en: With the words, "Protect me from contact with the earth," he places it so that it does not lie face down;
1. he cuts off an odd number of handfuls; 2. likewise [he prepares] the Nidhanas; 3.
According to some, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) serves the purpose of a sacrificial seat (*āsana*) for them; 4.
regarding the *prastara*, one may act according to one's desire; 5. whatever else there is, other than the *pariṣavaṇa* and the *utsarjana*, that is repeated in every case. 6.
"One cuts the prastara-bunch with the mantra, but the other [grass] silently"—this is the Vājasaneyaka.

Having cut everything, he touches the trimmed grass with the formula: "O divine sacrificial grass, grow with a hundred shoots! He makes a cord of three or five strands with the formula: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi. 7–10.
He replaces it with the formula, "The womb is well-established. 11.

Having spread it out with its tips pointing northward with the formula, "Thou art the girdle of Aditi," and having gathered the *nidhana* bricks upon it with the formula, "I gather thee, well-prepared," he places the *prastara* grass-bundle across the uppermost *nidhana* brick with the formula, "The womb is unbroken," and binds it with the formula, "The binding is for Indrāṇī.
12. He makes a knot with the formula, "May Pūṣan tie the knot for thee. 13.
"May he not strike thee," saying this, he conceals the knot from the front toward the west, or from the back toward the east.

"The waters have straightened thee, the Aśvins, and the seven ṛṣis; as the sacrificial grass (barhis) with the rays of the sun, I take hold of the banner of the dawns"—saying this, he takes hold of the sacrificial grass. "With the two arms of Indra, I lift thee up"—saying this, he lifts it up. "With the head of Bṛhaspati, I carry thee"—saying this, he places it upon his head.
Thus ends the fourth section.
"Go forward; go along the wide mid-air"—with these words, he turns back the two [stones] that were used for going.
"I set thee in the lap of Aditi"—with these words, he places the *andhas* within the altar, in the region of the enclosing-sticks.
"Thou art the sacrificial grass, going to the gods"—with these words, he consecrates the *barhis* that has been placed near.
With the words, "Thou art going to the gods," he places [the grass] so that it does not hang down, as he would have set it down previously.

"Of those herbs which were born for the gods in the three ages of old—of them may I obtain the joint while bringing the sacrificial strew (paristara). May the purity of the waters, fit for sacrifice, accompanied by the gods, be auspicious to me. May I, the cutter of you [grass], not come to harm; may I live for a hundred autumns. Of the immeasurable, I bind together these measured [blades] for the sake of good action. May I not go to any sin whatsoever; rising again, may they become abundant. With these verses, he lays down the sacrificial strew, and with the verse, "The cutter, the binder," he cuts and binds [the grass] according to the respective characteristics of each.
He prepares a sacrificial fuel (idhma) of twenty-one pieces of wood, either of *khadira* or *palāśa*.
There are three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
[The wood may be] from *palāśa*, *kārsmarya*, *khadira*, *udumbara*, *bilva*, *rohitaka*, or *vikaṅkata*, or from whatever trees are fit for sacrifice.
The fuel-sticks may be either moist or dry, provided they have their bark intact;
the middle one is the thickest, the southern one is the longest and thinnest, and the northern one is the shortest and thinnest.
There are two Āghāra-fuel sticks and twenty-one Anūyāja-fuel sticks.
Having made a cord as before from *darbha* grasses that are either with roots or without roots, he spreads it out with its ends pointing north.
(12) Thus ends the fifth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

"Since you, having assumed the form of a black antelope, entered the trees, therefore I gather you together in twenty-one parts, well-gathered: the three enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), the three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), those that move along for the life of the sacrifice, the fire-brick (*upaveṣa*), the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), and the fire-tongs (*dhṛṣṭi*)—I gather them well-gathered. With these words, he gathers the sacrificial fuel (*idhma*) upon the cord. (1)

"Thou art Kṛṣṇa, dwelling on the mountain peaks; O God, go forward; may I attain thee," with these words he girds himself. He conceals the knot from the front toward the back, or from the back toward the front. He does not let it hang down. (2) He places the wood-chippers there.

(3) "Through thee they found the altar and the earth; through thee the all-bestowing sacrifice is born. Knowing, thou followest the flawless sacrifice; through thee the Hotṛ priest extends the half-months. With these words he makes the *veda* of darbha grass. (4)

One whose desire is for cattle [prepares] the *vatsajñu*; one whose desire is for food [prepares] the *mūtakārya*; one whose desire is for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) [prepares] the *trivṛcchiras*.
(5) Having cut off a span from the cord, he sets aside the scrapings of the altar.

(6) Having trimmed all the leaves from the branch within the altar, and having cut the branch from its base, he fashions the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), saying: "Thou art the *upaveṣa*; they have held thee as a server for the sacrifice. While preparing the oblation for Indra, mayest thou be auspicious and helpful to us. (7)

"The Soma has been brought from the third heaven by the Gāyatrī; he takes a chip of bark within to bring together the drinking of the Soma. Having taken a chip from the pruning, he sets it aside in a known place.

(8) Having made a threefold filter of darbha grass, he hangs it loosely upon the branch with the formula, "Thou art the filter of the Vasus," with the roots [of the grass] at the base [of the branch] and the tips at the tip; he does not tie a knot. (9)

"May these three-fold palāśa blades of darbha grass, as large as a span, serve as the most excellent purifiers in the sacrifice; may they make my milk and oblation pure. "May these two, Prāṇa and Apāna, moving about as the purifiers that cleanse the oblation, circulate everywhere, nourishing all the limbs of the sacrifice. With these words, the sacrificer recites the mantra while the rite is being performed.
(10) They sweep the fire-hall and smear the sacrificial sites. (11) The sacrificer and his wife adorn themselves. (12)
The two *sāṃnāyya* pots in the new cart are smeared with cow-dung up to the level of the gravel.
Thus ends the sixth section (*kaṇḍikā*). Thus ends the second chapter (*paṭala*).
On the day of the new moon when they do not see the moon, on that day he performs the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. 1.
In the afternoon, or when the sun is directly over the trees, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
He brings sacrificial grass (barhis) that is pure and fit for sacrifice— either with its roots and cut in one stroke,
or else single blades of grass cut at their bases.

Having strewn sacrificial grass (*darbha*) with its tips pointing eastward around the southern fire, and having spread more grass to the south or behind it, he arranges the vessels for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña one by one, facing south-east: the *sphyā* (wooden sword), the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the mortar and pestle, the winnowing basket, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for the cooked rice-oblation (*carusthālī*), and whatever else he may require.
To the south stands a cart loaded with rice, its pole pointing eastward.
The Adhvaryu, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), places a single strainer (*pavitra*) inside the vessel and pours out the grain from the cart toward the south or the north.
Having filled it, he wipes it out.
He pours [the grain] into an earthen vessel, either with the formula, "I pour you out, acceptable to the ancestors," or silently.
To the west of the Anvāhāryapacana fire, upon a black antelope skin spread on which a mortar is placed, the wife stands facing south-east and threshes the grain, separating the husks from the grain.

He threshes the grain once (11). He cooks rice grains that are still alive in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire (12). Having dug up the altar with a single furrow, directed southward and eastward, either between the Gārhapatya and Anvāhāryapacana fires or to the southeast of the Anvāhāryapacana, with the formula: "Struck away are the Asuras, the Rakṣases, and the Piśācas who sit upon the altar" (VS 3.45), and having sprinkled it with water with the formula: "May the Fathers be purified" (VS 2.30), and having consecrated it with the formula: "May the Fathers come, swift as thought" (VS 2.31), he places the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)—cut in a single pull, soft as wool, pleasant—with the formula: "I bring thee, O grass, soft as wool and pleasant, for the Fathers. (VS 2.29)

"May my Soma-loving fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers sit here together with their followers"—with these words, he spreads the sacrificial grass that has been cut in a single stroke across the altar (13).
This is the seventh section.

Having sprinkled the *sthālīpāka* with clarified butter—either freshly churned butter or purified ghee—and having placed the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) on a single-bladed wooden sword (*ekasphyā*), he sets down the *sthālīpāka*. 1.
To the south, he places one by one a cushion, a pillow, collyrium, ointment, and a water-pot. 2.

The Adhvaryu, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, bending his right knee, having spread a base of ghee in the stirring-ladle and having taken a portion from it and sprinkled it with ghee, offers it in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the formula: "Svadhā! Adoration to Soma, drunk by the Pitṛs! 3. With the formula, "Svadhā! Adoration to Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs," he makes the second offering. With the formula, "Svadhā! Adoration to Agni Kavyavāhana," he makes the third offering. 4.
Having offered those rice grains which were in the stirring-ladle, he silently places the stirring-ladle [on the fire].
Some say that one does not offer to Yama.

May the Asuras who have the form of Pitṛs, who move about having assumed various shapes, depart! May Agni drive them away from this world—those who carry off *parāpur*s and *nipur*s. Those who are gods, those who are Pitṛs, and those who are humans; those who died in the womb and those who were cast away; those who were cast up and those who were buried—may they all, coming together here, rejoice. The Asuras who, assuming various shapes, move about with the *svadhā* offering; those who carry off *parāpur*s and *nipur*s—may Agni drive them away from this world.

"O Agni, drive away from this world those Asuras who, appearing as kinsmen, have entered among the fathers through illusion—those who support Parapura and Nipura. With these words, he takes a single glowing ember from the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. (7) Having once scratched the south-eastern intermediate direction with the wooden sword (sphya), and having sprinkled it with water while reciting "May they rise up, the lower ones," he places the ember at the edge of the scratch.
(8) From this point forward, the sacrificer performs the rites wearing the sacred thread over his right shoulder (prācīnāvītī). (9)
"May my fathers cleanse themselves; may my grandfathers cleanse themselves; may my great-grandfathers cleanse themselves"—with this [formula], he pours out three handfuls of water for each person.
Or, he sprinkles [the ground] three times from right to left.
The followers of the Vājasaneyi school prescribe three vessels of water.
Thus ends the eighth section (kaṇḍikā).

Bending his left knee and with his hand turned downward, he offers the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) on the sacrificial grass (barhis) that has been cut in a single stroke, ending toward the south, with these respective mantras: "This for thee, O Father, [Name], and for those who follow thee";
the fourth cake is offered silently. 1–2.
He, having performed [the rites], goes while pronouncing the names individually, starting from the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha) onwards, for those who have been prepared or not yet prepared.

If he has no kinsmen, he should offer the first rice-ball with the formula: "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth! the second with: "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in the intermediate space! and the third with: "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in heaven! (6) If he has two fathers, he should designate both for each individual rice-ball. (7) If his father is living, he should not offer [the balls]; having performed [the rites] up to the *homa*, he should desist. (8)

"Whatever my mother has done in negligence or has acted contrary to her vows, may my father take that seed; let another [seed] come to fruition. To the fathers who partake of the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Adoration! To the grandfathers who partake of the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Adoration! To the great-grandfathers who partake of the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Adoration! Having thus paid homage and said, "O fathers, rejoice here according to your respective portions," he turns away. (9) He waits until the steam has subsided. (10) Once the steam has subsided, he turns back, saying, "The Soma-loving fathers have rejoiced," or he turns back even before the steam has subsided. (11)

He smells what remains in the cooking pot [with the verse]: "O Pitṛs who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama, for them is this world; Svadhā! Homage! May the sacrifice be prepared among the gods. Bestow a hero, O Pitṛs! (12).
It should be eaten by one who is ill, or eaten by one desiring food, or eaten by one who, though capable of eating, does not eat. (13).
As before, having poured three handfuls of water into a single vessel, he gives collyrium, ointment, and clothing three times over each Piṇḍa. (14)

"Anoint [him], O father so-and-so; anoint [him], O grandfather so-and-so; anoint [him], O great-grandfather so-and-so"—with these words he offers the collyrium. 15 In the same way, for the ointment, he adapts the mantra as "Anoint [him].

16 If he does not know their names, he uses the collyrium with the formula: "May my fathers anoint themselves; may my grandfathers anoint themselves; may my great-grandfathers anoint themselves. In the same way, for the ointment, he adapts the mantra as "May they anoint themselves. 17

Thus ends the ninth section (kaṇḍikā). Having cut off the fringe of the garment, he places it down with the words: "O fathers, these are your garments; therefore, O fathers, do not deprive us of anything else. Or, if he is in the earlier stage of life, he places a tuft of wool. In the latter stage of life, he places his own hair. When the rice-balls have cooled, he mutters the salutations: "Homage to you, O fathers, to the essence! (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.5). 1–2.
"O fathers, give us houses; O fathers, we give you our seat"—with these words he worships the ancestors.

"You are strength, the great, immortality, clarified butter, milk, sweet drink, and flowing liquor; you are the *svadhā*—satisfy my fathers"—with this he pours out water. He worships with the verses beginning with "We call the mind hither."

"Arise, O fathers, you who have departed as heroes; follow the ancient path of Yama. Bestow upon us wealth that is auspicious, and announce us as partakers among the gods"—with these words he causes the fathers to rise.
(6) "Depart, O fathers, you who are worthy of Soma"—with this *pravāhaṇī* verse he causes the fathers to depart.
(7) "O Prajāpati, these things are not yours"—wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he goes to the place of the Gārhapatya fire. (8)
With the verse, "That which is the intermediate space," he worships the Gārhapatya fire with a *paṅkti* verse.
With the words, "I cause thee to consume the essence of the waters and the plants; bear a fetus created by the beings," he gives the middle ball of rice to his wife.

With the words, "O Fathers, bestow a fetus, a boy adorned with a lotus wreath, so that there may be a man here," the wife consumes it. It is known from tradition: "She will indeed give birth to a male child."

"Those who are born of the same womb, of one mind, living or dead, who are mine—may their prosperity be bestowed upon me in this world for a hundred years. With these words, the sacrificer eats one of the remaining portions. Or rather, having placed all the balls together in the pot, he throws the *sakṛdācchinna* grass into the fire with the verse, "Ye samānāḥ... (TS 3.3.9). "He has been our messenger for the oblation, Jātavedas; having made the offerings fragrant, he has carried them away. He has given them to the Fathers, and they have eaten them with the *svadhā* call. Knowing [the way], O Agni, come back again to the gods. Having thus thrown back a single fire-brand and sprinkled the vessels, he brings them up two by two.
The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is concluded.
15. One should either cast the rice-balls into water or have a Brāhmaṇa eat them. 16. This very rite, as prescribed, is also for one who has not established the sacred fires. 17.
The rules for cooking and the oblation are performed in the *aupāsana* fire;
or one may offer the oblation in the *atipraṇīta* fire (18–19).
One should perform the ritual worship (*upasthāna*) of whichever fire one offers the oblation into (20).
"In that case, the word *gārhapatya* would be omitted because of the prohibition of the consecratory rites" (Sūtra 21).
Thus ends the tenth section (*kaṇḍikā*) and the third chapter (*paṭala*).
On the night of the new moon, the sacrificer himself offers the *agnihotra* with barley-gruel and sets aside the remnants of the *agnihotra* for the purpose of curdling [the milk]. 1.
On this night, not even the children receive milk. 2.
When the evening Agnihotra has been offered, he milks the evening milk. 3.

Having strewn grass around the fires, or around the two fires, having washed the Sāṃnāyya vessels, and having spread Darbha grass to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, he sets them down in pairs, facing downwards. 4.

He prepares a pitcher, a branch-purifier (*śākhāpavitra*), a rope for tying, two cords for the ends, a wooden vessel, a milking vessel, an iron vessel or a wooden vessel for covering, the *agnihotra-havanī* ladle, and a fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*).
(5) He makes two purifiers (*pavitra*) from two blades of *darbha* grass with unbroken tips, each a span (*prādeśa*) long.
(6) Holding a blade of grass or a piece of wood between his fingers, he cuts them while reciting: "You two are purifiers belonging to Viṣṇu; may Vāyu purify you with his mind. (7)
He does not [clean] with the fingernail.

Having wiped [the vessels] with water while reciting "O Viṣṇu, you two are purified by mind," and having poured water into the *agnihotra-havaṇī* over which a strainer has been placed, he purifies the *prokṣaṇī* waters with the two strainers whose tips point north: first with "May the god Savitṛ purify you"; second with "With the flawless strainer"; and third with "With the rays of the Vasu Sūrya."

Having consecrated [the vessels] with the mantra, "O divine waters, you who flow first," and having turned the vessels face upwards, he sprinkles them three times with the mantra, "Be purified for the rite of the gods," and places the two known strainers [into them]. [He recites: "O divine waters, may you remain pure; purify these vessels. Purify also the leaf-cup of the gods for the sake of the *upātaṅka* sacrifice. Purified by the god Savitṛ with the rays of the bright Sun."

Having consecrated with the mantra, "O cow, purify the milk-pail, the strainer, the rope, and all the vessels," he awaits the cows as they approach, reciting: "These cows come hither, yielding honey, possessing offspring, glorious, and multiform; multiplying and being born again, may Indra cause you to delight here, O cows. This is the eleventh section.

"Scorched is the Rakṣas, scorched is the evil-plotters," with these words he heats the Sāṃnāyya vessels over the Gārhapatya fire. Having taken up the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) with the formula, "Thou art the bold one; grant us spiritual power (*brahman*)," and having drawn out embers toward the north from the Gārhapatya with the formula, "The fear of the enemy is driven away; the attacking armies are driven away," he places the cooking pot (*kumbhī*) upon them with the formula, "Thou art the heat (*gharma*) of Mātariśvan.
Or [he may place it] with the formula: "I set down the two churning-sticks (*ukhā*) so that the sacrifice may not slip; may they bear the curd cooked for Indra, brought together with the cattle."

"May you heat yourself with the ascetic fervor of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases," he says. Having strewn embers around it clockwise, he places a branch-purifier upon it with its tip pointing eastward, saying, "Thou art the purifier of the Vasus. 3. [He does so] toward the north in the morning. 4.
Holding on to the cooking pot, he restrains his speech. 5.
Or he remains seated holding the *pavitra*. 6.
"Thou art the girdle for Aditi," [with these words] he takes up the cord for the tethering-post.

7. "Thou art the thirty-third among the threads; come together with the *pavitra*. May this auspicious rope, the tethering-cord, serve the inviolable cow"—with this the sacrificer consecrates the cord as it is being taken up. 8.
With the words, "Thou art Pūṣan," he addresses the calf. With the command, "Announce to me when she has been joined with the calf," he gives the direction.

He addresses [the cow] with, "I join you. With the words, "Free from disease, I unite you with offspring; may you become abundant through the increase of wealth," he joins the calf [to the cow]. 9–11.
He issues the command: "Do not pass between the cow that has been milked and the sacrificial ground.

(12) If he should pass between her while she is being milked, he should say: "May the *sāṃnāyya* offering not be spoiled. (13) He addresses her with the words: "I approach you. He approaches the milch-cow with the mantra: "I unite you with progeny free from disease and with the abundance of wealth; becoming manifold, swelling with strength, milk, and ghee, may I sit near you while you live. (14)

A Śūdra should not milk; or rather, he may milk. (15) He milks using a wooden vessel. (16) The sacrificer consecrates the cow when she has been approached for milking, while she is being milked, and during the sound of the stream, with the mantra: "I unite you with offspring, free from disease. (He addresses her) when she has been approached: "May Heaven and Earth together milk this sacrifice for me; may Dhātṛ together with Soma, and Vāyu together with Vāta, bestow wealth upon the sacrificer. (He addresses her) while she is being milked. (17)

Thus ends the twelfth section (kaṇḍikā). Having milked the stream [of ghee] with the verse: "They milk the fountain, the four-holed jar, the divine Iḍā, honey-sweet and finding the light; O Indra and Agni, quicken that which is full of truth; may that establish the sacrificer in immortality," he carries it away. 1–2.

He asks him: "O milker of desires, tell us for Indra the oblation that provides power. 3. He points with his finger toward that [cow]. He replies: "In her the milk of the gods and of men is deposited. 4. He consecrates her with the mantra: "She is Viśvāyu. 5.
"May Savitṛ purify you with the filter of Vasu, with a hundred streams, well-purified," saying this, he pours [the milk] through the filter into the pot.
"The drop is offered, the speck is offered," with these words he consecrates the droplets.
In this same manner, he causes the second and third [cows] to be milked.
He follows the second [cow] with the mantra, "She who is all-pervading," and the third with, "She whose work is universal.

Having caused the three to be milked, he releases his speech three times with the words: "May she yield much milk for Indra and for the gods as an oblation; may she be fit again for milking for the calves and for men. Without touching [the cows], he causes the subsequent ones to be milked silently. Having poured water into the milking vessel, he pours the wash-water from the pot into it with the mantra, "Be united, O you who possess the immortal nectar," and while ensuring no spilling occurs, he makes it well-cooked.

"Strengthen the cows, strengthen the lord of the cows; may the master of the sacrifice not come to harm"—saying this, while making a path, he carries [the milk] out toward the east, or toward the north-east, or toward the north.

On one day, two days, or three days—on the first, second, or third day prior to the Upavasatha—he causes the cows to be milked for the purpose of curdling, and they milk them continuously until the Upavasatha. With that [milk], he curdles it so that the bottom remains cool.
"With *soma* I mix you for Indra; [I mix] you with curds.

(14) Having placed the remnant of the *agnihotra* beneath it with the formula, "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I continue thee along the continuity of the sacrifice," and having made this milk into *soma*, he adds the scrapings from the trimming with the formula, "May it go back to its own womb; the *parṇa*-bark is the purifier, belonging to Soma, fashioned from Soma. (15) Thus ends the thirteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
The options for the *ātañcana* (curdling agent) are: medicinal herbs, *pūtika* plants, *kvala* fruits, rice grains, or bark.
1. In the absence of the remnants [of the Soma], one should curdle [the milk] with rice grains; in the absence of rice grains, with medicinal herbs. 2.

"O Waters, be watchful among the oblations, as you are watchful among the gods; even so, be watchful for the sacrificer at this sacrifice. Having poured water into either an iron vessel or a wooden vessel, he covers it with the formula: "Thou art the support; I place thee for Viṣṇu, for the sacrifice; with waters from a non-empty vessel, those which flow pure. He recites over it: "May the divine vessel, not made of clay, be employed for the life of the sacrifice; hold fast the waters that have been led across the filter, do not let them be lost. The sacrificer mutters: "The divine vessel, not made of clay, is employed for the life of the sacrifice; the waters have been led across the filter; hold them fast, do not let them be lost. (3) If he should cover it with a clay vessel, he should thrust a blade of grass or a piece of wood into the covering. (4)
"O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation," saying this, he places it down so that it does not fall. 5.

"These two, the *parṇa* leaf and the *darbha* grass, are the purifiers of the gods' oblations; for the sake of the morning service, guard them, O Viṣṇu, for you indeed protect the oblation"—saying this, he places down the well-known branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*). 6.
With that same branch or with *darbha* grass, he drives away the calves for the morning milking, just as he did for the evening milking. 7.

Having placed the potsherds, he causes the morning milking to be performed as in the case of the evening milking. The curdling agent, the covering, and the setting aside [of the milk] are omitted. One who has not sacrificed with Soma should not perform the *saṃnayya* offering, or he may perform it. One who has not attained prosperity should not sacrifice to Mahendra; for it has been said, "There are three who have attained prosperity."
Aurva, Gautama, and Bhāradvāja—these, or whoever else [is qualified], should sacrifice to Mahendra immediately after the Soma sacrifice.

Then he issues the command: "Strew the sacrificial grass; enclose the fire. May the enclosed fire protect the sacrificer. May these golden neck-ornaments, the essence of the waters and the plants, be for the sacrificer as wish-granting cows in yonder world."
Some recite this as the *paristaraṇī* [verse].
(13) He strews the fires with *darbha* grass, both with tips pointing northward and with tips pointing eastward. (14) Those with tips pointing northward are placed behind and in front. (15)
Having performed this, he fasts.

(16) Having performed the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*), the preparation of the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*), and the altar (*vedi*) up until the northern boundary-line (*parigrāha*), on the following day, having poured out the remains of the water used for purification (*āpyalepa*), he should perform the subsequent boundary-line and the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*). On the previous day of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), there is the adding of fuel, the strewing of grass, and the fasting; however, on the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), these three occur on the same day. (17) Or, in the case of an immediate rite (*sadyaskālā*), everything is performed on that very day. (18)
Thus ends the fourteenth section; thus ends the fourth chapter.
When the sun has risen, he commences the ritual procedure for the full moon sacrifice; for the new moon sacrifice, he commences it before sunrise.
There are four officiating priests.

As before, he strews the fires, if they have not already been strewn. Having washed his hands with the formula, "May I be able for you two for the sake of the work of the gods," and having taken a step from the *gārhapatya* fire while reciting, "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I strew thee for the continuity of the sacrifice; for the continuity of the sacrifice, I strew thee," he strews a continuous line of *ulapa* grass from the *gārhapatya* up to the *āhavanīya*. He strews silently the southern and northern lines.
To the south of the *āhavanīya*, he prepares the seats for the Brahman and the sacrificer, the former to the east and the latter to the west.

To the north of the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires, having strewn darbha grass, he arranges the vessels in pairs, turned face down—ten on the west and ten on the east. Having arranged the ten western ones according to the traditional enumeration, beginning with "the wooden sword (sphya) and the potsherds," he then arranges the eastern ones: the dipping-spoon (sruva), the Juhū, the Upabhṛt, the Dhruvā, the Veda-grass bundle, the Pātrī, the butter-pot (ājyasthālī), the Prāśitra-vessel, the Iḍā-vessel, and the Praṇītā-water vessel. These [eastern] ones are to the north of the remaining [western] ones.

The anvāhāryasthālī, the stone, the upaveṣa, and the vessels for the morning milking—some authorities prescribe the carrying forward of the praṇītā waters before the arranging of the sacrificial vessels. The sruva spoon is made of khadira wood, the juhū of parṇa wood, the upabhṛt of aśvattha wood, and the dhruvā of vikaṅkata wood;
or one may have the spoons made from any one of these trees.
The ladles (sruk) are a cubit long or an aratni long, with their tips reaching to the tips [of the handles], having hollows for the blades and mouths like those of swans. 12.
The wooden sword (sphya), the yoke-pin (śamyā), and the vessel for the Prāśitra-portion are made of Khadira wood. 13.
Vessels intended for purposes other than the oblation (ahomārtha) are made of Vāraṇa wood. 14.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.

Here, as before, he prepares the two strainers (*pavitra*), provided that he does not perform the *saṃnayana* (the mixing of curds with milk). However, for one who does perform the *saṃnayana*, those two are available.

With the formula, "Thou art of the forest trees; be purified for the gods," he washes with water the *praṇītā*-water-carrying cup, silently washing both the bronze (*kaṃsa*) and the earthenware vessel. He should pour out [the water] with a bronze vessel for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), with an earthenware vessel for one who desires stability (*pratiṣṭhā*), and with a cow-milking vessel (*godohana*) for one who desires cattle. Having placed the cup, over which a strainer has been laid, to the west of the *gārhapatya* fire, he pours water into it with the formula: "Who takes you? Let him take you! For whom do I take you? For him I take you! For prosperity, you! (3). While taking the water and about to take it, he meditates upon the earth with his mind. (4)

Having filled the *camasa* with its mouthpiece and purified it like the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he consecrates it and issues the command: "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters; O sacrificer, restrain your speech. (5) Everywhere, he performs the action once the impulse (*prasava*) has been uttered.
(6) While the waters are being led forward, the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer restrain their speech until the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). (7)

"Who leads you? Let him lead you. O divine waters, may you lead the sacrifice; may you establish it for us. Rejoicing in refreshment, with ghee upon your backs, flowing upward, descending upon the sacrificer with thousandfold nourishment"—thus, holding [the water] level with his breaths and supporting it with the wooden sword (*sphya*), he carries it away without spilling it.

(8) He meditates on the earth with his mind. (9) "Who yokes you? Let him yoke you"—with these words, he places [the water] to the north of the Āhavanīya fire on *darbha* grass, without touching it. (10)

"They move about, they lie down; having covered [the ground] with *darbha* grass while standing, let the divine folk lie down. Having touched the vessels with his hand holding the *pavitra*, [he says]: "The vessels for the sacrifice to the gods.
Thus ends the sixteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
"You are of the forest trees; for dexterity, you!"—with these words he takes up the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle. "For service, you!"—with these words [he takes up] the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*).

Having heated [the implements] over either the *āhavanīya* or the *gārhapatya* fire with the formula, "The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away," he addresses [the sacrificer]: "O Sacrificer, I shall pour out the oblation.
If the sacrificer is away on a journey, he says, "O Agni, while I am away, I shall pour out the oblation."
"Go along the wide mid-air," with these words he proceeds toward the cart.
Behind the *gārhapatya* fire, a cart stands ready, its yoke fastened, with the pole pointing either east or north, and containing either rice or barley.
With the formula "Thou art the pole," he touches the right end of the yoke, or the left.
"Thou art the most bountiful of the gods," with these words he mutters while touching the northern of those [two] poles. 7.
"Viṣṇu has stepped upon thee," with these words, having placed his right foot upon the left wheel, he mounts [the cart], saying, "Thou art the unoffered oblation-holder. 8.
Having uncovered the enclosure with the words, "Wide path for the wind," he gazes at the rice for the sacrificial cakes, saying, "I gaze upon thee with the eye of Mitra. 9.

Having cast away [the husks] with the formula, "The Rakṣas is cast out; the one who utters evil is cast out," he should cast away whatever else remains from the materials for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśīya). Having consecrated them with, "For strength, I take you; place milk in me," and having explained the Daśahotṛ formula, he places the two strainers (pavitra) in the winnowing basket (śūrpa). Into that, he pours out the oblations with the Agnihotra-ladle, or with that same ladle provided with the strainers, either rice or barley.

Having taken a handful with the formula, "May the five [fingers] restrain [you]," and having poured that handful into the offering-spoon (sruk), he proceeds with the formula, "By the impulse of god Savitṛ... and then pours out three times with the Yajus formula, "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni," and a fourth time silently.
Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā).
In this manner, the subsequent [offerings] are according to the respective deities: "To Agni and Soma" at the full moon sacrifice; "To Indra and Agni" at the new moon sacrifice.

Having poured out four handfuls and having scattered [grains] over those already poured out, he touches the poured-out portions with the formula, "This for the gods," and the remaining [portions] with, "This is ours together."

With the formula, "For prosperity thee, not for misfortune," he consecrates the grains that have been poured out. Having stepped out with the formula, "Here I am released from the noose of Varuṇa," he looks toward the east with, "I have beheld the sun.

With "May I behold the light of heaven," he surveys the entire sacrificial ground (*vihāra*). With "The Vaiśvānara light," he addresses the Āhavanīya fire; with "Svāhā to Heaven and Earth," he consecrates the spilled grains. With "May the dwellings in Heaven and Earth be firm," he descends [the altar]; with "Follow the intermediate space," he carries [the grains] away.
With "I place thee in the lap of Aditi," he deposits them behind the Gārhapatya fire, according to the respective deity.
Or, if he cooks [the oblation] on the Āhavanīya fire;
if he should pour out [the grain] into a vessel, having placed the wooden sword (sphya) to the south, he should mutter all the cart-formulas over that vessel.
Thus ends the eighteenth section; thus ends the fifth chapter.

Having poured water into the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle while it still possesses its bristles, having purified it as before and consecrated it with a mantra, he addresses the Brahman priest, saying, "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle. Having recited "By the impulse of the god... (*devasya tvā...*), he sprinkles the oblation three times according to the respective deity, saying, "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni," and so forth, taking care not to sprinkle over the fire itself.
(1) He should sprinkle over the person whom he hates. (2)

Having turned over the vessels that were lying face up, he sprinkles them three times with the formula, "Be purified for the divine rite. Having set down the remainder of the sprinkling water in front of the Gārhapatya fire, he takes the black antelope skin with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," and shakes it three times at the rubbish-heap (utkara) with the formula, "The Rakṣas is shaken off; the enemies are shaken off," shaking it with its neck upwards and its hair side outwards.
He spreads it with its neck toward the north, either to the north of the Gārhapatya or in the place of the rubbish-heap, with its hair facing upward.
He places the hide of the cow (bhasad) in front of it, facing westward.
Without letting go of the black antelope skin, he places the mortar upon it with the formula, "Thou art the pressing-skin.
Without letting go of the mortar, he pours the oblation-grain into it with the formula, "Thou art the body of Agni," three times with the sacrificial formula and a fourth time silently.

Taking the pestle with the formula, "Thou art the stone, born of the tree," he strikes thrice with the call, "O preparer of the oblation, come! Or, without actually threshing, he calls for the preparer of the oblation.

"O preparer of the oblation, come!"—thus for a Brāhmaṇa; "O preparer of the oblation, approach!"—thus for a Rājanya; "O preparer of the oblation, run hither!"—thus for a Vaiśya; "O preparer of the oblation, run forth!"—thus for a Śūdra.
Or rather, [the first formula] may be used for all.
"I shall slay the Rakṣas, the rival from heaven," [saying this] he threshes the grain.
Thus ends the nineteenth section (kaṇḍikā). He issues the command: "Strike loudly! 1.
Having taken up the stone with the formula, "Thou art the Kuṭaru, honey-tongued," the Āgnīdhra strikes the large and small millstones together with the formula, "Bring us food; bring us strength. 2.
Moving it three times over the lower grinding stone and once over the upper grinding stone, he completes the process nine times.
Or, having taken a wooden pin with a verse addressed to Savitṛ, he strikes [the grain] with it.
Saying, "Thou art increased by rain," he places the winnowing basket in front or to the north.
Having consecrated [the grain] with the formula, "O you who have grown through the rains, stand firm," he scoops it out with the formula, "May the one who has grown through the rains recognize you.
With the formula, "The Rakṣas is blown away; the enemies are blown away," he winnows it on the rubbish-heap.
He consecrates the husks as they fall away with the formula, "The Rakṣas is cast forth; the enemies are blown away."

Having poured the husks onto the middle *puroḍāśa* pan, he scatters them beneath the black antelope skin with the formula, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases," in the northwestern intermediate direction;
"He scatters them by hand," so says the *Bṛhad-ṛcaka-brāhmaṇa*.

Having touched the potsherd with water and set it down in its known place, and having touched water, he separates [the grains] with the formula, "May Vāyu separate you. Having poured the rice-grains into the vessel with the formula, "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you," he looks at them with the formula, "I look upon you with unimpaired vision for the increase of wealth, for splendor, for good progeny, and for the protection of my sight; I invoke this blessing. Then he gives the command: "Pound [the rice] three times!
(11) She who is the sacrificer’s wife comes forward and pounds [the rice]; or anyone else may do so if she is not present. (12–13)
Thus ends the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā).

With the formula, "Be purified for the gods; be cleansed for the gods; be beautified for the gods," he makes the rice grains well-husked; or [he does so] silently. Having washed the rice grains while they are being thrice-husked, he pours out three times on the rubbish-heap the refuse that remains as the husks, with the formula, "O waters, carry away that which is the portion of the Rakṣases from here. 2.

Here, having performed the rites beginning with the taking up of the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina) prior to the turning [of the mortar], he places a wooden pin (śamyā) with its knob pointing north upon the black antelope skin with the formula, "Thou art the support of heaven. Having placed the large millstone (dṛṣad) upon the pin with the formula, "Thou art Dhiṣaṇā, daughter of the mountain," he places the small millstone (upalā) upon the large millstone with the formula, "Thou art Dhiṣaṇā, daughter of the mountain. 3. There is no relinquishing [of the materials] as before. 4.

Having consecrated the rice grains with the formula, "Ye are stalks, full of honey," and having recited "In the impulse of the god... (devasya tvā), he pours the rice grains onto the large millstone according to the respective deity with the formula, "I pour thee out, acceptable to Agni," three times with the sacrificial formula (yajus) and a fourth time silently. 5.

With the words, "For out-breathing (prāṇa) thee," he pushes forward an eastern stone; with "For in-breathing (apāna) thee," a western one; with "For diffused-breathing (vyāna) thee," he places one in the middle to separate them. With "For out-breathing thee, for in-breathing thee, for diffused-breathing thee," he grinds continuously. With "May I extend long life for the sake of longevity," he pushes the pestle forward to the end. With "May the god Savitṛ, golden-handed, receive you," he causes the flour to fall onto the black antelope skin. Having looked at it with the words, "I look upon you with unimpaired vision," he gives the command: "Grinding without scattering, make it fine. A female slave or the wife grinds it.
"Or rather, the wife husks and the Śūdra woman grinds"—this is the twenty-first section; thus ends the sixth chapter.
He cooks the sacrificial oblations either on the Āhavanīya fire or on the Gārhapatya fire.

Having taken up the *upaveṣa* with the formula, "Thou art bold; grant the Brahman," and having consecrated it with, "Burn the hand of the Rakṣas; thou art the serpent of the depths," he turns out two glowing coals from the Gārhapatya fire toward the west with, "O Agni, drive away the Agnimāda. With, "Drive out the flesh-eater," he throws one of the two toward the north-western intermediate direction. Having established the other on the south with, "Bring the one who sacrifices to the gods," he places upon it the lower cake-pan with, "Thou art firm."

"The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away"—having placed a coal on the potsherd with these words, he touches the second one to the east of it with "Thou art the supporter (dhartra). He places the third one to the east of the first with "Thou art the foundation (dharuṇa). With "Thou art the conscious one (cit), sit in all directions," he places [a brick] to the south of the middle one. With "Thou art the surrounding conscious one (paricit), sit in all directions," he places [a brick] to the north of the middle one. The others are placed according to their respective positions. Thus ends the twenty-second section.

"Thou art the host of the Maruts," with these words he places the sixth [potsherd]. "Thou art the law (dharma)," with these words the seventh. "Ye are piled up (citāḥ stha)," with these words the eighth.
In this same manner he places the subsequent arrangement of potsherds.

Alternatively, having placed the middle one and having touched it with a finger of his left hand, he places a coal upon the potsherd with the formula, "The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away. Then, with "Thou art the supporter (dhartra)," he places another [potsherd] behind that; with "Thou art the foundation (dharuṇa)," he places one before that; and the others according to their proper positions.
The Vājasaneyins prescribe the placing [of coals] with the finger and the turning of the coals for each respective [potsherd].
With the formula, "Ye are piled; ye are piled upwards," he piles eight [potsherds] upwards, or silently.
Having covered the potsherds with coals by means of the *veda*-grass-bundle while reciting, "Be heated by the heat of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases," he places the boiling water (*madantī*) over them.
Thus ends the twenty-third section; thus ends the seventh chapter.

Into a vessel that has been washed, heated dry, and fanned, and into which the strainers have been placed, he pours the flour while reciting the formula "Thee for the God," followed by "I pour thee, acceptable to Agni," according to the respective deity; he does this three times with the sacrificial formula and a fourth time silently. While pouring, he restrains his speech; he releases it when covering [the vessel] with ashes.

Having purified the flour as one does the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he mixes it with the *praṇītā* waters; or, having purified other [water] with a *yajus*-formula, if he should not find the *praṇītā* waters.

Having taken [the water] from the *praṇītā* vessels with the *sruva* ladle and supporting it with the *veda* grass-bundle, he pours it onto the flour with the formula, "The waters have united with the waters. Having moistened them with the heated water with the formula, "Those born around," and having mixed them together with the formula, "I unite thee for generation," and having formed a ball with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," and having divided it with the formula, "May you two turn apart according to your respective portions," and having made two equal balls, he touches them according to the deities: "This is for Agni" for the one belonging to Agni; "This is for Agni and Soma" for the one belonging to Agni and Soma. 5.

Saying, "I drive away the face of the attacking army," he drives the embers away from the potsherds with the wooden sword (*veda*). Then, saying, "Thou art the Gharma, belonging to all life," he places the cake for Agni (*puroḍāśa*) upon eight potsherds.
In the same way, he proceeds with each subsequent cake on its respective potsherds.
Thus, from this point forward, the ritual actions are performed in their proper sequence.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section (kaṇḍikā).
One performs each rite with an action of the same kind;
those rites which are possible are performed only once.
"O wide-expanding one, may the lord of the sacrifice expand wide for you"—saying this, as he spreads out the *puroḍāśa*, he spreads it so as to cover all the potsherds.
He makes it not high, not in the shape of a cake, resembling the form of a tortoise, and the size of a horse's hoof;
or he makes it as large as he thinks fit.
Some say that one does not separate it [the cake] from the vessel.
With the formula, "Take up the skin," he smoothes it with water without letting it flow away.

Having carried fire around all the oblations three times with the formulas, "The Rakṣas is excluded; the enemies are excluded," he heats them with embers with the formula, "May the god Savitṛ cook you."
"O Agni, do not consume his body," [saying this], he causes it to blaze up with *darbha* grass or with flames.
"Cooking without burning," [with these words] he releases his speech.
The Āgnīdhra priest ensures that the sacrificial oblations are well-cooked.
With the formula, "Be united with the sacred word," he spreads ash mixed with embers over the sacrificial cake using the wooden sword.
At this point, he may release his speech.
Having warmed the washing of his fingers and the rinsing of the vessel over a firebrand, he draws three lines within the altar with the wooden sword—either directed eastward or northward.
Pouring them out without mixing, he pours them out three times, ending toward the west, with these mantras respectively: "To unity, svāhā!
Having poured them out, he may heat them or he may not heat them.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section.
Thus ends the first question.

Having taken up the wooden sword (*sphya*) with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," and having consecrated it with, "Thou art the right arm of Indra," he cleanses it with a blade of *darbha* grass, saying, "May thy heat not depart. To the west of the Āhavanīya fire, he prepares the altar (*vedi*), either measured by the height of the sacrificer or of unlimited size, facing eastward; it should be so wide that the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) placed upon it may fit across it. 1. It should be oriented crosswise [from west to east] so that the oblations may be contained within it. 2.

"By means of the *veda* they found the altar; that earth spread out wide with its contents. She bears the embryo within the worlds; from that the sacrifice is born, bestowing all things. With these words, before or after the *stambayajus*, he sweeps the altar three times with the *veda*.
From the eastern third of the altar, he takes up the *stambayajus*.

With the words, "Thou art the armor of the earth," he places a blade of *darbha* grass there with its tip pointing northward or eastward. With the words, "O Earth, place of sacrifice for the gods," he strikes it with the wooden sword (*sphya*). With the words, "Araru is driven away from the earth," he takes up the dust along with the grass using the wooden sword and carries it away with the words, "Go to the fold, the stall of the cows. He looks toward the altar or the sacrificer with the words, "May the sky rain for thee.
With the words, "Bind him, O God Savitṛ," he pours out [the earth] on the northern side, in the eastern third part, at a distance of two steps to the north of the altar, or at an unlimited distance;
that is the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
"May you not leap up to heaven," [saying this], the Āgnīdhra catches with his joined palms the [grains] that have been poured out.
In this same manner he carries away the second and third portions.
While carrying away the fourth silently, he carries away all the remaining *darbha* grass.

Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā). "On the earth, the non-sacrificial ground of Araru"—this is for the second throwing. "May Araru not fall upon the sky"—this is for the third. "Araru is driven away from the sacrificial ground of the earth"—this is for the second taking away. "Araru is driven away from the non-sacrificial ground of the earth"—this is for the third. "Smitten is the Rakṣas"—at the second scattering, the Āgnīdhra holds [the earth]; "smitten is the malevolent one"—at the third; "smitten are the Yātudhānas"—at the fourth. 2.

"May your drop not leap up to heaven," he says, looking at the pit; then, with the wooden sword (*sphya*), he encloses the altar (*vedi*) on the south side with "May the Vasus enclose you with the Gāyatrī metre," on the west with "May the Rudras [enclose you]," and on the north with "May the Ādityas [enclose you]. 3.
"O earth, strike away the non-sacrificial spot, the non-sacrificial spot of the earth! With this, he scrapes away the uppermost layer with the wooden sword. 4.
The Agnīdhra throws the excavated earth three times onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).

"O men, prepare this altar for the gods in the lap of Aditi, which is dear to them. May all the gods take pleasure in it; may they enter the sacrificer with a desire for wealth. Thus he gives the command.

With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he digs it to a depth of two finger-breadths, three finger-breadths, four finger-breadths, or as far as the white part of the heel; it should be a span wide, or the width of a chariot-track, or the width of a furrow, or a span deep, and it must contain loose soil.
He does not dig deeper than these measures.
To the south [of the altar], it should be larger, sloping toward the east, or sloping toward the northeast.
This is the second section (kaṇḍikā).
He raises the two shoulders of the altar toward the east and the two hips toward the west. 1.
It is narrower in front, broader behind, and more deeply curved in the middle. 2.
That part which extends beyond the root, he cuts that with the wooden sword (sphya), not with his fingernail. 3.
That loose earth which extends beyond, he throws it onto the rubbish-heap (utkara). 4.
One desiring cattle should make the earth removable as dung.
Having performed that which is prior to the digging, he should dig with the mantra whatever he brings up.
Having addressed the Brahman priest, saying, "O Brahman, I shall perform the northern tracing," he traces around the altar with the wooden sword (sphya) from the south, saying, "Thou art Truth."

With the formula, "Thou art the seat of *ṛta*," [he draws the line] behind; with "Thou art the glory of *ṛta*," to the north. Some prescribe that the two enclosures (*parigrāha*) are performed in reverse order.
With the formulas, "Thou art support" and "Thou art self-support," he levels the altar toward the west with the wooden sword (*sphya*).
With the verse, "Taking up the earth, the life-giving one," he gazes at the altar (vedi).

Having fixed the wooden sword (sphya) crosswise at the rear third part of the altar, he issues the command: "Place the sprinkling waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladles (sruc); gird the wife; bring the clarified butter.
Or alternatively, he may not utter this command.

Having filled the *prokṣaṇī* vessels and pushed the wooden sword (*sphya*) toward the north, he pours water near it without touching the wooden sword on the south side; then, while meditating in his mind upon someone whom he hates, he places [the vessels] in the track of the wooden sword with the formula, "Thou art the seat of Truth" (*ṛtasadhastha*). 13. With the formula, "Thou art hundred-edged, made of wood, the slayer of enemies," he throws the wooden sword eastward against the west onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), meditating in his mind upon someone whom he hates. 14. Without washing his hands, he strikes the vessels [to clean them]. 15.
Having washed his hands, he washes the *sphya* (sacrificial wooden sword) without touching its tip.

To the north of the *āhavanīya* fire, he places the fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with their tips pointing eastward; the fuel to the south and the sacrificial grass to the north.
Thus ends the third section; thus ends the first chapter.

Some prescribe the binding of the wife first; others prescribe the wiping of the *sruk* ladles. Having taken up the *sruc* ladles with the formula, "The butter-dripping ones—Agni calls you for the sacrifice to the gods," and having heated them over the Āhavanīya or Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away," and having consecrated them with the formula, "You are sharpened, destroyers of rivals," he wipes the *sruc* ladles with the tips of the *veda* grass, either dividing them or not dividing them, holding them turned upwards, facing east or north.
Some say that only the *upabhṛt* ladle should be held facing north.

"May I not wipe away the cow-pen," [he says]; with the tips [of the blades] he performs an inward-facing stroke on the front, and a gathering-stroke all around the hollow; with the roots, the handle. (4) "Speech, breath," [he says]; with the tips [of the blades] he performs an inward-facing stroke on the front of the *juhū* ladle, with the middle parts an outward-facing stroke toward the east, and with the roots the handle. (5) "Sight, hearing," [he says]; with the tips [of the blades] he performs an inward-facing stroke on the front of the *upabhṛt* ladle, with the middle parts an outward-facing stroke toward the west, and with the roots the handle. (6)
With the formula, "The offspring, the womb," he cleans the *dhruvā* just as he does the *sruva*.
With the formula, "O vigorous one, may I not wipe away the form and color of the cattle; I cleanse thee, the conqueror of rivals," he cleans the *prāśitraharaṇa*, or silently.
He does not let those that have been cleaned come into contact with those that have not been cleaned.

"By the most intense brilliance of Agni, I heat you thoroughly," he says, heating it again, sprinkling it, and placing it on *darbha* grass either to the east or to the rear of the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
Having touched the implements for wiping the ladles with water, [the ritual is concluded].
This is the fourth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

"The craft of heaven is spread out; it rests upon the peaks of the earth. With that [craft], which has a thousand branches, we destroy our rival, Svāhā!"—with these words he offers it into the fire, or he throws it onto the heap of rubbish where it was heated.
1. "Seeking goodwill," with these words he girds the wife behind the Gārhapatya fire while she is sitting with her knees raised, or while she is standing.
2. Some say he makes her recite [the formula].
With a cord made of muñja grass, either with a noose at one end or as a simple yoke, he ties it inside his garment; or rather, he does not tie the garment at all—so say some.

Having made a knot with loose ends to the north of the navel and having wound it around from left to right, he places it below the navel on the right side. Then, rising, he worships the Gārhapatya fire, saying: "O Agni Gṛhapati, summon me! (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.3.1–6).

"O wives of the gods, call upon me; O wife, for you as a wife this is your place; homage be to you, do not harm me"—with these words he worships the wives of the gods. (7) Having stepped away from that spot, he sits down to the south facing north, saying: "May we be rich in offspring through you. (8) He mutters: "May I be like Indrāṇī, unwidowed; may I be like Aditi, rich in sons. O Gārhapatya fire, may I not be childless; may I have good offspring through you. (9)
"May she sit beside my sacrifice," thus the sacrificer gives the direction.
"He should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices using abundant clarified butter," so it is known.
Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā).

With the words, "May Pūṣan open your cavity," he uncovers the cavity of the butter-vessel. Having melted the clarified butter over the *dakṣiṇāgni*, and having taken the butter-pot with the formula, "Thou art Aditi, of unimpaired wings," he pours the butter into it while it is covered by a strainer, saying, "I pour out for thee—that which is the milk of the great ones, the sap of the plants—of thee, the imperishable, for the sacrifice to the gods. Having placed it on the *dakṣiṇāgni* with the verse, "Over this Vishnu strode," and having placed it on the southern half of the *gārhapatya* fire with the formula, "For strength (iṣe) thee," and having taken it down with the formula, "For vigor (ūrje) thee," and having supported it with the *veda*-broom, he hands it to his wife.
Closing her eyes, she looks at it and gazes without breathing, [reciting] "Thou art the water of the earth.
With [the formula] "Thou art brilliance," she places it over the Gārhapatya fire in the northern half.
In the absence of the wife, the [recitation of] "brilliance" and so forth is omitted, though the placing over the Gārhapatya remains.

Having taken it up with "For brilliance thee," he carries it away with "Thou art brilliance; follow after brilliance. Having placed it over the Āhavanīya fire with "May Agni's brilliance not depart from thee," he sets it down on the track of the wooden sword (sphya) with "Thou art the tongue of Agni. 5.
The Adhvaryu and the sacrificer, having closed their eyes and looked [at the ghee], gaze at the clarified butter without exhaling, saying "Thou art the ghee, thou art truth.
6. Then he purifies it by means of two strainers with tips pointing north, moving them back and forth. 7.
Thus ends the sixth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the formula "Thou art brilliance" he takes the first [portion], with "Thou art light" the second, and with "Thou art splendor" the third.

As before, having purified the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*) with two [spoons] smeared with clarified butter (*ājya*), and having made the *veda* the *upabhṛt* spoon, he takes the portions of clarified butter within the altar (*antarvedi*) using a dipping-spoon (*sruva*) from which no [butter] has been poured out.
Holding the mixture of equal parts sour milk and ghee, he takes four portions with the *juhū*, eight with the *upabhṛt*, and four with the *dhruvā* which is established on the ground (3).
For one desiring cattle, there are five portions in the *dhruvā*; for the other two ladles, it is according to the original model (4–5).
Some say that ten portions are taken in the *upabhṛt* ladle and five portions in each of the other two;
others say there are more in the *juhū* and fewer in the *upabhṛt*, with the most in the *dhruvā*.

With the three formulas beginning "The bright thee for the bright," and the two beginning "Of the five winds thee," he takes four or five times into the *juhū* ladle, reciting a mantra for each portion.

"I take thee for the support of the five directions; I take thee for the support of the five peoples; I take thee for the support of the five waters; I take thee for the support of the five ridges. "Thou art the abode, the beloved of the gods, the inviolable place of sacrifice for the enjoyment of the gods; I take thee. And with the formula, "For the sake of the five-holed ladle," he takes [the butter] into the *upabhṛt* eight times or ten times, reciting a mantra for each. (9) With the remainder, he pours it into the *dhruvā* four or five times, reciting a mantra for each. (10) He does not set down the clarified butters on the *utkara*. (11)
"They do not carry what has been drawn within the altar toward the west.
This is the seventh section (kaṇḍikā).
Thus ends the second chapter (paṭala).

Having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters as before and having addressed the *brahman*, he unties the fuel-bundle (*idhma*) and sprinkles it three times with the formula, "Thou art black, dwelling in the mountain. He sprinkles the altar (*vedī*) three times with the formula, "Thou art the altar," and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) three times with the formula, "Thou art the sacrificial grass. Having placed the sacrificial grass with its knot toward the east inside the altar, he sprinkles the tip with "For heaven thee!"; the middle with "For the intermediate space thee!"; and the root with "For earth thee!
Having caused the tips to be poured into the ladle (*sruv*), he causes the roots to be poured into it.

With the formula, "For nourishment thee," he sprinkles the knot from east to west with the *sruva* ladle; having poured out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water continuously from the southern hip to the northern [hip] with the formula, "Svadhā to the ancestors," he loosens the knot with the formula, "May Pūṣan untie thy knot.
(3) He draws it forward, hidden [from view], and pulls it back.

(4) With the formula, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s tuft," he takes up the *prastara* toward the Āhavanīya fire as if drawing it away; he does not lift it up, nor does he move it forward, nor does he move it backward, nor does he scatter it, nor does he wipe it, nor does he wipe it across, nor does he wipe it along. (5)

"May this Prāṇa and Apāna go unto the sacrificer; for they have become the two *potaḥ* priests, the purifiers who cleanse the oblation in the sacrifice. Having recited, "I place Prāṇa and Apāna in the sacrificer," he inserts them into that *pavitra* (strainer) and hands it over to the sacrificer with the words, "By means of Prāṇa and Apāna, I make you one whose body is whole. The sacrificer [hands it] to the Brahman priest, or the Brahman priest holds the *prastara* (grass-bundle), or the sacrificer [holds it].
Thus ends the eighth section (kaṇḍikā).
Having covered the altar with darbha grass, he spreads the binding-cord to the south, either straight across or diagonally.

With the mantra, "I spread thee, O wool-soft one," he covers the altar with sacrificial grass (barhis), spreading it thickly so that it is not seen through, ending toward the east or toward the west, in three layers or five layers.
He covers the roots with the tips [of the grass-blades].
He repeats the mantra for each respective element (*dhātu*).

Holding the *prastara* bundle in his hand, he lays down the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) so that they touch one another, using these mantras respectively: "Thou art Gandharva Viśvāvasu," and so forth; the middle one with its tip pointing north, and the other two with their tips pointing east.
The southern [fire] is directed toward the Āhavanīya with its tip pointing westward, and the northern one toward it with its tip pointing eastward.
Having consecrated the Āhavanīya with the mantra, "May Sūrya protect you from the front," he arranges the fire while holding the *prastara* grass-bundle over the Āhavanīya.
According to the Vājasaneyaka, he throws out two firebrands (*ulmuka*) toward the east for the sake of the after-offerings (*anūyāja*).
Having touched the middle enclosing-stick, he places two upward-pointing kindling-sticks for the *āghāra* libation:
with the formula "Thee, the one who seeks the sacrifice, O Kavi," he places the southern stick; with "For life, thee," the northern one.
Or [he may place them] silently.
He makes two darbha-blades with their tips level and containing a central knot into the *vidhṛtī*.

Having placed them inside the altar with their tips pointing north, saying, "You two are the restrainers of the people," he places the *prastara* upon them, saying, "May he sit in the seat of the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas.
The roots of the *prastara* are closer together than the roots of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
With the formulas, "Thou art the Juhū ladle, dripping with ghee," and so on, he places the ladles, one after another, without touching them, upon the Prastara grass-bundle.
Thus ends the ninth Kaṇḍikā.
Or rather, he places only the Juhū ladle upon the Prastara.

He makes the handle of the *juhū* equal in length to its base. To the north of the *juhū*, he places the *upabhṛt* so that it is slightly closer together with the two *vidhṛtis* below them. To the north of the *upabhṛt*, he places the *dhruvā* so that it is slightly closer together with the two *vidhṛtis* above them.

With the formula, "Thou art the bull, belonging to the Śakvarī meters, the son of the *ghṛtācīs*; sit in the beloved seat with thy beloved name," he places the *sruva* to the south of the *juhū*, or to the north of the *dhruvā*.

Having consecrated the *sruva*-ladles with the mantra, "These have sat down," and the clarified butter with, "You are Viṣṇu's portions; you are Vaiṣṇava abodes; you are Prajāpati's abodes," he removes the embers from the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) using the same procedure as for the potsherds. He consecrates [the cake] with, "O Surya, shine forth as light for great sensory power. Then he sprinkles the Agni-cake with the mantra: "May Agni, whose source is ghee, swell; may he approve the oblations. Anoint yourself; I sprinkle you, who are well-formed and a finder of wealth, with the luster of cattle, as one dear to Agni. The subsequent cake he sprinkles silently.

"O Soma, you whose self has entered into the animals, who have extended yourself according to the station of the gods—becoming possessed of self and rich in ghee, go to the gods and find the light for me, the sacrificer. Thus [he addresses] the morning milk. "May I prepare for you a pleasant seat;

with a stream of ghee I fashion it for you as a most gracious one. Having spread a base of butter in the vessel, he places the sacrificial cake upon it without turning it over, saying: "Moist, expansive, the guardian of the world, the cooked one, the progenitor of thoughts, he emerges.
Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).
Having wiped away the ashes with the Veda, he places [the cake] upon the vessel with the formula: "Sit upon this; be established in immortality; O essence of rice, be well-disposed. 1.
[He places] that made of barley silently. 2.

Having anointed the potsherds with the dipping-spoon (sruva) with the formula, "May the nourishment, the prosperity, the sap of the earth, not depart," and having anointed the potsherds with the dipping-spoon with the formula, "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey," he anoints the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) with the dipping-spoon, making it well-anointed, without spots like a tortoise, without leaving any part out, and without scratching it. 3.
One should anoint [the sacrificial grass] from above and moisten it from below.
One should set down the oblations at the full moon sacrifice with the *caturhotṛ* formula, and at the new moon sacrifice with the *pañcahotṛ* formula.
It is known from tradition that one should set down any other oblation besides those belonging to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* with this [formula]: "By your dear name, sit upon your dear seat."
With another [hand], he places the offering-spoons and the two *puroḍāśa* cakes down (7). [He places] the two later milkings (8).

Or rather, he joins the two *sāṃnāyya*-pots in the middle of the altar—the boiled milk on the east and the curds on the west. Then he moves them apart: he places the boiled milk on the southern hip of the altar and the curds on the northern one (9).

"This Veda has found the earth, which was hidden in secret, in the depths and in the caves. May it find a world for the sacrificer; may he of many deeds perform the flawless sacrifice. Having placed the *veda* grass-bundle either in front of or to the north of the *dhruvā* ladle, having strewn around the edges of the altar (*vedyanta*), and having prepared the seat for the *hotṛ*, he proceeds with the *sāmidhenī* verses.
(10) Thus ends the eleventh section; thus ends the third chapter. He issues the command: "Recite for the fire being kindled," or "Recite for the fire being kindled. (1)
He recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses; it has been stated that these consist of three sets of five.
At each *praṇava*, he places a fuel-stick upon the fire.
When the *sāmidhenī* verses are increased, the fuel-sticks are increased; when they are decreased, it is as in the archetype.
Having recognized [the verse] "O Agni, kindled with an oblation," he leaves aside one *anūyāja* fuel-stick and places the entire remainder of the fuel on the fire, or at the *paridhānīyā* verse.

Having fanned the fire three times with the *veda*-grass whisk, having taken clarified butter from the *dhruvā* vessel with the *sruva*-ladle, and having held it up with the *veda*-whisk while seated, he draws it along the northern junction of the enclosing sticks, meditating mentally on Prajāpati, pouring the *āghāra* libation straight, continuous, and radiant toward the south-east, causing all the fuel-sticks to touch it.
Regarding the two libations (*āghāra*), he says they should be offered straight forward, or obliquely, intertwined or not intertwined.

(8) Having taken clarified butter from the butter-pot with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), saying, "May the *dhruvā* be replenished with ghee," and having made the portions, he replenishes the *dhruvā*; this is the universal rule. (9) He issues the command: "O Agnīdh, cleanse the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) and the fire three times each. (10)

Thus ends the twelfth section (kaṇḍikā). With the fire-wood-binding cords, together with the *sphya* or without the *sphya*, the Āgnīdhra, moving around from left to right, should wipe the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) three times each, following the order of their placement and pointing toward the east, saying: "O Agni, winner of booty, I wipe thee who art about to run for booty, who art about to win booty, the vigorous one, the winner of booty, for the sake of winning booty; [I wipe] Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of eating food"—thus three times for the Agni facing east.
Having placed the *juhū* or the *vañcali* spoon in front of the *dhruvā* with the words "Thou art the world," he takes the *juhū* with "Come, O *juhū*! and the *upabhṛt* with "Come, O *upabhṛt*!"
"O well-sacrificed one, may you today become for me a *ghṛtācī* (ghee-dripping ladle), well-enclosed and well-surrounded"—with these words, he places the *juhū* upon the *upabhṛt*.
Having brought it forward from the front, he brings it back down from the front.
In every case, the placing upon and the bringing down down are performed in this manner.
He does not make a clinking sound, nor does he hold the two *sruva* ladles at his navel.

With the mantra, "O Agni and Viṣṇu, may I not step between you," he steps across to the south with his right foot, passing beyond the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) to the front of the *sruva* ladles and behind the *prastara* bundle, while he steps to the north with his left foot.
Or rather, it may be the reverse of this.
"Thou art the station of Viṣṇu," with these words he stands. 9. His right foot is within the altar and his left is outside. 10.
Then, standing upright and having lowered himself along the southern joint of the enclosing-sticks (paridhi), 11. [he recites the formula].

Thus ends the thirteenth section (kaṇḍikā). Beginning with the words "samārabhyordhvo adhvaraḥ," while pouring the ghee straight and continuously toward the east and the north with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse, he causes all the fuel-sticks of the fire-wood to touch [the stream of ghee]. 1.
Regarding one for whom he desires, "May he be liable to die," it has been stated that he should pour crookedly for him. 2.
Having poured upwards, one should cut [the stream] for one whom one hates;
[one should pour] downwards for one desiring rain.
According to some, [this applies] to one who is hated.
(6) For one desiring heaven, he should offer the majority of the oblations after the *āghāra* libations.
(7) Or rather, he should not perform the *āghāra* libations; he should offer [the oblations] in the eastern part, the middle, or the western part [of the fire]. (8)

Having offered the oblation, he breathes over it with the words, "Bṛhadbhā. Having lifted the offering-ladle (sruk) with the words, "Protect me, O Agni, from evil conduct; grant me a share in good conduct," he steps back toward [the fire] without letting the two ladles touch each other.
These very steps of advancing and retreating are accompanied by mantras.
With the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," he anoints the *dhruvā* with the *juhū* either twice or thrice.

With the formula, "Uplifted for wealth," having taken clarified butter from the *dhruvā* with the *sruva*, and having sprinkled the *juhū* with the formula, "For the sake of heroic sons, svāhā," and having removed the [butter] from the *juhū*, he sprinkles the *dhruvā* in return with the formula, "By sacrifice, sacrifice is continued," and places the two ladles in their respective places.
Thus ends the fourteenth section.

"Who will be the Adhvaryu here? He indeed shall be the Adhvaryu here. [The sacrificer says: "May the sacrifice perform the office of the priest for the sacrifice; may the mind perform the office of the priest. I take refuge in speech: Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ! May I stand in the place of Viṣṇu. Having taken hold of the faggot-bands with the wooden sword (sphya) and having taken a blade of grass from the edge of the altar, the two stand to the north for the Pravara invocation—the Adhvaryu to the east and the Āgnīdhra to the west.
The Āgnīdhra, having taken hold of the faggot-bands, modifies the mantra: "Who will be the Āgnīdhra here? He indeed shall be the Āgnīdhra here. 1–2.

Having addressed the Brahman priest, saying, "I shall cause the announcement for the Brahman-pravara," he causes the announcement to be made with the words, "Announce! Announce! Announce for me! Announce! 3. Standing to the west of the *utkara* mound, facing south, holding the wooden sword (*sphyam*) and the cleansing-grass (*saṃmārgān*), the Āgnīdhra responds with the call, "Let there be hearing! (*astu śrauṣaṭ*). 4. This applies to the Soma sacrifice as well. 5.
In every case, the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta* formulas are thus;
this is the fifteenth section (kaṇḍikā), and the fourth chapter (paṭala).
They proceed without speaking out of turn. 1.

Before the *āśrāvaṇa* call, one should not say anything else; once the *āśrāvaṇa* has been made, the *āgnīdhra* should not say anything until the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* response; once the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* has been given, the *adhvaryu* should not say anything until the word "yaj" (sacrifice); once "yaj" has been uttered, the *hotṛ* should not say anything until the *vaṣaṭkāra*.
(2) If he should say anything else, he should again perform the *āśrāvaṇa*. (3) Or he should mutter the *vyāhṛtis*. (4)

He chooses the Hotṛ seated with his knees raised [saying]: "Agni, the divine Hotṛ, shall sacrifice to the gods—he who is wise and observant, like Manu, like Bharata, like so-and-so, like so-and-so"—according to the lineage of the sacrificer.
(5) He chooses three Rishis who composed the mantras; or he may choose one, two, three, or five. (6–7)
He chooses neither four nor more than five; 8.
From here upwards the Adhvaryu chooses, and from there downwards the Hotṛ; 9.
The king chooses by means of the Pravara of the domestic priest. 10.
"May he speak with sacred knowledge; may the Brahmins be the promoters of this sacrifice"—with these words he recites the remainder of the *pravara* invocation.
Or rather, he does not choose a lineage of seers (*nārṣeya*); he should simply say, "Like Manu.
The Hotṛ sits down.
He pronounces the name of the Hotṛ in a low voice, and [the word] "human" (*mānuṣa*) aloud. He throws a blade of grass onto the altar.
Thus ends the sixteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

Having taken up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles while the word "ghṛtavatī" is uttered, having stepped across once toward the south, he performs five *prayāja* offerings facing eastward, to the west of the junction of the *āghāra* lines:
(1) either to each direction respectively—*samidh* in the east, *tanūnapāt* in the south, *iḍ* in the west, *barhis* in the north, and the *svāhākāra* in the center;
or (2) all of them together at once.
