Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, he first issues the direction: "Recite the offering-verse for the *samidhs*. For the others, he says: "Recite, recite! (4) If he should desire of someone, "May he become more prosperous," he should offer for him while stepping forward; if he should desire, "May he become worse off," he should offer while stepping backward; if he should desire, "May he be neither better nor worse," he should stand in the same place. (5) Having sacrificed three times, he pours half of what is in the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*. Having sacrificed the remaining [three] oblations and stepped back, he bastes the *dhruvā* with the remainder and then bastes the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) in order, ending finally with the *aupabhṛta*. (6)
One should not pour clarified butter over the oblations of one whom one hates. He places the two *sruva*-ladles in their proper place.
Thus ends the seventeenth section; thus ends the fifth chapter.
The two *ājyabhāga* (clarified-butter portions) for Agni and Soma consist of clarified butter as the oblation, [offered] with two [portions] taken four times each.

Now, one who is not a Jamadagni, even when dealing with the *pañcāvatta* (five-fold portioning) of the Jamadagnis, should address the descendant of Jamadagni and perform the *pañcāvatta* in all cases. While cutting the portions, he issues the direction for the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*): "Recite for such-and-such a deity. Having cut each portion and having anointed the *prastara* and the *barhis* grass with the *sruva*-ladle, he takes up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, steps across to the south, causes the announcement to be made, and once the response has been given, he issues the direction for the offering verse (*yājyā*): "Sacrifice to such-and-such. This is the universal rule. He makes the offering to Agni in the eastern part of the northern half of the fire.
In the eastern part of the southern half, he offers to Soma, level with the previous [offering]. Both [ladles] are provided with light.
He takes up the two ladles toward the first *ājyabhāga* offering and does not set them down until the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

He offers the other oblations between the two *ājyabhāga* portions. Having stepped back and made an under-layer of ghee in the *juhū* ladle, he says: "Do not fear, do not tremble; may I not harm you; may your brilliance not depart. Support yourself, rise up! I shall sprinkle you with water; I shall take portions from you. Saying, "Homage be to you; do not harm me," he cuts a portion from the middle of the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni, measuring the thickness of a thumb-joint and sliced crosswise. For one who performs the fourfold cutting (*caturavattin*), he takes a second portion from the eastern half, sliced lengthwise. For one who performs the fivefold cutting (*pañcāvattin*), he takes a third portion from the western half.
He cuts off portions of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with the two fingers joined by the flesh and with the thumb, without piercing them.
This is the eighteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
[He cuts] from the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the *sāṃnāyya* offering with the *sruva* ladle. 1.

For one who is younger in birth, having first taken a portion from the eastern half, he should place the *sruk* ladle in the eastern half; having taken another portion from the middle, he should place the *sruk* in the western half.
He should take the first portions for the eldest son of the eldest wife, or for one who has attained prosperity.
He should take the latter portions for the youngest son of the youngest wife, or for one who is younger in birth, or for one who desires to prosper.

Now, if the domestic priest or one desiring the office of domestic priest should sacrifice, having first taken a portion from the eastern half and having placed the ladle in the eastern half, he should offer it in the eastern half of the fire.

Having sprinkled the portions with clarified butter, [he recites]: "Whatever I have done contrary to the rule for myself while cutting the portions—this I anoint back with clarified butter; may that swell up again. Having thus re-anointed the oblation, he gives the two directions: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni," and "Sacrifice to Agni.
Having dripped clarified butter [onto the offering] as if covering it, and having offered it without spilling, he pours clarified butter over it from behind.
He offers the oblations by means of the division of the *āghāra* libations. 8.
He pours the *āghāra* from the *sruva*-ladle over each preceding joint [of the fire]. 9.
If he should hate anyone, he should offer the oblations while mentally scattering [the offering] against that person. 10.
When the fire has lost its flames and seems to flicker, then he offers the oblations.
At the full moon sacrifice, there is indeed the low-voiced offering (*upāṃśuyāja*) with clarified butter as the sacrificial material; it is dedicated to Viṣṇu, or to Agni-Soma, or to Prajāpati.
The principal part of this [offering] is performed in a low voice.
One who desires to become like Viṣṇu should sacrifice [to him].
This is the nineteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
One who has rivals [should sacrifice] to Agni and Soma.

With the subsequent oblations, he proceeds according to the respective deities, as in the case of the Āgneya offering. Having taken portions from both milkings, he takes a portion from the curd and then takes a portion from the boiled milk—or rather, it may be the reverse. He offers all liquid substances through the mouth of the ladle.

With the *sruva* ladle, he performs the two *pārvaṇa* oblations. "On the full moon day: 'We worship the bull, the vigorous, the full moon; may it yield for us excellent heroism and thousandfold abundance of wealth. To the full moon, the giver of good gifts, to Prāṇa, Svāhā! On the new moon day: 'The new moon is fortunate and very gracious, swelling again like a milch-cow; may she yield for us excellent heroism and thousandfold abundance of wealth. To the new moon, the giver of good gifts, to Apāna, Svāhā! (5)

He offers the *nāriṣṭha* oblations: "O Sacrifice, these ten bodies of yours are worthy of worship; may the sacrificer gratify them with clarified butter. Invoking the blessing of the two *nāriṣṭhas*, the sacrificer has become immortal in the divine realm of the gods. O you two of a hundred powers, that portion of strength which the gods ordained for you—by this he gratifies you; by this, be satisfied and remove our distress. I belong to the world of the gods who perform good deeds; what is sacrificed here for me shall not be in vain."

I, the knowing one, sacrifice after the two Nāriṣṭhas, when Indra bestowed their share upon them, which is inviolable. O divine Soma, be one who does not let us fall into the pit; O Maruts, be gracious to us at this sacrifice! Let not the overwhelming curse find us; let not the hateful host find us. Thus ends the twentieth section.

Brahman is the foundation of the mind, Brahman of speech, Brahman of sacrifices, oblations, and clarified butter. Whatever is redundant in the ritual and whatever is deficient, may the sacrifice, knitting together its joints, proceed by arranging it. May this oblation, consecrated with *svāhā*, go to the gods. "I unite your mind with my mind; I place your breath within my breath; I unite your out-breath with my out-breath; I place your in-breath within my in-breath. Having grasped [the vessel], the sacrificer becomes immortal. "Be auspicious to us, for the sake of bipeds and for the sake of quadrupeds, *svāhā*!"—with these mantras, one offers for each.
This is the time for the secondary offerings (*upahoma*): either immediately after [the main oblation], or after the principal offerings, or before the *samiṣṭayajus*.

Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhu* ladle, he cuts off a portion from the northern half of each of the sacrificial oblations once for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering. For one who follows the five-fold division, he cuts twice.
Among the portions for the deities, the *Sviṣṭakṛt*, the *iḍā*, and the fourfold distribution, each subsequent one is larger than the preceding.
Having sprinkled clarified butter over them twice, he does not sprinkle it back over the original oblation.

"Recite for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt"—this is the formal direction (*saṃpraiṣa*). He offers [the oblation] in the eastern part of the northern half [of the altar], so that it does not touch the other offerings. Having stepped back and having poured water into the *juhū* ladle, he pours it out within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the mantra: "I offer this oblation to Vaiśvānara; may this thousandfold, hundred-streaming spring nourish our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather in the heavenly world, *svāhā*. (He pours it out, he pours it out. Thus ends the twenty-first section (*kaṇḍikā*). Thus ends the sixth chapter (*paṭala*). Thus ends the second book (*praśna*).
Some prescribe the *iḍā* first, others the *prāśitra*.

Having split the cake for Agni—whether facing forward or across—and having separated it with the thumb and the ring finger, he cuts off the *prāśitra* from the middle, the size of a barley grain or a *pippala* fruit; larger than a barley grain [with the formula]: "May this not be harmed by the arrow; may we not consume the pure, well-offered oblation of the sacrifice.
He cuts off the [portion] from the northern part in the same manner.
Having spread [the underlayer of ghee], he does not pour [ghee] over it; or rather, it is the reverse. Or else, he both spreads [the underlayer] and pours [ghee] over it.

Some prescribe the carrying around and the eating of this [portion] at this very point. Having spread [an underlayer] in the *iḍā*-vessel, he cuts off the *iḍā* from all the sacrificial oblations, whether in four portions or in five portions.

"Having seen the *ghṛtapadī* [offering] ordained by Manu and impelled by Mitra and Varuṇa, I cut off from the southern half of the cake dedicated to Agni that which has a single face, without piercing through," with these words he first cuts the portion from the southern half of the *puroḍāśa* for Agni. (7) He makes a second cutting from the point of junction. (8) And from the eastern half, he cuts the sacrificer's portion, which is like a tiny speck and long. (9)
Having satiated it with clarified butter, he brings [the portion] from the *dhruvā* vessel;
or alternatively, having cut off the sacrificer’s share from the southern half, he takes it from the junction.
In the same way, he cuts off from the northern [half].
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
Having sprinkled the iḍā with clarified butter and handed it to the Hotṛ, he passes to the south of the Hotṛ without letting go of it.
With the iḍā, he encompasses the Adhvaryu from behind.
Alternatively, having moved the *iḍā* to the east and sitting to the south, he anoints the two finger-joints of the Hotṛ with the *sruva*—

either anointing the rear joint first and then the front, or conversely. Having offered water, sitting facing west in front of him, he cuts off the *avāntareḍā* from the *iḍā* into the hand of the Hotṛ.
The *adhvaryu* makes the first cutting; the *hotṛ* himself makes the subsequent one—or rather, this may be the reverse.
There are the spreading of the base (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) from the smearings.

One who follows the five-fold division (*pañcāvattin*) should pour over twice. While the portion is being invoked, both the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) touch it from behind. Recognizing the formula "The divine *adhvaryus* are invoked," the *adhvaryu* mutters: "May I, being invoked, possess cattle. Recognizing the formula "This sacrificer is invoked," the sacrificer [mutters] that same mantra.
When [the *iḍā*] has been invoked, he carries the *prāśitra* portion for the Brahman priest past the front of the Āhavanīya fire.

(9) When that has been consumed, the Hotṛ eats the *avāntareḍā*, saying: "I eat thee, offered to Vācaspati; I eat thee, offered to Sadaspati. (10) After the *iḍā* has been consumed, the five—[the priests] with the sacrificer as the fifth—consume the *iḍā*, saying: "Be pleased with our portion of the *iḍā*; quicken our cattle, quicken our horses. May we, with our whole selves and our whole retinues, be those who enjoy thee. (11)
Thus ends the second section (kaṇḍikā). They remain seated with speech restrained until the sprinkling (mārjana).

Having sprinkled themselves with water on the sacrificial grass (prastara) within the altar (antarvedi) with the mantra, "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]," he divides the cake dedicated to Agni (āgneya-puroḍāśa) into four parts and places it upon the sacrificial grass; or, having placed it upon the sacrificial grass, he divides it into four parts.
The sacrificer assigns it, saying: "This for the Brahman; this for the Hotṛ; this for the Adhvaryu; this for the Agnīdh.
[He assigns] either those beginning with the Agnīdh or those beginning with the Hotṛ.
Having pointed out the portion for the sacrificer, saying, "This for the sacrificer," the Adhvaryu prepares the largest piece as a sixfold portion (ṣaḍavatta) for the Agnīdh.
Having once spread [the ghee] underneath, he takes [the portion] twice; having spread it underneath, he pours [ghee] over it twice.
Or alternatively, he spreads [ghee] underneath twice, takes [the portion] twice, and pours [ghee] over it twice.
"Thou art the Āgnīdhra-hearth of Agni; thou art the Śāmitra-hearth of Agni; homage be to thee; do not harm me"—with these words, the Āgnīdhra consumes [the portion].
With the *veda* grass, he distributes the portions for the Brahman and the Sacrificer (9).
For the other two [the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu], he does so with separate vessels (10).
"Thou art the portion of the Earth," says the Hotṛ as he consumes his portion; "Thou art the portion of the Atmosphere," says the Adhvaryu; "Thou art the portion of Heaven," says the Brahman (11).
In the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, he cooks a large, unlimited amount of Anvāhārya rice;
some say it should be cooked in milk.
Having poured clarified butter over it—or not pouring it over it—he takes it down, places it within the altar (antarvedi), and sets it down.
Thus ends the third section (kaṇḍikā).
He issues the command: "Let [the gifts] be brought to those seated on the south.
The sacrificer says to those Brahmins who are on the north: "Come here to the south."
To them he gives the *anvāhārya* rice, saying, "O Brāhmaṇas, this is your boiled rice.
Once it has been accepted, he issues the command from the north, "Carry it around.

Having set aside the remnants of the oblation and having thrown the two firebrands together, he issues the command: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Āgnīdhra, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire thoroughly with the *sruva*-ladle."

Permitted by the Brahman, the Āgnīdhra places a kindling-stick (samidh) with the formula: "This is thy kindling-stick, O Agni; through it mayest thou grow and swell; may the lord of the sacrifice grow and swell; may we grow and swell, may we swell, svāhā! (6) Having wiped each of the enclosing-sticks (paridhis) once as before, he wipes the fire once while facing eastward with the formula: "O Agni, winner of booty, thee who hast run for booty, who hast won booty, the vigorous one, the winner of booty— I wipe thee for the winning of booty, Agni the eater of food, for the sake of eating food. (7)

Having sprinkled the faggot-binders with water, he offers them into the fire or deposits them on the rubbish-heap, saying: "O Rudra, Lord of beings, who moves along the threads, the bull—do not harm our cattle; let this be an offering for you, Svāhā! [He may also deposit them] in the hall, in a stable, in another cow-pen, or beyond the pasture. Thus ends the fourth section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the first chapter (paṭala).

Having brought the *aupabhṛta* ladle and having taken up both the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, he steps across once toward the south and offers three *anūyāja* offerings to the west of the junction of the *āghāra* lines. At each call for the *āśrāvaṇa*, when the response has been given, he first issues the direction: "Sacrifice to the gods! For the other two, he says: "Sacrifice! Sacrifice!
He offers the first offering on the eastern half of the fire upon the *samidh* fuel-stick, the second in the middle, and the last one forward, completing it while joining the other two together.
Having stepped back and placed the two ladles in their respective places, he separates them with the two *vājavatī* verses.

With the formula, "At the impulse of strength," he raises the *juhū* ladle together with the *prastara* grass-bundle with his right hand, palm upwards. Then, with the formula, "And [I drive] my rivals away," he lowers the *upabhṛt* ladle with his left hand.
With "The upward-grasping," he raises the *juhū*; with "and the downward-grasping," he lowers the *upabhṛt*.
With "The gods have increased the sacred word (*brahman*)," he pushes the *juhū* forward toward the east.

Then, with the formula "Now [I drive] away my rivals," he throws the *upabhṛt* ladle westward outside the altar with his left hand; having sprinkled it and lifted it up, he anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the *juhū* ladle: with "For the Vasus, thee! the middle one; with "For the Rudras, thee! the southern one; and with "For the Ādityas, thee! the northern one. (7) He does not place the *juhū* on the *prastara*.

Having removed the *prastara* from the two separating blades (*vidhṛti*) with the formula "May Heaven and Earth agree; may Mitra and Varuṇa favor thee with rain," and having placed the two separating blades back among the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he anoints the *prastara* over the ladles. (9)

Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā). With the verse, "Licking what is smeared" (*aktaṃ rihāṇā*), he anoints the tip [of the sacrificial grass] with the *juhū* ladle; with "Offspring, the womb" (*prajāṃ yonim*), the middle with the *upabhṛt* ladle; and with "May the waters and plants swell" (*āpyāyantām āpa oṣadhayaḥ*), the root with the *dhruvā* ladle. This is done three times. Alternatively: with "Be anointed in heaven" (*divyaṅkṣva*), the tip with the *juhū*; with "Be anointed in the intermediate space" (*antarikṣe'ṅkṣva*), the middle with the *upabhṛt*; and with "Be anointed on earth" (*pṛthivyāmaṅkṣva*), the root with the *dhruvā*.

Thus again: 3. Furthermore: [He takes] the root with "For the earth, thee! on the *dhruvā* ladle; the middle with "For the intermediate space, thee! on the *upabhṛt* ladle; and the tip with "For heaven, thee! on the *juhū* ladle. 4.

Having removed a blade of grass from the anointed [ghee] with "For life, thee!", having set it aside in its known place, and having taken the *prastara* bundle with his right and left hands and placed it upon the *juhū*, sitting down, having called for the announcement (*āśrāvya*) and the response (*pratyāśrāvite*), he issues the command: "The divine Hotṛs have been impelled for the auspicious speech; the human [Hotṛ] has been impelled for the *sūktavāka*; recite the *sūkta*! 5.
While the *sūktavāka* is being recited, at the words "the spotted deer of the Maruts," he throws the *prastara* together with the twig into the *āhavanīya* fire.
(6) He does not utter *svāhā*.
(7) He does not shake it, nor does he fan it away, nor does he scatter it, nor does he wipe it, nor does he wipe it back, nor does he wipe it along; nor should he throw it toward the north. (8)
Holding the hand transversely, as if drawing it along, he throws it into the Āhavanīya fire;
it has been stated that he does not break it off.
Having spread it out, he should throw it if he should desire, "May a female child be born to him."
He releases the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *āśis* [formula].
This is the sixth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
Turning his hand downward... 1.
He issues the command: "O Āgnīdhra, bring [the Prastara]! 2.

Three times the Āgnīdhra raises the Prastara upward with his joined palms, moving it in a non-circular direction, with each of these mantras: "May Agni cause you to go to the deity by means of the red [horse]," and so forth.
3. Then the Āgnīdhra says to him: "Throw it after [the oblations]! 4.
He throws back into the fire the blade of grass that was taken from the prastara-bunch with the formula, "May it be well with thy bodies.
Having pointed three times at the fire with his finger while saying, "This is this," he addresses the fire with the mantra, "O Agni, thou art long-lived; protect my life.
With the formula, "Thou art firm," he touches the earth within the altar.
Then the Āgnīdhra says to him, "Converse [with the Hotṛ]!
(8) The Adhvaryu says, "The Āgnīdh has come! The Āgnīdhra replies, "He has come. The Adhvaryu says, "Make it heard! The Āgnīdhra replies, "Śrauṣaṭ!
(9) Having taken hold of the middle enclosing-stick, he issues the command: "A good path for the divine Hotṛs; well-being for the human ones; pronounce the *śaṃyuvāka*! (10)
While the *śaṃyuvāka* is being recited, he throws the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the *āhavanīya* fire:

the middle one with the formula, "The enclosing stick which you placed around," and the other two with, "O paths of the sacrifice, you have been gathered together. He pushes the tip of the northernmost stick onto the embers.

Having consecrated the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the formula, "May you extend the sacrificer," and having placed the tip of the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *juhū* ladle, he makes an offering over the residue with the formula, "Those who have a share in the residue.
14. Right here the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) consume the remnants of the oblation.
15. Thus ends the seventh section; thus ends the second chapter.

Having washed the remnants of the clarified butter from the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* spoons along with the *sruva* ladle, the Adhvaryu takes them up; the Hotṛ takes the *veda* grass-bundle; and the Āgnīdhra takes the wooden sword (*sphya*), the vessel of clarified butter, and the water-pitcher.
(1) Intending to perform the offerings for the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*), they proceed westward, with the Āgnīdhra leading.
(2) The Adhvaryu enters by the front of the Gārhapatya fire, while the other two enter by the north. (3)

Having placed the two offering-spoons on the *kaṭa* post with the formula, "I place [you] in the seat of Agni Vāmapannagṛha," he wipes the two poles of the yoke with the formula, "O two bearers of the yoke, protect the yoke-animals.
(4) If he should perform the pouring out from a vessel, he should place the two spoons on the wooden sword (*sphya*) with these same two formulas.
(5) They perform the *saṃyājana* offerings for the wives with either the large spoons (*sruc*) or the small ladles (*sruva*). (6)

Having made the *upabhṛt* the vessel, [they sacrifice] with the *juhū* or with the *sruva*, according to some; others say they sacrifice behind the *gārhapatya* fire, sitting with their knees raised, either with a loud sound or in a whisper (*upāṃśu*).
The *adhvaryu* is to the south, the *āgnīdhra* to the north, and the *hotṛ* in the middle.
Having offered with clarified butter to Soma and Tvaṣṭṛ, they cause the wives to sacrifice together with the tail (jāghanī), either with clarified butter or as it has been taken up.
With the two calls, "Recite for Soma" and "Sacrifice to Soma," he offers in the northern half.
In the same way, [he sacrifices] to the others and to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Thus ends the eighth section (kaṇḍikā).
[He worships] "the wives of the gods" and "Agni, the lord of the house. 1. Tvaṣṭṛ is to the south, or alternatively to the north; Agni, the lord of the house, is in the middle. 2.
One should sacrifice to the wives of the gods either within an enclosed space starting from the Āhavanīya fire, or in an unenclosed space.
One desiring sons should sacrifice to Rākā; one desiring cattle, to Sinīvālī; and one desiring prosperity, to Kuhū.
Some authorities prescribe these [offerings] as being obligatory.

Some recite these [verses] before the Devapatnīs; others, after them, as previously described. Having touched water with his fingers and his lap, the Hotṛ causes four drops of clarified butter to be poured into his hand; from this, he cuts off the *iḍā* for the Hotṛ and six for the Āgnīdhra.
While the *iḍā* is being invoked, the Adhvaryu, the Āgnīdhra, and the wife touch it.
The Hotṛ and the Āgnīdhra consume the portion that has been invited.

Here, while the wife holds on to him, he offers the *saṃpatnīya* oblation with the wooden spoon (*sruva*), [reciting]: "May the wife go together with her husband through their good deed; may they become the two yoke-horses of the sacrifice. Being in agreement, may they cast away the enemies; may they grasp the unaging light in heaven, Svāhā!
Some recite this verse before the offerings to the wives of the gods, or after them; or rather, it is after the offerings of the flour-smears and the husks.
Having placed the wood-chips for the kindling on the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, he offers the oblations of the flour-smear and the husks. 12.
Thus ends the ninth section.

In the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one performs either the *phalīkaraṇa* oblation first or the other way around. Having poured the *phalīkaraṇa* husks into four ladles of clarified butter (*ājya*), he offers them with the mantra: "O Agni, whose strength is unfailing, whose body is cool! [I offer] what has adhered to the flour, in the mortar and pestle, and whatever has stuck to the winnowing basket; the drops and the scattered fragments—I sacrifice them together. May all the gods enjoy this oblation. Whatever many scattered drops there are in the sacrifice, all those I offer well-sacrificed and well-poured into the fire, Svāhā! (1)

"To Sarasvatī who brings fortune to the settlement, svāhā! To Sarasvatī who brings fortune to the household, svāhā! O Indra, make our minds intent upon the household, and make our kinsmen well-disposed, svāhā!"—with these mantras, he offers oblations one by one into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
(2) "Thou art the Veda," with this mantra, the Hotṛ throws the Veda-grass three times into the lap of the wife.
(3) "Drive away the hater, drive away the enemy," with this, the other [wife] pushes back each time as it is thrown in. (4)
Reciting "Stretching the thread," the Hotṛ, having stepped out from the Gārhapatya fire, spreads [the grass] continuously as far as the Āhavanīya fire, or up to the Vedi. 5.
Reciting "I loosen this," the wife unfastens the noose of her girdle. 6.
He pours the full vessel into her joined palms, which still hold the girdle. 7.
When [the water] is being brought with the words, "May you be equal in life-span, equal in offspring," he mutters [the formula].
Having poured it out and wiped his mouth, he rises with the thought: "May I be prosperous, possessed of cattle, possessed of offspring, and a mistress of the household.
Thus ends the tenth section; thus ends the third chapter.

Having gone to the Āhavanīya fire in this manner, he offers all the expiatory oblations (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) with the *juhū* or the *sruva* ladle. The verse is: "Brahman is the foundation of the mind; whatever in the sacrifice has been under-intoned, over-intoned, accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, or recited in excess, and whatever is deficient—may the sacrifice, smoothing over its joints, proceed as it ordains. May the offering consecrated with *svāhā* go to the gods. O gods, whatever we have omitted, or whatever offense against the gods has been committed through speech, even though we were intent on devotion—O Maruts, cast that away from us, for the enemy seeks to harm us; place it elsewhere than us!"

Stretched out for me is the water; that is stretched out again. The sweetest prayer is recited for the hymn. This ocean is the all-healing one; may you both be fully satiated by this which has been consecrated with *svāhā*. "Up from the darkness," "Up that bright one," "This for me, O Varuṇa," "That of thee I implore," "Thou for us, O Agni," "So thou for us, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art Ayāsya"—placed by the unwearied mind. Being unwearied, thou hast carried the oblation; as the unwearied, bestow healing upon us. "O Prajāpati"—this is the verse.

Svāhā to the desired; Vaṣaṭ to the undesired, Svāhā! To the remedy for ill-omened sacrifice, Svāhā! To the expiation, Svāhā! To misfortune, Svāhā! To the divine bodies, Svāhā! To prosperity, Svāhā! To complete prosperity, Svāhā! O Agni, you are the unerring one and free from reproach; you are indeed truth, you are the unerring one. Sustained by an unerring mind, you carry the oblation with an unerring [mind]; as the unerring one, bestow healing upon us. Whatever we have done amiss in this sacrifice, whether in the mantra or in the ritual action, I pacify all that with this oblation. May the gods be satisfied; may they rain down [blessings] with clarified butter. 2.

This is the eleventh section (kaṇḍikā). O Jātavedas, unite that which was known and unknown, and that which was thought and not thought; for you indeed know each thing as it truly is. Whatever was done in this rite, whatever was not done, whatever was left in excess, and whatever was not left in excess—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, being wise, make all of it well-sacrificed and well-offered. Whatever I have overdone in this ritual, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, being wise, make all of it well-sacrificed and well-offered. O Indra, from whatever we fear, from that grant us freedom from fear.

O Maghavan, grant us this for our protection; strike away the haters, strike away the mockers. The giver of well-being, the lord of the people, the slayer of Vṛtra, the dispeller of mockers, the controller—may Indra, the bull, go before us, the giver of well-being and the creator of fearlessness. O Lord of the Bay Steeds, increasing through these songs, fill up whatever is deficient for us here. When you burst open the great cow-pens for your praisers, may we then be those who receive the greatest portion. Whatever in the sacrifice is done incorrectly, whether unknowingly or knowingly—

O Agni, prepare this for him, for you indeed know it as it truly is. The sacrifice is commensurate with the person; the sacrifice is commensurate with the person. O Agni, prepare this for him, for you indeed know it as it truly is. Whatever mortals, with simple minds and limited skill, do not properly conceive of the sacrifice—may Agni, the Hotṛ who knows the ritual, discerning and most skilled in worship, sacrifice to the gods according to the seasons. Whatever the priests, whether knowing or unknowing, do in their confusion—may Agni and the goddess Śraddhā release me from that sin.
(Thus ends the twelfth section.)

Agni Jātavedas has sacrificed, having sat down within us as the first. Granting gain, release us with a good release; bestow upon us wealth, O Jātavedas, and whatever is auspicious. "Those hundred and those thousand sacrificial nooses of yours, O Varuṇa, which are spread in many places—from them may Indra, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, all the gods, and the Maruts release us with well-being. Having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* uttered separately and together, [one recites]: "O Agni, awaken among beings! Raise up the highest! etc.
As before, having replenished the *dhruvā* [ladle], standing upright within the altar (*antarvedi*) and reciting "O gods, you who know the way," he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* with the *dhruvā*.
(2) At the middle *svāhā*-utterance, he throws the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) after [the oblation].

(3) If the sacrificer should be away on a journey, he should place the sacrificer’s portion into the *dhruvā* with the words, "The world of Prajāpati named Vibhān," and offer it together with the *samiṣṭayajus*. (4)

"Strew [the grass] over it, enclose the altar; do not harm your sister as she lies there. These golden, bright-colored [blades] are the Hotṛ’s seats for the sacrificer, O Bradhna! Having thus strewn the altar with the Hotṛ’s seats, he sets down the *praṇītā* waters within the altar and releases them with the words: "Who has unyoked you? May he release you. 5.

"The Upaveṣa which the gods placed among men—those who are ill-disposed toward us, bring them here for us! O Upaveṣa, protect our offspring, our prosperity, and our wealth; make our bipeds and quadrupeds firm and unswerving. Having spoken thus, he hides the thick end of the Upaveṣa into the heap of earth (utkara) from the front toward the west.
This is the thirteenth section.
If he should practice sorcery, he says, "O Upaveṣa, let the spear reach that one whom we hate," and then, having uttered his name, he hurls it at him. 1.

"Drive away that rival who attacks us from our home; Indra has driven him away with the *nirbādhyā* oblation. Go beyond the three distant realms; go beyond the five peoples; go beyond the three luminous spheres as far as the sun is in heaven. May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, lead you to the furthest distance, from which you shall not return for eternal years. With these five verses, saying "He is slain! We have struck down so-and-so!", he should either cast [the enemy] out or bury him. 2.
"Loosed, fly away, O arrow sharpened by sacred knowledge; go to the enemies, enter them, and let not one of them remain. Or [he says]:
"The potsherds which were in the Gharma... With this four-footed verse, having loosened the potsherds and counted them, he removes them from the fire. The New and Full Moon sacrifices are concluded.

One should conclude the sacrifice on the Āhavanīya fire with the *śaṃyu* formula and on the Gārhapatya fire with the *ājyeḍā*. Or alternatively, one may conclude on the Āhavanīya with the *iḍā* and on the Gārhapatya with the *śaṃyu*.

(6) If the conclusion on the Gārhapatya is to be with the *śaṃyu*, then having taken a blade of grass from the Veda, one should anoint its tip in the *juhū* ladle, its middle in the *sruva* ladle, and its base in the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*). Its ritual procedure is like that of the *prastara* bundle, beginning with the *sūktavāka* and ending with the *śaṃyuvāka*.
(7) One who desires heaven [should perform] the New and Full Moon sacrifices. (8)
Whether desiring one thing or all things (9),
he may desire them simultaneously or separately regarding the food (10);
with these two [fires], he should sacrifice for as long as he lives (11).
Or he may sacrifice for thirty years;
or, being aged, he may desist. Having stated, "He who desires offspring should sacrifice at both full-moon and new-moon festivals," [the text] says, "But one should sacrifice at only one."
Thus ends the fourteenth section; thus ends the fourth chapter.
Having completed the Full-moon sacrifice, he subsequently prepares a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Vaimṛdha.
Some authorities prescribe that this should be performed with the same ritual procedure (*samānatantra*).
In its commencement, one may proceed according to one's desire; however, by the act of commencing, it is restricted [to a specific form]:
it consists of seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses, and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is according to one's faith.

The two *saṃyājyā* verses contain the word "strength" (*śardha*). [The verses are: "O Agni, exert thy strength for great good fortune; let thy splendors be most excellent. Make the lordship of the house well-governed; trample down the powers of those who act as enemies. Like a swift steed fanned by the wind, when thou standest spreading abroad thy food greedily among the desires, thy unaging strengths, O Agni, strive apart like chariot-horses to consume."

At the full moon sacrifice, he subsequently offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma; at the new moon sacrifice, a pap of rice cooked in ghee to Aditi, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a cake on eleven potsherds to Pūṣan and Indra for one who has rivals or who practices sorcery. For one who fears death or misfortune, he should perform a second offering of a pap to Indra the Protector as part of the Vaimṛdha rite. A castrated bull is the sacrificial fee. One desiring offspring, cattle, or kinsmen should subsequently offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Possessor of Power.
One should perform this as a secondary expiation,
or the other two,
whichever one suspects may have been committed.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.
He should offer [an oblation] to Indra Vaimṛdha for one who neither makes a sound nor hears; he should offer [an oblation] to Indra Aṃhomuc for one who neither makes a sound nor hears.
He who has rivals should offer [the sacrifice] to Indra, the subduer of Vṛtra;

and he whom no one at all can oppress should offer it to Indra alone. He who has rivals, having completed the Full Moon sacrifice, should subsequently perform this offering: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a pap for Sarasvant.
One who has rivals should sacrifice only on the full moon day, not on the new moon day;
for it is traditionally known that by performing the Pitṛyajña on the new moon day,
one hurls a thunderbolt at one's rival with every transition [of the sun].

At the new moon, when [the sun] moves into the third part of the zodiacal sign, there should be the principal offerings to Agni and Soma for one who has rivals or who is practicing exorcism. "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *sākaṃprasthāyīya*"; thus the new moon rite is modified.

There are two milkings in the evening and likewise two in the morning. (12) They proceed with the two evening milkings in the evening and with the two morning milkings in the morning. (13) Or rather, they proceed with all of them in the morning. (14)
At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out four vessels made of udumbara wood; their ritual procedure is like that of the *juhū* ladle.

Having performed the two *ājyabhāga* offerings and having offered the cake for Agni to the *āgnīdhra*, and handing over the two *srucaḥ* ladles, he steps forward together with the water-pitchers and issues the two directions: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra" and "Call for the *āśrāvaṇa*: 'Sacrifice to Indra! (15–17).
Thus ends the sixteenth section.

As many as there are jars, so many Brāhmaṇas, wearing their sacred threads over the left shoulder (upavītin), stand up to the south; having filled vessels from the jars, they offer with them following the Adhvaryu as he offers. There are neither portions for the Sviṣṭakṛt nor any ritual consumptions (bhakṣa).
From this point onwards, it is the same. The Sākaṃprasthāyīya sacrifice is concluded.
One who desires heaven should perform the Dākṣāyaṇayajña.
He should sacrifice on two full-moon days and two new-moon days.

On the first full moon day, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma; on the subsequent [full moon day], a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and curd for Indra. On the first new moon day, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni; on the second [new moon day], a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and clotted curds (āmikṣā) for Mitra-Varuṇa.
It has been stated that this is for one who desires distinction.
Or, one may approach his wife at the proper season.

Thus, at the commencement of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, there is this option: "One should sacrifice with these New and Full Moon sacrifices," or "Having sacrificed with them for fifteen years, one may cease, or one may continue to sacrifice. The Dākṣāyaṇayajña is thus concluded.
By this, the Eḍādadhā sacrifice, the Sārvaseniya sacrifice, the Vasiṣṭha sacrifice, and the Śaunaka sacrifice are explained.
Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā). Thus ends the fifth chapter (paṭala).
One most proficient in the Veda is the Brahman priest at the New and Full Moon sacrifices. 1.
He chooses him [as officiant] with the words: "O lord of the earth, O lord of the world, O lord of the great being, we choose you as the Brahman. Having been chosen, he mutters [the following].

I am the lord of the earth, I am the lord of the ground, I am the lord of the great being. Impelled by the god Savitṛ, I shall perform the office of the officiating priest. O god Savitṛ, they choose you, Bṛhaspati, the divine Brahman; that I announce to the mind. Mind to Gāyatrī, Gāyatrī to Triṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh to Jagatī, Jagatī to Anuṣṭubh, Anuṣṭubh to Paṅkti, Paṅkti to Prajāpati, Prajāpati to the All-gods, and the All-gods to Bṛhaspati.

"Bṛhaspati is the Brahman for the Brahman; Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvar. Bṛhaspati is the Brahman of the gods; I am the Brahman of men. O Bṛhaspati, protect the sacrifice," having said this, he steps across to the south behind the Āhavanīya fire and casts away a blade of grass from the Brahman’s seat with the formula: "Cast out is the one whose wealth is turned away, along with evil! Then he sits down with the formula: "In this seat of the one whose wealth is turned hitherward I sit, impelled by the god Savitṛ; I sit in the seat of Bṛhaspati. That I announce to Agni, that to Vāyu, that to Sūrya, that to Pṛthivī.
He remains seated, turning toward the Āhavanīya fire.
In each ritual act, he restrains his speech, or [he does so] during those rites accompanied by mantras; however, he may speak as he pleases during silent rites.
If, through negligence, he should utter a word, he should restrain his speech after muttering a verse addressed to Viṣṇu and the vyāhṛtis.
"O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters," when this is said—thus ends the eighteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

"Lead forward the sacrifice; cause the deities to prosper; may the sacrificer abide upon the back of the firmament. Where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer—Om, lead forward! Thus he gives the impulse.
In all *iṣṭis*, there is an invitation (*āmantraṇa-iṣṭi*); thus, by that ritual act, he invites [the deity] in whom he addresses [the offering].

(1) "Sprinkle the sacrifice" (*prokṣa yajñam*) is used at the sprinkling of the oblation (*havis*), the fuel-sticks (*idhma*), and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). (2) "O Bṛhaspati, enclose the altar; may the seats be yours, O gods; upon it let the sacrificial grass spread well; may the divine Earth be non-injurious to us"—this is for the enclosing of the altar (*parigrāha*). (3) "O Prajāpati, recite after [me] regarding the sacrifice" is said to one who is about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses. "O Lord of Speech, cause this speech to be heard; cause the sacrifice to be heard among the gods; [cause] me to be heard among men"—this is at the *pravara*.
He appends the formula "O deity, do thou increase" to every [portion].
(4) He gazes at the *prāśitra* being cut out with the formula, "I gaze upon thee with the eye of Mitra.
(5) He says, "Go along the path of Truth," as it is being carried around; and "I look upon thee with the eye of Sūrya," as it is being brought back. (6)

Having received [the portion] with the *sāvitra* formula, having spread out grass-blades within the altar (*antarvedi*) with the words "I set thee on the navel of the earth, in the place of *iḍā*," and having placed it down with its handle pointing eastward, he gazes at it with the words "I gaze upon thee with unimpaired vision. Then, taking it up with his thumb and ring finger with the *sāvitra* formula, he swallows it without chewing, with the words: "I consume thee with the mouth of Agni, with the belly of the Brāhmaṇa; I set thee in the stomach of Bṛhaspati, the Brahman, and Indra.
Thus ends the nineteenth section.

"May those deities who are within the waters pacify this; go to the belly of Indra, consecrated by *svāhā*, *svāhā*!"—having thus poured water over [the food] and sipped water, he touches the region of the navel with the formula: "Do not come into contact with my food; sit above my navel; I set thee in the belly of Indra. (1) He touches the limbs according to their respective marks with the formula: "Speech is in my mouth... (2) He touches the remaining parts with the formula: "May all [my members] be unharmed... (3).
Having washed the vessel and filled it, he pours it out toward the distant direction with the words, "May the quarters be gladdened"; he pours it toward himself with the words, "May I be gladdened.
When they bring him the portion for the Brahman, having accepted it, he does not consume it until the sacrifice is concluded.

"O Brahman, you are the Brahman; for the Brahman, I have offered you today; do not harm me; having been offered, be auspicious to me"—with these words, he touches the *anvāhārya* rice that has been placed within the *vedi*.

(7) When [the Adhvaryu] says, "O Brahman, we shall proceed," he gives the impulse: "O God Savitṛ, you have declared this; impel it and sacrifice it! Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; may he protect the sacrifice, may he protect the lord of the sacrifice, may he protect me! Om! Be established! (8) Thus he pronounces the impulse.

"May the ground go to the ground; may the mother go to the mother. May we abound with sons and cattle; may he who hates us be split asunder. With these words, whatever earthen vessel should break during the sacrifice, that he should consecrate with this mantra. (9) Having consumed the portion belonging to the Brahman priest, [he recites]: "Agni Jātavedas has sacrificed; may he sacrifice for us toward greater wealth. Unite us with a favor that brings strength. Having thus addressed the Āhavanīya fire, he goes out by the same way he entered. (10) Thus is prescribed the office of the Brahman priest for the *iṣṭi* sacrifices and the animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*). (11)
Thus ends the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā). Thus ends the sixth chapter (paṭala). Thus ends the third book (praśna).
We shall now explain the duties of the sacrificer (yājamāna). 1.
The patron of the sacrifice observes celibacy, gives sacrificial fees, prepares the ritual materials, and desires the objects of his wishes;
he mutters the mantras containing blessings directed toward himself, worships the instruments of the rite, and recites the consecratory formulas;
and on the new and full moon days, he has his hair and beard shaved.
"Let him shave even a small amount of hair," so says the Vājasaneyaka.
"Thou art lightning; strike away my evil; from the immortal I go unto the true"—with these words, one who is about to sacrifice touches water.
This touching of water occurs at all sacrifices.

I take up Agni, the good chariot, who is the source of bliss, who ascends the rising sun for the sake of the day—the Āditya, the highest light among lights—may he delight tomorrow in the sacrifice for the sake of the deities. The Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the deities together with Indra: these I first encompass within my own abode through my wisdom. Those gods who have entered this fifteenfold nourishment, them I first encompass.

"May Agni, the bearer of oblations, bring them here: 'This is their full-moon oblation for me; this is their new-moon oblation for me,'" he mutters over the Āhavanīya fire as it is being kindled, according to the respective signs.
"The cattle have come to the assembly of the gods between the two fires; those I first enclose within my own abode with my mind," he mutters while standing between the two fires.

"May the people of every form rejoice here, dwelling together with Agni, the lord of the household. As the first, I encompass them within my own abode by means of my wisdom. May the cattle of every form rejoice here, dwelling together with Agni, the lord of the household. As the first, I encompass them within my own abode by means of my wisdom"—with these words, he addresses the Gārhapatya fire.
Thus ends the first section.

"This is the fire of the ancestors; may it carry the oblation to the ancestors. With the words, "I first enclose it, so that it may make our food free from poison," he [encloses] the *dakṣiṇāgni*. With the words, "May the guardians of the assembly kindle you, the eternal one, who share in victory; O Agni, shine for me in the assembly for a hundred autumns for the sake of conquest," [he addresses] the *sabhya* fire. With the words, "May I bring food for the household for a hundred autumns; may Ahirbudhnya bestow prosperity and sacred knowledge upon this dwelling," [he addresses] the *āvasathya* fire.

"I announce this sacrifice to the Vasus, of whom Agni is the eldest; I announce this sacrifice to the Rudras, of whom Indra is the eldest; I announce this sacrifice to the Ādityas, of whom Varuṇa is the eldest"—with these words he mutters when the fires have been placed on the altar.

Before the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is brought, the husband and wife eat food that is rich in milk, prior to the driving away of the calves on the new moon day. On the full moon day, those intending to fast for the *Paurṇamāsa* sacrifice do not eat until they are quite well-satisfied.
They two should eat without beans and without meat, with clarified butter; in its absence, with curds or milk.

On the full moon day, one undertakes the vow with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); on the new moon day, after the calves have been separated from the cows. "One undertakes the vow when the *praṇītā* waters are being brought forward, or when the oblations are placed near"—this applies commonly to both occasions.

Some say: first the eating, then the adding of fuel to the fires, and then the undertaking of the vow; others say: the undertaking of the vow, the eating, and the adding of fuel to the fires; still others say: the adding of fuel to the fires, the undertaking of the vow, and the eating.
(8) With the verse, "The plants are rich in milk," he sips water or touches it.
(9) He steps across to the south behind the Āhavanīya fire. (10)
"From this point onward, this indeed becomes the path for the sacrificer to traverse.
This is the second section.
Standing to the south of the Āhavanīya fire, one who is about to undertake the vow meditates upon the ocean with his mind. 1.

Then he mutters: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow"—thus the Brāhmaṇa; "O Vāyu, lord of vows; O Āditya, lord of vows; O lord of vows among vows, I shall perform the vow"—thus the Rājanya and the Vaiśya. Or the Brāhmaṇa may recite all [the formulas]. Then he worships the Āditya, saying: "Thou art the sovereign, thou art the guardian of vows, thou art the lord of vows; this I declare unto thee; may I be able to do it; through that may I be able; through that may I prosper."
If one should undertake the vow after the sun has set, he should mutter this *yajus* while standing near the *āhavanīya* fire:

"Both fires I spread with sacrificial grass; may the deities dwell near me. I fast from the domestic animals for the sake of my lordship over cattle. He mutters this at evening while the fires are being strewn around.
At evening, he eats forest food, excluding beans and meat.

Or rather, he may eat as much as he desires from the path up to honey or from the *prāśātika* fruit, or even water; or he may eat nothing at all. He should not eat in the evening that which he intends to offer in the morning sacrifice.
One who intends to dwell in the forest eats water, or he does not; while stretching his limbs, he should say, "May skill and wisdom abide in me. He keeps watch on the night of the new moon.
Or rather, he may sleep on top [of the fire], but he must not lie down [on his back]; 14.
Or he may lie down on top, but he must remain a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*); 15. Some authorities prescribe staying awake in both cases. 16.
He sleeps either in the *āhavanīya* shed or in the *gārhapatya* shed.

(17) Thus ends the third section (*kaṇḍikā*). Having murmured: "O gods, exert yourselves among the gods; as the first among the second, as the second among the third—three times eleven—protect me here! May I be able to do this which I am doing; may the Self do it for the Self. This I shall do as a remedy; this is my all-healing remedy. O Aśvins, protect me both of you!"—on the following day, he chooses the *brahmán*. (1)

Having said, "O lord of the earth, O lord of the world, O lord of the great being, we choose you as the Brahman," he sits down to the west of the Āhavanīya fire, having passed between it and the Dakṣiṇā fire;
the Brahman sits to the east and the sacrificer to the west.

Bhū, ka, vāk, car, go, vaṭ, kha, dhū, nū, and pū—these are the ten monosyllables, the Virāṭ meters, which have pervaded this entire world. May those goddesses, being in harmony through their power and wisdom, lead our sacrifice to well-being; you are purified by the Brahman. Who yokes you? Let him yoke you for all desires, for the sacrifice to the gods. Those that flow from the front, from above, and from all sides—

With those [verses] containing the purifier (*raśmipavitra*), he consecrates the *praṇītā* waters as they are being brought forward, saying: "With faith, I begin the sacrifice. When it is said, "O Sacrificer, I shall pour out the oblation," he gives his permission loudly, saying, "Om, pour it out!
(4) He consecrates with the mantra, "Agni, the Hotṛ, him I invoke here," the oblation as it is being poured out.
(5) Or he touches the vessel used for pouring out the oblation, or he consecrates it with the mantra. (6)
Having uttered that speech, he restrains his voice.
Then he yokes the sacrifice with the formula:
"Who yokes you? May He yoke you. He gazes across the entire sacrificial ground.

Thus ends the fourth section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the first chapter (paṭala). [One recites: "The four-tufted maiden, well-formed, with ghee as her face, in the midst of the world; being cleansed for great good fortune, milk desires for me, the sacrificer. [This is said] while the altar (vedi) is being swept. [One recites: "O gods, whoever hates me with the heart, with the mind, or with speech; whoever hates me with sacred knowledge (brahman) or with ritual action; whoever with learning and with a burning heart—Indra, with his thunderbolt, I cut off his head. [This is said] while the *stambayajus* grass-bundle is being carried away.

"I build this mansion for him among you, O gods, who practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*); he is wise, a practitioner of austerity, moving with his mind through the quarters as an inner messenger among human beings"—with these words, [he addresses] the heap of earth (*utkara*) as it is being taken up.
"With the measure of the sacrifice, with its extension, with its counterpart, and with its increase, I enclose thee"—with these words, [he addresses] the altar (*vedi*) as it is being enclosed.

When we, digging up the earth, the plants, and the waters, have caused injury—O Adhvaryus who wield the wooden sword (sphya)—may the wide atmosphere protect us from that [injury] with the wooden sword. When we, desiring the gods, have caused injury while digging and have fashioned the altar (vedi) of this [earth] with our minds as something cruel—may we not come upon the wrath of the earth because of that; may she be auspicious to us along with all the worlds. Having become the earth, she has nourished her greatness; thereafter, the god increases the waters.

"Those worthy of sacrifice distinguish the sacrifice; may the plants and the waters, the Śakvarīs, be auspicious here"—this [is said] while the [sacrificial ground] is being prepared. "I, of holy will, invoke the divine waters; day and night they have flowed, the active ones"—this [is said] while the sprinkling waters are being set down. "Soft as wool, spreading out, pleasant for the gods, beloved for their seat—place me, the sacrificer, in the world of heaven, on the back of the firmament, in the highest sky"—this [is said] while the sacrificial grass (barhis) is being spread. 5.

"By means of water, purify the clarified butter; by means of clarified butter, purify the waters thoroughly with the purifiers of Savitṛ. O divine Śakvarīs, being in harmony, protect this sacrifice with the Śakvara [chant]. Thus they recite over the clarified butter and the sprinkling waters while they are being purified.
Both recite over the two ladlings of clarified butter.
This is the fifth section.

We have refreshed the sacrificial grass within the earth, causing the severed plants to grow anew. May those whose roots you have struck with the wooden sword (sphyá) become auspicious and easy for us to invoke. May the plants be well-disposed toward the sacrificer, as well as the waters and the *śakvarī* verses here. May Parjanya, who makes the heavens rain, cause them to sprout—those golden-colored, hundred-branched, and inviolable ones. Thus [he addresses] the sacrificial grass placed within the altar.

The four-tufted young woman, well-adorned, clothed in ghee as her face, wears the sacred ordinances. Being spread out for great good fortune, do thou milk desires for me, the sacrificer. Be auspicious and helpful to me; be pleasant and easy to sit upon for me; be full of vigor and full of milk for me. Make swell for me food and vigor; make swell for me spiritual power and luster; make swell for me dominion and strength; make swell for me the subjects and prosperity; make swell for me long life and the eating of food; make swell for me offspring and cattle—thus [he says] while it is being spread.

With each of these mantras—"Thou art firm"—he places the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) as they are being laid down. [He says: "In this sacrifice, for the sake of great abundance and for my lack of agitation, I place the enclosing sticks. Agni, the supporter, the sustainer, the most steadfast, shall drive away the enemies from here. And: "I yoke thee with divine prayer," [he says] regarding the Āhavanīya fire. And: "Thy most brilliant heats, thy lights, thy glowing splendors—O Agni, with those [splendors], clothe thyself on all sides like armor; let not the Piśācas, the destroyers of the sacrifice, harm thee. And: 4. "I yoke thee with divine prayer... [and so forth]. And: "Thy most brilliant heats, thy lights, thy glowing splendors—O Agni

With the two separating-sticks (*vidhṛtī*), I cut asunder my rivals—those born, those who are my kinsmen, and those yet to be born. With the two separators, I scatter them away; may I be the highest among my own people, O Gods! As the two separators drive away the enemy, all evil, lack of thought, and the ill-fated one, sitting as goddesses in the world of the well-performed deed—you two are the separators, the sustainers, the self-sustained ones; uphold the vital breaths in me, uphold offspring in me, uphold cattle in me. Thus [he says] when the two separating-sticks are being placed down. This is the sixth section.

"This sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) is the supporter of both; it is the supporter of the fore-offerings (prayāja) as well as the after-offerings (anūyāja). It has supported the kindling-sticks (samidh) of all forms; upon it I place the offering-spoons (sruk). Thus [he says] as the prastara is being placed down.

Ascend the path, O Juhū, the way of the gods, where the first-born ṛṣis of old are. O you with golden wings, swift and well-formed in limb, carry me to where the worlds of the doers of good deeds are. You are the Juhū, dripping with ghee; you are the Gāyatrī, measured by the poets and cherished by them. Without wavering, attend to the sacrifice; lead the sacrifice with good guidance toward the gods through the divine protection of Agni—thus [he addresses] the Juhū. "With the Upabhṛt, I drive away my rivals, those born enemies and those yet to be born."

With two *dohā* verses: "Like a cow that yields well, may I be the sacrificer; may my rivals be beneath me. O *upabhṛt*, well-sustained, dripping with clarified butter, possessing all knowledge through the *triṣṭubh* metre—unwavering, attend to the sacrifice! With good guidance, lead the sacrifice to the gods through divine protection belonging to Indra. [He takes up] the *upabhṛt*. "O Agni, whoever, ill-disposed toward me in speech or mind, seeks to harm me or assails me from afar..."

"This mind of mine is the lower; may I be the higher than the *dhruvā*. May my rivals be lower than I. You are the *dhruvā*, the supporter, full of wealth; you who possess all knowledge through the *jagatī* metre. Without wavering, attend to the sacrifice; lead the sacrifice with good guidance toward the gods by means of the divine protection belonging to all the gods"—thus [he addresses] the *dhruvā*. "Be pleasant for me, sit on the earth as one easy to sit upon; spread yourself out with offspring and cattle in the world of heaven."

"Sit in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space! May I be superior; let my rivals be inferior. This *sruva* ladle offers the oblations; it has a hundred syllables, with the *anuṣṭubh* metre. It anoints all the forms of the sacrifice through the divine protection of Bṛhaspati"—thus [he addresses] the *sruva*. "This vessel is full of clarified butter, with its stream of milk unbroken, a fountain with a hundred streams. Through the divine protection of the Maruts"—thus [he addresses] the *ājyasthālī*. (2) Thus ends the seventh section (*kaṇḍikā*).

"You are satisfaction; you are the Gāyatrī metre; satisfy me with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge. You are satisfaction; you are the Triṣṭubh metre; satisfy me with vigor and heroism. You are satisfaction; you are the Jagatī metre; satisfy me with offspring and cattle"—[with these words he addresses] the sacrificial cakes as they are being anointed with clarified butter.

"You are the sacrifice, resting on all sides; may the past and the future rest upon me from all sides. May there be for me a hundred blessings; may there be for me a thousand pleasant and nourishing truths. You are Prajāpati, resting on all sides; may the past and the future rest upon me from all sides. May there be for me a hundred blessings; may there be for me a thousand pleasant and nourishing truths. With these words, he touches the cake for Agni that has been placed in position, or indeed all the oblations.

"This sense-organ is immortal; with this vigor, Indra healed the cattle. With that, O gods, protect me here! May I win nourishment, strength, glory, power, and force. May the cooked [milk] rest within me!"—thus for the morning milk-offering. "That which entered the earth, by which Prajāpati sprinkled strength into Indra—that is this bright honey, full of vigor, with which he subsequently curdled Mahendra. May the curd strengthen me!"—thus for the curd. 3.

"May this sacrifice, rich in oblations, be established with the Ṛg, the Sāman, the Yajus, and the deities. Through it, may we conquer the worlds possessed of the sun; may I attain immortality as a friend of Indra"—with these words he addresses all the oblations.

"May Indra and Agni drive away from this world him who desires what is less for me, the sacrificer, at this sacrifice; may I obtain offspring rich in heroes"—with this verse he addresses the oblation to Indra and Agni.
With the section beginning "O Agni, let there be splendor for me in the invocations," or with eight verses, he should touch all the oblations that have been placed.

One desiring offspring should touch the oblations placed on the altar at the full moon sacrifice with the *caturhotṛ* formula; one desiring heaven should do so at the new moon sacrifice with the *pañcahotṛ* formula. Some authorities prescribe these as being performed regularly.
Thus ends the eighth section (*kaṇḍikā*). This concludes the second chapter (*paṭala*).
One should recite the *daśahotṛ* formula before the *sāmidhenī* verses.
"May the Aṅgirases protect this sacrifice with the Prātaranuvākas," he mutters at the beginning of the *pṛṣṭha*-verses (*pṛtanāṣāḍ-dhenu*).

While they are being recited, having explained the *Daśahotṛ* formula, he [recites] "O Agni, may your strength rise up! for the fire as it is being kindled; and "May Agni, kindled, invoked, and consecrated with *svāhā*, fulfill us; may this homage go well to the gods," for the fire once kindled.
"Thou art the mind, belonging to Prajāpati," [he says] over the *sruva*-ladle as the *āghāra* libation is being poured.
Having taken hold of the *sruva* ladle, he follows it with the mantra: "Thou art the speech of Indra.

(5) When the *hotṛ-pravara* and the *adhvaryu-pravara* are being recited, [he says]: "O gods, O fathers; O fathers, O gods! Who I am, as such I sacrifice. Him whom I belong to, I do not neglect. My own is the sacrifice, my own the gift, my own the piling of the altar, my own the toil, my own the oblation. For me, Agni is the witness, Vāyu the listener, Āditya the announcer, Heaven the father, Earth the mother, and Prajāpati the kinsman. Who I am, as such I sacrifice. (6)
Having explained the *caturhotṛ* formulas, he performs the *prayāja* offerings with each respective mantra as they are offered: "I gratify the spring among the seasons," and so on. With the mantras:

"One for me, one for him who hates us and whom we hate; two for me, two for him; three for me, three for him; four for me, four for him; five for me, nothing for him who hates us and whom we hate"—he offers with each respective mantra. With the mantra: "Through the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Soma, may I become possessed of sight," he offers the two *ājyabhāga* portions.
Or rather, there are two separate consecrations (*vihṛtānumantraṇau*):

"The sacrifice is endowed with sight through Agni; may I become endowed with sight through the sacrifice to the god Agni. "The sacrifice is endowed with sight through Soma; may I become endowed with sight through the sacrifice to the god Soma"—these are for the two separate [consecrations].
One should recite the *pañcahotṛ* formula prior to the cutting of the sacrificial oblation.

With the formula, "Through the sacrifice to Agni, may I become an eater of food," he consecrates the oblation offered to Agni; with "Thou art a piercer," the Upāṃśuyāja; with "Of Agni and Soma," the offering to Agni and Soma; with "Of Indra and Agni," the offering to Indra and Agni; with "Of Indra," the Sāṃnāyya offering to Indra; with "Of Mahendra," the offering to Mahendra; and with "Of Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," the offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Some teachers prescribe other deities before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.

"By the sacrifice to the god Indra Vaimṛdha, may I become free from rivals and full of vigor. By the sacrifice to the god Indra Trātṛ, may I become protected. By the sacrifice to the gods Heaven and Earth, may I prosper in both worlds; may I attain abundance and a firm foundation," so say some.

"Through the sacrifice to the god Pūṣan, may I be procreated with offspring and cattle; through the sacrifice to the goddess Sarasvatī, may I nourish speech and the eating of food; through the sacrifice to the Viśve Devas, may I attain union with the vital breaths; through the sacrifice to Aryaman, may I go to the heavenly world; through the sacrifice to Aditi, may I be born forth with offspring and cattle; through the sacrifice to Indra, the possessor of power, may I become powerful and an eater of food"—thus are the modified formulas according to their respective characteristics (1). "May Agni protect me from ill-sacrificed offerings"—this is said when the *prāśitra* portion is being cut off (2).
"O you of beautiful form and excellent color, come to the *iḍā*!

3 Come for abundance, come for prosperity, come for wealth; come, O mind, come, O curd, come, O joy, come, O truth—come! At the silent invitation (*upāṃśūpahava*) of the *iḍā*, he recites the seven divine cows: "Thou art consciousness, thou art thought, thou art intelligence, thou art delight, thou art enjoyment, thou art offspring, thou art the noble one. At the loud invitation (*uccair-upahava*), [he recites] the seven human cows.

"O divine waters, turn back toward me with the gods; being gracious, sprinkle me with gracious ghee! This is homage! As the physician, the seer, the Brahman, I offer this—like water rising from the ocean with a ladle; speech stands at the tip of the sage, pointing with its ten horns.

(4) While the [victim] is being invited, looking at the Hotṛ, he should meditate on Vāyu in his mind, [reciting]: "Vāyo, come hither! and "The earth is your mother. (5) In the case of blessings, [he recites]: "May that blessing of mine be true," and "The blessing for me is strength. (6)

"Through the sacrifice to the gods for Iḍā, may I become possessed of cattle"—thus [he recites] when Iḍā has been invoked. "Iḍā, the cow, has come to us with her calf, milking out nourishment, swelling with milk; may she come to us with food, with oblation, and with cows; may Iḍā come to us"—this is for the portion being brought for consumption. (7) The consumption of Iḍā and the ritual sprinkling have been explained. (8)

"O Bradhna, swell; may that which I give not diminish; may that which I do not fail me. You are the ordainer of the quarters; may the quarters be ordained for me; may the quarters be ordained for me—the divine and the human. May day and night be ordained for me; may the half-months be ordained for me; may the months be ordained for me; may the seasons be ordained for me; may the year be ordained for me. You are the ordainer; may it be ordained for me. With these words, he touches the sacrificial cake placed upon the *barhis* grass. Thus ends the tenth section.

Then he disposes it toward the quarters: "To you, from the four immortal guardians of the quarters, we offer this oblation for the overseers of what has come to be. Let those who possess a portion receive their share; let not the portionless one partake. Let us exclude the portionless one. Make the waters swell, quicken the plants, protect the two-footed, protect the four-footed, and send down rain from heaven. This is the oblation for the Brāhmaṇas, the Soma-drinkers who drink the Soma. The non-Brāhmaṇa is excluded; here there is no place for the non-Brāhmaṇa. (ŚB 9.3.1.24)

"Invoked is Father Heaven; may Father Heaven invoke me; from the Āgnīdhra fire, for life, for luster, for living, for merit. "Invoked is Mother Earth; may Mother Earth invoke me; from the Āgnīdhra fire, for life, for luster, for living, for merit"—this is the specific formula for the portion of the Āgnīdhra. 2. With the words, "O radiant one, swell," he touches the Anvāhārya mess placed within the altar. And [he recites]: "This vessel is full of nectar; it is a fountain with a thousand streams, inexhaustible. It supports the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky. By means of this rice-mess, may I overcome death. 3.

The instruction for the *anvāhārya* rice and its offering has been stated. [While the *anūyāja* fuel-stick is being placed on the fire: "This is thy fuel-stick, O Agni, with the *samit* [verse]. [When it has been placed: "O Agni, him whom I cut off, or he who wanders about having been driven away—cut down his offspring and his root, O Gods! O Agni, whoever assails us, whether he be our equal or a stranger—let nothing of him remain, as if of a withered fuel-stick! O Jātavedas, him who hates me and him whom I hate, and him who hates me—burn them all together, O Agni, and those whom I hate and those who hate me! Thus [he speaks] when the fuel-stick has been placed upon the fire.

"The altar, the sacrificial grass, the cooked oblation, the fuel, the enclosing sticks, the offering-spoons, the clarified butter, the sacrifice, the *ṛc*-verses, the *yajus*-formulas, the *yājyā*-invocations, and the *vaṣaṭ*-calls—may my convergences bow down; the fuel and the binding [of the grass] have been offered. With this, he offers the *saṃmārga* (cleansing) oblations.
He should recite the *saptahotṛ* formula either before or after the *anūyāja* offerings.
Thus ends the eleventh section.

1. With each of these formulas—"May I, through the sacrifice to the gods by means of the *barhis*, become possessed of offspring"—he [the Adhvaryu] offers the *anūyāja* oblations one by one as they are being sacrificed. 2. Both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ] mutter two verses containing the word *vāja*.

3. With each of these formulas—"I have satisfied the Vasu gods with the sacrifice; I have satisfied the Rudra gods with the sacrifice; I have satisfied the Āditya gods with the sacrifice"—[the Adhvaryu] addresses the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) while they are being anointed with clarified butter. With the formula, "May the *barhis* be anointed with the oblation, with clarified butter; may it be united with the Ādityas, with the Vasus, with the Maruts; may it be anointed together with Indra and all the gods; may that which goes to the heavenly sky, Svāhā! he addresses the *prastara* (handful of grass) while it is being anointed.
"May I follow Agni’s victory with my own victory"—thus, according to the indicative marks, he recites the *sūktavāka* for the deities.
(4) And when the Hotṛ pronounces the sacrificer’s name, he should then say: "These blessings have come, desiring to yield milk.

(5) "May this true blessing of mine go to the gods—more acceptable than the acceptable, more praiseworthy than the praiseworthy; may it go to the gods with a mind free from resentment. May the sacrifice go to the gods; may that [fruit] come to me. In the blessings of the *sūktavāka*, he pronounces the name of whatever he desires. (6)

With the formulas, “May Agni cause you to go to the deity through Rohita,” the *prastara* is thrown by the *āgnīdhra* with each mantra (7). When the *prastara* grass is being thrown, [the sacrificer recites]: “A wedge of heaven, stretched down from the earth, has arisen; with that thousand-jointed one, we consume our enemy. May he who hates me suffer greatly; O herb, may I not suffer” (8).
When the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are being released, [he recites]: “I release you” (9).

At the *śaṃyuvāka* [he recites]: "O Viṣṇu, may there be well-being (*śaṃyoḥ*). "O Sacrifice, homage to you; O Sacrifice, homage, homage to you! May you be established for me with auspiciousness; may you be established for me with comfort; may you be established for me with prosperity; may you be established for me with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Be established in accordance with the success of the sacrifice! Homage to you, O Sacrifice; homage to you; homage to you! "The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus as a giver of wealth, by the Yatis as a giver of blessings, and by the Vasus as full of blessings. From that sacrifice of mine which has been offered and consumed, may wealth come here. Thus [he recites] over the poured-out remains (*saṃsrāva*) when they have been offered.
Thus ends the twelfth section; thus ends the third chapter.
"By the sacrifice to Soma, the god, may I beget vigorous seed"—with these words, according to their respective characteristics, he performs the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings after each has been offered.

"By the sacrifice to Rākā, the goddess, may I become possessed of offspring; by the sacrifice to Sinīvālī, the goddess, may I become possessed of cattle; by the sacrifice to Kuhū, the goddess, may I become possessed of nourishment and cattle"—these are the optional (kāmya) formulas.

"Through the sacrifice to the goddess Rākā, may I become possessed of offspring; through the sacrifice to the goddess Sinīvālī, may I become possessed of cattle; through the sacrifice to the goddess Kuhū, may I become possessed of nourishment and cattle"—thus the wife recites the consecration.

"May Iḍā clothe us with ghee, she whose footprint the seekers of the gods purify; the Vaiśvānarī, the Śakvarī, increasing, has approached the sacrifice, she who belongs to all the gods"—with these words he recites over the Ājya-iḍā. Having placed the Veda-grass-bundle within the altar, he touches it, saying: "Thou art the Veda."

"O Purāvide," with these words, he should utter the name of whatever he intends against his rival; "it is known that he thereby seizes all of it. (6) "When the oblation of husks has been offered and the mouth has been wiped, [he recites]: 'Sarasvatī who is the bringer of fortune, from her grant me; may we be among those who partake of her. (7) He follows the *samiṣṭayajus* offering with the mantra: 'The sacrifice is wealthy, the sacrifice is possessed of wealth; may the wealth of that wealthy sacrifice come to me; may that [wealth] come to me. He utters the name of whatever he desires. (8)
With the words, "May the lord of the sacrifice [attain] his blessing," he eats the sacrificer's portion.
Thus ends the thirteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, for the sacrificer: with the mantra "I have performed the service for Dadhikrāvan," he consumes the evening milk; with "This is the oblation," he consumes the morning milk. 1.
A non-Brāhmaṇa shall not eat the *sāṃnāyya*.

Within the altar, while the waters have been led forward, the Adhvaryu causes a continuous stream of water to flow. He mutters, "May you be abundant for me," as the water is being brought to the assembly hall.
Both recite the *kapālavimocana* formula.

With the words "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he strides four steps toward the east with his right foot at the southern edge of the altar, each step further to the north than the preceding one, without crossing over his left foot. He does not step beyond the Āhavanīya fire.
Standing, he mutters the fourth [section]:
"The Viṣṇu-strides, the Viṣṇu-transcendings, the Atimokṣas"—some recite these as interwoven, others as separate.
"With the god Agni I conquer the armies" refers to the Viṣṇu-transcendings; "O gods who destroy the sacrifice" refers to the Atimokṣas.
"We have gone to heaven; we have gone to heaven"—with these words he worships the Āditya.
Thus ends the fourteenth section.

Rising today, O thou of friendly luster, destroy my rivals. With lightning by day, strike them down; as thou settest, cast them beneath us. Rising today, grant us our share, as a father bestows upon his sons. Thou art the lord of long life; grant that to us, O Sūrya. Rising today, O thou of friendly luster, ascending the highest heaven, O Sūrya, destroy my heart-disease and my jaundice. We transfer my jaundice to the parrots and to the *ropaṇākā* birds; then we deposit my jaundice among the *hāridrava* birds.

"Up has risen this sun together with all-pervading power; may he subject my enemy to me, and may I not be subject to my enemies. May Dawn and Night sweep away all the evil of him who curses us though we do not curse, and of him who curses us though we do curse.
(1) "I turn following the turning of Indra," saying this, he turns to the right.
(2) If he should practice sorcery, he should crush the heel of his right foot, saying: "I bind the breath of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so. (3)
"May that fortune which is meritorious prevail; may that which is evil be defeated. Having said this, he turns back again, saying, "May I be united with my offspring;

may my offspring be united with me. "Kindled, O Agni, shine for me; kindling thee, O Agni, may I shine," with these words he kindles the Āhavanīya fire. "May the sacrifice be wealthy; may I become more wealthy," with these words he stands in worship.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.

"O gods, whatever rival or hostile mortal seeks to harm us—may nothing of him remain, as if of a log being consumed by fire. With these words, and with the two verses addressed to Agni and Pāvamāna beginning "Agni, you purify our lives," he worships the Gārhapatya fire. And with the verse "O Agni, lord of the house," he pronounces his son's name; for one who has not yet been born, he says, "I invoke this blessing for you, O offspring"; for one who is already born, he says, "for so-and-so."
