"For light, for the thread, thee!"—with these words he sits down within the altar (*antarvedi*). "May the divine thread not be severed; may the human thread not be severed; may I not be cut off from the divine abode, nor from the human"—with these words he utters the name of his beloved son.
"O Agni, O bearer, cook for us a well-prepared meal for our offspring; may it be auspicious for our children and our bodies, providing comfort. With this verse he addresses the *dakṣiṇāgni*.
"For light, for the thread, thee!"—with these words he sits down within the altar. The utterance of the name is as before.
Having sat down with the mantra, "Thou art light, O thread," he mutters [the following].
(7) Having placed the Veda on his lap and sitting within the altar, he mutters the *atīmokṣa* formulas.
(8) Some authorities prescribe that at this point the spreading of the Veda-grass and the consumption of the sacrificer's portion take place. (9)
"Who yokes you? May he release you," with these words he releases the sacrifice.
"O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow," with these words he releases the vow.
"The sacrifice has come into being," with these words he mutters the re-attainment of the sacrifice.
Having gone out toward the east, he mutters the *gomatī* verse, "Possessing cows.
(13) Or, at this point, he may consume the sacrificer’s portion.

(14) Having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, or having sacrificed with Soma or an animal sacrifice, he mutters: "O Sacrifice, may blessing be mine, and may prosperity be mine; may life be mine, and may strength be mine. O Sacrifice, may you conclude auspiciously for me; O Sacrifice, may you conclude well-offered for me; O Sacrifice, may you conclude uninjured for me. (15)
"Thou art rain; rain away my evil; from untruth I have come unto truth," with these words, having performed the sacrifice, he touches water. This touching of water occurs at all sacrifices.
(16) "I shall satisfy the Brāhmaṇas," thus he gives the call. (17) When departing on a journey, facing the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), he mutters the *yājamāna* formulas. (18)
He strides the Viṣṇu-strides toward the east (19).
Having gone out toward the east, he mutters the Gomatī verse; he mutters it (20).
Thus ends the sixteenth Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the fourth Paṭala.
Thus ends the fourth question.
We shall now explain the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*).

"O Aśvattha tree, which has grown from within the Śamī tree, dwelling together with thee—I draw thee forth with a sacred prayer (*brahman*) and with the signs of sacrifice. With these words, he brings the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*) from an Aśvattha tree that has grown from within a Śamī tree.
"Even of one whose womb is the *śamī* tree," so says the Vājasaneyaka.

"From the *aśvattha* tree, the bearer of oblations, I gather the sacrificial body born of Agni; the *śamī*-wombed one, whose source is peaceful, for the procreation of Agni. Bestow long life upon me! Having thus consecrated the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) while saying "O sacrificer," he brings seven terrestrial materials. Likewise, he brings seven from trees. Or five each; or more than seven from the terrestrial ones.

"One should not collect the ritual materials," says the Vājasaneyaka. "The form of Vaiśvānara has flowed around upon the earth; may they enter us with comfort"—with these words, [he places] the sand. "That which is here from heaven, that which is there from earth—when the two worlds were born, they came together. May the saline soil protect the black [earth], and may the black [earth] protect the saline soil; may both come most readily to the sacrifice"—with these words, [he places] the saline soil. "When you moved across the earth, making channels and assuming the form of a mole for concealment—that which was hidden of yours, we, gathering it here, may we live a hundred autumns with brave sons"—with these words, [he places] the mole-dust.

"Bringing hither the vigor and essence of the earth, may we live a hundred autumns, many-lived. May we be free from deafness, for our hearing has been discovered by the ants in their secret holes"—thus [he addresses] the ant-hill. "For the destruction of hunger among the creatures created by Prajāpati, may there be well-being for us. I bring hither food and strength for the creatures, broth for the houses, and essence"—thus [he addresses] the broth-pot. "He who, assuming its form, found her who had entered the secret cave in the midst of the flood"—[with these words he addresses] the clay mold.
"Bringing this which was dug up by him, may we perform for him in this [earth] without failure"—thus [he places] the earth dug up by a boar.
This is the first section.

"With those [powers] by which he made firm the wide foundation of the world, the supporter of all people—may all those pebbles be auspicious for us"—thus [he places] the pebbles. "The gold is the bright seed of Agni, born from the waters, immortal among offspring. Collecting it and placing it to the north, may I cross over misfortune with ease"—thus [he places] the gold. This is the first section.

Thus [are] the earthen [bricks]. 2. If there are five [pieces] of Udumbara wood, an iron chip becomes the fifth. 3. Having assumed the form of a horse, when you stood upon the Aśvattha tree for a year, hiding from the gods—now we gather that which was hidden from you here; may we live a hundred autumns with brave sons. [With this verse] he [addresses] the Aśvattha. "You have arisen from the strength of the earth, O Lord of the Forest; grow forth with a hundred branches! Rejoicing in food and strength through you, may we rejoice in the increase of wealth along with nourishment. [With this verse] he [addresses] the Udumbara. "That leaf of yours which fell while being carried away by the Gāyatrī from the third heaven..."

"This is the *parṇa* (palāśa) leaf; for it was born from the leaf of Soma, therefore I take it for the attainment of the drinking of Soma. That which you heard while the gods were uttering the discourse of Brahman—you are indeed renowned as 'Suśravas' (the well-hearing). May that splendor of Brahman enter me! While collecting it, may I directly attain it"—with these two [formulas], he takes the *parṇa*. "That *śamī* wood with which Prajāpati extinguished the heat of the fire when it was created—this *śamī* I take for the sake of non-burning and for peace"—with this [formula], he takes the *śamī*.

"O Jātavedas, when you were being created, from which [part] the *vikaṅkata* tree attained its luster—with that luster, well-measured, shine forth for us a wide world"—thus [he addresses] the *vikaṅkata*. "O Jātavedas, when the Maruts, having moistened it with water, cut out your heart while you were exhausted"—[thus he addresses the *udumbara*].

"From that thunderbolt I gather this for thee; O Agni, be of one soul and of one heart with me"—this refers to a tree struck by lightning. "That which it beheld in the midst of the flood, the wide foundation of the world—that leaf, born from the abode of the lotus, the spreading of the earth, I bring hither"—this refers to a lotus leaf. These are the products of trees.
Thus ends the second section.

"O Jātavedas, you whom I have gathered together, just as the body is hidden within the elements—being thus gathered, sit down, auspicious for all creatures; as one who knows, lead us toward a wide world. Having thus gathered [the materials], he deposits them.
1. Now, regarding the lunar mansions (nakṣatras): 2.
A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires under the Kṛttikās; he becomes preeminent and endowed with spiritual luster (brahmavarcas). 3.
If one establishes the fires under Ārdrā, fire becomes a burner of his house.
If one establishes them under Rohiṇī, he rises to all heights.
Under Mṛgaśīrṣa, one who desires spiritual luster or who desires to perform a sacrifice [should establish them].

He who was previously auspicious but may become more wicked under the two Pūrva-phalgunīs; he who, under the two Uttarā-phalgunīs, should desire, "May my offspring be desirous of giving"; and he who [under the same] should desire, "May I be fortunate and an eater of food."
Some [perform] this very same [rite] in reverse.
10. Now another [method]: having performed the two preceding [rites], one becomes worse; having performed the two succeeding [rites], one becomes better. 11.
He who desires, "May it be given to me," [should perform it] with his hand. 12.
On the day of Citrā, a member of the royal caste who has rivals [should sacrifice].

On Viśākhā, one desiring offspring; on Anurādhā, one desiring prosperity; on Śravaṇa, one desiring nourishment; on the Uttaraproṣṭhapadas, one desiring firm standing. Some authorities prescribe all these rites as being obligatory.

Having stated, "One should establish the sacred fires on the full moon of Phalgunī," he says: "If one were to establish them on the full moon of Phalgunī, he would place him [the fire] upon the seat of the year; therefore, one should establish them two days or one day before [that full moon]. One should establish them on either the new moon or the full moon. Spring is for the Brāhmaṇa, summer for the Rājanya, or winter for the Vaiśya; the rainy season is for the Rathakāra.

This is the time for those of the three castes who perform this rite. (19) The cold season belongs to all castes. (20) One intending to sacrifice with the Soma should not observe the season nor the lunar mansion. (21)
Having moved away from his residence, one who is settled should establish the sacred fires; one who is a wanderer may do so without having moved away. Or he may travel for a single day.
Thus ends the third section.

"May the impurity being turned up destroy the sin of the sacrificer. May the four quarters be auspicious to us; may Mother Earth be propitious to us for the sake of offspring. Having thus thrown up the sacrificial ground (devayajana) which slopes toward the east, and having sprinkled it with water while reciting, "May the divine Waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drink; may they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity," he constructs a shelter over that site with its rafters facing north. In front of that, along the middle beam, is the location of the Gārhapatya fire.

Therefore, the site for the Brāhmaṇa’s Āhavanīya fire is eight steps to the east; for the Rājanya, eleven steps; for the Vaiśya, twelve steps. Or, it may be at twenty-four steps, or at an unlimited distance, or as far as one judges with the eye; "therefore it should not be established too far"—this is heard in the scripture as applying to all without distinction. To the south-east, in the third part of the space from the Gārhapatya, closer to the Gārhapatya, is the site for the Dakṣiṇāgni.
The chamber for the Āhavanīya fire is one place, and that for the Gārhapatya fire is another. 6.
In front of the Āhavanīya, in the assembly hall, is the Sabhya fire. 7. To the east of that, in the lodging, is the Āvasathya fire. 8.
He shaves his hair and beard, clips his nails, and bathes; the wife does the same, except for shaving her hair. 9 Wearing linen garments, the husband and wife should establish the sacred fires.
10 These two are given to the Adhvaryu priest at the time of the sacrificial fee. 11
In the afternoon, when the sun is behind the trees, having brought fire from the *aupāsana* hearth, he establishes the *brāhmaudanika* fire to the west of the site for the *gārhapatya* fire;
or he may establish the entire *aupāsana* fire there;
or it may be produced by friction.

If he should bring the entire *aupāsana* [fire], having taken two cakes—one made of barley and one made of rice—with two *audumbara* leaves, he should place them upon the hearth; the barley cake behind and the rice cake in front. Upon that [fire] he should place [the oblation].
Alternatively, even when bringing the entire *aupāsana*, he may place the two cakes upon the hearth.
This is the fourth section (*kaṇḍikā*). Thus ends the first chapter (*paṭala*).

On another night, he pours out four handfuls of rice for the *brahmaudana* on the hide of a red bull, with the neck toward the east and the hair upward, or on a mat; [he does so] at night. Having recited "In the impulse of the god... (VS 1.1), he pours out the first portion with the formula, "I pour out what is pleasing to Brahman, to Prāṇa"; the second with "to Apāna"; the third with "to Vyāna"; and the fourth with "pleasing to Brahman. Or he may pour out all of them silently.
He cooks it in four water-vessels;
he does not wash [the vessel] nor does he drain [the liquid].
Some say it is cooked in milk.
"It is known [from scripture] that he cooks it like rice grains with the husks removed.

(7) Having taken portions from the *brahmaudana* with a ladle, he either offers them into the fire or addresses them with the mantra: "To the penetrator, the seer, the pure one, the word of praise is offered—to the bull, the vigorous one; may there be for us freedom from fear from whatever causes fear. I sacrifice to the gods; come hither! (8) Having divided the *brahmaudana* into four parts and poured abundant clarified butter over them, he distributes them to the four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are descendants of seers (*ārṣeya*), moving them forward without breaking the continuity. (9)

The first morsels have been taken; the hands are unwashed. Then, having scraped the remainder of the *brahmaudana* (sacrificial rice) and poured the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*) into it, he places upon it three moist fuel-sticks from a variegated *aśvattha* tree—each a span long, with their leaves still attached, and covered in resinous exudations (*stibhiga-vatyaḥ*).
[This concludes] the fifth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

"O you [sticks], gathered from the variegated *aśvattha*, you are fashioned for the body. You are equal in measure to Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice; you are three, consisting of triplets, forming a pair for the sake of procreation. (1)

Then he establishes the fires with verses addressed to Agni containing the word "ghṛta": with *gāyatrī* verses for a Brāhmaṇa, with *triṣṭubh* verses for a Rājanya, and with *jagatī* verses for a Vaiśya.

"Honor Agni with fuel"—this is the [verse]. "O beloved Agni, let the ladles full of ghee, bearing oblations, approach you; graciously accept my fuel-sticks. "O Angiras, we strengthen you with fuel and ghee; blaze brightly, O youngest one"—this is for the Brāhmaṇa. "Being kindled, he is the first law (dharma), anointed with unguents, the possessor of all boons; flame-haired, clothed in ghee, the purifier, the excellent sacrificer—Agni [is present] for the sacrifice of the gods."

"Clarified butter is his face, clarified butter is his source; Agni, kindled with clarified butter, has clarified butter as his food. The rivers carry you, dripping with clarified butter; drinking the clarified butter, sacrifice to the gods with a perfect offering. "For the Kṣatriya: 'O Agni, giver of life... "Thee, O Agni, most youthful, being enkindled, the gods have made their messenger, the bearer of oblations. With wide strides, fed on clarified butter, invoked with offerings, they have established thee as a brilliant eye that impels the swift. "Thee, O Agni, from of old, invoked with clarified butter, those seeking favor have enkindled with excellent fuel."

"Growing strong, nourished by the plants, you spread across the wide expanses of the earth. With a face of ghee, they strive to kindle Agni, who sits at the yoke of the *ṛta*, like a friend. Kindling him, the unassailable one shining in the assemblies, may he raise up our bright-colored prayer. This is for the Vaiśya.
Thus ends the sixth section.
He gives three heifers at the fuel-sticks. 1.
The Brāhmaṇas eat the rice porridge (odana).
To those who have eaten, he gives a common gift.

On whichever lunar mansion (nakṣatra) he intends to establish the sacred fire (agnyādheya), on that same year, prior to it, he should place these fuel-sticks (samidh) either twelve days, two days, three days, or one day before.
The fires must indeed be established by one who is about to set them up.

Then he observes the vow: he does not eat meat, he does not approach a woman, and they do not carry his fire out from the house, nor do they bring it from elsewhere. He should live for a year according to the *brāhmaudana* rite.
If the *aupāsana* fire has been established, his fire-rites are performed in this [fire].
He should not set out on a journey,
nor should he follow [the fire] when it is moved.

If he should depart or follow after [the fire], having cooked the *brahmaudana* (sacrificial rice for the Brahmins), he should place the fuel-sticks on the fire according to this same procedure. 11. If the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) does not come to him within a year, having cooked the *brahmaudana* and placed the fuel-sticks, he should establish them as soon as it comes to him. 12. Regarding the rules for maintaining [the fires], he may act according to his own desire. 13.
One should observe the vow for twelve days, or for one day. 14.

One who is about to establish the sacred fires (agnyādheya) cooks the *brahmaudana* again. 15. He who is about to establish his fires observes this vow for that night: he does not eat meat, nor does he approach a woman. 16.

"O Agni, cause the subjects to dwell together with the quarters and with cattle; bestow upon him the kingdoms that were in the impulse of Savitṛ"—with this verse [RV 3.54.21], he binds a speckled goat to the north of the Gārhapatya hearth.
(Thus ends the seventh section.
Then the sacrificer enters the vow and restrains his speech, saying: "I enter from falsehood into truth; I enter from the human into the divine; I restrain my divine speech. (1)
They keep him awake during this night with the lute and the flute;
or indeed, he does not wake, nor does he restrain his speech.

He sits through this night kindling this fire with wooden chips, using the verse: "Kindling the fire with wooden chips, may I win both worlds; having prospered in both worlds, may I cross over death."

At that time, just before dawn, he heats the two kindling woods with the two verses: "O Jātavedas, pour here the seed of the world; that which shall be born from fervor... and "Generating from the Aśvattha tree Agni, the bearer of oblations, from the womb of the Śamī, the source of bliss... and "This is your seasonal womb. (5)

"The immortal Agni with bright luster drives away the demons; he is pure, purifying, and worthy of praise"—having thus consecrated the two fire-sticks (*araṇī*), [the Adhvaryu says]: "O great ones, mistresses of the people, in the seat of Order, come hither, you who support the treasures; pregnant with the kinsman Jātavedas, you two bring forth him who goes before the sacrifices. While the two fire-sticks are being brought forward, the sacrificer gazes at them. "Both the one to be milked for thee and the bearer of the milk—this wide earth is thy portion; I offer it to thee as thy share," [with these words] he hands [the fire-sticks] over to the sacrificer.

"Ascend, cling to me—my *śakvarī* verses—with my husband, O Agni, together with long life and splendor. Living long, may I behold each succeeding year, and perform the sacrifice at the new moon and the full moon. Having accepted [the bride], he says: "You two possess the power of the seasons; you have Agni as your seed. Conceive a fetus; I give it to you both. That is the truth: that you shall bear a hero and you shall bring forth a hero. Through me, you two shall procreate in the morning; having procreated through me, you shall cause [others] to procreate."
Having accepted [the gift], the sacrificer consecrates it with the formula: "With offspring, with cattle, with the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa), in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the eighth section; thus ends the second chapter.

Both [the priest and the sacrificer] mutter: "I first take Agni into myself" and "The Agni who is ours, O fathers. Having dug up the site for the Gārhapatya fire with the formula "Go away, depart," he sprinkles it with water using the verse "May the goddesses be for our aid."

In this same manner, [the procedure] for the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Āhavanīya, and the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires is performed. 2. Thus, from this point forward, the ritual acts are performed in their proper sequence. 3.

Having divided half of the sand into two parts, he pours one part into the Gārhapatya hearth and the other part into the Dakṣiṇāgni hearth. 4. Having divided the remaining half into three parts, he places them in the preceding [hearths].
In this very manner, he pours out all the earth-clods.

With the formula, "Thou art the ash of Agni," he pours out the sand; with "Consciousness," the saline soil (ūṣa). While pouring them out, he meditates in his mind: "Whatever black there was in the moon, may that be here."

"Go forth, O Agni, from the mother earth; enter the people from the great dwelling-place! Those seeking the gods who have established thee, the carrier of oblations and guardian of the world—[thus he says] over the mole-hill. "That immortal essence of the earth which came into being together with thee—that Agni gave to Agni; in that, let this one be established"—with these words, he pours a mound of ant-hills into the site of the Gārhapatya fire.
"With that which is of the atmosphere"—[this is for] the Dakṣiṇāgni. "With that which is of heaven"—[this is for] the fires in the east.

"From the ocean a honeyed wave has come, bestowing further sovereignty. May these wealthy ones and we together gather food, strength, sweetness, and delicacy. [He places] the earth dug up by a boar with the words, "In the beginning it was only this much. [He says], "When you, O Goddess, first expanding, were scattered apart by the gods, you spread out with your greatness; you made yourself firm with pebbles, and you conquered the three worlds and the four quarters. He places the pebbles while meditating on his enemy. Thus ends the ninth section.
"I spread the *ṛta* as a layer upon the earth; upon the *ṛta* I place the fire; upon the *satya* I place the fire"—with these words he arranges the materials in their respective places.

"Those bodies of yours which are dear..."—this is the verse. Having united the wooden vessels with the formula, "I unite your hearts; may your minds be united; may your breath be united," he pours in the sand with the verse, "From here Agni was first born."

"O Jātavedas, those auspicious bodies of yours which are in the intermediate space, in heaven, and on earth—with those, united with your retinue and in harmony, you whose source is gold, carry the oblation, O Agni. With these words, he places a piece of gold to the north among the ritual materials in the site of the Gārhapatya fire.

"He who is the moon-like Agni, with a moon-like chariot, green-skinned, Vaiśvānara, seated in the waters, the finder of light, the one who plunges through, the swift, surrounded by powers, the impetuous—may the gods establish him here, the highly glorious one. He consecrates the placed piece with this mantra. He gives silver to his enemy.
If he does not find someone to hate, he should cast [the fire] toward whatever direction that hateful person might be;
in this way, he performs the rite for all [directions].
Having removed the ashes from the *brāhmaudana* fire-pit, he churns the fire from within a *śamī* tree in that [pit].
While the rays are rising, he places the two kindling woods together with the *daśahotṛ* formula.

He stands by [the fire] with the mantra: "O Agni, be born together with Agni, together with wealth, together with prosperity, together with offspring, together with cattle, and together with Vedic splendor. He churns the fire on a horse.
The horse is white with unmoistened eyes, or red with knees like those of a female, or it may be any stallion whatsoever.

While the fire is being churned from the wood of the *śakti* tree belonging to Sāṃkṛti, he sings the *Sāman*; when smoke has arisen, [he recites] the verses of Gāthin Kauśika and [the verse] "Jātavedas is placed within the two kindling woods" (RV 6.16.43).
He consecrates the fire as it is being brought down with the formula, "Descend, O Jātavedas" (RV 10.88.12).
Thus ends the tenth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

In this rite, he causes the sacrificer to recite the *caturhotṛ* formulas. 1. "Agni was born first for the ancients; the purifying, bright, and cleansing one is worthy of praise"—with these words, he consecrates the [fire] once it has been produced. 2.
Once it is produced, the sacrificer gives a choice boon. 3.
A cow is a boon, another is a superior boon; a milch-cow is a boon, another is a superior boon; a draft-ox is a boon, another is a superior boon; a heifer is a boon, another is a superior boon.

The sacrificer breathes over the calf that has been born: "With the breath of Prajāpati I breathe over you; with the nourishment of Pūṣan, for my long life of a hundred autumns, for a hundred years of life, for vitality, for splendor, for living, and for merit."

"Mortals have generated the immortal, the tireless, the crossing one with firm jaws; may the ten unwedded sisters, moving together, embrace the male newborn. Having thus grasped the newborn with cupped hands, he kindles [the fire] with the formula: "Thou art the sovereign (*samrāj*), thou art the far-shining (*virāj*); may the two Sarasvatīs, the two springs, enkindle thee; thee, an eater of food, for the sake of offspring. Then, having lifted him up facing eastward while seated, at the end of all the formulas, while the *Rathantara* and the *Yajñāyajñīya* are being sung, he performs the first [offering] according to the *Ṛṣi-ādhāna*.
With the *vyāhṛtis*, or with the first two [of them], and with the first two *sarparājñī* verses, and with the first *gharmaśiras* verse.

With the formula, "O Lord of Vows of the Bhṛgus, the gods, I establish you with the vow," he should establish the fire for one of the Bhṛgu lineage. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows of the Aṅgirases, the gods, I establish you with the vow," [he should establish it] for one who is a Brāhmaṇa of the Aṅgiras lineage. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows of the Ādityas, the gods, I establish you with the vow," [he should establish it] for other Brāhmaṇa lineages. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows of King Varuṇa, I establish you with the vow," [he should establish it] for a king. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows, by the power of Indra, I establish you with the vow," [he should establish it] for a Rājanya.

"O Manu, O Grāmaṇī, O Vratapati, I establish thee with the vow"—thus for a Vaiśya. "O Ṛbhus, O Devas, O Vratapati, I establish thee with the vow"—thus for a Rathakāra. These are the *ādhānas* according to the respective *ṛṣis*. The *vyāhṛtis* are: *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*. The verses of the Sarparājñī are: *bhūmir bhūmnā*. "The Gharma is the head; may this Agni become dear to the cattle. Grant shelter to our children and descendants. Vāta is the breath; may this Agni become dear to the cattle. Cook well-pleasing food for our children and descendants."

The sun is the eye; thus he is Sūrya, and thus this Agni becomes beloved by the cattle. O bright one, with that which is your bright luster, your bright body, your bright and imperishable light—with that shine for me; with that I establish you, O Agni, by means of Agni and the sacred word (*brahman*). These are the *gharmaśiras* verses.

O Jātavedas, those auspicious forms of yours which are in the atmosphere and those which are on earth—with those, united with your host and in harmony, you who have a golden womb, carry forth the oblation, O Agni. I place you, the breath, in immortality; you, the eater of food, for the sake of eating food; you, the protector, for the sake of protection. With the vigor of heaven, the greatness of earth, the nourishment of the atmosphere, and the brilliance of cattle, I establish you as the possessor of all cattle.

"O Agni, lord of the house, dwelling in the depths, seated in the assembly, find a world from heaven, from earth, and from the intermediate space for the sacrificer. I set you down upon the head of the earth, in the world of sacrifice. "O Agni, whoever is an enemy to us, whether a stranger or one of our own kin, who seeks to harm us—here I suppress him with you," saying this, he places [the fire] among the ritual materials.

"May the Gārhapatya fire, burning away hostilities and making each dawn better than the last, O Agni, driving away our rivals, bestow upon us abundance of wealth, food, and strength"—with these words the sacrificer consecrates the fire as it is being established; and the Adhvaryu makes him recite the *gharmaśiras* verses.
Thus ends the twelfth section; thus ends the third chapter.
When the sun has half-risen, he establishes the Āhavanīya fire.
When [the sun] has risen, for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*),
he kindles a fuel-stick of *aśvattha* wood at the *gārhapatya* fire for the purpose of carrying forward the fire, and he prepares sand for the supporting-stand.

He raises it with these [verses]: "I raise thee for vigor, for strength; I raise thee for virility, for breath, for luster. Thou art the overcomer of rivals, the overcomer of Vṛtra. That greatness of thine among the gods which is heavenly, that soul of thine which has entered into the cattle, that nourishment of thine which has spread among men—with that, O Agni, come to us, being well-pleased. From heaven, from earth, from the intermediate space, from the wind, from the cattle, from the plants—from wherever, O Jātavedas, thou hast been born—therefrom, O Agni, come to us, being well-pleased.
With these four verses beginning "Upwards thee all the gods," he raises the fire as if holding it aloft.
He holds [the fire] as it is being raised and brought near.

Then, into the right ear of the horse, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "O powerful one, bring hither that dear body of Agni which is purifying among cattle; O powerful one, bring hither that dear body of Agni which is purifying in the waters; O powerful one, bring hither that dear body of Agni which is bright in the sun. He continues to hold the fire.

Then the Āgnīdhra, having brought a common fire or having churned one, sits with his knees raised and establishes the southern fire while the *yajñāyajñīya* is being sung, according to the *ṛṣi*-based establishment rite, with the second *vyāhṛti*, with the three *sarparājñī* verses, and with the second *gharmaśiras* verse: "O Agni Jātavedas, those auspicious bodies of yours which are in the atmosphere and those which are on earth—with those, having united, together with your host and in harmony, you who are gold-wombed, carry forth our oblation."

"I place you, the Vyāna breath, in immortality as an eater of food for the sake of eating food, as a protector for the sake of protection. With the vigor of heaven, with the greatness of earth, with the nourishment of the intermediate space, and with the splendor of cattle, I establish you, possessing all cattle. O Agni, drinker of food, source of bliss, most auspicious one, from heaven, from earth, and from the intermediate space, find a world for the sacrificer. I seat you upon the head of the earth, in the world worthy of sacrifice. O Agni, whoever, whether a kinsman or a non-kinsman, seeks to harm us—here I suppress him with you. Thus he places [the fire] among the ritual materials. Thus ends the thirteenth section (Kaṇḍikā).
From the house of a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who is as well-nourished as an Asura, one should fetch [the fire] and establish it for one desiring prosperity;

however, one should not eat from his house thereafter. For one desiring food, [it should be fetched] from a frying pan; for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), from the top of a tree that is burning.
While the Āhavanīya fire is being lifted up, they sing the Vāmadevya chant.

[The verse is: "Along the eastern direction," this one; "Stride forth, for you are great, O altar-seeker for the sake of men! Be watchful in the three worlds with offspring and wealth! May these riches attend me; may I dwell here together with these progeny! May the all-formed Iḍā stand here; shine in the midst of wealth, O Jātavedas! Thus they proceed eastward, preceded by the horse. To the south, the Brahman priest causes the chariot or the chariot-wheel to turn until the wheel has revolved three times.

Six times he carries the fire for the one who is to be hated: holding it at the height of the knees, he carries it a third of the way; at the height of the navel, a third; at the height of the mouth, a third. He does not lift it above the height of the ears. If he were to lift it up and then lower it, he should instead carry it along by his mouth and place it down.
One should not pass between the fire and the sun.
Having carried it while keeping it to the right, he brings it forward.
At the halfway point, the sacrificer gives a gift.
Having placed gold on the half-way point, he steps across with the formula, "Thou art the sky, the sun, the firm foundation, the stepping-stone.

(13) With the verse, "He has mounted the horse facing eastward," he causes the horse to step upon the materials from the south toward the north, so that the embers of the established fire may fall upon the footprint.
(14) Having turned the horse clockwise, he makes it step again with the verse, "When thou didst neigh. (15)

He holds the horse facing westward in front [of the fire]. (16) The horse is one that walks forward. (17) Regarding its absence, there is a Paiṅgāyani Brāhmaṇa which states: "A draft-animal that does not limp and walks forward performs these rites. (18)
Thus ends the fourteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
"He should place [the fire] on the footprint of a water-jar," so says the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa. "He should place [the fire] on the footprint of a goat," so says the Vājasaneyaka. 1.

Then the sacrificer mutters the *śivā* formulas: "O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Virāj and the Svarāj—may they enter me; may they quicken me! O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Samrāj and the Abhibhū—may they enter me; may they quicken me! O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Vibhū and the Paribhū—may they enter me; may they quicken me! O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Pramvī and the Prabhūti—may they enter me; may they quicken me! O Agni, with those bodies of yours which are auspicious, I establish you. (2)

"O Agni, with those forms of yours that are terrible, go to so-and-so"—with these words the sacrificer sends [the fire] against his enemy; by means of them, he brings about his defeat. (3) The *anu-vākyās* are recited in the forest.

(4) Having consecrated [the fire] with the mantra: "That which is here from heaven, and that which is there from earth—the two worlds, being in agreement, have come together. Upon their back let Jātavedas sit, the bringer of well-being, auspicious for offspring and pleasant to the body," he places the *āhavanīya* fire while standing facing west in front of it. (5)

While the *Bṛhat* is being sung, and while the *Śyaita*, the *Vāravantīya*, and the *Yajñāyajñīya* are being performed, [one should establish the fire] by means of the *Ṛṣis*, with all the *Vyāhṛtis*, with all the *Sarparājñīs*, and with the third *Gharmaśiras*: "O Jātavedas, those auspicious bodies of yours which are in the intermediate space and those which are on earth—with those, having united, together with your host and in harmony, you who are born from gold, carry the oblation, O Agni! I establish you, the out-breath, in the immortal, as an eater of food for the sake of eating, as a protector for the sake of protection."

With the vigor of heaven, with the greatness of earth, with the nourishment of the intermediate space, and with the brilliance of cattle, I place you, possessing all cattle. O Agni, sovereign, one-footed Aja, Āhavanīya fire, find a world from heaven, from earth, and from the intermediate space for the sacrificer. "I seat you upon the head of the earth, in the world worthy of sacrifice. "O Agni, whoever is hostile to us, whether a stranger or one of our own kin, who seeks to harm us—this person I now suppress by means of you," saying this, he places [the fire] among the ritual materials.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.

"He has attained, he has pervaded, he has pervaded all life. "I am yours; you are mine; this is mine; you are my source; I am your source. Being mine alone, O Agni, carry the oblations, O son, creating the world for your father, O Jātavedas"—with these words the sacrificer consecrates the fire as it is being established.
(1) In all fire-establishments, the sacrificer follows along with whichever [mantras] he uses for the establishment: the *vyāhṛtis*, the *sarparājñīs*, and the *gharmaśiras* verses.
(2) He does not touch the fire that has been established but not yet offered into. It must be appeased with clarified butter and with herbs. (3)

"O Agni, that dear body of yours which is purifying among cattle, which is on the earth, which is in the fire, which is in the *rathantara* [sāman], and which is in the *gāyatra* meter—with this, I sacrifice it for you; Svāhā! O Agni, that dear body of yours which is purifying in the waters, which is in the intermediate space, which is in the wind, which is in the *vāmadevya* [sāman], and which is in the *triṣṭubh* meter—with this, I sacrifice it for you; Svāhā! O Agni, that dear, pure body of yours which is in the sun, which is in the sky, which is in the sun-god (*āditya*), which is in the *bṛhat* [sāman], and which is in the *jagatī* meter—with this, I sacrifice it for you; Svāhā! With these mantras, he offers clarified butter and herbs at each verse. 4.
Some say that he should offer the fuel-sticks; at the establishment of the sacred fires, the Brahman priest sings Sāmans,
though for some these are prohibited.
"The *udgītha* becomes [constituted] by means of the *vyāhṛtis*," so says the Vājasaneyaka.
Thus ends the sixteenth section; thus ends the fourth chapter.
Then he establishes the *sabhyāvasathya* fires, having brought fire from a common source, or having churned it, or from the *āhavanīya*, according to the *ṛṣi*-based rite of establishment.

"O Agni, you purify our lives; O Agni, purify yourself as a skillful craftsman. "Agni, the seer, the purifying one, the domestic priest of the five peoples; we implore him for great wealth"—with these three verses, he places fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* wood on each fire-altar, or alternatively, he places all three on the Āhavanīya fire.

From the ocean a honeyed wave has arisen; together with the *upāṃśu* [cup], it has attained immortality. That which is the secret name of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is the tongue of the gods, the navel of immortality. Let us proclaim that name with clarified butter; let us sustain it at this sacrifice with our minds. May the Brahman priest hear the hymn being recited. The four-horned bull has bellowed this. Four are his horns, three are his feet, two are his heads, and seven are his hands.

With the verse, "Bound in three ways, the bull bellows; the great god has entered into mortals," he places three fire-sticks made of *śamī* wood, anointed with ghee, one by one onto each of the fires—or three onto the Āhavanīya alone. Likewise, he places sticks from various other trees. With the verse, "O Agni, kindled, shine before us," he places a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood. With the verse, "We worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni," he places a stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood. With the verse, "That wonderful [splendor] of the desirable Savitṛ," he places a stick of *śamī* wood.
Thereafter, he offers the Agnihotra oblation silently.
Alternatively, having filled the *sruk* with twelve portions (*dvādaśagṛhīta*), he offers it while meditating on Prajāpati in his mind; this serves as the substitute for the *agnihotra*.

With the words, "O Agni, those forms of yours that are terrible—with them may you go to so-and-so," the sacrificer sends [the oblation] against his enemy; by means of them, he causes him to perish. These are the verses recited in the forest (*araṇye’nuvākyā*).
Thus ends the seventeenth section.

Having filled the *sruk* ladle with twelve ladlings, he offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse containing seventy syllables: "Seven are thy fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues... When it has been offered, the sacrificer, having given a choice gift, mutters the *Śiva* formula: "The fires that are in heaven and those that are on earth, coming together and milking out food and vigor—may those fires, being worshipped and gratified, having become partakers of the oblations, bestow wealth upon us and return to their own abodes as they came, Svāhā! Thus he offers. 1.

Then the sacrificer worships with the *virāṭ* formulas: "O Atharvan, protect my food, the nourishment measured by breath; guarded by you, rejoicing in food and strength, may we delight in the abundance of wealth and in nourishment"—thus he addresses the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire. "O Narya, protect my offspring, the continuity of the world's root; I entrust to you that which was fashioned from the heart of my own self"—thus he addresses the *Gārhapatya* fire. "O Śaṃsya, protect my cattle, the wealth and treasure of every form."

"May I bestow upon you the prosperity and joy of houses," [he says] regarding the Āhavanīya fire. "O wide-extending one, protect my assembly hall, which increases sensory power and prosperity; may it be the shade for all people," [he says] regarding the Sabhya fire. "O Ahi Budhnya, protect my mantra along with fortune and glory; I entrust the mantra, fortune, and glory to Ahi Budhnya," [he says] regarding the Āvasathya fire. "The Virāj, created by Prajāpati, stepped forth fivefold as the fires;
rising upwards, she became the Rohiṇī, the womb and the foundation of Agni," [he says] regarding all of them. 2.
Thus ends the eighteenth section; this is the fifth chapter.

He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni. 1. The oblation has been set aside, placed near, and remains unbesprinkled. Then, having cleared a space for gambling in the middle of the assembly hall, having sprinkled it with water, having cast the dice, having placed gold upon the dice, and having swept together, spread out, and leveled [the ground], he offers the oblation for the Kṣatriya in the center of the gambling space with the verse: "He who sits down, firm in his vows... 2.

In the assembly hall, having placed gold in the midst of the assembly, he offers an oblation upon the gold with the mantra: "Now indeed Brahmaṇaspati utters the hymn worthy of praise, in which Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and the gods have made their dwellings. (3) "May Ahi Budhnya hear us, as well as Aja Ekapād, Pṛthivī, and the Ocean; may all the gods who increase the *ṛta*, being invoked, and the praised mantras recited by the seers, protect us. Having said this, while handing over a hundred dice to the sacrificer, he says: "Play for cows against rice-grains; do not cause injury; divide the limbs [of the victim]. (4)
They perform [the rites] according to the *saṃpraiṣa* (directions).
This is the nineteenth *kaṇḍikā*.
The sacrificer wins what has been performed. 1.
With that [milk], they prepare the food by which they perform the sacrifice, and having consecrated it, they offer it to the members of the assembly (sabhāsads).
They eat in the guest-house (āvasatha). The sacrificer worships the fires with the two *kḷpti-sāmanasī* verses: "May Heaven and Earth be well-ordered; may the fires be of one mind. 4.
He undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the sprinkling (prokṣa). At the time of the sacrificial fee for the offering to Agni, he gives the fee:
a goat, a full vessel, a pillow, and a thread made of all kinds of fibers, to the Āgnīdhra priest.
8. A horse for the *brahmán* or the *adhvaryú*.
9. An ox for the *adhvaryú* at the site of the *āhavanīya* fire.
10. A milch cow behind the *gārhapatya* fire for the *hotṛ*.
He gives a garment, a pair of cattle, and a new chariot; these are common to all [the priests].
Having stated, "He gives up to twelve," it is known from tradition that "one may give more at will for the attainment of the unlimited.
Beyond the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he says: "Six should be given, twelve should be given, twenty-four should be given."
Regarding those animals whose greater prosperity one desires, at the conclusion of the ritual, one should give a two-year-old female calf and a ram with testicles to those birds.
He gives an increasing sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 17.

If one who is not wealthy should establish the sacred fires, he may, if he so desires, give a single cow; it is known from tradition that this serves as a substitute for the [usual] cows. 18. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. 19.
Thus ends the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā).
One should offer the Pavamāna oblations immediately;
or on the twelfth day, or after two days, three days, four days, half a month, a month, a season, or a year.
One who does not intend to sacrifice with Soma should not offer [the oblation] before a year has passed. Some say he may offer it.
If he should offer it, he should offer three oblations of clarified butter to Agni Pavamāna, Agni Pāvaka, and Agni Śuci, or having offered to the deities associated with Soma, he may then offer it.
Whether they belong to the same ritual manual (*samānatantra*) or different manuals (*nānātantra*), they may be treated as having the same ritual manual by means of the *āgneya* offering.

If one should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," one should offer these oblations to him one by one. If one desires of someone, "May he be neither better nor worse," one should offer all of them together. If one should desire of someone, "May he become superior, better, and more prosperous," one should offer to Agni Pavamāna first, and then offer to Pāvaka and Śuci on the same sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
A gold coin weighing a hundred *mānas* is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

The two former oblations consist of thirty mānas each, and the latter consists of forty mānas. Having measured the gold with that [ladle] by which they are measured, he gives it away. The sacrifice is completed according to the established rule.
Thus ends the twenty-first section; this is the sixth chapter.
He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni, and a pap in clarified butter to Aditi.
There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.
At the time of the fourfold division, he hands over the sun to the Brahman priest. Four ṛṣis consume it;
to those who have consumed it, he gives an identical boon. Some prescribe the gift of a cow and a bull. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner.

He subsequently offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma, and a porridge cooked in clarified butter with three ladlings to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. (6) The sacrifice is completed as established.

(7) The Vājasaneyins prescribe an offering of porridge cooked in clarified butter for Aditi, with seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses and a cow as the sacrificial fee, in place of all the subsequent offerings. (8)
The sacrifice is concluded with the word *siddham*. 9.
One who is about to begin the Agnihotra, having mentally recited the *daśahotṛ* formula and offered the oblation along with the ladle into the Āhavanīya fire, then performs the evening Agnihotra. 10.
He should set it down with the *vyāhṛtis*. 11.
When the year has come to an end, he should set them down with these very same [verses].
For twelve days, while the fires are kept perpetually burning, the sacrificer, not being away on a journey, should himself offer the Agnihotra; he wears an unwashed garment.
Thus ends the twenty-second section.

The first [cow] that he milks for the Agnihotra, that he gives as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Now, according to some: having established the fires and washed his hands, and having offered the Agnihotra for a year, he then begins the New and Full Moon sacrifices; having sacrificed with those two for a year, he performs a Soma sacrifice or an animal sacrifice, and after that he performs other rites. 2.

Having worn unwashed garments for thirteen nights, the sacrificer himself should offer the *agnihotra* while not traveling abroad. Having performed a *soma* sacrifice or a *paśubandha* right here, he dismisses the sacred fires (*agnīn utsṛjati*). "It is just as if one were to release [cattle] after providing them with good pasture"—so says the *Śāṭyāyanibrāhmaṇa*.
(3) Having offered the two *Sārasvata* oblations with the verses, "Full behind" and "That which the gods placed," he performs the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice.
(4) It consists of a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Sarasvant. (5)
For one who desires, "May I be fortunate and an eater of food," [he should offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Bhagina; some recite this as if it were a permanent (obligatory) rite,
while others say it is a separate ritual procedure.

O blessed Agni, from you proceed all fortunes, like the branches of trees; through obedience come wealth, strength, and victory in the conquest of Vṛtra, as well as the rain of heaven and the flow of waters. You are Bhaga for us, for you grant treasures for our nourishment; with wondrous luster, you rule like one who traverses all. O Agni, like Mitra, you are the guardian of the great *ṛta* (cosmic order) and the dispenser of abundant wealth, O God—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses.
(9) Thus ends the twenty-third section.
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers the *jaya* oblations with the formulas beginning "Thought and thinking... (1).
"Cittāya svāhā! Cittyai svāhā!"—thus some recite.
"Prajāpati [gave] the *jayas*," with this they perform the thirteenth.

"O Agni, giver of strength, grant power and vigor to me as I step forth; for one who has been cursed, grant immunity from being cursed, for the sake of pre-eminence among this people"—with this they perform the fourteenth, for one who desires, "May I be distinguished among the people. He becomes distinguished, but a speckled mark appears upon his face.
A pair of bulls is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 5.
The sacrifice is completed as established. 6.

One who is about to begin the New and Full Moon sacrifices, having mentally recited the Caturhotṛ formula and offered it with its accompanying portion into the Āhavanīya fire, then begins the New and Full Moon sacrifices. 7.
One should set out the oblations with the *vyāhṛti*s; when the year has elapsed, one should set them out with these very same [formulas].

This applies to one who establishes the sacred fires on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). But on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), having completed the establishment of the fires together with the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice at the preceding festival, [the procedure continues].
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section.
On the following day, he performs the Full Moon sacrifice.
Immediately after the establishment of the fires, the observances of the one who has maintained the sacred fires begin:
he shall not speak untruth.

No Brāhmaṇa who has not eaten should dwell in his house. He should not keep out a guest who has arrived with the setting sun for the sake of lodging. He should not eat food cooked by a woman during her menstrual period.
One should not place wet wood [on the fire]. 7 One should not eat [food] from water that flows within a boat. 8 One should not dwell in a salt-flat created by oneself. 9
He should be meritorious;
having uttered the syllable *hiṃ*, he should approach his wife while restraining his speech,
or he may speak.
One should not eat in the evening until the evening oblation has been offered;
likewise in the morning.
In the house of one who has established the sacred fires, one must not eat in the evening until the evening oblation has been offered, and likewise in the morning; such is the vow for others as well.
At night, one should not give anything other than food;
some say one may give [other things].
But when giving food, one should not give it away [without first eating].

In this year, one should not eat meat without having sacrificed with an animal victim. [If he has been so instructed,] he should eat it after reciting this ritual formula: "I send the food to the fires with my mind; let them consume it together with my speech. Being heedful and vigilant, I move about; let him consume it with a propitious mind. Having spoken this formula, he should eat it. Thus ends the twenty-fifth section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the seventh chapter (paṭala).
We shall now explain the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*). Its ritual procedure is like that of the initial establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*).

He who, having established the fires, does not prosper within this year, should re-establish them—whether desiring offspring, desiring cattle, desiring prosperity; or when his wife has become barren, or when she bears only female children, or when she is neglected by her husband, or when he becomes impaired in some limb.

One who intends to extinguish the sacred fire should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, one on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara, one on ten potsherds to Varuṇa, one on eight potsherds to Agni Apsumat, and a pap to Mitra. 4.

O Agni, that dear body of yours which is the purifying one as it descends—enter the earth together with that, by means of the *Rathantara* Sāman and the Gāyatrī metre. O Agni, that purifying body of yours which is most beloved by the mind—enter the intermediate space together with that, by means of the *Vāmadevya* Sāman and the Triṣṭubh metre. From that, bestow strength upon us and increase our domestic prosperity. O Agni, that bright and dear body of yours which is established within the sun and the radiant light—[enter it].

Enter heaven with her by means of the *Bṛhat* Sāman and the *Jagatī* metre; then protect us with rain! O Agni, those milch-cows of yours, the portions that have been gathered together—by them milk for us here our desires: offspring, prosperity, and also wealth! Those provisions of yours, O Agni, which Indra and the boar brought hither—on those flames sit down here, namely the ash of Vaiśvānara.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

"O Agni, those materials of yours belonging to the trees which have been gathered together—go with them to the trees, to your own womb, each according to its proper place. Agni has gone to his world; he has settled in his own seat. I have approached the slaying of the sheep among the gods with my mind, saying 'So be it. With these words, before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he offers seven oblations. The sacrifice is completed as prescribed.
Having performed the Full Moon sacrifice, he releases the fires while they are still burning.
For a year, at the most, he remains one who has relinquished the sacred fires. 4.
Rohiṇī, Punarvasū, and Anurādhā are the lunar mansions [for this rite]. 5.
He should establish the fires during the rainy season or in autumn. 6.

The sacrificial materials (saṃbhāra) are both prepared and unprepared, as are the sacrificial formulas (yajus). Alternatively, he brings five terrestrial materials and likewise five forest-derived materials.
Having spread out old darbha grass in the sacrificial enclosures, he establishes the Gārhapatya fire with the Sarparājñī verses beginning with "Bhūmir bhūmnā."
At midday, he draws out the Āhavanīya fire while it is burning, using other *upolava* darbha grasses that are from the previous year and have been blown by the wind for a year.
With the verse, "When thou, being angry, didst scatter [the fire]," he draws out the Dakṣiṇāgni; with the verse, "That which was scattered by thy wrath," he draws out the others.
With the verse containing the word Bṛhaspati, "May the mind, which is light, enjoy [the offering]," he worships.
With the verse, "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues," he offers the Agnihotra.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section.
He offers an oblation to Agni on five potsherds, or on eight potsherds.
If it is on five potsherds, the two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *gāyatrī* meter; if it is on eight potsherds, they are in the *paṅkti* meter.
The entire offering belongs to Agni.
There are fifteen or seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.
He performs the sacrifice in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) starting from the *sāmidhenīs* up to the final *anūyāja*, but the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is performed loudly (*uccais*).
In the four *prayāja* offerings, he inserts the four case-inflections: "O Agni, O Agni," "in Agni, O Agni," "by Agni, O Agni," and "Agni, in Agni."
Having uttered the seventh case-ending, he performs the *vaṣaṭ*-call with the *prayāja* formula.
For one whom he desires to strike down, he should place the case-ending either after the *ye yajāmahe* formula or before the *vaṣaṭ*-call.

"Awaken Agni with a hymn" (*agnim stomena bodhaya*) is the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*) for the butter-portion (*ājyabhāga*) dedicated to Agni; "O Agni, you purify the lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pavase*) is that for the one dedicated to Soma. Or, one may use "Agni is the head" (*agnir mūrdhā*) for the one dedicated to Soma, [for a sacrificer] desiring offspring or cattle, or for one whose offspring have perished or whose cattle have perished.
The verses for the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings are characterized by the word *agni*.

Or rather, as with the two Ājyabhāga offerings, so it is with the Patnīsaṃyājas. The invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) consist of Akṣarapaṅkti meters: two for the offering to Agni and two for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, beginning with "O Agni, [bring] that horse today."
With the words, "Return with vigor, together with wealth," he offers oblations on both sides of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
16. Or rather, he offers with "Return with vigor" before the fore-sacrifices (prayāja), and with "together with wealth" after the after-sacrifices (anūyāja). 17. Or this [order] may be reversed. 18.
He gives both kinds of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
This is the twenty-eighth section.

[The fees] pertaining to the establishment of the sacred fires (āgnyādheya) and the re-establishment of the sacred fires (paunarādheya) are: a chariot repaired again, and a piece of gold weighing one hundred mānas.

Therefore, it is said that silver is gold. Furthermore, some say that a chariot [should be given] as a replacement for what was previously mentioned, a garment with its fringes resewn as a replacement for what was previously sewn, and a draught-ox for the attainment of desire. Even if the other items are not available, one should give at least a draught-ox; for the Paiṅgāyani Brāhmaṇa states: "In a draught-ox, indeed, these desires and even more besides reside."
He assigns the case-endings for two of the after-offerings (*anūyāja*), saying "O God, in Agni" and "The god in Agni"; [he does so] except for the last one.
He issues the call for the last one loudly.
The sacrifice is completed successfully (siddham iṣṭiḥ saṃtiṣṭhate). 8.

He subsequently offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Varuṇa in place of all the deities to whom subsequent offerings are normally made, or in place of those belonging to the two-deity class (dvidevatya). 9. The sacrifice is completed successfully. The re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) is concluded. 10.
He who establishes the third [sacrificial fire] should offer these oblations: "Leka, Saleka, Suleka.
If that which has been mounted upon the two kindling woods should be lost, or if both fires should go out while the sun sets or rises, for him the re-establishment of the fires is the expiation.
"Re-establishment [of the fires]"—so says Āśmarathya; "the establishment of the fires"—so says Ālekhana. Thus ends the twenty-ninth section (kaṇḍikā).
Thus ends the eighth chapter (paṭala). Thus ends the fifth book (praśna).

When the sun is over the trees or when the sun is visible, having taken up the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*) with the formula, "Thou art the bold one; grant me spiritual power," he addresses the Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "O good Gārhapatya. 2.

Then he awakens it with: "Awake, O Agni! Be watchful for him! May this man and the merit of his sacrifices and pious works unite in this higher common dwelling-place; may all the gods and the sacrificer sit down here!
(3) "Bring it forth!"—thus says the sacrificer in the evening; "Bring it forth!"—thus [he says] in the morning. (4) By that, he obtains a thousand wish-fulfilling cows. (5)

"By speech as the Hotṛ, by breath as the Udgātṛ, by the eye as the Adhvaryu, by the mind as the Brahman, and by the ear as the Āgnīdhra—with these five divine officiating priests (ṛtvij), I lift you up. With these words, he lifts the flaming Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya.

"O Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ! Being lifted up, lift me out from the evil that I have done unknowingly and that which I have done knowingly; from whatever sin has been committed by day, lift me up and release me from all that"—with these words the sacrificer consecrates the fire being lifted up in the evening. "From whatever sin has been committed by night, lift me up and release me from all that"—with these words he does so in the morning.

O Agnipati, O Agni, know me; O Agnipati, O Agni, be gracious to me. I offer the immortal oblation into the immortal [fire]—Agni upon the earth—for the winning of immortality. Through that, may I win infinite desire, which Prajāpati won first. To Agni in Agni, svāhā! (8) Thus ends the first section.

"O Agni, sovereign ruler, one-footed Aja, Āhavanīya fire! Find a world for the sacrificer from heaven, from earth, and from the intermediate space. I place you upon the head of the earth, in the world worthy of sacrifice. O Agni, whoever is our enemy, whether he be a kinsman or a stranger, him I trample down with you. Having walked around to the front, facing north or west, he establishes the fire in its evening place; facing east in the morning.
The sacrificer himself brings the fuel-wood with the verse, "Bringing [the wood] every day, O Agni, may we, your neighbors, not be harmed by a weary mind.
With these five verses, beginning with "Whatever [logs], O Agni," he places large pieces of fuel-wood upon the fires, one verse for each fire;
the longest piece is placed on the Āhavanīya fire.
Just as they have been established by him in due order, or starting from the Āhavanīya fire, so should the fire be installed so that the oblation does not pass between them;
one does not walk between the two fires.
If he has followed the former [fire], then he should perform the *saṃcāra* afterwards;
for he has already gone there.
Some say that the *saṃcāra* may be performed at will after the oblation has been offered.
He maintains the Āhavanīya fire at night. (11) For one who has attained prosperity, the [Āhavanīya] is maintained permanently. (12) The Gārhapatya fire is maintained permanently. (13)
Likewise, as for the Anvāhāryapacana fire: if it has been established by churning, [that is one case];
if it is brought from elsewhere, they bring it from the south day after day.
"They should bring it on the Upavasatha day, or they should bring it at the Navāvasāna," so says the Vājasaneyaka.
Thus ends the second section (kaṇḍikā).
They adorn the fires by sweeping around them:
the adornments are performed first at evening, and afterwards at morning.
Or this may be done in reverse order. Some say that the ornaments are for both [the sacrificer and his wife] at evening and likewise in the morning.

With the formulas, "O Agni Gṛhapati, be purified," he purifies the Gārhapatya fire; with "O Agni Vahni, be purified," the Dakṣiṇāgni; with "O Agni Samrāj, be purified," the Āhavanīya; with "O Agni Sabhya, be purified," the Sabhya; and with "O Agni Pariṣadya, be purified," the Āvasathya.
He strews around the fires, or the two fires, with Darbha grass or other grasses, having their tips pointing northward and eastward.
The *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood; the *agnihotra-havaṇī* is made of *vikaṅkata* wood, being either a cubit (*bāhu*) or a span (*aratni*) in length.
The *agnihotra-sthālī* (milk-pot) is shaped like a hand with fingers spread out, fashioned by an artisan, with its rim facing upward and turned on a lathe.

To the south of the sacrificial ground stands the *agnihotrī* cow; the sacrificer addresses her: "Thou art *Iḍā*, the bearer of vows; I shall perform the vow for both of us. Prosper, I shall perform the vow for both of us. O *Iḍā*, come! Rest in me! O *Svar*, come! O *Aditi*, come! O *Gauḥ*, come! O *Śraddhā*, come! I call thee by means of Truth."
Then, touching the place of the altar, he says: "Thou art this [earth]; Agni is thy calf; do thou milk for me heaven and immortality.
(9) Having let the calf loose to the south with the words, "Thou art Pūṣan," and having turned toward the east, he milks it—either facing north, or east, or north-east.
(10) A Śūdra must not milk it. (11)
Or he has arisen from what is non-existent, namely the Śūdra; or he might cause harm—
whatever he places upon the Gārhapatya fire, that very thing he purifies.
He milks [the cows] using the *agnihotra* vessel and the milking-pail.
This is the third section (*kaṇḍikā*).

One should milk the two front [cows] for the eldest son of the eldest wife, or for one who has completed his Vedic studies; one should milk the two rear [cows] for the youngest son of the youngest wife, or for one who is younger than his brothers, or for one who desires prosperity.
He does not stroke the udders;
he milks according to the ritual manual as it is perceived.
As before, the sacrificer consecrates the cow when she has been approached, while she is being milked, and the sound of the stream [of milk].
He milks when the sun has set;
the oblation is to be offered before the sun has set.
"This day-and-night is indeed the ocean; its two shallow fords are the two junctions (saṃdhi). Therefore, the oblation should be offered at the junction," so says the Śailāli-Brāhmaṇa.
Having seen the stars at evening, at night, or at twilight—whether before sunrise, at the rising of the sun, when the sun has just risen, or after it has fully risen—in the morning:

if he offers at sunrise, he thereby obtains the Agniṣṭoma; if he offers at midday, he thereby obtains the Ukthya; if he offers in the afternoon, he thereby obtains the Ṣoḍaśin. If he offers in the first watch of the night, he thereby attains the first round of the night; if he offers at midnight, he thereby attains the middle round of the night; if he offers in the last watch of the night, he thereby attains the final round of the night.

It is known from tradition that he should not think, "In all these times one must offer," but rather understand that even in times of distress, one should simply perform the obligatory offering (*nitya-homa*).
(Sūtra 11) That which is the time for the principal offering (*homa*) is also the time for its auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).
(Sūtra 12) Thus ends the fourth section (*kaṇḍikā*); thus ends the first chapter (*paṭala*).
His Agnihotra becomes possessed of a wife. 1. The wife sits down in her own place. 2.

Having approached from behind the Āhavanīya fire and sat down to the south, the sacrificer sips water, saying: "Thou art lightning; strike away my evil; from untruth I go unto truth; may faith abide in me. 3.

With the words, "I sprinkle thee with the Real through the Truth," he sprinkles [the fire] in the evening; with the words, "I sprinkle thee with the Truth through the Real," in the morning. First the Āhavanīya, then the Gārhapatya, then the Dakṣiṇāgni—or alternatively, the Gārhapatya, the Āhavanīya, and the Dakṣiṇāgni—just as they were established. Having stepped forth from the Gārhapatya with the words, "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I continue thee, the continuity of the sacrifice," he lets a continuous stream of water flow toward the Āhavanīya.

"Thou art bold; bestow the *brahman*," saying this, he takes the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*). Having pushed out the embers toward the north from the *gārhapatya* hearth with the formula, "Ye are the makers of beings; the danger from strangers has been warded off, the attacking armies have been warded off," and having separated them from the *gārhapatya*, he consecrates them with, "Ye are full of moisture," and then mutters: "From Agni I take Āditya; from day I take night," at evening. "From Āditya I take Agni; from night I take day," at morning. 6.

"O Jātavedas, enjoy this oblation, the footprint of Iḍā, rich in ghee, moving and unmoving. May there be delight here for these seven domestic animals, which are of all forms and diverse forms. For the increase of wealth, for good offspring, and for great heroism"—with these words he places the Agnihotra milk upon them.
(Thus ends the fifth section. The Agnihotra is indeed semen. One should not cook it too well, lest one ruin the semen; nor should it be uncooked, lest it remain merely within. 1.
It should be offered with the water still flowing; having made it flow, it should be sprinkled.

It should not be sprinkled for one who desires brilliance, for one who desires sacred luster (*brahmavarcasa*), for one who wishes to overcome evil, and also for all desires; and also for him who should desire, "May a hero be born to me."

Or [the milk] may be placed on the lap; with the words, "I gaze upon you with unimpaired sight," he gazes at it with a burning blade of grass. Having poured the rinsing water of the milking vessel into the *sruva* spoon, he sprinkles [the milk] with it, saying, "May I not lose your heat," or else with a drop of water.

"May I arise with offspring and cattle; may thy heat not reach me; may the world of heaven shine upon me in the three worlds. Having looked back again, [he says]: "The *rakṣas* is excluded, the enemies are excluded, failure is struck away, evil is struck away, the evil deed of the evil-doer is struck away. He who desires to perform an evil deed against us—may it recoil upon him. Having carried fire around it three times, while making a path with the formula: "Thou art the Gharma, the bestower of abundance of wealth;
establish vigor here," he carries it out toward the northeast, or toward the north, or toward the east. Some say that he does not make a path.

"Here, may he strengthen offspring and cattle"—having thus established [the fire] on the ground three times; "Ye are makers of the world; the danger from enemies has been warded off, the attacking armies have been warded off"—having thus pushed back the embers toward the Gārhapatya fire.
This is the sixth Kaṇḍikā.

Taking the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," and heating them over the Āhavanīya or Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "The demons are burnt up; the enemies are burnt up," he touches them together with the formula, "May the sacrificer and his wife be uninjured. Then, having consecrated the *agnihotra-havaṇī* with the formula, "Thou art golden-stalked, with immortal leaves, the stream of sacrifices," he says at evening, "Oṃ! I shall draw up the oblation for the gods; [protect] the sacrificer from evil. At morning, he says, "Oṃ! I am drawing it up."

"You are the oblation of the gods; may there be safety for me from death, may there be well-being for me, may there be freedom from fear for me"—having recited this in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), he gives permission with the loud call, "Lift up! In the event of the sacrificer being absent, he should give himself permission.
2. While the [soma] is being ladled out, both [the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer] must restrain their speech until the *homa*. 3. And the sacrificer stands without blinking. 4.
Having been lifted up, he sits down;
he draws up four times.
If one should desire, "May this one among my sons prosper," he should draw up a full vessel for him.

If he should desire, "May his offspring be prosperous according to seniority," he should draw the first cup full, and then each subsequent one less than the preceding. "According to juniority" is the opposite of this. "All [sons] shall be of equal vigor" means they are equal. In the obligatory rite, he draws them according to their availability.
Thus ends the seventh section.

"I draw you forth for Agni and for the Earth"—this is the first; "and for Vāyu and for the Atmosphere"—this is the second; "for Sūrya and for Heaven"—this is the third; "and for Candramas and for the Nakṣatras"—this is the fourth;
"and for the Waters and for the Plants"—this is the fifth, [belonging] to the Jamadagnis.
Or, alternatively, he may recite with each mantra: "The Earth is *iḍā*, the Atmosphere is *iḍā*, Heaven is *iḍā*, the Ritual is *iḍā*, the Earth is distinct *iḍā*."

Saying, "Give me cattle," he places [the fuel] either to the west of the Gārhapatya fire at the place of adding fuel, or closer to it; having warmed his hand over the Gārhapatya, he touches it: "In harmony with the gods who come in the evening, may the gods who come in the evening bring us safely across; may I be united with cattle, may I make my offspring firm"—thus in the evening. "In harmony with the gods who come in the morning, may the gods who come in the morning bring us safely across; may I be united with cattle, may I make my offspring firm"—thus in the morning. 4.
Having touched it with the *daśahotr* formula, while holding a palāśa fuel-stick of the length of a span above it, he carries it level with the flame of the *gārhapatya* fire.
With the words, "Go through the wide atmosphere," he steps forward. As he steps forward, he recites the *daśahotr*.
He draws [the breath] equally with the nostrils,
saying "Svāhā to Agni Vaiśvānara," and deposits it in the middle region;
saying "To Vāta," he lifts it up.

"Come hither! Restrain yourselves! Do not enter among those who have a share in the portion of the Seven Seers where the world of the righteous is; place this sacrifice and the sacrificer there. To the ancient [world]! To Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ! Grant me long life!"—with these words, he places [the vessel] upon the Darbha grass to the west of the Āhavanīya fire.
(11) Thus ends the eighth Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the second Paṭala.

When the fire is being drawn out, that which is offered therein becomes an offering to the Vasus. When it is established, it lies emitting smoke among the Rudras. When the flame first touches the fuel, it is among the Ādityas. When the entire fuel is completely ablaze, it is among the Viśvedevas. When the flame descends deeply and becomes as if a glowing pit of iron, it is an offering to Indra.

When there are embers, and from those embers the flame rises up, it is indeed an offering to Prajāpati. When the embers are covered over with grass (śara), and from that a dark-blue appearing flame rises, it is an offering to Brahman. 1.

When the embers have subsided and it shines as if flickering, that is the mouth of the gods; therefore, it is known that one should offer in such a way that one does not cover the mouth. 2. Saying, "You are lightning; strike away my evil; from the immortal I go to the true," he, about to sacrifice, touches water and places a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood—either one, two, or three. 3.

"O Agni, this is thy fuel"—with these words [he places the first]. "I place thee, a golden beam, a means of transition to the heavenly world"—this is the second. "Thee, silver-colored, with a green interior, having the light of fire, imperishable, a cow of plenty, leading to heaven—I place thee as a brick for the night, for the sake of the heavenly world; by that deity, mayest thou sit firm like Aṅgiras"—with these words he places the third at evening. "Thee, tawny, with a silver interior, having the light of the sun, imperishable, a cow of plenty, leading to heaven—I place thee as a brick for the day, for the sake of the heavenly world"—thus in the morning.
This is the ninth section.
Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, having exhaled and inhaled, having closed his eyes and looked, he should offer an oblation and meditate upon whatever desire he may have.
(1) Having offered, he gazes intently at the great [fire].

(2) He offers when it is blazing or when it is dark-colored, or when the flames have passed away and it seems to quiver; for one desiring a village, he offers when it is smoking; for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), when it is flaming; for one desiring splendor (*tejas*), upon the embers. (3)
He offers the fuel-stick over the root at a distance of two finger-breadths.
He offers in the evening stepping forward, and in the morning stepping back;
or in both cases, he may offer stepping forward.
While about to offer the oblation, he mutters "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ.
He offers the evening Agnihotra with "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! and the morning [Agnihotra] with "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!
Or, he may perform the combined offering: in the evening with "Agni is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā! and in the morning with "Sūrya is light, light is Agni, svāhā!"

With "For food, thee! he wipes off the evening smear from the front of the ladle; with "For strength, thee! the morning smear upwards. Having wiped the smear on the sacrificial grass with "For the plants, thee! Quicken the plants!", and having set down the ladle with "Grant me luster!", he gazes at the Gārhapatya fire with "O Agni, Lord of the House, do not burn me; I have placed immortality within myself; offspring is light; I gaze upon thee with unimpaired sight. Then, with "Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ," he offers the northern oblation on the fuel-stick in the eastern part, or silently.
Some say that one should not offer over a fuel-stick.
Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).
Having offered the subsequent oblation (uttarā-āhuti) which is larger, he leaves over more for consumption. 1.
If one should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," he should offer more of that person's portion first and offer less of the subsequent portion. 2.

Having offered the oblation and lifted up the *sruva* ladle, he thrice brandishes the ladle toward the north over the fire, saying: "O Rudra, be gracious; O son of Arbha, be gracious; O rogue, homage be unto you; O Lord of Creatures, protect him! (3)

As before, having wiped away the smearings, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), saying "Svadhā to the fathers; gladden the fathers," he wipes the smearings on the ground south of the altar, saying "Grant me offspring. Having set down the ladle (*sruk*) with the words "Thou art rain; cut off my evil; from the Untrue I have gone to the True," and having offered the oblation and touched water, the ladle remains within the altar. Then, taking a portion with his finger while saying "Thou art Pūṣan," he consumes the smearings silently, avoiding the sound of teeth.

Having sipped water in this manner, having again consumed [the remainder] and sipped water, having taken hold of the *barhis* grass, having turned toward the north and stepped aside, he says: "For the embryos thee! Make the embryos rejoice! This is an oblation for Agni; may it be generative for me, with ten heroes and a full troop, for my well-being. May it win for me the self, progeny, cattle, safety, the world, and rain. May Agni make my progeny abundant; bestow upon us food, milk, and seed.
