May he maintain for us the increase of wealth, nourishment, and vigor—*svāhā*! With these words, he sips water using a ladle whose handle points either northward or eastward. This is the eleventh section (*kaṇḍikā*).
He modifies the morning mantra to "The oblation for Sūrya.

Having twice licked the ladle and filled it with water, he pours it out toward the west with the words, "Quicken those who partake of the remnants. Having sipped water, he washes the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle with *darbha* grass in front of the *āhavanīya* fire.
It is known from tradition: "The gods do not eat what has been washed with meat."

Having filled the ladle with water, he pours it out toward each of the quarters, saying: "For the serpents thee! Quicken the serpents! Having poured out three ladlesful, saying: "Quicken the ants! Quicken the other folk of the serpents! Quicken the divine folk of the serpents!", and having filled the fourth ladleful, he says: "I offer the nectar upon the earth; svāhā! Having poured [the water] behind the Āhavanīya fire, he places the remainder in the joined palms of his wife, saying: "For the houses thee! Quicken the houses! (4) If the wife does not attend, he should pour it into her place, saying: "To the wives of the gods I offer the nectar; svāhā! (5)

Furthermore, having taken [the butter] with the *sruk* ladle and poured it out at the place of pouring while saying, "Thou art the pacification of the droplets," one should heat the *sruk* over the *āhavanīya* fire. Then either the hand should be placed [over the fire], or the hand should be heated and placed into the *sruk*. He directs it toward the north, saying, "For the Seven Sages, thee; gladden the Seven Sages.
Thus ends the twelfth *kaṇḍikā*; thus ends the third *paṭala*.
"O Agni Gṛhapati, seated in the assembly, enjoy [this]—svāhā! With these words, he offers one, two, three, or four oblations into the Gārhapatya fire using the *sruva* ladle.
Some recite this [formula]: "To Agni Gṛhapati, lord of wealth, lord of prosperity, to Kāma, to the eating of food—svāhā!
Others [recite it] with an accumulation [of verses].
"O Agni, invincible one, worthy of the assembly, enjoy [this]—svāhā! With these words, he offers one, two, three, or four oblations with the *sruva* ladle into the *anvāhāryapacana* fire.
He offers the second oblation with the mantra: "O Lord of food, give us food.
Or, without eating, he may offer it into the other two fires.

The oblation is offered in the Āhavanīya fire, not in the two others. It is known from scripture: "If, having offered in the Āhavanīya, one were to offer in the two others, it would be as if one were descending from the heavenly world. Indeed, all these fires are established for the purpose of offering. One offers four oblations in the Gārhapatya, four in the Anvāhāryapacana, and two in the Āhavanīya. Thus they total ten. "The Virāj consists of ten syllables; the sacrifice is commensurate with the Virāj"—so says the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa.
"Shine forth! Thou hast shone; thou hast shone"—this is prescribed for the kindling of the fire-altar (agnyupasamindhana).
Or, [he may do so] with each mantra individually: "Shine forth! Thou hast shone; thou hast shone; may I shine; shine thou!
He does this either with the fire as it was originally established or by stepping out from the Āhavanīya fire in the proper sequence.
Having poured water within the altar (antarvedi), [he recites] "iti trayodaśī kaṇḍikā" (thus ends the thirteenth section).
He sprinkles around the fires as before; [but] not a continuous stream (na dhārām).

"O Agni, having offered up thy own body, do thou satisfy Heaven and Earth; bestow strength upon us. Having smeared a blade of grass with the contents of the *agnihotra* vessel, he throws it into the fire;
for this indeed is the conclusion of the *agnihotra*.
He should not throw a blade of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into the fire; for it has been said, "This sacrifice, namely the *agnihotra*, is indeed incomplete [if concluded otherwise]."

Having washed the *agnihotra* ladle, he pours out [the remains] at the place where the water is brought forward, saying: "I offer what is imperishable for the sake of imperishability; Svāhā! Or he pours it out within the altar (*antarvedi*). Having sipped water with the formula, "Thou art rain; cut off my evil; from the Untrue I have gone to the True; faith in the waters," the sacrificer purifies himself within the altar, saying: "Ye are food-eaters; may I be an eater of food. Ye are glory; may I be glorious. Ye are faith; may I be faithful. (ŚB 2.3.1.1–6)

"Water indeed first came into being as phlegm (śleṣman), by which Varuṇa was sustained, by which Mitra, and by which the gods consecrated Indra for kingship—with that I consecrate myself for splendor. With these words, he pours water onto his head.
(7) For one desiring cattle, he should offer oblations with the milk of two [cows]:
he milks the first into the *agnihotra* pot, and the second with a milking vessel. (8–9)
Having first placed [the vessel] on the fire, he brings the latter [milk].
If Rudra should destroy one's cattle, one should offer the evening and morning oblations with the milk of two cows according to this same procedure.

If he should fail [to obtain it], he should offer clarified butter at evening and morning with the mantra: "O Jātavedas, together with the gods, partake of this oblation of ghee from heaven and earth; Svāhā! (10–12).
"O Agni, who art not to be appeased, whose body is difficult to soothe, accept [this] with Svāhā! Having offered ghee thus for twelve days, one should thereafter pay no further heed to it.

This is the fourteenth section (kaṇḍikā). One should offer milk for one desiring cattle; curds for one desiring sensory power; barley-gruel for one desiring a village; cooked rice for one desiring food; and rice grains for one desiring vigor. Some say [one should offer them] for one desiring strength. One should offer meat for one desiring fame; Soma-juice for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); and ghee for one desiring splendor (*tejas*).
He cooks the gruel for the consecration; 2. when it is cooked, he sprinkles it with water while reciting a Yajus formula; 3.
in the same manner, [he prepares] the meat; 4.
He does not sprinkle clarified butter [over the ghee], thinking, "May your heat not carry it away. He throws either two or one tip of a *darbha* blade [into the vessel].
He does not place curd over it, for that is already cooked; it is known that he does not sprinkle it, because it has already been mixed with the coagulant (*ātāñcana*).
In this same manner [he treats] the rice grains, the boiled rice, and the *soma*.
One for whom there is need for sprinkling [with water] should offer oblations with clarified butter, rice-gruel, boiled rice, or Soma.
(8) One desiring splendor should offer oblations with clarified butter for a year or for twelve days.
(9) One should not perform this sacrifice for a Kṣatriya. (10)

At the time of the fire-oblation, one should send food from one's house to a Brāhmaṇa; by that, indeed, his oblation becomes as if offered. 11. One should always cause [the sacrificer] to recite the *agnyupasthāna* (prayers to the fires). 12.
Or, one should offer the oblation for one who is a Soma-sacrificer and a speaker of truth. 13.

Day after day, the sacrificer himself should offer the Agnihotra, or on the new and full moon days (parvan). Or a student (brahmacārī) may offer it, for he has been purchased by means of sacred knowledge (brahman); or a milk-offerer (kṣīrahotṛ) may offer it, for he has been purchased by means of wealth—so says the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the fifteenth section; thus ends the fourth chapter.

We shall now explain the worship of the fires (*agnyupasthāna*). 1. When commanded, "Perform the worship," one should worship the *Āhavanīya* fire alone; [one may worship] another [fire] only by virtue of a specific scriptural injunction. 2.
Having approached the northern oblation, he should stand near it as if slightly sideways with the six verses beginning, "Approaching the sacrifice... (RV 10.176.1–6).

With the seventh verse, "O Agni and Soma, this [sacrifice] well... (RV 1.93.1), he should worship during the bright fortnight; with the seventh verse addressed to Indra and Agni, he should worship during the dark fortnight.
With the verse, "I have performed [the praise] of Dadhikrāvan," he offers on both occasions with the eighth [verse].

(6) With the four verses beginning, "O Agni, may my word be [effective] at the invocations," he offers before the Agniṣomīya sacrifice during the bright fortnight; likewise before the Aindrāgna sacrifice during the dark fortnight.
(7) With the six verses beginning, "O Agni, you purify the lives," he offers every year, or always. (8)
Or, one should offer the Pavamāna oblations every year in place of these [standard offerings].
The rite up to "O Agni, giver of life" (Āyurdā agne) is established; it continues until the verse addressed to Citrāvasu.
One worships with the Citrāvasu formula three times in the evening; three times in the morning with the Arvāgvasu formula: "O Arvāgvasu, may I reach your end in safety."

Having performed the worship with the verse, "Kindling thee for a hundred winters," he offers four fuel-sticks, one in each fire, with the formulas: "Thou art the fuel of Agni; protect me from imprecation. Thou art the fuel of Soma; be my protector against others. Thou art the fuel of Yama; protect me from death. Then, having performed the worship with the remainder of the section beginning, "Thou, O Agni, hast united with the splendor of the Sun," he wipes his mouth with the verse, "O Soma, in thy service, bearing our minds within our bodies, may we, possessing offspring, attain prosperity.
(12) Thus ends the sixteenth section.
He gazes at the houses with the verse, "I behold the offspring. (1)
"May I partake of your water, O Ambhas and Stambhas," with these words he stands worshipping the cow-pen (goṣṭha). 2.
"O wealthy ones, rejoice," with these words he mutters while standing between the two fires. 3.
"You are united, possessing all forms," with these words he touches the calf. 4.
"Thou art the collection, possessing all forms"—with these words [he addresses] the calf; or "Thou art the world, nourishing with a thousandfold prosperity"—with these words he addresses the calf.
With three *gāyatrī* verses beginning "Up to thee, O Agni, day by day," and with four *dvipadā* verses beginning "O Agni, thou art our nearest," he worships the *gārhapatya* fire.

"Be mindful of us; hear our call; deliver us from every malicious person"—this is the fourth [verse]. (8) "With strength I behold you; with strength may you behold me"—with these words he looks at his house or his cattle.

(9) "Great shall be the protection of the three, the celestial one of Mitra and Aryaman, the unassailable one of Varuṇa. For neither in the home nor on the perilous paths does a wicked enemy have power over them. For they, the sons of Aditi, grant eternal shelter; they bestow desirable boons upon the donor. With this triplet addressed to Prajāpati, he worships. (10)
If one should desire, "May he return safely," one should look upon him with these [verses]. "He returns safely indeed"—this is a ritual procedure not connected with a sacrifice.

"May the curse of the stingy mortal, his malice, not reach us. Protect us, O Brahmaṇaspati! May he who is wealthy, the remover of disease, the finder of goods, the increaser of prosperity—may he, the swift one, attend to us. May your unassailable chariot, with which you protect the worshippers, reach us from every side.
Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā).

Having performed the worship with the verses: "That excellent glory of Savitṛ," "The exhilarating Soma, the resonant one," "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people," "O Mitra, never indeed art thou a slayer," "Never indeed dost thou fail us," and "Around thee, O Agni, as a fortress we [stand]," [he should proceed].

"Thou art the crusher; may I crush him who hates us and whom we hate"—with this, he should tread upon the heel of the right foot if he should compete with one who is inferior. "Thou art the overcomer; may I overcome him who hates us and whom we hate"—with this, he should press down on the right side of the foot if [he competes] with an equal. "Thou art the subduer; may I subdue him who hates us and whom we hate"—with this, he should tread with the forepart of the foot if [he competes] with one who is superior.

"May Pūṣan, the guardian of cattle, protect me; may Pūṣan, the guardian of paths, protect me; may Pūṣan, the guardian of lords, protect me; may Pūṣan, the overlord, protect me. Having thus worshipped the worlds, [he continues]: "The eastern direction has Agni as its deity; may he reach Agni who seeks to harm me from this direction. The southern direction has Indra as its deity; may he reach Indra who seeks to harm me from this direction. The western direction has Soma as its deity; may he reach Soma who seeks to harm me from this direction."

"The northern direction—Mitra and Varuṇa are its deities; may Mitra and Varuṇa strike him who seeks to harm me from this direction. The upward direction—Bṛhaspati is its deity; may Bṛhaspati strike him who seeks to harm me from this direction. This direction—Aditi is its deity; may Aditi strike him who seeks to harm me from this direction. Having thus worshipped the directions according to their respective characteristics, [the eighteenth section ends].

Having kindled the fires, he worships with the verse: "May Dharma protect me from non-Dharma; may Non-Dharma protect me from Dharma. May life and further life, sight and wide-sight, the forward-moving and the downward-moving, the wide-striding one—O wide-strider, through your speech may we obtain a share of food. Having thus worshipped, he worships the Gārhapatya fire with the two *Āgnipāvamānī* verses, "O Agni, you purify lives," and with "O Agni, Lord of the House. He pronounces the name of his son, saying, "I invoke this blessing for [the child]," using the word *tantave* (for the offspring) if he is unborn, and "for so-and-so" if he is already born.

Whatever the Agnihotrin may desire, he should ask the fires for that; "it comes to him," so it is known. It has been stated: "Should the fires be worshipped or should they not be worshipped? [The answer is: He worships them at night, not in the morning.

"One should not descend to the fire in the morning, nor should one who has established the sacred fires think [of descending] in the morning"—so says the Vājasaneyaka. "With the words: 'Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! May I be rich in offspring through my offspring, rich in heroes through my heroes, rich in splendor through my splendor, and rich in nourishment through my nourishments,' one should thus pay homage"—so says the Vājasaneyaka. Or else, with the thought, "May I be able to support you; may my faith not depart," he should do so. Some say that one should pay homage with the Vātsapra hymn alone, both evening and morning.
With the *Go-sūkta* or the *Aśva-sūkta*.
Thus ends the nineteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*). This is the fifth chapter (*paṭala*). One should worship [the sun] in the morning with the *Prātar-avaneka* hymn.

While the oblation is being placed on the fire or being ladled out, one should mutter the four verses beginning with "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations," and then, having sprinkled [the water] three times on the ground with the formula: "O Lord of Waters, that which is your portion of the waters—this is it! Repelled are the enemies! Repelled are the enemies! Repelled are the enemies!"—one should say: "I have washed you for the sake of Time, for victory, for prosperity, for the sake of food, and for the sake of good deeds. Here I cause this evil-mindedness to float away; may I become the highest among my rivals and co-spouses."

Having washed his hands with the mantra, "May the water [be] friendly toward me," reciting: "O Dhātṛ, bestow prosperity upon me; make me the lord of prosperity; may Indra, the Maghavan, as the ruler of the people, lead me with glory"; and having recited: "The waters, risen at dawn, impelled by the gods, firm destroyers of curses—may they drive away curses from among us like dirt," he should sip water and say: "Today I shall utter speech endowed with sensory power; I am one of long breath, unbroken, and an undeceived guardian."

"May the divine light be unceasing; may the eyes be those of Suparṇa; may the ears be well-hearing, ears that hear the gods; may the hair be the sacrificial grass (barhis) and the top-knot be the strewing-wood (prastara); arrange [the parts] according to their places; may there be well-being for the heart; do not harm me!"—having thus touched the limbs according to their respective characteristics, [this concludes] the twentieth section.

"Thou art luster; bestow luster upon me! Thou art the maker of long life; [thou art] the consort of long life. *Svadhā*! Ye are my protectors; guard me, protect me! Ye are seated within myself; let no one strike us down, nor let us perish. To the ancient [time], to *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, grant me long life! Having thus worshipped all [the fires], he worships the Āhavanīya with the following section: "O Gharma, [grant] me, the eater of food, vigor in the belly; may I today among this people be an eater of food; may I not be a non-eater of food—he who hates us."

O Mātariśvan and Kavi, make me rich in cattle today among this people; may I be rich in cattle today among this people, while he who hates us remains without cattle. O Aṅgirases, make me glorious today among this people; may I be glorious today among this people, while he who hates us remains inglorious. O Agni, whoever curses us—be he near or far, whether he be one of our own kin or a stranger seeking to harm us—burn him up as he stands facing you, O Jātavedas, in union with Vaiśvānara and in harmony with him.

O Agni, with that which is your *arcis* (flame), strike back at him who hates us and whom we hate; O Agni, with that which is your *śociḥ* (glow), burn him back who hates us and whom we hate; O Agni, with that which is your *tapaḥ* (heat), scorch him back who hates us and whom we hate; O Agni, with that which is your *haras* (fierce heat), seize him back who hates us and whom we hate; O Agni, with that which is your *tejas* (splendor), pierce him back who hates us and whom we hate. Thus ends the twenty-first section (*kaṇḍikā*).

"O Agni, Lord of lights, homage to you! Bestow light upon me. O Arvāgvasu, may I attain your well-being at the further shore; O Arvāgvasu, may I attain your well-being at the further shore; O Arvāgvasu, may I attain your well-being at the further shore. You are the thread; do not cut me off from that. May there be well-being for [Name]! May there be well-being for [Name]! May there be well-being for [Name]!"—thus he pronounces the names of his sons, three times for each one.

May it be well with you! May those who follow me protect me—the six broad expanses, the impetuous force, the sky and the earth, the waters and the plants, and the light and truth. Just as you, O Vasus, worthy of worship, released the buffalo cow that was stuck in the foot-print, even so release us from this distress. O Agni, lengthen our life-span further. The Suparṇa birds, the Priyamedha seers, approached Indra with their prayers. Dispel the darkness, fill our vision, and release us like those bound in a snare.

"O Agni, you purify our lives; I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan"—these two [verses]; "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations"—these four; "O Agni and Soma, this [sacrifice] of mine..."—this one; "We choose that nourishment of the god Savitṛ, the best, the most sustaining, the swift; we meditate upon the fortune of Bhaga. For of this Savitṛ, there is nothing more self-glorious or dear; they do not diminish his sovereign rule. This is the twenty-second section.

O God Savitṛ, impel auspicious fortune for us today, rich in progeny; drive away evil dreams. O God Savitṛ, drive away all difficulties; impel that which is auspicious for me. Sinless before Aditi, under the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may we attain all desirable things. For he, Savitṛ, as Bhaga, impels treasures for the donor; we seek that wonderful portion from him. O Savitṛ, grant us what is desirable today, what is desirable tomorrow, and day by day grant us what is desirable—grant us auspicious fortune.

"O God, through this prayer, may we be partakers of the desirable and abundant dwelling; Dīkṣā, Tapas, Mātariśvan, and Bṛhaspati are the womb of this speech. May the Vedas and auspicious sciences abide within me; O Agni and Soma, bestow glory upon us! By that through which Agni shines, by which Soma shines, by which the Sun shines, by which Virāj shines—by that may I shine forth everywhere here, increasing alone. Having thus performed the worship, he removes the grass-blades from the fire. "He becomes radiant and endowed with spiritual luster," so it is known.
Thus ends the twenty-third section; thus ends the sixth chapter.
One who is about to depart gives the command: "Kindle the fires!
He then stands near them while they are burning.

"O Śaṃsya, protect our cattle; guard them for us until our return," he says regarding the Āhavanīya fire. "O Narya, protect our progeny; guard it for us until our return," he says regarding the Gārhapatya fire. "O Budhnya, protect our food; guard it for us until our return," he says regarding the Anvāhāryapacana fire. Standing between the two fires, he mutters: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two guard these houses of ours; may Pūṣan protect them, unharmed and undisturbed, until our return."
Having worshipped with the *virāj* formulas as before and having eaten, one who is about to go on a journey says, "Prepare the fires.

He worships the blazing fires: with the formula, "O manly one, protect my offspring; guard it for me until my return," he worships the *gārhapatya*; with "O deep-seated one, protect my food; guard it for me until my return," the *anvāhāryapacana*; and with "O praiseworthy one, protect my cattle; guard them for me until my return," the *āhavanīya*. And [he worships] with the verse, "My name was first, O Jātavedas... (RV 10.55.3).

Restraining his speech, he proceeds [to the fire] with the mantra: "May we, O Indra, not stray from the path, nor from the sacrifice, we who possess Soma; may no enemies stand within us. Lead us upward, O Agni, you who are offered with clarified butter; unite us with the increase of wealth and with progeny; make us many.
(8) He releases his speech at a distance from the fires. (9) Thus ends the twenty-fourth section.
At the time of departure, facing the monastery, he mutters the *agnyupasthāna* formula:

"Remaining right here, I support you, O fires, who are there, with my breath, speech, and mind. May life not abandon me while I am away; I worship you with the Vaiśvānara light. If he should depart without having performed this worship, he should perform it with this very same formula.
Having prepared fuel-sticks, he returns.

Just as sons run toward their father who has returned from a journey, even so do the fires run toward him. He goes bringing either wood-shavings or logs, just as one goes bringing [food] for his sons; such is the understanding of this. (4) He restrains his speech at a distance from the fires. (5) If a king, a father, or a teacher should come between him and the fires, he should not pay them attention until they have passed beyond the sight of the fire-hut. (6)

"Bringing [offerings] at all times with an unailing mind, O Agni, may we, as your neighbors, not come to harm. Homage be to you, the bounteous one; homage to you, who delight in the *upasada* sacrifice. O Agni, adorn your bodies; unite me with wealth"—with these words he approaches. (7) "Kindle the fires," [he says].
(8) He stands in attendance over them while they are blazing. (9)

"O Śaṃsi, you have protected our cattle; give them back to us," he says, breathing over the Āhavanīya fire: "O Agni, thousand-eyed, hundred-headed, a hundred are your out-breaths, a thousand your in-breaths. You rule over thousandfold wealth, over milk with a thousand streams. Grant that to us; may I partake of it; may we become the greatest sharers of it. Thus ends the twenty-fifth section.

"Protect our offspring for us, O manly one; give that back to us," he says, breathing over the *gārhapatya* fire. "O Agni, lord of the house, may I be a good lord of the house through you as lord of the house; may you be a good lord of the house through me as lord of the house. For a hundred winters, may we two, uniting our blessings and not parting our bodies," he says, [breathing over] the *gārhapatya*. "Protect our food for us; give that back to us," he says, breathing over the *anvāhāryapacana* fire. Standing between the two fires, he mutters [the formula] as in the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation) for one about to depart.
He modifies the mantra, changing "you have protected" (*ajūgupat*) to "you two have protected" (*ajūgupatam*) and "he has guarded" (*abhyarākṣīt*) to "you two have guarded" (*abhyarakṣatam*).

With the four verses beginning "My name and thine, O Jātavedas," he worships the Āhavanīya fire; with "O thou who protectest my progeny, give that back to me," he worships the Gārhapatya fire; with "O thou who hast increased my food, give that back to me," he worships the Anvāhāryapacana fire; and with "O thou who hast protected my cattle, give them back to me," he worships the Āhavanīya fire. Having worshipped them, he approaches them as before with the Virāṭ-krama formulas. He modifies the mantra to "thou hast protected" (*ajūgupas*). Here, the worship of the fuel-sticks and the quarters is performed just like the worship of the fires.

If he should travel abroad on the ninth day, he should perform the attendance with the verse, "The Friend, knowing, impels the people" (*mitro janānyātayati prajānan*), and then offer an oblation with the formula, "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]" (*mano jyotirjuṣatām*).
Some teachers prescribe these—kindling-sticks, the oblation, and the attendance—in this specific sequence.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section.

Regarding this, they say: "The fire should not be approached [with a request for safety], for who would awaken one who is sleeping in a state of bliss? One should simply say: "O Giver of Fearlessness, grant me fearlessness; may it be well with me; may there be fearlessness for me. The Vājasaneyins record these formulas concerning the approach when about to depart and the approach upon returning:
"Homage be to you, I shall depart; homage be to you, I have returned," so say the Bṛhad-ṛcas.

O houses, do not fear; do not tremble. Bearing strength, we come to you. Bearing strength, a wise and well-disposed one comes to your houses, rejoicing in his mind. To those houses where the traveler goes, where there is much goodwill—those houses we invoke; may they recognize us as we recognize them. Invoked are our friends, possessors of abundant wealth, who delight in sweet pleasures. May our houses always be free from harm to all their inhabitants. Invoked here are the cows, invoked are the goats and sheep;
and the sweet essence of food is invoked in our houses. Thus he approaches the houses.

"For your safety and for peace, I enter that which is auspicious, propitious, and health-bringing—health and well-being. Thus he enters. (4) "Bearing strength for you, well-disposed and wise, I have come to the house, rejoicing in my mind. Carrying nourishment and sprinkling clarified butter, in them I settle down with a well-disposed mind. Having entered, he mutters this while settling down.
(5) Thus ends the twenty-seventh section; thus ends the seventh chapter.
When about to depart with his household, he offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati. While it is still unoffered, they load the goods onto the vehicles.
They should not bring back anything that has been left behind.
If it should be something that cannot be carried by vehicle, they should first carry it forward or remove it away.
Where he intends to dwell for a series of nights—whether five, seven, nine, or ten—he should offer oblations when departing from there.
Or, having returned to the site of his previous nine-night stay and having dwelt there for one night, he should offer oblations when departing again.

The right horse is yoked, while the left remains unyoked; or else, the right horse of the one standing by the fire is yoked, while the thong of the left is merely passed over [the pole]; or when all have been yoked, having recited "O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate*) and offered the oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with the following verse, and having thoroughly washed the embers, he consigns the fires into the separate fire-drills (*araṇī*)—those fires which are maintained.
Holding the two fire-drills over the fire, he mutters: "This is thy seasonal womb."
Alternatively, the sacrificer himself deposits [the fire] within himself:

"O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice, come, ascend it; entering your own self, bestow upon us many human riches. Having become the sacrifice, sit upon the sacrifice as your own womb, O Jātavedas, being born from the earth; come, O dweller, to this abode. Having warmed his hand, he takes it to his mouth. "Descend, O Jātavedas, knowing the way; carry again our oblation to the gods. Bestow upon us long life, progeny, and wealth; shine upon us, unaging, in our home. With these words, he causes [the fire] to descend into the common (worldly) fire.

Or, having caused [the fire] to descend into the two kindling woods, he should churn it. 13. If the fire should become mounted upon the two kindling woods while being extinguished, he should mutter this mantra.
14. Thus ends the twenty-eighth section.

"This is the most auspicious conclusion that I have arrived; may Heaven and Earth be gracious to me. May the quarters be free from disease for me—rich in cattle, rich in wealth, rich in horses, rich in men, rich in gold, and rich in heroic sons, svāhā! With these words, he offers the oblation when the recitation has concluded. (1) One who has established the sacred fires must not eat of the new grain until he has performed the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.
(2) He should sacrifice of the first-fruits of rice, barley, and *śyāmāka* millet. (3)
On either the new moon day or the full moon day, 4.
the ritual procedure (tantra) is that of the new moon sacrifice; 5. there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. 6.
At the time of the offering, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni made of old rice;
"as one yokes an unbroken horse with a broken one, so is that," it is known.
It is known that in whatever sacrifice one desires to prosper, one should perform it, and therein [one should offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni.

For the nine [oblations], there are the other offerings: a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni, or one for Agni and Indra; a pap cooked in milk for the Viśvedevas; a pap of *śyāmāka* grain for Soma; and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.
Some authorities prescribe the offering to Heaven and Earth before that to Soma.

When the oblation has been poured out and set down, but before it has been sprinkled with water, he then offers five *ājyānī* oblations with the mantra: "To him who has a hundred weapons, who has a hundred powers... (RV 6.75.18).
Either before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering (13), or after it, the ritual procedure beginning with the sprinkling (*prokṣa*) is undertaken (14).
There is either one mortar and pestle, or a separate pair for each seed (15).
In all [offerings], the mantra for the threshing of the *haviṣkṛt* [is recited] (16);
the scattering of the husks (17); having thrown in the last [grain], he releases his speech (18).
This is the ritual procedure for other various seeds that have been combined. 19.
At the time of decoration, he fills the single-pan cake (ekakapāla) with clarified butter. 20.
Or, having made its back exposed, he sets it down. 21.

At the time of the performance, having taken up the portion placed on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*), having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, having placed [the oblation] therein, having brought it along the place of rest, and having poured clarified butter over it, he performs the offering in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
This is the twenty-ninth section.
He should offer it entirely, without turning it back, straight and firmly established; he should not offer it with his hand.
If the oblation, once offered, should turn back, one should adjust it with the tip of the ladle,
not with the hand;
it must be adjusted only when the boon has been granted.
Having placed [the cake] and having sprinkled it with clarified butter, some say it should be offered again.
Alternatively, one should not offer a cake on a single potsherd; rather, one should sacrifice to Heaven and Earth with clarified butter.
He gives the first-born of those calves that are born before the Ekāṣṭakā festival; [he gives] a garment at the Śyāmāka sacrifice.
"O gods, you have led us from good to better"—with these words he eats the portion belonging to the sacrificer. (8) Or rather, there may be a substitution for all the mantra-accompanied portions.
"May Agni eat first; for he knows how the oblation is. May he, who dwells among all people, make the plants auspicious for us"—this is for the *śyāmāka* grains. (10)
The sacrifice is concluded successfully. 11.
Or rather, one should perform the Āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi on either the new moon day or the full moon day. 12.
Or rather, one should sacrifice with the new grains on either the new moon day or the full moon day. 13.
Alternatively, having caused an Agnihotrī cow to eat a bunch of rice or a bunch of barley, he should offer oblations in the evening and morning with her milk.
Alternatively, he should offer oblations in the evening and morning with a gruel of new grain.
Alternatively, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* on the *gārhapatya* fire using new grain, he should offer it on the *āhavanīya* fire to the deities of the *Āgrayaṇa*, with Sviṣṭakṛt as the fourth.
Alternatively, having cooked four śarāvas of rice for the nine [deities], he should feed four Brāhmaṇas; 17.
in this same manner, he should sacrifice with barley; 18. in that case, the offerings to Agni and Śyāmāka do not take place. 19.

He gives the first-born of those calves that are born after the Ekāṣṭakā. He eats the sacrificer’s portion with the mantra: "This very barley, mixed with honey, they ploughed upon the banks of the Sarasvatī; Indra, the lord of a hundred powers, was the master of the plough, and the bounteous Maruts were the ploughmen. Or rather, there may be a substitution for all the mantric consumptions. The sacrifice is concluded. Thus ends the thirtieth section.
If one should perform the Śyāmāka sacrifice according to various ritual manuals, he gives the command: "Bring up the śyāmāka grains.
For that sacrifice, there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; the two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain the word "sad"; and the two *saṃyājyā* verses are *virāj*s.

"O Agni, you are far-extending, the beloved and excellent Hotṛ; through you they extend the sacrifice. [He recites] "O Soma, those [powers] of yours which bring bliss," and "Possessing the seat," as well as the two Virāj verses, "Enkindled, O Agni" and "These, O Agni.
4. The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is a garment, curd-mash, honey-mash, honey-offering (madhuparka), honey-spoon, or a brown or tawny [cow].
5. The sacrifice concludes with the established rite. 6.
Regarding green barley, potherbs, *śamī* seeds, fresh grains, and fresh fruits, one may eat them at will even if they have not been offered in sacrifice.
Some prescribe a sacrifice for bamboo-grains (*veṇuyava*).
When the bamboo-grains are ripe, he issues the command: "Let the bamboo-grains be winnowed."
This very [sacrifice] is its ritual framework; this is its deity:
[it belongs to] Agni, Mitra and Varuṇa, or Prajāpati.
There are two *dhāyyā* verses beginning with "sa pratnathā"; there are four [verses] for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, ten for the oblations, and two for the *sviṣṭakṛt*.

"Having sacrificed with rice, one should sacrifice again with rice, not with barley; likewise, having sacrificed with barley, one should sacrifice again with barley, not with rice. Or rather, one may sacrifice with rice at both [times]. For these [grains] are indeed the most easy to prepare," so says the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa*. (13) "In the rainy season one should sacrifice with *śyāmāka* grains, in autumn with rice, and in spring with barley, or according to the season with bamboo-grain (*veṇuyava*)," so it is known—so it is known.
(14) Thus ends the thirty-first section (*kaṇḍikā*). Thus ends the eighth chapter (*paṭala*).
Thus ends the sixth question:
One who performs the animal sacrifice (paśubandha) conquers all the worlds.

One intending to sacrifice with it, on either the new-moon day or the full-moon day, having mentally recited the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula, offers an oblation together with the ladle into the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "The sun is your eye."
He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu;
this serves as a substitute for the adding of fuel to the fires. The sacrifice is concluded in the established manner.
He maintains the Āhavanīya fire.
With the formula, "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely," he offers the oblation for the sacrificial post (yūpāhuti) into the Āhavanīya fire with the dipping-spoon (sruva);
or rather, with the offering-ladle (sruk) using four portions of ghee.
One should not offer oblations for one who has been initiated.
Having recited a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he should either stop or he may offer oblations.
Or, having churned fire in the vicinity of the sacrificial post, he should offer oblations in it.
(12) The Adhvaryu takes up the *sruva* ladle and the remainder of the clarified butter; the carpenter takes up his tool.
(13) They proceed to where the sacrificial post stands. (14)
The trees suitable for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) are the *palāśa*, *khadira*, *bilva*, and *rauhītaka*.

One who desires splendor or the performance of sacrifice [should choose] a *palāśa* post; one who desires heaven or virility, a *khadira*; one who desires food or Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*), a *bilva*; and one who desires offspring or sight, a *rauhītaka*.

[The post should be] grown on level ground, not produced from a branch, possessing many leaves and branches, with an unwithered top, not hollow, not twisted, not crooked, straight, upright, with its bark undivided at the top, and slightly inclined toward the east, north, or west.
"If one should desire that [the sacrificer] be without a firm foundation," it is said;
having passed over the sacrificial posts, he chooses another and consecrates it with a mantra.
This is the first section (kaṇḍikā).
"Going beyond others," [he says].

Then he touches it, saying: "I take pleasure in you, the one belonging to Viṣṇu, for the sacrifice to the gods. With the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), he anoints it all around the base, saying: "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey."
Having placed a blade of *darbha* grass with its tip pointing upwards between [the tree and himself], saying, "O herb, protect him," he strikes it with an axe, saying, "O axe, do not harm him.
(4) He brings back the first chip that falls away.
(5) He should cut it at the height of the ankle, or at the height of the knee, or so as not to reach the axle. (6)
"Lest you should scratch the sky with your top," [saying this] he causes it to fall eastward, or northward, or both eastward and northward.
(7) "O Tree, grow with a hundred shoots!"—with these words he offers an oblation on the stump.
(8) "May we grow with a thousand shoots!"—having touched himself [with the tree], he cuts off the finger-joints along the grain [of the wood], saying, "The axe which [has cut] thee. (9)
He trims the tip [of the sacrificial post] with the verse, "Uninterrupted is the wealth, rich in heroes.
(10) "Five aratnis long" refers to the optional [lengths].
(11) Some authorities prescribe [the lengths] from one aratni up to thirty-three aratnis without interruption. (12)
As tall as the sacrificer with his arms raised,
or as tall as one standing on a chariot with his arms raised.
A man’s height is its minimum measure; however, it should be larger than that. Some say it should indeed be made larger.
It should be three *arati*s or four *arati*s long, made of *pālāśa* wood for the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* sacrifice; for the *saumya-adhvara*, it should be different from this—so says the Vājasaneyaka.
Thus ends the second section.

1. The upper fire-stick (upara) is unplaned at its base; it has eight facets, which become progressively finer toward the tip, with the facet facing the *agniṣṭha* stone being clearly defined, neither too thick nor too thin.
2. From the wood-shavings, the *svaru* and the splinter for the churning-sticks (*adhimanthana-śakala*) are fashioned.
The *caṣāla* at the top [of the sacrificial post] should be one span (*pṛtha*) in measure, eight-sided, and curved in the middle.
(4) For one whom he desires, "May another world ascend for him," he should make the *caṣāla* out of another tree according to its own natural form.
(5) As far as the uppermost finger-joint extends, so far above the *caṣāla* the post should have an excess of two, three, or four finger-breadths. (6)
The altar for one who has performed the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice is the size of a chariot.
It is measured by the axle behind, by the pole transversely, by the front yoke in front, or as far as the outer holes;
or it is four cubits behind, six cubits long towards the east, and three cubits in front.

Having prepared that altar, excluding the bending of the grass as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and having performed everything up to the northern *parigraha* line, he constructs the *uttaravedi* on the altar, measuring ten steps in extent for a Soma sacrifice;
some say it should be narrower in the front. Having measured it with a yoke or by the sacrificer's own steps, he measures it out with a *śamyā*.
The *uttaravedi* for the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* sacrifice is the measure of a *śamyā*.

Having placed a *śamyā* in front with its tip pointing north, he scrapes the interior toward the north with the wooden sword (*sphya*), saying: "Thou art my path to wealth. Likewise on the south, [he scrapes] eastward, saying: "Thou art my path to refreshment. Behind [the altar], [he scrapes] northward, saying: "Protect me from distress. On the north, [he scrapes] eastward, saying: "Protect me from agitation.
Thus ends the third section (kaṇḍikā), thus ends the first chapter (paṭala).
From the northern shoulder of the altar, at a step toward the north, he prepares the *cātvāla*.

Having measured it silently with a yoke-pin (*śamyā*) like the *uttaravedi*, he takes up the spade (*abhri*) with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... and, having traced around it three times clockwise with the formulas, "The Rakṣas is enclosed; the enemies are enclosed," he digs it knee-deep or three spans deep, silently. He then carries away the earth for the *uttaravedi* with the word, "Vider. He scatters it upon the *uttaravedi* with the formula, "Thou art a lioness."

With this same [formula], he takes a second [shovelful] with "on the second," a third with "on the third"; the fourth he takes silently. Having spread it out with "Spread wide, O thigh; may the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for thee," and having pressed it down with a wooden pin (śamyā) saying "Thou art firm," he consecrates it with "Be prepared for the gods. Having sprinkled it with water with "Be purified for the gods," and having scattered sand over it with "Be beautified for the gods," he pours the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water to the north of the high altar (*uttaravedi*) with "Carry away the impurity, O waters. Having drawn out a single line toward the north with the wooden sword (*sphya*) while reciting "Vibhrāj, the great one, let him drink the Soma-like [draught],"...

"May he bestow honeyed life upon the lord of the sacrifice, unimpaired; he who, impelled by the wind, protects by himself, nourishes the subjects, and shines forth in many ways"—with these words he fashions the edges of the high altar (uttaravedi).
Some say he touches them.
Thus ends the fourth section (kaṇḍikā).

Then, having made a four-cornered *uttaranābhi* in the middle of this [altar], measuring a span, or the size of a cow’s hoof, or the size of a horse’s hoof, he consecrates both with the verse: “The two young maidens with four tufts, whose face is ghee, in the midst of the world; may the gods dwelling upon them rejoice here on the highest firmament. Then he sprinkles the *uttaravedi* according to the respective marks with these formulas: “May Indraghoṣa protect you from the east with the Vasus” (for the east); “Tvaṣṭṛ protect you from above with forms” (for the middle). 1–2.
He should pour out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water to the south of the *uttaravedi*, meditating in his mind on someone he hates while saying, "I afflict you with pain. 3.

As before, having drawn out the single *sphya* to the south, and having taken five portions of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, placing gold in it at every step, he sprinkles [the butter] across the *uttaravedi* or over its northern *nābhi*. 4.
He sprinkles the southern shoulder, the northern hip, the southern shoulder, the northern shoulder, and the middle, with the respective mantras beginning, "Thou art a lioness. 5.

Having lifted the *sruk* ladle with the formula, "To the beings thee," he encloses the *uttaravedi* altar with enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *pūtudru* wood: with the formula, "Thou art all-living," the middle one; with "Thou art firmly seated," the southern one; and with "Thou art immovably seated," the northern one.
He offers all oblations through the junction of the enclosing-sticks.
Thus ends the fifth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

With the formula, "Thou art the ash of Agni," he pours the ritual materials (*saṃbhāras*) onto the *uttaravedi*: bdellium, fragrant reed-grass, a white tuft of wool, and a hornless goat's horn from one that has not previously had its horn cut off. Some teachers prescribe that everything from the sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*) until the pouring of the materials should be performed while the fire is being held over the *uttaravedi*. Having performed the rites up to the sprinkling, he covers [the altar] with branches of the *udumbara* or *lakṣa* tree and dwells there if the animal sacrifice is not to be completed on the same day.

Having kindled the fuel-stick to be carried forward at the Āhavanīya fire and having supported it with sand, he issues the command: "Recite for the fire being carried forward," or simply, "Recite for the fire being carried forward.

Having lifted the fire, he offers the *udyata-homa* at the Āhavanīya with the verse: "Whatever sin we have committed against you, O Purifier, whether you were previously [near] or now become further away—strengthen your body with clarified butter; do not harm me, who have approached you from the front. Svāhā!
When the first [verse] has been recited three times, he carries [the fire] forward, supporting it with the supporting sands.

"O thou with the tuft of hair, sit first upon the womb!"—reciting this, he recognizes the Hotṛ. "O Agni, drive away the adversaries, push them aside; banish sickness and ward off the demons! From this great ocean of heaven, release for us here an abundance of waters. O Sacrifice, be established in a benevolent and most gracious mind; may riches enter thee in many ways. Granting long life to the sacrificer, then anoint the singer here with immortality. Having thus established [the fire] on the sacrificial materials with the words, "The sacrifice has been established," [the rite concludes]. This is the sixth section.

Having placed the supporting coals (*upayamanī*) to the north with the formula, "Thou art the soil of Agni," and having kindled the fire with the verse, "As among men we have established thee, as among men we kindle thee; O Agni Aṅgiras, sacrifice to the gods for the one who seeks the gods," he fills the ladle with twelve portions and offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the seventy-verse hymn beginning, "Seven are thy logs, O Agni, seven thy tongues.

He then offers four *atimukti* oblations with the formulas: "May Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, and Viṣṇu lead the sacrifice, knowing it; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it; announce the sacrifice to the gods; further extend the lord of the sacrifice, Svāhā! (ŚB 3.8.5.1–2).

This [fire] from which he carries forth [the fire] for the animal sacrifice is the Āhavanīya; that [fire] from which he carries it forth is the Gārhapatya. (3) If the time for the Agnihotra has arrived when the fire has been carried forth, he should offer the Agnihotra in this very [Āhavanīya] fire. (4) The same applies in other cases where the ritual procedure has been interrupted. (5)
He brings the sacrificial fuel and the grass-bundle.

The fuel consists of twenty-three pieces of wood; the *prastara* is made of *aśvavāla* grass; the two *vidhṛtis* are made of sugarcane; and the enclosing sticks (*paridhis*) are made of *kārṣmarya* wood.
Thus ends the seventh section; thus ends the second chapter.
Having strewn grass around the fires, he undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the washing of the hands (pāṇiprakṣālana). He arranges the vessels according to their purpose:

the wooden sword (sphya), the Agnihotra-ladle, the Vasā-homa-ladle, a second Juhū-ladle, the Pṛṣadājya-vessel, a second Upabhṛt-ladle, two vessels for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), the heart-spit (hṛdayaśūla), a knife (asi), a pot (kumbhī), a branch of the Plakṣa tree, a leaf-strainer (śākapavitra), two omentum-roasting spits made of Kārṣmarya wood—one with two prongs and one with one—and a staff for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest made of Udumbara wood, reaching either to the mouth or to the chin, as well as two ropes (raśanā).
Having made the two strainers, he issues the command: "O sacrificer, restrain your speech.

Restraining his speech, having touched the sacrificial vessels, prepared the *prokṣaṇī* waters, and addressed the Brahman priest, he sprinkles the vessels; at this point, he releases his speech. Taking up the wooden sword (*sphya*) and performing the second tracing of the altar, he issues the commands as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice. He modifies the final command to: "Bring the clarified butter and the curds. At the time of wiping the spoons, having wiped the *sruva* ladle, he wipes the axe on its handle.
The *vasāhomahavanī* is like the *juhū*, and the *pṛṣadājyadhānī* is like the *upabhṛt*. Having poured out the clarified butter (*ājya*), he pours out the curds (*dadhi*).
(7) Regarding the curds, the act of placing them on the fire is omitted. (8) Furthermore, there is another view that no ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*) is required for these curds. (9)
Thus ends the eighth section (kaṇḍikā).
At the time of taking the clarified butter, he takes four portions into the *juhū* ladle and four into the *upabhṛt*.

Having poured clarified butter into the vessel for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), he takes five portions of speckled butter into the *pṛṣadājya-dhānī* vessel with the formula: "Thou art the milk of the great ones," or alternatively: "Thou art light, multiform, the fuel of the All-gods."
At the time of placing [the vessels] on the four-fold *dhruvā*, he places the clarified butter offerings;
he places the *pṛṣadājya* vessel together with the *upabhṛt*.

Having consecrated the clarified butter as before, he traces around the pit for the sacrificial post (yūpāvaṭa) in front of the Āhavanīya fire, with half [of the pit] within the altar and half outside the altar. 6.
The taking up of the spade and the tracing around are as before. 7. Then he digs so that the bottom [of the pit] will not be visible. 8.

Having placed the sacrificial post (yūpa) facing east into the hole, he washes it with the verse: "Whatever a skillful carpenter has hewn away from thee with his hand and axe—may the pure, life-giving waters cleanse all that. Then he sprinkles it with water containing barley, saying: "For the earth, thee! to the root; "For the atmosphere, thee! to the middle; "For the sky, thee! to the top.

Having poured the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water into the pit with the formula, "May the world, the seat of the Fathers, be purified," and having cast a barley grain into it with "Thou art barley," and having spread sacrificial grass over it with "Thou art the seat of the Fathers," and having cast a first-fallen splinter into it with "Thou art easy of access," and having offered an oblation upon the splinter with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) while reciting, "O Heaven and Earth, fill yourselves with ghee"—this is the ninth section.
He issues the command, "Recite for the post being anointed," or alternatively, "Recite for the post being anointed; recite for the post as it is being anointed."

Then the sacrificer, standing in front, anoints it with unconsecrated clarified butter using a wooden splinter, saying, "Thou art for Indra. Having anointed the top-ring (*caṣāla*) with the formula, "For the plants that bear good fruit," he fixes it on with, "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey. Then, with the *sruva* spoon, pouring a continuous stream without interruption, he anoints the rear-most corner facing the fire with, "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey. At the place where the rope will be fastened, he touches the sacrificial post from all sides three times.
The sacrificer does not release the sacrificial post, which has been anointed and so forth, until its encircling with the rope.
He issues the command, "Recite for the post being raised," or "Recite for the one being raised.
He raises it with the formula, "Support the sky, fill the mid-region."
With the verse "Those various abodes of yours," he places [the post] into the pit.
With the two verses beginning "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu," he erects the post facing the Āhavanīya fire.
Regarding the one for whom he desires, "May he be endowed with splendor," it has already been stated.

Having brought the top of the Āhavanīya fire near [the base] and having bent down the root of the sacrificial post (yūpa), he covers it with dust in a clockwise direction while reciting, "Thee, the winner of the priesthood, the winner of the nobility," making the lower part invisible; then, with the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, he makes it firm in the ground level with the earth while reciting, "Make the priesthood firm, make the nobility firm.
Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the formula, "Unfold the earth," he sprinkles [the post] with water.
There are two girdles made of darbha grass: the animal-girdle is double-stranded and two spans long; that of the sacrificial post is triple-stranded and three spans long.
Having taken up the girdle with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he wipes the sacrificial post with his hand holding the girdle, saying, "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu."

He gazes at the top [of the sacrificial post] with the verse, "That highest step of Viṣṇu... He issues the command: "Recite for the post being encircled," or "Recite for that which is being encircled.
With the formula, "Thou art encircling," he thrice encircles the post from left to right with a cord at the height of the navel, or at its middle part.
Regarding the one whom he desires, it has been stated: "May he be possessed of vigor."
One should wrap it far down for one who desires rain, and far up for one who does not desire rain—so say some (7).

For him for whom one should desire, "May a female be born to him," one should intertwine the ends near the edge but not wrap them around (8). For him for whom one should desire, "May a male be born to him," one should wrap them all the way to the end; having inserted the thick part into the thin part, he takes the *svaru* with the formula, "Thou art the son of heaven," and hides it on the northern side of the post that stands nearest the fire, in the middle loop of the cord, with the formula, "I hide thee on the ridge of the atmosphere" (9).

[The animal] is for the *uttama* [cup], or for all [the cups]; or, according to the Vājasaneyaka, for the two lower ones. Thus ends the eleventh section (*kaṇḍikā*), and thus the third chapter (*paṭala*).
They bathe the sacrificial animal, excluding those with crooked ears, one-eyed, lame, crippled, or seven-hoofed.

If he should be deficient in a limb, or if a limb should become diseased, then according to some, having offered oblations to Viṣṇu, to Agni-Viṣṇu, to Sarasvatī, and to Bṛhaspati, one should employ [the animal]. It is known from tradition: "That which is not eaten is the impurity of animals."

With the words, "For strength, thee," he takes two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*). With the words, "Thou art the one who comes near," he takes a branch of the *plakṣa* tree that has many leaves, with its tip not dried out and free from holes.
For one whom he desires to be without cattle, he should perform the introductory rite for him using a branch that is leafless and has a dried-out tip.
Some say that he performs the introductory rite using a blade of grass.

With two blades of *barhis* grass and a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, he dedicates the animal facing westward from the east. While touching it, he recites these two verses: "The divine hosts approach the gods," and "The offspring of Prajāpati being born. Then he says: "I dedicate you, acceptable to Indra and Agni. (8) There are five instances of announcing the deity: at the dedication (*upākaraṇa*), the binding (*niyojana*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the extraction of the omentum (*vapā-uddharaṇa*), and the sprinkling over the heart (*hṛdaya-abhighāraṇa*).
(9) Having offered the five oblations with the verse, "Knowing [the way], they receive the first," he churns the fire. (10)
Alternatively, having churned the fire, he should perform the *upākaraṇa* rite.

With the formula, "Thou art the birthplace of Agni," he places the lower churning stick upon the fire-drilling board. With the formula, "Ye two are the testicles," he places two blades of *darbha* grass pointing eastward.
With the formula, "Thou art Urvaśī," he takes up the lower churning stick; with the formula, "Purūravas," the upper churning stick.

"May the god Savitṛ anoint you both with honey," [saying this] he anoints the two [kindling woods] in the cavity of the butter-pot; "Anointed with ghee, do you two support the bull," [saying this] he consecrates both; "Thou art life," [saying this] he places them together. (14) Thus ends the twelfth section.
"Recite for the fire being churned," he gives the command; or rather, "Recite for the fire being churned. (1)

When the first verse has been recited three times, he churns the fire three times clockwise, saying: "Be born following the Gāyatrī metre" for the first time; "following the Triṣṭubh metre" for the second; and "following the Jagatī metre" for the third. Then he churns as rapidly as possible. If the fire is not produced while being churned, he should recite verses that slay the Rākṣasas.
"Recite for what has been born," he commands when [the fire] has been produced. "For that which is being cast forth," he says as he casts it;
with the formula, "May you two be of one mind for us," he casts it into the Āhavanīya fire in front of the northern enclosing stick, or at the junction.
Having cast it with the formula, "Fire moves within fire, having entered," he makes an offering over it with the *sruva* ladle.

Having taken the rope with the *sāvitra* formula and having passed it around the right foreleg of the animal, he pulls it upward and fastens the noose diagonally across the right half of the head with the formula, "I seize thee, the divine oblation of Ṛta, with the noose. Then, with the formula, "Be bold against men," he binds [the animal] to the north of the sacrificial post. (Sūtra 8) Those belonging to the group of eleven are bound to the south.
(Sūtra 9) He sprinkles [the animal] with the formula, "I sprinkle thee for the waters and for the plants. (Sūtra 10)

With the words, "Thou art the drinker of the waters," he causes [the sacrificer] to sip. With the words, "O divine waters, may you season this well-prepared oblation for the gods," having inspected [the butter] from above, below, and all around, and having placed the *veda* grass-bundle down, he proceeds with the *sāmidhenī* verses.
Thus ends the thirteenth section; thus ends the fourth chapter.
Having poured the clarified butter from the *sruc* and having stepped back, he anoints the victim with the *juhū* ladle:
"May your breath unite with the wind," on the head; "May your limbs unite with those worthy of sacrifice," on the two shoulders; "May the lord of the sacrifice unite with his blessings," on the hip.
He proceeds with the ritual beginning from the anointing of the *dhruvā* ladle, which is the same up to the *pravara* invocation.

Having chosen the six officiating priests (ṛtvij), as well as the two Hotṛs—both the divine and the human—and having called for the formal announcement (āśrāvaṇa) once more, he chooses the Maitrāvaruṇa, saying: "Mitra and Varuṇa are the Praśāstṛs; [I choose] from the office of the Praśāstṛ.
While the animal sacrifice stands ready, he performs the eleven fore-offerings (prayāja).
He first issues the command, "Prompt for the *samidhs*! For the others, he says, "Prompt!
Prompt! Having combined the fourth and eighth offerings, after offering ten, he leaves over the eleventh portion of clarified butter.

The sacrificer, having consecrated the first four with the four original formulas, consecrates the next three beginning with *Dvāraḥ* by means of the formula for the fourth, and the remainder with the final formula.
Having stepped back, he anoints the *svaru* and the *svadhiti* with the *juhū* ladle; he anoints the *svaru* three times and one of the edges of the *svadhiti* once.
Having placed the *svaru* between them, he anoints the animal with the *svadhiti*, saying, "O you two anointed with ghee, protect the animal," at its head.
Or rather, he does not use the *svadhiti*, but only the *svaru*.
He cuts off the cooked portion with the anointed [spoon] and dissects the animal with the other. 13.
Handing over the knife to the slaughterer, he says: "O slaughterer, this is your edge; let it be sharpened. 14.
Thus ends the fourteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
He issues the command: "Recite for the fire being carried around," or "Recite for the fire being carried around.

Taking a firebrand from the Āhavanīya fire, the Agnīdhra carries the fire around the animal, the sacrificial post, the Āhavanīya, the place of the Śāmitra, and the Cātvāla pit three times clockwise, with the verse: "The wise Lord of Strength has gone around... Some say he also carries it around the clarified butter.
Having thrown back the firebrand, he goes around three times in the opposite direction.
"Knowing, they receive it first"—this is said when the fire is being carried around; he offers the *apāvya* oblations, one, two, three, or four times.
"The cattle of Paśupati are diverse as well as similar; may the self-ruling Lord approve that one which the gods have chosen"—this is the second [verse].
"When they bind him"—this is recited while he is being bound. "While releasing"—this is recited while he is being led forward.

"O Revatīs, enter the lord of the sacrifice with a friendly disposition"—with these words, the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer touch the animal from behind with the two omentum-roasting spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*). Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and the response having been given, he issues the command: "O Hotṛ, give the impulse; bring the oblations to the gods!
Upon the Hotṛ’s signal, "Bring Agni forward for him! Spread the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)!", the Āgnīdhra takes a firebrand from the *āhavanīya* fire and goes out first.
The slaughterer (*śamitṛ*) leads the animal.
"O chest, O atmosphere!"—saying this, they lead the animal northward between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap.
"May the breath of the sacrificer be distinct from that of the animal," the Adhvaryu murmurs.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.
"Dig a pit for the entrails, O King," [the Adhvaryu says], and recognizing this, he digs the pit for the entrails. 1.
In a place surrounded by fire, he places a firebrand; 2.
that is the *śāmitra* (the slaughtering fire). 3.

Having stationed the animal facing west to the south [of the fire], he places *barhis* grass beneath it with the formula, "Protect [the animal] from contact with the earth," using either of the two [bundles] used for the preliminary dedication (*upākaraṇa*). Upon that [grass], they cause it to be quieted, with its head toward the west and its feet toward the north.
Having said, "Quiet it, making it free from groaning," the Adhvaryu turns away.

You are the finder of heaven; having found heaven, come to heaven; [bring] heaven for me, heaven for my cattle. You are the finder of the world; having found the world, come to the world; [bring] the world for me, the world for my cattle. You are the finder of the way; having found the way, come to the way; [bring] the way for me, the way for my cattle. You are the finder of refuge; having found refuge, come to refuge; [bring] refuge for me, refuge for my cattle. Indeed, you do not die here, nor are you harmed; you go to the gods by easy paths.

"Where the doers of good deeds go, and not the doers of evil—there may the god Savitṛ place you. "I unite you with honey from all quarters for the guardians of the quarters; may the waters and plants be free from disease; may this sacrificer drive away his enemies; may all animals be unseized"—having said this, the sacrificer turns away. "The breath of the sacrificer is distinct from that of the animal," thus the Adhvaryu mutters. Thus ends the sixteenth section.

"May those whose udder has four openings, filled with honey and ghee, be full of milk for us in this stall, increasing our vigor. Here let the cattle of every form rejoice; in this sacrifice, may they who know all things, dripping with ghee, and dwelling together in Agni as their home, protect us with milk and ghee. While looking at the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer remain silent. 1.

"Bestow Indra’s portion for our prosperity; protect this sacrifice and the sacrificer at the sun's rising. May he who hates us cry out against him!"—with these words, they look toward the bellowing [animal].
When it has been slaughtered, he offers the *saṃjñapta-homa* with the verse: "That the animal has made a lowing sound...
The Adhvaryu and the sacrificer approach the animal with the two omentum-roasting spits, saying: "O slaughterers, come hither!"
"Aditi releases the bond of the victim; may Aditi release this bond," [he says].
Having wound the cord around the necks [of the victims] and having fastened it with a single pin, he throws it into the *cātvāla* pit, saying, "I make him who acts as an enemy low.
If he should practice sorcery, he should say, "I make low him who acts as an enemy; upon him whom we hate, I cast the bond," and with that [cord] he should tie down a tree, a stump, or a post.
Thus ends the seventeenth kaṇḍikā; thus ends the fifth paṭala.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife forward. 1.
With the words "Homage to thee, O Expander," the wife worships the sun. 2.
With the words, "Go forward, unhindered," he leads her toward the east; some say he addresses her with this mantra.
3. With the words, "O divine waters, you who seek purity," the wife, the officiating priests, and the sacrificer touch the water at the *cātvāla* pit.
4. Some say the wife does not participate. 5.

With water, he causes all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the animal to swell; the Adhvaryu sprinkles all its limbs, and the wife causes them to swell. Or rather, it is the reverse: with the formulas beginning "May your speech swell," they do so according to the respective characteristics of each part. With "The pain that has reached your vital breaths," he [sprinkles] the region of the heart.
"May your penis swell," [he says] over the penis (9). "Pure are our ways," [he says] over the feet (10).
Having caused each one to swell, he mutters [the verse] while the drops have not yet reached the ground: "Peace to the waters" (11).

Having poured the remainder on the ground with the formula, "Welfare from the plants! Welfare from the earth!", he places what remains of the two cutting blades across his navel to the south with the formula, "O plant, protect him! and then cuts across the side with the axe, saying, "O axe, do not harm him.
He takes the tip of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with his left hand.

Then, having taken the middle portion from where he draws it out, and having smeared both sides with blood, he throws it away toward the north-western intermediate direction with the formula, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases. Then he stands upon it with his left foot, saying, "Here I crush the Rakṣas; here I lead the Rakṣas to the lowest darkness.
(Thus ends the eighteenth Kaṇḍikā.

Having extracted the omentum with the formula, "For food thee," and having covered the two-pronged spit with the omentum using the formula, "May Heaven and Earth be enveloped by ghee," he finally inserts the single-pronged spit into the thinnest part [of the omentum] with the formula, "For strength thee."

Having consecrated it with "Be prepared for the gods," having sprinkled it with water with "Be purified for the gods," and having wiped the omentum with the flaying-knife with "Be cleansed for the gods," he cuts it off with "May wealth with good heroes be cut off for you; I cut you out, acceptable to Indra and Agni.
(2) The slaughterer, having covered the omentum-extractor with his fist, remains there until the offering of the omentum.

(3) Having heated the omentum over the *śāmitra* fire with "The demon is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away," and having worshipped the sun with "Homage to the sight of the sun," he proceeds forward with "Go through the intermediate space. (4)
Taking a portion of the firebrand, the Āgnīdhra goes forward first;
the sacrificer again takes hold of the two omentum-spits;
he throws the remaining portion of the firebrand back into the Āhavanīya fire.

"The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away," he says. Having placed the omentum upon the outermost embers of the Āhavanīya fire, and having carried it southward between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya, he hands it to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
(8) Sitting to the south, the Pratiprasthātṛ roasts it on the Āhavanīya fire.
(9) This is the nineteenth Kaṇḍikā.
With the formula, "O Vāyu, come to the drops," he throws the tip of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) beneath the omentum (*vapā*).

With the formula, "Thee they have established as the bearer of oblations," he makes an offering over the omentum with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*). When the drops have appeared, he issues the command: "Recite for the drops."

Having made it bloodless and well-boiled, and having placed it upon the sacrificial grass at the southern corner of the altar on a branch of the *lakṣa* tree with the formula, "Make the plants well-peppered," he draws out the two omentum-spits with the formula, "May hostilities be driven away," and sets them down. Having taken up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles over which ghee has been poured, having stepped across to the south, and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, when the response has been given, he issues the direction: "Prompt for the *svāhākṛtis*," or "Prompt for the *svāhākṛtis*.

Having offered the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, having returned, and having sprinkled the *dhruvā* with the remainder, he sprinkles the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) and then the omentum. Or rather, this [order] may be reversed; however, the *upabhṛt* is not [sprinkled].
He offers the two *ājyabhāga* portions. He does not perform them at the animal sacrifice; some say not even at the Soma sacrifice.

Having offered the first *parivapya* with "Svāhā to the gods," having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, having placed a piece of gold therein, having taken the entire omentum as an oblation-portion, and having placed a piece of gold on top, he pours clarified butter over it.
Thus it becomes five-fold;
even for one who offers four-fold portions, it should indeed be five-fold.
This is the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā).
"Recite for Indra and Agni the omentum and fat of the goat; give the command for Indra and Agni regarding the omentum and fat of the goat"—these are the two calls.

Having offered the oblation at the *vaṣaṭ*-call with the verse, "O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum," and having stepped back and offered the northern *parivapya* oblation with "Svāhā to the gods," he, standing to the north, pours clarified butter over the vessel from which the omentum was removed.

The Pratiprasthātṛ throws the two omentum-spits into the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Svāhā! Go to the Maruts of the upward sky!"—the two-pronged spit pointing eastward and the single-pronged spit pointing westward; or it may be the reverse of this.
Then the Adhvaryu makes an offering over them with the residue of the oblation.
At this point, the sacrificer gives a boon—either three uncastrated bulls or three milch-cows as the sacrificial fees.

Having stepped out together with their wives, they purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit with five verses: the three beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," and [the following two]: "O Waters, carry away this impurity and whatever filth there is; whatever falsehood I have committed through malice, or whatever harsh word I have uttered—O Waters, release me from that sin, from all transgressions. "I release myself from curses, I release myself from Varuṇa; I release myself from the fetter of Yama, from every offense against the gods and likewise from offense against men.
Thus ends the twenty-first section (*kaṇḍikā*). Thus ends the sixth section.
One undertakes the ritual procedure for the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), beginning with the setting out of the vessels.
1. The arrangement of the vessels is according to their purpose.
2. At the time of the pouring out [of the grain], one pours out the animal-cake made of rice, on eleven or twelve potsherds. 3.
Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), he gives instructions regarding the animal:

"The heart, the tongue, the breast, the liver, the two kidneys, the left foreleg, both sides, the right hip, and the third part of the rectum—these are for the deities (*daivata*). The right foreleg, the left hip, and the third part of the rectum—these are for the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. He extracts the lungs, the spleen, the mesentery, the large intestine, the omentum, the fat, and the tail.
He issues the command: "Do not let the rectum be torn apart."

The meaning is "do not let [the animal] perish. 8. Having placed the animal in a water-purifying vessel (*udakapavitra*) within the cooking pot (*kumbhī*), and having prodded it with a spit, he cooks its heart on the *śāmitra* fire. 9.
He proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the threshing (*avahanana*). 10.
Having performed the rite with the omentum, he proceeds with the cake-offering. When the animal has been cooked, the two formal calls are:

"Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and Agni regarding the cake," and "Direct the call for Indra and Agni regarding the cake"; or alternatively, "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and Agni regarding the cake being cut off," and "Direct the call for Indra and Agni regarding the cake. For the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the two formal calls are: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni," and "Direct the call for Agni."
Thus ends the twenty-second section (kaṇḍikā). Having taken the *prāśitra* portion, [he takes] the *iḍā*, but not the sacrificer’s share. 1.
The sacrifice, beginning with the oblation of the sacrificial food (*havis*) and ending with the *iḍā*, is concluded. 2.

Having consumed the portions offered with the Maitrāvaruṇa as the sixth, having performed the purification over the *prastara* grass-bundle as before, and having taken a portion of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the *sruva* ladle and supported it with the *veda* grass-bundle, he asks three times: "Is the oblation cooked, O *śamitr*?
To which the other replies: "It is cooked. (1–4)
Having reached the second half-way point, he takes the second [portion];

at the third, [he recites]: "May Pūṣan, the protector of cattle, protect me. At the first [half-way point] he sets out, saying: "May Pūṣan, the protector of the path, protect me"; at the second: "May Pūṣan, the protector of the way, protect me"; at the third: "May Pūṣan, the protector of the region, protect me.

Having extracted the heart from the spit and placed it in a pot, he sprinkles the heart with speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), having gone around to the north, while reciting: "May thy mind unite with my mind."
With the mantra, "The self which has entered into the animals," [he offers] with clarified butter.
8. With the mantra, "Svāhā! May I not be harmed by the steam," he consecrates the rising steam as it rises.
9. Carrying the animal, he holds the heart-spike at its side, without touching himself or others. 10.

Having carried [the sacrificial portions] southward between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the *āhavanīya* fire, he places them on the southern hip of the altar with either the *pañcahotṛ* or the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula. He spreads [clarified butter] upon four [vessels]: the *juhū*, the *upabhṛt*, the *vasāhomahavaṇī*, and the *samavattadhānī*.
Having placed pieces of gold in the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*, while cutting off the portions upon the *plakṣa* branch over the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he issues the call.
Thus ends the twenty-third section (*kaṇḍikā*).
"Recite for the *manotā* as the oblation is being portioned out. First, he portions from the heart; then from the tongue; then from the chest; for the others, he may portion as he desires.
It has been stated: "He portions from the middle of the rectum."
Or as it has been extracted (4):
having cut off portions twice each from the portions for the deities, he places them in the *juhū* ladle; [he cuts] once each from the portions for *Sviṣṭakṛt* into the *upabhṛt* ladle (5).

Having divided the rectum into three parts and set aside the thickest part for the *upayaj* offerings, he divides the middle part into two and places one portion among the portions for the deities (6), and the thin part among those for *Sviṣṭakṛt*.

Alternatively, having divided [the fat] into two parts, he should set aside the thickest portion for the *upayaj* offerings; the remainder he divides into three parts, and having divided the middle part into two, he places it among the *daivata* portions. He places the thinnest portion among the *sauviṣṭakṛta* portions, and the thickest portion in the *iḍā*. He cuts the fat three times: twice into the two ladles and once into the *samavatta-haraṇī*. Having placed the fat into the broth, covered the two ladles with fat, and placed pieces of gold on top, he pours the clarified butter over them.
