From the portion of grain that has been evenly divided, he cuts off six portions for the *iḍā*, making the *vaniṣṭhu* (the rectum) the seventh. Or rather, he cuts from six [portions] and the *vaniṣṭhu* as the seventh.
He increases the *iḍā* with boneless parts.
Having placed the *kloman* (lungs), the *plīhā* (spleen), and the *purītat* (omentum) underneath, he sprinkles it with broth and pours clarified butter over it.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section; thus ends the seventh chapter.
"I take the essence of the waters and of the plants," with these words he takes the fat-oblation into the vessel for the fat-oblation. He cuts the stream [of fat] with the sharp-edged knife.
For one who offers five cuttings twice, he mixes the fat-oblation with the side [of the knife] while reciting, "Thou art glory" (ŚB 1.2.1.20).
He covers it with that same [side] while reciting, "Thee for the gliding of Vāta" (ŚB 1.2.1.21). Or he mixes it with the blade; some say he covers it with the blade.
Now, those parts which he does not cut off—the head, the two shoulders, the *aṇūka*, and the two hind thighs—are the non-offering portions;
having placed them together with the boiled portions, he touches them while reciting, "Indra’s breath is in every limb.
Then he proceeds with the oblation.
"Recite the invitatory verse for the goat-oblation for Indra and Agni; give the command for the offering of the goat-oblation for Indra and Agni"—these are the two calls.
At the half-verse of the *yājyā*, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the fat-oblation (*vasāhoma*) with the verse, "O drinkers of ghee, drink the ghee.
With the remainder, he offers in each direction with the formula, "The quarters, the intermediate directions," and in the center with the fifth [formula].
Having established the final [offering] facing eastward, he worships with the formula, "Homage to the quarters! (VaikhŚS 10.12).
He offers at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* (VaikhŚS 10.13).
Or, in this case, he may sacrifice toward the quarters; either after the *vanaspati* offering or after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering (VaikhŚS 10.14).

Having stepped back, having spread a base of ghee in the *juhū* ladle, having taken a portion of the *pṛṣadājya* once, and having poured ghee over it twice, he issues the two calls: "Recite for Vanaspati" and "Prompt for Vanaspati. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
(15) Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* cutting, the sacrificer recites the following mantra.
(16) Placing the *aupabhṛta* portions upon the *juhū* in the *āhavanīya* fire while turning them upside down, he issues the two calls: "Recite for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" and "Prompt for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. (17)
Having offered when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, having stepped back and returned to his place, he sets down the two offering-spoons (*srucau*) in their respective stations.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
Here, some authorities prescribe the taking out of a portion for the *iḍā*.
He cuts off the intermediate *iḍā* portion;
having spread a layer of fat underneath, he bastes it with fat.
It has been stated: "For whomsoever he should desire, 'May he be without cattle,' for him [he should cut] without fat."
They consume [the portions] after they have been invoked, with the Maitrāvaruṇa as the sixth; the Pratiprasthātṛ is the seventh. 5.
He prepares the rectum for the Āgnīdhra as a sixfold portion. 6.
He carries the adhyūdhnī [portion] to the Hotṛ. 7.

"O Āgnīdhra, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings (aupayaja); O Upayaṣṭṛ, sit down; O Brahman, we shall set forth; having placed the fuel-stick, O Āgnīdhra, cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire once each," thus he issues the command.

He brings the embers for the supplementary offerings from the Āgnīdhra hearth. He performs the supplementary offerings at the Hotṛ's station. In the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice, [he performs them] at the northern corner of the altar from the Śāmitra hearth.

Having cut the rectum into eleven pieces crosswise—without piercing them and without turning them over—the Pratiprasthātṛ offers each piece of the rectum with his hand at every *vaṣaṭ* call of the after-offerings (*anūyāja*), with these mantras respectively: "Go to the ocean, svāhā! (and so on).

Having offered all of them, he wipes the smearings upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the mantra, "To the waters, to the plants," and mutters, "Grant me mind and heart. Having taken the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) into the *juhū* ladle and having made the *upabhṛt* the vessel for the speckled butter, he performs the eleven after-offerings with that.

He gives the first direction with "To the gods, *preṣya*! and the others with "Direct, direct! (13). The sacrificer consecrates them with the standard formulas (14). Thus ends the twenty-sixth section.
With the first [verse], he offers the first four [oblations] and the tenth; with the second, [he offers those] prior to the *vanaspati* [offering]; with the last, the remainder.
In the variations of the two subsequent [verses], both the Adhvaryu and the Maitrāvaruṇa urge the Hotṛ, saying, "Recite the offering-verse (*yajya*).
Regarding this, some prescribe the anointing of the *svaru* [wooden splinter].

Having stepped back and placed the *svaru* on the *juhū* ladle, he offers it at the end of the *anūyāja* offerings with the mantra: "May your smoke go to heaven, your flame to the intermediate space; fill the earth with ashes, Svāhā! (4).
The procedure is the same up to the call for the response (*pratyāśrāvaṇa*). (5) The *sūktavāka* direction (*praisha*) is modified. (6)
The Maitrāvaruṇa should say to him, "He has chosen Agni as the Hotṛ today.
He makes offerings over the four enclosing sticks, excluding the Dhruva stick.
Having brought the tail of the victim to the south of the sacrificial ground, they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives with it.

With clarified butter, having caused Soma and Tvaṣṭṛ to be invoked, he cuts portions for the wives of the gods from the tail-tendon held upward; for Agni Gṛhapati from the one held downward. He cuts the *iḍā* portion for the Hotṛ from the tail-tendon held upward; for the Āgnīdhra from the one held downward.
He hands it to the wife; she gives it to the Adhvaryu or to another Brāhmaṇa.
[He offers] the arm to the immolator (if it is not a Brahmin).
If he is a non-Brahmin, [he offers] that to a Brahmin.

Having offered the three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations with the formula "O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice," and touching [the heart-spike], he goes northward, pours water in a place where no path crosses, and sets down the heart-spike at the junction of the dry and the moist, meditating in his mind on someone whom he hates, with the formula "Thou art pain. 15.

"May the waters and plants be gracious to us"—having performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*) at that *cātvāla* pit together with his wife, he worships the sun with the verses "From every station, O King... and "Lift up the highest...", places fuel sticks on the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra "O Fuel, may we prosper through thee...", and they worship [the fire] with the mantra "I have moved along the waters.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section.

"One animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) follows the pattern of an *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offering), while another follows the pattern of a *soma* sacrifice. When one brings forward the water, pours out the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), and strides the *viṣṇukrama* steps, it is of the *iṣṭi* type; other than that, it is of the *soma* type—so says the Vājasaneyaka."

The sacrificer pays homage to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with the mantra: "Homage to the *svaru*-staves! May you not reach me while set up; may I not be left behind as one who has failed. Like the horns of horned animals, the *svaru*-staves with their *caṣāla*-tops appear upon the earth. These divine *svaru*-staves stand firm; homage to my friends! May you not reach me while set up.
And also: "May I obtain great heroic power. Having thus paid homage, he mutters the formula:
"O Sacrifice, prosperity for me! (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.9).

Indeed, they cause this [sacrificial post] to move away from the trees for the sake of the oblation; when the humans have sacrificed, they depart. The sacrificial post (yūpa) indeed takes upon itself whatever is ill-sacrificed in the sacrifice. If one should touch the post, he would take that ill-sacrificed portion of the sacrifice upon himself; therefore, he should address it with these mantras: "O Vāyu, this is yours, O Vāyu"—for one [post]; "O Vāyu, these two are yours, O Vāyu"—for two; "O Vāyu, these many are yours, O Vāyu"—for many. The *Nirūḍhapaśubandha* sacrifice is dedicated to Indra and Agni, or to Sūrya, or to Prajāpati. With that, one should sacrifice every year; some say every six months.
At the change of seasons, or at the beginning of the turn when there is good pasture, [the fires] should be moved.

Indeed, the fires of a sacrificer who does not offer oblations become desirous of meat; they fix their thoughts solely upon the sacrificer and intend him for slaughter. For in other fires, people cook meat for pleasure, but for these [sacrificial fires], no other desire for meat exists. Furthermore, for one who possesses these fires, the year should not pass without his sacrificing with an animal. "This [offering] is life-giving and a ransom for the self," so it is said in the Vājasaneyaka. 8.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the eighth section.
Thus ends the seventh book (praśna).
Truly, the merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices becomes inexhaustible. 1.
On the full moon day of Phālguna or Caitra, he performs the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

On the preceding parvan, having mentally recited the Pañcahotṛ formula and offered the Sagraha oblation in the Āhavanīya fire, he prepares the Anvārambhaṇīyā offering: a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara and a pap for Parjanya.

"Vaiśvānara with his aid, he who is not touched by heaven"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for Vaiśvānara. "Sing forth to Parjanya, the son of Heaven, the bountiful one; may he seek out pasture for us. "Address the powerful one with these songs; praise Parjanya and strive to win him with homage. Bellowing like a bull, the swift-giver, may he place seed as a germ within the plants"—these are the verses for Parjanya. One gives gold to the [priest] for Vaiśvānara and a milch-cow to the [priest] for Parjanya. The sacrifice is thus completed. 4. One sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva [offering] on ground sloping toward the east. 5.
Carrying forward the fire from the *gārhapatya* as in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), he offers the *udyata-homa*.

Having recognized the signal from the Hotṛ with the verse, "Sit down first upon the woolly womb," he places a tuft of wool at the site of the *āhavanīya* and establishes the fire upon it. Another view holds that the carrying forward of the fire for an animal sacrifice is not permitted where there is no northern altar (*uttaravedi*).
Having added fuel to the fires and brought back a branch, he drives away the calves for the sake of the *āmikṣā* offering to the Viśvedevas (9).
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the *prastara* bundle consist of fresh shoots (10). It is tied up in three places, and then again in one place (11).
In that [context], there is the mantra (12),
likewise the fuel (13), and the twenty-three pieces of wood (14).
Having bound together three bundles, he binds them once again as one.
15 As before, he causes the evening milking for the Vaiśvadeva offering to be performed.
16 Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
On the following day, at the time for arranging the vessels, he sets out either a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood for the whey or a *sruk* ladle.
At the time of the pouring out [of the grains], he pours out the eight oblations as they are prescribed in the text, beginning with the cake on eight potsherds for Agni.
Of these, five end with that for Pūṣan and are the common (optional) offerings.
He cooks the sacrificial cake for Pūṣan from the flour.
He pours the evening milk into the warm morning milk;
that which coagulates is the *sāmicī*, and that which remains liquid is the *vājina*.
The summons regarding the animal victim is as before. Likewise for the clarified butters (*ājyāni*).

There is a modification regarding the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*): with the formula, "Thou art the milk of the great ones," he takes twice the clarified butter into the vessel for the speckled butter—twice the curds and once the clarified butter.
At the time of taking down [the hot milk], having coagulated the *āmikṣā*, having drawn it out into two vessels, he sprinkles it with a portion of the whey (*vājina*).
At the time of the decoration, he fills the single-pan cake with clarified butter, or having made its back exposed; he places the sacrificial oblations down with the *vyāhṛtis*.
He places the whey on the rubbish heap.
With the *pañcahotṛ* formula, the sacrificer touches all the oblations that have been set down.
He is to be churned like an animal, and there are *sāmidhenī* verses;
there are nine *prayāja* offerings; between the fourth and the last [of these], there are four *pāśuka* (animal-related) *praisha*-prefixed *yājyā*s beginning with "O Doors" (*duraḥ*). 13–15.
The driving-in of the sacrificial animal is as before.

At the time of the ritual performance, having performed the rite with the *upāṃśu* Sāvitra formula, he proceeds as previously with the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*). With the four names of the months, "Madhu and Mādhava," he makes an offering over the cake on one potsherd.
At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives the first-born calf, or a pair of cattle (19).
Having poured the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) into the *juhū* ladle and having made the *upabhṛt* the vessel for the speckled butter, he performs nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with it (20).
Thus ends the second section (*kaṇḍikā*).
The first eight [offerings] belong to the animal sacrifice, excluding the *pariṣava*.
With the last [verse], he performs the last [offering].
He gives the first command: "Sacrifice to the gods! and for the others, "Sacrifice, sacrifice!"
He pronounces the blessing: "He desires well-being for a year; he desires the divine abode. Thus the Hotṛ continues with the blessings of the *sūktavāka*.
In this same way, the sacrificer mutters [the formula]. He modifies the mantra to "he desires" (*āśāse*).

Having thrown the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the fire and having performed the rites up to the pouring out of the remnants, he spreads an under-layer of butter in the vessel for the whey (*vājina*), and while pouring along the sacrificial grass within the altar, he takes the whey.
He does not pour over [the oblation].

"Recite for the Vājins! Sacrifice to the Vājins!"—these are the two calls. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers with the cup; or, while the ladle is being poured out, he offers at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* call.
Sitting with his knees raised, the Hotṛ recites the offering prayer without pausing.
He performs the after-offering with the formula, "O Agni, partake of the *vājina*.

For he indeed takes portions from three oblations for the *sviṣṭakṛt*: from the *soma*, the *vājina*, and the *gharma*. With the remainder, as in the animal sacrifice, he offers to the quarters; then, having invited one another, they all consume what remains within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*).
He addresses him by the name of the ritual action, saying, "N.N., do you invite [us]!
(13). The response is, "I have been invited!
(14). The Hotṛ eats first, and the sacrificer last; however, some say that the sacrificer eats both first and last. (15)

May the portion of the swift ones protect us; may the swift one protect us. May the seed that has been sprinkled, the nectar for the sake of strength, bestow upon us sensory power and wealth. May we not come to harm while consuming the swift one. "Of thee, who hast been made a portion by the swift ones, who hast been pressed by the swift ones, who hast been drunk by the swift ones—of thee, the swift one, being invited, I, invited, partake," with these words he consumes it.
(16) The *samiṣṭayajus* offerings are performed as at the animal sacrifice. (17) The sacrifice is completed successfully. (18)

Thus ends the third section (kaṇḍikā). On the following day, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice, [the sacrificer], permitted by the divine Savitṛ, says: "May the divine waters moisten your body for long life and luster. Then, using a three-colored porcupine quill, a stalk of sugarcane, or a sugarcane splinter, and an iron razor made of Udumbara wood, he has his hair trimmed and his beard shaved.

"Truth alone is the Supreme Lord; nothing whatsoever transcends Truth. Upon Truth the ocean is set; upon Truth this earth rests. Agni with his sharp flame has overcome the heat; the head is placed within the heat by the brilliance of Vaiśvānara. By Truth I turn it back; by Satya I turn it around; by Tapas I follow it; by the auspicious I turn it toward me; by the helpful I turn it hither. With these words he turns [the head].

"That is Truth, that is Satya, that is the Vow; may I be able to do that; by that may I be able; by that may I prosper"—with these words the sacrificer murmurs. And [he recites] the section beginning, "The Brāhmaṇa is the one Hotṛ. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.5.2.16–20)
During the intervals between the ritual festivals, he observes these intermediate vows:
4. He does not eat meat; 5. he does not approach a woman, or [he may approach] his wife during her season.
He does not sit facing upward; he should loathe falsehood; he sleeps facing the east.
"He eats honey"—one [view] is that this refers to the eating of honey; another is that it is for the sake of a condiment. "The Ṛtayājī is one, and the Cāturmāsyayājī is another."

He who sacrifices thinking, "Spring has been, the rainy season has been, autumn has been," is a performer of the Seasonal Sacrifices (*ṛtuyājī*). Now, he who sacrifices every four months is a performer of the Four-Monthly Sacrifices (*cāturmāsyayājī*). It is known from tradition: "In spring he sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva; in the rainy season with the Varuṇapraghāsas; in autumn with the Sākamedhas.
This concludes the fourth section (*kaṇḍikā*), and thus the first chapter (*paṭala*).
Then, after four months, having departed [from the winter residence] on the full moon of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa, he sacrifices with the Varuṇapraghāsas.
"When the *kakṣa* grass has grown up, one should sacrifice"—thus says the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa*.
Its ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is like that of the *Vaiśvadeva*.
Having prepared two altars (*vedī*) in front of the *Gārhapatya* fire, they are level and oriented toward the east.
The Adhvaryu performs the northern [side] and the Pratiprasthātṛ the southern. The Adhvaryu operates in the northern sacrificial area (vihāra) and the Pratiprasthātṛ in the southern.
The entire ritual procedure (tantra) is performed in both places. The Patnīsaṃyāja offerings are also performed in both.
There is a single *saṃpraiṣa* (direction) for the calf;
the Brahman gives his permission twice.
The two altars are separated by two finger-breadths, three finger-breadths, four finger-breadths, a span, the width of a chariot track, a *mītā*, or by a *prādeśa* across, without being joined.
The space between the two altars is the path for the Pratiprasthātṛ.
To the west of the northern altar, while carrying away the *stambayajus*, he carries it around so as to pass behind the Adhvaryu. He throws it down upon the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
The rubbish heap is common [to both].
14. There are five officiating priests. 15. Whatever the Adhvaryu does, that the Pratiprasthātṛ does as well. 16.
Whatever involves vocal action, the Adhvaryu alone should perform it; likewise,
the simultaneous recitations (nigadas),
and the purificatory rites involving common materials.

Having performed the enclosure from the northeast, he connects the two altars with a single wooden splinter (sphya). Starting from the northern hip of the southern altar and proceeding to the southern shoulder of the northern altar, he pours out the high altar (uttaravedi) on the northern altar according to the ritual for the animal sacrifice (paśubandha).
At the proper time, they lead forward the fires from the Gārhapatya according to the ritual for the animal sacrifice.
Those who have not yet raised their ladles do not offer oblations.
23. The Pratiprasthātṛ takes his position between the two altars; the Adhvaryu, to the north of the northern altar. 24.
First, the Adhvaryu establishes the fire on the northern high-altar (uttaravedi); subsequently, the Pratiprasthātṛ [establishes it] on the southern one. 25.
Having added fuel to the fires, they bring two separate branches (26), as well as the sacrificial wood and the sacrificial grass (27).
The Pratiprasthātṛ drives away the calves for the offering to Marut; the Adhvaryu does so for the offering to Varuṇa (28).
The offering-spoons (sruva) are made either of *śamī* wood or of gold.
They cause the evening milk to be milked according to the respective deities. Or else, the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings are performed on the same day.
This being the case, the curd would be for the purpose of the *āmikṣā* by means of worldly [preparation].
32 Some say that the *āmikṣā* and the *payaḥ* (milk) are modifications of the morning milking.
33 At the time of the offering, he pours out nine subsequent oblations, beginning with "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni. 34
All [the grains] are barley;
or alternatively, the *karambha* vessels and the two rams belong to Pūṣan, while the others consist of both barley and rice.
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently pours out the barley for the *karambha* vessels.
The Adhvaryu prepares the portions for the ram with the *yajus* formula; the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the portions for the ewe. (38) The deity for these two is the same as that for the *āmikṣā*.
(39) The wife prepares the *karambha* vessels from grains that are to be ground raw. (40)
There are as many ram and ewe effigies made of raw dough as there are members of the sacrificer’s household, including the wives, with one additional [effigy].
(41) The Adhvaryu makes the ram, and the Pratiprasthātṛ makes the ewe. (42–43)
Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā). 1.
The female characteristics of a woman; 2. the male characteristics of a man. (8.6.1)
Alternatively, on the previous day, having husked barley grains as it were on the Anvāhāryapacana fire, the wife prepares the *karambha* vessels from those slightly parched grains.
Regarding this, the Vājasaneyaka states: "She also prepares a ram and a ewe.
Having placed the offerings up to those for Indra and Agni upon the fire, she places the ewe on eleven potsherds and the ram on eight.
Or they may be two *kumbhīpākya* [vessels].

Having placed the single-pan body-vessel (*kāyam ekakapālam*) on the fire and having poured [the contents] into these [vessels], they lead forward the fires; so says the Vājasaneyaka. The summons (*saṃpraiṣa*) is like that for the animal sacrifice. Likewise the clarified butters (*ājyāni*).

There is a modification regarding the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). With the formula, "Thou art the milk of the great ones," he takes the clarified butter once into the vessel for the speckled butter; twice the curds and twice the clarified butter.

Now, if indeed on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa he should take it after mixing [the ingredients], then at the time of taking down [the oblation], they fashion two hairy effigies of rams out of wool from sheep that are not ewes.
In the absence of that, having mixed *kuśa* grass and wool together, he places a ram in the northwestern (māruti) enclosure and a ewe in the western (vāruṇī) enclosure.
Then, into these two, he scatters *śamī* leaves and *karīra* shoots, more than a hundred or more than a thousand in number.
Having added them to the *karambha* vessels, he places the sacrificial oblations upon the northern altar.
The Pratiprasthātṛ places one offering for Māruta and the bowls of parched grain (karambha-pātra) on the south side. 15 Here they exchange the two ram-effigies.
16 He places the ewe upon the offering for Māruta and the ram upon the offering for Varuṇa. 17
The two churning-sticks are like those for an animal sacrifice, and there are *sāmidhenī* verses; however, there are neither *prayāja* nor *anūyāja* offerings.
With the verse, "We invoke the Praghāsya gods," the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife forward and makes her recite this.
He asks her: "Wife, how many lovers do you have?"

"May Varuṇa seize those whom he names," thus he points them out. (21) If one were not to declare him who is a paramour, one would obstruct a dear kinsman. "This one is my paramour"—thus he should point him out. "Having pointed him out, he causes him to be seized by the noose of Varuṇa," so it is known.

(22) The northern fire is swept clean, while the southern remains unswept. Then, having gone between the two altars, the sacrificer and his wife—either to the north or along the northern altar—having placed the vessels of *karambha* in a winnowing-basket made of *aiṣīka* grass and having set it upon their heads, they stand facing west in front [of the fires] and offer with the winnowing-basket into the southern fire. (23)
The sacrificer recites the *puro'nuvākyā* verse beginning with "mo ṣū ṇa indra"; both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ] recite the *yājyā* verse beginning with "yad grāme.
24. They both mutter the two verses in reverse order, beginning with "akrankarma karmakṛtaḥ.
25. Or rather, either the Adhvaryu or the Pratiprasthātṛ may offer the oblation, while the other two should hold on from behind. 26.
Here he cleanses the southern fire (27).
Having performed the rites up to those for Indra and Agni, the Adhvaryu begins [the next stage] (28).
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts off the entire female sheep for the Maruts together with the first portion; he cuts the *śamī* leaves and *karīra* fruits with the second portion (29).
Then he proceeds with the offering. 30.
Then the Adhvaryu, with the first portion, cuts off the entire ram for Varuṇa; with the second, the *śamī* leaves and *karīra* fruits. Then he proceeds with the offering.
31. Thus ends the sixth section.
"Recite for the body! Sacrifice to whom!"—these are the two calls regarding the cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla).

He offers the cake on one potsherd with the four names of the months: "Nabhas" and "Nabhasya. Now, some indeed cut off portions for the *iḍā* separately; one should not do so in that manner. Having taken portions from all seven oblations together, the Adhvaryu hands them to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
Into that [vessel], the Pratiprasthātṛ adds the portion for the Maruts.
3. They consume it after it has been invited. 4. A bull that is as if aged is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 5.
If he so desires, however, he may give even more than that;
some say a cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

He invokes the blessing: "He prays for prosperity lasting a full year. In the blessings of the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ recites, "He prays for the divine abode. In this manner, the sacrificer mutters [the formula]; he modifies the mantra by saying, "He prays for... (instead of "He has prayed for...").

Both proceed with the two *vājina* offerings. Having poured the remnants together, they consume them in the northern sacrificial area as before, [reciting]: "May the drops enter me; O throat, fill my essence with the essence of the flowing streams. Of that which has been made into food by the *vāja*s, [I partake]"—the rest is the same. With the exception of the full-vessel offering (*pūrṇapātra*), he concludes the sacrifice as before.
In place of the *pūrṇapātra* (full vessel), there is the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) belonging to the Soma sacrifice.
There are four portions of clarified butter (*ājya*) taken up in four ladlings.
They perform the *avabhṛtha* with the dregs and the scrapings of the vessel dedicated to Varuṇa.
The Tuṣas receive the status of those who consume the *ṛjīṣa*.
Some recite a cake on one potsherd for Varuṇa.
He does not give a long-life offering, nor does he recite the mantra for departing, nor does he sing the Sāman.
The departure for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in all directions is prescribed.
Some say one should not go toward the north. Others say that they should proceed facing the direction in which they are going.
If flowing waters are available, one should approach standing waters. 21.
In their absence, one may act as one pleases. 22.
Having prepared an altar ending with the spreading of grass at the edge of the water, he places the sacrificial oblations upon it. 23.
Alternatively, there is no altar.
24. Having seen water, he mutters: "A hundred physicians are yours, O King, a thousand. 25. They step onto the edge of the water with the formula: "The noose of Varuṇa has been stepped upon. 26.
Having stepped into the water and standing therein, they perform the avabhṛtha rite.
(27) Having thrown a blade of grass [into the water], he makes an āghāra libation with the sruva-spoon.
(28) Or, if there should be a blade of grass already there, he should offer the oblation upon it. (29)
Thus ends the seventh section (kaṇḍikā). He issues the command: "O Agnīdh, wipe the waters thrice! 1. He adapts the mantra:

"O waters, winners of the prize, as you flow toward the prize, or as you are about to win the prize, you who are full of vigor, for the sake of winning the prize, I wipe you for the victory of the prize—O waters, eaters of food, for the sake of food-eating. 2.
With the words, "The face of Agni has entered the waters," he pours the butter from the ladle;
the sacrificer follows with the mantra, "Speech is yours, belonging to Agni. The *pravara* invocation is omitted.
Having performed the *prayāja* offerings excluding the *barhis*, he sacrifices the two *ājyabhāga* portions containing the word "water" (*apsumantau*).

"O Agni, in the waters... is this [verse]. "Soma has told me that within the waters are all remedies; both Agni, the source of universal well-being, and the waters, which possess all remedies"—these are the two containing the word "water. Having taken a portion from the *niṣkāsa* (remnant of the offering), and having sacrificed to Varuṇa, he takes the entire *niṣkāsa* and sacrifices it to Agnīvaruṇa for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
No response is made.
Or rather, having poured the contents of the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, he performs two after-offerings (*anūyāja*) excluding the one for the *barhis* grass.
He issues the first direction, "Sacrifice to the two gods," and the subsequent one, "Sacrifice."
Having filled a pot with husks, he stirs them in the water with the mantra: "In the waters is thy heart, within the ocean. 12.
Or rather, there is no *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) belonging to the Soma sacrifice; he should silently throw the scrapings of the husks into the water. 13.
With the mantra, "I untie this," the wife unfastens the bond of the *yoktra* (sacrificial girdle). 14.

Having consecrated the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) with the mantra "O divine waters... (*devīrāpaḥ*), the sacrificer, having stepped into the water with the mantra "May the waters and plants be friendly to us" (*sumitrā na āpa oṣadhayaḥ*), bathes together with his wife; both, including their heads, bathe without wiping themselves dry.
Then they run over each other's backs.
They may give these two garments to whomever they wish; for, according to the Vājasaneyaka, they do not remain the garments of the initiated.

Having worshipped the sun with the mantra, "We have risen above the darkness," and having gone back to the water's edge with the mantra, "The noose of Varuṇa is loosened," he prepares fuel-sticks and returns silently without looking back. Having placed fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra, "O Fuel, may we prosper through thee," they worship [the fire] with the mantra, "I have followed the waters. 18. At this point, after performing the Full Moon sacrifice, the returning [of the student] begins as before, starting from the washing of the feet.
19. Or, he may shave his hair entirely. 20.

The mantra and other elements are modified: "That which Varuṇa has turned back from the ends of the earth and from heaven—Agni, ruling by his might, Varuṇa together with his prayers, Indra with his friends the Maruts. "Agni with his sharp [flame]" and so forth is the same as before.

Alternatively, having bathed and shaved off his hair and beard, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇis*), and having moved away, he churns out the fire and performs the Full Moon sacrifice.
Indeed, this Varuṇapraghāsa is a sacrifice; for it is not appropriate that one should offer the Agnihotra on the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), according to the Vājasaneyaka.
Thus ends the eighth section; this is the second chapter.
Then, having commenced on the first full-moon day among four months, he sacrifices with the Sākamedha offerings for two days: 1.
He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavat, simultaneously with the rising of the sun. 2.
Or they proceed together with the *raśmi* formulas; the sacrifice is completed as established. At midday, [he offers] a pap (*caru*) to the Maruts Sāṃtapanas.

He does not throw the *barhis* grass after [the oblation]. The sacrifice is completed as prescribed. In the evening, he prepares a pap (*caru*) cooked in the milk of all [the cows] for the Maruts Gṛhamedhins.
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used for the *sāṃtapana* offering is the same as that for the *gṛhamedhīya*.
Alternatively, there is no fuel-stick (*idhma*) or sacrificial grass (*barhis*). He does not recite the *sāmidhenī* verses; neither the *prayāja* offerings nor the *anūyāja* offerings are performed.
Having driven away the calves without the accompaniment of a sacrificial formula (*ayajuṣka*), he milks the cows with a strainer (*apavitra*).

Having indeed driven away the calves with a leafy branch and having milked the cows while the *pavitra* strainers are present, some say that he cooks that *caru* oblation in the same manner as it is performed on the new moon day.

Having added fuel to the fires, prepared the *veda* grass-bundle, and strewn around the fires, he proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the washing of his hands. He arranges the vessels according to their purpose, placing a cooking pot (*sthālī*) in the place of the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*).
"At the time of the offering" (nirvapaṇa-kāle)—
this is the ninth section (kaṇḍikā).
Having measured out four handfuls, he pours in much more grain.

At the time of placing the potsherds, he places the *caru* with the first *kapāla* formula; he modifies the mantra to "Thou art firm" (*dhruvo 'si*). At the time of sifting the flour, he sifts the rice grains.
At the time of placing [the vessel] on the fire, having caused all the cows of the sacrificer to be milked—just as for the morning milking—he cooks it in that [milk].

At the time of the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*), he issues the command for everything other than the fuel and the sacrificial grass. At the time of taking the clarified butter, he takes it only in the *dhruvā* ladle.

Having consecrated the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), having addressed the Brahman priest, having sprinkled the altar (*vedī*), having poured out the remainder of the sprinkling waters, and having thrown back the two strainers (*pavitra*), he places the two separating blades (*vidhṛtī*) within the altar and sets down the *dhruvā* ladle and the *sruva* spoon. He modifies the mantra to "May these two sit down" (*etāvasīdatām*).
At the time of serving the food, having placed a blade of *śara* grass, he draws out as many portions of cooked rice as there are members of the sacrificer's household.
If there is more than this, he places many grains of boiled rice—
removed [from the husks], not winnowed, adorned, and sprinkled with ghee.
He cooks the neighbor's rice for the wife on the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni).
He does not pour clarified butter over it. 11.
The Vājasaneyins record the removal of two [portions]. "From the south he sacrifices to the Maruts Gṛhamedhinas.
12. Thus ends the tenth Kaṇḍikā.
From the northern [portion], he performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

Having made a depression between the two portions of boiled rice (*odana*) and having poured clarified butter (*ājya*) there, he prepares the portions for the clarified butter, or according to the Vājasaneyaka, from the *ājyasthālī* (the vessel for clarified butter).
While doing so, he should not take [the portion] from the *dhruvā* ladle.

Having performed the offerings of the two *ājyabhāga* portions, and having made an under-layer of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle and taken portions from all [the sacrificial foods], he sacrifices to the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins (4).
Having taken a single portion each from the northern half of all [the portions] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt (5),
there is neither the *prāśitra* nor the sacrificer’s portion (6).
The Iḍā ceremony concludes. 7.

Those who are the dependents of the sacrificer and who are entitled to eat the remnants of the sacrificial oblation eat the remains of the cooked rice; these may be either the officiating priests or other Brāhmaṇas. 8.
The Brāhmaṇas eat the cooked rice that is in the cooking pot. 9.
Well-satisfied and contented, they dwell this night with their faces turned toward non-retrogression.
Even their neighbors cook for them;
they slaughter cattle for them. 10–12.
They anoint and rub [the body]; they let the calves stay with the cows;
he sets down the vessel without having removed it.

He places the fuel-sticks on the fire one after another, without wiping them with the stirring-ladle. 16. During the latter part of the night, he binds two calves—one to the cow that has been milked for guests and the other to the Agnihotra cow.
17. When it has dawned, before the Agnihotra oblation is offered, they proceed with the rite of the full ladle; or, once the Agnihotra has been offered. 18.

Having filled a ladle with the charcoal from the hearth, he should summon a bull; while the bull is bellowing, he should run forward and, with the following verse, offer the full ladle into the Gārhapatya fire: "The full ladle has flown away at the bellowing of the bull.
(19) If the bull does not bellow, the Brahman priest should say, "Offer it! (20) He gives as a sacrificial fee that [ladle] into which he offers while the bull is bellowing. (21)

He offers a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts, the sportive ones, or to the Maruts who possess their own wealth. They proceed together with the rising sun, or together with its rays. The sacrifice is concluded in the established manner.
Thus ends the eleventh section. Then he commences the ritual procedure for the Mahāhavis.
The ritual procedure for this has been explained by means of the northern sacrificial enclosure (vihāra) used for the Vāruṇapraghāsa sacrifice.
At the time of the pouring out of the oblations, he pours out eight subsequent offerings, beginning with the cake on eight potsherds for Agni.

In the place of the *caru* for Indra, some recite a *caru* for Indra Vṛtrahan: "O Agni, perform the office of the *hotṛ*; perform the office of the messenger; stand upright at the sacrifice. May Heaven and Earth protect you; may you protect Heaven and Earth. Be the *sviṣṭakṛt* for Indra and the gods; enjoying this oblation of clarified butter, partake of it, Svāhā! With these words he pours the clarified butter from the ladle. The sacrificer follows with the mantra: "Speech is yours, belonging to Agni. 4.

He offers oblations on a single potsherd with the four month-names: *saha*, *sahasya*, *tapaḥ*, and *tapasya*. A cow is the sacrificial fee, or a bull that is aged. "He invokes the well-being of the year," and "He invokes the divine abode"—with these words from the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ recites the blessings. The sacrificer likewise mutters them. He modifies the mantra to "He invoked.
He places the husks dedicated to Indra and Agni into the water. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner.
Thus ends the twelfth section; thus ends the third chapter.
At that very time, he commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*).
Having prepared the sacrificial grass-bundle (*veda*), he constructs a four-cornered altar (*vedi*) of the height of the sacrificer in front of the *anvāhāryapacana* fire. 2.
The corners extend toward each direction, and the middles toward the intermediate directions.
(1) It is dug out; it becomes excavated.

(2) The altar is not to be dug out facing east, for this is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). (3) Nor is it to be dug out facing south, for this is a [sacrifice] to the gods. (4) Both directions are to be dug out in between, for it is known from scripture that both the gods and the ancestors are to be worshipped. (5)
He modifies those mantras associated with the gods that begin with "To the gods, to the ancestors," so that it becomes: "O Earth, the place of sacrifice for gods and ancestors.
Or rather, there is no modification, because one hears the words of another [in the original text].
Having performed [the rites] prior to the northern boundary-line (parigraha), he brings fire from the southern fire and places it upon the middle of the altar.
In this Pitṛyajña, the rites pertaining to the Āhavanīya fire are performed.
Having added fuel to the fires, he brings the sacrificial wood and the grass.
He cuts the grass together with its roots.

Or [the fuel] may be cut near the root; the sacrificial wood (idhma) for wealth and other purposes should be twelve years old and longer. Having strewn around the fires, he proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the washing of the hands. The arrangement of the vessels is according to their purpose.

At the time of the offering, having enclosed the altar on all sides and made a door to the north, he, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), offers the oblations to the south; or [he may do so] to the north while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), according to the traditional recitation: "To Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs... and so forth as prescribed. Now, according to some: [there is] clarified butter for Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs; a cake on six potsherds for the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass (barhiṣad); parched grains (dhānā) for the Pitṛs consumed by fire (agniṣvātta); a stirred drink (mantha) for Agni Kavyavāhana, or for Yama, or for Yama accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs.
A water-pot serves as the vessel for the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī).

Having mixed barley with the surplus *prokṣaṇī* water and having husked the rice grains three times, he divides them with the verse for division (*vibhāga-mantra*), setting aside those intended for the parched grains (*dhāna*) and grinding the others into flour. Having placed six potsherds on the southern half of the *gārhapatya* fire, he places the potsherd for the parched grains upon the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire with the first verse for the potsherds (Sūtra 18). At the time of placing [the grains], having poured the rice grains onto it with the verse for placing, he makes the parched grains multiform (Sūtra 19). "They remain lying around while being scorched," so it is known (Sūtra 20).
Thus ends the thirteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
At the time of the formal command (saṃpraiṣa), he issues the commands with the exception of the wife.
1. At the time of taking the clarified butter (ājya), he takes four portions of clarified butter to the north of the Gārhapatya fire. 2.
He proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* waters.
At the time of strewing, while strewing the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) three times from right to left around the altar, he goes around it.
Holding the wooden sword (*sphya*) aloft, he goes back around three times without strewing.
The *prastara* bundle belongs to Auddhava;
its taking up and placing down are performed silently;
there are no *vidhṛti* blades.
He lays down two enclosing-sticks (paridhi):
the middle one and the upper one.

Or he may lay down all of them; or, if at the time of the invocation he recognizes [the fire] by saying, "The enclosing-sticks are opened," he should place the southern stick together with the middle one.

At the time of carrying forth [the oblations], having carried forth the parched grains (dhānā) and divided them with the *vibhāga* mantra, he mixes half of them with clarified butter. 13. Having made groats from the other half according to the procedure for ground flour, he pours those groats into half a jar of the milk of an *abhivānyā* cow; then, facing south, he stirs them three times counter-clockwise without touching [the vessel] using either a single cane-stick or a stalk of sugarcane. 14. Having placed the stirred drink (*mantha*) on the stick, he sets down each of the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) one by one. 15.
To the south, having placed one by one a cushion, a pillow, collyrium, ointment, and a water-pot, and having laid down the *veda* grass-bundle, he proceeds with the *sāmidhenī* verses.

(16) He issues the command: "Recite for Agni, being kindled, for the gods, and for the ancestors! (17) He recites one *sāmidhenī* verse three times: namely, this one beginning with "We invoke you, who desire us" (*uśantas tvā havāmahe*). (18)

Leaving aside one *anūyāja* fuel-stick, he divides the remaining fuel-wood into three equal parts and places them on the fire three times. (19) [The procedure] is the same up to the *pravara*. (20) He does not choose an ancestral lineage (*nārṣeya*), nor does he choose a *hotṛ*. (21)
Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sit down, O Hotṛ! This much constitutes the *pravara* (the invocation of the ancestral lineage).
22 Having performed the *prayāja* offerings excluding the one for the *barhis* grass, he performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings containing the word "living" (*jīvat*).

23 "O Agni, with your beautiful light, grant us wealth that nourishes all life and compassion so that we may live. O Soma, you bestow great fortune upon the aged, and you [bestow it] upon the youth who follows the cosmic order (*ṛta*)."
"You bestow skill for the sake of living," thus [they become] possessed of life. 24.
Regarding this, some prescribe the enclosing of the altar. 25.
Thus ends the fourteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

Having loosened their sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*), they place them over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*). The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) walk around in reverse order; they transpose the offering-spoons (*sruk*), the oblations (*havis*), and the enclosures.

To the south of the *juhū* spoon, he places the *upabhṛt*; to the south of the *upabhṛt*, the *dhruvā*; to the south of the *puroḍāśa* cake, the parched grains (*dhānā*); and to the south of those, the stirred drink (*mantha*).
The *juhū* and the six potsherds (*ṣaṭkapāla*) are placed in the same location.
Some say that the Brahman and the sacrificer [are the two who eat].
(4) For those who offer five cuttings, there is a six-cutting; for those who offer four cuttings, there is a five-cutting.
(5) He cuts from the sacrificial cake while breaking it apart. (6)
One who performs the five-fold cutting should cut twice from the first portion.
Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, he issues the command: "Recite the *anuvākyā* for Soma accompanied by the ancestors; pronounce the *svadhā*!
He cuts once from the sacrificial cake, once from the parched grains, and once from the stirred drink.
Having cut off the portion from the south, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, and having stepped across toward the north, he stands facing south and causes the announcement:

"O Svadhā! He responds: "Let there be Svadhā! He issues the command: "Soma accompanied by the ancestors, Svadhā! He performs the sacrifice with the verse: "Those who [deserve] the Svadhā... He utters the *vaṣaṭ* call as "Svadhā namaḥ.
However, having prohibited the utterance of *svadhā*, for the Bahvṛcas and Vājasaneyins, he prescribes only the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta* formulas.

He recites two invitatory verses (*puro'nuvākyā*). Having recited the first verse, he utters the *praṇava*; having recited the second, he utters the *praṇava*. These verses, beginning with "O Soma, you are observant" (*tvaṃ soma pracikito*), are traditionally handed down.

There is one *yājyā* verse: "O Agniṣvātta fathers... (RV X.15.13). "Those who are Agniṣvātta and those who are not Agniṣvātta, the fathers who release from distress, who are worthy of Soma—whether they be higher or lower, being immortal—may they speak for us and may they protect us. Enjoying the groats (*karambha*) milked from the cow Vānyā, rising up, both the lower and the higher ones—the Agniṣvātta fathers, in harmony with the seasons and accompanied by Indra—may they enjoy this oblation. [This is] for the Agniṣvātta fathers.
(17) They perform the Pitṛyajña in a screened enclosure while whispering. (18)
In this very manner, he sacrifices to the Barhiṣad Pitṛs and the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs;
he sacrifices to Agni Kavyavāhana for the sake of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
He cuts off the first portion of the oblation for whichever deity he is sacrificing to.
And that is the Avadānakalpa: 22.
He cuts off the *iḍā* from the stirred drink (*mantha*), or indeed from the stirred drink itself; 23.
He places the stirred drink before the *hotṛ*. 24.
The Hotṛ smells it with the words, "25. This is the fifteenth section.
The Brahman, the Adhvaryu, the Agnīdh, and the sacrificer [smell it]. 1.
Or rather, the sacrificer does not [consume it];
or else, having divided it into equal portions and consumed it from the front, they wipe the remnants on the *barhis* grass.
Taking a water-pot, the sacrificer goes around the altar three times, pouring water to the left while saying, "May the ancestors be purified."
Having placed the water-pot, he walks around three times from right to left, sprinkling water as he goes, with the verse: "Making the earth his jar, producing various works.

Having pressed together the remnants of the oblation and formed them into balls, he places them on the three corners—namely, the eastern, the southern, and the western—with these mantras respectively: "This for you, O father, [Name], and those who follow you"; "This for you, O grandfather, [Name], and those who follow you"; "This for you, O great-grandfather, [Name], and those who follow you. He thus addresses three further ancestors: the sixth ancestor at the first ball, the fifth at the second, and the fourth at the third.

In the northern corner, he should wipe away the remnants of the *ripla* with the formula, "O Fathers, enjoy here according to your portions. Having spoken thus, they go out toward the north and worship the Āhavanīya fire with the verse addressed to Indra, "May we behold thee well," or with verses addressed to Indra until the sun sets.
Then, with the *paṅkti* verse, "They have eaten, they have rejoiced," they worship the Gārhapatya fire.
By this same [verse], they enter the enclosed space (*pariśrita*).
Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the eating and the sprinkling [of water].
(11) All [the portions] are to be smelled. (12) From the application of collyrium onwards, it is like the Piṇḍapitṛyajña until the end of the row. (13)
With the verse, "That which is the intermediate space," he returns with the *paṅkti* [meter].
Having untied their *prācīnāvīta* [arrangements], they make them into *yajñopavīta* [arrangements]. The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) move around; they transpose the offering-spoons (*sruk*).
They remove the enclosures.

Having poured the contents of the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, he performs two after-offerings (*anūyāja*) without the *barhis* grass. He gives the first summons, "Sacrifice to the two gods," and the second, "Sacrifice.
(17) At the *sūktavāka*, they turn their sacred threads over to the right. (18) They do not perform the offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*). (19)
He does not offer the *samiṣṭayajus* oblation; everything else is performed. The Pitṛyajña is concluded.
Thus ends the sixteenth section; thus ends the fourth chapter.
He prepares single-pot-sherd cakes for each person, as many as there are attendants of the sacrificer including his wives, with one additional cake.
While the cakes are being prepared, the sacrificer mutters: "For as many as we are, the householders, I have performed this service."
They attend to them silently.
He places them over the Gārhapatya fire on its northern half.

Having sprinkled them with clarified butter—or without sprinkling them—he removes them from the fire, places them within the altar, and pours them into a bag with the formula, "Thou art the protection of the animals."
Either in bags or within bags; according to some, they carry them away covered with a sheath.
"Rudra is indeed one; he did not stand for a second," [saying this], he carries a single firebrand from the Dakṣiṇāgni, emitting smoke.
Having gone to the intermediate direction between the north and the east, he scatters one *puroḍāśa* cake upon a mole-hill, saying, "O Rudra,
this mole is your animal," or while mentally meditating on someone whom he hates, "This [person] is your animal. If he does not hate anyone, he should say, "The mole is your animal."

Having kindled a single firebrand at a crossroads and having strewn grass around it, he takes a portion once from the northern half of each of the sacrificial cakes and offers them with either a middle or a terminal leaf of the *palāśa* tree, saying: "This, O Rudra, is thy share; together with thy sister Ambikā, enjoy it, Svāhā! With these two verses, "A remedy for the cattle... and "Down, O Mother, we have appeased Rudra...", he sprinkles water around the fire at the crossroads. The sacrificer mutters: "We have appeased Rudra here, O Mother... This is the seventeenth section.

With the verse, "We worship Tryambaka," they circumambulate the fire three times to the right. (2) A wife of the sacrificer who desires a husband should circumambulate with the verse: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the finder of a husband; like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from here, not fall [into misfortune]. (3) Having thrown out the sacrificial cakes so that they stand upright and having picked them up, they pour them into the joined palms of the sacrificer with the verse, "We worship Tryambaka"; then, taking them away with the words, "You are fortune; may I obtain you for fortune," they should pour them back together three times according to this same procedure. (4)
And those who desire husbands should likewise scatter [the grain] while adapting the mantra accordingly.
Some say they should scatter it after going around [the fire] both ways. He scatters them into two bundles, or into the bundles themselves.
"This is your portion, O Rudra," he says, as he hangs [the offering] on a tree, or on two trees, or on many trees;

or else, having gathered it in two bags, having made a carrying-pole, and having placed it upon a dry stump or in the mound of an anthill, they descend three times with the words, "With bow unbent, pināka in hand, clad in a skin.

Having sprinkled water around, they return silently without looking back. Having offered fuel-sticks into the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "O Fuel, may we prosper through thee," they stand worshipping with the words, "I have followed the waters."
Thus ends the eighteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
He offers a sacrificial pap (caru) of ghee to Āditya as before.
A white horse is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 1–2.
A cow that is white, or one whose limbs are white—3. The *iṣṭi* sacrifice is concluded. 4.

One desiring sight should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu; one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a pap (*caru*) to Bṛhaspati; one desiring cattle should offer [a cake] to Indra; one desiring offspring should offer [a pap] to Sarasvatī; and one desiring a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) should offer [a pap] to Pūṣan. 5.
Of these, he should offer whichever one he desires; thus the sacrifice is completed. The Sākamedha rites are concluded.

In this rite, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), the shaving of the beard and so forth is carried out as before; or he may have his entire hair shaved. The beginning of the mantras is modified: "He who on the skin of this earth shaves away the plants—Agni, ruling by his might, Varuṇa together with his prayers, Indra with his friends the Maruts. The formula "Agni with the sharp [blade]" is the same.
Thus ends the nineteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*). This is the fifth chapter (*paṭala*).
Then, after two days, three days, four days, half a month, a month, or in four months, he performs the *Śunāsīrīya* sacrifice.
The ritual procedure for this is like that of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
At the time of the offering, he pours out ten oblations in ascending order, beginning with a cake on eight potsherds for Agni.
The ritual procedure for the milk for Vāyu is like that of the morning milking.

Now, according to some: having offered five *saṃcarā* oblations, there is a barley-gruel for Vāyu, a *pratidhuk* (fresh milk) for Indra, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra Śunāsīra. "O Indra Śunāsīra, do you with the ladle offer our oblation; may the wise one enjoy it. Bring forth the ghee-rich offerings to him, the Lord of the bay horses, with one accord. O Indra, increasing through the seasons and through prayer, enjoy this oblation of Śunāsīra"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the sacrifice to Śunāsīra. There is a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya. (5) There are nine *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s. (6) According to some, there are five *prayāja*s and three *anūyāja*s. (7)
With the formula, "The gliding one; for Aṃhaspatya thee," he makes an offering of a cake on one potsherd to the month-names.
The sacrificial fee is a plough with twelve oxen, or one with six yokes.
According to some, [the offering] is for two camels (uṣṭārau);
or it is for one camel (uṣṭāram); or a white horse for the cake on one potsherd, or a white cow.

Thus ends the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā). The Hotṛ recites the blessings of the *sūktavāka*, saying, "He invokes the well-being of the year-long [rites]; he invokes the divine abode," and so forth. The sacrificer likewise mutters these; he adapts the mantra by changing it to "he invokes. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. The Cāturmāsya rites are concluded. Here, after performing the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), the shaving of the beard and so forth proceeds as before. Or, one may have all the hair shaved off. The beginning of the mantras is modified: "Parameṣṭhin released [one] month for the sake of creatures."

Therefore, bringing great bounty from them, [you brought] immortality to mortals. You are born again according to your offspring; that indeed is your immortal state, O mortal one. By which [power] the months, the half-months, the seasons, and the years [were established], by which they turned back for you, O Prajāpati, as you were sacrificing—with that sacred word (*brahman*) do I turn [the breath] back for this man so that he may live. "Agni with his sharp [flame]"—[this is] the same [as before]. (1) Having sacrificed with the Cāturmāsya offerings, he sacrifices with Soma or with an animal sacrifice.
(2) When the moon has risen on the full moon day of Phālguna, he undergoes initiation for the Soma sacrifice. (3)
If he does not drive it out from there, another Phālgunī [full moon] should pass him by.
This indeed is the rule for one who is letting go [of the ritual];
but for one who is taking it up again, having sacrificed with the Śunāsīrīya on the fourteenth day of the month of Phālguna.
Thus ends the twenty-first section (kaṇḍikā).
On the fifteenth day, he performs the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
One who desires cattle should perform this very sacrifice on that season of the year when there is most milk in his cows.

By this very [rite], one desiring offspring or desiring cattle should sacrifice. Now, according to some: in place of the other seasonal festivals (*parvan*), one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva until he obtains a thousand cattle; then he should sacrifice with the others at their own proper times.
One desiring a village should sacrifice with the Śunāsīrīya in the rainy season in water.
Having settled down by rainwater, he then performs the rites requiring water.
By this very [rite], one who desires offspring, cattle, prosperity, spiritual luster, or food should sacrifice.
He designates the months by means of the joints during the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
We shall explain the five-year cycle (pañcasāṃvatsarika).
Having performed sacrifices for three seasons and three years, he does not sacrifice for one month. Having performed the two subsequent [seasons], he ceases.
Or, having commenced on the full moon of Caitra, having performed two [seasons], and having failed to sacrifice for one month, he ceases after performing the next three [seasons].
Then, one should practice these very same [vows] for fifteen years— twice,
thrice, or for an unlimited time.
And it is known from scripture that "he does not sacrifice for one month during each set of three years"; this repetition refers to that statement.
(15) In the five-year cycles, however, the Vaiśvānara-Pārjanya offering and the Pañcahotṛ rite do not recur, because they constitute a single undertaking. (16–17)
"As in the Anvārambhaṇīyā, as in the Anvārambhaṇīyā.
Thus ends the twenty-second section (kaṇḍikā). Thus ends the sixth chapter (paṭala).
Thus ends the eighth book (praśna).
An expiation characterized by scriptural injunction is prescribed for the transgression of a rule.
(1) When multiple expiations are heard in relation to a single fault, they should be combined because they serve distinct purposes.
(2) These include recitation, burnt offerings, and sacrifice. (3)
4. They are for the purpose of expelling defects.
5. Immediately after a defect, [the following] should be performed.
6. Once the defect has been removed, the entire ritual action is to be performed again.

There is no re-performance of the rite merely because of his silence. (7) One who has maintained the sacred fires, when about to depart, should offer oblations with the verse, "To you, O best of Angirases.
(8) Having consigned the fires into separate sets of kindling woods, he sets out. (9)
Wherever he may dwell, he should conclude this *iṣṭi*.

10 If the *āhavanīya* fire of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*anvāhitāgni*) should go out, he should lead forward another fire with the verse, "Agni has looked toward the forefront of the dawns," and having worshipped it with "Bhūḥ," he should offer a full *sruva*-ladle as a universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) with the formula, "To him who, possessing oblations, seeks to win Agni for the feast of the gods—O Purifier, be gracious to him, Svāhā! Then he should offer an oblation with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode across this [world].
11 Some say he should merely recite [the verse]. 12

Mentally, he should mutter the *yajus* formula for undertaking the vow. 13. Whoever should follow [the fire], he should repeat this same procedure, omitting the leading forward [of the fire]. 14. He should churn the *gārhapatya* fire. 15.
Whatever is the nature of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire:

if the fire of one who has established the sacred fires should go out, he should walk three times around it from left to right as far as the range of the throwing of the yoke-pin, reciting, "The lord of booty, the sage Agni... (RV 10.87.21), and then he should gather it together with the formula: "This is one for thee, and another beyond; enter into union with the third light. Be pleasant for the body through entering into union; be dear to the gods in the highest birthplace. (VS 12.54). If it should go out further away, he should move forward along it and settle there.
One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt.
One should fetch sacrificial grass from near a path. An ox is the sacrificial fee. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner.
Then, when the next day has dawned, he settles back into his domestic duties.
If the calves set aside for the oblation should suckle [the mother cows] instead of that [intended] place, he should offer a barley gruel to Vāyu in their stead.
Then, having set aside the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should observe the fast.
If the evening milk used as the oblation should meet with misfortune, one should set aside rice for Indra and fast;
whatever [milk] there may be in the morning, that he should have cooked. Then the other [offering] should be a cake for Indra.
Having taken portions from that [milk] and the morning milking together, he should proceed with the offering. 28.
This very same rite is the expiation when the morning milking has failed. 29.
Having taken portions from that [milk] and the evening milking together, he should proceed with the offering. 30.
If both udders of a cow should suffer distress, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and five measures of boiled rice to Indra.
(31) One should sacrifice to Agni with the cake and to Indra with the five measures of rice. (32) Or, one may sacrifice to both deities with the five measures of rice alone. (33)
Then, having driven away the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should fast.
(34) Thus ends the first section. If on the day of the vow his wife should be in her courses, he should perform the sacrifice after having sent her away. (1)
Behind the altar, or within the altar, he should spread out the cord for binding toward the north.

When she has been impregnated for three nights, then he should invite her with these words: "I am heaven, you are earth; I am Sāman, you are Ṛc. Come, let us unite; let us both deposit seed for the sake of obtaining a male son, for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor."

If one’s *agnihotra* or *sāṃnāyya* should spill, he should go away toward the north, dig up a mound of earth from an anthill, pour [the spilt milk] onto that anthill-mound with the verse addressed to Prajāpati, “O Prajāpati, these [beings] are not thine,” and having worshipped it with the word “bhūḥ,” he should milk another cow and offer again. If the *sāṃnāyya* has been lost, he should bring in another.

If an insect should fall into it, he should pour it out within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the verse addressed to Heaven and Earth, “The great Heaven and the Earth for us...,” using either a middle or the lowest leaf of a *palāśa* tree; then, having milked another cow, he should offer again. If the *sāṃnāyya* has been lost, he should bring in another.

"If one's *agnihotra* should rain upon it, [one should offer] with [the verse]: "Mitra, the wise one, ordains people; Mitra has supported the earth and the sky; Mitra gazes upon the tribes with unblinking eyes; for the sake of truth, he offers the oblation rich in ghee. Having done that and having milked another [cow], he should sacrifice again. (6)

If, when the first oblation has been offered, the second oblation should spill over, or if one should offer the first oblation with the second verse, then—having recited the verse addressed to the tree, "O Lord of the Forest, where you know the secret names of the gods, there cause the offerings to go"—and having placed a fuel-stick upon it, he should offer silently from that very spot, milk another cow, and offer again.

(7) If, when the first oblation has been offered, the Āhavanīya fire should go out, he should offer [the oblation] either on a nearby wood-shard or on gold, while saying, "Fire is in the wood; in the wood is fire. (8)

If, prior to the *prayāja* offerings, a burning coal should fall outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he should press it down with the base of the *sruva* ladle, saying: "Do not let darkness overcome me; do not let the sacrifice perish; do not let the sacrificer perish. Homage be to you as you come; homage, O Rudra, as you go away; homage where you sit down! Do not harm the *adhvaryu*; do not harm the sacrificer!"—if it falls in the east. "Do not harm the *brahman*; do not harm the sacrificer!"—if it falls in the south.

"Do not harm the *hotṛ*; do not harm the wife; do not harm the sacrificer," [he says] if it is from behind. "Do not harm the *āgnīdhra*; do not harm the cattle; do not harm the sacrificer," if it is from the north.
Having taken hold of him [the horse] with the words, "I take up the sacrifice from the lap of Nirṛti; I entrust it to the gods," [this is the second section].

"The thousand-horned bull, Jātavedas, whose back is the *stoma*, who is rich in clarified butter and fair of count—may he not abandon us; may we not abandon you when you are kindled. Grant us prosperity in cattle and prosperity in heroes. With these words, he throws it into the fire (1).
Or, having thrown it, he should make an offering over it (2).
If, at the close of the time, the fire is not produced while being churned, he should fetch another fire from wherever he can find one and offer there (3).
Then, without hurrying, he should churn again;
if he cannot find another [fire-drill], it should be offered into the right ear of a she-goat.
However, he must not eat from that goat.
If he should not find a goat, the offering is to be made in the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa;
however, one should not detain a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of lodging.
If he should not find a Brāhmaṇa, the offering is to be made into a clump of Darbha grass.
One should not sit upon *darbha* grass;
if one cannot find *darbha*, the oblation should be offered in water.
One should not discriminate against water, saying, "This is fit for drinking" or "This is unfit for drinking."
One should observe this [rule] even regarding food that is unfit to be eaten for the duration of this year;
however, one should not wash one's feet with water. Āśmarathya maintains that these vows last for one year, while Ālekhana maintains that they last as long as one lives.
After a year has passed, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati.

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat for those among whom both preceding and succeeding members die in succession. Or, in the event of a house fire, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Viviciya for one whose consecrated fires have been mixed with other fires, or have become intermingled with one another.

To Agni Vipṛc, an offering on eight potsherds, if the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires [are separate]. "Through Agni Vipṛc, we meditate upon the hymn with our songs; may he grant us thousands. "Agni, the sage, is kindled, the inspired priest who perfects the sacrifice. Granting us wealth by distributing it, may you bestow riches upon us"—these are the invitatory and offering verses (yājyā-anuvākyā). To Agni Vīti, an offering on eight potsherds, if the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgni fires [are separate], or if the Dakṣiṇāgni and Āhavanīya fires [are separate].

To Agni Śuci, an offering on eight potsherds, if [the fire] has been kindled by a forest fire, a funeral pyre, or a corpse-fire. To Agni Saṃkusuka, an offering on eight potsherds, if [the fire] has been kindled by the fire of birth-impurity. "Saṃkusuka, Kusuka, the scatterer and the one who scatters—by means of beans, clarified butter, and Nala fuel, we pacify the flesh-eating fire. In this Saṃkusuka fire, we wipe away our blemishes; we have become worthy of sacrifice, purified. May he prolong our lives"—these are the invitatory and offering verses.
To Agni Apsumat, an offering on eight potsherds, if [the fire] has been kindled by lightning. 22.

If all [the verses] should come together, one should examine them and, having determined them, offer the *vrātabhṛt* as the third, the *apsumatī* as the fourth, and the *kṣāmavatī* at the end; one should cause it to proceed around the perimeter.
Some recite the *vrātabhṛt* as the second and the *vrātapati* as the last.
Thus ends the third section (kaṇḍikā).

"May Agni, Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Bṛhaspati make the leaking embryo free from poison; may it flow away upon the earth, and may it not reach Nirṛti. Having consecrated the leaking *agnihotra* vessel with this mantra, he should join it together with the mantra, "The moon that has fled...

(RV 10.72.8). "One who performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt," so it is said. Or, if the main sacrifice is performed within the same ritual framework (*samānatantre*), the primary offering should be made.

Now, according to some: "The sacrifice of one whose sacrifice is interrupted by the performance of this *iṣṭi* during its extension is indeed split apart. One should offer that same cake on eight potsherds for Agni which belongs to the full moon or the new moon to Agni Pathikṛt (the Maker of the Path). By that very act, he finds his way back again and does not cut off the sacrifice; so it is known.
Furthermore, it is taught that the two *saṃyājyā* verses themselves should belong to Pathikṛt.
It has already been stated regarding him whose sacrificial oblation has been set out when the moon rises in the east.
If the sun rises before the oblation has been poured out, one should offer it with the *prākṛtī* verses; thus says Āśmarathya.
One should remove [the offering] when the rice grains have become [separated];
thus says Ālekhana, [saying they belong to those whose portion is failed].
If the moon rises after the [milk] has been set aside, one should remove the remainder from the original [oblation] portions once they have become rice-grains.

For one whose oblation has not yet been taken out when the moon rises, or who did not intend to undertake the vow of observance, he should divide the rice-grains into three parts as before. Then, having driven away the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should fast.
Now, if the moon should rise while the sacrificial oblation has already been taken up, that same expiation applies and that same observance of the vow is required.
Having reunited the calves with their mothers and having driven them away again, one should set aside on the previous day the milk and curds for the purpose of mixing with the oblation.

One who has established the sacred fires, having acted as if he has violated his vow—whether by traveling abroad or by eating meat or approaching a woman on a day when the vow is to be observed—should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati. 13–15.

If one should shed tears due to distress, [he shall offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratabhṛt. "O Agni, you who bear the vows, pure one, seat the gods here; O Agni, for the carrying of the oblation! Bearing the vows, the protector of vows, undeceivable, worship the gods for us—you who are ageless and rich in heroes—bestowing jewels, easy to find, O Agni, protect us that we may live, O Jātavedas! These are the invitatory and offering verses. Some prescribe the *Vrātabhṛtī* [offering] during a journey, and the *Vrātapatī* at the time of shedding tears.
Thus ends the fourth section; thus ends the first chapter.

If the cow consecrated for the *agnihotra* should low while being let loose, one should offer an oblation or address her with the mantra: "From whatever fear you have lowed, from that grant us security; grant us security for our cattle; homage to Rudra, the bountiful giver. (1)

If she should sit down, he should address her with this very [verse]: "From whatever fear you have sat down," and then, having raised her up with the words, "The goddess Aditi, of all forms, has placed life in the lord of the sacrifice; making a portion for Indra, for Mitra, and for Varuṇa," he should cause her to stand. Having milked her, he should give her to a Brāhmaṇa whose food he would not otherwise eat. "He thus fastens misfortune and evil upon him," so it is known.
Alternatively, having crushed her repeatedly with a staff, he should raise her up and take her for himself.

"O blessed one, may you have good pasture; may we also be blessed. Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you come. Having plucked a bunch of *darbha* grass, he should make her eat it.

(4) If she should indeed yield red milk, having said, "Step aside," and having enclosed the southern fire, he should cook this [milk] upon it. Having offered it with the *vyāhṛtis* or silently, he should give it to a Brahmin whom he does not intend to visit again. (5)

If the milk being milked should spill, he should consecrate it with the mantra: "Whatever milk today has clung to the earth, whatever has flowed into the plants, whatever into the waters—let there be milk in our houses, milk in the cows, milk in the calves; let that [milk] be mine. Having thus consecrated it, he should pour water over it with the mantra: "I send you forth to the ocean.
If the vessel being milked should break, he should wash another one and milk into it, or he may milk into that very same one.

If the milk being milked, or being carried away, or already carried away, or being placed on the fire, or already placed on the fire, or being removed from the fire, or already removed, or being ladled out, or already ladled out, should spill, then it should be offered exactly as it is, regardless of its state; or else, another portion should be milked over it.

If what has been ladled out once should spill, or twice, or thrice, one need not pay heed to it. But if what has been ladled out for the fourth time should spill, one should pour the remainder back into the pot, ladle it out four times again, and offer it; or else, another portion should be milked over it.
Thus ends the fifth section.

If it should spill while being hurriedly carried, he should sit down, take it up again, and offer it exactly as it was, whatever its condition may be; or else, having milked another cow, he should offer again. Or, having recited the verse addressed to Varuṇa over clarified butter, he should sacrifice with that verse to Varuṇa.
If it should spill toward the east, he should offer it exactly as it was, whatever its condition may be, or it should be milked again by means of another [verse].

Now, according to some: if it should spill while being carried forward, one should consecrate it with the mantra, "Thou art offered as the body of Prajāpati, the sustainer of all, svāhā! and this itself shall be the *agnihotra*, says Āśmarathya; [but] Ālekhana says that one should milk another cow and offer again. If it should spill after having been carried forward, one should carry it back, pour four spoonfuls into it, and offer it; or else, one should milk another cow. If it should spill before the [milk] has been set down, one should offer it just as it is, however it may be; or else, one should milk another cow.

Now, according to some: if the oblation that has been presented but not yet offered should spill, it should be offered again exactly as it was, in whatever state it may be. Then, having milked another cow, it should be offered again; or else, one should offer with clarified butter—this part is the same.

"Sky and earth have spilled; the young bull has spilled upon the cows. May this entire world, having spilled, cause the sacrifice to procreate.
