From what has spilled, the progeny is born; from what has spilled, the bull is born. From what has spilled, may we procreate. Having thus consecrated the spilt [milk], he should pour water over it with the mantra, "O Earth, be moistened.
If it is only a mere drop that is not a full oblation, that is indeed just a droplet (vipruṭ).
If it should spill in the evening, he shall not eat until the morning offering; if it should spill in the morning, he shall not eat until the evening offering.

Indeed, a divine thunderbolt falls upon him whose *agnihotra* makes a hissing sound (*śiriśirā*). He should say, "May it burn that one," naming the person whom he hates. If a dog should run between the fires while the *agnihotra* has been placed on the fire-stand, he should take ashes from the *gārhapatya*, scatter them from the *āhavanīya* while reciting the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, "Viṣṇu strode across this," and having stepped forward, he should fill the dog's footprint with those very ashes.

If the sun should set while someone’s fire has not been carried forth, and he sees it shining elsewhere, he should carry that [fire] from there and enter this [fire]; thus indeed is this [fire] established. (12) This is the ritual procedure for re-establishing the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) when it has gone out. (13) If the sun should set while someone’s fire has not been drawn out... (14)

Thus ends the sixth section (kaṇḍikā). Having tied a piece of gold with a blade of *darbha* grass, he should carry it in front. A Brāhmaṇa who belongs to a [Vedic] lineage (*ārṣeya*) and is well-versed in the scriptures should carry the fire behind him. He should follow behind the Agnihotra oblation. Having established the fire upon the gold in its proper place, having set down the regular Agnihotra, and having sat without breathing until the sun sets, he should stir the fire, offer the oblation, and after worshipping with "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ," he should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) to Varuṇa.
Some authorities prescribe the *vrātabhṛtī* offering as the second. Some [prescribe] the carrying forward of the fire even without the gold.

If the time for the evening *agnihotra* should pass by, one should offer the oblation that compensates for the lapse of time with the formula, "To Vastor, homage! Svāhā! Then, having set down the regular *agnihotra*, one should remain seated without breathing until the sun sets; then, having stirred [the milk] and offered it, one should worship with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. If the morning [time] should pass by, one should offer the oblation that compensates for the lapse of time with the formula, "To Vastor, homage! Svāhā! Then, having set down the regular *agnihotra*, one should remain seated without breathing until the sun rises; then, having stirred [the milk] and offered it, one should worship with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. A choice gift is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Having offered into the Āhavanīya fire and extinguished it with the verse, "Agni has looked upon the forefront of the dawns," one should lead forward another fire with the formula, "Be secure right here; do not abandon me, [Name], the son of [Father's Name]. Having worshipped the Sun, he should offer a pap (caru) to Mitra.
Some authorities prescribe a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya.
When the sacrifice is completed, on that very day, the sacrificer and his wife, maintaining the Āhavanīya fire, remain without eating and restrained in speech.

In both cases, one should offer the evening *agnihotra* with milk as before. If the sun should rise while the fire has not yet been carried forward (*anudghṛta*), one should carry four ladles of clarified butter (*ājya*) in front. A Brahmin of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) who knows much of the sacred lore should carry the fire behind him. He should follow the fire with the *agnihotra* offering. Having established the fire in its proper place, he should sacrifice toward the west with clarified butter, saying: "May Uṣas with her banner rejoice in the sacrifice accompanied by the gods; to the gods, the most honey-sweet, Svāhā! This is the ritual procedure for the *agnihotra* offering itself. That same expiation which applies to one who has let the morning time pass applies here as well.
The difference is only this much: here he does not follow the *āhavanīya* fire [when it goes out].
12. Now, according to some: "If the sun should set or rise while his fire has not been carried forth"—this is the seventh section (*kaṇḍikā*).
One should offer two portions of four ladles each with the verses: "May the mind, the light, enjoy it" and "The thirty-three threads.

(1) If the sun should rise upon one whose Agnihotra has been set out but not yet offered, that is as if one who is about to give birth were not to give birth; indeed, the sacrificer obstructs his own self or suffers the loss of everything. Having placed the perpetual Agnihotra [fuel] down, sitting without breathing until the stars appear, and having stirred [the fire], he should offer and then worship with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ. (2) A one-year-old calf is the sacrificial fee.
(3) Āśmarathya says that after offering and removing that [fire], the re-establishment of the fire (*punarādheya*) is its expiation.

Now, according to some: if [the fire] should go out at the end, having drawn [the milk], he should run forward toward the east. Having set it down, he should sit until he faints. When he faints, then he should offer with "bhūḥ svāhā. Prajāpati is indeed "bhūta" (become); he thus resorts to him, and he (Prajāpati) raises him up from there; the sacrificer does not meet with ruin—so it is known.
If one's Agnihotra should be interrupted for two days, three days, or four days, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat.

"The bull with sharpened horns, shining brightly, making for himself a path easy to traverse and free from exhaustion, looking back toward his ancient dwelling place, Agni has stretched out the celestial thread. "Thou art our thread and our bridge, O Agni; thou art the path that leads to the gods. By thee, O Agni, may we ascend to the ridge, and then may we rejoice in the communal feast with the gods"—these are the invitatory and offering verses (yājyānuvākyā).
"Stretching out the thread, wake up, O Agni! "Up from the highest [darkness]," "Up from the darkness," "Up that bright [light]"—these are the secondary offerings (upahoma).
We invoke Agni Sviṣṭakṛt—the bearer of oblations, the overcomer of adversaries, the slayer of Rākṣasas, the victor in battles, the radiant, the shining, the far-seeing.
O Agni, fulfill this well-offered sacrifice; O God, overcome all hostile armies for us. Show us the wide path, shine forth, and grant us a long life, full of light and free from decay.
These are the two *saṃyājyā* verses. Thus ends the eighth section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the second chapter (paṭala).
Some prescribe this same *iṣṭi* for every case of [the fire] having gone out.

The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are: "Come, O Agni, among the people with your heat, purifying with your flame; come to this my excellent praise. "Come to us, O Agni, among the people with your heat, shining, O Purifier; placing our oblations among the gods.
When the *āhavanīya* fire has gone out, he offers an eight-potherd cake to Agni Jyotiṣmat.

If, when the evening *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, the eastern fire should go out, one should place the *agnihotra* milk on the fire, heat it, and then follow after [the fire] with both the fire and the *agnihotra*. A Brāhmaṇa who is well-versed in the Veda should carry it forth; he should give whatever wealth he had previously intended to give. It is known from scripture: "By means of the imperishable, he causes him to move forward.

If, when the morning *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, the western fire should go out, one should cause the former fire to go out, churn a new fire as before, draw forth the latter fire as before, and then offer the oblation.
If he should hasten, having settled first [the fire], he should then draw it out toward the east and offer.

But that is a repetition (*jāmi*), for he makes what was previously behind into what is behind again. Having settled elsewhere, having churned as before, and having drawn out the latter fire as before, he should offer. Then, on the following day, [the rite] beginning with "To Agni Tapasvat Janadvat" is the same.

Now, according to some: if one's fire goes out, he should not wait for the [prescribed] time. Having followed the fire [to its end], he should churn out another fire as before; having drawn it out as before, he should offer oblations. Or he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara and a porridge of barley to Varuṇa. If either the Gārhapatya or the Āhavanīya fire goes out, it should be churned from those very embers. If there are no such embers remaining, he should touch the two kindling woods with ashes and then churn; "he thus generates him from his own womb," so it is known. This same procedure applies when the fuel consists of wood chips or grass.

"To Agni, the ascetic, the one who possesses people"—this is the same [as before]. 13. Or, in place of the *anugateṣṭi* sacrifice, he should offer these oblations: "To Mitra, svāhā! To Varuṇa, svāhā! To Agni, svāhā! To Agni, lord of vows, svāhā! To Agni, the ascetic, the one who possesses people, the purifier, svāhā! To Agni, the pure, svāhā! To Agni, the luminous, svāhā! To Sūrya, svāhā! He should offer them with the *vyāhṛtis* both separately and combined. 14. Thus ends the ninth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
If the Āhavanīya fire should go out before the time of the oblation, one should lead forth another from the Gārhapatya.

(1) If at the time of the oblation the Prāṇa has gone into the Udāna, one should offer in the Gārhapatya. (2) If the Udāna has gone into the Prāṇa in the Gārhapatya, one should offer in the Āhavanīya. (3)
If the Dakṣiṇāgni has gone out, [one should offer] in the Gārhapatya, thinking, "The Vyāna has entered the Udāna.
(4) If all the fires should go out, one should churn the fire and, having carried it toward whichever direction the wind blows, offer it with the formula, "To Vāyu, svāhā!

(5) Or, indeed, if it is windless, after churning the fire and establishing the sacrificial hearths (*vihāra*), the sacrificer, having sat down behind the Āhavanīya, should himself drink the Agnihotra milk; for it is known from tradition that this constitutes a substitute for the Agnihotra offering. (6)
If he should offer before sunset, he should offer again after sunset and worship [the fires] with the verse, "May you two be of one mind toward us.

(7) If [he offers] at the dead of night, he should offer again at dawn and worship with this same [verse]. (8) If, while sprinkling the oblation, he should sprinkle over the fire, he would be sacrificing with a burnt sacrifice.
"May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again"—with these words, he should rekindle the fire.
(9) This applies in the case of all impairments of the fires.
(10) One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Agnivān for him whose fire they might carry out from another fire. (11)
Āśmarathya says that they should perform an expiation in whatever manner they might recover [the fire].
Ālekhana says that if they should perceive it while it has not yet been formally deposited, they should follow it [to its source] and there is no expiation.
It has been stated: "To Agni Jyotiṣmat, an offering on eight potsherds. 12–13.

Then he should offer an oblation with the verse: "Thirty-three are the threads... (VS 2.28). If, while the *sāṃnāyya* has been placed on the fire or the sacrificial food (*havis*) has been set out, a man, a dog, a chariot, a wild boar, or a water-snake should pass between the two fires, he should sprinkle water there and drive a cow through that spot, saying: "May prosperity increase; may the sacrifice release the lord of the sacrifice from distress through curds and clarified butter—Svāhā! (VS 2.29).

"May the sacrifice reach the gods, the Agni, and the Yajña; may the blessing of the sacrifice come to me from there! May the sacrifice reach the Pitṛs, the Pañcajanas, the quarters, the waters, the plants, and the trees; may the blessing of the sacrifice come to me from there! Having offered these six oblations, he should sweep together the path with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode across this," or he should mark out the footprint. 16.

If his cart or chariot passes between the two fires, he should extinguish the Āhavanīya and re-establish it from the Gārhapatya with these two verses: "O Agni, that place of yours which was first set forth, for it has extended along the rays of the sun; bring back thence that which abides in wealth, and unite us with your favor accompanied by strength. "O Agni, you are far-reaching"—with these two [verses]. Then he should offer the *pāthikṛtī* oblation as before. He should offer this very same [oblation] again. Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).
If one is deluded during the *stotra* or the *śastra*;
or if they should separate the fires with their own breaths; or if someone else should separate them;
or if they should carry the fires apart from the fires [of the altar].
For one who has died among the people,
he should offer the Agnihotra with the milk of a cow that suckles another's calf until the body has been touched by the fires;
all this, however, should be performed silently.
He causes [the cow] to be milked while wearing the sacred cord over the right shoulder (pācīnāvītī).

Having taken those darbha grass blades which were pointing eastward and turned them so that their tips point southward, he places the vessel upon the cool ashes in the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire-hearth. Having removed it from the fire toward the south, he pours all of it out in a single motion silently. Holding a fuel-stick beneath [the vessel], he steps out toward the south of the sacrificial ground (vihāra). For it is known from scripture: "For one holds [the offering] above for the sake of the gods. (Sūtras 7–9)

Having approached and placed the fuel-stick on the fire, he should offer everything at once in silence. Alternatively, he may designate Soma Pitṛmant for the first oblation and Agni Kavyavāhana for the second. The acts of tasting, pouring out, and sprinkling around do not exist here.
He gives the sacrificial implements to the Brahmins;
he indeed gives those made of iron. They cast the earthen vessels into the water; [this is] immortality itself.

If a son should die, [there should be] a stone [as the sacrificial fee]. (16) If they should hear that he has died when he was previously thought not to have died, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat.
(17) If the sacrificer should die after the first oblation has been offered, one should pour the subsequent oblation onto the cold ashes from the south. (18)
Or he should cause [the fire] to go to the heap of ashes (19).
Some say that one should perform here that very same first oblation which is performed in the Pitṛmedha (20).

If the sacrificer should die while the sacrifice is in a state of disorder, one should take portions from all [the offerings], recite the names of all the deities, and offer with the utterance "svāhā" (21).
If an Āhitāgni who has gone abroad should die and his death be unknown, they should burn a thicket with his fires in the direction toward which he had set out. 22.

Alternatively, they fashion a human figure on a black antelope skin using three hundred and sixty palāśa stalks. Having wrapped the joints with palāśa bark or *kuśa* grass, they form the head with forty stalks, the neck with ten, the chest with twenty, and the belly with thirty. With fifty stalks they form each arm; from those same [fifty], they fashion five fingers for each by means of five stalks each. With seventy stalks they form each leg; from those same [seventy], they fashion five toes for each by means of five stalks each. With eight stalks they form the penis, and with twelve the testicles.

Having fashioned a human figure out of those [skins] upon a black antelope skin, having bathed and adorned it, and having spread the black antelope skin within the sacrificial altar (vedī) with its neck toward the south and the hair facing downward, they lay the deceased upon it supine; having covered him with a new cloth with its fringes toward the feet, the relatives sit around him. The attendants touch him, saying, "This is he, whose these fires were," once he has passed away. From this point, the ritual procedure is undertaken. Having performed that, they should burn him with the fires; so says the Vājasaneyaka. 23

If, when the sacrificial oblations have been set down, a black bird should fly over them repeatedly, as if shaking its wings, and alight upon them, one should offer an oblation with the verse: "Viṣṇu strode across this [world].
(24) If it should fly away high, one should not take heed of that.
(25) If, while being erected, the sacrificial post or its top-ring should fall, one should offer an oblation with the verse: "The Brahman is the foundation of the mind. (26)
Thus ends the eleventh section (kaṇḍikā).

If one should cause the after-offerings (anūyāja) to be announced while the remnants of the oblation have not yet been removed, he should offer an oblation with the verse: "O gods, whatever I may have overstepped among you... (RV 10.2.31).

If the *praṇītā* waters should spill or run out, he should take them up again with the three verses beginning, "O Waters, you are indeed refreshing" (RV 10.9.1–3), and then offer an oblation with the verse, "That which has been stretched out for me, O Waters... (RV 10.9.6).

If, at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the sun should not become visible, one should offer oblations with the verses: *ud vayaṃ tamasas pari*, *ud u tyaṃ citram*. If jackals should howl after him, saying, "The jackal has howled! The one-footed has howled! We are beset; make for us a boundary," he should add fuel to the fire with a *pālāśa* wood and offer six oblations with the verses: *imaṃ me varuṇa*, *tattvā yāmi*, *tvaṃ no agne*, *sa tvaṃ no agne*, *tvamagne ayāsi*, and *prajāpate*. Then he says: "I set up this boundary for the living, so that no other may reach their midst."

"May they live a hundred long autumns, placing death beyond them with a mountain"—with these words, he places a stone as a boundary-marker on the south. The fuel for a Kṣatriya is from the Nyagrodha tree, at the boundary of his kingdom;
that of a Vaiśya is from the Aśvattha tree, at the boundary of his domain.
One should offer eight oblations with the formula "To the beloved ones, svāhā! These may optionally replace all the expiatory rites (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

(7) If one sees an evil dream or perceives another cause for fear, one should offer oblations with the verse, "From what we fear, O Indra... Some say that one should merely recite [the verse]. (8) "Indeed, the *gharma* of all luminaries shines; therefore, upon hearing that the *pravargya* is being prepared, or while the *pravargya* is being performed, one should offer oblations with the verses beginning 'With these songs...'. Some say that one should merely recite [the verses]. (9)

If the sacrificer should eat while the fires have been kindled for the *homa* but the oblations have not yet been offered, he should offer two oblations with the verses, "That which we [have done] as it were... (*yatte vayam yathā ha tat...*) or he should add two pieces of fuel-wood. Some say he should merely recite them. (10) With these two verses, "Whatever flaw has occurred in my self" (*yan ma ātmano mindābhūt*) and "Agni has given back my sight" (*punar agniś cakṣur adāt*), one who has seen the sun set while the fire is unextinguished, or who has seen it rise while the fire is unextinguished, or who has neglected the sacred fires, or who has superseded his younger brother in marriage, or who has been superseded by a younger brother, or who has married before his elder brother, should offer oblations. Some say he should merely recite them. (11) One should offer three oblations with the verse, "The unknown sin" (*anājñātam*) when the offense is unknown. Some say he should merely recite them. (12)
Thus ends the twelfth section; thus ends the third chapter.

If one's clarified butter (*ājya*), before it has been purified (*anutpūta*), should spill, he should give [a substitute] after cutting out a living creature. If it has been purified (*utpūta*), a variegated object should be given.
According to some, a boon should be given (3).

If there is anything in his ladle or whatever may be abundant in his house, that he should give. With the words "I sprinkle thee," he should either pour [the water] over it or consecrate it with the mantra (4).
According to some, immediately after the clarified butter, he recites the verse, "The sacrifice has gone to the people of the gods" (5).

"By the measure of the sacrifice, by the over-measure, by the counter-measure, and by the up-measure, I encompass thee"—having thus encompassed it, he measures a span eastward with the formula, "To Bhūpati, svāhā!"; southward with "To Bhuvanapati, svāhā!"; westward with "To Bhūtānāṃ pati, svāhā!"; northward with "To Bhūti, svāhā!"; and upward with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ.

It is heard in the scripture as a general rule for all oblations that one should consecrate what has been spilled with the formula, "To Bhūpati, svāhā; to Bhuvanapati, svāhā; to Bhūtānāṃ pati, svāhā! without exception.

If the potsherd should break, he should join it together with the formula, "With the Gāyatrī of a hundred syllables, I join you," and then, while it is being held over the Gārhapatya fire, he should offer an oblation upon it with the mantra, "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering].
Then he should pour water over it with the formula, "The Gharma is unbroken, the giver of life.
Then, having prepared another one, he should place it among the potsherds with the formula, "Thirty-three threads. This applies if it breaks before the pouring of the milk.
Now, if one should place another [potsherd] with this very same mantra after those already placed,
or if there should be a displacement from the place of a mantra;

or if, among those already employed, a potsherd should be lost before the performance of the purposeful rite (*arthakarman*), one should offer a two-potsherd oblation to the Aśvins and a single-potsherd oblation to Heaven and Earth.

The Bhārgava is the Hotṛ; a one-year-old [cow] is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Regarding this, the Vājasaneyins prescribe a spoon-offering with the verse addressed to Heaven and Earth: "May the great Heaven and Earth...
Thus ends the thirteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

"If a cake on one potsherd should leap away or roll back, [he recites]: 'Follow the path of Prajāpati; may we prosper with heroes, with cattle, with horses, with all nourishments, with offspring, and with sensory power. May the gods lead our sacrifice straightway. Thus he restores it to its proper place."

The sacrificer consecrates it with the mantra: "I establish myself in the kṣatra, I establish myself in the kingdom; I establish myself in horses, I establish myself in cattle; I establish myself in progeny, in what is to be. One [brick] has increased everything; that is placed upon the other. To Dyaus Viśvakarman and to Pṛthivī, I have paid homage. Then he should offer oblations with the formula, "May Dyaus not leap over Pṛthivī.
If, while performing the *saṃyājana* of the wives, he should drop a potsherd, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
It is said: "He who is a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices should offer this very same [oblation]."
One should offer this very oblation if one should eat of the new grain without having performed the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.
For he who has established the sacred fires is brought near to the gods; if he were to eat his allotted portion before it is prepared, he would meet with misfortune.
One should offer a cake on thirteen potsherds to the Maruts for him whose twins are born, whether they be two cows or two men.
A man indeed desires lack of vigor; a cow desires the absence of offspring.

One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu for him whom they might cause to sacrifice in another's fires, or for him in whose fires another might sacrifice. One should offer a pap made of vāstu-grain to Rudra for him whose cattle Rudra might seek to destroy.

With this very same procedure, one should cause the Niṣādasthapati to sacrifice; for that is his sacrifice. It is known from tradition that the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is either a black antelope skin, or a horn, or a donkey, or a deer, or a spotted deer, or a vessel of Śyāmāka grain, or a hoof-ring.
Thus ends the fourteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
If a religious student (brahmacārī) should approach a woman, he should sacrifice a donkey as an animal offering. He should bake a cake on one potsherd (ekapāla-puroḍāśa) upon the ground.
They should proceed with the portions [of the victim] in water;
[otherwise] it would have the Rakṣases as its deity or Nirṛti as its deity.
One should worship Nirṛti with a Pākayajña.
If the oblation of anyone is burnt, Nirṛti seizes that sacrifice. Having completed that [original rite], he should offer another oblation intended for that same deity.

Now, according to some: if the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) of anyone is burnt, Nirṛti seizes that sacrifice. He should proceed with whatever remains as the residue; he should give that sacrificial fee and the remnant of the oblation to his enemy. "He thus causes Nirṛti herself to seize him," so it is known. This is the expiation for the burning of everything.
If he should not be able to offer the oblations,
or if the sacrificial offering intended for a particular deity should be spoiled, he should offer another oblation to that same deity;
in that case, the mantras beginning with the taking up of the ladle (sruc) should be repeated.
Or, if it should be spoiled at the end,

he should conclude the remainder with clarified butter (ājya) dedicated to the respective deity. If all his sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) should be lost, spoiled, or stolen, he should perform the sacrifice by enumerating those deities with clarified butter.
Then he should perform another sacrifice that is not excessive; for a sacrifice is indeed the expiation for a sacrifice.
It is known from tradition: "One pours spoiled sacrificial food into water.
One should not sacrifice with that which is unfit to be eaten by the Aryas.

It is known from scripture: "The sacrificial oblation for which the *puroḍāśa* is poorly cooked belongs to Yama; it goes to Yama. Having completed that [rite], one should cook four *śarāva*-measures of boiled rice on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire and feed four Brāhmaṇas.
Among those who eat, there should be one who is a descendant of Bhṛgu.
That sacrifice by which one sacrifices without giving a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is emaciated and does not lead to long life; one should give a fertile field as a gift.
If one should omit the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), an excellent and established gift should be given; that is the expiation (21).

If one should invoke a deity who has no share [in the sacrifice], one should worship her with clarified butter (*ājya*) according to how she was invoked, either before or after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering (22).

If one should fail to invoke a deity who does have a share, one should rise up at the moment one remembers her, invoke her mentally, and offer an oblation with the verse: "Whatever, O gods, I may have overstepped" (*yad vo devā atipādayāni*) (23).
Thus ends the fifteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

If, before the fore-offerings (prayāja), an oblation should fall outside the enclosing sticks (paridhi), he should say to the Āgnīdhra: "Having gathered this [offering], offer it. He offers it with his joined palms (añjali). A full vessel (pūrṇapātra) should be given to him.
Whatever earthenware vessel should break during the sacrifice, that he should throw into the water with the mantra: "Earth has gone to earth."
The implements are made of wood for the Āhavanīya fire.

If a failure in the sacrifice should occur on account of the Ṛgveda, one should offer an oblation into the Gārhapatya fire with the word "bhūḥ. If it occurs on account of the Yajurveda, one should offer into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the word "bhuvaḥ. If it occurs on account of the Sāmaveda, one should offer into the Āhavanīya fire with the word "suvaḥ.
If it occurs on all accounts, one should offer into all three fires.

Āśmarathya says that this universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) should be performed in all cases. Ālekhana says it should be performed only where it has not been specifically prescribed. There is yet another view: there should be an accumulation [of expiations] in every case. If he should encounter danger while in the sacrificial enclosure (*vihāra*) or outside it, he should offer an oblation with the mantra: "Prajāpati Viśvakarman—may I succeed through sacrifice with his mind as the deity. O Lord of the dwelling-place, may the wealth of him who has abandoned me find a dwelling for me. If his prepared oblation (*havir-nirupta*) should spill, he should give a living creature as a gift. If it spills after it has been purified (*utpūta*), a multi-colored object (*citra*) should be given. According to some, a choice gift (*vara*) should be given.

If one should transpose the deities of the portions (*avadāna*), the oblations (*havīṃṣi*), or the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses; or if the portion taken for a deity should spill before it has been offered; or if there is a transposition of deities—one should give whatever is abundant in his house as a substitute.
Some say that in every case of such a transposition, one should offer these two oblations with the verses, "Thou art ours, O Agni" (*tvaṃ no agne*) and "So thou art ours, O Agni" (*sa tvaṃ no agne*).

If one's sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) should fly away or become disintegrated, having removed it and placed it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he should consecrate it with these two [verses] and pour [clarified butter] over it: "Why do you fly up? Why have you flown away? Being pacified, come here for the sake of peace. Becoming non-terrible and worthy of sacrifice, sit in your own place; sit in your own place. Do not harm us, O god sent forth; be anointed with clarified butter and with splendor. Do not injure anything of ours. For the sake of the peace of acquisition and security, sit upon this sacrificial grass.
11. The sacrificer becomes powerful when they perform this expiation at his sacrifice. 12.

Thus ends the sixteenth section; thus ends the fourth chapter. The sky has spilled, the earth has spilled, this entire world has spilled. All beings have spilled; from that which has spilled, let the oblation be born. Here let cattle multiply, here horses, here men. Here let the abundance of wealth, accompanied by a thousand sacrificial fees, settle down. May this sacrifice increase with cattle and horses; may this altar be rich in offspring and heroic sons. May this sacred grass surpass other grasses; may all the gods protect this sacrifice.

With these four verses beginning with *payasvatīroṣadhayaḥ*, one should consecrate the spilled *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter), pour water over it, wash the ladle, place a *śatamāna* weight of gold in the ladle, take another portion of *pṛṣadājya* while reciting *idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame*, have a horse smell it, and set it down in its proper place. Now, according to some: if *pṛṣadājya* is spilled, having taken up more *pṛṣadājya* from the remaining *pṛṣadājya*, he should offer an oblation with the verse *mano jyotirjuṣatām*.
Likewise, if *soma* is spilled, having taken up more *soma* from the remaining *soma*, he should offer it.

"Whatever the bird has touched with its beak, O Nirṛti, may Agni, the bearer of oblations, the purifier of ghee, purify all that"—with these words he consecrates what has been touched by a black bird. The disposal and so forth are as before; however, the vessel is scraped clean here. "Whatever the dog-eater has licked with his mouth, O Nirṛti, may Agni, the bearer of oblations, the purifier of ghee, purify all that"—with these words he consecrates what has been licked by a beast of prey. The disposal and so forth are as before; however, no vessel is used here, for he takes [the remainder] in another [vessel].

If the animal, having been brought forward for sacrifice, should bleat, one should offer an oblation with the verse: “Whatever [is] beyond this region...”; and one should offer or address it with the mantra: “From whatever you fear, O Bleater, from that grant us freedom from fear; be gracious to all our offspring; homage to Rudra, the Bountiful.

(6) If, however, it should sit down, one should offer a second oblation with the same verse: “From whatever you fear, you have sat down. (7) Once it has sat down, the Adhvaryu should make it rise with the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa. (8)

Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā). "Rise up, O bull; stand firm; do not perish; do not harm this sacrifice or the sacrificer. Place the sacrificer in the world of heaven; be a source of well-being for our two-footed ones and a source of well-being for our four-footed ones.
(1) With "Rise up, goat! he addresses the goat; with "Rise up, ram! the ram; with "Rise up, cow! the cow. (2)
Because of fear of whom you trembled most—[reciting] the second [verse] while trembling;
"because of fear of whom you fled"—[reciting] the second [verse] when he has fled;
if he does not come, one should sacrifice after having offered another animal of the same form, color, and age, dedicated to that same deity.
Because of the fear of whom the known things stand still—this is the second [verse] for the unconscious immolation;
"Homage to him who has done this, to him Svāhā!"—this is the third [verse] everywhere.

Or rather, one should not do so; having caused the animal to enter the water with these four verses—"Verily you do not die here," "Thee, O all quarters," "The quarters of all quarters," and "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss"—and having offered another animal of similar form, color, age, and deity, one should sacrifice.
Because of fear he urinates, thus he makes a second urination; because of fear he voids excrement, thus he makes a second voiding of excrement.
(9) He consecrates with the mantra "Upwards, up for us, for our protections" the one who is being raised up.
(10) If, while being offered to drink, he does not drink, one should make him drink with the words "Or else you will die here. (11)

12. He addresses the omentum as it flows with the verse: "The womb that leaks, the Agada, the Hotṛ, the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky—from wherever it has fallen, let that reach Agni alone; let Nirṛti go away. 13. It has been stated [in the ritual manual]: "When they lead the consecrated animal toward the north... 14. If those who have disturbed the animal should be desired by him so that they may meet with misfortune, he should offer an oblation in the Āgnīdhra fire with the verse beginning "kuvidaṅga" which contains the word "namovṛkti"; or in the Āhavanīya or Śāmitra fire in the case of the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice.

If the omentum, the oblation, or the portioning should spill, he should take it up with the mantra: "I take thee for glory and for heroism; O inviolable ones, do ye bestow upon us power and milk. Then he should offer an oblation with: "Thy drop, thy overflow, the divine banner which has entered the entire world—protect us for our safety, Svāhā!

(15) If he should realize that [the vessel] has eight feet, he should offer two oblations with the mantras: "The Ordainer, the Giver, the Sun, the god who dwells in heaven," and then, having wrapped an eight-pronged golden ornament with a turban, [he should place it on the head].
(16) Thus ends the eighteenth section.
Having placed [the embryo] in the first sheath, having placed it in the second, he places it in the third.
Having made the sheaths as if hollowed out, the Adhvaryu then consecrates it with the mantra: "O you whose embryo is golden.
Having turned the embryo clockwise with the words, "Turn back, O Turner," he strips away the amnion with the words, "I split open your caul."
Let her be outside; having cast out the embryo from within her thighs, having impaled it on a spit and carried it to the *śāmitra* fire, he cooks it.
(4) With the verse, "The wide-dropping, all-formed drop," he brings a vessel near for the essence of the embryo.
(5) Having offered the sacrificial cake for the animal victim, he offers the sacrificial cake for the embryo, as well as a one-potsherd cake for Heaven and Earth. (6)

Having performed the ritual with the *paśupuroḍāśa*, he proceeds with the *garbhapuroḍāśa* (the sacrificial cake of the embryo), following the division for the *dyāvāpṛthivī* offering. (7) While cutting the portions for the deities of the animal victim, having first cut one portion from the region of the embryo's navel, he places it among the portions for the deities; the other portion he places later among the *sauviṣṭakṛta* portions. (8) He distributes the essence of the embryo into three parts, among those for the deities, the *sauviṣṭakṛta*, and the *iḍā*. (9)
He offers with the verses "The one-footed, the two-footed" prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering (10).
Gold weighing eight *prūḍ*s is the sacrificial fee (11).
Having cut off the right forefoot of the fetus, he sacrifices to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa with the verse, "I proclaim today thy name, O Śipiviṣṭa," or with the following verse (12).

With the verse, "O Maruts, he whose dwelling... [he places] the embryo and the embryo-cake to the north of the Gārhapatya or the Śāmitra fire, having covered them in cold ashes. Then, having gathered them together with cold ashes using the verse, "May the great Heaven and Earth for us...", he worships it with the five verses beginning, "This youth...
(13). Āśmarathya says that this expiation for a pregnant [cow] should be performed everywhere; Ālekhana says it should be performed only where it is specifically prescribed. (14)

If the sacrificial post (yūpa) should sprout before it has been released [from its consecration], one should offer a Tvaṣṭṛ-related animal sacrifice, taking as the victim for the *savanīya* a castrated, hairy, tawny, multicolored bull.
Regarding this, the Vājasaneyins prescribe an oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Some, however, say that one should offer only spoonfuls (*sruvāhuti*) dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ at this point.
Thus ends the nineteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

If the sacrificial post (yūpa) should be hollow, the sacrificer would die from dysentery. Having offered oblations with the verses addressed to Viṣṇu, the Vyahṛtis, and the verse addressed to Prajāpati, he should cut that post down, cast it into the fire, and then prepare another.
If it is infested with worms, worms will devour him; the expiation is as before.

If it should leap over the cutting-block, one should know: "The wife will act improperly toward him. The subsequent ritual, beginning with the *vyāhṛtis*, is the same. (3) If it should fall to the south, or if it should break back toward [the sacrificer], or if it should become entangled in the branches, the sacrificer will die. In place of the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, one uses a verse addressed to Yama. The subsequent ritual is the same. (4) If it should fall into the water, he will die in the water. In place of the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, one uses a verse addressed to Varuṇa. The subsequent ritual is the same. (5)
If they should seize everything by force, one would be defeated; at the place of the Vaiṣṇavī [verse], there is an Aindrī; the rest is the same. 6

If the root [of the sacrificial post] should wither, one should know that he will not perform the ancestral rites as before. If it withers in the middle, he will die of hunger. If it withers at the top, he will not go to the heavenly world. If the part near the fire (the base) should break, the sacrificer will die. If the eastern part [breaks], his wife will die; or conversely, this may apply to the other parts. If the southern part [breaks], a son born of a buffalo-woman will die. If the northern part [breaks], the eldest son will die. If the south-eastern part [breaks], the Brahman priest will die. If the south-western part [breaks], the Hotṛ priest will die. If the north-western part [breaks], the Adhvaryu priest will die. If the north-eastern part [breaks], the Āgnīdhra priest will die. 7.

In all cases beginning with the dry wood, the subsequent procedure for the southward direction and so forth is the same. (8) If reddish lines should circle the sacrificial post counter-clockwise, one should know: "He will not perform a sacrifice involving a thousand [cows]. If they are white and circle it clockwise, one should know: "He will soon perform a sacrifice involving a thousand. (9) If, when the oblation has been offered, black smoke should strike toward the southern direction, or if the wind should swirl the smoke counter-clockwise, the sacrificer would die. One should offer the universal expiation; one should offer it. (10)
Thus ends the twentieth Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the fifth Paṭala;
thus ends the ninth Praśna.

One who is about to sacrifice with Soma chooses Brāhmaṇas as Ṛtvij priests who do not claim descent from a famous Vedic lineage (anārṣeya), who are either young or old, who are learned (anūcāna), whose speech is clear, and who are free from physical defects.

To them he announces the Soma. He asks them: "Who are the officiating priests? Who are performing the sacrifice? Is it not an Ahīna rite? Has the office of the priest not been abandoned? Are the sacrificial fees auspicious? For thus says the *Chandoga Brāhmaṇa*.

Then he mutters: "Greatness you have spoken for me; splendor you have spoken for me; glory you have spoken for me; praise you have spoken for me; prosperity you have spoken for me; enjoyment you have spoken for me; everything you have spoken for me; may that protect me, may that enter me, through that may I enjoy."
Or rather, [he thinks]: "Since you are the path named *sruti*, the channel for Soma, may I go to the Soma"—with this thought he stands upon the path.
(5) "May the god go to the god; may Soma go to Soma; by the way of Truth, leaving behind all evil deeds"—with these words he proceeds forward.
(6) Turning to the right, he worships the ancestors with the formula: "O Fathers, Bhūr! (7)
He chooses all four of them, either collectively or one by one:

the Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and the Unnetṛ—these are the Adhvaryus; the Brahman, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Āgnīdhra, and the Potṛ—these are the Brahmans; the Hotṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Acchāvāka, and the Grāvastut—these are the Hotṛs; the Udgātṛ, the Prastotṛ, the Pratihartṛ, and the Subrahmaṇya—these are the Udgātṛs. The Kauṣītakins prescribe the Sadasya as the seventeenth.
He becomes a supervisor of the ritual acts: 11.
if there are four [priests] at the beginning; 12.
or else, the *varaṇas*. 13.

"Agni is my *hotṛ*, Āditya is my *adhvaryu*, Candramas is my *brahmán*, Parjanya is my *udgātṛ*, Ākāśa is my *sadasya*, the Waters are my *hotrāśaṃsin*s, and the Rays are my *camasādhvaryu*s"—this is the silent announcement of the deities (*devatādeśana*). "So-and-so is the human [priest]"—this is said aloud. Thus ends the first section (*kaṇḍikā*).
One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma in the spring.
2. The Agniṣṭoma is the first sacrifice. 3. Some prescribe the Atirātra as preceding it. 4.

"Every spring, one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma; its sacrificial fees are three," so says the Chandoga Brāhmaṇa. One should perform the first sacrifice with either the Rathantara-sāman, the Bṛhat-sāman, or both sāmans.
Some say that one should not undertake the Bṛhat-sāman without having previously performed the Rathantara-sāman.

If one should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, or with an animal sacrifice, or with Soma, he should sacrifice either on the new moon day or on the full moon day. (8) "O divine Varuṇa, grant me a place for sacrifice," thus the sacrificer should beg the king for a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*).

(9) If he grants it, [the king] says to him, "May you become possessed of a sacrificial ground. If he does not grant it, [the sacrificer says], "On whatever sacrificial ground I know, there I shall consume you. (10)

Then they address him with these words: "The Brahman priest says, 'You have struck down the mind; the mind will desert you. The Hotṛ priest says, 'You have struck down speech; speech will desert you. The Adhvaryu priest says, 'You have struck down the breath; the breath will desert you. The Udgātṛ priest says, 'You have struck down the eye; the eye will desert you. The Sadasya says, 'You have struck down the self; the self will desert you. The Sacrificer says, 'You have struck down progeny; progeny will desert you. The Hotrakas say, 'You have struck down the limbs; the limbs will desert you. All the officiating priests say, 'You have struck down all beings; all beings will desert you.'"

Thus ends the second section (kaṇḍikā). The King requests the sacrificial ground (devayajana): "Agni is the Hotṛ; he is my Hotṛ. O Hotṛ, give me the sacrificial ground," thus [addressing] the Hotṛ. "Āditya is the Adhvaryu; he is my Adhvaryu. O Adhvaryu, give me the sacrificial ground," thus [addressing] the Adhvaryu. "Candramas is the Brahman; he is my Brahman. O Brahman, give me the sacrificial ground," thus [addressing] the Brahman. "Parjanya is the Udgātṛ; he is my Udgātṛ. O Udgātṛ, give me the sacrificial ground," thus [addressing] the Udgātṛ.

"Space is my *sadasya*; may that *sadasya* grant me a place for the sacrifice to the gods"—thus [he addresses] the *sadasya*. "The waters are my *hotrāśaṃsins*; may those *hotrāśaṃsins* grant me a place for the sacrifice to the gods"—thus [he addresses] the *hotrakas*. "The rays are my *camasādhvaryus*; may those *camasādhvaryus* grant me a place for the sacrifice to the gods"—thus [he addresses] the *camasādhvaryus*.

Alternatively, one need not request a place for sacrifice. One should instead stand near the deities [with these words]: "Look at this, O Vidhartṛ; look at this, O Nāka; look at this, O Ramati. They call him the most praiseworthy, the highest, the immortal. Sūrya, the most excellent, shines with his rays across heaven and earth, the two who have the gods as their sons.
With the words, "We have come to this sacrificial ground of the earth," he settles upon the sacrificial ground.
According to the Vājasaneyaka, he mutters [this] while grasping the central pillar of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall.
Then he offers the *saṃbhāra-yajus* oblations;
the section beginning with "Agni with the *yajus*-formulas, Savitṛ with the *stoma*-chants" is prescribed [in the text].
At this point, having brought the King (Soma), they serve him with milk-rice until the time of purchase.

"Sit here on your own skill, O father of skill; in the favor of the gods, for great delight. Resting in your own seat, settle yourself with your body; be like a father to his son, very gracious. As the auspicious one, enter me as the auspicious; my soul is truth, my faith is imperishability, and austerity is my foundation. May the quarters, impelled by Savitṛ, consecrate me. 'I am Truth'—with these words, before the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, the sacrificer worships the Āhavanīya fire. Having mentally recited the *Saptahotṛ* formula and offered it into the Āhavanīya along with the cup (*graha*), [the ritual proceeds].
Thus ends the third section. He initiates the procedure for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering.
He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; or rather, a caru-oblation in clarified butter to Agni and Viṣṇu.

A cake is for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); a caru-oblation in clarified butter is for one who desires offspring or cattle. Some authorities prescribe a second caru-oblation in clarified butter to Aditi for one who desires both offspring and cattle.
There are fifteen or seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. Some prescribe the *prāgvaṃśa* hall first; others [prescribe] the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering. The *dīkṣaṇīyā* concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
He holds the clarified butter firmly.
(8) He performs the rites silently from the point prior to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.

(9) Now, according to some: he recites as much of his speech as he possesses during the Dīkṣaṇīyā offering; lower than that during the Prāyaṇīyā; lower still during the Ātithyā; in a whisper during the Upasads; and loudly at the Agniṣomīya. (10)

In the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering], one uses a low tone; in the *prāyaṇīyā*, a lower tone; in the *ātithyā*, an even lower tone; in the *upasad*s, in a whisper; and in the *agnīṣomīya*, loudly. Alternatively, in the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, one may use a whisper; in the *prāyaṇīyā*, a quieter whisper; in the *ātithyā*, an even quieter whisper; in the *upasad*s, in a whisper; and in the *agnīṣomīya*, loudly. (11) In the *soma* sacrifice, which has the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as its archetype, the following do not take place: the piling of the fire (*agnyanvādhāna*), the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*), the eating of forest food (*āraṇyāśana*), the keeping of the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*), the giving of the *anvāhārya* rice, the girding of the wife (*patnyāḥ saṃnahana*), and her untying (*vimocana*). (12)
The adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) should be performed at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, as well as the girding of the wife.
During the initiatory rites (*dīkṣās*), he has the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) prepared;
[or rather, it is prepared] after the King Soma has been purchased, or during the *upasad* days.
Thus ends the fourth Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the first Paṭala.
He constructs the hall with the beams pointing eastward (prācīnavaṃśa), high in the front and low in the back, enclosed on all sides, with corners in the intermediate directions. 1. 2.

He places the *ārokas* on the corners; there are doors in each direction: a door in the east for one who desires heaven; in the south for one who desires, "May I prosper in the world of the fathers"; in the west for one who desires the world of men; in the north for one who desires, "May I prosper in the world of the gods"; in the northeast for one who desires, "May I prosper in both worlds"; and on all sides for one who desires, "May I prosper in all directions."

To the north, outside the *prāgvamśa* hall, in an enclosed space, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved. First the armpits, then the beard, then the hair; or alternatively, first the beard and armpits, then the hair. With the formula, "May the waters moisten [you]," he moistens the right side of the head where the hair is parted. Having placed a blade of *darbha* grass with its tip pointing eastward between [the hair and the skin] with the formula, "O herb, protect him," and having applied the razor with the formula, "O axe, do not harm him," he shaves the hair with the formula, "The gods' beard."
In this manner, [the sacrificer] mutters the subsequent [verses]:
"O herb, protect me! O axe, do not harm me! May I attain safety through what is beyond.
He has his nails trimmed on the inside. 10–11.
Starting from the little finger of the left hand, [he cleanses] twelve times;
then, starting from the tip of the forefinger, he cleanses with water thirteen times.
He brushes his teeth with an Udumbara twig, taking care not to cause blood to flow.
He bathes in still waters that contain shells, that do not foam, at a hairy bathing place;
having placed gold in a pool, he bathes therein—so says the Vājasaneyaka.
Thus ends the fifth section.

"May the waters, our mothers, purify us," [he says]. "The golden-colored, pure, and purifying waters have moved forward, leaving behind all that is blameworthy; for within them a hundred filters are stretched out—by means of these may the god Savitṛ purify us. With these two verses, beginning with "The golden-colored, pure, and purifying," he murmurs as he steps out from the water, saying, "Pure and purified, I emerge from the waters. He drinks the water.
The wife does the same, except for the hair.

Then he gives him a large garment of linen cloth. He accepts it with: "Dīkṣā (Consecration) art thou, the womb of austerity; austerity art thou, the womb of the Brahman; the Brahman art thou, the womb of the Kṣatra; the Kṣatra art thou, the womb of Truth; Truth art thou. O Earth! I undertake faith with my mind, consecration with austerity—the sovereign lady of the whole world. May all the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled."

"You are the body of Soma; protect my body. You are the consecration (*dīkṣā*); you are the body; may I clothe myself in you, who are auspicious and pleasant. Having thus clothed himself, he arranges the fringe (*nīvi*) with the formula, "You are the fringe of Soma. 6. With the words, "For strength (*ūrj*) you," he eats food mixed with clarified butter, curds, and honey as an addition.
7. He eats whatever is dear to his heart. 8.
It is known that this very same [state] occurs for him in the other world. He should eat such food that he may observe a progressively lighter vow during the consecrations (*dīkṣā*).
Some prescribe eating before the shaving of the hair or the putting on of the garment.
With the formula, "Thou art the milk of the great ones," he scrapes out fresh butter with two bunches of *darbha* grass.

With the mantra "Thou art the bestower of luster," he anoints himself three times from front to back: first the face, then the limbs in the direction of the hair. "He becomes well-anointed"—thus ends the sixth section.
With the formula, "Thou art the eye of Vṛtra," he applies collyrium made from the *traikakuda* plant.
According to the Vājasaneyaka, if he cannot find *traikakuda*, he may apply any kind of collyrium whatsoever.
With a blade of *darbha* grass together with its tuft, or a blade of *śara* grass, or a bunch of *darbha* grass, he applies it twice internally on the right eye without blinking; once on the left.

Or rather, he sprinkles the right [hand] twice and the left three times; or he sprinkles both three times each. Then, to the north of this [spot], outside the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, he purifies him with bunches of *darbha* grass. It has been stated: "He purifies with two [verses]; he purifies with three [verses]."
With twenty-one [straw blades] divided into three sets of seven each, he wipes upwards from the navel twice; once downwards.
Some say he purifies him by wiping along the length [of the body].
He should purify one whom he hates by wiping across or diagonally.
With each of these mantras, beginning with "May the Lord of Thought purify you," he recites them one by one;

to every one of them, he adds the phrase "with an unbroken strainer" (acchidreṇa pavitreṇa). While being purified, he mutters: "May the Lord of Thought purify me; may the Lord of Speech purify me; may the divine Savitṛ purify me."

And [he recites] "O you whose garment is the purifier" (*tasya te pavitrapate*) and "The purifying one, who dwells in the light, the all-seeing, with his purifier—may he, the Purifier, cleanse me. With that golden purifier of a hundred strands, belonging to Prajāpati, we who know the *brahman* purify the *brahman*" (13).
And [he recites] "Whatever offense against the gods, O Agni, you have...
(14). Or he may offer oblations before the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice; some say he should merely mutter [the mantras]. (15)
Thus ends the seventh section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the second chapter (paṭala).

Having entered the *prāgvaṃśa* hall by the eastern door with the verse, "O gods, we entreat you," and having passed to the south of the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula, "Indra and Agni, Heaven and Earth," he sits down near the *āhavanīya* with the formula, "Thou art the lord of consecrations.
1. From this point onwards, this indeed becomes the path for the sacrificer's movement. 2.
Regarding this, some prescribe the *dīkṣaṇīyā* (initiation offering) [at this point];

others [prescribe] the *saṃbhārayajūṃṣi* (formulas for the gathering of materials) before the *dīkṣāhutis* (initiation oblations). From the *dhrauva* clarified butter used for the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, he offers four *dīkṣā* oblations with the *sruva* spoon, and the fifth with the *sruc* ladle, using these formulas respectively: "To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā! and so forth.
Having filled the *sruk* ladle with twelve portions, he offers the sixth full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse, "Of the god who is the leader... (RV 1.89.6).

At the point where the Adhvaryu offers the *audgrahaṇa* oblations, the sacrificer, holding onto the Adhvaryu, offers five oblations: "May my speech be consecrated by speech, svāhā! May my breath be consecrated by breath, svāhā! May my sight be consecrated by sight, svāhā! May my hearing be consecrated by hearing, svāhā! May my mind be consecrated by mind, svāhā! (TS 6.1.1.5–6).
Or, he may recite these formulas over the Adhvaryu while he is offering.

"We take hold of the wind, the breath, with our mind, [and] Prajāpati, who is the guardian of the world. May he protect us from death, may he save us from distress; living long, may we attain old age"—with these words, he recites this mantra over the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as it is being offered. (9) Some [teachers] say that here the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas are recited.
(10) He consecrates the sacrificer with a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). (11)
One should consecrate oneself with two [skins] joined together, with the flesh on the inside and the hair on the outside.
If there should be only one, one should sew it to the right foreleg, or to the edges.
Some say that one should fasten two [skins] crosswise, or sew them to the leg.
Within the altar, he spreads a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair facing upward.
With the words, "You two are the artistic forms of the Ṛg and Sāman," he touches the white and black stripes. According to some, he strokes them.
Thus ends the eighth section.

"O Indra Śākvara, I take refuge in the Gāyatrī; I yoke it for you. O Indra Śākvara, I take refuge in the Triṣṭubh; I yoke it for you. O Indra Śākvara, I take refuge in the Jagatī; I yoke it for you. O Indra Śākvara, I take refuge in the Anuṣṭubh; I yoke it for you. O Indra Śākvara, I take refuge in the Paṅkti; I yoke it for you"—with these mantras, he touches the black antelope skin in each direction respectively. With the final mantra, he touches it in the middle. Then, facing eastward and bending his knees, he creeps forward.
With the verse, "This prayer of one who strives," he mounts the black antelope skin upon the ashes.

While ascending, he recites: "I ascend Sutrāman... When he has ascended, he recites: "I have mounted this good ship... and also: "I have ascended the consecration (dīkṣā), the consort of the Eternal (ṛta), with the Gāyatrī metre and with the sacred word (brahman). Order (ṛta) has been established in Truth (satya); Truth has been established in Order. Both Order and Truth have become mine. I have become light; I have gone to the sun; I have reached the heavenly world, the back of the firmament, the summit of the radiant one.
At this point, the wife places a braid of hair upon her head. According to the Vājasaneyaka, it is a black braid of wool.
They call a net *kumbakurīra*.

With the formula, "Thou art the protection of Viṣṇu," the sacrificer covers his right shoulder with an unwashed garment. With the formula, "Protect [me] from the glare of the stars," he covers his head.
According to the Vājasaneyaka, he should wrap his head with a turban in a clockwise direction.
It has been stated that one should not uncover [the head] before the purchase of the Soma (10).
He consecrates the wife with a garment whose fringe is directed toward the east (11). They say that it should be a garment with the fringe turned upward (12).
The girdle is made of reeds or of muñja grass, triple-stranded, thick, with a loop on one side. With it he consecrates the sacrificer; with a yoke-tie, the wife.
[He says] "Thou art vigor," while meditating in his mind upon someone he hates, as he winds it around the navel.
Having made a loose knot above the navel, having wound it around from left to right, he settles it below the navel on the right side.
In this case, he girds the wife as at the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; the modification is: "I gird thee.
(16) He hands the black antelope horn to the sacrificer with the formula: "Thou art the womb of Indra; do not harm me.
(17) Some say that he ties it [to his finger]. (18)
It has three or five folds and is turned to the right; some say it is turned to the left.
This is the ninth section.
With the formula, "For the sake of cultivation, for good crops," he digs up a clod of earth from the altar.
When the intention "for the sake of well-fruited plants" has been reached, he scratches his head;
[he says] "O horn, loosen this knot, that which is knotted in his ankle, and that which is knotted in his heart"—thus [he touches] the limbs.

He hands over to the sacrificer the sacrificial staff made of *udumbara* wood, which belongs to the tree-dwelling deities, with the formula: "Seated above, O glorious one, bestow glory upon the sacrificer."

Or whatever sacrificial tree bears fruit—reaching to the mouth or reaching to the chin—the sacrificer, having taken hold of it with the formula, "The divine Vanaspati is well-established," and having consecrated the cup used for the offering of the *vrata* with the formula, "Thou art wide-extending, the supporter of people; O self-enjoyer, protect me," he mutters the *keśinī* *dīkṣā*: "Agni is consecrated, the earth is the consecration; may that consecration consecrate me; through that consecration, I am consecrated. Vāyu is consecrated, the intermediate space is the consecration; may that consecration consecrate me; through that consecration, I am consecrated."

The Sun is consecrated; heaven is the consecration. May that consecration consecrate me; with that consecration, I am consecrated. The Moon is consecrated; the ear is the consecration. May that consecration consecrate me; with that consecration, I am consecrated. Prajāpati is consecrated; the mind is the consecration. May that consecration consecrate me; with that consecration, I am consecrated. By speech, may my speech be consecrated for Agni, together with the all-pervading one. By breath, may my breath be consecrated for Vāyu, together with the all-pervading one. By sight, may my sight be consecrated for Sūrya, together with the all-pervading one.

"May my ear be consecrated by the ear; may it unite with the Moon. May my mind be consecrated by the mind; may it unite with Prajāpati. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Penance is my consecration, Truth is the master of the house. 6. Then the Adhvaryu addresses him with this mantra.
7. Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).

The earth is consecration; by that consecration Agni was consecrated—by that same consecration I consecrate you. The atmosphere is consecration; by that consecration Vāyu was consecrated—by that same consecration I consecrate you. The sky is consecration; by that consecration Āditya was consecrated—by that same consecration I consecrate you.

The quarters are the consecration; by that consecration the moon was consecrated—by that same consecration by which the moon was consecrated, I consecrate you. Water is the consecration; by that consecration King Varuṇa was consecrated—by that same consecration by which King Varuṇa was consecrated, I consecrate you. Plants are the consecration; by that consecration King Soma was consecrated—by that same consecration by which King Soma was consecrated, I consecrate you.

Speech is the initiation; by that initiation the breath is initiated. By that initiation with which the breath is initiated, by that initiation I initiate you. May the earth initiate you as you are being initiated. May the intermediate space initiate you as you are being initiated. May the sky initiate you as you are being initiated. May the quarters initiate you as you are being initiated. May the waters initiate you as you are being initiated. May the plants initiate you as you are being initiated. May speech initiate you as you are being initiated.

"May the *ṛc*s consecrate you as you are being consecrated; may the *sāmans* consecrate you as you are being consecrated; may the *yajus* verses consecrate you as you are being consecrated. Day and night, plowing and rain, brilliance and honor, the waters and the plants, light and truth—may these consecrate you as you are being consecrated.
Thus the Adhvaryu makes him recite the *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas.
Then he bends his fingers.

"Oblation! To the sacrifice with the mind!"—these two [verses]. "Oblation! From heaven!"—these two. "Oblation! From earth!"—these two. "Oblation! From the wide mid-region!"—these two. "Oblation! I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind"—with this he closes his fists and restrains his speech.

Then he announces him three times in a whisper and three times aloud: "This Brāhmaṇa has been initiated, so-and-so, son of such-a-one, grandson of such-a-one, great-grandson of such-a-one; son of such-a-woman, granddaughter of such-a-woman, great-granddaughter of such-a-woman."
He who undergoes initiation is born from Brahman; therefore, even a Rājanya or a Vaiśya, one announces as "a Brāhmaṇa. Thus ends the eleventh section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the third chapter (paṭala).
One should initiate him in the afternoon.

If he should desire of someone, "May he become an ascetic," he should sit facing the east in the forenoon, restrained in speech, performing austerity until the stars rise. Having caused the cow to be milked for his vow, leaving one teat of the calf, [he recites]: "Those words of cattle that are in the bull, those bright ones in the sun, send them forth; as is your portion here, may they come back to us auspiciously. Having murmured this, he releases his speech with the words, "Perform the vow! (ĀpŚS 15.19.1–4)

With the words, "Thee for the impellers," he releases four fingers—two on one side and two on the other. He keeps watch that night. When the King [Soma] has been purchased, he keeps watch the second night;
on the day of the pressing, he keeps watch the third night.
He places the names at the ends [of the formulas]: "Canasita" and "Vicakṣaṇa. "Canasita" refers to a Brāhmaṇa; "Vicakṣaṇa" refers to a Rājanya and a Vaiśya.
With the *pariṇaya* formula, he utters human speech.

He should not converse with a woman nor with a Śūdra (10); he should not follow after such a person (11). If a conversation with a Śūdra should occur, he should tell one among Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, or Vaiśyas, "Tell him this," or "Say this to him"—this is the Vāsasaneyaka tradition (12).
"One may indeed converse with a Śūdra who is not characterized by sinful conduct; so says the Śāṭyāyanaka.
(13) "He addresses [them] but does not perform the formal salutation (*abhivādana*) toward his teacher, father-in-law, or king; so says the Śāṭyāyanaka.
(14) Thus ends the twelfth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
Agni, indeed, is the consecrated one; therefore, one should not touch him (the sacrificer).
1. Nor should one utter his name. 2. One should not throw away the black antelope horn before the leading forth of the sacrificial gifts. 3.

He does not show his teeth; nor does he smile while covering [his mouth] with his hand. He should avoid honey, meat, women, untruth, sleeping on elevated beds, spitting, going out at improper times, and staying away from the sacrificial shed of one who has been consecrated.
One should not void urine or feces during the day;
if one must do so, it should be in the shade.

Desiring to urinate, one should take a blade of grass or a clod of earth with the words, "This is your sacrificial body, O Niyat. Having released the urine with the words, "I release the waters, not my offspring; O deliverers from distress, may you, consecrated by Svāhā, enter the earth," one should sip water and replace what was taken with the words, "Be united with the earth. 9.

"What of my milk here you have offered out of satisfaction—that I take back again, as one takes back the *agnihotra* with *soma*"; with this he consecrates the spilled semen. "Whatever of my essence I have here spat out unintentionally—that may Agni, Soma, and the Earth restore again into myself"; with this he speaks after having vomited or after having sneezed. "The food which you eat at night does not satisfy hunger in the morning; do not harm us, for that has not been seen by day"; with this he speaks after eating food in a dream. "To the waters belonging to Rudra, svāhā!"; with this he speaks upon seeing blood that has flowed out.
Thus ends the thirteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

"O waters named Bībhatsā, consecrated by Svāhā, enter the earth"—with these words [he pours out] the sweat. "O waters named Kṛpā, consecrated by Svāhā, enter the earth"—with these words [he pours out] the tears. "O waters named Tapasyā, consecrated by Svāhā, enter the earth"—with these words [he pours out] the perspiration.
1. He does not exit through the western door. 2.
He does not offer an oblation unconnected with a sacrifice;
he does not perform the Agnihotra; he does not sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
He does not give [gifts] (6), nor does he cook (7).
He remains consecrated for at least twelve days; another view is that he remains so for a month, a year, or as long as he may be emaciated (8).

And it is known: "When the consecrated one becomes emaciated, then he becomes fit for sacrifice (*medhya*); when there is nothing left within him, then he becomes fit for sacrifice; when his skin and bone are joined together [i.e., when he is reduced to skin and bone], then he becomes fit for sacrifice; when the blackness vanishes from his eyes, then he becomes fit for sacrifice.

It is known: "He undergoes consecration while fat; he performs the sacrifice while emaciated. Whatever of his limbs wastes away, that indeed he offers as an oblation. Thus ends the fourteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

There is one initiation (*dīkṣā*), three *upasads*, and the soma-pressing on the fifth day; or there are three initiations, three *upasads*, and the soma-pressing on the seventh day; or there are four initiations, three *upasads*, and the soma-pressing on the eighth day. The initiation takes place either on the new moon day or on the day of sacrifice; the soma-pressing day occurs either on the full moon day or on the day of sacrifice. Or rather, it may be the reverse of this.

The initiation (*dīkṣā*) takes place on the new moon day or on the day of sacrifice; the soma-pressing day (*sutyamahaḥ*) takes place on the new moon day or on the day of sacrifice. Or, the initiation takes place on the full moon day or on the day of sacrifice; the soma-pressing day takes place on the full moon day or on the day of sacrifice. (4) One should not let the sun set or rise while he is outside the initiation-hut (*dīkṣitavimita*).
(5) Having watched the sun set, he should mutter the verses addressed to Varuṇa; having watched it rise, those addressed to Sūrya. (6)
If he sees something impure, he mutters, "The mind is unbound. (7) When it has rained, he mutters, "Wetting [the earth], bestow strength.
(8) He lies down to the south of the Āhavanīya fire facing east, neither turned downward nor with his back upward, and he should not turn away from the fire. (9)
If he should turn away, he should mutter: "May all the gods turn toward me.
(10) He should not sit on anything other than a black antelope skin. If he should sit elsewhere, he should mutter: "The gods have gone to the assembly, the sacrifice has gone.
(11) He should not be separated from his staff and black antelope skin. Having set both aside, he may void urine and excrement. (12)
As for the characteristics of the initiated wife that have been stated:
(13) the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the same [for both]. (14) She should not wear the garment of one who is initiated. (15) One should not proclaim her evil, nor should one eat her food.

Or, when [the meat] has been assigned for the sake of the sacrifice, they may eat from the remainder; or when the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice] is concluded; or when the omentum (*vapā*) has been offered. Thus ends the fifteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*); thus ends the fourth chapter (*paṭala*).

One should not release speech before the appearance of the stars. If he should release it, he should restrain his speech after muttering: "This is Viṣṇu" and "O Agni, you are the guardian of the vow."
Or alternatively, he may undergo initiation again.
Now, according to some, having recited the verses dedicated to Viṣṇu, those dedicated to Agni-Viṣṇu, that to Sarasvatī, and the last one to Bṛhaspati, he should restrain his speech.
Ālekhana says that he should release his speech only when the milk has been poured out.
"It is said that for a Kṣatriya there is gruel (yavāgū).
"One should consume either gruel or milk mixed with a single [milk] addition," so some teachers instruct without specifying a particular caste.
Regarding this, some indeed consume milk as the fast-food; however, one should not do so. One should cook the gruel in milk itself and then consume it as the fast-food.
If the cow yielding the vow-milk should yield little, he should milk another; 8.
If there should be no other, having mixed [the milk] with water, he should cook it; 9. If there should be no milk, having cooked gruel in water itself, he should consume it as his vow-food. 10.
At the very least, he should offer *pippala* fruits; he must not fail to observe the vow for the sake of ensuring that the *agnihotra* is not interrupted.

If he should desire curd, they should provide him with this very curd. If he should desire grain, they should pour parched grains (*dhānā*) for him; they should pour flour (*saktu*) for him; they should bring clarified butter (*ghṛta*) for him.
One may subsist on the very oblations of the *agnihotra*, excluding meat, as a fast-food.

Indeed, they say that this is the speech pertaining to the consecration (*daikṣa*). However, the rule regarding the teats for all [the cows] is handed down independently of the *upasad* days. In the afternoon, when the sun is above the trees, the one who provides the fast-food restrains his speech. Having issued the command, "Make the fires luminous; O consecrated one, restrain your speech; O wife, restrain your speech," he sends forth the call.
Thus ends the sixteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
When the stars have risen, the release of speech is as before. 1. In this manner he restrains his speech until near sunrise. 2. Once the sun has risen, he releases his speech. 2.

He observes the vow at midday and at midnight; or, having passed the human time [of the day], he does so. According to some, he consumes the milk of the evening milking in the latter part of the night, and the milk of the morning milking in the afternoon.

He cooks the vow-food (*vrata*) for the initiated sacrificer on the *gārhapatya* fire; that for the wife on the *dakṣiṇāgni*. Whatever expiation is prescribed for spilled *agnihotra* milk, that same applies to the vow-food.

Having silently drawn it up as in the *agnihotra*, and having carried the vow-food across behind the *āhavanīya* fire, he hands it over while saying: "O one observing the vow, observe the vow! Enter the vow! (6–8).

Having washed his hands with the mantra, "We meditate upon the divine intellect" (*daivīṃ dhiyaṃ manāmahe*), and with the mantra, "Those gods who are born of mind, joined with mind" (*ye devā manojātā manoyujaḥ*), he consumes the fast-food (*vrata*) within an enclosed space to the south of the Āhavanīya fire. (9) Those who have not been initiated do not see him while he is consuming the fast-food. (10) Having consumed it with the mantra, "O Waters, be auspicious when drunk; be very kind to us in our womb and belly; full of nourishment, free from disease, and sinless—be auspicious to us for life," he touches the region of his navel. (11)
Having drunk water, he mutters [the formula] silently; the wife observes her vow in her own place. Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the fifth chapter (paṭala).

1. "O Agni, be well awake," with these words he addresses the Āhavanīya fire when about to sleep. 2. Having awakened, he may release his fists, his speech, or utter the words used by one who is not consecrated (*adīkṣita*), saying: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows. 3. Having awakened, he mutters: "May all the gods turn toward me; may mind come back, may life come back, may breath come back, may intention come back. May Vaiśvānara, the undeceivable protector of the body, drive away all misfortunes. And [he recites]: "May Vaiśvānara... and so forth.

Therefore, one who has been initiated should seek wages for twelve days; it is known from scripture that he thereby gathers the sacrifice itself. 4. With the formula "Pūṣan is the winner," he instructs those who bring the winnings. 5.
With these formulas beginning with "The moonlight," he accepts them according to their respective characteristics. 6.
"May the god Savitṛ [bestow] wealth, the giver of wealth"—with these other verses; "For Vāyu thee"—with this he points out one that has been lost;
"For Varuṇa thee"—with this, one that has died in the water.
"Be unto Nirṛti!"—this refers to one that has fallen down or is shattered;
this is the eighteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
"Be unto the Maruts!"—this refers to one struck by lightning, killed by a ram, or submerged in water.
1. With "For Rudra thee," [he offers] that which has been struck down by Mahādeva. 2. With "For Indra thee, O victorious one," he should find that army which is threatening. 3.
With "For Yama thee," [he offers] one who has died from an unidentified wasting disease (*yakṣman*).
He should not let the cows graze upon the plants that have been assigned [for sacrifice].
Having consigned the fires into separate fire-drills, he proceeds by chariot;
in the absence of a chariot, he takes a part of the chariot.
8. "From good may I attain better"—with these words he sets out. 9. "O divine waters," with these words he plunges into the water.
10. "May I follow the unbroken thread of the earth"—with these words he crushes a clod of earth with his hand as far as the opposite bank.

Saying, "Arise from the earth," he places either sand or a clod of earth in the middle and at the far end. 11. Likewise, one who is crossing while seated in a boat. 12. [The fire is produced] by means of two kindling-sticks; according to some, by means of [multiple] kindling-sticks. 13.
One should not be separated from one's chariot or its wheel. 14.
Some prescribe the settling upon the sacrificial ground at this point.
15. He who settles here should set out; he who does not settle from the beginning does not set out. 16.
"The sacrificial grounds for the gods are eternal.
This is the nineteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
Thus ends the sixth chapter (paṭala).

The sacrificial ground for the gods (*devayajana*) should be elevated toward the south, sloping toward the north, inclining toward the east, or inclining toward the northeast; or it is where many Brahmins may gather in harmony.
