Indeed, the fires themselves are the sacrificial ground for the gods; for it is known from scripture that "wherever one establishes the fires and sacrifices, there one sacrifices on the very sacrificial ground of the gods."
The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is indeed the place of sacrifice for the gods. Some say that if one gives beautiful sacrificial fees, he sacrifices at the very place of sacrifice for the gods.
4. The offerings made before the principal oblation are optional. 5. One performing a malevolent rite should sacrifice on wood that has been stripped of its bark. 6.
From whatever tree [the wood] was taken, from that they should carry it away or dig it up;
they should perform the sacrifice for one who is being falsely accused in secret, in a cave in the forest.
They should employ the *pṛṣṭha* chants in secret; everything should be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*); he should sacrifice on dry ground.

If one should desire, "May I go forth as a manifestation to both gods and men," he should not clear away even a mere measure of ground for the sacrificial site toward the east from the place of sacrifice. He should cause him to sacrifice at a spot where a path runs between the water and the place of sacrifice. If one should desire, "May no further sacrifice come to him," he should purchase the King (Soma) from a Kautsa or from another Brāhmaṇa; having said this, he adds, "Or even from a non-Brāhmaṇa."

On the site of the *uttaravedi* or the site of the *uparavas*, having spread out a red bull-hide with its neck toward the east and the hair facing north, he pours out the King [Soma] on the southern side of the hide. The Soma-seller sits down on the northern side. Having enclosed the area on all sides with a water-pot, the King, and the Soma-seller, having made an opening to the north, it has been stated: "The Somas are to be selected. 14.
Having said to the Soma-seller, "Purify the Soma," he turns away;
he should not look back at it. The sacrificer should not sort the Soma.
Neither his own servant, nor the Adhvaryu, nor the Adhvaryu’s assistant should do so.
There should be witnesses for the king as he is being examined.
With the two verses beginning with "I am yours, O Ājuhvāna," the sacrificer pays homage to the Āhavanīya fire.
This is the twentieth section.
He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *prāyaṇīyā* offering.

Having prepared the *veda* grass-bundle and strewn around the fires, he undertakes the ritual actions beginning with the washing of his hands. He arranges the vessels according to their respective purposes, placing a cooking pot (*sthālī*) in the position of the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*).
At the time of the offering, there is a *caru* oblation of milk for Aditi as the introductory rite (*prāyaṇīya*).

Having performed the rites prior to the formal summons (*saṃpraiṣa*), he issues the summons, excluding those pertaining to the wife. That same altar which is prescribed for the prepared altar serves as their altar; that same sacrificial grass (*barhis*) which is prescribed when the grass has been strewn serves as their sacrificial grass.

At the time of taking the clarified butter, he takes four portions into the *juhū* at the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice, provided there are no *anūyāja* offerings, for the purpose of pouring them together into the *upabhṛt*.
At the *udayanīya* sacrifice, which has no *prayāja* offerings, he does not take any into the *juhū*; he takes four into the *upabhṛt* for the purpose of the *anūyāja* offerings.
He places the *prāyaṇīya* offering upon the altar with the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula.
It has been stated that there are no *anūyāja* offerings, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.

He performs four *ājyabhāga* offerings in the respective directions: Pathyā Svasti in the east, Agni in the south, Soma in the west, and Savitṛ in the north. In the center, he offers to Aditi with the oblation.

Having offered to Aditi and recited the verse addressed to the Maruts, he fills the *caru* with clarified butter and sacrifices to these deities—or from the *dhruva* ladle. The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is the sixth.
The sacrifice should be concluded with the *śaṃyu-formula*, or it may be left unfinished;
however, one should not perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. But one should perform those *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings on the day of the concluding oblation (*udayanīya*).
Or, if the ritual action is the same,
he retains the clarified butter for the *dhruvā* vessel (16).

In the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, he sets aside for the sake of the *udayanīya* offering the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the pot (*sthālī*) from which no portion has been removed, and the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) (17–18).
Thus ends the twenty-first section; this is the seventh chapter.

Having taken eight portions from the *dhruvā* ladle into the *juhū* for the *prāyaṇīyā* offering, or four, he ties a piece of gold with a *niṣṭarkya* knot using a blade of *darbha* grass and places it therein with the formula: "This, O *śukra*, is thy body.
To the east, facing westward, stands the *somakrayaṇī* cow—one year old, two years old, or older.
"Without deception, listen!"—these are the forms [of the cow].
Some say that one should purchase [the Soma] with a Rohiṇī cow that has reddish-brown hair, speckled tail-hair, speckled hooves, clear eyes, and a white appearance.
For a Rājanya, it should be a cow of two colors.
With *śuṇṭhī*, *adhī*, *lodhra*, and *karṇī*, [he prepares] for the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
(6) Then, looking at the cow for purchasing Soma (*somakrayaṇī*), he offers that clarified butter with the mantra, "Thou art speed" (*jūr asi*).

(7) Having taken another fourfold portion of butter and having placed a piece of gold behind it with the mantra, "Thou art light" (*śukram asi*), and having looked at the clarified butter with the mantra, "The oblation for the Viśvedevas" (*vaiśvadevaṃ haviḥ*), and having worshipped the Sun with the mantra, "I have mounted the eye of the Sun" (*sūryasya cakṣur āruham*), he consecrates the cow for purchasing Soma with the mantra, "Consciousness thou art, mind thou art" (*cid asi manāsi*). (8)
[The bride] becomes bound at the foot with [the verse], "May she not be seized by the ear.
With the words, "May Mitra bind you at the foot," he gazes at her right forefoot. With the words, "May Pūṣan protect the paths," he addresses her as she walks toward the east.
She steps forward six steps following him, with her right foot, reciting these mantras one after another: "Thou art a Vasu; thou art a Rudra."

"Bṛhaspati shall delight you in happiness"—with these words, the Adhvaryu, having grasped the seventh footprint with his joined palms and having placed gold upon that footprint, offers an oblation into the gold with the formula, "I sprinkle you upon the head of the earth," and then takes away the gold. Taking up the wooden sword (*sphya*) with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he traces around the footprint three times clockwise with the formula, "The *rakṣas* is enclosed; the enemies are enclosed," as far as the clarified butter has spread.

Having traced around [the vessel] with a black antelope horn and having poured as much cooked rice as there is into a pot with the words, "May wealth be ours," he hands it to the sacrificer with the words, "In thee be wealth" (3); to the wife with the words, "In thee be wealth" (4).
The wife consecrates the footprint being given away with the formula, "May I not be separated from the abundance of wealth" (5).
"O Goddess, look together with the goddess Urvaśī," with these words he causes the wife to look at the Soma-purchase cow.
"May we, accompanied by Tvaṣṭṛ, gaze upon thee," with this the wife addresses the Soma-purchase cow.
"May we, accompanied by Tvaṣṭṛ, gaze upon thee," with this the sacrificer [addresses her].

From whichever footprint it was taken, having washed both hands along with the gold in that [footprint], and having poured water over it with the mantra, "Make the earth swell," he divides the footprint into three parts. He scatters one third upon the cool ashes to the north of the Gārhapatya fire; one third [he scatters] at the Āhavanīya fire; one third he gives to the wife.
She places that in her house. Thus ends the twenty-third section.
In this context, some authorities prescribe the worship of the sun and the rites beginning with the sowing for the king.
With the verse "We have entered upon the path," they proceed toward the Soma in a wagon whose front plank has been removed, which is enclosed and covered with a roof, moving eastward.
They carry the purchased Soma on their heads up the mountain.
To the west or north, with its pole facing east or north, the sacrificer addresses the King Soma while it stands on a cart with yoked poles resting upon his chin:
"May thy stalk be joined with my stalk.
Regarding one for whom he desires, "May he be without cattle," it has been said that [the cart] should be without spokes.
He spreads out upon the hide a linen garment that is double or triple [in size], with its fringe toward the east and its border toward the north—or with its fringe toward the north.
Upon it, holding the threads with his thumb and little finger, he measures them while reciting the *aticchandas* verse, "Him, the god Savitṛ," casting each thread one by one.
Thus, he measures with each individual verse.
He holds the thumb down against all [the fingers]. (10) He does not use the same [finger] with which he measured the first [line] for the fifth; he uses that very same one for the last.
He measures five times with the formula. Five times silently. (12)

Thus, having gathered the remaining stalks twice, thrice, or an unlimited number of times with the formula, "For the offspring thee," and having bound them together with a linen cloth, he ties them with a double-folded turban with the formula, "For the out-breath thee"; then, loosening it with the formula, "For the diffused breath thee," he gazes at them with the formula, "Do thou breathe after the offspring; may the offspring breathe after thee.
With the formulas, "This is thy Gāyatra portion," and so forth, the sacrificer worships the King Soma.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section (kaṇḍikā).

"O divine Sūrya, we shall buy the Soma; we announce it to you. Do you arrange the ritual acts for all the gods; arrange the sacrificial fees according to the season and according to the deity. Having thus worshipped the Sun and handed over the King (Soma) to the Soma-seller, he bargains with him:
"O Soma-seller, is this Soma yours for sale? (1-2)
"It is for sale," the other replies.
Having said, "I buy from you Soma, full of vigor and full of milk," he says to him, "I buy it from you for a cow's tail-hair.
To each subsequent offer, the Soma-seller replies, "King Soma deserves more than this," until there is no further bargaining.
"I will buy it from you with a *kuṣṭha* plant," he says for the second time; "I will buy it from you with a hoof-print," for the third; "I will buy it from you with a footstep," for the fourth.
Thus three times [in total].
Or, he may do so once each, three times over.
"Let me buy [the Soma] from you with a cow," he says at the end;
or rather, he may say, "Not with a cow. Pointing it out with the word "this," he mutters: "Her is the self, her is the form, her is the offspring, her is the milk, her is the kinship.
Having muttered, "I buy your bright [Soma] with the bright," he buys it with gold.
Having muttered, "Thou art the body of austerity," he purchases [the Soma] with a goat (ajā). 12. With each of the remaining [animals], he purchases it one by one. 13.
If he were to purchase it with a bull, he would be purchasing it with Prajāpati; in that place, therefore, there is a castrated yearling (vatsatara). 14.
"With two pairs" means a young bull and a young cow (15);
having purchased those two simultaneously, he completes the transaction at the end with a garment (16).
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section (kaṇḍikā).
[The sacrifice] of one who gives twelve hundred as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) [is performed] with ten [stomas],
or mostly [with eleven],
or with four; according to some, [it is performed] with cows, gold, or a garment for victory.

With one [verse] for one who gives twenty-one as the sacrificial fee; with three for one who gives sixty; with an unlimited number for one who gives an unlimited amount. (4) With twenty-four [verses] for one who gives a thousand or all his possessions;
or with thirty for one who gives a thousand. (5–6)
Twenty-seven cows, gold, a goat, and a garment—this makes thirty.
(7) With a hundred [cows] for the Vājapeya; with two hundred for the Rājasūya; (8) with a thousand for the Aśvamedha. (9)
With the words, "May there be moonlight for us," he takes the gold from the Soma-seller.
With the words, "May there be light for us," he gives a tuft of white wool to the sacrificer; at the proper time, he makes it the center of the fringe-filter.
The filter of the white, bright-colored [wool] remains unsewn.
For one whom he hates, he should make two strainers, one black and one red.

Having moistened a black tuft of wool with water, he ties it [to the other] with the formula: "This I tie around the necks of the biting serpents. With that [tuft], he strikes the Soma-seller with the words: "In the Soma-seller, darkness! He addresses the animals used for the purchase of Soma with: "O dog, run away!

Then, pointing toward the animals used for the purchase of Soma, he takes the King (Soma) from the Soma-seller with the formula: "Thou art self-born; thou art self-produced; born for this rite, I take thee by Truth; protect me by Truth. 15.
"If he should suffer from distress, let him remove it by means of heat alone" (16);
"here the sacrificer uncovers himself" (17).
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section.

With the verse, "The birds of fair wings," he hands the staff of the consecrated over to the Maitrāvaruṇa, saying: "By the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the directors, I give you; may I become straight and not crooked. With the formula, "Come to us like Mitra," the sacrificer takes the King (Soma), saying, "Enter the thigh of Indra," and having seated him on his right thigh, he remains holding him firmly with both hands.
In this context, some authorities prescribe the worship of the Sun, the handing over of the staff, and the assignment of the Soma-purchase animals.
Having turned the Soma-purchase cow clockwise with the formula, "May Rudra turn you back," and having ransomed her with another cow, he releases her in the sacrificer’s cow-pen.
If the Soma-seller should dispute, they should cause him to be destroyed by striking him with a spotted wooden splinter of a leather thong.
Some say they strike them with clubs;
some prescribe the execution as a constant rule.
Taking the King [Soma] with the words "With long life! With good life!", the sacrificer rises and proceeds toward the cart with the formula, "Go through the atmosphere! 9.

With the formula, "Thou art the seat of Aditi," the Adhvaryu spreads a black antelope skin upon the cart-seat with its neck toward the east and the hair upward; with the formula, "Sit upon the seat of Aditi," he places the King [Soma] thereon. With the verse, "In the woods has he spread out the mid-air," he wraps it around with a cloth; with the solar verse, "Up that Jātavedas," he fastens the black antelope skin in front from the outside with its neck pointing upward, leaving an opening on the far side.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the ninth Paṭala.

Here, as at the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, having touched the two poles, he pulls the cart with the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa"; having propped it up with the formula, "May Varuṇa prop thee up"; having fixed the pin with the formula, "Thou art the support of Varuṇa"; having driven near the two oxen with the formula, "Come hither, ye two oxen that draw the pole"; and having passed the hitching-rope around the yoke with the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa," he throws the head-stall with the formula, "The noose of Varuṇa is cast off. In this same manner, he yokes the second ox. Carrying two green branches, the Subrahmaṇya priest creeps between the two shafts; these are either branches of the Palāśa tree or branches of the Śamī tree.
Then, having called the Subrahmaṇyā, the Adhvaryu, while holding onto the cart, issues the command: "Recite for King Soma as he is being carried away; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā! 4.

In all *subrahmaṇyā* recitations, having taken hold of the *subrahmaṇyā*-priest, the sacrificer mutters: "Thou art the *subrahmaṇyā*; of thee, the earth is one foot. Thou art the *subrahmaṇyā*; of thee, the intermediate space is one foot. Thou art the *subrahmaṇyā*; of thee, the sky is one foot. Thou art the *subrahmaṇyā*; of thee, the quarters are one foot. Beyond the dust (the sun) is thy fifth foot. Do thou milk for us food, strength, luster, sensory power, spiritual splendor, and the enjoyment of nourishment. Thus he does so three times at each invocation. At the first [invocation], it is recited three times after being uttered.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth section (kaṇḍikā).
Having proceeded eastward with the words, "Depart, O Lord of the World," they turn to the right.
With the words, "Becoming a hawk, fly away," the two Adhvaryus consecrate the King (Soma) with a mantra.
"May we go upon the path," says the Adhvaryu; then the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer pass by the King (Soma) either to the south or to the north.
With a goat dedicated to Agni and Soma, its ear seized, the sacrificer awaits the King being carried forth, saying, "Homage to Mitra...
The goat is hornless; it may also be not hornless. It is either black-spotted or red-spotted.
[The Udumbara post] is thick, stout, and bearded;

it has a head-piece (śīrṣaṇya) and side-pieces (anūcya) reaching the length of an aratni, with its base reaching to the navel. It is bound with girdles of muñja grass. All the Adhvaryus lift it up in front of the Prāgvaṃśa hall while the King [Soma] is being carried forward.
They kindle the fires, or they kindle the fire-altars.

Having stationed the cart in front of the *prāgvaṃśa* shed with its pole facing east or north, having dug it up and propped it up as before, he pulls out the pin with the formula, "Thou art the support of Varuṇa. Having untied the noose of the yoke-thong with the formula, "The noose of Varuṇa is loosened," he releases the head-stall with the formula, "The noose of Varuṇa is released.
(9) In the same way, he unyokes the northern ox. (10) It may be that the left ox is unyoked while the other remains unyoked. (11)
Thus ends the nineteenth section (kaṇḍikā). Now he commences the ritual procedure for the guest-offering (ātithyā): 1. The fire-pan consists of twenty-two wooden pieces;
2. [The fuel is] twenty-two pieces of wood.

The *prastara* is made of *āśvavāla* grass; the two *vidhṛtis* are made of sugarcane; the enclosing sticks (*paridhis*) are made of *kārṣmarya* wood. Having prepared the *veda* and strewn around the fires, he proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the washing of the hands.
(3) The arrangement of the vessels is according to their purpose.
(4) At the time of the pouring out [of the oblation], having caused the wife to hold onto the cart, he pours out the *ātithya* offering. (5)

Or [he may take it] with the hand of his wife, or from her hand. While pouring from hand to hand, he should mutter all the cart-formulas (śakaṭamantra) with each respective mantra, beginning with "Thou art the guest-offering for Agni" (agner ātithyam asi). 6–8.
There is a substitution for the instruction regarding the deities;
one appends the *sāvitra* verse and the word *juṣṭam* to five [verses],
according to some, but not to the two following ones.
There is a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) on nine potsherds for Viṣṇu (12). From this point onward, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are performed as for Viṣṇu (13).
Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he unyokes the northern ox (14).

Having taken the garment with the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa’s," and having taken the King [Soma] with the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa, firm in thy vow," he descends [with him] with the formulas: "With unbroken leaves, descend unto the subjects who desire thee; O Soma, King, being pleasant, descend unto the pleasant subjects; may all subjects descend unto thee. Having thus descended, he proceeds forward with the formula, "Follow the intermediate space. This is the thirtieth section. The Pratiprasthātṛ, taking the throne-seat (āsandī), goes first.

With the verse, "Those abodes of yours," he enters the *prāgvaṃśa* hall by the eastern door, carries the King [Soma] around to the south of the *āhavanīya* fire, and places the royal throne (*rājāsandī*) to the south of the *āhavanīya* with the formula, "Thou art the seat of Varuṇa, established in the truth. (2) Upon it, the spreading of the black antelope skin is performed as on the cart, and the King [Soma] is set down.
(3) He consecrates the King [Soma] with the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa, whose vow is firm. (4)
With the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa’s," he girds [the sacrificer] with a cloth.

With the verse, "Thus worship Varuṇa, the great; pay homage to the wise guardian of immortality. May he grant us a triple-layered shelter; may Heaven and Earth protect me in their lap," he should mount the King [Soma] at every stage.
He issues the command: "Do not walk between Agni and the King."
The ritual acts beginning with the threshing are performed; 8. four portions of clarified butter are taken up; 9.
having presented the guest-offering according to the Caturhotṛ formula, he recites the Saṃbhāra-yajus formulas; 10.
Some say that he causes the sacrificer to recite [the formulas]. 11.
Like the animal sacrifice, there is the fire produced by friction and the *sāmidhenī* verses. 12.
There are five *prayāja* offerings. 13.

In the fourth [offering], he pours all the butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle together. 14. It concludes with the *iḍā*. 15. He retains the clarified butter in the *dhruva* vessel. 16. [He retains] the clarified butter. 16.
Thus ends the thirty-first section;
thus ends the tenth chapter; thus ends the tenth book.

Regarding the morning pressing of the Agniṣṭoma: from the *dhruva* vessel, he takes the *tānūnaptra* portion into the *sruc* or the cup (*camasa*). It is either fourfold or fivefold. He takes it with each of these formulas: "I take thee for Āpati," and so forth. 1.
"Thou art unassailable," [saying this], the officiating priests, with the sacrificer as the seventeenth, touch the *tānūnaptra* together.

(2) "May my consecration... [saying this], the sacrificer [touches it]. (3) Whomever he should desire, thinking, "May he attain glory through the sacrifice," him he should let touch first. If he should desire [this] for all, he should let them all touch it together. (4)
Therefore,
having recited, "Of those who have performed the *tānūnaptra*," the sacrificer smells the *tānūnaptra* three times with the formula, "I offer you in Prajāpati, in the mind.
Or he may cause [the sacrificers] to enter into the vows day by day.
"O waters, you delight the fires," he asks.
"The divine, immortal ones, increasing the cosmic order, delight," the Āgnīdhra replies.
"Come with them," he issues the command.

Having touched the boiling waters and untied the garments of those who have performed the *tānūnaptra* vow, they cause the King [Soma] to swell with their hands holding gold, saying: "O divine Soma, may each of your stalks swell.

(11) Then they perform the concealment (*nihnuvate*). Having placed the *prastara* grass-bundle at the southern edge of the altar and having made their right hands upward and their left hands downward, they say: "May wealth be sought; may fortune be sent forth.
(12) Then the sacrificer enters the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). (13)
"O Agni, Lord of Vows, you are the lord of vows among vows," with these words he worships the Āhavanīya fire.
"By this very [formula] he places a fuel-stick upon it," so says the Vājasaneyaka.
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
He fastens the girdle more tightly; he draws his fists closer together;
he becomes one whose vow is heated;
he purifies himself with the *madantī* waters.
From this point onward, he observes the vow with the formula, "O Agni, that body of yours which belongs to Rudra.
Having performed the *pravargya* rite, they proceed with the *upasad* rites; or rather, it may be done in the reverse order.
One should not perform the *pravargya* at one's first sacrifice.
One may perform the Pravargya rite;
one may perform it for a wicked Brāhmaṇa;
some say [one may perform it] for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
"One should perform the *pravargya* for one who is learned in the Vedas and a master of the *śruti*; thus says the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa*.

The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used for the *ātithyā*, the *upasad*s, and the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is the same; likewise the *prastara* and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). Some say that the sacrificial grass already spread out is that very same grass, and the enclosing sticks already placed are those very same enclosing sticks."

He commences the procedure for the Upasads. 13. The sacrificial fuel (idhma) is either of the standard type or consists of ten pieces of wood. 14. Having prepared the Veda-grass-bundle and having strewn grass around the fires, he undertakes the ritual actions beginning with the washing of his hands. 15. He arranges the vessels according to their respective purposes.

Having arranged the wooden sword (*sphya*), the *āgnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, the *sruva* spoon, the *juhū* ladle, the *upabhṛt* ladle, the *dhruvā* ladle, the *veda* grass-bundle, and the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) in pairs, and having prepared the two strainers (*pavitra*), he issues the command: "O sacrificer, restrain your speech.

(16) Restraining his speech, having touched the vessels, having prepared the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), and having addressed the Brahman priest, he sprinkles the vessels. (17) At this point, he releases his speech. (18)
Taking up the wooden sword (sphyam ādāya)—this is the second section (kaṇḍikā).

Having taken the Stambayajus from the hair [of the altar], and having performed the second tracing (parigrāha), he issues the command: "Place the sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇīḥ) down; set the fuel (idhma) nearby; cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladles (sruc); bring the clarified butter (ājya) hither. 1.

At the time of taking the clarified butter, he takes it only from the *dhruvā* vessel. Having consecrated the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), having addressed the *brahmán*, and having sprinkled the fuel and the altar, he pours out the remainder of the sprinkling waters, inserts the two strainers (*pavitra*) back [into the vessel], places one kindling-stick for the *āghāra* libation, and having laid down the two separating blades (*vidhṛti*) within the altar, he sets down the *dhruvā* and the *sruva* ladle. He modifies the mantra "May these two sit down" [to "These have sat down"].
Having placed the *veda* grass-bundle, he proceeds with the *sāmidhenī* verses.
He recites nine *sāmidhenī* verses.

Three verses are recited three times, or nine in succession. One should not offer another oblation beforehand; one should only pour the *sruva*-ladle [oblation]. This remains the same up to the *pravara* invocation.
He does not choose an *ṛṣi* lineage nor a *hotṛ*. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sit down, O *hotṛ*. This much constitutes the *pravara*. 8.
He takes eight portions from the *dhruvā* vessel into the *juhū*. 9. Four into the *upabhṛt*. 10.

Taking both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt* while the word "ghṛtavatī" (rich in clarified butter) is uttered, he steps across once toward the south and proceeds with the offering like that of the *upāṃśuyāja*.
With half of the *jauhava* [clarified butter] he sacrifices to Agni; with the other half, to Soma.

Having poured the *aupabhṛta* [butter] into the *juhū*, and having sacrificed to Viṣṇu and stepped back, he offers the *upasat* oblation with the *sruva*-ladle, saying: "O Agni, that body of yours which is devoid of desire... [He calls out:
"O Agnīdh, the waters are rejoicing! 11–12.
Having performed these and other such acts of concealment (*nihnava*), [the Adhvaryu] says: "O Āgnīdhra, recite the names of the wives of the gods; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā.

Sitting down to the west of the Gārhapatya fire, the Āgnīdhra recites the names of the wives of the gods: "Sena is the milch-cow of Indra," and so forth. On the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he invokes the Subrahmaṇyā. The sacrificer follows this with the same formula as before.
Thus ends the third section (*kaṇḍikā*). Thus ends the first chapter (*paṭala*).

In the early forenoon, they perform the Pravargya and Upasad rites belonging to the forenoon; in the late afternoon, they perform those belonging to the afternoon. At evening, the removal [of the vessels] is done with the left hand turned upward. This is the first [set of rites].
In this way, with the following two [verses],
he offers on the second day at Rajāśayā, and on the third day at Harāśayā;
it has been stated that those which are the morning *yājyā*s [are used].
There are exactly three *upasads* for a one-day sacrifice (*sāhna*), and twelve for a multi-day sacrifice (*ahīna*).

(7) If they should fight in battle or before [the enemy], he should place iron in the first [offering] and offer it; silver in the second; and gold in the last. (8) "Pointed at the tip"—this is the rule for the breast-ornaments (*stanakalpa*). (9)

On the day they purchase the Soma, they should milk four cows in the evening, three in the morning, two in the evening, and one on the final day; all [the milk] is used for the *āśira* mixture in the evening. 10.

Between the *Pravargya* and the *Upasad* rites, they prepare the altar (*vedi*). 11. Having measured three steps eastward from the central forehead-mark of the *Prāgvamśa* hall, they drive in a wooden peg (*śaṅku*). 12.

Therefore, fifteen [steps] to the south; likewise to the north. These two are the hips. Thirty-six [steps] to the east from the first peg; from that, twelve to the south; likewise to the north. These two are the shoulders. "I measure thee, the milk-abounding cow of the gods, well-milking and not shrinking away; may Indra drink the Soma; may there be peace for us"—with this verse he measures. On all sides he stretches it around with a cord.
"In the middle, on the spine" (16)—this is the fourth section.

"O men, come here and prepare this altar, rich in Vasus, rich in Rudras, and rich in Ādityas, on the height of heaven, at the navel of the earth, so that this sacrificer may not come to harm, by the impulse of the god Savitṛ"—with these words he issues the command. 1.
They construct the altar with a wooden sword (*sphya*), a winnowing basket (*vighana*), a rib-bone (*parśu*), and an axe (*paraśu*).

Having performed the rites up to the northern enclosure (*parigrāha*) as in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, except for the formal bending of the knees, he consecrates it with the mantra: "The four-crested, youthful, well-formed one, whose face is ghee, stands in the midst of the world; upon her are seated two birds—of these two, the gods have their share. (1) At twelve steps west of the *cātvāla*, there is the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). On that same path, to the north, the location is determined according to where the *cātvāla* was. (2–4)
The *cātvāla* pit and the *uttaravedi* altar have been explained;
[the sacrificer] dwells there sheltered by branches of the *udumbara* or *plakṣa* tree.
On the following day, he combines the final *pravargya* and *upasad* rites.
Having performed the morning rites, he then performs the afternoon rites.
Here, having extinguished the *pravargya* vessel, he leads forward the fire as in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*).
This is the *āhavanīya* fire for the *soma* sacrifice; that from which he leads it forward is the *gārhapatya*.
He performs the subsequent tracing of the altar with the formula containing the word "fire.
11. At this point, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having brought a branch, drives away the calves for the curdled milk offering (payasyā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
12. Thus ends the fifth Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the second Paṭala.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he sprinkles the altar (*vedi*) three times.
(1) They do not perform the sacrifice upon that which has not been sprinkled.

(2) Then, having spread the sacrificial grass thickly across it from west to east, he washes the two carts that were previously yoked, whose yokes have already been fastened and whose pins have been removed; having untied the knots tied first on them and making new ones for identification, he places them with their covers on, on either side of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line in front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, without letting the line descend, within an enclosed space. (3)
Then he anoints these two with the third part of the foot-print [clay], mixed with clarified butter, using the verse,
"May a hero be born to us," twice; he anoints the right side of the axle-hole with his right hand, palm upwards, facing eastward,
and he does not turn his hand back.
In the same way for the other [side],
either once or likewise he anoints the northern *havirdhāna* cart.

Having offered the verse beginning with *yuñjate manaḥ* on the Uttaravedi fire, he issues the command: "Recite for the two Havirdhāna carts as they are being moved," or "Recite for them as they are being moved.
When the first verse has been recited three times, they move the carts forward while lifting them up, saying: "Go forward, O sacrifice!
If there should be the sound of an axle, he should follow it with the mantra: "O fair-spoken one! (suvāk).
Having placed gold on the track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, or on both tracks, the Adhvaryu offers an oblation upon the gold with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode across this. 13.
In the same manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ [offers] on the northern one. 14.
Thus ends the sixth section.
He offers with the verses, "The two [worlds], rich in food and rich in cows...

(RV 10.133.1–2). With the verse, "Drive away the fear of men, turn back the wheels; go to the house of Soma," the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, the Brahman, or the Maitrāvaruṇa kicks away [the earth] at the third part of the altar, or throws a clod of earth outside the altar.

Leaving three steps behind the Āhavanīya fire towards the west, [the Adhvaryu] says, "May you two rest here," and having placed [the two Havirdhāna carts] so that they are level with the nave, he supports them with the formula, "Thou art Vaiṣṇava; may Viṣṇu support thee. Then, with the formula, "Or from the sky, O Viṣṇu," the Adhvaryu drives the wedge into the southern corner-joint of the southern Havirdhāna cart. He fastens the pole-axle to that wedge. In the same way, the Pratiprasthātṛ [does so] for the northern cart with the formula, "Now, indeed, of Viṣṇu... into the northern corner-joint. Having pulled up the pegs upright, they encircle [the carts] from above.
For it is known that "the divine oxen indeed carry [the burden] on their backs";
with the words "Or for the great Viṣṇu," he measures out the pillars on all sides,
leaving space for the *khara* mound in front.
He places two bamboo poles pointing northward, one behind and one in front.
9. The procedure for the Sāṃkāśina rite regarding the Śālāmukhīya, the Hotrīya, and the Uttaravedi is the same.
10. Thus ends the seventh Kaṇḍikā.

With the formula, "Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu," he holds a bamboo beam crosswise over the front *rarāṭya* (ridge-pole). Having sewn it with the formula, "Thou art the needle of Viṣṇu," and having made a knot known as "the firm one of Viṣṇu," he lays down the forward-pointing beams. With the formula, "Thou art the back of Viṣṇu," he places the middle roof-covering upon them; it is three *aratnis* wide and nine long.
Having silently placed the other two roof-coverings, he inserts reed-bundles (*tejanī*) into the intervals between the coverings with the formula, "Thou art the mat.
These become the internal partitions.

Having enclosed [the altar] on all sides with the verse, "O lover of songs, may the songs encompass thee," he loosens the two ends of the forehead-band with the formula, "Ye are the two corners of Viṣṇu’s nose. According to some, he touches them together. Having sewn the right arm of the door with the formula, "Thou art the needle of Viṣṇu," the Adhvaryu makes a knot in the well-known place with the formula, "Thou art the fixed point of Viṣṇu. According to some, they prescribe making the knot first.
"That which he should first tie as a knot," so it was said (7).
In the same way, the Pratiprasthātṛ [ties] the subsequent one (8). In the same way, the two others sew (9).
The *havirdhāna* shed is high in front and low behind;
he touches it when it has been measured, saying, "Thou art Vaiṣṇava; for Viṣṇu, thee!
Thus ends the eighth section; thus ends the third chapter.

"Viṣṇu is praised for that heroic deed: like a fearsome beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains, in whose three wide strides all beings abide. Having stepped forward from the *saṃmita* [post] toward the east, the sacrificer steps out from the *āhavanīya* fire three steps toward the east with the verse, "In whose three wide strides... (RV 1.22.18). 1. The *adhvaryu* should not pass beyond the two *havirdhāna* sheds while facing east; 2. if he should pass beyond them, he should proceed with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu. 3.

At a distance of six steps from the utkara toward the west, he erects the āgnīdhra shed; half within the vedi and half outside the vedi. It has its beams facing east, four pillars, is enclosed on all sides, and has its entrance to the south.
At three steps to the east of the western edge of the vedi, he measures out the sadas crosswise.
For one whom he hates, it is measured diagonally.
It is nine cubits wide and twenty-seven cubits long from north to south;
or it may be of unlimited size, as far as one considers sufficient for the priests, the hearth-mounds (dhiṣṇiyas), and the attendants—this is another view.
To the south, at the first step from the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, he erects the Audumbara post in the middle of the *sadas*.

One should draw the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) toward the Sadas hall so that there may be no conflict with the Sāṃkāśina rite. 10. The preparation of the pit for the Audumbarī post is like that for the sacrificial post, excluding the use of wood-shavings.

11. Having placed it in front of the pit facing east and having silently washed it, one then sprinkles it with water containing barley-grains: "For heaven, thee! over the top; "For the intermediate space, thee! over the middle; "For earth, thee! over the root. 12.

"Supporting the sky, fill the mid-air," with these words the Udgātṛ priest simultaneously raises the post whose top-knots point eastward; or [he says], "Rise up, O Lord of the Forest, in harmony with the divine Barhis.
This is the ninth section.
"May Dyutāna Māruta set thee up," with these words he sets up the post whose top-knots point eastward, together with the Udgātṛ.
Above the part buried in the ground, it is equal in height to the sacrificer.
2. The acts of scattering earth around, firming it up, and sprinkling water are performed as with the sacrificial post (yūpa).

3. Having placed gold at its two prongs (viśākha), while pouring ghee from the dipping-spoon (sruva) onto the gold with the mantra, "O Heaven and Earth, may you be filled with ghee," he causes the stream to flow down along the Audumbara post until it reaches the end. 4.
This [post] is the tallest among the pillars of the *sadas*.
It is at the level of the *nābhidaghnya* [posts].
The surrounding [posts] are lower. One who desires rain should erect the *sadas* low; some say one who does not desire rain should erect it high.

Having laid down bamboo beams pointing northward and eastward with the formula, "Thou art Indra's," he places three middle roof-coverings upon them with the formula, "For the shelter of all people. He places three southern coverings with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s seat," and three northern ones.
Both the southern and northern coverings are positioned so that they overlap the Audumbarī post.
It is known that one makes the southern [fires] northern.
(11) There are nine layers for those [altars] performed for specific desires (*kāmya*).
(12) There are nine in the *agniṣṭoma*; fifteen in the *ukthya*; sixteen in the *ṣoḍaśin*; seventeen in the *vājapeya* and the *atirātra*; twenty-one in the *sattra* and *ahīna* sacrifices. (13)
The inner partitions, the enclosure, the *sāṃkāśina* (the space for looking out), and the two doors are like those of the *havirdhāna* shed.

14. With the formula, "Thou art Indra’s seam," he sews [the cloth]. Having made a well-known knot with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s firm [seam]," he touches the finished [cloth] with the formula, "Thou belongest to Indra; for Indra thee! 15.
The Adhvaryu should not pass beyond the *sadas* toward the west, nor past the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths or the Hotṛ. 16.

If he should pass over [the altar], he should proceed with the verses addressed to Indra: "Ā ghā ye agnimindhate... and "stṛṇanti barhirānuṣak... yeṣāmindro yuvā sakhā. Some recite this very *staraṇī* verse [first].
(17) Or he may proceed with the verses dedicated to Kṣetrapati.
(18) Some prescribe the ritual of the *uparava* holes first; others the ritual of the *sadas* shed. (19)
Thus ends the tenth Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the fourth Paṭala.

Beneath the southern *havirdhāna* cart, in front of the axle and in the intermediate directions, he makes four *uparava* holes, each with a span (*prādeśa*) for its mouth and a span for the distance between them.

Having taken up the spade with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he traces around the first one three times toward the southeast, saying, "The *rakṣas* is traced around; the enemies are traced around. 1–2.
In this manner, he circumambulates the others from left to right, ending toward the north. (3) Thus, from this point forward, the ritual acts are performed for these [fires] in successive order.
(4) They are covered with grass underneath; they are not joined together above. (5)
Having silently dug [the pits] to the depth of an arm's length, he digs them while reciting: "I dig you, the slayers of Rākṣasas, the slayers of secret spells (valaga), belonging to Viṣṇu.
(6) Some authorities hand down the formulas for the *uparava* pits as being singular.

(7) Having lowered his arm with the formula, "Thou art Virāj," and having thrown up the earth with the formula, "Here I cast up that secret spell," he presses it down at the edge of the *uparava* pit with the formula, "The secret spell has been pressed down by the Gāyatrī metre. (8)
"I take away the Vaiṣṇavas," he says as he takes [the earth]. "Trampled down is the evil-doer," with these words he pours [the earth] in front of the support-post.
He performs this for all [the posts] in the same way. This much is different: having lowered the arm with each preceding mantra, he presses down [the earth] with each subsequent meter.
The Gāyatra, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Paṅkti are those that are traditionally recited. 12.
This is the eleventh section (kaṇḍikā).
Or rather, [the first] among all. 1.

"You are the Virāj, the slayer of rivals; you are the Samrāj, the slayer of enemies; you are the Svarāj, the slayer of the malevolent; you are the Viśvārāj, the slayer of all destructive powers"—with these words, the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer lower their arms.

"Touch these for long life and splendor; you are the treasure-store of the gods, the repeller of hatred. Drive away from us all hatreds whatsoever that we have committed. This which has been deposited here belongs to the gods; thus protect the four quarters, making our other rivals inferior. Having touched the *uparava* holes [with this], the sacrificer touches the southeast one, and the Adhvaryu touches the northwest one.

Then the sacrificer asks, "Adhvaryu, what is here? The other replies, "Auspiciousness. Having said, "May that be for us both," the sacrificer touches the northeast corner, and the Adhvaryu touches the southwest corner. In the same manner, there is a question and a reply; the sacrificer says, "May that be for me."

"Driving away the Rakṣases, driving away the spell-weapons, I sprinkle you, who belong to Viṣṇu"—with these words, having sprinkled the sounding-holes (*uparava*) with water containing barley, he pours the remainder of the sprinkling-water into the pit with the subsequent mantras, saying, "I pour down. Having cast a barley grain into it with the formula, "Thou art barley," and having spread sacrificial grass over it with the formula, "I spread thee," he makes an offering over it with clarified butter, saying, "I offer upon thee.
He performs this for all [the holes].
With the formula, "Driving away the Rakṣases, driving away the spell-weapons, I sprinkle you, who belong to Viṣṇu," he sprinkles the two pressing-boards (*adhiṣavaṇaphalaka*).
Thus ends the twelfth section (kaṇḍikā).
[The cart] is made of udumbara wood, or of kārṣmarya wood, or of palāśa wood; it is dried and planed, with the two side-pieces (pradhī) joined at the front and cut apart at the back.
On a one-day sacrifice (ekāha), he does not join them together; from that point onward, they should be joined.
Or he joins them together during the Ukthya and other rites;
then he places them upon the sounding-holes (uparava) with the formula: "I place you two, the Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-destroyers, belonging to Viṣṇu.
He covers two with the southern [hole] and two with the northern [hole].
The two [holes] in front are joined together by two finger-breadths, while those behind remain unjoined.

Then, with the subsequent mantras, having strewn around [the holes] clockwise with the dust from the *uparava* pits using the mantra "I surround them," and having spread sacrificial grass (*barhis*) around them with the mantra "I strew around," he consecrates them with the final mantra.
In front of this very *havirdhāna* cart, at the support-post, he makes a square mound (*khara*) with the dust from the *uparava* pits, sufficient for the Soma vessels.
He leaves a path for movement in front. 9.
Between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, or between the *āgnīdhra* and the *cātvāla*, the Adhvaryu and those seeking a view may pass. 10.
Some say that after the Soma has been pressed, those seeking a view may pass everywhere. 11.
Thus ends the thirteenth section; thus ends the fifth chapter.
He scatters the *dhiṣṇya* hearths from the *cātvāla*. (1) The *āgnīdhrīya* hearth is between the *āgnīdhra* shed and the northern edge of the altar, leaving a passage to the north. (2)
In the eastern half of the assembly hall, having left a path for movement in front, he places the *hotrīya* shed on the *pṛṣṭhyā* line. To the south of that is the *praśāstrīya* shed;
to the north of the *hotrīya*, he extends the others toward the north: those of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, the *potṛ*, the *neṣṭṛ*, and the *acchāvāka*.
Outside the *sadas*, to the south of the edge of the altar, having left a path for movement to the south, level with the *āgnīdhra* hearth;
[he sprinkles] with the eight verses beginning with "Vibhūr asi," one mantra at a time.
Some authorities prescribe these same formulas both for the worship (*upasthāna*) and for the sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*).

"Pointing out the others by way [of the path], O Lord of the Path, homage be to you; do not harm me"—with these words, he approaches each one in turn. (9) "You are the sovereign, Kṛśānu"—[this for] the Āhavanīya fire. "You are the one to be attended, the purifying one"—[this for] the Bahiṣpavamāna laud. "You are the swift one, possessing the mist"—[this for] the Cātvāla pit. "You are the unpolished, the sweetener of the oblation"—[this for] the Śāmitra fire. "You are the one to be gathered, the supporter of all"—[this for] the Utkara mound. "You are the abode of Truth, the light of heaven"—[this for] the Audumbarī post. (10) Thus ends the fourteenth section.

"Brahman-light art thou, the sustainer of heaven," [with this he addresses] the Brahman. "Thou art the Sadasya, the robber," [with this] the Sadasya. "Thou art the ocean, the supporter of all," [with this] the Sadas. "Thou art the goat, the one-footed," [with this] the Śālāmukhīya fire. "Thou art the serpent of the depths," [with this] the Prājahita fire. "Thou art the Kavya, the bearer of the Kavyas," [with this] the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. "May I attain that long life; may it protect me; by its name I cut off him who hates us and whom we hate."

"May I attain the Vāmadevya, which is the life of all; may it protect me. By its name I cut down him who hates us and whom we hate. May I attain the Rathantara, the lord of life; may it protect me. By its name I cut down him who hates us and whom we hate. With these mantras, one [addresses] the Havirdhāna, Āgnīdhra, and Sadas sheds respectively.
"With the fierce army..."—this phrase is appended everywhere.
He issues the command: "Strew the sacrificial grass; extend the vow."
Or, at the previous spreading, he should give this command:
"While spreading here, he should spread the *nābhi* over the *uttaravedi*, the *khara*, and the *uparava-dhiṣṇiya*s.
At this point, he gives the one-breasted *vrata* milk to the sacrificer.
The Vājasaneyins prescribe a half-vow here: "Half [of the vow] is omitted between the last Pravargya and the Upasad. Thus ends the fifteenth section; thus ends the sixth chapter.
He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma. 1.16.1.
The ritual procedure for this is like that of the established Animal Sacrifice (Paśubandha).
The Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula and the animal-offering sacrifice (paśviṣṭi) are not found among the subsidiary parts. He silently binds the sacrificial grass used for the Guest-offering (Ātithyā).
And those enclosing-sticks (paridhi) are included in the sacrificial fuel (idhma) for the animal sacrifice;
at the time of arranging the vessels, he employs the *pracaraṇī* ladle as the seventh. Its ritual procedure is like that of the *juhū*.
At the time of taking the clarified butter (ājya), having first taken four portions silently into the *pracaraṇī* ladle, he takes the *pāśuka* (animal-sacrifice) portions of clarified butter. 8.
With the words "May the wife of the Brahman go forward," the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife away. 9.
Then, with the words "And I, being desirous [of offspring]," the wife, having sat down near the *śālāmukhīya* fire, mutters the verse: "May we, possessing good progeny, [worship] thee. 10.
Brahmā places the King (Soma) upon his lap. 11. He issues the command: "Summon those who share the same vows! 12.
They summon the attendants of the sacrificer. 13.
The sacrificer takes hold of the *adhvaryu* from behind; the wife takes hold of the sacrificer; and the other sons and brothers take hold of the wife.

Having covered the members of the household with a new, unwashed garment and having tied the handle of the offering-ladle to the end of the garment, he offers the *vaisarjana* oblations with the *pracaraṇī* spoon.
With the two verses beginning "O Soma, you [protect] us from those who harm our bodies" (*tvaṃ soma tanūkṛdbhyo juṣāṇa*), he offers half [of the oblations] in the *gārhapatya* fire.
"Bring the Soma!"—this is the sixteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

They bring forward the pressing-stones, the vessels for Vāyu, and the wooden trough (droṇakalaśa). They lead up the wife. They cause the carts to move forward, including those belonging to the Yāyāvara which are at the other Gārhapatya fire. They lead forward a goat. They carry after [the sacrificer] the fuel, the sacrificial grass, the clarified butter, and the sprinkling water.

Having kindled the fuel for the leading forward [of the fires] at the *śālāmukhīya* fire and having covered it with sand, he issues the command: "Recite for Agni and Soma as they are being led forward," or "Recite for those being led forward.
When the first verse has been recited three times, they proceed eastward, preceded either by Agni or by Soma, with the verse: "May this Agni of ours create wide space.
Having established the fire on the *āgnīdhrīya* altar, he offers half of the remaining clarified butter with the verse: "O Agni, lead us."
The Āgnīdhra causes the pressing-stones and the Vāyavya cups, along with the Droṇakalaśa, to remain overnight.
Having gone to the north of the Āgnīdhrīya fire and the Āhavanīya fire, he offers the entire remainder of the clarified butter with the mantra, "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely.
Once the offering has been made, the attendants turn to the right and return by the same way they came.
With the verse, "Soma goes forth, the knower of the way," he causes the King to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the western door. Those who have already attained prosperity enter by the eastern door;

the sacrificer enters by the eastern door. In the interior of the southern *havirdhāna*, the spreading of the black antelope skin and the placing of the King [Soma] are performed as previously described.
Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā).
Then the sacrificer hands him over to the deities with the words: "O God Savitṛ, this Soma is yours. 1.

Having consecrated [the Soma] with the mantra, "O divine Soma, you have approached the gods," and having turned clockwise with the words, "I, a human, [have approached] humans," he makes a reverential salutation with joined palms toward the east, saying, "Homage to the gods. Toward the south, he says, "Svadhā to the ancestors. Having stepped out with the words, "I have emerged from the noose of Varuṇa," he gazes toward the east, saying, "The light has become manifest to me. He surveys the entire sacrificial ground, saying, "May I behold the light. [Gazing at] the Āhavanīya fire, he says, "The Vaiśvānara light.
At this point, the sacrificer releases the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*).
"O Agni, Lord of Vows, you are the lord of vows among vows," with these words he worships the Āhavanīya fire; "by this very [formula] he places a fuel-stick upon it," so says the Vājasaneyaka.
He loosens his girdle more widely; he opens his fists more widely.
At this point, some prescribe the handing over of the staff.
"Svāhā! [I offer] the sacrifice with the mind; svāhā! To heaven and earth; svāhā! From the wide atmosphere; svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind"—with these words he loosens his fists.
"Svāhā! Or rather, release it into the wind"—with this he releases his speech. The vow is concluded.
On the day of the Soma-pressing, he consumes the remnants of the Soma and the oblations (10).
To the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he places the fuel and the sacrificial grass with their points directed eastward; the fuel to the south and the sacrificial grass to the north (11).
Thus ends the eighteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
One commences the ritual procedure beginning with the consecration of the sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇī).
At the time of spreading the sacrificial grass (barhis), one spreads it to the west of the high altar (uttaravedi). 2.
The mantra for spreading [the grass] is repeated three times.
The ritual pertaining to the animal sacrifice (pāśuka), beginning with the placing of the clarified butter (ājya), is undertaken; it proceeds identically up to the *pravara* invocation.
Having chosen both the divine and the human *hotṛ*s, and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he chooses the Soma-officiating priests (*saumika ṛtvij*) by means of the *ṛtu-praiṣa* and other formulas.
Having cast aside a blade of grass with the wooden sword, [he assigns the priests]:

"The Ādityas from the Agnīdhra"—thus the Agnīdhra; "the Aśvins as Adhvaryus from the office of the Adhvaryu"—thus the two Adhvaryus; "Mitra and Varuṇa as Praśāstṛs from the office of the Praśāstṛ"—thus the Maitrāvaruṇa; "Indra as Brahman from the office of the Brahman"—thus the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; "the Maruts from the office of the Potṛ"—thus the Potṛ; "the Gnas from the office of the Neṣṭṛ"—thus the Neṣṭṛ.

"Agni is the leader of the divine clans; this sacrificer is the leader of men. May the household-fire of these two shine with its wide domain for a hundred winters. O you two, mingling your gifts yet not mingling your bodies"—with this [formula] he addresses the sacrificer (8).
Or: "This sacrificer, pressing the Soma, [is the leader] of men" (9).
Some prescribe the choosing of a priest at the *savanīya* [offering]; in that case, he should say "pressing the Soma" (10).
In all cases, the utterance of the name is done in a low voice; "mānuṣa" (human) is uttered aloud.
Thus ends the nineteenth *kaṇḍikā*. This is the seventh *paṭala*.
Whenever he has been initiated (*pravṛta*), he performs two *pravṛta* oblations with these two [verses]: "May I be beloved of speech; may I fulfill the hymn with the Ṛg-verse."
Having performed the fore-offerings (prayāja) during the day, they wait with the after-offerings (anūyāja) as the sun sets.
When the omentum has been offered and they have performed the purification (mārjana), he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇyā-priest, summon the Subrahmaṇyā litany addressed to the Father and Son.
From that point onward, the Subrahmaṇyā litany is indeed addressed to the Father and Son.
When the Vasatīvarī waters have been summoned, he stands facing west and draws them from the flowing waters of the mountain-breaker with a jar;
he should not let the water flow past the last [jar];
he draws them at the junction of shade and sunlight.

If he cannot find the shadow of himself, he should take [the water] in the shadow of a tree or of a riverbank, moving against the current while reciting: "These waters are rich in oblation" (RV 7.49.2). If the sun should set before the water has been taken, he should offer five *arka* oblations with the formula, "The heat is light, svāhā! (VS 38.26), and having given a choice gift, he should take [the water] while holding a firebrand above it, or having placed gold [in the vessel].

Or one may take [the water] from the jars of a Brāhmaṇa who performs many sacrifices; for it is known that "one who sacrifices with Soma becomes a performer of many sacrifices. With the formula, "I set you down in the seat of Agni whose house is unassailable," he places [the water] to the west of the Śālāmukhīya fire. At all the depositions of the Vasatīvarī waters, the sacrificer mutters: "O gracious ones, for the sake of grace, bestow grace upon me. He then proceeds with the ritual beginning with the setting out of the vessels for the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) of the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice.

The sacrificer does not eat of the offering to Agni-Soma; or he may eat. He does not offer the *svaru* splinter, nor does he remove the heart-spit. The same applies to the *savanīya* animal sacrifice.
The *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Thus ends the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā).
At night, he carries around the Vasatīvarī waters while the sacrificer and his wife are seated within the altar (antarvedi).
He should not carry them around one who has not been initiated.

Having placed [the cup] on the left shoulder with the formula "On the left shoulder! and having gone around behind the *prājahita* fire, having carried it out by the eastern door, and having gone south of the altar, he circumambulates the *mārjālīya* hearth on the south and sets it down on the northern corner of the southern *uttaravedi* with the formula, "Thou art the portion of Indra and Agni. Having placed [the cup] on the right shoulder with the formula "On the right shoulder! and having returned by the same way, having carried it out by the eastern door, and having gone north of the altar, he circumambulates the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth on the north and sets it down on the northern corner of the northern *uttaravedi* with the formula, "Thou art the portion of Mitra and Varuṇa."

Placing [the vessel] on his left shoulder with the formula "OṂ! and returning by the same way he came, he sets it down behind the Āgnīdhrīya hearth with the words, "Thou art the portion of the Viśve Devas.
Having set it down, he consecrates it with the formula, "Be watchful at the sacrifice.
At this point, the Pratiprasthātṛ milks the evening milk for the sake of the curd-mixture (payasyā).

The Adhvaryu gives the command: "Prepare the milk-mixture for the cow that provides the *vratadhuk* milk for the sacrificer; for the one that provides the milk for the wife, prepare curds for the *dadhighraha*; for the one that provides the *gharmadhuk* milk, prepare curds for the *dadhigharma*; for the Maitrāvaruṇa, prepare curds that are heated but not coagulated; for the Ādityagraha, prepare coagulated curds (*śṛtātaṅkyam dadhi*). O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; do not fast at the Sadas. They perform these acts according to the command.
At this point, he binds the sacrificial fuel and the grass-bundle for the *savanīya* animal and the *savanīya* offerings.

Or rather, there is no *barhis* grass; they cause the sacrificer to remain awake at the *prastara* alone, either at the *āgnīdhra* shed or in the *havirdhāna* shed. They cause the wife to remain awake in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall.
The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) dwell in the *āgnīdhra* shed for this night.
The sacrificer protects the King; he protects him. 14 Thus ends the twenty-first section (kaṇḍikā). Thus ends the eighth chapter (paṭala).
Thus ends the eleventh book (praśna).
Having awakened at the end of the night, he touches the Āgnīdhra fire with the verse, "O Agni, lead us" (*agna ā naya*).

With the verse, "Viṣṇu strode through this" (*idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame*), [he touches] the *havirdhāna* shed. With the verse, "O Agni, you purify our lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pavase*), [he touches] the offering-spoons (*srucaḥ*). With the verse, "Come, O Vāyu, drinker of the pure" (*ā vāyo bhūṣa śucipā*), [he touches] the vessels for Vāyu (*vāyavyāni*). With the verse, "Those who kindle Agni" (*ā ghā ye agnim indhate*), [he touches] the *sadas* hall. With the formula, "Prajāpati, blind with his mind, went toward [the sacrifice]" (*prajāpatir manasāndho 'ccheta*), he offers thirty-three oblations of the body of the sacrifice (*yajñatanū*) in the Āgnīdhra fire. Having offered with the first mantra, he recites each preceding one in sequence and offers with each subsequent one.
The Vāyavya cups are one span in height, with raised rims at the top for pouring, and concave in the middle.

Of these, those for which no specific wood is prescribed should be made of *vaikaṅkata* wood, or of any other sacrificial tree that bears fruit. He places the vessels on the mound (*khara*) with the formula, "Who yokes you? May he yoke you," for those vessels for which no mantra has been specifically enjoined.
"Agni is the deity"—with this [formula], he places the Upāṃśu cup on the southern shoulder [of the altar]. 7. "Soma is the deity"—with this, he places the Antaryāma cup on the northern [shoulder]. 8.
With the formula, "Thou art great," he places the Upāṃśusavana stone between those two cups, facing southward and touching both vessels. 9.
To the west of that [post], he places the vessels for the two-deity offerings (dvidevatya) facing westward:

one with a garland for the Indra-Vāyu vessel, saying "Indra is the deity"; one with a goat's horn for the Maitrāvaruṇa vessel, saying "Bṛhaspati is the deity"; and one with two corners for the Aśvin vessel, saying "The Aśvins are the deity. To the west of those, he places the Śukra and Manthin vessels side by side: the southern one made of Bilva wood for the Śukra, saying "Sūrya is the deity"; and the northern one made of Vikaṅkata wood for the Manthin, saying "Candramas is the deity."

To the rear of those two, there are two *ṛtupātra* cups made of *aśvattha* wood, with bases shaped like horse-hooves and openings on both sides; the southern one belongs to the *adhvaryu*, and the northern one to the *pratiprasthātṛ*.

(13) With the formula "The Viśve Devās are the deity," he places the *āgrayaṇa-sthālī* on the southern hip [of the altar]; with "Indra is the deity," the *ukthya-sthālī* on the northern hip. The *ukthya-pātra* is placed to the north of that [cup]. (14) Between the two *sthālīs*, three *atigrāhya* cups are set facing northward: the one for Agni, the one for Indra, and the one for Sūrya. (15)
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
On the northern shoulder [of the altar], there is a four-cornered vessel made of udumbara wood for the Dadhigraha offering;
it is of the same form for the Aṃśu and Adābhya offerings.
If one should take the Soma-draught for Soma, this very [vessel] should be placed there.
In front of the support of this very Havirdhāna cart, [one places] the Āditya bowl and the Āditya cup to its north.
With the formula "The Earth is the deity," [one places] the Dhruva bowl on the ground in front of the support of the northern Havirdhāna cart.
The *ṣoḍaśin* cup is made of *khadira* wood, four-cornered; if there is a *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, it is suspended in the middle like the handle of a ladle.
Ten *camasa* cups, made of *nyagrodha* or *rohitaka* wood, with or without handles, are placed according to available space.
There are exactly ten *camasādhvaryu* priests.

With the formula, "I yoke for thee the earth with light," he places the *droṇakalaśa*—provided with a fringe-filter (*daśāpavitra*)—beneath the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, toward the west.
Its attachment to the tree is by means of *vāyavya* [ropes].

"Yoking Vāyu for you together with the intermediate space," with these words, he places the Ādhavanīya jar upon the interior seat of the northern *havirdhāna* cart. "I yoke speech for you together with Sūrya," with these words, he places the *pūtabhṛt* jar on the front beam (*pradhura*).
12. Beneath this very *havirdhāna*, behind the axle, [he places] three *ekadhana* jars—five, seven, nine, or eleven. 13.
Over that upon which he measures [the soma], there is the pressing-skin, a prepared mound (*khara*) with four corners and a hollow at the top for pouring. 14.

Having sprinkled the skin for pressing with the formula, "I sprinkle thee, the slayer of Rakṣases, the slayer of spells, belonging to Viṣṇu," and having spread the two pressing-boards with their hair-side upward using the formula, "The slayer of Rakṣases, the slayer of spells, belonging to Viṣṇu, I spread thee," he places upon it four stones as pressing-stones, each a span in size, with their upper surfaces facing upward and shaped like striking-tools, saying, "The slayers of Rakṣases, the slayers of spells, belonging to Viṣṇu, I set you down.
The fifth stone, which is the largest, is placed in the middle;
they face toward it.

Thus ends the second section (kaṇḍikā). "The largest-mouthed ones, the abodes of the waters, the embryos of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), the guardians of the world, the hawks, the guests of the mountains, the peaks, like those who protect the swift-moving [chariot]—with your voice call Indra, with your roar drive away disease. You are yoked; carry [the sacrificer] to the heavenly world; carry the sacrificer forward! Having consecrated the yoked [animals] with this mantra, he sets out the vessels for the *agnīṣomīya* and the *savaniya* offerings. He takes the portions of clarified butter (*ājya*) as in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. 2.

Now, according to some: one takes the clarified butter for the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice in the Prāgvamśa hall; that for the Savanīya sacrifice in the Āgnīdhra shed; and that for the Anūbandhyā sacrifice on the Uttaravedi altar.
According to others, one takes the clarified butter for both the Savanīya and the Anūbandhyā sacrifices behind the Uttaravedi.
Whatever wood one intends to add as fuel on that day, one should sprinkle it together with the sacrificial fuel.
6. Up to the placing of the offering-spoons (*sruc*) is the same. 7. With the formula, "I yoke the three separate ones of the Sun for thee," he consecrates the placed spoons.
8. Some prescribe the placing of the Soma-vessels at this point.
"Protect me from this seat, from the mantra, and from any curse," with these words he should offer oblations before the Prātaranuvāka;
and the Pañcahotṛ formula at the Āgnīdhra fire for one who desires heaven; some authorities prescribe this as a regular (obligatory) rite.

In the middle of the fire, he offers oblations of clarified butter, oblations of animal victims, and oblations of sacrificial cakes; on both sides, he offers oblations of Soma. Here, within the *antareṣa* space, he pours down the King [Soma] upon the pressing-stones with these two verses: "For the heart, O King Soma, thee...
Prior to the utterance of speech, and prior to the calling of the birds, he begins the *prātaranuvāka*.

"Recite for the gods who come early in the morning; O Brahman, restrain your speech; O Pratiprasthātṛ, pour out the *savanīya* offerings; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the *subrahmaṇyā*," thus he issues the command.
Some transmit the instruction: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the *subrahmaṇyā*.
The Adhvaryu says to the Hotṛ: "I receive your speech with my mind."
Here, the Pratiprasthātṛ undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the washing of the hands for the Savanīya offerings;
he arranges the vessels according to their purpose.
Thus ends the third Kaṇḍikā.
There are two potsherds for the purpose of roasting; eight cake-potsherds [are used] at the morning pressing; eleven at the midday pressing; twelve at the third pressing.
Some prescribe all the cakes dedicated to Indra on eleven potsherds at each pressing.
These are the vessels for the morning milk-offering.
In the *prāgvamśa* hall, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours out the *savanīya* offerings.
All of them consist of barley, with the exception of those intended for the parched grains (*lāja*).

[The offerings are]: parched grains (*dhānā*) for Indra accompanied by the Haris; groats (*karambha*) for Indra accompanied by Pūṣan; parched flour (*parivāpa*) for Sarasvatī Bhāratī; a cake (*puroḍāśa*) for Indra; and curd-mixture (*payasyā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa.

When the offerings have been poured out, one proceeds with the ritual beginning with the formula, "This for the gods," and so forth. At the time of threshing, one threshes the other grains, excluding those intended for the *lāja* (parched grain).
At the time of placing the potsherds, one places the potsherds for the *dhānā* (fried grain) and the *lāja* upon the fire using the first mantra for the potsherds.

At the time of placing [the vessel] on the fire, having poured the rice grains with the mantra for placing on the fire, he prepares the *dhānās* (parched grains). Having poured the *vrīhi* rice, he prepares the *lājās* (fried grains). Having placed the *puroḍāśa* on the fire, he prepares the *payasyā* (curd-mixture) as in the case of the *āmikṣā*.

At the time of taking it off the fire, having taken down the *dhānās*, he divides them with the mantra of division and mixes half of them with clarified butter (*ājya*). Half of them he turns into flour-meal (*saktu*) according to the procedure for grinding.
They call a mixture of *mantha* "karambha. They call parched grains "parivāpa.
13 He removes the husks from the parched grains with his fingernails.
14 Upon the fingernails, he performs the functions of the mortar and the pestle. 15
Thus ends the fourth Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the first Paṭala.
When he recognizes [the verse], "Dawn has appeared, the bright beast," then he offers with the *pracaraṇī* ladle [the verse]: "May Agni hear our call along with the fuel.

Having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter, he issues the command: "O Hotṛ, proceed! O Camasādhvaryu of the Maitrāvaruṇa, come hither! O Ekadhanins, come hither! O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife! O Unnetṛ, with the Hotṛ’s cup and the Vasatīvarī waters, go toward the Cātvāla pit!"
Saying, "Come, come out," the Neṣṭṛ leads forth the wife, or saying, "Come hither, come out. Holding the *pānnejani* vessel, they proceed toward the *tīrtha*.
There, at a place where they may hear the Hotṛ reciting the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*), the Adhvaryu takes water from the flowing stream.
If he does not hear, he becomes deaf; his speech is indeed cut off.
(6) If they should be at a distance, he should go out toward them and take [the water].
(7) Having placed a blade of grass in between with the words "O divine waters," he makes the offering upon it. (8)

Or, if there were previously a blade of grass, he should offer into that with the formula, "Thou art the furrow" (Kārṣir asi). Having caused the oblation to overflow with *darbha* blades, he draws [the Soma] from those offered portions with the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup using the formula, "For the imperishability of the ocean, I draw you up. He draws the Ekadhana vessels with the formula, "I draw your juice from the Soma of the Mūjavat mountains."
Standing facing west, the wife takes up the *pannejanī* waters with the formula, "For the Vasus, for the Rudras, for the Ādityas.
The Neṣṭṛ leads the wife away, saying, "Come forth! Come out! or "Come! Come out!
Behind the Neṣṭṛ's station, the wife, standing facing west, sets down the *pannejanī* waters with the formula, "For the Vasus, for the Rudras, for the Ādityas."
In this very same manner, he causes [the cups] to sit down following the Ācchāvāka as he sits.
This is the fifth section (kaṇḍikā).
Having poured water from the Vasatīvarī jars into the Hotṛ’s cup, and having touched the Hotṛ’s cup and the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup together over the Cātvāla pit, he pours the Vasatīvarī waters into them.
Knowing that they are coming together, the Maitrāvaruṇa pours from the Hotṛ’s cup into his own cup; then from the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup into the Hotṛ’s cup. Or rather, it may be the reverse.

While being held over the *catvāla* pit, he anoints both types of spoons with the formula: "May Varuṇa anoint you together, may Indra, may Pūṣan, may Dhātṛ, may Bṛhaspati, and may Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu, bestowing offspring, grant wealth to the sacrificer. [He adds: "May the poles be made ready by the poles according to their respective order.
"O Adhvaryu, have you seen the Soma?"—thus the Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu.
Having replied, "I shall offer it," he offers the *kratukaraṇa* oblation from the remains of the *pracaraṇī* ladle with the verse, "O Agni, that mortal whom you [protect] in battles.
In the absence of that, he offers with four spoonfuls (*caturgṛhīta*).
It has been stated that if it is an *agniṣṭoma*, he offers.

Now, according to some: if it is an *agniṣṭoma*, he makes an oblation; if it is an *ukthya*, he wipes the remnants on the enclosing stick (*paridhi*); if it is a *ṣoḍaśin*, having made the oblation and wiped the residue on the enclosing stick, he touches the *droṇakalaśa* and the forehead-piece (*rarāṭī*). In the *vājapeya* and the *atirātra*, he neither offers the oblation nor does he touch [the vessels]. Reciting this *yajus*, he enters by stepping up directly. He causes the waters to enter through the western door; one who has already attained prosperity enters through the eastern door; the sacrificer enters through the eastern door.
He places the *pracaraṇī* ladle on the front beam of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
This is the sixth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

Beneath this very *havirdhāna* cart, in front of the axle, he places the cup for the Maitrāvaruṇa; on the northern track, in front of the wheel, the cup for the Hotṛ; beneath the northern *havirdhāna*, in front of the axle, the *vasatīvarī* waters; and behind the axle, the *ekadhanā* waters. Or rather, it may be the reverse of this. It is known from scripture: "The sacrificer steps toward the waters; thus glory indeed comes to him."
Here he proceeds with the *dadhighraha* (curd-offering).
He takes it in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood.

Having taken the curd with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, the luminous, I take thee, the luminous," he carries it forward with the formula, "O Indra, [ward off] the mind of the hater. He offers it with the formula, "For out-breath thee, for in-breath thee."
The *dadhighraha* (curd-draught) is both obligatory and optional. The other two are optional. It has been stated: "One desiring splendor should take the *ājyagraha*.

If one should take the *somagraha*, having poured the King [Soma]—obtained for a single draught—into the lower stone, and having moistened it with the *vasatīvarī* waters, he consecrates it with the mantra: "O well-born ones, you have increased by my mind. Then he presses with the Soma-making verses: "The gods, the seekers, made three kindling-sticks for the mighty one who moves around; they assigned one of them to the mortal as enjoyment, while two, the sisters, went toward the world. Thus he presses.
He consecrates the first splashing drop with the mantra, "May it splash toward me" (ā mā skān). He consecrates the droplets with the mantra, "The drop has fallen" (drapsaś caskanda).
The rule that the one with golden hands (Hiraṇyapāṇi) presses, takes, and offers is an absolute injunction.
And this applies with the exception of the verse, "Three [streams] of the mighty one" (tisro yahvasya).
Having offered it in the assembly hall, he consumes it while facing westward with the formula "Consume [it]," according to the specific characteristics of each portion (14).
Or rather, one who is not authorized [for the Soma sacrifice] may consume it, because it is a modification of the Dadhigraha and thus possesses the characteristics of Soma (15).
Those other [substances] which serve as the means for preparing the Soma possess the characteristics of Soma (16).
He first draws either the Aṃśu or the Ābhya cup with the formula:
"I take your bright [portion] with the bright. [He takes it] from curds, milk, or the Nigrābhyā waters.
He plucks three stalks from the King Soma that has been tied up.
Thus ends the seventh section (kaṇḍikā).

With the mantras beginning "May the Vasus draw you forth with the Gāyatrī metre," he shakes him four times with each mantra, or five times, or seven times. Having distributed those [mantras] beginning with "In the Māndā waters for you," [he proceeds].

With the verse beginning "In this [cup] the fierce ones have shaken," he takes the *kakuha* (the large stalk) and carries it away; with the verse "O Soma, that invincible name of yours which is watchful," he offers it.

Having set aside the *ādhavana* (shaking) stalks so they are well-identified, he mixes one stalk at each of the great pressings during each *savana*, using these formulas respectively: "O divine Soma, you are mixed with the *gāyatrī* metre.

While taking a stalk for a single cup, having placed the King (Soma) on the lower stone, having pressed it once, and singing the *vāmadevya* hymn mentally without drawing breath, he draws the cup with the verses of the *vāmadevya*: "By what [splendor] has the wonderful one come to us? and so forth.
It is to be taken by one who is turned away, either while breathing out or breathing in, or having breathed out and inhaled, or having exhaled.
If he should breathe out, the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer should both exhale over a hundred-measure weight of gold with the verse: "May our breath come from afar.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ causes them to touch it with the gold and sprinkles it with water.
