"May Indra and Agni create splendor for me"—having touched water, the Adhvaryu offers [the libation] while breathing out, breathing in, and breathing across, with the undefined verse addressed to Prajāpati, beginning with "When they have run after him.

(9) If he is unable to take it or to offer it, he may take it or offer it once a boon has been granted. (10) In the case of the Aṃśu cup, he gives twelve first-calving four-year-old cows and a garment with a fringe. It is the same for the Adābhya cup. (11)
The Ābhya cup should be drawn by one who has rivals; the Aṃśu cup by those desiring prosperity.
These two are not to be drawn in every sacrifice; rather, they are to be drawn at the Vājapeya, the Rājasūya, the Sattras, or when the entire property is given away.
They should be drawn for one who is very dear to him, as if he were well-tested.
Thus ends the eighth Kaṇḍikā; this is the second Paṭala.
Having filled the Hotṛ’s cup with the Vasatīvarī waters along the northern track, he makes the sacrificer recite over the Nigrābhya waters: "You are the Nigrābhyās, heard by the gods.

Having taken up the Upāṃśusavana pressing-stone with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he consecrates it with, "Thou art a stone, the performer of the sacrifice. While taking it up, he restrains his speech; having drawn the Āgrayaṇa cup, he releases his speech.
Then, having placed it upon the lower pressing-skin, he measures it out with the *aṃśu* stalks as in the purchase [of Soma].

This much is the difference: [he measures] with each of these formulas, "For Indra, thee, the slayer of Vṛtra," and so forth, one mantra at a time. He measures five times with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*), and five times silently.
He does not gather the rays [of light].
He prepares a larger portion of the King (Soma) for the morning pressing and a smaller portion for the midday pressing.

Having bound it and placed it back on the stone, having poured the King (Soma), which has been obtained for a single drawing, onto the lower stone, and having placed the shoots in the Hotṛ’s cup, he holds the Upāṃśusavana pressing-stone over it and, while pouring water around it three times clockwise, he performs the *nigrābha* rite with the words: "To the east, to the west, to the north, to the south."
Whichever wife he should desire, let him meditate upon her in his mind, saying, "O Mother, come forth!
She indeed will desire him.

With the words, "Ye are refreshing, O conquerors of Vṛtra," having sprinkled a portion of those [waters] and having taken six moist, connected stalks of the King [Soma] that have been touched, and having placed them upon the skin, he consecrates the King with the verse, "O Soma, that light of yours which is in heaven. 10.
Thus ends the ninth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the mantra, "O Dhiṣaṇās, be firm," [he places] the two pressing-boards.

With the mantra, "I have increased you with my mind, O well-born ones," he addresses the King Soma himself. Having lifted the pressing-stone with the mantra, "Do not fear, do not tremble," and having placed a blade of grass between [the stone and the Soma], he presses it with the mantra: "We, being sinless and sent by Indra—may Vāyu be your portion; may Mitra be your portion; may Varuṇa be your portion. King Soma is unslain. Thus he presses.
Or, if there were previously grass, wood, or a root, he should strike [the soma] upon that.
He presses eight times first.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, holding the Upāṃśu vessel, places two stalks between it and the [stalks of the] shoots already set aside.
Into that [vessel] the Adhvaryu, when it has been pressed, takes [the Soma] with his joined palms, saying: "O Vājin, flow pure for Vācaspati.
There is no strainer, no under-vessel, and no placing [of the vessel).
This is the first round. The second and the third are prescribed in the same manner.
Or rather, he presses for the second time eleven times, and twelve times for the third.
The taking of the *nigrābha* water and the pouring of it over [the soma] occurs twice, either at the beginning or at the end.
He presses the stalks belonging to the *hotṛ*'s cup during the final round.
The Pratiprasthātṛ places two stalks each between the remaining [stalks]. 12.

Having taken up the cup with the formula, "Thou art made one’s own," the Adhvaryu steps across to the south of the Hotṛ with the formula, "Follow the atmosphere. 13. Or he may step by whichever way the Hotṛ causes him to proceed. 14.
One should offer oblations while bowing low toward him whom one hates.
(2) If he should desire, "May Parjanya be rainy," he should wipe [the vessel] inwardly, wiping downward with his hand inside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
(3) If he should desire, "May it be dry," he should wipe outwardly, wiping upward with his hand turned palm-upward outside the enclosing sticks. (4)

One should pour all the remnants into the Āgrayaṇa vessel with the formula, "This is thy womb; for breath thee! Having set down the empty vessel in its place, having placed the *aṃśu* stalk therein, and having mixed it at the third pressing, one should press it. 5. Now, these [rites] are for one practicing sorcery. 6.

Having drawn the Upāṃśu cup, he sets it down with the formula, "I set thee in the breath of so-and-so. Having taken it up with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," and having covered it with his hand with the formula, "I cover the breath of so-and-so," he should say, "Slay so-and-so! Then I shall offer thee. 7.
If it should be far away, he should stand until darkness falls.

While intoxicated by the exhilaration of the *madira* liquor, standing with his body bent, thinking "May this [enemy] be dead," he should offer the oblation and deposit it with the formula: "I deposit you in the breath of so-and-so.

According to some, one who performs sorcery offers an oblation over a stalk of grain that is entangled in his garment, arm, or chest, saying: "O divine stalk, for whomsoever I have cursed, let that be true; may he be struck down by a non-floating fracture—phaṭ!"

"O Soma, that name of yours which is 'unassailable' (adābhya) and 'vigilant' (jāgṛvi)—with these [names], he inserts two shoots each from the Upāṃśusavana stones at each pressing during the great pressings.
Thus ends the eleventh section; thus ends the third chapter.
Having inserted the Adābhya shoot and the two Upāṃśupāvana shoots, all the Adhvaryus press the great pressing from all directions.

The Adhvaryu stands in the east, the Pratiprasthātṛ in the south, the Neṣṭṛ in the west, and the Unnetṛ in the north. According to some, the Adhvaryu is in the west and the Neṣṭṛ in the east. Having placed King Soma on the lower pressing-stone and having set the stalks in the Hotṛ’s cup, they press with the other pressing-stones silently, except for the Upāṃśusavana stone, from the point of adding water onwards. In this same manner, they add water and press a second and a third time.
The Adhvaryu pours the pressed [Soma] with his joined palms;
the Unnetṛ, having drawn it out through the filter, pours it into the Ādhavanīya jar from the north.
This indeed is the path for both the waters and the Soma.
This is the first method.
[In] three methods [it is done].

Having gathered [the Soma], having placed the pressing-stones face-to-face upon the lower stone, and having pressed it, he places the dregs (*nīṣa*) into their mouths; "he gives them fodder," so it is known.

The Udgātṛ priests, having established the *droṇakalaśa* among them, spread out over it a filter (*pavitra*) with its fringes pointing northward. The sacrificer consecrates the filter as it is being spread, reciting: "O Brahmaṇaspati, thy filter is stretched out; thou, the lord, encompassest the limbs on every side. He whose body has not been heated [by austerity], being raw, does not partake of that; only those who are cooked [purified] and carry it have attained it. Thus ends the twelfth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
Having made the navel of the *pavitra* the [support] for the sacrificer, he causes a stream to flow into it from the *hotṛ*-cup.
(1) The *unnetṛ* pours [the Soma] from the *ādhavanīya* into the *hotṛ*-cup with water.
(2) The stream must be poured continuously; "thus his desire becomes fulfilled," so it is known. (3)
One should cut off [the draught] for one whom one hates.
From that point, he draws the Antaryāma cup from the stream; and from there, all the cups up to the Dhruva.
The Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups have the same Brāhmaṇa explanation and are used for malevolent rites.

The difference is only this much: having taken [the draught] with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; restrain the inner breath," he passes beyond the Hotṛ to the north. Or, by the way the Hotṛ may direct him, standing to the north, having led it along the northern joint of the enclosing-sticks, he offers it in the northern half.

7. Some authorities prescribe two reversed locations. 8. Having poured the entire residue from the Āgrayaṇa vessel into the mixing-vessel with the formula, "This is thy womb; for out-breathing thee," and having set down the non-empty vessel in its place, [he pours the residue] between the pressing-stones and the Upāṃśusavana stone, facing south, so that it touches both vessels, with the formula, "For through-breathing thee. 9.
It has been stated that for one for whom it is desired, "May he be short-lived," the two [libations] should remain untouched.

(10) One should not offer the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma libations before the sun has risen. (11) However, if one is in a hurry, one may offer the Upāṃśu before sunrise and the Antaryāma after sunrise. (12)
"Some say that both [libations] should be offered before the sun has risen.
This is the thirteenth section (kaṇḍikā). Thus ends the fourth chapter (paṭala).

If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; if it has the Bṛhat-sāman, those beginning with the Śukra cup; if it has the Jagat-sāman, those beginning with the Āgrayaṇa cup.
If it is a sacrifice with both *sāman*s, one may act according to one's desire;
or rather, one should draw the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava.

He who would cause [the sacrificer] to step forward [to a higher world] should draw the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava, so that his offspring may be established in due order. These are the optional sequences for the cups.
Regarding those [vessels] prior to the Āgrayaṇa, it has already been stated.
(5) Whichever optional cup one might take before the Aindravāyava, one should not set it down. (6) It is set down following the setting down of the Aindravāyava. (7)
He draws the draught for Indra and Vāyu.

Having recited, "O Vāyu, come hither, O drinker of the pure," and having drawn it with, "Thou art taken with a support; for Vāyu thee," he pours it out. Having recited, "O Indra and Vāyu, these [Somas] are pressed," and having drawn it with, "Thou art taken with a support; for Indra and Vāyu thee," he wipes it around with the fringes of the filter and deposits it with, "This is thy womb; for the two who are in harmony (sajoṣas) thee. He wipes all the draughts around with the fringes of the filter and deposits them according to their respective deities and their respective places with, "This is thy womb."
For this purpose, there should be a second filter with ten fringes (daśāvat).

Having drawn the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa with the verse, "This [cup] is for you two, O Mitra and Varuṇa," and having mixed it with warm milk that has been boiled and cooled with the verse, "May we, having won through wealth, rejoice; may the gods [rejoice] through the oblation, as cows through pasture; O Mitra and Varuṇa, do you two grant us that cow every day, one that does not kick," he deposits it with the formula, "This is your womb; for Ṛta and Ayu, you!
Having drawn the Śukra cup with the verse, "This Vena has impelled," and having mixed it with gold, he deposits it with the formula, "This is your womb; protect heroism."
With the words, "For Śaṇḍa thee," [he takes a portion] from the one he hates.

Having taken the *manthin* cup with the verse, "As of old... (RV 8.42.3), he mixes it with groats while not letting himself be defiled, using the verse, "O you two who, at our invocations, like a mind, winning the prize through your skill, hasten hither; he who, full of great valor, has mixed the directions with his arrows in his hands" (RV 8.42.4).
He deposits it with the formula, "This is thy womb; protect the offspring. 14–16.
Thus ends the fourteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the formula "For Marka thee," [he takes from] one whom he hates.

If he should desire, "May I drive out from the village him who is in the village, and may I place in the village him who is outside the village," he should draw out the *śukra* cup with the formula: "Here I drive out N.N., the son of N.N., of the lineage of N.N., from this people. He should set down the *manthin* cup upon that [spot] with the formula: "Here I settle N.N., the son of N.N., of the lineage of N.N., in this people."
With the verse "The gods who are in heaven" (*ye devā divi*), using either the *upayāma* formula or the *yajus* formula, he draws the *āgrayaṇa* from the vessel with two streams.
Having poured the Soma that was in the *āgrayaṇa* vessel into another vessel, he makes it the second stream.
With the verse containing the word "thirty-three" (*triṃśat trayaś ca*), he should draw [the draught] for one who has enemies or who is practicing sorcery.

Saramā found the breach of the mountain; she, moving in unison, secured the great, ancient path. The swift-footed one led the way for those who flow in syllables; being the first to know, she went toward the roar as her ford. Thus [it is said] regarding the one who acts with magical power. Having taken the Āgrayaṇa draught, having uttered "hiṅ" three times, he releases his speech.

"Soma purifies himself; Soma purifies himself; Soma purifies himself. He purifies himself for well-being; he purifies himself for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); he purifies himself for this priesthood (*brahma*); he purifies himself for this nobility (*kṣatra*); he purifies himself for this people (*viś*); he purifies himself for the waters; he purifies himself for the plants; he purifies himself for the trees; he purifies himself for heaven and earth; he purifies himself for this sacrificer who presses the juice; he purifies himself for me, for preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*). As you purified yourself for the gods, so purify yourself for me. Thus he recites three times—first softly, then loudly, and finally very loudly.

Having set it down with the formula, "This is thy womb; for the Viśve Devas thee," he draws three *atigrāhya* cups at the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice: one for Agni, one for Indra, and one for Sūrya. The formulas for drawing and setting down are: "O Agni, [grant] long lives... and "Arising, thou art the spreader...
He draws the *ukthya* cup from the vessel with the drawing and setting-down formulas: "Thou art taken with a support; for Indra, the mighty and vigorous, thee."
Thus ends the fifteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the verse, "The head of heaven, the messenger of earth," he takes the *dhruva* ladle full from the *sthālī*.
He should take only a little if he desires that someone should be short-lived. He should take it half-full if he desires that someone should attain a longer life.

"This is your womb; for Agni Vaiśvānara, you," [with these words] he should place it upon gold in its proper station for one who desires long life. 3. A prince guards it until the time of its being brought down. 4. If he should desire, "May the one who has entered be excluded, and may the one who is excluded enter," he should uproot the *dhruva* [ladle] with the formula: "Here I uproot so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, from the clan of such-a-one. He should then set it down again in that very same place with the formula: "Here I set down so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, in the clan of such-a-one. 5.
If one were to do this, he would disturb the lifespan of living beings. With this mantra, one should pass a blade of grass back and forth over [the person].
(6) If one intends to practice sorcery, saying, "I cause the life of such-and-one, the son of such-and-one, to depart," he should cause the *dhruva* star to depart.
(7) Or, saying, "Thee, who art firm and of firm abode, I displace from this place," he should strike him with the *vyaṅga* star. (8)
Here the stream ceases (9). Having pressed [the Soma], he places the strainer (pavitra) down (10).

Having poured all the *ekadhana* waters into the *ādhavanīya* jar according to their purpose, and having poured the waters from the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup into the *ādhavanīya*, and having spread the strainer with its fringes pointing north over the opening of the *pūtabhṛt* jar, he should touch the King Soma that is in the *ādhavanīya* jar with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati thee! (11). With "For Indra thee! he touches the *ādhavanīya*; with "For the All-gods thee! he touches the *pūtabhṛt*. (11)
Those Pavamāna cups all have the *upayāma* formula [added] at the beginning;
the sacrificer, using the Pañcahotṛ formula, touches all the cups.
With the verses, "The drop has fallen," "Thy drop," "The drop which," and "Thy drop," he offers the oblations of the drops (*vaipruṣa-homa*) with each mantra.
(15) The first [verse] is attached everywhere; some recite the following three as *anṛta* (uninterrupted) at each pressing.

(16) Having mentally recited the *Saptahotṛ* formula and offered the cup (*graha*) in the *Āhavanīya* fire, the five officiating priests, having bent forward and holding on to one another, proceed toward the north for the *Bahiṣpavamāna* chant. (17)

Thus ends the sixteenth section (kaṇḍikā). The Prastotṛ takes hold of the Adhvaryu; the Pratihartṛ takes hold of the Prastotṛ; the Udgātṛ takes hold of the Pratihartṛ; the Brahman takes hold of the Udgātṛ; and the sacrificer takes hold of the Brahman. 1.

Now, if the sacrificer himself should be the Hotṛ, he should simply proceed [with his duties]; for it is stated in the Bṛhad-ṛca Brāhmaṇa: "For his [the sacrificer's] singing belongs to the Upagātṛs. 2.
As if crawling, as if gliding, as if lowering their heads, they creep along;

for the sacrifice is like a wild animal. First, the Adhvaryu creeps forward, shaking a handful of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), saying: "Let Speech go before, let it lead the way! The Gāyatra path, with the Vasus as its deity—may he reach the Vasus in safety by a path that is neither rough nor obstructed.
Looking toward the *cātvāla* pit, they chant; or [they chant] on the northern shoulder of the altar.
Then the Adhvaryu introduces the Stotra.
This introduction is performed in this same manner for all Pavamāna chants.
With the formula, "Speech has been released, Indra’s power has been released; come hither," he introduces the other Stotras following the Pavamānas with two blades of sacrificial grass (barhis).
Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa should approach the Bahiṣpavamāna; for it is a means of purification. It is known from tradition: "He whom he hates, he should exclude from the Bahiṣpavamāna.
While it is being chanted, the sacrificer joins in the singing. There are at least four assistant singers (upagātṛ).
The Adhvaryu does not join in.
"Utter the *hiṅ* for Vasvī; chant the *prastāva* for her; praise her; [do this] for my acquisition!"—with these words, the sacrificer mutters before the *bahiṣpavamāna*.
He also recites the *daśahotṛ* formula. While the *stotra* is being chanted, he mutters the *daśahotṛ* formula.
At the middle *stotrīyā*, he performs the *anvāroha* with the formula: "Thou art the falcon, having the *gāyatrī* metre."

At the second *pavamāna*, [he recites] with the second mantra; at the third, with the third. 16 Now follows the rule for the subsequent [recitations]: he consecrates the *stotra* with the formula, "Thou art the praised, the praise"; [he consecrates] the *śastra* with the formula, "Thou art the recited, the recitation. 17 To both, he appends the phrase, "We win the powers of the senses. 18
When the *stotra* has been chanted, the *adhvaryu* gives the command: "O *āgnīdh*, spread the fires; strew the sacrificial grass; prepare the sacrificial cakes. 19.

Now, according to some, as he rises while the *stotra* is being chanted, he says: "O *āgnīdh*, spread the fires; strew the sacrificial grass; prepare the sacrificial cakes; O *pratiprasthātṛ*, come with the animal victim. 20.
They perform [the rites] according to the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*). 21.
Thus ends the seventeenth section; thus ends the fifth chapter.
He distributes the hearths from the Āgnīdhra fire-altar:
with embers at two pressings, and with sticks at the third.
He pours [the dust] onto the dhiṣṇiya hearths in that same sequence in which they were originally set out.

Having taken five portions of clarified butter in the *pracaraṇī* ladle, and having drawn Soma from the *droṇakalaśa* with the *pariplu* spoon, he, sitting facing west in front [of the hearths], sprinkles the dhiṣṇiyas with those very same formulas, or silently.
[He spreads the sacrificial grass] for the *āhavanīya*, *āgnīdhrīya*, *hotrīya*, and *mārjālīya* fires with *soma*; the others with clarified butter (*ājya*). [With the formula:

"Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I spread thee for the continuity of the sacrifice; for the continuity of the sacrifice, I spread thee," he begins from the *gārhapatya* fire and spreads the sacrificial grass continuously along the spine-line (*pṛṣṭhyā*) up to the *āhavanīya* fire. Having returned with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, the sacrificer worships the King [Soma] with: "O Viṣṇu, thou art our nearest [kinsman]."
With this very [verse], the Adhvaryu, having touched the vessels, draws the Āśvina cup. (9) "O you two, with your hair-braid..."—this is the formula for drawing and setting down.
(10) The stream-drawings are taken from the Droṇakalaśa by means of the dipping-spoon; [they may be] from elsewhere because of a specific scriptural statement. (11)
Having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted rope, he dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni (12).

At the Ukthya sacrifice, [he dedicates] one to Indra and Agni; at the Ṣoḍaśin, one to Indra; at the Atirātra, one to Sarasvatī (13). Some authorities prescribe these as cumulative additions: at the Agniṣṭoma, he immolates the animal for Agni; at the Ukthya, a second for Indra and Agni; at the Ṣoḍaśin, a third, a ram for Indra; and at the Atirātra, a fourth, a ewe for Sarasvatī (14).
Having performed the rites up to the omentum, and having offered the omentum and performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), they proceed toward the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).
As they are about to proceed, they look at the cups (*graha*).
"Two oceans," [they say] regarding the *pūtabhṛt* and *ādhavanīya* vessels.
With "The two firm ones," [he takes] the *droṇakalaśa* (18);
with "Encompassing Agni," the entire *rājā* (Soma) (19);
with "For my out-breath," the *upāṃśu* cup; with "For my in-breath," the *antaryāma* cup; with "For my diffused breath," the *upāṃśusavana* stone; with "For my speech," the *aindravāyava* cup.

"May [the draught] for my *dakṣa* and *kratu* [be purified]"—thus for the Maitrāvaruṇa cup; "for my two eyes"—thus for the Śukra and Manthin cups; "for my hearing"—thus for the Āśvin cup; "for my self"—thus for the Āgrayaṇa cup; "for my limbs"—thus for the Ukthya cup; "for my life-span"—thus for the Dhruva cup. "O giver of splendor, be purified for splendor for me"—thus for the clarified butter (*ājya*) offerings; "O giver of splendor, be purified for splendor for my cattle"—thus for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*); "O givers of splendor, be purified for nourishment for me"—thus for all the cups (*graha*);
"O givers of splendor, be purified for splendor for my two breasts"—thus for the two seasonal cups (*ṛtupātra*).

With the formulas, "For my brilliance, for my vital energy, for my luster, for my heroism; O giver of luster, flow for luster," he takes the *atigrāhya* cups and the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, one with each mantra. With "Thou art the belly of Viṣṇu," he takes the *droṇakalaśa*. With "Of Indra," the *ādhavanīya*. With "Of the All-gods," the *pūtabhṛt*.
Thus ends the eighteenth section. "Who art thou? What is thy name? [he asks] regarding the *āhavanīya*.

"O Soma, we choose you as the Udgātṛ, the observer of men; carry us across for our well-being. With the words, "From all my forms," one who desires to become a king should gaze upon the entire King (Soma). One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), or one who is ill, or one who is straying from his path, [should do so].
With the *śṛtaṃkāra* formulas, the sacrificer worships all the cups (*graha*).

"Ye two are cooked; cook my out-breath and in-breath," [he says] regarding the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups. "Thou art cooked; cook my diffused breath," [he says] regarding the Upāṃśusavana stone. "Thou art cooked; cook my speech," [he says] regarding the Aindravāyava cup. "Thou art cooked; cook my skill and will," [he says] regarding the Maitrāvaruṇa cup. "Ye two are cooked; cook my two eyes," [he says] regarding the Śukra and Manthin cups. "Thou art cooked; cook my hearing," [he says] regarding the Āśvina cup. "Thou art cooked; cook my self," [he says] regarding the Āgrayaṇa cup.

"You are cooked; mix my limbs," [he says] regarding the *ukthya* cup. "You are cooked; mix my life-span," [he says] regarding the *dhruva* cup. "You are cooked; mix my luster," [he says] regarding the clarified butter (*ājya*) cups. "You are cooked; mix my cattle," [he says] regarding the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). "You are cooked; mix my nourishment," [he says] regarding all the *graha* cups. "You are the belly of Prajāpati; you are cooked; as such, mix me," [he says] regarding the *droṇakalaśa*. "You are the belly of Indra; you are cooked; as such, mix me," [he says] regarding the *ādhavanīya* vessel.

"You are the belly of all the gods; you are cooked; do you cook me," [he says] regarding the *pūtabhṛt* vessel. "You are cooked, I am cooked; my out-breath is cooked, my in-breath is cooked, my diffused breath is cooked; my eye is cooked, my ear is cooked, my speech is cooked, my self is cooked, my oblation is cooked, my Soma is cooked, my cups are cooked. O Indra, drink this pressed juice, the most excellent, immortal exhilaration. The streams of the bright [Soma] have flowed toward you at the seat of the Cosmic Order (*ṛta*)."

O Soma, you are a bull, brilliant; O God, you are a bull whose ordinances are bull-like. You uphold the laws as a bull. Bull-like is your manly power; you are a bull in the wood, a bull in exhilaration. As such, O Bull, you are a bull indeed. Like a neighing horse, the bull Indra has gathered together the cows and the steeds. Open wide for us the doors to wealth—thus [he says] to the King, the All.

"Agni is the purifier; may he purify me. Soma is the purifier; may he purify me. Sūrya is the purifier; may he purify me. Having performed the worship with these [verses] according to their respective characteristics—saying "The cows are invited; I am invited among the cows"—he throws the implements used for making the altar onto the *utkara* heap with the formula "The wooden sword (*sphya*) is well-being," and then worships it.
He worships Heaven and Earth with "May Heaven and Earth favor me," and the place for the *vahiṣpavamāna* chant with "The place of praise (*upastāva*).
Thus ends the nineteenth section.
"Kalaśa"—thus [he addresses] the *kalaśa* vessel; "Soma"—thus Soma; "Agni"—thus Agni; "Upa devāḥ"—thus the gods; "Upa yajña"—thus the sacrifice; "Upa mā hotrāḥ"—thus the *hotrakas*.
He appends these phrases everywhere according to their respective gender, saying, "Let them call," "let them call," "let them call.

"Homage to Agni, the slayer of Makha"—thus [he addresses] the Āhavanīya fire; "Homage to Rudra, the slayer of Makha"—thus the Āgnīdhrīya fire; "Homage to Indra, the slayer of Makha"—thus the Hotrīya fire.

"Ye two are firm, ye two are relaxed, ye two are united"—with these words he worships Heaven and Earth. [He worships] Sūrya, Vāyu, Agni, Yama, Sarasvatī, and the two doors of the assembly hall. In every case, he appends the formula "Protect, protect! according to the respective gender of the deity.
As he is about to step forward, he mutters, "Homage to the Beholder"; having stepped forward, [he mutters], "Homage to the Witness."
With the verse, "By the front [door] to the seat of Brahman, the dwelling-place of the sacrificer," he enters either by the eastern door.

Having paid homage with "Homage to the *sadas*," he pays homage to the *sadas*; with "Homage to the Lord of the *sadas*," he pays homage to the Brahman; with "Homage to the friends who go before," he pays homage to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); and with "Homage to Heaven, homage to Earth," he pays homage to Heaven and Earth. Then, having cast out a blade of grass from his seat with "O son of a remarried woman," he sits down with the words, "May I go along the downward slopes and the upward slopes. (8) Having sat down, he mutters: "Protect me today, O Heaven and Earth. (9)
"Come, O Fathers; you who have fathers," with these words he gazes across toward the southern half [of the altar].
(10) Both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer mutter these two [formulas]; or rather, the sacrificer alone.
(11) At this point, the Pratiprasthātṛ places the *savanīya* offerings. (12)
With these [formulas], the Adhvaryu proceeds.
He takes portions of the deities' shares from all the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) into the *juhū* ladle, and the portions for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice into the *upabhṛt* ladle.

The two calls for direction (*saṃpraiṣa*) are: "Recite the invitatory verse (*anuvāka*) for the sacrificial cakes for Indra at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsāva*)," and "Prompt the Hotṛ to recite the offering verse (*praṣya*) for the sacrificial cakes for Indra at the morning pressing. Or alternatively: "Recite the invitatory verse for the sacrificial cakes for Indra being cut at the morning pressing," and "Prompt the Hotṛ to recite the offering verse for the sacrificial cakes for Indra set forth at the morning pressing."

"Recite for Agni; give the command for Agni"—thus [he says] for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. Having cut off the entire portion of the clarified butter and having set aside the Prāśitra, he does not take the Iḍā nor the portion for the sacrificer. Having brought the Iḍā to the Hotṛ and while going toward the Havirdhāna shed, he issues the command: "Recite for Vāyu and for Indra-Vāyu."

"You are taken with a support; you are the seat of speech"—with these words, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having taken the counter-portion of the draught for Indra and Vāyu from the *droṇakalaśa* using the Āditya vessel, does not set it down.

(19) The Adhvaryu, taking the draught for Indra and Vāyu and the King Soma from the *droṇakalaśa* by means of the *pariplava* ladle, both go out, stand to the south, and, having moved along the southern joint of the enclosing sticks, he pours the libation with the *pariplava* ladle, saying, "May this sacrifice be a peaceful one for the gods," so that it becomes offered like the *upāṃśu* libation. (20) At this point, he offers all the Soma oblations. (21)

From the point where he thinks, "I shall offer without stepping forward," standing there and holding either the *sruva* ladle or the *vāyavya* cup, he should cause the announcement (*āśrāvaya*) to be made. Or, having taken up a *graha* or having drawn out the *camasa*, they should commence the *stotra*; this is the ultimate rule.

(22) Having caused the announcement and the response (*pratyāśrāvita*) having been made, he issues the command: "To Vāyu, to Indra and Vāyu, *preṣya*! (23) He offers when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered; they both offer again when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered once more. (24)
If the sacrificer should think, "My rival has passed me by," [he should act] thus—this is the twentieth section.
Before the oblation, he should grasp a finger with his thumb, saying, "He who seeks to harm us, O Indra and Vāyu"; or if it is the other way around, he should grasp the thumb with a finger.
Having offered the oblation, he worships the Sun with the formula: "Thou art the earth, the best of rays, the protector of breath; protect my breath.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue from the Adhvaryu's vessel into his own; the Adhvaryu pours it into the Pratiprasthātṛ's. Or rather, this may be done in reverse.
With the formula, "For the gods thee," the Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue from the Āditya-vessel into the Āditya-pot.
The Adhvaryu, having taken the cup, quickly runs toward the Hotṛ and hands the cup to the Hotṛ with the formula, "May I be wealthy.
(5) Having received it in this very manner, the Hotṛ places it on his right thigh, holds it with both hands, and remains seated. (6) In the same way, they proceed with the two subsequent cups. (7)
The *āghāra* and *punarvaṣaṭkāra* offerings do not take place (8).

The calls for direction (*saṃpraiṣas*) are according to the respective deities (9). The drawing of the *pratinigrāhya* cups, their non-drawing, the worship of the sun, the pouring down, and the offering are performed with the successive mantras (10).
"Thou art pervasive, the best of rays; thou art the protector of the vyāna breath; protect my vyāna"—with these words, the third worship of the Āditya [cup] is performed.
(11) "O Viṣṇu of the wide stride, this is thy Soma; guard it"—with these words, the Pratiprasthātṛ covers the Āditya-sthālī with the Āditya-pātra.
(12) Having handed over the cup for the Aśvins to the Hotṛ, while going toward the Havirdhāna shed, he issues the command: "Recite for the cups being filled! (13)

He draws nine goblets, with the *hotṛ*’s goblet as the foremost. Having spread an underlayer of ghee from the *droṇakalaśa* and having drawn [the soma] from the *pūtabhṛt*, he pours an overlayer of ghee from the *droṇakalaśa*. This is the procedure for all the goblets.
At the time of drawing the draughts, there are optional ritual procedures for the cups belonging to two deities (dvidevatya). 17.
If the sacrificer should think, "My rival has surpassed me," he should draw first by means of the Pratiprasthātṛ, offer first, and set it down first. 18.

If he should desire, "May I make him equal in strength with his rival," they should draw simultaneously, offer while standing side-by-side, and having offered simultaneously, they should set them down side-by-side. 19. [End of section]
"Equal" is the meaning.

(20) If he should desire, "May they confine him who has already been confined, and may he who is confined gain release," [he should do as follows]: with the formula, "This one, the son of such-a-one and grandson of such-a-one, I draw out from such-a people," he should draw out the Adhvaryu's cup; with the formula, "This one, the son of such-a-one and grandson of such-a-one, I set down in such-a people," he should set down the Pratiprasthātṛ's cup upon it. (21) If they are for specific desires, the *pratinigrāhya* cups should be drawn separately with separate vessels. (22)
Thus ends the twenty-first section; this is the sixth chapter.

Then they proceed with the Śukra and Manthin cups. "Thou art praised, O sustainer of people; may the gods who drink the Śukra lead thee forward"—with these words, the Adhvaryu takes the Śukra cup. "Thou art praised, O sustainer of people; may the gods who drink the Manthin lead thee forward"—with these words, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the Manthin cup. The Camasādhvaryus take the cups.

Having covered [the two pits] with two sprinkled wooden chips, they both scatter earth from below with two unsprinkled chips, saying: "Śaṇḍa and Marka are driven away along with so-and-so! Or the Adhvaryu, meditating in his mind upon the one he hates, says: "Śaṇḍa is driven away! and the Pratiprasthātṛ says: "Marka is driven away!
Having grasped [the chips], they both go out toward the east.
"Go along the wide mid-air," [he says] as they proceed forward.
"With Indra as my ally, with fury, may I drive away those who attack; slaying the Vṛtras, irresistible"—with these words, the sacrificer takes hold of the *śukra* cup from the point of its offering.

With the other [formula], "Unite the *uttaravedi*, or the two cups, or the two *aratni*s; unite the *brahman*, may you quicken that for me; unite the *kṣatra*, may you quicken that for me; unite the *iṣ* (food), may you quicken that for me; unite the *ūrj* (strength), may you quicken that for me; unite wealth (*rayi*), may you quicken that for me; unite prosperity (*puṣṭi*), may you quicken that for me; unite offspring (*prajā*), may you quicken that for me; unite cattle (*paśu*), may you quicken those for me," they join together the two cups or the two *aratni*s on the north side of the *uttaravedi*.
With the formula, "Thou art unassailable," they grasp the *uttaravedi* with both thumbs and walk around it as if they were two falcons gliding through the air.

"Generating offspring rich in heroes, go around, O bright one, with bright luster!"—with these words the Adhvaryu proceeds by the south. "Generating offspring rich in progeny, go around, O stirred one, with stirred luster!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ proceeds by the north.

With the front [of the yoke], they join together either the two cups or the two axle-pins over the northern altar, saying: "Uniting from heaven and from earth, join together my life-span; quicken that for me! Join together my out-breath; quicken that for me! Join together my in-breath; quicken that for me! Join together my diffused breath; quicken that for me! Join together my eye; quicken that for me! Join together my ear; quicken that for me! Join together my mind; quicken that for me! Join together my speech; quicken that for me! (8)

Then the Adhvaryu addresses them two with the mantra: "You are life; bestow life upon me; bestow life upon the sacrifice; bestow life upon the lord of the sacrifice. You are breath; bestow breath upon me; bestow breath upon the sacrifice; bestow breath upon the lord of the sacrifice. You are sight; bestow sight upon me; bestow sight upon the sacrifice; bestow sight upon the lord of the sacrifice. You are hearing; bestow hearing upon me; bestow hearing upon the sacrifice; bestow hearing upon the lord of the sacrifice. (22nd Kaṇḍikā)

"O you two gods, Śukra and Manthin, fashion the divine subjects; fashion the human subjects; bestow upon us food and vigor; bestow life-breaths upon the cattle, and offspring upon me and the sacrificer.

(1) They throw away the two un-sprinkled wood-shavings outside the altar, saying, "Śaṇḍa and Marka are cast out along with so-and-so! Or the Adhvaryu, meditating in his mind on his enemy, says, "Śaṇḍa is cast out! and the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Marka is cast out! (2) They place the two sprinkled [shavings] down: the Adhvaryu with "Thou art the kindling-stick of Śukra," and the Pratiprasthātṛ with "Thou art the kindling-stick of Manthin. (3)

Having called for the response and once it has been responded to, he issues the command: "O Camasādhvaryus of the central performers, announce the Soma-pressings for Indra—the morning pressings of the *śukra* and *manthin* vessels, dripping with sweetness; offer them! O Camasādhvaryus of the Hotrakas, having offered each once, come back after having drawn more from the *śukra* vessel!
4. They act according to this command. 5. The two Adhvaryus offer from the front toward the west; the Camasādhvaryus offer from behind toward the east with the goblets. 6.
Having recited the counter-announcement for the *śukra* and *manthin* cups, the offering is made.

(7) "He is the first, the fashioner, the maker of all; he is the first Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; he is the first Bṛhaspati, the wise one. To that Indra I offer the pressed [soma], Svāhā!"—with these words the Adhvaryu offers. "To that Sūrya I offer the pressed [soma], Svāhā!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ offers.
(8) These two offerings are either accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*-call or without the *anuvavaṣaṭ*-call. (9)

In the *sarvahuti* (the all-oblation), or alternatively, having set down the *śukra* cup in its place like a *sūda*, the *pratiprasthātṛ* draws out a coal from outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) from the northern half [of the fire] and offers the residue of the *manthin* cup upon it with the formula: "This, O Rudra, is your portion, which you requested.

This *manthin* cup is a vessel for one who is afflicted; if he should hate any of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), he should offer it to him. It is known from tradition: "He indeed becomes afflicted right here."

Then he issues the summons: "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward; let the Brahman’s, let the Udgātṛ’s, let the Sacrificer’s go forward. Some recite: "Let the Udgātṛs’ [cups] go forward"; [others say] "Let the Sadasya’s [cup] go forward" or "Let the Sadasyas’ [cups] go forward.
(13) Then they perform the joint offerings for the Hotṛs.
(14) For him, the Camasādhvaryus, having drawn wine from the Droṇakalaśa into each of their respective cups, carry them forward. (15)

Having taken the cup belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa, having gone to the Āhavanīya fire, and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, when the response has been given, he issues the command: "O Hotṛ, recite the offering prayer; O Praśāstṛ [recite the offering prayer]," or [simply] "O Hotṛ, recite the offering prayer.
Having offered it at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* calls, he brings the portion for consumption. He proceeds in this same manner with the subsequent cups; only this much is different.
Thus ends the twenty-third section (kaṇḍikā).
At the second [cup], he issues the command: "O Brahman, sacrifice! At the third: "O Potṛ, sacrifice! At the fourth: "O Neṣṭṛ, sacrifice! At the fifth: "O Agnīdh, sacrifice!
In all cases, there is an *anuvaṣaṭ* call, with the exception of the cups for the dual deities (*dvidevatya*), the seasonal cups (*ṛtu-graha*), the Āditya cup, the Sāvitra cup, and the Pātnīvata cup.
Taking the Āgnīdhra’s cup, he goes to the Sadas and announces, "The Āgnīdhra has offered!
(3) The others reply, "He has performed a good deed; he will cause us to drink Soma.

(4) If he should officiate for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya and that person should desire to consume Soma, [the Adhvaryu] should fetch branches of the Nyagrodha tree, grind them, mix them with curds, and strain them. While the cups are being offered, he should take out a coal from within the enclosing sticks, scoop some of this [grain-mixture] into the cup with a young blade of Darbha grass, offer it on the coal with the formula, "I am you; you are me," and then give that portion to him as his share to consume. (5)
Among those gathered at the vessel, the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* first consumes [the Soma].

Looking toward the Soma as it is being brought for consumption, he says, "Come, for consumption! Having received it with the words, "May I be united with you through the arms of the Aśvins," and having gazed at it with, "O divine Soma, you who are the watcher of men," he consumes all the cups dedicated to Indra at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) with the formula, "The gladdening overcomer... He consumes the *nārāśaṃsa* cups with, "...drunk by Narāśaṃsa. At the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), he consumes all the cups dedicated to Indra with, "...of the troop belonging to Rudra," and the *nārāśaṃsa* cups with, "...drunk by Narāśaṃsa."

At the third pressing, he consumes all the cups dedicated to Indra with the formula, "Of him who belongs to the troop like the Ādityas. He consumes the *nārāśaṃsa* cups with the formula, "Of that which was drunk by Narāśaṃsa.
Whatever [formula] precedes the one for the Vasu-group, he attaches it everywhere.
Even for those [cups] belonging to other deities, [he uses] the formula, "Of that which was drunk by Indra."
Or, according to the respective deity:
"May Vāk, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma"—thus some prescribe the consumption of all the Soma;
or else: "May the goddess Vāk be satisfied with the Soma."
Having consumed [the Soma] with the mantra, "Impel my limbs, O Lord of the Bay Steeds," they touch the region of their navels.

(13) One should not drink Soma unless invited; for one who drinks without being invited becomes excluded from the drinking of Soma. (14) He addresses [the other participants] by name and by the designation of the ritual action, saying, "So-and-so, so-and-so, invite [me]! The response is, "I am invited. (15)
He desires an invitation (*upahava*) from those who eat from the same vessel or from similar vessels; or from those who share a single bowl.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

First he consumes the draught for Indra and Vāyu, grasping it within the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). First [he consumes] the draught for Mitra and Varuṇa, grasping it within the two eyes. He consumes the draught for the Aśvins by moving around [the cup] on all sides, grasping it within the two ears.

Without setting down the vessel, they consume the draught for Indra and Vāyu twice—either both consume it or one consumes it. The other two [draughts] are consumed once each. Regarding this, the meaning of "they consume" (*bhakṣayanti*) is that the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ [consume them]; the meaning of "they consume" (*bhakṣayanti*) is that the two Adhvaryus and the Hotṛ [consume them]; the meaning of "he consumes" (*bhakṣayati*) is that he alone [consumes it].
Having consumed [the soma], they pour the remnants (sampāta) into the Hotṛ’s cup, whether [the other cups] have been consumed or not.

At this point, they set aside the vessels. He places a fragment of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa-śakala) into the vessel for Indra and Vāyu; the curd-mixture (payasyā) into that for Mitra and Varuṇa; and the parched grains (dhānā) into that for the Aśvins.
He places them on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart. "They remain there until the third pressing for the continuity of the sacrifice," so it is known.
7 Some prescribe the cutting off of the *iḍā* portion here.
8 Here the Hotṛ invokes the *iḍā*. The cup-bearers lift up their cups; the Hotṛ’s cup is touched within the *iḍā*. 9
They eat what has been invited, as in the archetype; 10 he places a fragment of the sacrificial cake for the Acchāvāka;
11 they consume the remnants of the oblation in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed. 12

In this context, the following acts are performed for the *savanīya* offerings: the throwing of the branch (*śākhā-praharaṇa*), the procedure regarding the whey (*vājina-caryā*) within the altar (*antarvedi*), the sacrificer’s touching of the *veda* grass-bundle, the two oblations of the flour-smear (*piṣṭalepa*) and the husks (*phalīkaraṇa-homa*), the wife’s disposal of the *veda*, the sprinkling (*mārjana*) upon the *praṇītā* waters, the removal of the *upaveṣa*, and the release of the potsherds (*kapāla-vimocana*).
(13) For these [acts] do not displace the specific [rites] that are incidental (*prāsaṅgika*). (14) According to another view, one should indeed displace them. (15)
The Hotṛ obtains the portion by means of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance;
the Adhvaryu [obtains it] by means of both the oblation and the pressing; not by either one alone.
They also obtain the portion by means of the designation (*samākhyāna*).
The Hotṛ consumes all the cups once (19),
and his own cup twice (20).
The Hotrakas consume their respective cups twice each (21).
The Adhvaryu causes them to consume what has been consumed once, in the same order as before; the others do so at the end.
Having consumed, they cause [the cups] to swell with the mantra: "Swell up; let [the essence] come together unto thee."
Those are the *nārāśaṃsa* cups;
there are two *nārāśaṃsa* cups at the first two pressings, and one *nārāśaṃsa* cup at the third pressing.
Having been consumed and replenished, they set them down beneath the southern *havirdhāna* cart, leaning against its support.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section; thus ends the seventh chapter.

The Acchāvāka priest sits down outside the Sadas hall, in front of his own Dhiṣṇiya hearth. Placing a fragment of the sacrificial cake before him, [the Adhvaryu] says: "O Acchāvāka, speak what is to be spoken by you."

When he recognizes, "They are calling upon us Brahmins, O Brahmins," then he announces him to the *hotṛ*: "This *acchāvāka* desires an invitation; invite him, O *hotṛ*. 3. And when the cows have been invited with the words, "Invited are we," this being the signal from the *hotṛ*, [the *maitrāvaruṇa* says]: "Recite for the one being drawn out! O *camasādhvaryu* of the *acchāvāka*, draw out [your cup]; make it bright on both sides! 4. Having taken that [cup] and gone to the *āhavanīya* fire, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and when the response has been given, he issues the command: "O *acchāvāka*, sacrifice! 5.
Having offered at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*, he carries away the portion for consumption.
He does not consume it with him; he does not seek permission to consume from him. If he should desire permission to consume from him, he should say to him, "Consume!
Having consumed and caused [the cup] to swell, they set down the two cups of the Neṣṭṛ and the Āgnīdhra between them and proceed with the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*).
They are drawn from the *droṇakalaśa* vessel; they are not set down. 9.
From the remnants of the preceding [libations], they draw the subsequent ones. 10.
The Adhvaryu draws first, and the Pratiprasthātṛ follows last, each with his own formula: "Thou art taken with a support; thou art Madhu... and so on for each respective mantra. 11.
Some recite: "For Madhava thee! For Mādhava thee! (12). All [the cups] have the *upayāma* formula at the beginning (13).
One should not follow after the other. The Adhvaryu enters by the south in the established manner; the Pratiprasthātṛ enters by the north in the established manner (14).
Having passed right through the door (15), as the Adhvaryu is entering, the Pratiprasthātṛ receives him from behind with a cup; as he is going out, [he receives him] with a vessel (16).
"Recite the *praisha* for the seasons!"—thus the Adhvaryu issues the command during the first three [libations]. The Pratiprasthātṛ does likewise (17).
Turning the two vessels around at their openings, the Adhvaryu says, "With the seasons, *preṣya*," for both; likewise the Pratiprasthātṛ.
(18) Turning them around again, the Adhvaryu says, "With the season, *preṣya*," once; likewise the Pratiprasthātṛ.
(19) Thus ends the twenty-sixth section.
Twelve, thirteen, or fourteen [verses] are taken.
(1) In the case of twelve, the first two are taken together; (2) the last two are taken together;
(3) in the case of thirteen, there is the taking and giving together of the last two.
Likewise, among the fourteen [verses], of the first and the last, there is a transition;
the thirteenth and fourteenth, "saṃsarpa" and "asyaṃhaspatyāya tvā," are indeed held apart.
Having recognized [the signal] with "O two Adhvaryus, sacrifice! O Gṛhapati, sacrifice!", he gives the call for both simultaneously: "O Hotṛ, sacrifice this!"

In this manner, at the conclusion of his own directions, the householder [performs] the two pourings together like those for the dual-deity cups. With an unblessed vessel, the Adhvaryu draws the draught for Indra and Agni, using the verses "O Indra and Agni, come to the pressed juice" for both the drawing and the setting down. The Pratiprasthātṛ carries away the portion for consumption.
Both Adhvaryus consume their respective portions according to the *vaṣaṭ* call.
10. All the *somapātra* vessels that have been consumed are washed at the *mārjālīya* shed.

11. Taking this vessel, the *adhvaryu* sits down facing east in the *sadas* hall; intending to respond to the *śastra* recitation with the formula "The *iḍā* is the invocation of the gods," he murmurs [the following].
12. Recognizing the signal of the *hotṛ* with "Śaṃsāvoṃ," turning clockwise, he responds with "Śaṃsā modīva" or "Śaṃsā modiva."

Holding the *ṛtupātra* cup, he responds while standing facing west at the seat of the *sadasya*; or else, while bowing low, he responds at the half-verses with "Othā moda iva," and at the pauses with "Omothā moda iva. At the very end, there is only the *praṇava*.
"Othā moda ivaṃ hotar moda iva, omothā moda iva, om"—these are the alternatives.
The [verse] after the half-verse is not omitted; he does not respond with the *abhipratigara*.
16 At the calls of *oṃ*, *śauṃsā*, *moda iva*, and *authā moda iva*, he performs both [the *pratigara* and the *abhipratigara*].
17 Having responded to the *śastra*, the Adhvaryu takes up [his cup], and the Camasādhvaryus take up their cups. 18
Having caused [the Āgnīdhra] to call out and having received the response, he issues the command: "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
This is the twenty-seventh section.
They shake the *nārāśaṃsa* cups following the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls.
They take away the portions;
the consumption of the draught has been explained. Likewise are the consumption, the swelling, and the setting down of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups.
He draws the *vaiśvadeva* cup with the *śukra* vessel; "Omāsas carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ" is the formula for both the drawing and the setting down.
With the words, "He has been created, he has been created," he introduces the *stotra* with two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Prior to the *ājya* offerings, the sacrificer mutters: "Utter the *hiṅ* for Iḍā; chant the *prastāva* for her; sing the *stotra* for her; may it be secured for me. He also recites the *Caturhotṛ* formula.
And while the *stotra* is being chanted, he mutters the *Caturhotṛ* formula.
It is known from tradition: "Having explained the Caturhotṛ formulas, he chants the Udgītha with the Ājya-stotras.
When the Stotra has been chanted, the Śastra response is like that of the Aindrāgna, excluding the Ṛtu-cups; and there are the Grahas and Nārāśaṃsa cups.
All the Camasa cups are for consumption.

"You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Mitra and Varuṇa, for the gods. Having taken the third Ukthya portion with the Ukthya vessel, saying "O gods, you two [are] for the gods who are worthy of praise," and having set it down with "This is your womb; for Mitra and Varuṇa, you," he touches the vessel with "Thou art a sacrificial oblation again. (11) Whatever cups have the Maitrāvaruṇa as their chief, he responds for that one and consumes it along with them. (12) Having drawn the cups with the Maitrāvaruṇa cup as the chief, he introduces the Stotra as before. (13)

The *stotra* is chanted as before; having responded (*pratigīrya*), the *adhvaryu* takes up the cup, and the *camasādhvaryus* take up the goblets. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and it being responded to, he issues the direction: "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the *soma*s! At the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ* calls, they offer the oblations. They bring forth the portions for consumption (*bhakṣa*). 14. From this point onward, the procedure for the groups [of cups] is the same, with the exception of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups.
15. With the formula, "I mix thee, who belongest to the gods, for the gods; I fill thee for the life of the sacrifice," he pours the residue into the principal vessel. 16.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth section (kaṇḍikā).
If the Adhvaryu should desire, "May I endow myself with the glory of the sacrifice," it has been stated [above];
in this manner, the two subsequent turns (paryāyas) are prescribed.
The Pratiprasthātṛ proceeds with those two. The difference here is this:

he modifies the second drawing and setting by saying, "For Indra thee," and he draws half of the remnant of the Ukthya. He touches the vessel as before. He pours out the goblets, with the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s goblet at their head.
He does not introduce a goblet that has not been consumed with the Stotra.
The Pratiprasthātṛ does not consume from the *ūrdhvapātra* vessel. He pours the residue into the principal vessel.
With the formula, "For Indra and Agni, thee," he performs the drawing and placing of the third cup, and he draws the entire remainder of the *ukthya*. He does not touch the *sthālī* vessel.

Having spread the filter with its fringes pointing northward over the opening of the *pūtabhṛt* vessel, he pours all that King [Soma] which was in the *ādhavanīya* into the *pūtabhṛt*. While drawing out the cups, beginning with the cup of the *acchāvāka*, and having drawn out the entire King [Soma], he wipes the two jars with the fringes and turns them face down. He pours the residue from the principal [cup] into [the *droṇakalaśa*]. Having responded to each *śastra* at the morning pressing, he says, "O reciter of the *uktha*! (9–11).
They proceed with the first two pressings without hurrying; they hurry with the third pressing.
When the morning pressing has concluded, he offers an oblation with the mantra: "May Agni protect us at the morning pressing.
He issues the command: "O Praśāstṛ, give the impulse! Give the impulse! or simply "Impulse! (prasu).
"Creep away," he replies.
(15) They creep out by the same way they crept forward. (16) The morning pressing concludes; the morning pressing concludes. (17)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the eighth chapter (paṭala).
Thus ends the twelfth book (praśna).
The midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana), beginning with the pressing of the Soma, is now performed.
The ritual procedure for him is explained by that of the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana).

Having poured [the soma] from the Hotṛ’s cup into the Vasatīvarī waters, he prepares the Nigrābhya waters. There are no cups for the dual deities, no seasonal cups (ṛtugraha), and no spoon-offerings (darvihoma).

Having loosened the king [Soma], he hands the Soma-turban to the Grāvastut. (5) Without being prompted, he recites the verses belonging to the Grāvastotra. (6) In the same manner, the great pressing takes place. (7)
But [the chant] is resonant:
"And they propitiate, they press here, O3! Here! (9).
In the middle round of the final pressing, he places the *bṛhat* [sāman]: "The great, the great" (10).

When the supreme pressing has been pressed and the King Soma has been collected, the stones have spoken: "The drop belongs to Indra. They have caused Indra to come from the furthest distance, from this vast firmament, the intermediate space. They have pressed out prosperity; they have pressed out for me spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). In the conflict, they have slain the demons; the oppressors of sacred knowledge have been struck down. Thus the Pratiprasthātṛ gives thanks to the pressing-stones.

(11) Having offered the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), the *savanīya* offerings are made, excluding the curd-mixture (*payasyā*). (12) Having performed the ritual with that, he proceeds with the *savanīya* offerings. (13)

The *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* portions, however, are common [to both]. (14) That [procedure] may be either performed or not performed. (15) From the gathering [of the materials] up to the pouring [of the libations], the Adhvaryu draws the cups when it has been performed. (16)
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
Then [he draws] the Śukra and Manthin cups, and the Āgrayaṇa from three streams.
Having poured out [the Soma] from the Āgrayaṇa vessel, he forms the second stream; from the water-vessel, the third.
Having drawn the Ukthya cup, [he draws] the two Marutvatīya cups. This, however, is the reverse order. Some say that the Ukthya is in the middle and the two Marutvatīyas are on both sides.

With the formula "The Marut-possessing one," the Adhvaryu first draws the first Marutvatīya with his own Ṛtu-vessel; with "O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts," the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the latter with his own vessel. Some prescribe that for these two, the vessels belonging to other deities are used for the one who is to be hated.
He ceases from the *dhāraikadhana* offerings; this and the following constitute the five *pañcahotṛ* formulas (6).

Having performed the worship with the *grahāvakāśa* and *śṛtakāra* formulas, and having offered the *vaipruṣa* oblations and the *saptahotṛ*, they proceed to the *mādhyandina-pavamāna* chant as at the *bahiṣpavamāna* (7).
"The path is in the *triṣṭubh* meter, the Rudras are the deity; by the path that is not too far, may we safely reach the Rudras"—this is the modification for the procession (8).

Having gone to the north of the *havirdhāna* shed, having passed around the *mārjālīya* hearth on the south, and having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, the Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer stand in front of the Hotṛ. Having passed either to the south or to the north of the Praśāstṛ’s hearth, the Udgātṛs chant the Mādhyandina Pavamāna.
Thus ends the second section.

"Sing the *hiṅkāra* for the light; chant the *prastāva* for it; sing the *stotra* for it—for my attainment of it," thus the sacrificer mutters before the midday *pavamāna*. He recites either the *caturhotṛ* or the *pañcahotṛ* formula, and also [the formula]: "Sing the *hiṅkāra* for long life; chant the *prastāva* for it; sing the *stotra* for it—for my attainment of it. And while the *stotra* is being chanted, he mutters either the *caturhotṛ* or the *pañcahotṛ*. And during the middle *stotrīyā*, he performs the second *anvāroha*.

When the *stotra* has been chanted, the *adhvaryu* issues the summons: "O *āgnīdh*, spread the fires; strew the sacrificial grass; prepare the sacrificial cakes; O *pratiprasthātṛ*, follow with the *dadhigharma*. 1.
The *pratiprasthātṛ* takes up the *dadhigharma* in the *āgnīdhra* shed. 2.

Having spread a base of butter in the ladle made of Udumbara wood, and having taken curds with the formula, "As great as are heaven and earth," and having poured butter over it, he says: "May speech and mind mix you; may out-breath and in-breath mix you; may sight and hearing mix you; may skill and strength mix you; may vigor and power mix you; may life and old age mix you; may self and body mix you. You are cooked; you have been made cooked; for the cooked you, for the cooked ones you! Having placed it on the Āgnīdhra fire, he says, "O Hotṛ, speak what is to be spoken by you. 3.

When he recognizes that it is cooked—saying, "If it is cooked, offer; if it is not cooked, let it simmer"—at this moment, having replied, "The oblation is cooked," and having taken it, gone to the Āhavanīya fire, called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, and received the response from the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, he issues the command: "Sacrifice the Dadhigharma.
This is the third section. "Sacrifice the Dadhigharma. 1.

"He whom they call Indra, whom they call Varuṇa, whom they call Mitra, whom they call Truth; he who is the most divine among the gods, born of ascetic fervor—to that Indra I offer the pressed soma, Svāhā! With these words, he offers at the *vaṣaṭ*-call. Having offered at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call with "Svāhā Vaṭ! To Indra!", he carries away the portion for consumption. Those who have participated in the *pravargya* rite consume it. Its formula for recitation in the forest (*araṇye’nuvākyā*) is the mantra for the consumption.
"It should not be performed without the *pravargya*," so says another [teacher].

(5) Having consumed [the soma] with the mantra, "Mitra [governs] the people; Mitra [governs] them forth," they touch their navel regions. (6) The procedure for the *savanīya* offerings has been explained. (7)
The difference is this much: at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), he modifies the call beginning with "for Indra, the rice-cakes" (*indrāya puroḍāśānām*).
(8) Having brought the *iḍā* to the Hotṛ and going toward the *havirdhāna* shed, he issues the command: "Recite for those being drawn up" (*unnīyamānebhya anubrūhi*).
(9) [This continues] from the drawing up until the placing of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups. (10)
In that regard, there is a modification:
he draws the *acchāvāka*’s cup as the tenth; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* being responded to, he issues the formal command.

"O Soma-pressings for Indra, belonging to the midday libation, to the portion of the Viṣṇvevya hymn, accompanied by the Śukra and Manthin vessels, dripping with sweetness"—this is the beginning of the formal summons (saṃpraiṣa).
14. There are six Hotṛ-offerings. 15. They proceed with the Agnīdhra’s cup first, followed by the Acchāvāka’s cup. 16.
These same *hotrā* formulas are used at the third pressing (17).

Thus ends the fourth section (*kaṇḍikā*); thus ends the first chapter (*paṭala*). When the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down, he gives the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*): much, or an unlimited amount—seven, twenty-one, sixty, a hundred, twelve hundred, a thousand, or all one's possessions (1).
Or, having excluded the eldest son from his share, he gives away all his possessions (*sarvavedasa*). 2.
At a sacrifice involving a thousand cows (*sāhasra*) and at one where all possessions are given away, he gives a mule.

3. He gives a sheep, a goat, a cow, a horse, a man, an elephant, a garment, a cart, a chariot, boiled rice, a stirred drink, beans, sesame seeds, rice, barley, and a donkey—these are the additional items which are not fixed. 4.
The number of cows becomes five.

When the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) have been placed to the south of the altar, he goes to the north of the *havirdhāna* shed, passes around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth, and enters the *prāgvaṃśa* hall by the eastern door. Having performed here the acts beginning with the summoning of the sacrificer’s kinsmen and ending with the lowering of the ladle-handle, he offers the southern oblations with the *pracaraṇī* ladle.
Having tied a piece of gold and placed it in clarified butter, he offers two oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire with the two verses, "Upwards that" (*ud u tyam*) and "The bright one" (*citram*).
Having offered gold with the words, "Go to heaven, fly to the sun," he takes it up.
Holding both [the gold and the vessel], he approaches the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) with the words, "By means of your form, I approach your form.
Some authorities recite the division after having passed over [the gifts].

"May Tutha, the all-knowing, distribute among you," he says; having thus caused them to be scattered by means of a black antelope skin, the sacrificer divides them into four parts for the Adhvaryus. 11.
As much as he gives to the Adhvaryu, half of that goes to the Pratiprasthātṛ, a third to the Neṣṭṛ, and a fourth to the Unnetṛ. 12. By this, the distribution to the others is explained. 13.
Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā).
He first gives to the Agnīdhra a piece of gold, a full vessel, a pillow, and a thread of all colors;
finally, he gives them to the Pratihartṛ.
In such a way he should give to the Brahman priest that he might not think of any other sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having given the various limbs [of the body], he redeems them one by one according to their respective characteristics, if he intends to depart.
"O Hotṛ, I give you speech; I redeem it for you with this," [he says].

In this manner, he gives his mind to the Brahman, his breath to the Adhvaryu, his sight to the Udgātṛ, his hearing to the Hotrakas, his limbs to the Camasādhvaryus, his body-hairs to the Prasarpakas, and his self to the Sadasya—excluding the sacrificial fees, the Camasādhvaryus, the Prasarpakas, and the Sadasya.

With golden-handled reins, he leads [the horse] in front of the Gārhapatya fire and behind the Sadas. Between the Āgnīdhra shed and the Sadas, he releases those [reins] toward the north through the *tīrtha*.
"O Agni, this gift of thine..."—with these words, the one who leads the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) forward [recites].
(9) In the same manner, whether the participants have taken hold of one another or not, he offers on the Āgnīdhrīya fire with the verse, "O Agni, lead us... (10).

If a forest [product], a carriage, a garment, or an upper garment is given, or if it is intended to be given, he offers the second oblation with the verse, "He has stretched out the atmosphere over the forests. (11) If a man or an elephant is given, or if it is intended to be given, he offers the third oblation with the verse, "O Prajāpati, none other than you... (11)

"May I today win a Brahmin," [thinking thus], he gives gold to the first Ātreya, or to the second or third; in the absence of such, he should give it to one who is an *ārṣeya* (descendant of seers) and well-connected. Having addressed those who have been led away with the words, "Go among the gods through our gift," and having come to the *sadas*, he looks around with the words, "Behold the light of heaven," if he should distribute [the gold] after leading it away.

He should give [the dakṣiṇā] to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) seated within the assembly hall; he pays homage to the officiating priests in the two Havirdhāna sheds. It is known from the tradition of the *prasarpakas* that one should proceed toward whichever sacrifice one has come to attend.
Thus ends the sixth section (kaṇḍikā).
He gives [the gifts] to the attendants (prasarpaka) seated to the south of the Sadas, but not outside the sacrificial ground (vedī). 1. Not outside the vedī. 2.
Not when solicited; 3 not out of fear;
4 not from the Kaṇvas or Kaśyapas; 5.

It should not be given to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, nor even to a Brāhmaṇa who is ignorant. One may give it even to a non-Brāhmaṇa who possesses knowledge; whatever knowledge he knows, that he secures through that gift.
Whatever [knowledge] he knows, whether it be for a learned Śrotriya, a kinsman, or a non-priest who has approached him, that he secures through that gift.
That [gift] by which one attains preeminence through that deity for the sake of the eldest—he secures it by means of that [gift].
(9) That [gift] which belongs to one who is of noble lineage and learned—he attains the heavenly world by means of that.
(10) If another should not desire her when she is being given away, he should give her to one whom he hates, together with other wealth. (11)

If one should drive back a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) among the cattle, or if one should take it back, a female jackal (*salāvṛkī*), having become that [gift], will cause him to perish. 12. The cattle depart after that sacrificial gift which one gives to an unworthy recipient. If he should think, "I have given to an unworthy recipient; I have not deceived this [gift," he should mutter this *yajus* or give a cow to a Brahmin. 13.
When the verse addressed to Marutvat has been recited, then it should neither be given nor accepted. 14.

When the omentum of the Anūbandhyā cow has been offered, he should give [the gift], and they should receive it. When the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) have been led away, he throws the black antelope horn into the Cātvāla pit with these two verses: "The healing medicine upon the head of the swift-moving antelope—by means of that horn, he has destroyed the hereditary disease spreading in all directions. "After thee the antelope has stepped with its four feet; O horn, loosen this knot, that which is knotted in his ankle, and that which is knotted in his heart. Having offered the five Vaiśvakarman oblations on the Āgnīdhrīya fire with the verse, "The seers have said that the lord of the sacrifice was struck by sin," [he concludes].
Thus ends the seventh section (kaṇḍikā).
They proceed with the two Marutvatīya offerings.

"Recite the invitatory prayer for Indra accompanied by the Maruts; give the command for Indra accompanied by the Maruts"—these are the two calls, which may be either with the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* cries or without the *anuvaṣaṭ*. Or, only one of them may be with the *vaṣaṭ* cry. Having poured out the remnants of the two double-deity cups (*dvidevatya*) as is customary, the Adhvaryu takes the third Marutvatīya draught with the cup that has not been consumed.

The two acts of drawing and setting down [the cup] are performed with the formula, "O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts. The Pratiprasthātṛ carries away his portion for consumption. Both Adhvaryus consume their portions in turn.
Taking this vessel, the response to the Śastra is as in the case of the cup for Indra-Agni; and there are the cups for the draughts and the Nārāśaṃsa verses.
He draws the Māhendra cup with the Śukra vessel. The drawing and setting down are performed with the formula, "Great is Indra by his might."
He introduces the hymn for Mahendra.
When it has been chanted, the *śastra* and the response (*pratigara*) are like those of the Vaiśvadeva; and there are the *graha* and *nārāśaṃsa* offerings.
The *atigrāhya* cups are offered following the *māhendra* cup.
Together with the *adhvaryu*, the *pratiprasthātṛ* takes the portion for Agni; the *neṣṭṛ* takes that for Indra; and the *unnetṛ* takes that for Sūrya.

Having offered the portion for Agni with the formula, "O Agni, full of splendor," the *pratiprasthātṛ* consecrates it with, "Thou art the knower of splendor. Having offered the portion for Indra with the formula, "O Indra, full of vigor," the *neṣṭṛ* consecrates it with, "Thou art the knower of vigor. Having offered the portion for Sūrya with the formula, "O Sūrya, full of radiance," the *unnetṛ* consecrates it with, "Thou art the knower of light.
Having offered these, they consume them in the *sadas* facing westward, each his own portion according to its respective mark, with the verses beginning, "In me, wisdom."
In the same way, there are variations regarding the *ukthya* cups;
this much is the difference. At every instance, he modifies the formulas for drawing and setting down the cups with "For Indra, thee! For Indra, thee!

Having responded to each *śastra*, he says, "The *uktha* has been spoken," referring to the midday pressing. When the pressing is concluded, he offers an oblation with the formula, "O Viśve Devas, O Maruts."
In the same manner, the summons and the creeping [of the priests] take place;
thus the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana) is concluded.
This is the eighth section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the second chapter (paṭala).
The third pressing has the Ādityas as its starting point.
Having closed both doors of the *havirdhāna* shed, he should take [the draughts] on the altar when it is crowded with many people;
or, if his rival should have entered there, he should take them while the rival is within the altar.
When the sun is being drawn at the sacrifice for a rival, he should stand outside the sacrificial altar (bahirvedi).
He draws Soma from the remnants of the double-deity cups (dvidevatyagraha) that were in the Aditya vessel, using the Aditya cup, with the verse: "Never art thou barren" (RV 8.91.3).
With the verse: "Never art thou neglectful" (RV 8.91.4), he [draws] the curd for the boiled milk (śṛtātaṅkya).

Having again taken the Soma with the formula, "The sacrifice of the gods," and having placed the *upāṃśusavana* pressing-stone upon it with the formula, "O Vivasvat Āditya," he stirs it with that stone.
Having mixed it with curds from a heated vessel, or with milk for one who desires rain, using the formula, "With that which is the divine rain, I mix thee," he lifts up the pressing-stone.
If, once lifted, a drop should immediately fall, Parjanya will be rainy; if it takes a long time, he will not be rainy.
He does not set it down.
(10) If he should desire, "May cattle miscarry their embryos," he should look at the sun after lifting it up.
(11) Having covered it with *darbha* grass or with his hand, he rises, saying: "May the god Sūrya protect me from the gods. (12)
Saying, "I [hold] from behind," the sacrificer takes hold of the Āditya cup until the oblation is offered (sūtra 13).
Saying, "The sage stretches out the path of the sacrifice," he carries it (sūtra 14).
Saying, "As far as the ocean," he causes it to flow down with *darbha* grass blades (sūtra 15).
Thus ends the ninth section (kaṇḍikā).

"Recite for the Ādityas—those who are dear, whose abodes are dear, whose vows are dear, the lords of the great year, the overseers of the wide mid-region—for the Ādityas, give the command! "Recite for the Ādityas—those who are dear, whose abodes are dear, whose vows are dear, the lords of the great year, the overseers of the wide mid-region—for the Ādityas, give the command! These are the two calls for direction (*saṃpraiṣau*). Or alternatively: "Recite for the Ādityas; give the command for the Ādityas.

Having thrown darbha grass into the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "O Agni, those kindling-sticks of thine which exist in their entirety," he offers the oblation to the Ādityas while looking elsewhere.
One who desires rain should offer with the verse, "Unfold the earth.
(3) Having offered, he should not look around.

(4) Having placed the Āditya-vessel in its proper place like a cook, and having poured the shoots from the two Adābhya vessels and the shoot from the Upāṃśu vessel into the *ṛjīṣa*, the great pressing is performed as at the morning pressing. (5)
They press only the *ṛjīṣa* [residue]; the *savanīya* offerings are made except for the *payasyā*.

Having churned the *patnyāśira* milk in the *āgnīdhra* shed, he causes it to be brought into the *havirdhāna* shed by the western door; those who have already attained prosperity do so by the eastern door.
The sacrificer enters by the eastern door (9).

Having spread the filter with its fringes pointing north over the opening of the *pūtabhṛt* vessel, the sacrificer, standing in front facing west together with his wife, pours the *āśira* (milk mixture) into it with the four verses beginning, "O gods, look upon us for beauty" (10).
At the time of the cup-drawings, he pours from the *āgrayaṇa* itself into the four streams (11).

Having drawn from the Āgrayaṇa vessel, he makes the second stream; from the Āditya-sthālī, the third; and from the residue of the Āditya-graha, the fourth. If it is an Ukthya sacrifice, he draws the Ukthya cup here. He stops the stream for the Ekadhana vessels as required, and so forth, according to the procedure of the midday pressing.

Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā). The path is that of the Jagatī; the deity is the Ādityas. "By the path that is not too far away, may I safely reach the Ādityas"—this is the modification for the gliding (sarpaṇa). "For life, utter the *hiṅ*! For it, chant the *prastāva*! For it, sing the *stotra*! For its attainment by me!"—with these words, the sacrificer mutters before the Ārbhava-pavamāna. He recites either the Pañcahotṛ or the Saptahotṛ formula, and also: "For life, utter the *hiṅ*! For it, chant the *prastāva*! For it, sing the *stotra*! For its attainment by me!"

While [the chant] is being praised, he mutters either the *pañcahotṛ* or the *saptahotṛ* formula. During the middle *stotrīyā* verse, he performs the third *anvāroha*. When the praise has been completed, the *adhvaryu* issues the command: "O *āgnīdh*, spread the fires; strew the sacrificial grass; prepare the sacrificial cakes; O *pratiprasthātṛ*, hold the conversation regarding the animal sacrifice. At this point, he should not sprinkle the already distributed glowing hearths with the wooden sticks; rather, the sprinkling takes place afterwards. The oblation is cooked.
Beginning with the formula "O pacifiers," he undertakes the animal ritual pertaining to the *eḍā* offering.
He carries the collected portions (*samavatta*) either to the south of the *havirdhāna* cart or to the north.
Once the *iḍā* has been consumed, [the procedure continues] from the *savanīya* offerings up until the setting down of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups.
