In that regard, there is a modification: [the formula] "for Indra, the cakes of the third pressing" is used for the *saṃpraiṣa* (direction), and so forth. Thus ends the eleventh section.
At the time of the performance, the Adhvaryu takes up the Hotṛ’s cup, and the Camasādhvaryus take up their respective cups.

Having caused the announcement to be made and having received the response, he issues the command: "For Indra, the Somas of the third pressing—possessing abundance, possessing pervasiveness, possessing power, possessing vigor, possessing Savitṛ, possessing Bṛhaspati, accompanied by the Viśve Devas, intense and full of blessings. This is the beginning of the command. (2) Then he offers the goblets.

(3) He offers at the *vaṣaṭ*-call with the formula: "To the flying falcon, svāhā! He offers at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call with the formula: "Vat! Adoration to him who has spontaneously approved; svāhā! (4)
Having offered, he carries away the portion for consumption;

in this manner he proceeds with the subsequent [oblations]. This much is the difference: he offers with each preceding mantra at every *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, and with each succeeding [mantra] at every *anuvaṣaṭ*-utterance.

Having offered all the *hotrā* oblations with the formula, "May they satisfy themselves," he mutters [the following]. (8) When the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down, the cup-bearers (*camasin*) follow their respective cups; they each cast three pieces of sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa-śakala*) into them, reciting these formulas one by one: "This for you, Father N.N., and those who follow you. (9) They mutter the salutations: "Homage to you, O Fathers, to the essence! (10)
The sacrificer recites the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula (11).
With the two verses addressed to Prajāpati, "O Prajāpati, these [worlds] are not yours... (12), they conclude.
Thus ends the twelfth Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the third Paṭala.
Having drawn the Sāvitra cup from the Āgrayaṇa vessel with the Antaryāma vessel, saying, "O Savitṛ, take the left [cup] today," he does not set it down.
He issues the two commands: "Recite for the god Savitṛ" and "Prompt for the god Savitṛ.
He does not utter the *anuvaṣaṭ* call.
With this very remnant, he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup from the *pūtabhṛt* vessel. "Thou art taken with a support; thou art good protection"—these are the formulas for the drawing and the setting down.
There is no *stotra*.
He responds with the *vaiśvadeva* chant:

"O Heaven and Earth, increase through the sacrifices according to the cosmic order (*ṛta*). Having recognized this, he responds with joy on both sides, saying: "Joy! Joy! As if with joy! Joy! As if with joy! (7–8).
Or he may respond with joy on only one side, saying: "Joy! As if with joy! Othā! Joy! As if with joy! (9).
Some recite [the verses] with an interval: *madā moda iva othā moda iva modā moda iva*.
(10) Up to the call (*vyāhāva*).

(11) Having recognized [the signal], "O Vāyu, unyoke those [horses] here with your teams," the Pratiprasthātṛ unyokes the vessels for the dual-deity offerings with the formula, "May Vāyu unyoke you. Having carried them out by the western door, having washed them at the Mārjālīya fire-altar, and having brought them back by the eastern door, he places them in their respective positions. (12)
The *graha* and *nārāśaṃsa* cups are like those of the *vaiśvadeva*.
He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *saumya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*).
The ritual procedure for the *caru* has been explained.
Having cooked [the oblation], wearing the sacred cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he proceeds with the offering to Soma.
He first cuts the first portion with his hand; the second with the stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa). Or this may be done in the reverse order.

Having cut from the south, having sprinkled [clarified butter] over it, having stepped across toward the north and standing facing the south, and having called for the announcement (āśrāvya), when the response has been given, he issues the direction: "Recite the offering-verse (yajya) for the Soma-oblation."
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers in the southern half [of the fire].
(19) He performs the *pariyajana* of the *saumya* [oblation] with clarified butter, silently, on both sides; or on one side only.
(20) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and having received the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, he issues the direction: "Sacrifice the clarified butter! (21)
Having offered at the *vaṣaṭ*-call and having stepped back, he fills the *caru* with clarified butter. (22) Thus ends the thirteenth section.
They carry [the offering] to the Udgātṛs. (1)
The Udgātṛs shall look down upon him, saying, "This belongs to you; that which is yours here.
He who does not see his own self should make a mirror with clarified butter and look into it.
He whose mind has wandered away should look at it, saying: "My mind that has gone astray..."
Furthermore, here he sprinkles the fire-hearths (dhiṣṇiyas) that have been spread out while burning with splinters, using clarified butter taken eight times.

If someone should say to him, "Sprinkle the Āgnīdhrīya hearth for me again," he takes [butter] nine times, sprinkles the Āgnīdhrīya first and last, and holds the remaining butter over the other hearths.
Having drawn the Pātnīvata cup from the Āgrayaṇa vessel with the Upāṃśu vessel, using the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; of thee, pressed by Bṛhaspati... he does not set it down.

Having sprinkled [the butter] with the remainder of the *vyāghāraṇa* and having caused [the Āgnīdhra] to call for the *śrauṣaṭ*, when the response has been given, he issues the command: "O *Āgnīdh*, sacrifice to the *pātnīvata*! At the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ*, he offers [the oblation], saying: "O Agni, accompanied by the wives (*patnīvān*)!
He does not pronounce the secondary *vaṣaṭ*;
or rather, he may pronounce the secondary *vaṣaṭ* in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

Then he issues the command: "Sit on the lap of the Neṣṭṛ; O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife; O Unnetṛ, fill the Hotṛ’s cup following [the others], and provide space for the Dhruva in the Hotṛ’s cup; cause the wife to be counted by the Udgātṛ; let the waters flow forth. They act according to this command. Having stepped between the Neṣṭṛ and the Dhiṣṇiya hearth, the Āgnīdhra consumes [the portion].
With the words "of that which has been drunk by Agni," he modifies the mantra for the consumption [of the Soma].
This is the fourteenth section.
One should not sit upon one's lap; if one were to sit upon one's lap, one would become a eunuch.
While pouring out the cups, beginning with the Hotṛ’s cup, and having poured out the entire King Soma, he wipes the two jars with the fringes of the cloth and turns them face down.
He introduces the *yajñāyajñiya* chant.
They kindle the hearths.
They chant the Yajñāyajñiya either with their ears covered or uncovered.
All those who have entered [the sacrificial ground] should join in the chanting of the Agniṣṭoma.
The sacrificer recites the Saptahotṛ formula.

With the words, "Of thee who art all-pervading, of the universe," he causes the wife to look at the *hiṅkāra* together with the *udgātṛ*. And [he does so] until three *stotriya* verses have been chanted, and [with the verse], "The gods have come. 8.

The wife causes water to flow forward along her right thigh, which is bare, directed eastward and northward, between her thighs. 9. Some say that she should cause it to flow forward between her thighs. 10.

One should raise [the voice] high above for the one who reveals the flanks; it is known that [this is done] for the one born from the foremost of the shameless. 11. He responds to the Āgnimāruta hymn when it is imminent. 12.
Having recognized [the verse], "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss," he responds while pouring water. 13.
Recognizing [the verse], "Truly, this is sweet, and this is honeyed," he responds with joy on both sides, saying, "Joy! Joy! and "Joy! Joy! until the *vyāhāva* (the call for the next response). 14.
From the settling of the *dhruva* vessel until its pouring out, the sacrificer does not void urine.
15. Thus ends the fifteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

"Thou art the existent; place me in the existent," with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ looks at the *dhruva* cup. Having grasped it with his joined palms, saying, "I encompass thee for Heaven and Earth," and having moved it while saying, "May the All-gods, common to all men, move thee forth," he pours the *dhruva* into the *hotṛ*-cup while seated facing west, using the formula, "The *dhruva* with the *dhruva*. It is to be poured before the *ukthya* draught, or in the middle, or at the end.
Or [he may do so] when the verse addressed to the Viśvedevas, "And let Ahi Budhnya hear us, and Aja Ekapād," is being recited.
Or, when the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*) has been recited once by the Teacher—
whether it be the middle or the final one— he says,
"The hymn (*uktha*) has been spoken for Indra," having responded to the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). Or, he does so after each individual recitation (*śastra*).

At the time of the procession, the Adhvaryu takes up the Hotṛ’s cup, and the Camasādhvaryus take up their respective cups. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and received the response, he issues the direction: "O reciter of the *uktha*, offer the *soma*s! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*, they make the offerings. They then bring the portions for consumption.

The Adhvaryu partakes of the Hotṛ’s cup with the formula: "Thou art well-being, the best of rays, dear to the gods, worthy of being seated together. May the gods enter thee, O auspicious one! Thou art impetuous, thou art brilliant, thou art manly, thou art mighty, thou art the sacred law, thou art heaven, thou art the warder-off. Of thee, who art impetuous, brilliant, manly, mighty, the sacred law, heaven, and the warder-off—of thee, the Śūdra and the Ārya, may I enjoy! (8) With the formula, "As you, O Sūrya, are visible to all, so may I become visible to all," the sacrificer worships the Sun. (9)
"Grant me life and sense-power; let not this [evil] come to me," he says as he approaches the Āhavanīya fire (10).
He pronounces the name of whatever he desires (11).
"O Agnīdh, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings," with these words he commences the ritual pertaining to the animal sacrifice (12).

Thus ends the sixteenth section; thus ends the fourth chapter. Once the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) have been thrown into the fire, the Unnetṛ draws the Hāriyojana cup. Having taken the entire Āgrayaṇa draught with the wooden trough (*droṇakalaśa*) while reciting, "Thou art taken with a support; thou art tawny," he does not set it down. Having mixed it with many parched grains (*dhānā*), and having placed it upon his head, he goes out and issues the two directions: "Recite the invitatory prayer for Indra accompanied by the tawny ones (*harivat*); give the command for Indra accompanied by the tawny ones! Or alternatively: "Recite the invitatory prayer for the Soma-parched grains; give the command for the Soma-parched grains that have been set forth!"
"Ye two are tawny; ye are the grains for the tawny ones"—having stepped forward and offered at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*, he takes away the portion for consumption.

Having placed the *droṇakalaśa* behind the *uttaravedi* and having sought permission from the *unnetṛ*, they all consume the *hāriyojana* portion with the formula, "O divine Soma, [thee] whose sacrifice is performed.
Without crushing the grains, they make hollows; having made the hollows, they suck them out as it were.
They eat [the portions] in the form of *ciściṣā*.
Having eaten them with the formula, "For cultivation, for security, for wealth, for prosperity," they mutter [the following]:

(7) "May you be full; fill up! Having thrown the remnants upon the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), they worship the Āhavanīya fire with the *minda* [offering], reciting: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self... (8).

"Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods; thou art the expiation for sin committed against men; thou art the expiation for sin committed against the fathers; thou art the expiation for sin committed by oneself; thou art the expiation for sin committed by another; thou art the expiation for every sin"—having spoken thus, he places wood-chips upon the Āhavanīya fire. Then, having thrown yellow *dūrvā* grass into the remnants of the *ekadhana* waters, having pressed them down, and having made them strong, he distributes them according to the cups. To the west of the *cātvāla* or in the *āstāva*, the cup-bearers, facing west, consume their respective cup-remnants with their noses, saying: "O God Soma, of thee who art washed in the waters... (9)

Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā). "I send you forth to the ocean; go back to your own source. May our heroes be unharmed; let not our property be scattered. "O Maruts, may this song of praise reach you; may it reach Viṣṇu, the protector of the poured seed, with his aids. And bestow strength upon the progeny and the singer. Do you protect us always with your blessings. Having poured the remnants [of the curd] within the altar (vedī), they consume the drops of curd at the Āgnīdhra fire-altar, reciting: "I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan..."

"Both are young seers; they are true, the lords of the cosmic order (dharman). With the words, "O Lord of the Cosmic Order of Truth, we dissolve our bonds of friendship," those who have performed the *tānūnaptra* rite dissolve their bonds of friendship.
2. The *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are performed as in the animal sacrifice. 3.

When the altar (*veda*) has been strewn, having taken nine portions of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, he stands upright within the altar and offers the nine *samiṣṭayajus* oblations continuously and in equal portions, with the formula, "Dhātṛ is the giver... and so forth. 4.
If he should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," he should offer to him one by one while standing crookedly, either with the *sruva* spoon or taking [the portions] separately.
When the third pressing of the seers has concluded, he offers an oblation with the verse: "This is the third pressing of the seers.

At this point, the followers of the Vājasaneya school prescribe the throwing away of the girdle and the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit with the formula: "Do not be a *māhiḥ*, do not be a *pṛdāku*!"
"By means of the god Agni, may I conquer the hostile armies," saying this, the sacrificer strides the Viṣṇu-steps according to the Jagatī metre.

"By means of all the gods, may I conquer the hostile armies; by means of the Anuṣṭubh metre, the twenty-one-fold Stoma, the Vairāja Sāman, the Vaṣaṭ-call, and the thunderbolt, I cast down all my kinsmen and rivals; I press them down, I drive them away from this dwelling, from this world of earth—him who hates us and him whom we hate. By the stride of Viṣṇu, I stride over them. Some recite this as the fourth [formula].
With the words, "United with Indra, may we... the sacrificer worships the Āhavanīya fire.
Thus ends the eighteenth Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the fifth Paṭala. He commences the ritual procedure for the Avabhṛtha bath.
Having prepared the Veda and strewn grass around the fires, he proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the washing of the hands. The arrangement of the vessels is according to the requirements.
At the time of the pouring out [of the grain], he pours out the offering for Varuṇa on a single potsherd.
Having taken four portions of clarified butter and having adorned the oblation for Varuṇa, he places it upon the northern shoulder of the high altar.

Here the sacrificer digs up the Audumbarī post while reciting: "Bestowing support upon the mother, the supporter suckling; may the Lord of Prosperity bestow nourishment here. May he maintain for us abundance of wealth, food, and vigor.

(5) He places it on the skin used for pressing, along with all the Soma-soiled implements, between the Cātvāla pit and the rubbish heap, or on the northern shoulder of the altar, on the Audumbarī stand. This excludes the four Soma-vessels.
(6) With the mantra, "O Varuṇa, let thy wrath depart through our prostrations," the sacrificer throws a piece of black antelope skin into the Cātvāla pit. (7)

One may undergo initiation again with this [wood], or wear it; or one should have a piece of it fashioned for the purpose of placing it in the *sruva* ladle, or for the purpose of threshing the sacrificial offering (*havis*). Some say that after emerging from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), one should give it to a son or to a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
When about to enter the purificatory bath, one should offer an oblation with the verse, "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation," and also with the verse, "O purificatory bath, Nicaṅkuṇa."
Thus ends the nineteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
"Salutation to Rudra, the Lord of the Dwelling, at the coming, the fleeing, the going forth, the departing, the turning back, and the turning away;
him who protects, him I invoke"—with these words, and also with "For wide indeed has King Varuṇa made," they say as they proceed toward the altar (vedī), or from the pit (cātvāla).
"O Prastotṛ, chant the Sāman! 3.
At the halfway point, all [the priests], together with their wives, reach the *nidhana* of the Sāman three times; having reached the end, they reach it for the third time. 4.
Everywhere he issues the call. 5.
It is prescribed that one should go toward all directions for the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*); such is the beginning of the ritual conduct.
Or, as in the case of the *niṣkāsa*, having performed the rite with the *vāruṇa* offering, he performs two after-offerings (*anūyāja*) without the *barhis* grass. Or not [so].

With the five verses addressed to Soma containing the word "drop" (*drapsa*), beginning with "That which [is pressed] by the stones," "Swell up," and "Be united," and with curds, he sprinkles the *urjīṣa* (the dregs of the soma) with a branch of the *udumbara* tree. There are seven or thirteen [verses].
Or, having struck [the vessel], he should offer [the contents] into the fire.
Having filled the ladle with the *ṛjīṣa*, he dips it into the water with the mantra: "In the ocean is thy heart, within the waters.
Then, whatever drop flows out, he should either touch it or consume it with the mantra: "O divine Soma, of thee who art washed in the waters..."

"I send you to the ocean"—with these words, he throws all the items smeared with Soma into the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). "The noose of Varuṇa is loosened"—with these words, the sacrificer unties his girdle; "I loosen this"—with these words, the wife unties her waist-band.
At this point, having thrown the waist-band, the girdle, the two garments, the net, and the black antelope skin into the purificatory bath.
Thus ends the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā).

Having consecrated the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) with the mantra "O divine waters... (*devīrāpaḥ*), the sacrificer, having plunged into the water with the mantra "May the waters and plants be friendly to us" (*sumitrā na āpa oṣadhayaḥ*), both the wife and the sacrificer—having bathed and not rubbing their heads against each other—run over each other's backs. 1–2.

Whatever I consecrated with the mind and whatever with speech; or whatever with the vital breaths, the eye, and the ear; or with semen, through the couple, and through the self—from the waters the worlds received brilliance and sensory power. O pure ones, you who release from consecration and from austerity, may the waters release brilliance and sensory power within me. Whatever I consecrated with the *ṛc*, the *sāman*, and the *yajus*; on the skin of animals, and with the oblation; or with the meters, the plants, and the tree—from the waters the worlds received brilliance and sensory power.

"O bright ones, releasers from the consecration and from austerity; O waters, releasers, bestow upon me luster and sensory power! That by which the Brahman, the Kṣatra, Indra and Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, and King Varuṇa; by which the All-gods and the seers, the vital breaths, and the worlds have received luster and sensory power from the waters—O bright ones, releasers from the consecration and from austerity; O waters, releasers, bestow upon me luster and sensory power! Having sprinkled [the water] three times with his joined palms, he says: "O Unnetṛ, draw up more for me."

"When the [sun] has risen, our songs most excellent in winning wealth, our hymns of praise go forth—conquering all, winning riches, with unfailing protection, like chariots seeking booty. Like the Kaṇvas, like the Bhr̥gus, like the Sūryas, they have attained everything that is to be attained"—thus the sacrificer gives the command.
This is the twenty-first section.

"Arising, bestowing progeny, life-span, and luster, may we be in the houses of both [father and mother]. Let them take hold of the Gāyatrī and the meters; may wealth and sacrifices attend us. Well-pleased, he has entered the light of heaven"—with these words, the Unnetṛ priest leads [the waters] up. 1.
Having risen while wearing two unwashed garments, the sacrificer puts on the *uṣṇīṣa* turban of Soma; the wife [puts on] the Soma-veil or the Soma-envelope.
These two are given to the Adhvaryu at the *udavasānīyā* offering.

Having worshipped the sun with the verse, "Upwards from the darkness... (RV 1.50.10), and having stepped back to the water's edge with the formula, "The noose of Varuṇa is loosened," they return without looking back, holding fuel-sticks in their hands and preceded by the Unnetṛ, while reciting the *mahīyā* verses: "We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal; we have reached the light, the gods have known us. What sin, what transgression of the waters, what debt to Yama I have incurred while living under his power—while remaining right here, we discharge that; as the living, we pay this back to the living. May we be free from debt in this world, free from debt in the next, and free from debt in the third world.
May we fulfill all paths, those leading to the gods and those leading to the fathers, being free from debt. (ŚB 4.2.5.1–5)
Having placed fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Fuel art thou; may we prosper," they worship it with the formula, "I have moved along the waters.
Thus ends the twenty-second section (kaṇḍikā). This is the sixth chapter (paṭala).
The Udayanīyā [offering] is like the Prāyaṇīyā.
He cooks [the oblation] in that very pot without removing it. That is the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); that is the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*). They proceed with the rites at the *Śālāmukhīya* fire.
In those very locations, he first sacrifices to the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), and lastly to Pathyā Svasti.
It has been stated that [the verses] which are the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā*) of the *prāyaṇīya* [offering] are used here.
(5) He immolates a barren cow (*vaśā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa as the *anūbandhyā*.
(6) Its ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is like that of the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*. (7)
"Recite for Mitra and Varuṇa the omentum and fat of the cow; give the command for the omentum and fat of the cow for Mitra and Varuṇa"—these are the two calls.
(8) In the same way, he modifies the endings of the portions from the oblation to "of the oblation.
(9) Some authorities prescribe three Anūbandhyā cows. (10)
[They offer] one for Mitra and Varuṇa, one for the Viśvedevas, and one for Bṛhaspati.
11. The [cow] for Mitra and Varuṇa is two-colored; the one for the Viśvedevas is multicolored; the one for Bṛhaspati is red. 12.
They proceed with the [offering] for the Viśvedevas in a low voice (upāṃśu) through the middle [of the sacrifice]. 13.

One should not offer them at every sacrifice—neither at the Vājapeya, nor the Rājasūya, nor a Sattra, nor at a thousand-fold sacrifice, nor at one where all one's possessions are given away (sarvavedasa). 14.
He who desires, "May my entire sacrifice be complete and full of essence," should offer these three Anūbandhyā animals. 15.
When the omentum of the Anūbandhyā has been offered, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved at the southern edge of the altar. 16.
The animal-cake offering for the Anūbandhyā cow.
Thus ends the twenty-third section. He offers the oblations of the Devikās. 1.
"A cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ"—thus there are five [offerings].
In those same vessels in which the Soma-pressings take place, he cooks the four subsequent oblations.
However, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* are common [to all].
"One desiring offspring should offer the Devikā oblations"—these are the optional rites.
5 At the Anūbandhyā sacrifice, he offers the *svaru* splinter; he removes the heart-spit.
6 He performs the Viṣṇu-strides. 7

For the King or one worthy of kingship, he subsequently offers eight *devasū* oblations following the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the Anūbandhyā cow, beginning with [the offering] to Agni Gṛhapati (8). However, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* are common [to all] (9). The Bahvṛcas prescribe a curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa (*maitrāvaruṇīmāmikṣā*) in place of the Anūbandhyā cow. Seated in front of the *havirdhāna* cart, the Hotṛ performs the sacrifice without pausing. It concludes with the *iḍā*, starting from the offering of the oblation; or it starts from the *prayājas* or the *ājyabhāgas*. Some prescribe that it ends with the *iḍā* (10).
Some perform the Kṛtsnasaṃsthā sacrifice; after that, he offers the Devikā oblations. However, the Sviṣṭakṛt and the Iḍā portions are common to both.
Having untied the first knots tied [to the poles] of the *sadas*, the *havirdhāna* shed, or the two *havirdhāna* sheds, he turns the *havirdhāna* carts toward the north outside the altar. 14.
Taking a firebrand from the *āhavanīya* fire, the sacrificer burns the edge of the altar with the verse: "Whatever debt remains unpaid... 15.
If he should act as if mixed up, he should offer groats with his joined palms into the forest fire with the formula: "O Viśvalopa, for thee who consumest all... 16.
With the three verses beginning "yadākūtāt," he consecrates the smoke;
17 with "ahnāṃ vidhānyām," as has been stated; 18 and having performed the worship with the verses beginning "ayaṃ no nabhasā puraḥ," according to the Brāhmaṇa. 19
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section (kaṇḍikā).
Having placed the Veda on his lap and sitting within the altar (antarvedi), he mutters the *atīmokṣa* formulas.
Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the Viṣṇu-strides (*viṣṇukrama*).

Having placed the *prājahita* fire on the altar and having moved the second fire to the *śālāmukhīya*, those who have attained prosperity should move out either to the east or to the north, [saying]: "To this more excellent dwelling-place we have now come; may both these, Heaven and Earth, be auspicious for us. Rich in cattle, rich in wealth, rich in horses, full of vigor—may we, with brave sons, move along with our heroes. Having settled upon the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), he begins the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *udavasānīyā* offering by means of churning the fire. Having added fuel to the fires, prepared the *veda* grass-bundle, and strewn around the fires, he proceeds with the rite beginning with the washing of the hands. The arrangement of the vessels is according to the requirements.

At the time of the offering, he offers a cake on five potsherds for Agni, or one on eight potsherds. If it is on five potsherds, the two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *gāyatrī* meter; if it is on eight potsherds, they are in the *paṅkti* meter. An ox is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or gold of the value of an ox. The sacrifice is concluded in the established manner. The Vājasaneyins prescribe a full-offering to Viṣṇu in place of the concluding rite (*udavasānīyā*).
Having filled the *sruva* ladle with twelve scoops, he offers it while standing upright within the *vedi*, reciting, "Viṣṇu strode across this [world].
(8) That sacrifice concludes at night; then he performs the evening *agnihotra*. At the proper time, he performs the morning *homa*.
(9) The *agniṣṭoma* is concluded; the *agniṣṭoma* is concluded. (10)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the seventh chapter (paṭala).
Thus ends the thirteenth book (praśna).
The Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma are modifications of the Agniṣṭoma by way of added qualities.

One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Ukthya; one desiring virility, with the Ṣoḍaśin; one desiring offspring or cattle, with the Atirātra; and by means of the Aptoryāma Atirātra, one obtains all desires. 2. Their ritual procedure is like that of the Agniṣṭoma. 3. And the modifications have been stated. 4.
Just as there are the sacrificial hall, the implements for the sacrifice, the sacrificial animals, the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, the cow for purchasing Soma, and the vessel;
if it is an *ukthya* [sacrifice], while drawing out the *agnistoma* cups, he leaves over the King [Soma] for three groups of cups.

The call is: "O Agnīdh, sit in the lap of the Neṣṭṛ! O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife! O Unnetṛ, fill the Hotṛ's cup following [the others]; make space in the Hotṛ's cup for the *dhruva* [cup]; cause the wife to be counted by the Udgātṛ; let the waters flow forth! 5–7.

Having performed the rites with the Agniṣṭoma cups, he draws the Ukthya libations as at the morning pressing; this much is the difference. At the first drawing and setting down, he modifies the formula to "For Indra and Varuṇa, thee!"; at the second, "For Indra and Bṛhaspati, thee!"; and at the third, "For Indra and Viṣṇu, thee! (Sūtra 8). "O Unnetṛ, pour out the entire King Soma; do not leave any remainder. Having wiped the two jars with the fringes of the cloth, [the Adhvaryu] says, "Set them down," thus giving this command at the final group of rites in all the sacrificial forms (saṃsthās). (Sūtra 10)
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
"O Āgnīdhra, bring the embers for the after-offerings (aupayaja)"—this and the subsequent ritual actions pertaining to the Agniṣṭoma are common to all sacrificial forms (saṃsthās).
However, if indeed, while drawing the last group of cups (camasa) for the Ṣoḍaśin or the Ukthya, he leaves over the King Soma (rājā) for one additional cup-group.
The drawing of the Ṣoḍaśin cup occurs at the morning pressing; it is the last of the stream-cups (dhārāgraha), or it may be drawn at each pressing.

Now, according to some: in the first two pressings, one should draw [the cup] from before the last *ukthya* turn; when the ritual has been performed with all [the cups], in the third pressing, it is drawn from the *āgrayaṇa*.
Or rather, in the third pressing alone, it is drawn from the *āgrayaṇa* for one who desires cattle. One should not draw it at the *ukthya* [sacrifice]; or one may draw it.
At the Atirātra for one desiring cattle; at the Atirātra for one desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa).
One may also take [the draughts] at the Agniṣṭoma for a Rājanya; it becomes one where the Stotras and Śastras have been recited.
"Mount [the chariot], O slayer of Vṛtra!"—with these words, the seizing and the setting down [of the cup] are performed.

"He than whom no other has been born superior, he who has entered into all beings; Prajāpati, in harmony with his progeny, attends the three lights—he is the Ṣoḍaśin. He is the Brahman, he who is seasonal. Known by the name Indra in the troop, I shall proclaim your two bay steeds at the great sacrifice. I win for you that which is seasonal; I win the desirable intoxication of the conqueror. Known by the name Indra, he who pours forth the ghee-like [soma] beautifully with his bay steeds—the renowned troop, may they enter you."
Having consecrated the seated [victim] with these four verses beginning with "harivarṣasaṃ giraḥ," [the ritual proceeds].
Thus ends the second section (kaṇḍikā).
When the sun has half-set, he begins the *ṣoḍaśin* chant with gold.
It takes place at the spot where the sacrificial grass (barhis) is located.
They hold a white horse in front, or one that is reddish-brown.
"Othā moda iva made madā moda ivomathā"—this is the interlaced response (pratigara) containing joy on both sides, used for the verses in the Anuṣṭubh meter.

"O Indra, lord of lords, you are the lord of the gods; make me, long-lived and full of splendor, a lord among men"—having offered thus, he consumes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with the formula: "Indra the sovereign and Varuṇa the king, they two first made this your portion; following their consumption, I consume it; may Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma. He modifies the consumption mantra for the cups by saying, "With the troop that has Āditya as its leader, with the *anuṣṭubh* metre. A reddish-brown horse is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or else a mule.
If it is an *atirātra* sacrifice, while drawing the *ṣoḍaśi-camasas*, he leaves over the King Soma for thirteen groups of cups.
Having performed the *ṣoḍaśin* rite, he proceeds with the rounds of the night.

The first group has the *hotṛ*-cup as its chief; the second has the *maitrāvaruṇa*-cup as its chief; the third has the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*-cup as its chief; the fourth has the *acchāvāka*-cup as its chief.

With the formula, "For Indra thee, belonging to the night," he pours after [the soma] into each principal cup. (11) The entire night belongs to Indra. (12) With the words, "The *anuṣṭubh* is the metre," he modifies the *bhakṣa*-mantra in every instance. (13)
The Adhvaryu proceeds with the first two groups; the Pratiprasthātṛ with the latter two. This is the first round. In this manner, the second and third rounds are prescribed.
Thus ends the third section (kaṇḍikā).
Now, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the cake on two potsherds for the Aśvins;
he draws the cups for the junction-formulas (saṃdhicamasa), with the Hotṛ’s cup as the principal one.
The *saṃdhi* chant is the *rathaṃtara* consisting of three verses; the *āśvina* recitation consists of more than a thousand verses.
That [recitation] is performed when the sun has risen.
When that has been put on, the Adhvaryu takes up the Hotṛ’s cup, the Camasādhvaryus take up their cups, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the sacrificial cake.

[The Adhvaryu issues] the two directions: "Recite for the Soma-draughts belonging to the Aśvins from the previous day; give the command for the Soma-draughts belonging to the Aśvins from the previous day.
Or he says: "Command for the Soma-draughts belonging to the previous day that have been set forth."
Or rather, he should not send it forth.
The Pratiprasthātṛ offers the cake together with the Soma cups as a complete oblation.
He modifies the consumption formula by adding, "The Paṅkti is the metre."
If it is the Aptoryāma sacrifice, while drawing the *saṃdhi* cups, he draws out the King Soma for four sets of cups.
(12) As in the first round of the night, so do they become the principal ones.
(13) He draws the cups for Agni first; those for Indra second; those for the Viśve Devas third; and those for Viṣṇu fourth. (14)

Regarding them, some say the ritual procedure for their distribution is like that of the *saṃdhi-camasa*. (15) One modifies the *bhakṣa-mantra* everywhere by adding "the *aticchandas* metre" [at the end].
(16) Thus ends the fourth section (*kaṇḍikā*), thus ends the first chapter (*paṭala*).
The *kratupaśus* and the *aikādaśina* animals are subject to option.
When they occur together, the consecratory rites (*saṃskāras*) are performed according to the scriptural injunctions. The auxiliary elements (*aṅgas*) apply as a common ritual framework (*tantra*).
The rites whose objects are perceptible are repeated at each consecration (pratisaṃskāra). 4.
There is an adaptation (ūha) according to the specific object.
5. Having offered the oblation for the sacrificial post (yūpāhuti), he cuts thirteen sacrificial posts, beginning with the one nearest the fire (agniṣṭha), while reciting the mantra. 6.
For all [the sacrificial posts], there are the rites of bringing the chips, the cutting, and the oblations (7).
He has the entire upaśaya post fashioned (8). He cuts the pātnīvata post in such a way that it will be level with below the navel (9).

Having performed that which is prior to the measuring of the altar, he measures out a rope eleven times the length of Daśaratha’s axle; having measured it, he measures the altar with a twenty-fourth part of that [rope].
(10) It serves as the substitute for the *prakrama* step.
(11) Having encircled the *agniṣṭha* post with two ropes, and having encircled the eleven [posts] with the ropes, he causes them to rest upon the *agniṣṭha*. (12)
The sacrificial posts are double the [usual] height. On the following day, having drawn the Āśvina cup, he erects the sacrificial posts,
or together with the post standing nearest the fire.
The taking up of the cord from the cloud (the sky) is the tracing; it is repeated. 16.
The intervals between the sacrificial posts are the size of a chariot-axle. 17.
Having traced around the southern one starting from the post standing near the fire (agniṣṭha), he traces around the northern one starting from the post standing near the fire. 18.
In this manner, he erects the sacrificial posts (yūpas) with their tops turned toward the north in alternating fashion.
For each post there are wooden chips (svarus).
The ground to the south becomes elevated.
One should measure it higher on the north side for one who desires the world of the ancestors (22).
Thus ends the fifth section.
For one who desires stability, all [sides] should be equal (1).

Those three which are middle-sized, he should make equal for one desiring cattle; he should interlink the others. For one practicing sorcery, [the altar] should have a point like an awl. The middle part is elevated, and the two ends are gradually sloped downward.
For one desiring rain, it should flow evenly; it is depressed in the middle, with the two edges gradually rising higher.
It should be interlaced for the sake of overcoming rivals;
it is said to be measured by a pit.

If he should desire, "May the ruling power (kṣatra) be more powerful than the common people (viś)," he should erect the southern [posts] higher than the one at the fire-altar (agniṣṭha). Or, conversely, if he desires, "May the common people be more powerful than the ruling power," he should do the opposite.

He should erect it level with the top for one who desires the world of the fathers; level with the middle and level with the girth-rope for one who desires the world of men; and level with the cross-piece (caṣāla) for one who desires sensory power.

The upper parts [of the stakes] should be equal in length; the middle parts and the girdles should be equal in width; and the *caṣāla* rings should be equal in thickness. Having encircled the *upaśaya* with two girdles, he places it facing eastward at the front of the southern sacrificial post, or to the south of it, while meditating in his mind upon the one he hates, saying: "Here I place so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, beneath Indra’s thunderbolt. He dedicates a black-necked animal to Agni at the central post (*agniṣṭha*), a ewe to Sarasvatī on the northern post, and a brown animal to Soma on the southern post.
In this manner, he dedicates the animals in reverse order, ending toward the south. 14. Finally, he dedicates the animal to Varuṇa on the south side, facing north. 15.
It has been stated that if one should desire, "May he who is excluded be further excluded," [this is the procedure]. 16.

Thus ends the sixth section (kaṇḍikā). He should designate a wild animal or a mouse as the victim for the supplementary offering (upaśaya), saying, "This is your animal," while mentally contemplating his enemy. 1–2.
If he does not hate [anyone], he should say, "The rat is your sacrificial animal.
For each animal there are sacrificial grasses (*barhis*), omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), pots (*kumbhī*), and heart-spikes (*hṛdayaśūla*).

The carrying forward of the fire is common to all, as is the *ādhṛgu* formula, the oblation for the immolated animal (*saṃjñaptahoma*), the removal of the ropes, the two *parivapya* portions, the throwing into the fire of the omentum-spits, the secondary oblation (*abhihoma*), and the sprinkling (*mārjana*).
The *manotā* hymn is repeated for each [animal],
or it is performed as a single common ritual (*tantra*); the three portions [of the omentum] and the collected offering (*samavatta*) belong to all of them.
Having equalized the excesses, he offers to the quarters.

9 At the last animal, he sacrifices to Vanaspati and to Sviṣṭakṛt. 10 He performs the *upayaj* offerings with the entire rectal sections of all [the animals]. And they perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the tails. 11

When the omentum of the Anūbandhyā cow has been offered, he erects the Pātnīvata post in front of the Śālāmukhīya fire; it is below the navel, without a base-covering, and without a top-ring (caṣāla).

Having dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ an animal that is a castrated bull, hairy, and tawny, and having performed the rite of carrying fire around it, he should release it and complete the remainder of the sacrifice with clarified butter.
He should take portions of the clarified butter as many times as there would be portions from the animal victim.
The clarified butter belongs to the animal sacrifice;
it is known that they proceed with the offering at the Śālāmukhīya fire.
Alternatively, one may simply discard what has been prepared on the Ārya fire; one should not bring the rite to a formal conclusion.

One should conclude the remainder of the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice after the *paśupuroḍāśa* and other offerings. (18) If there is a set of eleven animals belonging to the Kāpeyas, there are two animals dedicated to Indra on both sides of the one dedicated to Agni: to the north, those for Sarasvatī, Soma, Pūṣan, and Bṛhaspati; to the south, those for Savitṛ, Viśve Devas, Maruts, and Varuṇa.
(19) The Kāpeyas know this [set]; one should immolate it at the end of the *atirātra* sacrifice. (20)
"Among those who have already sacrificed, because of the connection with the word [of the guest],
it becomes other than the *sattra*";
thus ends the seventh section (*kaṇḍikā*), and this is the second chapter (*paṭala*).

The Vāsiṣṭha Brahman [is the officiant] at the Jyotiṣṭoma; or whoever may know the stomabhāgas [may be]. In the duties of the Adhvaryu and during the Stotra and Śastra recitations, he restrains his speech; and also during the Antardhi.
If he should speak while distracted, he shall mutter a verse addressed to Viṣṇu and the *vyāhṛtis*, and then restrain his speech.

While the king is being measured out, while the great altar (*mahāvedi*) and the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) are being prepared, while the fire is being measured, ploughed, and poured in, while each layer of the altar is being laid down, and during the rites of the piled altar and the rites of the bricks—while these are being performed—he sits to the south.

While the fire is being carried, he should go toward the fire as it is being led forward; while the *ukhā* is being carried, he should go toward the *vasatīvarī* waters and the *savanīya* offerings; while they are being brought in, he should go toward the *nairṛtī* bricks that are to be laid down. He goes to the south of the piled fires (*cityagni*) as they are being led forward.

(6) While the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds are being constructed, he goes between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), passes to the north of the *uttaravedi*, and sits down to the south.
(7) He remains seated until the time of the *vaisarjana* offering. (8)

While the oblations are being offered, he passes by them, goes to the north of the *havirdhāna* shed, circumambulates the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth to the north, enters the *prāgvaṃśa* hall by the eastern door, passes to the south of the *śālāmukhīya* fire, and sits down.
(This is the eighth section.
With the words "Thus do thou worship," he places the King [Soma] upon his lap.

When the offering has been made, he goes out first and follows behind the fire. Having reached the Āgnīdhrīya shed and handed over the King [Soma] to the Pratiprasthātṛ, he passes to the north of the Āgnīdhrīya, crosses to the south, and sits down. He places the King in his lap as before. When the offering has been made, he goes out first, leads the King into the Havirdhāna shed by the western door, hands him over to the Adhvaryu, goes to the north of the Havirdhāna, passes to the south of the rear of the Uttaravedi, and sits down. He remains seated until the offering of the omentum of the Agniṣomīya animal; once the omentum has been offered, he performs the ritual purification (mārjana).

While the *vasatīvarī* waters are being carried around, he sits on the south side. When they are waking up at the dead of night, he wakes up. Once the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) has been introduced, he restrains his speech until the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*). When the *savanīya* oblations are being brought forward, having entered the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door and having passed to the south in front of the *khara* mound, he sits down.
While the King Soma is being measured, while it is being pressed, and while the cups are being drawn, he restrains his speech until the drawing of the *āgrayaṇa* cup.
He offers the drops (*vaipruṣa*) as they are being poured into the *juhū* ladle.
While the Pavamāna chants are being recited, [the sacrificer], having taken hold [of the Brahman], creeps forward.
When it is said, "O Brahman, we shall chant the Stotra; O Praśāstṛ," he recites, "O God Savitṛ, this is declared to you," and follows it with the appropriate verses.
Thus ends the ninth section.
"You are the ray; for dwelling, I impel you, the dwelling; Om, praise!"—with these words he gives the impulse.
This is the ritual rule for all stotras. He places the Stomabhāgas one after another, each subsequent one higher than the preceding.
There are twelve [stotras] in the Agniṣṭoma; fifteen in the Ukthya; sixteen in the Ṣoḍaśin; seventeen in the Vājapeya; twenty-nine in the Atirātra; and thirty-three in the Aptoryāma.

When the Pavamāna has been chanted, having returned by the way he came and having passed to the south of the Uttaravedi, he sits down behind it. He remains seated until the offering of the omentum of the Savanīya animal.

When the oblation has been offered, having performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), while they are proceeding toward the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), he should worship with the *grahāvakāśa* formulas and the *śr̥takāra* formulas. Having gone north of the two *havirdhāna* sheds, having passed south of the *mārjālīya* hearth, and having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, he sits down after passing to the south of the *praśāstṛ*'s hearth. (6) When they bring him the *brahman’s* cup (*brahmacamasa*), he receives it and consumes it just as he does the other cups. (7) Once the chant (*stotra*) has been introduced, he restrains his speech until the concluding offering verse (*yajyā*) of the recitation (*śastra*). (8)
When the pressing has concluded, he departs by the way he came. 9.
Thus is prescribed the movement between the two subsequent pressings and the office of the Brahman priest. 10.
From this point onward, all other ritual acts are prescribed for the Brahman as being the duties of the Adhvaryu. 11.
He goes to the south of those who are going to the final bath (avabhṛtha). 12. Thus is prescribed the office of the Brahman for all Soma sacrifices.
13. This is the tenth section; thus ends the third chapter.
When about to accept a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should turn away and turn back seventeen times, and then accept it with the following:

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I accept you. May King Varuṇa lead you, O divine sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). For Agni, [I accept] gold; through this may I attain immortality. May there be vigor for the giver and joy for me, the receiver. Who has given this to whom? Desire to desire. Desire is the giver, desire is the receiver. Enter the ocean of desire; I accept you with desire. O Desire, this is yours."

"O Kāma, this is your sacrificial fee; may Aṅgīras Uttāna receive you. To Soma, a garment; to Rudra, a cow; to Varuṇa, a horse; to Prajāpati, a man; to Manu, a bed; to Tvaṣṭṛ, a she-goat; or to Agni; to Pūṣan, a ewe; to Nirṛti, a mule and a donkey; from the Himavat, an elephant; to the Gandharvas and Apsarases, a garland and ornaments; to the Viśve Devas, grain; to Vāc, food; or to Ūrj; to Brahmán, boiled rice; to Samudra, water; to Aṅgīras Uttāna, a chariot; to Vaiśvānara, a cart.
One should accept the chariot with a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara: "Vaiśvānara has ascended the vault of heaven, the back of the sky, as of old, being praised by those of good thoughts" (RV 3.2.14).
This is the eleventh section.
"He, like before, brings wealth to the living being; the watchful one goes around the common path" (RV 3.2.13). 1.
Whatever is not specifically prescribed, one should accept it with the formula: "Uttāna Āṅgirasa, may you accept this. Or rather, whatever lacks a prescribed mantra, [one should act thus].
In all cases, the *sāvitra* formula is placed first, and the *anvādhi* formula follows at the end.
Regarding the garment, he joins the formula—"The *gnās* cut you, the *apases* stretched you, the *varūtris* wove you"—before the deity-invoking portion.
These [formulas] are for the acceptance of the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) belonging to the *tantra* (the ritual framework).

It is also known from scripture: "The gods, indeed, caused Varuṇa to sacrifice. Whichever deity he brought as a sacrificial gift, that deity he pierced with his gaze. They said, 'Let us accept the gifts after turning away; thus the sacrificial gift will not pierce us. They accepted them after turning away. Then, indeed, the sacrificial gift did not pierce them. He who, knowing this, accepts the sacrificial gift after turning away—him the sacrificial gift does not pierce. This refers specifically to the *tantra*-gifts. One should accept a cow or a horse with the sacred grass (*barhis*).
One wins over a man with food, or an elephant with perfumes; one wins over a bed with pleasant speech.
Thus ends the twelfth kaṇḍikā; thus ends the fourth paṭala.

One of the four [priests] shall not eat for a year; it is known as the vow for one who recites the Caturhotṛ formulas. Indeed, these Caturhotṛ formulas constitute the sacrifice for one who has not established the sacred fires. He who is not propagated with offspring or cattle shall drink warm water for twelve days, wearing a garment of bark and sleeping on the ground.

On the morning of the twelfth day, having moved forward and breathed out and in with the formula, "Go to Indra, svāhā," he should breathe out again, explain the *daśahotṛ* formula, and offer the *caturhotṛ* formula with clarified butter taken four times. Or, he may offer half with the first ladleful and half with the subsequent one. He who desires, "May I procreate," should fill the offering-ladle with twelve ladlefuls, mentally recite the *daśahotṛ* formula, and offer it along with the ladle upon a clump of *darbha* grass; or he may offer half with the first ladleful and half with the subsequent one.

If glory should not reach a Brahmin who is learned and possesses sacred knowledge, he should go to the forest, tie up a bundle of *darbha* grass, seat a Brahmin to his right, and recite the *Caturhotṛ* formulas.

According to Āśmarathya, he should recite all of them together with the *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas; according to Ālekhana, he should recite only the *Hotṛ* formulas. He gives a boon to the one who sits to his right.
Now, these are the wives of the gods. With them, one should perform a sacrifice for one who desires offspring or who desires cattle.

(10) One should sacrifice by counting four steps each between Tvaṣṭṛ and the wives of the gods. (11) If [the result] is not produced within a year, one need not pay further attention beyond that. (12)
One seeking to practice sorcery should sacrifice with the Daśahotr formula (13).
One should offer the oblation on a self-made barren spot or in a cleft (14).
Thus ends the thirteenth section.

Whatever is cruel in speech, with that he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call. He cuts him down by means of the cruelty of his own speech; "He shall swiftly meet with misfortune," so it is known. If one should desire, "May a hero be born to me," he should offer the *caturhotṛ* formula with ghee taken four times. He should offer half with the first ladling and half with the second. A hero is born to him. But no other [son] is born after him.
The sacrificial fee is excellent.
4. With this very Caturhotṛ [offering], one should cause a king to sacrifice when a battle is joined. 5. Whatever they may win therein, from that a hundred and twelve is the sacrificial fee. 6.

One desiring cattle should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the Pañcahotṛ [offering], using clarified butter taken in four ladlings; half with the first drawing and half with the second. He gives four sacrificial fees: a horse, gold, a cow, and a garment.
By this very same [rite], omitting the sacrificial fees, one should cause him who is afflicted by illness or who desires heaven to sacrifice.

One should offer for one desiring heaven with the *manas* [verse]. One should cause one who has failed in a sacrifice to perform the *saptahotra* rite with clarified butter taken in four ladlings—half with the first drawing and half with the second.

He who desires, "May I become more than many," should employ the *daśahotṛ*. He who desires, "May a hero be born to me," should employ the *caturhotṛ*. He who desires, "May I possess cattle," should employ the *pañcahotṛ*. He who desires, "May the seasons be favorable to me," should employ the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*. He who desires, "May I be a drinker of Soma, a sacrificer of Soma; may a drinker of Soma, a sacrificer of Soma, be born to me," should employ the *saptahotṛ*. Now, this *ṛtumukhīya* is the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*: "Vāk is the Hotṛ. Regarding it, he says, "One should offer at each beginning of the season (*ṛtumukha*). This [rite] fulfills all desires.
Thus ends the fourteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

If they should expel him while he has been chosen for the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*), he should offer the *Daśahotṛ* formula with clarified butter taken in four ladlings in the *Āgnīdhra* fire, standing facing west, reciting it backwards and with distinct pauses. "He thus causes his vital breaths (*prāṇa*) to perish. If they should later admit him again, he should offer the *Daśahotṛ* formula with clarified butter taken in four ladlings in the *Āgnīdhra* fire itself, sitting facing east, reciting it in the natural order and without pauses. "He thus restores his vital breaths for him"—so it is known.

If one should desire, "May I be beloved," or if one should desire of another, "May he be beloved," for him one should fashion this *sthāgara* ornament, explain the *Daśahotṛ* formula in the east, the *Caturhotṛ* in the south, the *Pañcahotṛ* in the west, the *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* in the north, and the *Saptahotṛ* above; having adorned his face with the *saṃbhāras* and the *patnīs*, he should go half-way with it. "He indeed becomes beloved"—so it is known. 2.

These Caturhotṛ formulas should be employed where they serve the purpose of oblations, accompanied by the *graha* cups and the *svāhā* utterance; where they do not serve the purpose of oblations, they are without *grahas* and without *svāhā*; and where there are recitations (*japa*) to be performed by the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Among those [Caturhotṛ formulas], one should apply those connected with the ritual separation (*vihāra*) to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*); for both [types of sacrificers], one should apply the others.
Thus ends the fifteenth section; thus ends the fifth chapter.

Men have generated the praiseworthy Agni from the two fire-sticks by means of their thoughts and the movement of their hands—the far-seeing master of the house, the active one. By Agni is Agni kindled. Seven are yours, O Agni. May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]. Thirty-three. Whatever flaw is in my mind, or in my speech, or in my heart—may this god Bṛhaspati fill that up with wealth. Viśvakarman, enjoying this oblation, may he extend this sacrifice with continuous threads.

Those dawns that have shone forth and those that have set, I unite them with oblation and clarified butter. *Ayāścāgne 'si*. *Tvaṃ no agne*. *Sa tvaṃ no agne*. "O Gods, may we hear what is auspicious with our ears; O Holy Ones, may we see what is auspicious with our eyes. With firm limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain the lifespan ordained by the Gods. May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being."

May Tārkṣya with unharmed wheels grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us. May the Maruts, whose horses are spotted, who have Pṛśni as their mother, who move toward splendor, and who frequent the assemblies, come here. May all the gods—those men whose tongue is Agni and whose eyes are the sun—come here for our protection. A hundred autumns indeed are before us, O gods, during which you have ordained the aging of our bodies, when sons become fathers; do not harm our life-span in its course. "O Agni, kindled, shine forth"—this is the sixteenth section.

To the one with listening ears, the seer, the one to be known—I approach the firmament with salutations, praising him. O Agni, grant us that from which there is fear as freedom from fear; protect us from the wrath of the gods; come hither to sacrifice. Make Agni your god, in harmony with the fires, the most excellent sacrificer, the messenger at the rite—he who is steadfast among mortals, the upholder of *ṛta*, whose head is heat, who feeds on clarified butter, the purifier. Agni has clarified butter for his face, clarified butter for his back; kindled by clarified butter, clarified butter is his food.

The rivers, dripping with ghee, carry you; drink the ghee, O God, from the sacrifice, together with the gods. O Agni, giver of life! These [oblations], O Agni! Seven are yours, O Agni! May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]. Thirty-three [gods]. That which is of my mind. Viśvakarman. I yoke Agni. Kindling you... May Agni, being praised, protect us with the gods worthy of praise who belong to the earth. May Vāyu, being praised, protect us with the gods worthy of praise who belong to the intermediate space. May Sūrya, being praised, protect us with the gods worthy of praise who belong to heaven.

May Viṣṇu, praised by the gods worthy of praise who dwell in the quarters, protect us; may Agni with the *yajus* formulas and Pūṣan with the *svagā*-utterances protect this sacrifice. May they protect me; may I follow you; may you follow me; *svāhā*. With these three sections (*anuvākas*), in the case of an unrecognizable transgression regarding the *soma*, he offers thirty-three oblations.
(1) And thirty-three [oblations] of the limbs of the sacrifice in the *āgnīdhra* fire.

(2) Having offered seven oblations over the *vasatīvarī* waters or the *savanīya* offerings when they have been spilled, [with the verses]: "O Earth, thou art the great one," "O Sinīvālī," "O Urandhrā," "O Ācitti," "O Manas," "O Bhūvas," and "O Vivastā. (3)

Thus ends the seventeenth section (*kaṇḍikā*). "May I prosper with that wave of yours which is fit for oblation, potent, and most intoxicating. You are the clarified butter of Soma; you are the oblation of the oblation, the light of lights. With the deities of all you gods, I take you. Having consecrated [the water] thus: "May the Maruts pour you together, may Indra, may Bṛhaspati; may this Agni pour you together with long life and wealth. May he grant me a full span of life. The gentle ones, the lowing ones; the auspicious waters. From the beginning I behold them."
With these seven verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss," he should either pour [the Soma] together or consecrate it with these mantras.

1. If at the morning pressing he sees that there is excess Soma before the oblation has been offered, he should pour it into the cups or offer it as a libation. 2. Having seen it after the oblation has been made, he should perform the rite accompanied by the Stotra and Śastra. 3.
Having drawn the cups, with the *hotṛ*’s cup as the principal one, he introduces the *bṛhat* stotra. 4.
They should chant on verses containing the word "suckles," beginning with "The cow suckles for the Maruts.
5. Or they may chant on these same verses with the *gaurivīta* form of the *bṛhat* sāman, beginning with "This Soma has been pressed. 6.

The Hotṛ recites the *anuśaṃsa* for Indra and Viṣṇu (aindrāvaiṣṇavam). 7. He modifies the *bhakṣa*-mantra to "for Indra and Viṣṇu, who have drunk [of this]. 8. If this occurs at the midday pressing, it is exactly the same. 9.
In the *stotra*, there is a modification: with the verses addressed to Sūrya beginning "baṇ mahām̐ asi sūrya," they should chant using either the *Bṛhat* or the *Gaurivīta* [Sāman].

(10) The Hotṛ recites the *anuśaṃsa* in the same manner. (11) Likewise is the *bhakṣa-mantra*. (12) If there should be a surplus at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), one should perform the *ukthya* rite. (12)

If [the sacrifice is] an Ukthya, [they perform] the Ṣoḍaśin; if it is a Ṣoḍaśin, an Atirātra; if it is an Atirātra, a Dvirātra; and if it is a Dvirātra, then there is only a single Stotra. In that case, they should chant with verses addressed to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa, using either the Bṛhat or the Gaurīvīta Sāman.
The Hotṛ recites the *anuśaṃsa* in the same manner, and likewise is the mantra for the consumption [of the Soma].
Thus ends the eighteenth section; this is the sixth chapter.

If two Soma sacrifices should be performed in conjunction (*saṃsuta*), having offered at the outset the four *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas, he offers at the great night (*mahārātra*) after the *prātaranuvāka* has been commenced, while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, with the formula: "For lying down, for sitting down, for the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, the Anuṣṭubh, the Paṅkti, for victory—Svāhā! (1) In the same manner, at the beginning of each pressing (*savana*), he offers with the subsequent sets of four *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas and with each subsequent Vedic meter (*chandas*) up to the Paṅkti. (2)

The sacrifice has five pressings (*savana*): the three pressings, the final bath (*avabhṛtha*), and the *anūbandhya* animal sacrifice. Five oblations are offered into the kindled fire with the formula: "O Prāṇa and Apāna, protect me from death; O Prāṇa and Apāna, do not abandon me. 3.

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the animal sacrifice, the Adhvaryu mutters the *ājyā* verses containing the words *eti* and *preti*. 4. The opening verses (*pratipad*) are those addressed to the Maruts or those containing the word *vṛṣan*. 5.
The *Abhīvarta* is the *Brahmasāman*.
Both the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* are employed.

If the Soma sacrifice that follows is an *Agniṣṭoma*, one should perform an *Ukthya*; if it is an *Ukthya*, a *Ṣoḍaśin*; if it is a *Ṣoḍaśin*, an *Atirātra*; if it is an *Atirātra*, a *Dvirātra*; if it is a *Dvirātra*, a *Trirātra*; and if it is a *Trirātra*, only a single *stotra*.

The Abhijit sacrifice is to be performed for the sake of victory; the Viśvajit sacrifice is to be performed for the sake of universal conquest. It is known from scripture: "The Atirātra consists of all the Pṛṣṭhas and all the Stomas, for the attainment of everything and the securing of everything. (9) The *Sajanīya* hymn is to be recited; the *Vihavya* hymn is to be recited; the *Kayāśubhīya* of Agastya is the *Niṣkevalya*. One should recite these.

(10) One should insert the *Sajanīya* into the Vaiśvadeva hymn of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). One should insert the *Vihavya* into the Marutvatīya hymn of the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina*). One should insert the *Kayāśubhīya* of Agastya as the *Niṣkevalya* into the Vaiśvadeva hymn of the third pressing (*tārtīyasavana*). (11)

Thus ends the nineteenth section (kaṇḍikā). In this regard, there are these injunctions for the Sāmans: "The Tauraśravasa should be performed; the Vasiṣṭha-nihava should be performed; perform the Abhīvarta as the Brahman-sāman; perform both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara; perform either the Abhijit or the Viśvajit sacrifice; perform the Krośa and Anukrośa"—thus he issues the command before the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana).

The former [Soma sacrifice] is to be established; or rather, it is to be performed after the pressing has been completed. Or, one should perform a more extensive sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) with more sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). 3.

A joint Soma-pressing (*saṃsava*) may take place when there is an interval of a chariot’s day, or when a mountain or a river separates them, or when there is an intervening mountain, or between two different kingdoms; however, a joint pressing does not exist between those who are not at peace with each other—thus says the *Kaṅkatibrāhmaṇa*. 4.
Where there is illness among those initiated (*dīkṣita*), he should lie down in the sacrificer’s station (*yajamānāyatana*). 5.
Having taken hold of it, he should lead it to the Āgnīdhra fire. [He recites:

"I entrust this to you for the sake of the sacred word (*brahman*); may the sacred word entrust it to the deities. May the *vaṣaṭ*-call heal you together with all the gods. O Vasus, this is your morning pressing; O Rudras, this is your midday pressing; O Viśve Devas, this is your third pressing. Guard it! Heal it! Protect it! Let it not fail you!"—he joins these phrases to every [pressing].

Having kindled the fire at the Āgnīdhrīya altar and strewn grass around it, he should seat a Brāhmaṇa to the south upon Darbha grass, place a water-pot to the north, and having placed twenty-one barley grains and bunches of Darbha grass into that pot, he should respond: "You are the Jīvās by name; revive him! You are the Jīvikās by name; revive him! You are the Saṃjīvikās by name; revive him! (8) Thus ends the twentieth section. With the Oṣadhi-hymn beginning "The plants that have been born," he sprinkles him with these waters. (1)

"The waters are the breaths of Prajāpati; they are the medicine of the sacrifice"—with these words, they cause him to sip water. Then they touch him [with the following formulas]: "May the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma grahas protect your out-breath and in-breath. May the Upāṃśusavana stone protect your diffused breath (vyāna). May the Aindravāyava graha protect your speech. May the Maitrāvaruṇa graha protect your skill and resolve (dakṣa-kratu). May the Śukra and Manthin grahas protect your two eyes. May the Āśvina graha protect your hearing. May the Āgrayaṇa graha protect your self. May the Ukthya graha protect your limbs. May the Dhruva graha protect your life-span."—to each of these, he adds the formula "May so-and-so protect you. In every case, he appends the phrase "asāvasau" (so-and-so) [to the name of the deity]. 4.
Then he touches himself with the formula: "May the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [cups] protect my out-breath and in-breath.
He proceeds in this manner up to the Dhruva cup.

Having offered an oblation with the formula, "To the Lord of Prosperity, prosperity; to the Eye, the eye; to the Breath, the breath; to the Self, the self; to Speech, speech—bestow these back upon him, Svāhā!", he performs the touching as before.
If he should die before the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), they should perform the fire-*avabhṛtha*.

Or, having led him to the *avabhṛtha*, having sprinkled him [with water] and carried him out, they should cremate him with his own fires according to the available space. This much is the case for a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*).

In the case of *ahargaṇa* sacrifices, having been told "Bring [the fire]," one brings the fire from the *dakṣiṇāgni* or burns [the body] with fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*). The cremation of the deceased takes place to the south of the *mārjālīya* fire-altar (11).
Having completed that day silently, at the end of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, he collects the bones in a jar and places them on the *mārjālīya* (12).
The *udgātṛ* priests should chant the praises with the three *sarparājñī* verses, performed without the *pratigara* response (13).
This is the twenty-first section (kaṇḍikā).

The officiating priests, led by the Hotṛ, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītinaḥ), reciting the Yāmya verses and proclaiming the Sarparājñī verses, having tied up their right hair-tufts and loosened their left ones, striking their right thighs and fanning themselves with their fringed garments (sigbhiḥ), go around three times counter-clockwise (prasavyam) while reciting: "May our sin be burnt away" (*apa naḥ śośucadagham*). 1. Having tied up their left hair-tufts and loosened their right ones, striking their left thighs and not fanning themselves, they go around three times clockwise (pratipariyanti) while reciting: "May our sin be burnt away" (*apa naḥ śośucadagham*). 2.

When they have moved toward the north, then the Adhvaryu places a stone as a boundary-stone (*paridhi*) to the south of them with the verse: "I set up this boundary for the living; let not another half of us go to the nether world. May they live a hundred abundant autumns; we place death beyond by means of this mountain.
(3) The *agniṣṭoma* Soma sacrifice has cups beginning with those for Indra-Vāyu, or those beginning with those for Mitra-Varuṇa.
(4) They chant the praises with the *yāmya* hymns. (5)
At each hymn of praise, he places a jar of bones [nearby].
At the Mārjālīya fire-altar, they pour out the portions for consumption. They should take "O Agni, you purify the lives" as the introductory verse (pratipad).
Their Soma sacrifice should have the *rathantara* as its *sāman*.
"They place life-breath within themselves and go forth having cast off evil," so it is known.

If, however, he should have no protector, they should cremate him, bind his bones in a black antelope skin, and deposit them. Then, having initiated in his stead the one who is his own nearest relative, those intending to sacrifice should sit together with him.
In the course of a year, they should perform the sacrifice with the bones;
according to Āśmarathya, [this begins] from the *vyāpāta* [offering]; according to Ālekhana, from the *odavasānīyā* offering;
[the ritual] beginning with the *agniṣṭoma* Soma sacrifice is the standard procedure.
As before, there are twelve hundred as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Thus ends the twenty-second section (kaṇḍikā) and the seventh chapter (paṭala).

If, having pledged to perform a sacrificial session (sattra), one does not perform it, he should sacrifice with the Viśvajit Atirātra, which includes all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras, all the Stomas, and has all one's possessions as the sacrificial fee.
Some prescribe the Traidhātavīya sacrifice with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having been initiated for a *sattra* sacrifice, if he should rise [from it] prematurely, he should, after distributing the Soma, perform a *viśvajit* *atirātra* sacrifice as previously described.
If he should rise while the initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*) are still in progress, he should scrape out the clay from the fire-pan (*ukhā*), mix that clay with other earth, and have another fire-pan made.
Having drawn [the figures] of the animal heads, he should join them silently. (5) If there should be a layer that was piled during the Upasad days, he should repeat it;
(6) he should repeat it silently. (7)
"Accompanied by mantras"—this is another view.
(8) When one rises after the fire has been piled, no further piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*) is required; or one may pile the fire silently. "Accompanied by mantras"—this is another view.
(9) Once the fire has been carried forward (*praṇīta*), one should carry forward another fire silently; "accompanied by mantras"—this is another view. (10)

One should remove [the fires] from the implements—the Great Altar (*mahāvedi*), the Northern Altar (*uttaravedi*), the hearths (*dhiṣṇya*), the under-world pits (*uparava*), the sounding-holes (*khara*), the *sadas*, and the two *havirdhāna* sheds. One should acquire them again even from others.

(11) If the night should pass while the chanting has not been completed by all the rounds (*paryāya*), they should chant for the Hotṛ with six verses addressed to Indra and Viṣṇu; for the other [priests], with three verses each.
(12) If [only] two [rounds] have been performed, they should chant for the Hotṛ and the Maitrāvaruṇa during the first round, and for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin and the Acchāvāka during the latter. (13)
If they should chant for the Hotṛ with fifteen [verses] by means of one [set], and for the others with five each,
he should place "O Agni, O radiant Dawn" as the introductory verse (*pratipad*) for the Āśvina [śastra].
Thus ends the twenty-third section (*kaṇḍikā*).
If the sun does not appear while the *Aśvina* hymn is being recited, one should sacrifice a multi-colored animal dedicated to Sūrya.
One should also recite all the verses of the ten Maṇḍalas.

If the *Āhavanīya* fire of those who have been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) should go out, one should fetch it from the *Āgnīdhra*. If the *Āgnīdhra* goes out, one should fetch it from the *Gārhapatya*. If the *Gārhapatya* goes out, one should churn it anew from that very same place.
One should make the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) from the wood from which smoke rises;
the kindling-stick (*krumuka*) is for rekindling.
One should give four boons to the chief officiating priests (*mahartvij*).

If one's *soma* should run out, he should cut a piece of gold into two parts; having placed one half in between, he should press [the *soma*] together with the *r̥jīṣa*. Having poured the other half back in, they should proceed with the cups.
He should give four boons to the great officiating priests (*mahartvij*).
If they should steal his un-purchased *soma*, he should simply purchase it again.
If he has purchased [the Soma], he should press it after bringing it from whoever is nearest.
(10) He should give to the one who brings the Soma or to the Soma-seller as much as he pleases.

(11) In the absence of Soma, he should press *pūtīka* plants. In the absence of *pūtīkas*, [he should press] *ādāra* plants and *phālguna* plants that have white woolly tufts. In their absence, whatever milky herbs there may be, or red *dūrvā* grass, or green *kuśa* grass—so says the Vājasaneyaka. (12)

At the very least, one should mix all the Soma juices at the morning pressing with fresh milk (*pratidhuk*), at the midday pressing with boiled milk, and at the third pressing with curds—or with the mixture of boiled milk and curds (*nītamiśra*).

Now, according to some teachers: at the morning pressing there is both fresh milk and *pūtīka* plants; at the midday pressing there is both boiled milk and *pūtīka* plants; and at the third pressing there is both curds and *pūtīka* plants.
The Agniṣṭoma Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara as its Sāman (16).
Those very priests who were chosen [for the original rite] should officiate for him (17).
He should give one cow as the sacrificial fee to those same [priests] (18).

One should purchase the Soma again. Having emerged from the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), before the twelfth day, one should undergo initiation again for that very same sacrifice. In that case, one should give whatever one intended to give in the previous [sacrifice].
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section (kaṇḍikā).
If the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds should be consumed by fire, the Adhvaryu should protect the cups (*grahas*), the Udgātṛ the chants (*stotras*), and the Hotṛ the recitations (*śastras*).
If the Soma has not been burnt, they should settle upon the sacrificial ground from the side and proceed from the very point where the ritual was interrupted.
But if it is burnt, the penance for that is the same as for when it has been stolen.

One should give five cows in place of the [missing] cow, or five excellent bulls. If one does not find the pressing-stone at the morning libation, having fetched a Palāśa staff, one should press with that very thing; it is known that this indeed constitutes the penance for this.
If at the midday pressing, or if at the third pressing,
or even if at the morning pressing a pressing-stone should break, they should chant the *brahmasāman* of the *dyutāna-māruta* hymn before the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant;
or indeed, they may simply chant the *brahmasāman*.

If [the jar] should break at the midday pressing or at the third pressing, they chant this very same [hymn] before the Pavamāna chants. If the jar should break at the morning pressing, it has been stated that [they should chant] on verses addressed to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.

Now, according to some: "If the *kalaśa* jar should break at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), one should perform the *brahmasāman* with the *vaṣaṭkāra* as its final syllable. Having offered thirteen oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the formulas: "To Asu, svāhā! To Vasu, svāhā! To Vibhu, svāhā! To Vivasvat, svāhā! To Śūṣa, svāhā! To Sūrya, svāhā! To Candra, svāhā! To Gaṇaśrī, svāhā! To Malimluca, svāhā! To Jyotis, svāhā! To Abhibhū, svāhā! To Adhipati, svāhā! To Divāmpati, svāhā!"—thus [it is said]. This is the twenty-fifth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

You are the draught of Indra; you have been taken, you are to be taken, you are the foremost of the gods. Into you I enter, together with the draughts, together with the fore-draughts, together with offspring, together with cattle, together with the officiating priests, together with the Soma-pressers, together with the members of the assembly, together with those entitled to the sacrificial fees, together with the sacrifice, and together with the lord of the sacrifice. Indra and Agni are my protective enclosures; Vāta is my divine fortress. The sacred word (*brahman*) is my inner armor. Into you, O draught of Indra, I enter—along with the cows and along with the horses.

May Heaven and Earth be my armor; may Agni be my armor; may Sūrya be my armor; may Brahmaṇaspati be my armor. May no fear come upon me from this. Indra and Agni are my ramparts; Vāta is my divine fortresses. The sacred word (*brahman*) is my inner armor. As such, O Seizer Indra, enter me—along with my cows, my horses, and my men—with whatever belongs to me, even that which is shattered. With these words, the sacrificer consecrates [the altar].

"Unto safety and freedom from distress, unto lying down and sitting down, unto the Gāyatrī for its overcoming—Svāhā! Unto safety and freedom from distress, unto lying down and sitting down, unto the Triṣṭubh for its overcoming—Svāhā! Unto safety and freedom from distress, unto lying down and sitting down, unto the Jagatī for its overcoming—Svāhā! Unto safety and freedom from distress, unto lying down and sitting down, unto the Anuṣṭubh for its overcoming—Svāhā!

Unto safety and freedom from distress, unto lying down and sitting down, unto the Paṅkti for its overcoming—Svāhā! With these mantras, at each pressing, some offer five oblations when [the vessel] has been cracked.
