If the Prastotṛ should be cut off while they are proceeding with the *bahiṣpavamāna*, the head of the sacrifice would be severed; having given a boon to the Brahman, that same [Prastotṛ] must be engaged again. (3) If the Pratihartṛ [is cut off], the sacrificer would be deprived of his cattle; he should give away all his possessions (*sarvavedasa*). (4) If the Udgātṛ [is cut off], the sacrificer would be deprived of the sacrifice; that sacrifice, being without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*), should be concluded, and then another [Udgātṛ] should be brought in. (5)

In that case, one should give that which he would have given previously. 6. But if both are cut off simultaneously, the expiation belongs to the Udgātṛ; for the Pratihartṛ, it is the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta). 7.
In the case of being cut off first and then later, the expiation belongs to whichever one is cut off last. 8.
If this same [defect] occurs at the midday pressing, or if it occurs at the third pressing, one should offer the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section; thus ends the eighth chapter.

If the water-jar (*kalaśa*) should run dry, one should divide a piece of gold into two parts, place one underneath [the jar], pour water into it, and then pour milk into it. Having drawn up half [of the mixture], they should proceed with the ritual using the cups (*graha*).
He should give four boons to the chief officiating priests.
Now, according to some: if the *kalaśa* vessel should run dry, he should draw [the Soma] from the *āgrayaṇa*; if the *āgrayaṇa* [runs dry], from the *kalaśa*.
If either the cup (*graha*) or the *kalaśa* should run dry, he should draw [the Soma] from the *āgrayaṇa*, excluding the *śukra* and the *dhruva*.
It is known from the tradition regarding all the *grahas*—whether they have been spilled, lost, or broken—that they are to be taken from the *droṇakalaśa*.

If the *dhruva* cup should be lost, spilled, or broken, one should consecrate it with the mantra: "Thou art the bestower of life, O *dhruva*; bestow life upon me! Thou art the bestower of splendor, O *dhruva*; bestow splendor upon me! Thou art the protector of the body, O *dhruva*; protect my body! Having placed a piece of gold weighing a hundred *mānas* within it, he causes it to swell with the formulas: "Svāhā! Swell from the sky! Svāhā! Swell from the intermediate space! Svāhā! Swell from the earth! Thus he makes it swell.

O gods, let this sacrifice be a holy rite for the plants, for the animals, and for my wealth. O gods, let there be a holy rite for every living being. Swell with abundance, O divine sacrifice, rich in clarified butter! Be right here; do not waver. Like a mountain, be immovable. Like Indra, stand firm here; uphold the sacrifice here. Indra has supported it firmly with a firm oblation. For him the gods have spoken, as has this Brahmaṇaspati.

With these four verses—"Firm is the sky, firm is the earth, firm is this entire world; firm indeed are these mountains, firm is this king of the people"—he consecrates the one who has sat down and gives him a boon.
This is the twenty-seventh section.

If the Nārāśaṃsa cup should fail, the Adhvaryu should take the previous draught; having offered it at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ* calls, he should hand it over to the Camasādhvaryu. With that, the latter causes it to swell, [reciting]: "Swell up! Let [the drops] gather unto thee. 1.

If the Soma or the oblation should spill at the morning pressing, the midday pressing, the third pressing, at night, or during the *tiroahnya* days, one should consecrate it with the verses beginning "The sacrifice has gone to the gods, to the people" (*devāṃ janam agan yajñaḥ*) according to the preceding order, and then offer an oblation with the verse "May the mind, as light, enjoy [it]" (*mano jyotir juṣatām*). (2) Thirty-three. With the verses "The drop has fallen," "Thy drop," "The drop which," and "Thy drop," some say that one should offer five oblations at each pressing whenever a spilling occurs, reciting one mantra for each. (3)

If, while performing the seasonal offerings (*ṛtugraha*), the two [officiants] should become confused, they should offer oblations with these mantras, one by one: "May the rivers, having released their flow, drip with ghee; may spring, summer, and the honey-sweet rainy season, the autumn and winter—the seasons that bring delight—dwell together in the waters and the atmosphere. May Prajāpati produce offspring for us; may Dhātṛ, being well-disposed, grant us a happy mind. May the Year, together with the seasons, being watchful, and the Lord of Nourishment, bestow nourishment upon me. With the mantra "Come to us," and with "Thou, O Agni, art the guardian of vows," and "Whatever we have violated of yours," and "The honey-sweet," he offers the oblations. 4.
"May they protect this sacrifice; may they protect me; I take hold of you; take hold of me, Svāhā!"—thus he appends the names of the seasons.

(5) If the Soma should spill, having said, "O Brahman, the Soma has spilled," and having recited, "Now the god Savitṛ is to be praised by us," he measures five spans with the formula, "To Bhūpati, Svāhā," as performed previously.
(6) Thus ends the twenty-eighth section.

If one should set down the unconsumed cup with a hymn, let him say: "May she who is our thought by day come to us with protection; may Aditi, with her aid, grant us peace and drive away our enemies. And may those two divine physicians, the Aśvins, bring us well-being; may they ward off calamity from us and drive away our enemies. May Agni, with his fires, grant us peace, and may Sūrya shine warmly upon us."

Having offered three oblations on the Āgnīdhrīya fire with the verses, "May the wind blow auspiciously," "O you who are free from harm," and "Away with the adversaries," and having consumed that [remnant] in the Sadas while covered with an upper garment, he carries it out along the right door-post, washes it at the Mārjālīya fire, and brings it back by the eastern path with the verse: "The wise one does not discern that place, whither the dead man returns again to the living."

"Threefold is that which is of the world, like a chariot-wheel; the living one is not dead, he shall live. Having poured that [mixture] into the cups, he offers an oblation with the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," and then causes it to swell with the verse, "Swell up, O most intoxicating Soma, with all thy protections; be thou for us most far-reaching. 1.

"Bring [the offering] to this one who desires to drink, who knows all things, who comes readily, who has arrived, and who leaves no remnant behind, O men!"—having thus consecrated the portion that has been sprinkled, he consumes it with the formula: "The Moon has gone to the Moon; Indra drank from the Moon. Of thee, O Moon, drunk by Indra, full of sweetness, invited, I, being invited, partake. Thus he consumes it. 2.

If the consecrated one should spill [the offering], [he recites] this verse: "O Agni, burn down the enemies within us; burn away the curse of the hostile stranger. O Vasu, being observant, burn the unobservant; let your ageless, tireless flames stand around him. O Agni, great as Mitra, whoever from afar seeks to harm us, or whoever from near would attack us—burn him with your own ageless, bull-like flames; O most burning one, burn him with your heat! May he indeed create a signal even for one who sits far away at night."

When the ageless purifier drives the trees before him, no mortal can harm your body, O Agni. The monkey devours his own sharp point, as a cow consumes her own afterbirth. When he moves toward and away like a ram, when he chews upon the form of the Apsaras, shaking his head on the mountain and his chest with his chest, moving the stalk with his green hands—having offered these six full oblations, one should give boons for each oblation.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth section.

Having offered ten oblations with the verse, "Whatever offense against the gods... (*yad devā devaheḍanam*), he should consecrate [the sacrificer] with this section beginning, "Pavamāna, the winner of heaven" (*pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*). If the two Soma-offerings, the one already offered and the one yet to be offered, should become mixed, he should draw out a coal from within the enclosing sticks and offer it with the mantra: "For you two are the timely ones of the sacrifice, O Indra and Agni, of the conscious one. Be satisfied with the offered and the unoffered, with the unoffered and the offered; with the offered and the unoffered, with the unoffered and the offered. O Indra and Agni, enjoy and drink of this Soma; may you take pleasure in it. Having offered this into the coal, he should give that portion to him for consumption.

"May darkness not find the sacrificer, nor the officiating priests, nor these progeny; may he who would drink this Soma—this mixture of both [the pressed and the unpressed]—not do so," with these words he consumes it. (3) "May our fathers and our heroes not be harmed; may neither one of our own kin nor one of a different kin, nor one of evil eye or wicked intent, have power over us. May this offered oblation go to the gods," with these words he addresses the one who is consuming it. (4)

"Seven are the officiating priests, seven the seats; of these, ten fingers, the two Aśvins, five strengths, breath, diffused breath, downward breath, mind, intention, Agni, and the oblation consecrated with *svāhā*—may the gods eat it. Having consecrated the spoiled portion (*bhakṣa*) with this mantra, he should pour it out into the northeastern or the northernmost pit with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode across this [world]. For one who has vomited Soma, he should offer this sacrificial pap of millet (*śyāmāka*) to Soma and Indra.

Thus ends the thirtieth section; thus ends the ninth chapter. If a black bird flies repeatedly over the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds while shaking its wings as if from both sides, one should offer an oblation with the verse: "Viṣṇu strode across this [world]. If it should fly high, one should not take heed of that. If a cart or a chariot should pass between the two fires, or between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*, one should offer the *pāthikṛtī* oblation as previously described.

If the *havirdhāna* shed should fall, he should offer an oblation on the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula: "Savitar, Mitra, and Aryaman have lifted it up; he has slain all enemies with his power. He has made me great and possessed of heroes. Rest in the *rathantara*, svāhā!

(3) With this same formula, if it is the *sadas* shed, he should offer on the *hotrīya* fire: "Rest on the earth in the *vāmadevya*, svāhā! (4) If it is the *āgnīdhra* shed, he should offer on the *āgnīdhrīya* fire: "Rest in the atmosphere in the *bṛhat*, svāhā! (5)
If he should offer in the *śālāmukhīya* fire with all [the formulas] for the *prāgvaṃśa*, the formula "With the great [Sāman] I prop thee up in heaven" is common as the prop for all of them.

If they should expel him while he has been chosen for the office of the *ṛtvij*, he should offer in the *āgnīdhra* fire with the formula: "May this entire sacrifice come to me—the Viśve Devas, the Maruts, the Sāmans, the Ṛks, the Āprīs, the meters, the Nivids, and the Yajus—whatever is worthy of sacrifice belonging to this earth."

Having consumed the *soma* at another sacrifice, one should offer a supplementary portion of clarified butter into the *Āhavanīya* fire for the fires with the following [verses]: 31. "Thou art the flower of the waters, the essence of the plants, the beloved abode of Soma, the most beloved oblation of Agni; *svāhā*! Thou art the flower of the waters, the essence of the plants, the beloved abode of Soma, the most beloved oblation of Indra; *svāhā*! Thou art the flower of the waters, the essence of the plants, the beloved abode of Soma, the most beloved oblation of the Viśvedevas; *svāhā*! 1.

"O Soma, may we, filling our minds and bodies with your law, obtain offspring"—this is the remainder [of the mantra]. Having consumed [the portion], he offers oblations in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with each respective mantra: "Svāhā to the gods and the fathers! Svāhā to the Somya fathers! Svāhā to the Kavya fathers!

(2) Having spread Darbha grass behind that [fire] with its tips pointing south-east, he gives curd [to them], saying: "O gods, rejoice here! O Somya ones, rejoice here! O Kavyas, rejoice here! (3) He worships [them], saying:
"The Somya fathers have not been excluded from the drinking of Soma. (4)

When danger arises and it is impossible to sacrifice, one should collect portions from all the *havir* offerings and from the *soma* juices into the *droṇakalaśa* vessel and offer them with the formula: "To those gods to whom this portion belongs, whose are the *prayāja*s and the *anūyāja*s—to the gods whose chief is Indra, whose king is Varuṇa, and who have Agni as their Hotṛ—*svāhā*! Having sacrificed with the *droṇakalaśa*, one may sacrifice again once the danger has passed. If a verse should be omitted or if one should respond with the *abhipratigara* chant, one should offer four oblations with the verses: "O Agni, you for us...", "So you for us, O Agni...", "O Agni, you are the messenger...", and "O Prajāpati..."; and likewise the *vyāhṛti*s.

If a flaw should occur in the sacrifice through the Ṛgveda, one should offer an oblation into the Gārhapatya fire with the word “bhūḥ. If through the Yajurveda, [one should offer] into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the word “bhuvaḥ. If through the Sāmaveda, [one should offer] into the Āhavanīya fire with the word “suvaḥ. If it occurs through all three, one should offer into all of them.
(Thus ends the thirty-second section.
Or else, the Brahman priest should remain seated, meditating in his mind.

"If the Audumbarī post should break, [the Adhvaryu] should cut another and raise it with the formula: 'O straight one, place vigor in me; stand firm, established in prosperity. Having propped up heaven and the mid-region, be firm upon the earth! O supporter, sustainer, progenitor, restrainer! With these words, the Adhvaryu, the Udgātṛ, and the sacrificer raise it. He touches the firmly established post with the regular Yajus formula.

If the two Havirdhāna carts should fall, the Adhvaryu should lift the southern one and the Pratiprasthātṛ should support it; the Pratiprasthātṛ should lift the northern one and the Adhvaryu should support it."
The two [Adhvaryus] support it with verses addressed to Viṣṇu; they level it with verses addressed to Viṣṇu; the two Aśvins fashion it.

With the three verses beginning "O Agni, of booty consisting of cattle," and with the six Uṣṇih-Kakubh verses beginning "Auspicious to us be Agni when invoked, auspicious the gift, O fortunate one, auspicious the sacrifice, and auspicious the praises; and auspicious the praises—make our mind auspicious in the conquest of Vṛtra, wherewith thou mayest prevail in battles; wherewith thou mayest prevail in battles, stretch out thy firm [bow] against many who defy us; may we win through thy aids," they offer oblations on the Āgnīdhrīya fire-altar.
The Adhvaryu [performs] with the preceding *uṣṇih* verses; the Pratiprasthātṛ with the subsequent *kakubh* verses.

"Let the head of the sacrifice be established—immortal, consisting of the deities; let it be made with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, let it be established with one addressed to Aśvin. With these words, they both offer two identical oblations using clarified butter taken five times.
If the fire-pan (*ukhā*) belonging to the Āgnīdhra should break, he should scrape it together and make another.
"If it has been baked, one should grind it and, mixing it with other clay, fashion a new fire-pan (ukhā).
This is the thirty-third section (kaṇḍikā).

"If the fire in the fire-pan (āhavanīya) goes out, one should bring forth another from the Gārhapatya fire. That very same fire is to be carried around again; thus it is known: 'He generates him from his own womb. 1.34.1.
A black garment, a black cow, a black bull, and gold weighing a hundred mānas constitute the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
By that which is performed on the preceding day for the sake of the following day, he connects the two days; by that, he makes the sacrifice continuous.

In that he takes up the *vasatīvarī* waters for the following day on the preceding day, by that he connects the day; by that he makes the sacrifice continuous. In that he causes the milks to be set out for the following day on the preceding day, by that he connects the day; by that he makes the sacrifice continuous. In that he issues the call for the *atipraiṣa*, by that he connects the day; by that he makes the sacrifice continuous.

If even one of these [rites] is not performed, one should offer an oblation with the formula: "Homage to Brahman, homage be to Agni; homage to the Earth, homage to the Plants; homage to Speech, homage to the Lord of Speech; homage to the Great Viṣṇu—I perform [this]; Svāhā! and then one should offer the *sarvaprāyaścitta* (expiation for all faults). One should offer it, one should offer it. Thus ends the twenty-fourth section (*kaṇḍikā*). Thus ends the tenth chapter (*paṭala*). Thus ends the fourteenth book (*praśna*).

One who is about to collect the materials for the *pravargya* ceremony, on the new moon day, the full moon day, or under an auspicious lunar mansion during the waxing fortnight, silently places a stick of *kaṇṭakī* wood upon the fire and offers four spoonfuls of clarified butter with the verse, "They yoke the mind.

(1) Now, if he is already consecrated (*dīkṣita*), he should place that very *kaṇṭakī* stick upon the fire with this [same] formula; some say he should merely recite the sacrificial formula (*yajus*).
(2) Having taken up the spade with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he consecrates it with the formula, "Thou art the spade; thou art no woman. (3)
This is explained by [the rules for] the *sāgnikī* [offering].
(4) With the words, "Arise, O Brahmanaspati," he summons the Brahman priest.
(5) The Brahman priest stands up. Both recite the latter half-verse. They take up the black antelope skin. They lead away the goat, the male kid, and the stallion. (6)

"May Brahmanaspati go forth!"—saying this, they proceed toward the east, preceded by the horse, to where they are about to dig for the clay. Alternatively, these materials may have been brought forward while the site was enclosed. The clay-digging pit is in front of the Āhavanīya fire; each subsequent one is further to the east than the preceding one.

To the north of the clay pit, having spread out a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair side upward, he consecrates the clay pit with the mantra, "O divine Heaven and Earth. Having struck at the clay pit with the wooden shovel while reciting, "May I succeed today," and having taken up [the clay] with the mantra, "The head of Makha," he carries it away with the mantra, "For Makha, thee. He pours it onto the black antelope skin with the mantra, "For the head of Makha, thee.
In this same manner, he carries away a second portion.
He carries away the fourth portion silently, as much clay as he deems sufficient for the Pravargya vessels.
In the same way, there is a modification regarding the consecration of the other ritual materials. Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).

With the words, "So much was there at the beginning," he takes earth dug up by a boar; with the words, "The divine ants," he takes the mound of an anthill; and having mixed together *pūtīka* plants, goat-hair, and black antelope hair with the words, "Thou art the vigor of Indra;

thou art born of Agni, the seed of Prajāpati," he causes the horse to smell it with the words, "Bestow life, bestow breath. With the words, "May Madhu make thee sweet," he causes a she-goat to lick it.
Some teachers prescribe that the licking should take place before the smelling.
Many noble men take possession of it and carry it away.
To the north of the monastery, on ground that has been dug up, sprinkled with water, strewn with sand, and enclosed, they place it.
With the words, "May honey make thee sweet," he pours in the boiling water.
Those materials which are for the mixing of the boiled rice, and whatever else he considers necessary for the sake of firmness—this is the intermediate rule (upārdha).
Now follows the absolute rule:
whatever water-related rite occurs in the Pravargya, that is performed with the boiling waters (madantī) alone.
Neither a woman nor a Śūdra looks at him (9). He does not blow upon it while making it (10).
Having turned away from his mouth, he makes it with a flute without blowing upon it (11).
One should not allow the *pravargya* and the sun to be separated.

(12) If, at any point while the *pravargya* has been set aside, the sun should set, one should cease from that very point where the procedure was interrupted. On the following day, one should complete the remainder.

(13) Having thoroughly kneaded the clay and formed a lump with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," and having pressed it down with both thumbs with the formula, "Ye two are the feet of the sacrifice," he fashions the *mahāvīra*. It may have five elevations, or an indefinite number of elevations; it is a span high, with a ridge on top, provided with a pouring-surface above, and curved in the middle, shaped like a *vāyavya* vessel. (14)
Thus ends the second section (kaṇḍikā).
"I fashion you with the Gāyatrī metre," he says for the first; "with the Triṣṭubh metre," for the second; "with the Jagatī metre," for the third.
Or alternatively, he may fashion each one with all the metres.
With the formula, "Thou art the girdle of Makha," he makes a girdle around the opening.
With the formula, "May Aditi grasp thy opening," he makes the opening with a bamboo joint.
He extends it beyond the third fold.
He should do so until he considers himself fit for the consumption of the portion belonging to the deity, to the *sauviṣṭakṛt* offering, and to the *agnihotra*.
Having placed it on the sand to the north with the words, "Be warmed by the heat of Sūrya," he gazes at it with the formula, "Thou art Makha.
He performs this a second and a third time in the same manner.
The others are made silently.
From this same clay he fashions two milking-vessels (*dogdhrī*), with handles as thick as an elephant's tusk and provided with pouring-spouts, just like a ladle with a handle.
The vessel for the Adhvaryu is larger than that for the Pratiprasthātṛ.
The clarified-butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*) and the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds should be circular and shaped like a mortar;

[he places] the *gharma-iṣṭakā* and the *kulāyinī*, provided that there is a piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*). According to another view, these two should not be present if the *pravargya* rite is not performed.
They smooth it with smoothing agents:
with unwashed *caṇḍātaka* cloths, *gavīdhuka* seeds, *klītaka* salts, bamboo splinters, and clarified butter.
Having kindled the dung of a stallion at the Gārhapatya fire, he holds the first-made Mahāvīra pot with two hooves and fumigates it, saying: "Thou art the footprint of the stallion."
In this same manner, he fumigates the second and the third [mahāvīra]. The others [he fumigates] silently. 18. From this point onward, he takes up the mahāvīras with the two hooves alone. 19.
Having dug a pit in front of the Gārhapatya fire and having strewn it with the red-cooking materials, he brings down the mahāvīras into them. 20.
Thus ends the third section (kaṇḍikā).
"Thou art flame" is the first; "Thou art glow" is the second; "Thou art light, thou art heat" is the third.

Having silently placed the other [bricks] along with them and covered them with the red-coloured materials for cooking, he ignites blades of *muñja* grass at the Gārhapatya fire and offers them, one by one in each direction, with these mantras: "For the flame, thee! and so forth.
Or alternatively, with all [verses] from every side,
he attends to those being cooked with the verse "He who, through his greatness, makes the heaven non-terrible" (RV 10.89.4);
or with the following verse (RV 10.89.5).

When they are cooked, [the Adhvaryu] takes the two rubbing-sticks with the formula, "For success," removes the ashes, grasps the first-made *mahāvīra* with the two lifting-prongs, and carries it out with the formula, "May the god Savitṛ carry thee out. Having carried it out, while it is not yet set down upon the earth, he establishes it on the sand to the north with the formula, "Filling the regions and the quarters," and gazes at it with the formula, "I gaze upon thee with the eye of Sūrya.
He carries out the second and the third in the same manner; the others [the remaining *mahāvīras*] are carried out silently.

Then he surrounds them on the right with sand, saying: "Here I surround so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, with subjects, cattle, and Vedic splendor. For a Kṣatriya, he says "with subjects"; for a Vaiśya, "with cattle. (9) Then he moistens them with abundant goat's milk, saying: "I moisten thee with the Gāyatrī metre," and so on with each of these three [metres] for each [brick].
Or else, he moistens each one with all [the metres]. The others [the remaining bricks] are done silently. (10–11)
Then he ties them up on a spotted antelope skin and attaches them with the mantra: "O God who goes before, may I attain you. (12) Another view is that this mantra is to be used at a later time.
(13) Thus ends the fourth section; thus ends the first chapter.

When they are about to proceed with the *pravargya* ceremony, they close the doors and enclose the area for the wife. The *hotṛ* sits down to the west; the *adhvaryu* to the east; the *brahman*, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and the *prastotṛ* to the south; and the *pratiprasthātṛ* and the *āgnīdhra* to the north.

Having touched the boiling waters and performed the *śānti* rite with the first *anuvāka*, he spreads *darbha* grass in front of the *gārhapatya* fire and brings down the *mahāvīra* vessels upon them with the mantra: "O God, you who go before, may I attain you. (4) This mantra is to be used at the later time; this is the settled rule. (5) At this very point, all that pertains to the *gharma* is completed. (6)

Now, regarding the udumbara wood: they construct the *samrāḍ-āsandī* (the sovereign’s throne) from it; some authorities prescribe that it be larger than the *rāja-āsandī* (the king’s throne). It is woven with single-strand ropes made of muñja grass.
There are four offering-spoons (*sruk*), two of which are not bound [with cords].
The two pressing-stones are firmly fixed; the supporting-wood is larger than the vessel for the sprinkling-water (prokṣaṇī).

There are two offering-spoons (sruva) as the two hooves, and two fire-sticks (araṇi) equal in size to the Mahāvīra vessel. There are two stirring-sticks (dhr̥ṣṭī), a central post (methī), pegs (mayūkha), six splinters (śakala), and a kindling-stick (samidh) made of kāṇḍakī wood. There are thirteen enclosing-sticks (paridhi) made of vikankaṭa wood, and fuel for the Gharma-vessel made of the same. [There are also] sticks made of khadira, palāśa, udumbara, arka, kārṣmarya, bamboo, or śamī wood. There are three fans (dhavitra) made of black antelope skin with white and black hair.
It is known that their bamboo staffs are the length of an arm;
another view is that they are made of udumbara wood.
There are two plates, one of silver and one of gold.
There are two [weights] of a śatamāna (16).
Now, [there are] two girdles of muñja grass (17) and two Veda-strainers (18).
One of the two [carts] has been fumigated (parivāsita).

At the beginning, there are three *viśākhadāma* cords; abundant bundles of *muñja* grass; flour of *rauhiṇa* rice that has not been husked; sand for the donkeys; and two strainers (*pavitre*) made of *muñja* grass—this is one version—and another version says they are made of *darbha* grass. Having prepared the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*) according to the ritual procedure for the sprinkling waters, he addresses the Brahman priest.

Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā). "O Brahman, we shall proceed with the Pravargya ceremony. O Hotṛ, recite the hymn for the Dharma-vessel. O Agnīdh, place the two Rauhina cakes on the fire. O Pratiprasthātṛ, spread the fires. O Prastotṛ, chant the Sāmans.
With the formula, "Yoked by the Yajus, anointed by the Sāmans," he gives permission in a low voice; with "Accompanied by Indra, proceed," he gives permission aloud.
Or [he says], "Move forward!
(3). With the formula, "For Yama thee, for Makha thee," he sprinkles everything that is to be encircled three times, moving from front to back. (4) He causes the sprinkled items to be spread out. (5)
The Āgnīdhra places the two Rauhiṇa cakes on the fire; they have been prepared silently.
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the clarified butter according to the procedure for a Darvihoma.
According to another view, no such preparation of it exists.

Here he places the curd upon the fire. Then, having taken this royal throne-seat (samrāḍ-āsandī) and carried it around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he sets it down to the east of the King’s throne-seat (rāja-āsandī).

Upon it, having spread a black antelope skin with the neck pointing eastward and the hair facing upward, he brings down the two Mahāvīra vessels that are not to be used for the ritual, [saying]: "O God, you who go before, may I attain you."
Furthermore, this mantra is for the subsequent time.

Then, having taken this central post (methī), the pegs (mayūkha), the forked poles (viśākha), and the cords (dāmāni), he carries them out by way of the southern door, passing in front of the Hotṛ and behind the Gārhapatya fire; he then drives the central post south of the southern door for the Hotṛ to inspect it.
To the south of the eastern door-post of that same door, he fixes a peg for the calf.
To the south of this very other door-post, inside, he ties a goat; 15.
to the north, a ram; 16.
upon them, he stretches out cross-ropes. 17.
These very [stakes] remain extended until they are removed; with them they bind these [animals] at the proper time;
then he scatters the donkey-dust over them.

To the north of the Gārhapatya fire he prepares one [mound]; to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, another (21). He makes the mound for the leavings facing the northeast door, provided with an outlet on the outside (22).
To the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he places the boiled curds (23).
Thus ends the sixth section (kaṇḍikā).
[He takes] the wood-shavings and a fuel-stick of Kaṇṭakī wood.
Then, having grasped this Mahāvīra vessel used for the performance with two hooves, he cleanses it from above with the Veda-grass whose tips are uncut, saying: "O God, go forward; may I attain thee."

Having offered seven or eleven oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) into the *āhavanīya* fire with the wooden spoon (*sruva*), saying, "Svāhā to Prāṇa! Svāhā to Vyāna!", and having anointed the Mahāvīra pot on top of the *āhavanīya* with the wooden spoon, saying, "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey," and having placed a silver disk (*rukma*) upon the other mound (*khara*) while saying, "Protect the earth from heat," and having set down the Mahāvīra or handed it over to another, he takes two bundles of *muñja* grass and ignites their tips in the *gārhapatya* fire with the formula, "For the flame, thee! (*arcisse tvā*).

With [the formula] "For radiance, thee," he places the roots of those [reeds] facing north upon their tips; with "For light, thee," the roots of those facing south upon their roots; and with "For heat, thee," the tips of those facing north upon their roots.
He places them crosswise above the gold plate with [the formulas], "Thou art flame, thou art radiance, thou art light, thou art heat.

Having established the Mahāvīra vessel upon them with [the formula], "Sit down, for thou art great," he anoints the Mahāvīra with the *sruva* spoon while reciting, "They anoint him who spreads it out. Or rather, he fills it completely.

Without touching the Mahāvīra vessel, the sacrificer, holding a span-length [of grass] facing eastward, mutters these formulas according to their respective characteristics: "Invincible in front... (TS 1.3.4.a–f).
To the north, he touches the earth with the formula: "Thou art the horse of Manu, O thou of many sons" (TS 1.3.4.g).
The Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ take up the two stirring-sticks with the formula: "For success, thee! (TS 1.3.4.h).

With the verse, "O Agni, burn up the enemies within," he draws out embers from the Gārhapatya fire toward the north. With the formula, "You are piled, you are piled around," he surrounds them with the embers, moving clockwise.
This is the seventh section.
They enclose [the altar] with enclosing-sticks made of *vaikaṅkata* wood.
"Thou art the measure," says the Adhvaryu, placing two [stones] facing eastward; "Thou art the counter-measure," says the Pratiprasthātṛ, placing two facing northward.
In this same manner, for the remaining stones, the Adhvaryu uses each preceding formula and the Pratiprasthātṛ each succeeding one.
The Adhvaryu alone places the thirteenth stone on the south side with the formula, "Thou art the internal support of the atmosphere."

Having covered [the fire] with a golden plate (*rukma*) while reciting, “Protect the heaven from the heat,” and having consecrated it with the three verses beginning with “With these songs,” he takes up the fans (*dhavitra*). He takes the first with, “Thou art the *gāyatra*”; the second with, “Thou art the *traiṣṭubha*”; the third with, “Thou art the *jāgata*.
With these, he fans it upwards three times, saying, “Honey! Honey!
He gives one of them to the *pratiprasthātṛ*, and one to the *āgnīdhra*.
Led by the Āgnīdhra, they walk three times around [the fire] clockwise, fanning it upward.
They sit down around it facing it: the Adhvaryu in the east, the Pratiprasthātṛ in the south, and the Āgnīdhra in the north.
Without interweaving their movements, fanning upward, harmonizing with the *praṇavas*, kindling [the fire], and anointing it, they remain seated, restraining their speech.
"It is known from scripture that he took up the gold [vessel] when it was blazing.

At the point where [the Hotṛ] recognizes [the verse], "With which you released the swallowed quail," then the Adhvaryu consecrates the Mahāvīra vessel with the section beginning, "Ten rays toward the east, ten thou shinest to the south.
At the point where [the Hotṛ] recognizes [the verse], "O Aśvins, may our speech be effective," then the Adhvaryu, rising up, says, "The Gharma has been made radiant."
With the Adhvaryu at their head, they walk around three times without fanning.
(14) Taking the fans, the Adhvaryu hands them to the Pratiprasthātṛ. Having carried them around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ places them on the *samrāḍ-āsandi* throne.
(15) Standing each in his own place, all the officiating priests and the sacrificer, reciting the verse "I have seen the Guardian," gaze upon the Mahāvīra vessel. (16)
In an enclosed space, the Pratiprasthātṛ causes the wife to recite the remainder of the *anuvāka*, beginning with "tvaṣṭīmatī te sapeya" (17).
Thus ends the eighth section (*kaṇḍikā*) and the second chapter (*paṭala*). Then he issues the command: "O Agnīdh, set down the two *rohiṇa* rice-cakes."

He places the two sacrificial cakes, which have been spread with a base of ghee and sprinkled over with ghee, upon the two unobstructed ladles: one following the southern junction of the enclosing sticks, and the other following the northern junction of the enclosing sticks.

Having taken the rope with the formula addressed to Savitṛ, and having consecrated it with "Thou art the girdle of Aditi," he goes out by the eastern door and calls the cow that yields the Gharma-milk three times in a low voice: "O Iḍā, come! O Aditi, come! O Sarasvatī, come! Having returned and taken the two udder-straps with the formula "The two supports for milking," he goes out by the southern door and calls her three times aloud according to her name: "O So-and-so, come! O So-and-so, come!"
With the formula, "Thou art the turban of Aditi," he fastens the milch-cow of the Gharma with a rope; with "Vāyu art thou, the ewe," [he addresses] the calf;
having let it loose with "May Pūṣan let thee loose," he consecrates the milch-cow of the Gharma with the verse, "That teat of thine which is inexhaustible.

Having set down the calf with the words, "O cow, leave some of the Gharma; O cow, protect the Gharma; leave some for the Gharma," he sits down near her with the formula, "May Bṛhaspati sit down near thee."

Having touched the udders with the formula, "O generous ones, you are flowing," he milks the larger cow for the one who is the milker, using the formulas: "Flow for the Aśvins; flow for Sarasvatī; flow for Pūṣan; flow for Bṛhaspati; flow for Indra; flow for Indra.
The Pratiprasthātṛ silently milks the smaller goat.

When he recognizes [the verse], "Arise, O Brahmanaspati," then both, having given the two milks to the Āgnīdhra, having stepped forward as before, take up the two vessels with their handles (*śapha*). [The Adhvaryu takes] the first with the formula, "Thou art Gāyatra"; the second with, "Thou art Traiṣṭubha"; and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the supporting vessel (*upayamana*) with, "Thou art Jāgata.
When he recognizes [the verse], "Come hither, O milk-maid, with the milk," then the Āgnīdhra follows after.
He awaits the milk being brought with the formula, "Come hither together with a portion of strength."
Thus ends the ninth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the words, "O Indra and Aśvins, [I take] of the honey of the bee," he pours it into a cow's horn at the Mahāvrata.
1. With the words, "Svāhā! I offer you to the ray of the sun, to the rain-maker," he consecrates the rising steam. 2.
"Thou art honey, the oblation"—with these words [he takes] goat's milk;
some authorities prescribe the bringing of the goat's milk first.
"The heat of the sun, do thou burn"—with these words [he takes] the heat.

"By means of Heaven and Earth, I enclose thee," saying this, he encloses the Mahāvīra with his two hooves; then, having wiped away the ashes with the *veda*-grass whose tips have been cut off, the Pratiprasthātṛ supports it with the support-stand, saying, "By means of the intermediate space, I support thee. 6.

Having taken it up, saying, "May I be able to bear thee with the approval of the gods and the fathers," and having stood up, he carries it forward, saying, "Thou art brilliance; follow after brilliance. 7. While walking, without taking breath, he recites five names of the winds: "To the ocean wind, svāhā! and so forth. 8.
Having moved away, he offers five additional oblations with the formula, "To Agni accompanied by the Vasus, svāhā!

At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the established southern Rauhiṇa cake with the formula, "May the Day, the light, enjoy it with its banner; may the beautiful light, among lights, [enjoy it] with its light, svāhā!"

Passing to the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he looks at the Brahman priest with the words, "Seated in the south, [protect] all the quarters. He looks at the Hotṛ priest with the words, "He has sacrificed here to all the gods. Having consecrated the Gharma with the formula, "Of the Gharma consecrated by Svāhā," and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and received the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, he gives the command: "Recite the offering-verse for the Gharma! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering with the words, "O Aśvins, drink the Gharma! At the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* (anuvaṣaṭ), he offers with "Svāhā! To Indra, hail!

Having performed the worship with the remainder of the section beginning, "The Gharma you have drunk, O Aśvins," the Pratiprasthātṛ fills the Gharma—which is being held over the Āhavanīya fire—with boiled curds.
"Flow for sap, flow for strength," he says, consecrating it as it flows out.
(13) Thus ends the tenth section.
Then he causes it to flow toward the quarters with the formula: "For brilliance thee, for glory thee, for power thee, for prosperity thee. (1)

Having stepped back and taken up the supporting-stand (*upayamana*), having brought the remainder [of the milk], and having placed the supporting-stand within the altar (*antarvedi*), he places a silver disk (*rukma*) on the eastern mound (*khara*) and sets the *mahāvīra* vessel upon it with the formula: "Thou art the Law (*dharma*), the good Law; maintain the sacred formulations (*brahman*) for us. For a Kṣatriya, he says: "Maintain the ruling powers (*kṣatra*). For a Vaiśya, he says: "Maintain the people (*viś*). [He adds: "May the wind not spill thee.
If he should practice sorcery, he should set it down with: "I set thee down in the breath of so-and-so."
Here, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the northern Rauhiṇa cake as before.
Then, anointing these wood-shavings (*śakala*) upon the supporting-wood (*upayamana*), he offers them with these formulas one by one: "To Pūṣan, the essence, svāhā! and so forth.
Having smeared the sixth wood-shaving with all the residues, he throws it out toward the north without looking back, saying: "To Rudra, whose priest is Rudra, svāhā!"
Some prescribe that pieces of wood be placed before the Rauhiṇa oblations.
Then, having touched water and silently offered a thorn-tree fuel-stick, he offers the Agnihotra from this very remnant with the *upayamana* ladle, saying "bhūḥ svāhā," or he does so silently.
Having invoked one another, they all consume the remnant in the *upayamana* ladle.
With the words "Do you, so-and-so, invite [me]?", he addresses him by name; "I am invited" is the response. 11.
The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Āgnīdhra, and the sacrificer—12.
all [of them respond] directly. 13.

Or rather, the sacrificer himself [eats] directly. The others eat by smelling [the offering], saying, "The oblation is honey, the oblation is honey. Having eaten, he hands the support-vessel (*upayamana*) to the Pratiprasthātṛ. Having washed it on the mound for the remnants (*ucchista-khara*), he places the support-vessel within the altar (*antarvedi*). Having placed two gold plates (*rukma*) upon it and brought the boiling water (*madantī*), he purifies [himself] with the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses. Having poured out the water and having placed all the implements related to the *gharma* (*parigharmya*) right there, [he concludes].

Thus ends the eleventh section (kaṇḍikā). He gives the command: "Recite for the Gharma being set down," or "Recite for that which is being set down. Having recognized [the vessel] with the verse, "In whom the seven Vasus... and having carried it around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it on the royal throne (samrāḍ-āsandī) with the formula: "Svāhā! To thee, for the rays of Sūrya! in the morning; "Svāhā! To thee, for the constellations! in the evening. 2.

When he recognizes [the cow] with the words, "O inviolable one, eat grass always," he releases the cow, touches the boiling water (*madantī*), and they perform the *śānti* rite with the final *anuvāka*.
(3) In this manner, they proceed with the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites morning and evening.
(4) In a sacrifice with three *upasad*s, it is performed six times; in one with six *upasad*s, twelve times; and in one with twelve *upasad*s, twenty-four times. (5)

With this much variation, he offers the *rauhiṇa* oblation in the evening with the following mantra: "Carry me from day to night; protect me! This is your fuel-stick, O Agni; by it may you be kindled. Grant me life; anoint me with splendor. With these words, he places the fuel-stick in the evening. "Carry me from night to day; protect me!"—with these words in the morning.
"Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā!"—with this he offers the *agnihotra* in the evening. "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!"—with this he offers it in the morning.
Or he performs the combined oblation; he chooses the fires for the Agniṣṭoma,
but he should not choose them for the Ukthya.
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, which includes all the *pṛṣṭha* chants, he undergoes the consecration (*pravṛñjati*).

Having been thus consecrated, for one year he shall not eat meat; he shall not approach a woman; he shall not drink from an earthen vessel; and no woman shall drink his leavings. "He thereby sharpens his spiritual luster (*tejas*)," so it is known. This is the twelfth section (*kaṇḍikā*), and thus ends the third chapter (*paṭala*).
Intending to remove the *pravargya* vessels, he gives a goat to the *agnīdh*, a four-year-old cow to the *brahman*, a milch-cow to the *hotṛ*, and two gold plates to the *adhvaryu*.

Having placed another mound upon the previous mound and having scraped away the remains of the *ucchiṣṭa-khara*, he establishes the *samrāḍ-āsandī* throne to the north of the *āhavanīya* fire. Having placed all the implements for the *gharma* rite upon it, and having taken four spoonfuls of clarified butter in a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, he offers oblations with the formulas "O *Gharma*, that heat of yours which is in heaven," etc., according to their respective characteristics.

Alternatively, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having taken three handfuls of splinters together with their tips, lights one of them in the Āhavanīya fire and holds it at the height of his mouth; the Adhvaryu offers an oblation over it with the formula: "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in heaven..."

Having kindled another [fuel-stick] in that [Gharma] and having cast the previous one into the Āhavanīya fire, he holds it at the height of the navel. The Adhvaryu makes an offering over it with the formula: "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in the intermediate space. Having kindled another [fuel-stick] in that [Gharma] and having cast the previous one into the Āhavanīya fire, he holds it at the height of the knee. The Adhvaryu makes an offering over it with the formula: "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is on the earth.
He casts this very [Gharma] after [the fuel-sticks] into the Āhavanīya fire.
Within the enclosed space, the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife forward with the verse: "May Anumati favor us today..."
Saying, "Following the consent," they go out;
they carry away the sacrificial post, the wooden mallet, the pegs, the forked pole-ropes, and the two seats.
He carries the seat for the impure remains around to the south.
Having established two legs of the sovereign’s throne-altar (samrāḍāsandi) within the altar-ground and two outside the altar-ground, he issues the command: "O Prastotṛ, chant the Sāman!

All, together with their wives, join in the finale (nidhana) of the Sāman three times: the second time at the *adhyardha* [mark], and the third time having reached the western side of the high altar (*uttaravedi*). At all these points he issues the command. Thus ends the thirteenth section.

With the words, "For the protection from heaven thee," they set out on the first [day]; with "For the protection from Brahman thee," on the second; and with "For the protection from breath thee," on the third.

Having established the *samrāḍ-āsandi* throne to the north of the *uttaravedi*, he issues the command: "O *prastotṛ*, sing the *vārṣāhara* *sāman*; sing the *iṣṭāhotrīya* *sāman*. They reach the *nidhana* finale of the *iṣṭāhotrīya* *sāman*, but not that of the *vārṣāhara*.
If he were to pour water around [the fire] afterwards, then he should cause the *vārṣāhara* to be chanted there.

Taking the water-pitcher, the Adhvaryu goes around the northern altar three times, pouring water clockwise while reciting, "Thou art a wave, a source of peace for the sacrifice. Having set down the pitcher, he goes back around three times without pouring water, reciting, "Bring us peace and bring it all around. 4.

Having touched the northern altar with the words, "The navel of the Truth is four-cornered," and having poured out the two *khara* heaps to the north of the *uttaranābhi* with the words, "The seat is for all," he spreads them out.
5. With the words, "Away with hatred, away with the heart's pain," he prepares the *ucchiṣṭa-khara* in the region of the *mārjālīya*.
To the north of the *uttaranābhi*, having placed gold on the mound, he brings down the *pracaraṇīya* Mahāvīra into it.
Right here, he places the other two [Mahāvīras], either east and west or south and north.
Right here, he fashions the entire vessel for the *gharma* into a complete circle, the form of the sun.

With the formula, "Thou art the milk of the earth," he pours cow’s milk into the *mahāvīra* vessel; with "Thou art the light of the trees, the sap of the plants," he pours honey; and with "Thee, the vigorous one, we pour down, O vigorous ones," he pours curds.
In this same manner, he fills it a second and a third time.
Alternatively, he may pour only clarified butter in the first [filling], honey in the second, and curds in the third.

"O Gharma, this is your food, this is your sediment," [saying this] he fills with curds mixed with honey those vessels that have pouring-spouts; the others he sprinkles with water. "This is for the sake of non-emptiness," so it is known.
Thus ends the fourteenth section.

Now, if he intends to fashion it in the form of a man, [the procedure] is the same up to the first removal [of the clay]. Having removed the other two right here, he fashions the form of the head. He places a blade of *veda*-grass with its tip uncut upon it; this is the form of the tuft of hair (*śikhā*). On both sides [he places] the two milking-bowls; these are the form of the ears. On both sides [he places] two pieces of gold and two offering-spoons (*sruva*) filled with clarified butter; these are the form of the eyes. On both sides [he places] two *sruva* spoons; these are the form of the nostrils. The vessel for the sprinkling-water (*prokṣaṇī*) is the form of the mouth. The vessel for the clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) is the form of the neck.

On both sides, the two *dhṛṣṭī* are the form of the collarbones (*jatrūṇām*). On both sides, the two *śapha* are the form of the shoulders (*aṃsayoḥ*). On both sides, the two *rauhiṇahavanyau* are the form of the arms (*bāhvoḥ*). The eastern *methī* is the form of the ribs (*pṛṣṭīnām*). On both sides, the two fans (*dhavitre*) are the form of the flanks (*pārśvayoḥ*). In the middle, the third [fan] is the form of the chest (*urasaḥ*). In the middle, the supporting stand (*upayamanam*) is the form of the belly (*udarasya*). Upon it he places everything made of rope; this is the form of the entrails (*āntrāṇām*). The northern spade (*abhri*) is the form of the hips (*śroṇyoḥ*). On both sides, the two pegs (*śaṅkū*) are the form of the thighs (*sakthyoḥ*).

In the middle, the third [layer] is the form of the penis. On both sides, the two *rauhiṇa* potsherds are the form of the heels. He scatters the remains of the *rauhiṇa* flour; this is the form of the marrow. Having loosened the *veda*-grass mat, he scatters it along [the altar]; this is the form of the sinews. He covers it with *avakā* plants and *dhūpa*-grass; this is the form of the flesh. He sprinkles it with curd mixed with honey; this is the form of the blood. He covers it with a black antelope skin with the hair upward; this is the form of the skin and the body hair. Having loosened the royal throne (*samrāḍāsandi*), he places it on top; this is the form of sovereignty. Thus ends the fifteenth section.
One should remove [the fire] onto the *uttaravedi* for one who desires splendor; [one should remove it] onto the *uttaravedi* for one who desires food.
Alternatively, one may remove it further away or behind. One should remove it into the midst of waters. One should remove it onto an island in a river.
If one removes it onto an island in a river, one should not sprinkle water around it.

In whichever direction he may hate someone, he should remove [the fire] onto an *udumbara* branch in that direction. The *udumbara* is vigor; breath is food, and heat is pain. With the formula, "Here I burn away the breath of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, by means of pain," he indeed burns away his breath with pain. It is known from tradition: "He swiftly meets with distress. 4.
Where the *darbha* grasses are covered with *upadīka* insects, there he should remove it for one who desires rain. 5. They prescribe the regular rite on the *uttaravedi*. 6.
The birds should not settle upon this [fire] after it has been removed until the leading forward of the Āhavanīya fire.
7. Regarding this, some prescribe the sprinkling of water around [the fire].
8. Then they pay reverence to it with the formula: "Thou art delight by name, the divine Gandharva. 9.

Having consecrated [the water] with the mantra, "O divine Gharma, you have approached the gods," and having turned clockwise with the mantra, "I, a human, [approach] humans," he purifies himself at the site of the *mārjālīya* on the mound for the remnants (*ucchiṣṭakhara*) with the mantra, "May the waters and plants be friendly to us. Then, having worshipped the sun with the two mantras, "We have risen above the darkness" and "That bright [light] yonder," he offers oblations into the *gārhapatya* fire with the two mantras, "Upward that [light]" and "The bright [light]. Some say they worship [the fires]. He offers into the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra, "This very one, for us... Some say they worship [the fires]. This is the sixteenth section; thus ends the fourth chapter.
If the *gharma* should spill, he should consecrate it with these two verses: "The sky has spilled upon the earth... and [the second verse].

If lightning should strike while they are performing with the *gharma*, he should offer oblations according to the respective signs with the formulas beginning, "The lightning that struck in the east... and so forth.
If it strikes from all sides, he should offer all the oblations.
"Prāṇāya svāhā, Pūṣṇe svāhā"—these two sections (anuvākas) are the expiations for the Gharma. 4.
He lays down the Gharmeshṭakā with the section beginning "udasya śuṣmād bhānur naiti.

He lays down the Kulāyinī with the section beginning "yāste agne ārdra yonayaḥ. With the section beginning "agnir asi vaiśvānaro 'si," the Adhvaryu touches the piled fire-altar (cityāgni) using the Aiḍikī verse. 5.
With the words "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he performs all the expiations. (6) If the Mahāvīra pot should fall, he should lift it up with the two verses beginning "ūrdhva ū ṣu ṇaḥ" and "ūtaye.

(7) If it should break, he should join it together with the verse "vidhuṃ dadrāṇam. Then, with whatever substances serve for strengthening and adhesion, he should smear it, using the formula: "Whatever [is other] than meat and beans, even that which is apart from the joining. (8)
If they do not carry the *gharma* around, or if they do carry it around, they should carry it around him with these two verses: "With vigor again, together with wealth...
(VS 38.26) and "O *gharma*, do not harm us" (VS 38.27). These eight are the expiations when the *gharma* has been harmed.
Alternatively, one should consecrate the very *gharma* that has been harmed with four of these [verses].

If the sun should set while the *gharma* is being performed, one should tie a piece of gold to a blade of *darbha* grass at the western door, worship with the two verses "ud vayaṃ tamasas pari" and "ud u tyaṃ citram," and having offered oblations in the *gārhapatya* fire and cast the remnants, they worship the sun on the following day with the verse "vayaḥ suparṇāḥ.
This is the seventeenth section.

If the cow that yields the *gharma* milk does not arrive at the time for milking, one should milk another cow, cast the remnants, and give her to a Brāhmaṇa whom one does not intend to visit again at the time of the Soma-pressing.
If there should be no milk from the Gharma-cow, one should make the fourth foot of the *ṛc* into a teat and cause it to swell. 2. If one should milk curds, one should recite the hymn to Bṛhaspati. 3.
If [one milks] milk, [one should recite] the hymn to the Aśvins together with the *udarka*. 4.
If it should yield blood, one should offer oblations with verses addressed to Rudra (5).
If it should perish, one should offer oblations with two verses addressed to Dhātṛ (6).
If its calf should perish, one should offer an oblation with a verse addressed to Vāyu Niyutvat (7).
If she should sit down upon something impure or unfit for sacrifice, one should offer an oblation with a verse addressed to Agni; some say with one addressed to Agni and Varuṇa.
(8) If a bird should alight upon her, one should offer an oblation with a verse addressed to the Aśvins.

(9) If she should fall down, or become disoriented, or if a tiger should kill her, one should mix the milk of a female *arka* plant with goat’s milk, sprinkle it [upon her], and proceed with that. (10)

Some authorities prescribe the *pravṛñjana* (the heating of the milk) during the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing day). Regarding this, there is an inquiry: when the sun becomes reddish in the east, then it should be heated—either at the first appearance of light, at the break of dawn, at the time when the sun is half-risen, when it has just risen, or when it has fully risen; or [it may be done] at the morning *pavamāna*, at the *saṃgava* [period], or at the midday *pavamāna* after the chant has been performed.
He is to be initiated in the Āgnīdhra shed;
it is known that he is to be initiated only once.
These [rites] may optionally be performed together with the initiations belonging to the Upasads.
They consume the curd-heat offering (dadhigharma) with the Anuvāka beginning "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ. 17.
Thus ends the eighteenth Kaṇḍikā.
The Ghoratanu verses have been explained; the Gaṇa to be recited in the forest (araṇye'nuvākyo gaṇaḥ) and the two subsequent Anuvākas [are now to be discussed]. 1.

If he should rise up as a lone wanderer while performing the *gharma* rite, [the officiant] should consecrate him with the mantra, "O Indra, as you move about, bind the cows," and then, having kindled a firebrand at both ends, throw it toward him with the words, "O Agni, converse with Agni.
Then they pay homage to him with the remainder of the section beginning, "Once to thee, O Agni, be homage."

Now, if a vulture, a female wolf, a jackal, a long-faced owl, one possessed by a spirit, or a bird with blood on its face should speak—[reciting] "That which," "If impelled," "O long-faced one," "Thus the owl," and "Having entered into these beings," [and] "Stretching out the thighs"—having consecrated [the victim] with these [mantras] according to their respective gender-marks, the procedure beginning with the casting away of the firebrand (*ulmuka*) is the same. 5. If the cow that provides the *gharma* milk should be infested with worms, he should kill the worms of this cow with the section beginning, "With the devourer (*atriṇ*), I kill you, O worm.
6. Or rather, this expiation may be performed as a universal rule for all such cases.

7. Against whom one intends to practice sorcery, having taken blood as the sacrificial portion from him, one should offer it while reciting the section beginning with *ahar-avadya śṛtasya*. 8. If one intends to utter a curse against someone, having practiced celibacy for at least three nights and having gone to that person, one should utter the curse against him while reciting the section beginning with *brahmaṇā tvā śapāmi*.
9. Against whom one hates, one should bury a *svaja* plant in his cow-pen while reciting the section beginning with *uttuda śimijāvari*.
Or else, he should move the southern door-post of the cow-pen with this very [Sāman].
(10) If the Udgātṛ should not sing the Puruṣasāman, the Adhvaryu himself should sing that Sāman with the Anuvāka beginning "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ.
(11) Thus ends the nineteenth Kaṇḍikā; thus ends the fifth Paṭala.
We shall now explain the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*).

On a festival day during the northern course of the sun, or under an auspicious lunar mansion in the waxing fortnight, having had his hair and beard shaved, he goes out in the afternoon toward the east or the north. Having established the fire in a fallow place where no roof-coverings are visible, and having strewn grass around it, he performs the introductory rite as before. Having touched the *madantī* water and performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the first Anuvāka, he places four fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood, anointed with clarified butter, upon the fire with these mantras: "The earth is the Samit... and so forth. 2.
Then he worships the deities with the formula: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow.
(3) Then he causes him to recite the introductory verses of all the sections, or those of the first and the last.
(4) Having performed the *śānti* rite with the final section, he then closes his eyes and restrains his speech. (5)
Then, having wrapped his head from left to right with an unwashed garment while facing it, he causes him to enter the village after sunset.

He remains for that night either standing or sitting, maintaining silence. On the following day, having kindled the fire on a cleared spot where no roof-covering is visible and having strewn grass around it, he shows him six things—some say seven: the fire, the sun, a water-pot, a stone, a calf, and a woman who has not yet borne a child; gold is the seventh.
Or, having played three [notes] and demonstrated them, he plays the others as they occur. 9.
Having given this garment to the teacher, he worships the sun with the verse, "The birds, the fair-winged ones... 10.
Now follows his student life (brahmacarya). 11.
12. He should not eat at night during the Nitya [observance]. 13. If he should eat, it must be when the fire is blazing. 14. [If he eats otherwise, he incurs a fault.]
He should not place his feet on anything made of clay;
15 he should not converse with a woman or a Śūdra; 16 nor [should he step on] sandals or an umbrella. 17
He should not mount anything that has wheels like a chariot; he should not look at one whose life has departed; he should not bathe;
and on the eighth days and the festival days (parvan), he should fast while restraining his speech.
"And he shall not lie down" (21)—this is the twentieth section.
He should observe this vow for one year; he should study during that very year. 1.
If he does not study during this year, he should observe this vow for as long as it takes to complete his studies.

When the year has elapsed, while the ground is barren and no roofs are visible, he should kindle the fire, strew grass around it, and having dismissed [the fires] as before, touch the boiling water, perform the *śānti* rite with the first *anuvāka*, offer fuel sticks with the mantras recited in reverse order, worship the deities with the mantras recited in reverse order, perform the *śānti* rite with the last *anuvāka*, give a choice gift to the teacher, and have his hair and beard shaved.
Then his daily private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) resumes.
One should not study without having first recited the preceding section;

nor at night; nor after having committed an excessive transgression of the vow of celibacy; nor after eating meat; nor after having shaved the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, or the nails; nor after having groomed the hair; nor after having washed the teeth.

Not when it is night, nor when he has anointed himself, nor when he is wet, nor when the ground is wet, nor when it has not rained, nor when there is a cloud, nor in the shade, nor when the sun has set; not while looking at green barley, nor in the vicinity of domestic animals, nor of wild animals, nor in the vicinity of water;
not having seen anything uncooked, nor anything that has sprung up, nor blood; not near mansions, nor corpses, nor a dead body, nor an impure vessel.

When about to begin his studies, having gone out toward the east or the north, having established the fire on a barren spot where no roof-covering is visible, having strewn grass around it, and having touched the *madantī* water, he should perform the rite of peace (*śānti*) with the first *anuvāka*. Then, sitting behind the fire on *darbha* grass and holding *darbha* or *dūrvā* grass in his hands, he should recite [the Veda] while facing away from the teacher. Or, having given a gift, he may study in the vicinity of the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). When about to begin his studies, he should not speak other words [than those pertaining to the lesson].
If he should see anything performed that causes lack of peace anywhere, he should perform a rite for peace again and then study. 13.
Having studied, he should do so with the highest [concentration]. 14.
Having gone out for the Pravargya ceremony, he should not study anything else until he has re-entered; he should not study anything else. 15.
Thus ends the twenty-first section (kaṇḍikā); thus ends the sixth chapter (paṭala).
Thus ends the fifteenth book (praśna).
One who is about to pile the fire-altar (agni) procures the ukhā [fire-pan] on the new moon day, the full moon day, or on the eighth day of the waning fortnight.

Regarding the Aṣāḍhā bricks, some recite: "The gods whose domestic priest is Bṛhaspati; the gods of the gods; the first-born gods; O gods, exert your power among the gods! As the first among the second, as the second among the third—thrice eleven, thrice thirty-three—may I take hold of you; may I be able to do this which I am doing. May they protect me; may they inspire me in this sacred formulation (brahman), in this dominion, in this blessing, in this priesthood, in this rite, in this invocation of the gods. He offers an oblation of four ladlings.

Having cleansed the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles, and having taken eight portions of clarified butter into the *juhū*, he offers a single oblation with the verses beginning "He harnesses the mind first" (*yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ*), with the *yajus* formula being the eighth, while standing upright within the altar-ground.
If he should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," he should offer to that person one portion at a time while standing sideways.
If he should desire, "May I endow the meters with the glory of the sacrifice," it has already been stated [how this is to be done].

With the verse, "Fulfill the hymn with the Ṛc," he takes another fourfold portion [of ghee]. Then, with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... and so on with the four [verses], he takes the spade (*abhri*)—made of bamboo, variegated, either hollow or solid, sharpened at both ends or sharpened at one end, measuring a span (*prādeśa*), a cubit (*aratni*), a fathom (*vyāyāma*), or of unmeasured length; made of *khadira*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *arka*, *kārsmarya*, *vikaṅkata*, or *śamī* wood, or whatever tree is fit for sacrifice and bears fruit.
Thus ends the first section (*kaṇḍikā*).
Taking the horse’s halter with the verse, "They have taken this rein of the Order," he fastens it on the horse with the words, "Run forward, O steed!
He takes the donkey’s halter silently and fastens it on the donkey with the verse, "Yoke ye two the ass.
With the three verses beginning, "In every yoking, the most powerful," they set out toward the place where they intend to dig for the clay, with the horse leading the way.
If he should desire, "May there be a reversal of fortune," they should proceed with the donkey first.
He mutters: "O Agni Purīṣya, come hither like Aṅgiras!
(4). With the words, "O Agni Purīṣya, we come hither like Aṅgiras," he addresses the one with whom he has a grievance; not seeing him, he points him out. (5–6).
"We shall carry Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras," [saying this], he digs up the ant-hill; until the sun rises, having dug it up, he stands worshipping it.
"Agni has looked toward the forefront of the dawns," [saying this], he steps forward from the ant-hill.

Having returned, and having made the horse step upon the earth with the two verses, "O steed, come to the path" and "O steed, having stepped upon the earth," he strokes the back of the horse with the verse, "The sky is your back."

"Trample those who attack; let the enemies be beneath you. Stand like Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, conquering the waters and the fields. With the verse "Thou art trampled," he meditates with his mind upon him whom he hates as being beneath the feet of the horse.

With the two verses, "He has stepped forth" and "He has stepped forth," having made the horse step out toward the north from the clay-digging pit, and having poured water into the horse's footprint with the words, "O divine waters, flow forth," and having placed gold in the footprint—this is the second section.

Having offered a single oblation into the gold with the two verses containing the word "mind" (*manasvatī*), namely, "I sprinkle Agni" and "I sprinkle thee," and having taken up the gold, he traces around the clay pit for the spade with three verses beginning, "Agni, the wise lord of booty. He traces it successively further outward, making each subsequent circle larger.
He digs with the two verses beginning, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ."
If he should desire, "May he become more prosperous," he should collect [the materials] for him using both types [of verses].

He collects with eight verses. Having touched the clay with the verse, "Be born, O noble one," and having stirred up the clay-digging pit with the verse, "Thine is Vāyu," he pours water into the pit. Having lifted it up, he ties the ends of the black antelope skin with a hempen, a muñja-grass, or an arka-plant cord, with the formula, "Well-born with light, together. He binds it with a knot.
With the two verses addressed to Savitṛ, "O thou of good sacrifice, stand up erect" and "Stand up erect for our aid," he rises.
With the verse, "Once born, thou art the embryo," he carries [the fire]. With the verse, "Be firm, O thou of strong limbs," he places it upon the back of the donkey.
"Be auspicious to the subjects," with these words he consecrates the fire that has been established.
With the three verses beginning "Let the steed go forth neighing," they return without hurrying.
With the verse, "We bear Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras," he addresses whichever hateful person he encounters; looking away, he points him out.
And whatever else he considers to be for a firm purpose, [he does so].
Having gathered the earth with the verse, "The Rudras, having gathered the earth," and having mixed it with the three verses beginning, "Mixed by the Vasus," he hands it to the maker.

Having formed a lump with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," he touches the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf with the formula, "Ye two are the feet of the sacrifice," and he presses down upon the clay with his thumb and forefinger.
With the four formulas beginning, "May the Vasus fashion you with the Gāyatrī metre," the Mahiṣī prepares the fire-pan for one who has many wives; the Adhvaryu does so for one who has only one wife.
While it is being made, the sacrificer consecrates it with these very same formulas.
It may have three elevations, five elevations, or an unlimited number of elevations.

It may be square or circular; it is one span (prādeśa) in height, one cubit (aratni) in width, and one fathom (vyāyāma) in circumference, or it may be of unlimited size. Or it may be five spans in measure, according to the Vājasaneyaka, if there are five sacrificial animals.
While performing [the rite], he raises four corners toward the cardinal directions.
One should make it eight-cornered for one desiring prosperity, or nine-cornered for one practicing exorcism. Two finger-breadths below the cavity—
this is the fourth section.
With the words, "Thou art the girdle for Aditi," he makes a girdle.
At the junction of the girdle and the [cooking] potsherds, he fashions two, four, six, or eight breasts.

Having made an opening with the words, "May Aditi grasp thy opening," and having placed it upon the sand to the north with the words, "Having fashioned it, [place] this great pan," he entrusts it to Mitra with the words, "O Mitra, I entrust this pan to thee so that it may not be broken; may it not shatter. 3.
He who makes the fire-pan (ukhā) also makes from this same clay a brick called the *aṣāḍhā*, which is square, marked with three lines, and fashioned silently.
With the seven formulas beginning, "May the Vasus fumigate thee with the Gāyatrī metre," he fumigates the pan with the hair of a horse's tail;
some say [he uses the hair] of a stallion. 4–6.
The two hearths for baking the pots are located to the east of the *gārhapatya*.

(7) Having dug a pit to the east of the *gārhapatya* with [the mantra], "May the goddess Aditi [dig] thee," and having spread it with the red-baking materials, he places the *ukhā* into it with [the mantra], "The wives of the gods [place] thee.

(8) Having silently placed the *aṣāḍhā* brick upon it and covered it with the red-baking materials, he adds fuel to the fire in the *ukhā* with the four [mantras] beginning, "The goddess Dhiṣaṇās [place] thee. (9)
"O Mitra, cook this fire-pan," he says; while it is being cooked, he attends to it with three verses addressed to Mitra.

When it is cooked, he takes it off the fire with the words, "May the god Savitṛ take thee up. While it is being set down, he establishes it on the sand to the north with the words, "Fill the regions and the quarters of the earth. Having established it, he entrusts it to Mitra with the words, "O Mitra, I entrust this fire-pan to thee so that it may not be broken; may it not break. He silently takes down the *aṣāḍhā* brick.
Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the four [verses] beginning, "May the Vasus anoint thee with the Gāyatrī metre," he anoints the fire-pan (ukhā) with goat's milk.
Taking seven or twenty-one beans, he goes toward the head of a man—either that of a Vaiśya or a Rājanya who has been killed by a weapon or struck by lightning.

Having scattered beans, he cuts off the head of a human corpse with the formula, "This is that which you are, whose this head is," and replaces it in the place of the head at the anthill mound—which has been split into seven parts and covered with grass—with the formula, "By this, may you be provided with a head here. 3.

With three *Yamagāthās* he sings around [the horse], [reciting]: "He who alone is the ruler of this earthly realm that is within the belly; sing of Yama, Bhaṅgyaśravas, the king who is not to be obstructed. Sing of Yama, Bhaṅgyaśravas, the king who is not to be obstructed. By whom the waters, the rivers, and the deserts [are held], by whom the sky and the earth are made firm—[he who gave] the horses that do not perish, with golden girths, well-yoked, golden-eyed, and iron-hoofed; King Yama presides over this gift. Some say that he recites [these verses] while bringing [the horse].

"May this serve as enjoyment for our arms," [saying this] he takes the human head and brings it forward with the verse: "O Agni, rise up from the mother earth. He carries it around with three verses: "Agni goes around the sacrifice like a charioteer, bestowing food upon the gods"; "The sage, the lord of booty"; and "The divine Agni has gone forth, the slayer of demons, the driver away of disease; driving away all enemies, burning the Rākṣasas at every turn. Having carried fire around it and smeared it with clay, he sets it down. Thus ends the sixth section (Kaṇḍikā).

He offers animals to the fires for the sake of desire; they must be castrated. Having brought forward a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati, he recites twenty-one or twenty-four *abhidhenī* verses in a continuous sequence, including eleven standard verses and ten verses addressed to Agni beginning with "The seasons, O Agni...

(*samāstvāgne*). If there are twenty-one, he recites the verse: "O Agni, we kindle thee for the great gift of wealth; praise the two great ones, Heaven and Earth, for the office of the Hotṛ. (ŚB 13.2.6.1–3)

Desiring strength, I have approached with eloquence; may the Son of Waters accept my songs today. Will he, the swift-moving, bestow beautiful forms upon us? For he shall surely take pleasure in them. "The others come together"—this [verse] follows. "For the Son of Waters has taken his seat in the lap of the reclining ones, standing upright in their lap, self-glorious. He moves toward and away from both most beloved meeting places, knowing them well"—these three verses contain the word *ap* (water). If there are twenty-four [verses], then [one should use these]. For one who is ill, one should use [the hymn beginning] "From that world beyond" (*amutrabhūya*).
For one who is not ill, one should use "O Bṛhaspati, O Savitṛ, awaken him."

He concludes with the verse containing light, "Up from the darkness we have risen," (RV 1.50.10). He pours the oblation into the ladle with the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning" (RV 10.121.1).
"His fuel-sticks rise upward" (RV 10.88.3)—these are the Āprī verses for the fore-offerings (prayāja).
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the oblations dedicated to Agni are *triṣṭubh* verses addressed to Agni (10).
For the oblation dedicated to Prajāpati, the verses are "He who [gives] breath" and "He who gives the self" (11).
Alternatively, having cut off the heads of the animals once they have been immolated, he coats them with clay and sets them aside (12).
Thus ends the seventh section (kaṇḍikā).
They throw the headless trunks (kabandhas) into the water.
It is known from tradition that he concludes with the rite dedicated to Prajāpati.
Alternatively, in place of all these [animals], he immolates for Vāyu Niyutvat a white, hornless goat.
The invitatory and offering verses for the omentum are addressed to Vāyu and contain the word "white. The verses for the principal oblation are addressed to Vāyu Niyutvat.
Having cut off its head and smeared it with clay, he sets it aside.
It has been stated that the offering for Vāyu should be prepared (6).
For that [animal sacrifice], he offers a cake on twelve potsherds as the animal-puroḍāśa to Agni Vaiśvānara (7).
Some say that whichever animal is sacrificed in the fire, its animal-puroḍāśa should be one on twelve potsherds dedicated to Vaiśvānara (8).
Having sacrificed with that, for one year he should not eat meat, he should not approach a woman, and he should not sleep on a raised bed.

Or rather, he may eat meat and sleep on a raised bed, but he must certainly not approach a woman; so says the Vājasaneyaka. Having performed what precedes the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiation offering], he prepares the *dīkṣaṇīyā* consisting of three oblations.

The third [offering] consists of a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara, prior to the year-long maintenance [of the fires]. Having performed that which precedes the *dīkṣā*-offerings, he offers five *adhvarika* oblations with the formulas beginning "To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā! and six *āgnikī* oblations with the formulas beginning "Ākūtim agnim. He offers the seventh as a full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse, "Of the god who leads... (RV 1.89.5).

If one should desire of someone, "May he be liable to die," he should offer for him after reciting [the formulas] only once; this pierces his vital breaths. It is known from tradition: "He becomes deaf."
Thus ends the eighth section (kaṇḍikā). One who is consecrated (dīkṣita) carries the fire in the ukhā pot for a year; or for three days, six days, or twelve days.
Some say that even one who is less than a year [consecrated] is indeed [one who has carried the fire]. 1–2.
It has been said, "By means of Agni, indeed, [is] consecration.
