Having performed that which precedes the action of the fist-closing, he covers the *ukhā* with a nest of *śaṇa* grass or a nest of *muñja* grass, and with the two verses beginning "Do not break," he places it upon the *āhavanīya* fire.
With the verse "O Mitra, heat this *ukhā*," he surrounds it on all sides with embers, moving from left to right.

"Obeisance to the wood-eater, whose libation is clarified butter"—in this [verse], having anointed a piece of *krumuka* wood that has been scraped with a tool, he places it [into the fire], as well as blades of *muñja* grass;
"for one who has lost his prosperity," so it is said.

He should fetch [wood] from a forest fire for one whom he desires that his kingdom may be prone to internal strife. For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), [he should fetch it] from the top of a tree while it is burning.
For one who desires food, [he should perform] roasting.

(8) One who is performing the *kāmya* fire-sacrifice should not pour [the oblation] into the *āhavanīya* fire. (9) Once [the fire] has been produced in the *ukhya*, he follows it to the *āhavanīya*. (10)
With the words, "Over the assembly of another," he places a fuel-stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood;
with the words, "From the furthest distance," he places one of *śamī* wood.
Or rather, these two may be reversed.
With the three verses beginning, "Sit down upon the lap of this mother," he worships the newly born fire.
Thus ends the ninth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the five verses beginning, "O Agni, whatever [fires] there are," he places as fuel a piece of Udumbara wood that has not been cut by an axe.

For one practicing exorcism against a Tailvaka, he places a fuel-stick of *aśvattha* wood with the verse, "With your two fangs, [O Agni], [seize] the thieves" (RV 7.104.2). With the verse, "Those who among men are thieves" (RV 7.104.16), he places a fuel-stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood.
"Whoever would act with hostility toward us"—with this [verse], he offers a fuel-stick made of *śamī* wood.
Therefore, one should not proclaim the evil of one who has built the fire-altar, nor of one who maintains the fire, nor of one who knows the fire.
Reciting "Sharpened is my sacred power; I have extended their arms," while causing the sacrificer to recite the final [verse], he silently places two fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood upon the altar.

"Like a mother her son, may the earth bear Agni Purīṣya in her own womb—this ukhā. Being in agreement with all the gods and the seasons, may Prajāpati Viśvakarman join it [to the yoke]. With these words, he places the ukhā upon a sling made of muñja grass, having six or twelve suspension-ropes.

(8) The gold plate has twenty-one knobs and is strung on a cord; "the shining gold plate is visible. Sitting down, the sacrificer fastens it so that the knobs are inside and makes the knobs face outward. (9) With the verse, "All forms," he fastens the loop of the sling. (10)
With the verse, "Night and Dawn," he places a black antelope skin over [the fire].

(11) Having looked at the *ukhya* fire with the formula, "Thou art Suparṇa, Garutman," and having taken it up with the same formula, "Thou art Suparṇa, Garutman," he rises and, holding it above his navel, strides four *viṣṇukrama* steps toward the east with the formula, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu. (12) Having recited the verse, "Agni has roared," he turns clockwise three times with the four verses beginning, "O Agni, come back! (13)

Having untied the sling-rope with the verse, "The highest," and having brought it up with the verse, "I have brought thee hither," he worships it with the verse, "Great and lofty, he has risen before the dawns.
(14) He should meditate upon him in his mind for whom he desires, "May he become a ruler.

(15) The Audumbara throne-seat has its head-piece one cubit long, its side-rails knee-high, and its legs a span long; it is bound with Muñja grass, spread with wooden planks, or smeared with clay. (16)

"Sit down in the lap of this mother"—with these four [verses], he places the *ukhya* fire upon her; with three [verses], he places it on a pebble. "He worships it with the *haṃsavatī* verse," say some.
Thus ends the tenth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
With the verse, "By which the gods went upward to the light," he kindles the fire in the *ukhya* pan with pieces of wood a span long.
(1) It burns perpetually.
(2) At the time of the vow (*vrata*), having anointed a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood with the formula, "O Lord of Food, give us food," he places it upon the fire. (3)

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the Gāyatrī metre, I place thee, the night-brick; by that deity, like Aṅgiras, sit thou firm"—with these words he places a fuel-stick in the evening.

With this same formula, substituting "the day-brick" and the Triṣṭubh metre, he places it in the morning. He worships with the Vātsapra hymn using eleven, twelve, or thirteen verses beginning with "From the sky."
On the previous day he strides the Viṣṇu-steps; on the following day he performs the worship. Thus it is always from the time of the purchase [of the Soma].
On the day one purchases the Soma, on that day one should combine both [rites]: one should both stride forward and perform the worship.

From the time of forming the fist, he undertakes the ritual action. (10) If, while the fire is being carried forward, this god should feel affection for these creatures, he should place three fuel-sticks with each of three Āgneyī verses containing the word "physician" (*bhiṣaj*). "O Agni, you who have blackened tracks, bring the physicians; you are our worshipful Hotṛ. O Agni, be our physician among the gods, O carrier of oblations. You are the bearer of oblations to the gods. We invoke you as physicians; we kindle you as physicians. Be our physician among the gods. (11)

If he should desire, "May it rain," he should place three fuel-sticks with those three verses addressed to Sūrya that contain the word *raśmi* (ray). "Sūrya plunges into the waters with his rays, the greatest winner of booty; awaken for the singer, O increaser of vital strength! He who has measured out the ends of heaven and earth with his ray has filled both worlds with his greatness. With your most excellent steeds, you go weaving the thread, spreading out the dark [woof], O God, bestowing wealth. The rays of Sūrya, shaking [the darkness] like a skin, have driven away the gloom within the waters. (RV 1.50.10) 12. If he should desire, "May it not rain," he should place three fuel-sticks with those three verses addressed to Sūrya that contain the word *bhrājasvatī* (radiant).

13. This is the eleventh section. "His banners have become visible; his rays extend over the people, shining like fires. This [verse] is: "The one who crosses over, visible to all, the golden ornament of heaven rises, far-reaching, crossing over, radiant. Truly, men impelled by Sūrya shall go about their business and perform their works. 1.

If the *ukhya* fire should be lost while it is being carried, the sacrificer should worship it with these four verses: "O Agni, who returns," "O Agni Aṅgiras," "With vigor again," and "Together with wealth.
It is known from tradition that he indeed recovers it.

On the day he departs, having lifted the *ukhya* fire with the verse, "Thee all the gods have raised up," he places the *ukhya* fire on the front of a two-seated cart with the four verses beginning, "Sit thou in the lap of this mother."
He places [the vessels] down with three verses. According to some, he worships them with the *haṃsavatī* verse.
Having gathered those two fires together and having re-ascended them, he sets out with the words, "Come forward, O Agni, full of light!
He consecrates the sound of the dice with the verse, "Agni has roared."
With the verse, "Worship the fire with the fuel of resolve," he places a fuel-stick anointed with ghee once the [fire] has been established.
(8) For a Kṣatriya, he uses a Triṣṭubh verse; for a Vaiśya, a Jagatī verse.
(9) When the kindling of the fuel and the formal resolve coincide, he first places the stick anointed with ghee. (10)

If one should sit down in the ashes of the fire-pan (*ukhā*), let him take the pan, go to the edge of the water, and say: "Descend, O mighty one, into this well-formed, golden vessel with a thousand spikes; enjoy the honeyed spring, the wide expanse; enter your oceanic dwelling. Suckle this honeyed breast of the waters, which is swollen in the midst of the flood, O Agni."

With the two verses, "Delight in the well of honey, O wide one; enter your oceanic seat," he takes out the fire from the pan (*ukhā*) and, without setting it down, places the pan upon the tripod (*śikyā*). With the three verses, "O divine waters, receive this ash," he causes the ash to enter the water. (11) Having taken up the ash, having kneaded it, and with the two verses, "Having settled in the ash... he places it back into the pan. With the verse, "Return again with vigor and wealth," he brings it back up.
(12) With the verse, "May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again," he rekindles the fire in the pan. (13)
Thus ends the twelfth section (kaṇḍikā).
He worships with the two verses beginning "Be awake, O Awakening" (*bodha* and *bodhī*).

1. For one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*), the constant throwing of ashes into the water occurs once the *iṣṭakā* offerings have been performed; if they have not been performed, it is for the purpose of purification from contact. 2.
One desiring cattle should prepare [the altar] in cow-dung;
one who is a wanderer should cast it into the waters.

He prepares the bricks for the consecrated person during the ritual procedures of consecration lasting a month or more, prior to the consecration; in other cases, after the consecration, following the animal sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati.

He makes the bricks of clay: measuring a foot, measuring a cubit, measuring a thigh-bone, or measuring a knee-bone; they have straight lines, turned to the right, turned to the left, and marked with three lines.
They bake them over a fire produced by friction.
They remain unbroken.
One should not place [bricks] that are broken, black, or marked with spots. [The materials to be placed are:

a lotus leaf, a golden plate, a golden man, two offering-spoons (*srucau*), seven naturally perforated stones (*svayamātṛṇāḥ*), pebbles, golden bricks, five ghee-bricks, a clump of *dūrvā* grass, a tortoise, a mortar, a pestle, a winnowing basket, stones, the heads of sacrificial animals, and serpent-heads; these bricks must not be made of clay. One building the fire-altar for the first time should pile it knee-high with a thousand bricks. For the second time, one should pile it navel-high with two thousand bricks. For the third time, one should pile it mouth-high with three thousand bricks. Each subsequent altar is larger than the preceding one.
"One desiring heaven should pile the great, vast, and immeasurable [altar]," so says the Vājasaneyaka.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.

When the duration of the consecration has expired, having dug up a site for the Gārhapatya altar measuring one fathom (vyāyāma) square or circular with the words "Go away, depart," and having swept it with a branch of *palāśa* or *śamī* wood that is tawny-colored, and having pulled out the branch toward the east or the north, and having sprinkled it with water with the verse "May the goddesses come to us for our aid," he pours sand down with the formula, "Thou art the ash of Agni."
While scattering the saline earth (ūṣa), he recites: "Consciousness," and meditates with his mind: "Whatever is black in the moon, may that be here.

"Prepare the cow-pen, for it is your protector; sew many wide shields. Make iron forts, unassailable; let not your cup leak, make it firm. Having consecrated pebbles with this, he places four bricks facing east in the middle of the Gārhapatya altar with the formula, "This is that Agni... (VS 12.54).
Two [bricks] are placed in front, facing each other, either aligned or transverse, with the formulas, "O Agni, [bestow] the *iḍā*," and "This is your seasonal womb" (VS 12.55–56).
In the same way, two are placed behind with the formulas, "Thou art the layer" and "Thou art the surrounding layer" (VS 12.57–58).
He covers the remainder with thirteen *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.
With two mantras for each—one being "Fill the space! Be thou a milch-cow for him" (*lokaṃ pṛṇa tā asya sūdadohasaḥ*)—he lays down each individual *lokaṃpṛṇā*.
In all the bricks, he places the *tayādevata* formula at the end.

Thus ends the fourteenth section (kaṇḍikā). Having brought earth from the site of the Cātvāla pit, he spreads it over the altar with the verse addressed to Vaiśvānara, "Thou art asked about heaven" (pṛṣṭo divi). That constitutes the layer (citi). 1–2.

One who is building for the first time should pile it with five layers; for the second time, with three layers; for the third time, with one layer. From that point onward, he should pile it with only single layers.
Having touched the Gārhapatya layer with the verse, "Mortals have brought forth the immortal," he pours the *ukhya* fire onto that layer with four verses beginning with "United" (*samitam*).

It is known: "These two indeed hate each other—the one who is in the *ukhā* and the one who is being piled. The *brahman* is the *yajus*. In that he separates them after having mixed them together, he truly commands them through the *brahman*.

(He recites: "For together with the pure ritual power (*kratu*), the pure *praśāstṛ* has been born; knowing his firm vows, may you grow like branches. Having addressed the two while they are thus mixed, and having lifted the *ukhā* from the sling with the words "As a mother her son," he takes up the sling with a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara: "When his stream was silver... (TS 5.2.10.3–4).

There are three black Nairṛta bricks baked with husks. Taking a sling, a gold thread, and a stool, he goes to the southern intermediate region (the southwest) and, having placed the sling on a self-made salt-flat or a crevice with the mantra, "Homage to thee, O Nirṛti," he lays down the loop [of the sling] over those bricks with the three verses beginning, "Of this thy cruel mouth I offer.
These are laid down facing away, not touching one another, ending toward the south.
He does not perform the *tad-devatā* rite for them.

Thus ends the fifteenth section (kaṇḍikā). "O Goddess Nirṛti, that bond which you have bound... With these words, having covered them with a net of hair-sieve (*śikyajāla*), and having placed the gold-thread (*rukmasūtra*) and the stool (*āsandī*) beyond, [he recites]: "May Nirṛti depart from us; may she leave here nothing at all. We drive away the cattle-less, destructive evil—every bit of it. Away from us the fetters of Nirṛti, the deaths numbering one hundred and one! Away those snares of yours, the deaths numbering one hundred and one, which you cast forth! Those hundred and one snares of yours, O Death, for the slaying of mortals—all those we expiate through the power of the sacrifice."

Having consecrated the fire-altars with these four verses—"I subdue the goddess Nirṛti, taming her as a father does his son with his words; she who knows the head of every being that is born, the wise one beholds each head"—and having sprinkled around it with the verse addressed to Vaiśvānara, "That which is beyond this region," and having worshipped it with "Homage to Bhūti," they return without looking back. It is known from scripture: "They have escaped from the concealment of Nirṛti.
They purify themselves with water using the verse, "May the goddesses be for our aid."

"Carrying strength, wealthy-minded, wise, and full of luster, I approach my home with a joyful heart. With an eye that is not terrible, but auspicious, may I look upon my kin and prolong their lives. May we extend the life of our homes; may our homes extend our life. I enter the homes that are well-disposed, free from harm to heroes, abounding in heroes, and rich in brave sons"—with these words he approaches the house.
"An abode, a gatherer of riches"—with this verse they worship the Āhavanīya or the Gārhapatya fire.
Thus ends the sixteenth section (Kaṇḍikā).
The king undertakes the ritual actions beginning with the sowing of seeds.
Having performed the *prāyaṇīyā* offering, he measures out the altar (*vedi*).
According to the Vājasaneyaka, he releases his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).
The ritual procedure beginning with that [offering] is undertaken from the *dhruva* ladle at the *prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice.
Having performed the *ātithyā*, he measures out the fire-altar.
According to the Vājasaneyaka, he releases his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).

Having brought a clump of green darbha grass together with its roots and having planted it in the middle of the fire, he takes five portions of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle and offers five oblations upon the darbha clump with the verse: "May the year be in harmony with the half-months.
(7) He measures out the fire-altar with a bamboo pole as long as the sacrificer is when his arms are raised:
three [units] towards the east and four towards the north. (8–9)
The wings and the tail are each ten man-lengths;
the body is four man-lengths;
he extends the right wing by one cubit on the south side.

Thus, to the north [the altar] is increased by one span (prādeśa) or a cubit (vitasti); behind it is the tail. The first fire-altar is of one kind, the second of two kinds, and the third of three kinds; they proceed in this very manner up to the one-hundred-and-one-fold altar.

Therefore, one should indeed pile it in sevenfold form; for the original fire-altar is sevenfold, and from that point upward, they increase by one each time—so says the Vājasaneyaka. With the two verses, "O Earth, be pleasant, thornless, and a place of rest; grant us wide protection" and "Thus indeed among the mountains," they step upon the measured fire-altar.
Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā).
"Provide the leather thongs," he issues the command.
1. From the pit, he pours water into the troughs, saying, "The pit whose hollow has been prepared. 2. In those [troughs], they give drink to the oxen. 3.

He extends the pair of ploughs, [using the formulas]: "The incitement, the inner-restraint, their yoke-pole, the ploughshare, the goad, the crossbar, the fastening-strap, and both the two frog-shaped [plough-ends] as the yoke-animals.
With the two verses beginning "They yoke the ploughs," he yokes the plough, which has either six oxen, twelve oxen, or twenty-four oxen.

"Of the two camels, of the two *pilva* trees, and also of the two binding-ropes—we know the name of you all: 'O draft-animals, you who are skilled at drinking the sweet juice. Having consecrated the yoked animals with this, he rises up [with the mantra]: "Winning cattle, winning wealth, winning horses, winning gold, surrounded by pleasant speech—may Savitṛ go over the earth, filling it with a share of vigor on his single-wheeled chariot. With this, he raises the plow.

"Born of Brahman"—this is the verse. "That first [oblation] of yours which they do not obtain, in which they perform their rites—do not deceive us there; I place that before you. "Flow forth well for the winning of booty, overcoming the Vṛtras; you go as a debt-collector to cross over our enemies. "In the thousand-streamed [soma], those honey-tongued and unfailing ones have resounded together in the vault of heaven. "His watchful spies do not close their eyes; at every step there are ensnarers and fetters"—with these words he offers the *brahmavarmāṇi* (armor-of-prayer oblations). 7.
"Thou art named Malimluca, the thirteenth month; thou art Indra's armor, thou art Indra's protection, thou art Indra's shelter; unto thee I resort. Thus ends the eighteenth section.

"I enter the *gāyatrī* with my hair; I enter the *triṣṭubh* with my skin; I enter the *jagatī* with my flesh; I enter the *anuṣṭubh* with my bone; I enter the *paṅkti* with my marrow. May the formidable and thick armor belonging to Indra and Agni, which even the all-gods and the heroes cannot pierce, protect us from all sides. O gods, may we, being long-lived, reach old age. With these words, they step upon the measured fire-altar.
(1) He plows with two verses beginning, "The plow, tipped with iron... (2) The plowmen drive the oxen. (3)
He plows over the head of the question;
saying, "O cow that milks desires, milk out desire," he turns to the right and plows three furrows joined together.
In the middle, there is a gap between them.
From the right wing to the left; from the left to the right. From the southern hip to the northern shoulder; from the northern [hip] to the southern [shoulder]. Or this may be reversed.

"Be unyoked, O inviolable ones, you who go to the gods! We have crossed over the further shore of this darkness; we have reached the light; may we attain prosperity!"—having thus unyoked the oxen on the right shoulder or the left, and having released them toward the north or the east, he gives them to the Adhvaryu.
The Vājasaneyins record that the sacrificial altar (cātvāla) is square, not divided, and consists of sixteen furrows.
He pours out fifteen water-pots: twelve on the ploughed ground and three on the unploughed.
With the fourteen [verses] beginning with "The plants that have been born," he sows the seeds; it has been stated that this is done along every furrow.
Sesame, beans, rice, barley, millet, small grains, wheat, bamboo seeds, wild *śyāmāka*, wild *nīvāra*, wild sesame, and *gavīdhuka*—these are to be known as the wild *markaṭaka* grains.
With *gārmuta* as the seventh, or with *kulattha* as the seventh, there are seven cultivated grains for ploughed land; seven wild grains are for unploughed land. This is the nineteenth section.
If one should not find the specific herb, one should sow barley mixed with honey in its place;
or one should mentally meditate, "Thou art sown by me.
Once the herb has been found, one should tie it onto the first kindling-stick that comes along.

Having bound together as fuel those branches of the trees that bear fruit, he should sprinkle them with water while reciting the four verses beginning, "May he who is the progenitor of the earth not harm us. He collects clods of earth from the various directions—those which have fallen from the interior of the wood-pile to the exterior—and throws them together.
From whichever direction he hates someone who might be there, he should bring a clod from that direction, saying: "I take from here food and strength."
With the formula, "Ghee for the furrows," he touches the spaces between the furrows, or rather, the *uttaravedi*.

He pours out the *uttaravedi* to the same extent as the fire-altar. Having performed the rites up to the sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*), he scatters sand with the six verses beginning, "O Agni, may thy fame and vigor... Then, with the formula, "Ye are piled, ye are piled around," he encloses the site of the *āhavanīya* altar with an unlimited number of pebbles, just as he did for the *gārhapatya*.

With twenty-one [verses] for one desiring cattle; with twenty-seven for one who has rivals; with ten each for one desiring food; with an unlimited number for one desiring the unlimited. It has been stated:
"For whomsoever he should desire, 'May he be without cattle,' for him [he should do so] without counting.
With the verses, "Swell up! Let it come together to thee," he spreads out the sand.
With the following *triṣṭubh* verse, [he should offer] for a *rājanya*:

"The ruddy bull Soma has been pressed; like a king, the wondrous one has bellowed toward the cows. Purifying himself, he goes around the woolen filter to sit upon his ghee-filled womb like a hawk. With a *jagatī* verse, [he should offer] for a *vaiśya*.
Thus ends the twentieth *kaṇḍikā*.
The ritual procedure beginning with the *dhruvā* [offering] for the guest-offering (*ātithyā*) is undertaken.

Having performed the morning rites, he deposits the bricks of the first layer on a red bull’s hide in front of the *prāgvamśa* hall, with the neck pointing eastward and the hair facing upward. Alternatively, he may deposit three *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks and three *viśvajyotis* bricks.

Having sprinkled them with clarified butter using a handful of the tips of *darbha* grass and lifted them up, he issues the command: "Recite for the *cityagni*s as they are being led forth," or simply, "Recite for those being led forth."
When the first [verse] has been recited three times, they proceed forward with the horse leading the way, chanting "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre.
They lead a white horse in front.

Having touched the high altar (uttaravedi) while reciting, "May Prajāpati seat thee; by that deity, like Aṅgiras, sit thou firm," and having taken Agni into himself with the two verses, "I take Agni first" and "The Agni who is ours, O fathers," he touches the self-altar (svayaṃcit) while reciting, "O Agni, those fuel-sticks of thine... 4-6.
The Adhvaryu or the sacrificer piles the fire-altar with bricks.
When piling it himself, he takes the fire into his own self; he does not touch it with the formula for self-piling (svayaṃcit).
Regarding the groups [of bricks], there is a statement concerning their arrangement: "He lays them down facing east," "He lays them down facing west."
"He places one facing east, he places one facing west"—this is a figurative expression regarding the agent's orientation. 10.
A white horse stands to the south. 11.
Having touched it, one should place an *iṣṭakā* (brick) as a stepping-stone within the joint at the northern end of the tail, with the verse: "All have made Indra grow great. 12.
The fire for the ritual service is to the north or behind [the altar].
Reciting "May speech be in my mouth," he murmurs this at every ascent and descent; or he may do so once at the end.
This is the twenty-first section.

Having offered an oblation in the *śālāmukhīya* fire with the verse, "I approach the principles, adoring with the sacred word," he steps toward the east upon the horse with the verse, "Upon all [beings]. Having caused the horse to step upon a bunch of *darbha* grass with his right foot and having turned it clockwise, he causes it to step again with the verse, "When you neighed.
With the formula, "Thou art the back of the waters," he places a lotus leaf face upwards in the horse's footprint and issues the command: "Sing the *nidhana* of the waters."

Having placed a gold disk with a handle on top of a lotus leaf with the verse, "The Brahman was born," and having placed upon it a golden man facing east and lying supine, with his head toward the south, while facing east himself, he gives the command: "Sing the Puruṣasāman. Having touched the man with the verse, "The drop has fallen," and having consecrated him with the three verses beginning, "Homage be to the serpents," he pours butter over the man in the manner of the high altar (uttaravedi) using the five verses beginning, "Make thy body" (kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ); thus it is said that he places two offering-ladles (sruc) [upon him]. 4.

Alternatively, with the formula, "By the brilliance of Agni, I settle thee," he places a ladle made of *kārṣmarya* wood, full of clarified butter, to the south of the man. With the formula, "By the vigor of Indra, I settle thee," he places a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, full of curds, to the north of the man.
He worships the *kārṣmarya* ladle with the verse beginning, "Agni is the head," and the *udumbara* ladle with the verse beginning, "Of the sacrifice... This may also be done in the reverse order.
Some say that he deposits them with two verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhan*) and worships them with two *yajus* formulas.
In this case, having scattered gold like a man [over the earth],

this is the twenty-second section. Having touched the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the formula, "Thou art firm, a supporter, spreading," and having caused a horse to smell it, he places it in the middle of the fire-altar together with an unlearned Brāhmaṇa, using the formula, "May Prajāpati settle thee on the back of the earth," and with the *vyāhṛti*, "Bhūḥ."
Having offered the oblation with the formula, "I offer consciousness," he breathes over the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
An ignorant Brāhmaṇa gives a boon—one, two, or three times.
He lays down the first *svayamātṛṇṇā* while sitting; the second with his arms raised; the third while standing.
He gives the command: "Sing the *sāman* on the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
In the same way, having laid down the second and the third, he gives the command.

If the sacrificer should think, "My rival has surpassed me," he should lift up the brick already laid down toward the east with the formula, "Thou art the wide one" (*prathaḥ asi*). Or, if [he thinks] the other [has surpassed him], he should lift it toward the west with "Thou art the earth" (*pṛthivī asi*). If they are equal, he should shift it with "Thou art the world" (*bhūr asi bhuvanam asi*).
"Thou art brilliance; grant me brilliance," [with these words] he lays down the gold brick (8).
"The earth, the stronghold, with food," [with these words] he lays down the mandala brick (9).

"Thou art *bhūḥ*, the seed of the world; thou art a brick, the heavenly world. With speech I ascend thee. Agni is light, light is Agni. By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm. "Thou art *svāḥ*, the seed of the world; thou art a brick, the heavenly world. With mind I ascend thee. Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya. By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm. These two [formulas] are for the ascending (10).
Thus ends the twenty-third section (kaṇḍikā).

With the two verses beginning "Growing up from joint to joint" (*kāṇḍātkāṇḍāt parohantī*), he places a *dūrveṣṭakā*—a clump of green *dūrvā* grass with its root-clod, its tips uncut—in such a way that its tip reaches the *svayamātṛṇā* brick when it has been laid down.
Having placed pieces of gold on the *prabāhu* brick, he places the *vāmabhṛt* brick with the two verses beginning "Those splendors of yours, O Agni, which are in the sun" (*yāste agne sūrye rucaḥ*).

"Virāj jyotiḥ"—these three are the semen-droppers (*retaḥsic*). Of these, he should place two in the first layer for a youth; all [three] in the middle layer for one of middle age; and one in the first layer and one in the last layer for an old man.
He may place either [of the two] for one whom he hates.
With a *yajus* formula he lays down both this one and that one; with his mind, the middle one.

"May Bṛhaspati settle thee on the back of the earth, the luminous one"—with these words [he lays down] the *viśvajyotis* brick. "Thou art the path of Agni"—with these words [he lays down] two *saṃyānī* bricks.
"Madhu and Mādhava"—these two seasonal bricks have the same deity. He places them in all the seasonal layers using *avakā* plants. According to some, he settles them upon *avakā* plants.
With the two verses beginning "aṣāḍhāsī," he places the aṣāḍhā brick above, marked with a sign [on the upper side].

It has been stated: "For him whom he desires, 'May he become more prosperous,' one should place it for him with the sign on the northern side. Having placed the gharmestakā brick, he places the kulāyinī.
The two mantras for the Pravargya rite are as follows:
[15]. Thus ends the twenty-fourth section.

With the three verses beginning "The winds are honey for the one who follows the Truth" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*), he anoints a tortoise with curds mixed with honey; then, with the verse "May the great Heaven and Earth... (*mahī dyauḥ pṛthivī ca naḥ*), while facing eastward, he places it alive, turned westward, in front of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick. 1.

Having placed [the brick] with the words, "Let the four quarters proceed for the fires," and having covered it all around with *avakā* plants and concealed it with a net, he fixes it in place with pegs and consecrates the deposited brick with the mantra: "Go to the deep waters; let not the sun envelop you, nor Agni Vaiśvānara. Without malevolence, look upon the creatures; may the divine rain attend you. O bull among bricks, lord of the waters, glide through the three oceans to the heavenly worlds.
Go there where the ancients have departed, clothing yourself in the soil (*purīṣa*), each to his own womb. (2)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section (kaṇḍikā).

"O mortar, for indeed you are joined house after house; here, speak most brilliantly, like the drum of the victors. With this verse, he places a four-cornered mortar made of *udumbara* wood, one span in measure, upon the northern shoulder [of the altar].
The pestle is of unlimited size.

And also, O Lord of the Forest, the wind blows around your tip; so, O mortar, press out the Soma for Indra to drink! Having filled it with all kinds of herbs and brought it down, he places it in the middle of the fire-altar with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode across this [world].
He places the pestle with the verse, "That highest step of Viṣṇu.
He places the winnowing basket with the verse, "Or from heaven, O Viṣṇu."

"Stitched by the gods with immortality, the sister has mounted the fire-pan upon the altar. May Agni, who was awakened to truth by the ancient seers, being wise, perform that here. With these words, he fills the pan with clarified butter—either with curds, honey, sand, or all of them combined—and he must not look at it while empty; for if it were empty, it would be pierced by pain.
Then he pours milk into it.
Some prescribe filling [the gaps] after having piled them up;
it has been stated: "If one should desire, 'May he be hungry,' for him [he piles] deficiently.
With the formula, "Thou art firm, thou art the earth," he places [a brick] in the middle of the fire-altar.

"O Earth, sit upon the earth; as a mother upon her mother, as a pleasant one upon the pleasant; the sister has mounted the fire-pan (ukhā) upon the altar. May Agni, who was established here by the ancient seers, the wise one, establish that truth"—with these words he places the mortar, according to the Vājasaneyaka.

With the two verses, "O Agni, yoke those [steeds] which are yours" and "Yoke, O Agni, those who best invoke the gods," having offered oblations into the fire-pan, he throws pieces of gold into the head of the man.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section.
With the verse, "The drop has fallen," he places it in the mouth; or with the verse, "This has come into being for the whole world.
With "For radiance (*ṛc*), thee! he places it on the right corner of the eye; with "For luster (*ruc*), thee! on the left;
with "For brilliance (*dyut*), thee! on the two ears.
With the words "For speech, thee," he [offers] upon the right nostril; with "For light, thee," upon the left. 4.
With the formula "The fuel flows," he fills the human head with curds mixed with honey, using a ladle made of *śṛtātaṅka* wood. 5.
The Vājasaneyins prescribe that for all the animal heads, there should be both the placing of a gold plate and the filling [of the cavities]. 6.

With the verse, "In it the fair-winged one, the honey-maker, nest-builder," he takes the head of a man; with the verse, "The sun is the embryo," he places it in the fire-pan (ukhā) in front, with the chin facing eastward, supine and facing east. Having offered oblations on the two eye-sockets with the half-verses of the hymn, "The bright face of the gods," he places the heads of the sacrificial animals. It has been stated that for one whom he desires, "May he be without cattle," he should place them facing in various directions.
With the verse, "The course of the wind," he places the horse's head in front, facing westward.
With the mantra "ajasram indum" (VS 13.45), he places [the brick] from west to east for Ṛṣabha;
with "varūtrīṃ tvaṣṭuḥ" (VS 13.46), from south to north for Vṛṣṇi;
and with "yo agnir agneḥ" (VS 13.47), from north to south for Vasta.
He worships them with these offerings without interruption:
(13) "Do not harm this biped," for the man; (14) "Do not harm this single-hoofed one," for the horse. (15)
"imaṃ samudram" (RV 10.75.5) belongs to Ṛṣabha; "imām ūrṇāyum" (RV 10.75.8) belongs to Vṛṣṇi;
"ajā hi agne" (RV 6.48.2) belongs to Basta.

If it were for the primary [brick] belonging to Vāyu, one should, after laying down all the *upadhānas* in its place, worship with the *utsargas* of all [the bricks]. Or rather, having laid down each [brick] in its respective place, one worships with the *utsarga* of that very [brick].
It has been stated: "For whomsoever one should desire, 'May his food be less,' for him [one should place the brick] more closely together. 19–21.
With the formula, "Homage be to the serpents," he should place the head of a serpent on the southern shoulder, pointing away from the animal heads.
Or rather, he should merely recite the sacrificial formula (yajus) and not place it there.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section.

Mā is the metre; that is the earth, Agni is the deity; with that Ṛṣi, with that Brahman, with that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras. Pramā is the metre; that is the intermediate space, Vāta is the deity. Pratimā is the metre; that is the sky, Sūrya is the deity. Asrīviś is the metre; those are the quarters, Soma is the deity. Virāj is the metre; that is speech, Varuṇa is the deity. Gāyatrī is the metre; that is the goat, Bṛhaspati is the deity. Triṣṭubh is the metre; that is gold, Indra is the deity.

The Jagatī is the metre; its deity is Prajāpati, the Bull. The Anuṣṭubh is the metre; its deity is Vāyu, Mitra. The Uṣṇih is the metre; its deity is Cakṣus, Pūṣan. The Paṅkti is the metre; its deity is Parjanya, Agriculture. The Bṛhatī is the metre; its deity is Aśva, Parameṣṭhin. With these twelve verses—repeated three times—with "By that seer, by that Brahman, by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras," he piles the form of a man facing westward in front.
With the verse, "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads," the sacrificer worships the brick that has been placed by the Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa.

He lays down the Apasyā bricks: five facing west in the east with the formula, "I settle thee in the impulse of the waters"; five facing north in the south with the formula, "May he sit in the ocean, his seat"; five facing east in the west with the formula, "I settle thee in the seat of the waters"; and five facing south in the north with the formula, "The Gāyatrī metre. This is the twenty-eighth section.

Those gods who have grasped the sacrifice from among the gods—may Gāyatrī, knowing the way, lead them to the heavenly world, milking out immortality. Those who establish the lights, ascending to the world of immortality.

May they go forth, knowing and discerning the sacrifice, to the world of the well-done. Those sacrificial animals which have come together toward the womb of the sacrifice—the seers, the wise ones, discerning the sacrifice, bestow them upon the world of the well-done. That path extended for the journey of the gods, held apart by the meters, goes forth; by it he has ascended to heaven and the intermediate space, taking hold of the sacrifice and the world of the well-done. That sacrifice, with its thousand streams, was fashioned over heaven and earth.
With the formula, "Therefore let the sacrificer go by a path of well-being; from heaven he has ascended to the back," he places five gold bricks in each direction and one in the center.

"To Āyu, Svāhā! To Yoṣkṛta, Svāhā! To Yoṣpatvan, Svāhā! To Viṣṇu, Svāhā! To Bṛhaspati, Svāhā!"—having thus laid down five [bricks], he lays down this one: "Born from the waters and from the essence of the earth, he came into being from Viśvakarman. Tvaṣṭṛ, fashioning his form, entered him; that was the first birth of the Puruṣa, the All. Having laid this down, he says: "Thou art the seat of the Ṛtus; thou art the seat of Truth; thou art the seat of splendor; thou art the seat of luster; thou art the seat of glory; thou art praised. Thou art a foundation; for the sake of the foundation, thee! For the foundations, thee! Sit in the foundations!"

Thou art gain; for the sake of gain, may I obtain thee. Thou art acquisition; for the sake of acquisition, may I acquire thee. Thou art power; for the sake of power, may I be able. Thou art prosperity; for the sake of prosperity, may I prosper. Thou art action; for the sake of action, may I perform it. (2) Thus ends the twenty-ninth section.

Thou art a roar; for the roar thee, for the roars thee; sit in the roar! Protect the kṣatra; swell the kṣatra; quicken the kṣatra; restrain the kṣatra; make firm the kṣatra. Thou art the kṣatra; for the kṣatra thee, for the kṣatras thee; sit in the kṣatra! I settle thee among all earthly things. I settle thee among all atmospheric things. I settle thee among all celestial things. I settle thee among all the gods. I settle thee in all the waters.

I settle you in all plants; I settle you in all trees; I settle you in all directions. Sit in heaven! You are the winner of light, the winner of battles, the winner of much, the winner by conquest, the winner of all, the winner of everything, the ever-conquering, the winner of wealth. You are the radiant one, the widely radiant one, the preeminent radiant one. I settle you, the thunderbolt that slays rivals; I settle you, the thunderbolt that slays the malevolent; I settle you, the thunderbolt that slays the enemy.

I set you down, the thunderbolt that slays the Yātus; I set you down, the thunderbolt that slays the Piśācas; I set you down, the thunderbolt that slays the Rakṣases. I set you down, the Indra-thunderbolt that slays enemies, slays foes, slays rivals, and slays Asuras. You are the one rising up; you are the rising; you are the one about to rise; you are the one treading upon; you are the one treading; you are the treading; you are the one stepping together; you are the stepping together; you are the stepping together; you belong to heaven; you are heaven.

Sit upon the *ṛṣi*, sit upon strength, sit upon fortune, sit upon wealth, sit upon the auspicious, sit upon the earth worthy of sacrifice, sit upon the back of Viṣṇu, sit upon the place of Iḍā, sit upon that which is rich in ghee, sit upon that which is swelling— thus [ends] the thirtieth section.

Sit in the *saṃvatsara*; sit in the *parivatsara*; sit in the *idāvatsara*; sit in the *iduvatsara*; sit in the *vatsara*; sit in the *vatsara*. Sit in one; sit in ten; sit in a hundred; sit in a thousand; sit in ten thousand; sit in a hundred thousand; sit in a million; sit in ten million; sit in a hundred million; sit in a billion; sit in ten billion; sit in a hundred billion; sit in the middle; sit in the lotus; sit at the end; sit in the highest number (*parārdha*). You are swelling; for the swelling one you, for the swelling ones you—sit in the swelling one!

"Thou art *ṛta*; for the sake of *ṛta*, for the sake of the *ṛtas*, sit in *ṛta*. Thou art truth; for the sake of truth, for the sake of the truths, sit in truth. Thou art the junction; for the sake of the junction, for the sake of the junctions, sit in the junctions. Thou art the union; for the sake of the union, for the sake of the unions, sit in the unions. Thou art the attainment; for the sake of the attainment, for the sake of the attainments, sit in the attainments"—with these two sections (*anuvākas*), one should place the *ṛṣi*-bricks with each mantra, using the formulas of placement and the successive turns (*paryāyas*).
Thus ends the thirty-first section (*kaṇḍikā*).

"This one was in front of the earth"—with this [formula], he places fifty *prāṇabhṛt* bricks: ten in each direction, ten transversely, and ten in the middle. Having placed the innermost first, he places the outermost last. "The eastern direction of the directions"—with this [formula], he places fifty *apānabhṛt* bricks in the same manner as the *prāṇabhṛts*. Having placed the outermost first, he places the innermost last.

"Continue the breath from life-force; continue the out-breath from the breath; continue the diffused breath from the out-breath; continue the eye from the diffused breath; continue the ear from the eye; continue the mind from the ear; continue speech from the mind; continue the self from speech; continue the earth from the self; continue the intermediate space from the earth; continue the sky from the intermediate space; continue the world of heaven from the sky—thus are the twelve continuities. 3.

The earth is the barren cow; the new moon is the embryo; the trees are the placenta; Agni is the calf; and the *agnihotra* offering is the colostrum. The intermediate space is the barren cow; Dhātṛ is the embryo; Rudra is the placenta; Vāyu is the calf; and the *gharma* oblation is the colostrum. The sky is the barren cow; thunder is the embryo; the stars are the placenta; Sūrya is the calf; and rain is the colostrum. The *ṛc* is the barren cow; the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* chants are the embryo; the *praiṣas* and *nivids* are the placenta; the sacrifice is the calf; and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇās*) are the colostrum. The people (*viś*) are the barren cow; the nobleman (*rājanya*) is the embryo; the cattle are the placenta; the king is the calf; and the tax (*bali*) is the colostrum. These are the five barren cows.

"O you who are for the sake of wealth, stand firm; you have gone to the path of Agni; I take you with the most brilliant splendor by means of the deities"—having thus filled the *kumbha* and *kumbhī* with water, and having placed them along the furrows starting from the east with the mantra, "You are a shelter (*śarma*), you are a protection (*varma*); at the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I settle you, full of sweetness," he throws two pieces of gold into them with the mantra, "For light, you two. In the same way, the subsequent [pots] are placed along the furrows in each direction with the subsequent mantras. Four are placed in the middle with the mantra, "You are bright, full of vigor; I take you, belonging to Indra, the possessor of power, by means of the deities. (Śulba Sūtra 5–7)

Thus ends the thirty-second section (kaṇḍikā). "You two are the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and you two are the truth (*satya*). At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I set you down, full of sweetness. For the sake of sight, I take you two. "You two are pleasant and victorious. With the deities of all the gods, I take you. You two are slayers of rivals and slayers of enemies. At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I set you down, full of sweetness. For the sake of seed, I take you two. "You two are sovereign lords, full of vigor. With the deities of the Ādityas, the gods, I take you."

You are destroyers of demons and destroyers of enemies; by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I set you down, full of sweetness, for the sake of progeny. You two are supporters of the ruling power (*kṣatra*) and possessors of vigor; with the sacred word (*brahman*) and with the deities, I take you who belong to Mitra and Varuṇa. You are wealth and you are desirable; by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I set you down, full of sweetness, for the sake of splendor. You two dwell in the pen and are established on high; with the sacred word and with the deities, I take you who belong to Bṛhaspati.

"You are the past, you are the future; by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I settle you, full of sweetness. With the formula "For splendor, you two," he performs the taking up, settling, and re-setting of the jar-bricks (kumbheṣṭakā).
He consecrates those that have been laid down with the verse beginning "Golden-colored.
With the formula "Mount to heaven," he places the cooked rice-oblation (caru) of millet for Bṛhaspati in milk in the center of the jar-bricks.

With the verse, "Coming together," and with these two verses, "Golden-hued, he who is golden-appearing, the lord of the waters; he indeed is golden-hued, having sat down from his golden womb, the givers of gold give food to him," one [offers] the *naivāra* (rice) oblation.

"O Agni, the *trivṛt* is your head; that, O Agni, is my head. The *pañcadaśa* are your two arms; those, O Agni, are my two arms. The *saptadaśa* is your body (*ātman*); that, O Agni, is my body. The *ekaviṃśa* are your two thighs; those, O Agni, are my two thighs. The *triṇava* are your two knee-bones (*aṣṭhīvantau*); those, O Agni, are my two knee-bones. The *trayastriṃśa* is your foundation (*pratiṣṭhāna*); that, O Agni, is my foundation. With these [formulas], he places them on the head, the two wings, the middle, or the tail. "O Agni, the *trivṛt* is your head; protect me with it"—thus the sacrificer worships each one while bending down.

Having laid down the *ṛṣabha* brick with the verse "O Agni, you the bull," he covers the remainder with an unlimited number of *lokapṛṇā* bricks using the formula "Fill the space; they are the milkers of the well. (7) He should make all the bricks multicolored. (8) Thus ends the thirty-third section.
The rule for drawing lines is known:
one should place those that turn to the right on the south side; those that turn to the left on the north side; straight lines at the back and in front; and triple-lined ones in the middle.
Having placed gold upon the altar-site, he touches it with the *citiklpti* formula: "The thought and the non-thought... (VS 15.60).

Whatever has been piled by you, O Agni, whatever has been piled for you, whatever was deficient, or whatever was excessive therein—may all the gods, the Aṅgirases, and the Ādityas pile it up; may they fill your layer. Whatever fuel-sticks of yours, O Agni, [are there], [with that] consciousness and lack of consciousness... May we, O Agni, be possessors of wealth, sufficient for the sacrifice and for the sacrificial fee. May the pressing-stone speak over the stalk of Soma; may we serve Indra with the pressed drop. Bestow upon us, O Jātavedas, abundance of wealth, a portion of vigor, full of sweetness and truth.

We establish the sacrifice; we shall press the Soma; by means of the sacrifice, O Śakra, may we serve you. We have heard that you are the lord of riches, O Agni, Lord of Wealth; come among us with abundant food consisting of cattle, horses, and gold. May Heaven milk for you, may the Earth yield her milk; let the serpent glide along with water. With Prajāpati I satisfy myself; my self was empty. To that Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants, and who has entered all beings—to that Rudra, O gods, let there be homage! With these verses, he touches the *svayaṃcit* (self-piled) altar. 4
To the north stands a black horse, or one that is dark-brown;
having sacrificed it and having brought earth from the *cātvāla* pit, he scatters it over the altar with the verse addressed to Vaiśvānara, "Thou art asked about heaven" (*pṛṣṭo divi*).
This constitutes the layer.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth section (kaṇḍikā). That Agni who is within the waters, who is in Vṛtra, who is in man, who is in the stone; he who has entered into all beings—to those Agnis, let this be offered. He who is within Soma, who is within the cows, who has entered into birds, who is in wild beasts; he who has entered into the bipeds and the quadrupeds—to those Agnis, let this be offered. "He is questioned in heaven"—this is the verse. He by whom they equipped the chariot of Indra, he who belongs to Vaiśvānara and to the Viśvedevas.

"May this oblation be offered to those Agnis: to the steadfast Śakra, the overcomer, the invincible; to that Agni whom they call the eater of oblations, whom they call Desire, whom they call the giver and the receiver; to him who is the most divine among the gods, born of ascetic heat—to those Agnis, may this oblation be offered. Having laid down each layer (*citi*), he makes an offering with these six verses beginning, "To the bull-eater, to the cow-eater... (VS 17.80–85). (1) Having laid down each layer, he makes an offering with the verse addressed to Agni, "O Agni, many are [thy abodes]... (VS 17.86), which conceals the dwelling-places. (2) Some say that he should worship [the altar] [with the verse VS 17.87]. (3)
It has been stated: "One should touch the first layer with the Gāyatrī verse addressed to Agni. [The verse is:
"O Agni, being born, bring the gods here for him who has strewn the sacrificial grass."

You are our Hotṛ, worthy of praise. We have approached with a great mind the youngest [Agni], who has shone forth, well-kindled, in his own dwelling—of wondrous luster, between the two wide worlds, well-invoked from every side, facing all directions. Agni, the maker of wisdom, the accomplisher of the sacrifice, the Hotṛ, the most pervasive thought—men choose you alone for the small oblation as they do for the great; none other than you. Like Manu, we establish you; like Manu, we kindle you.

"O Agni, O Aṅgiras, like Manu, sacrifice to the gods for the one who seeks the gods; for Agni, the lord of all people, bestows a prize-winning steed upon the clan. Agni [bestows] wealth that is self-sustaining; may he, being pleased, go toward what is desirable. Bring nourishment to the singers!"—these verses are thus recited. (5) There are six *upasad* days.
(6) For two days at a time, he offers oblations with each individual *upasad* mantra. (7)

He piles the fire-altar with daily attendance for two days; the last layer is the ninth. There are three vows consisting of four oblations each, three consisting of three oblations each, three consisting of two oblations each, and one consisting of a single oblation.
Having performed the afternoon rites and having led the white horse around, they dwell [there]. They dwell.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth section (kaṇḍikā).
Thus ends the sixteenth book (praśna).
On the following day, having performed the morning rites, he piles the second layer (*citi*).

He lays down five *āśvinī* bricks with the formula, "The firm-seated one. Having laid down the five *ṛtavyā* bricks with the formula, "In harmony with the seasons," he subsequently lays down the five *āśvinī* bricks.
Having laid down five *prāṇabhṛt* bricks of the seasons with the formula, "Protect my breath," he lays down five *apasyā* bricks while moving around [the altar] with the formula, "Unfold the waters.
He lays down two *saṃyānī* bricks with the formula, "Thou art the path of Vāyu."
"Śukra and Śuci"—these two seasonal deities share the same deity-form.

"Tryavi the age"—five [bricks] on the southern buttock; "Paṣṭhavād the age"—five on the northern [buttock]; "Basta the age" on the southern shoulder; "Vṛṣṇi the age" on the northern [shoulder]; "Vyāghra the age" on the southern wing; "Siṃha the age" on the northern [wing]. Or rather, this may be reversed. "Puruṣa the age" in the middle. "Viṣṭambha the age"—four age-bricks in front, facing westward. It has been stated: "For one whom he desires, 'May he be without cattle,' for him [he places] the age-bricks."
From the *Ṛṣabha* up to the *Citi*, on the following day,
having performed the morning rites, he piles the third layer (*citi*).

Having touched the *Svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the verse, "O Indra and Agni, [place] this unshaking one," and having caused a horse to smell it, he places it in the middle of the fire-altar together with a Brāhmaṇa who does not know [the ritual], using the formula, "May Viśvakarman seat thee on the back of the atmosphere," and with this *vyāhṛti*, "Bhuvaḥ."
Having offered on the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the formula, "I offer consciousness," he breathes out.
13. With the formula, "Thou art light; grant me light," [he offers] on the gold brick. 14.
With the formula, "Above the sky," [he offers] on the *maṇḍaleṣṭakā* brick. 15.
Here, [the verses] for the two *retaḥsic* bricks are "vi vayaḥ" (16); for the *viśvajyotis* brick, "viśvakarmā tvā sādayatu antarikṣasya pṛṣṭhe jyotiṣmatīm" (17);
and for the two *saṃyānī* bricks, "antarikṣasya yānyasi" (18).
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
"Nabhaḥ" and "Nabhasyaḥ"—these four are the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*), two for each pair, having the same deity.
"Thou art a queen, the eastern quarter"—these five are the directional bricks (*diśyā*): one for each direction and one in the center.

Having placed ten "breath-bearers" (prāṇabhṛt) in front with the formula, "Protect my life," he places thirty-six *bṛhatī* bricks: twelve to the south with "The *mā* metre," twelve behind with "The *pṛthivī* metre," and twelve to the north with "Agni as the deity. He places seven *vālakhilyā* bricks in front facing west with "Thou art the head, the sovereign," and seven behind facing east with "The controller, the sovereign."

"Diagonally for the one you hate; for instigation thee; for the support thee; for the pit thee; for the ocean thee; for the sustainer thee; for wealth thee; for the river thee; for the sea thee; for Sarasvatī thee; for the all-encompassing thee; for well-being thee; for the intermediate space thee"—with these [formulas], he lays twelve *bhūteṣṭakā* bricks.
The altar is completed with the *ṛṣabha* and the others as the final layer.
On the following day, having performed the morning rites, he piles the fourth layer.

Having laid down [the bricks] according to the Brāhmaṇa with these two sections beginning with "Thou art the swift, threefold portion of Agni," he lays down two *saṃyānī* bricks with "Thou art the atmosphere;
for the atmosphere thee," and two *ṛtavyā* bricks with "Saha and Sahasya," having the same deity.
Then he lays down seventeen *sṛṣṭi* bricks with "They praised with one [hymn]."
"This is indeed that which first shone forth"—thus [are] the sixteen dawns (vyuṣṭis).
"The bull and so forth, ending with the altar-mound (cit).
This is the second section (kaṇḍikā).
On the following day, having performed the morning rites, he piles the fifth layer.

He places [the brick] in the east with the verse, "O Agni, drive away our born enemies"; in the west with, "By force, those who are born [enemies]"; in the south with, "The forty-fourfold Stoma"; and in the north with, "The sixteenfold Stoma.
Having spread earth upon the brick, he places the Purīṣavatī brick in the middle of the fire-altar with the formula, "Thou art the earth's soil."
With the formulas "The *chandas* is *eva*, the *chandas* is *varivas*" [he places] forty *virāj* bricks, ten in each direction diagonally.
4. With the formulas "Thou art a ray; for dwelling thee; quicken the dwelling," [he places] the *stomabhāga* bricks, seven in each direction. The remaining ones are in the middle. 5.
With the formulas "Thou art the queen, the eastern quarter," [he places] the five *nākasad* bricks, one in each direction and one in the middle. 6.

Having scattered soil upon them, he places five *coḍā* bricks upon them with the verses beginning, "This one, the golden-haired in front... (VS 15.6–10), while meditating in his mind on someone whom he hates, placing the last one toward the west and facing eastward.

Having touched the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the words, "I set thee down in the seat of Āyu," and having caused a horse to smell it, he places it in the middle of the fire-altar together with an unlearned Brāhmaṇa, using the verse, "May Parameṣṭhin set thee down on the back of heaven," and with this *vyāhṛti*, "Svar. Having offered an oblation on the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the verse, "I offer consciousness" (VS 15.12), and having moved away, he places the *vikarṇī* brick on the northern shoulder of the altar with the verse, "The neighing horse... (VS 15.13).
"Therefore, he places it down with other bricks.
This is the third section (kaṇḍikā).
"Thou art light; may light come to me," [with these words] he places the gold brick (hiraṇyeṣṭakā).
"May the sky be unconquered"—with this [formula], he lays down one brick of the mandala;
here, for the elder, there is one *retaḥsic* brick.
"May Prajāpati settle thee, the luminous one, on the back of the sky"—with this, he lays down the *viśvajyotis* brick.
*Tapaḥ* and *tapasya*: these two are the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavye*), having the same deity (Agni).
"Thou art the one belonging to the gods; thou art the path of the gods to the gods": these two are the *saṃyānī* bricks.

Some authorities prescribe that the *saṃyānī*, the two seasonal bricks, the *viśvajyotis*, the *retahsic*, the golden brick (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*), the circular brick (*maṇḍaleṣṭakā*), the *vikarṇī*, and the *svayamātṛṇṇā* should be laid down in this specific sequence.

Having performed the afternoon rites, he soaks the Udumbara fuel-sticks in clarified butter. On the following day, having performed the forenoon rites, he piles the Yājñasenī layer as the remainder of the fifth layer.

He places three Gāyatrī verses beginning with "Agni is the head" in the east; likewise the next three sets of three verses. Triṣṭubhs in the south; Jagatīs in the west; Anuṣṭubhs in the north; Bṛhatīs, Uṣṇihās, Paṅktis, and Akṣarapaṅktis—these various meters according to the available space. An Aticchandas verse in the middle; Dvipadās at the end.
Except for one desiring cattle, he builds the Gociti altar for one who desires a thousand [cattle].
(11) There are a thousand bricks measuring one foot. (12) He should place them in the first layer, the middle layer, or the topmost layer. (13)
Thus ends the fourth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the anuvāka beginning "O Agni, come to us with cattle," there is a repeated recitation for each mantra. 1.
With the eight mantras beginning "I yoke thee with Indra and Agni, with a companion, as a companion," [he offers] the eight *sayuj* oblations. 2.

"In the red clouds I settle you; in the ruddy clouds I settle you; in the black clouds I settle you; in the blue clouds I settle you; in the white clouds I settle you"—thus [he settles] the five clouds (3).
"Thou art Ambā by name"—thus [he settles] the seven Kṛttikās (4).
"Thou art the wind from the front, the winner of rain"—thus [he settles] the five rain-winning [clouds], moving around them (5).
With the formula "For the water thee," he lays down eight Āditya bricks (6).
With the formulas "For the Ṛc thee" and "For the luster thee," he lays down five Ghee bricks around [the altar] in successive order (7).
According to the Vājasaneyaka, ghee-clods are to be placed intertwined with the Āditya bricks (8).
"Thou art Yaśodā"—five [bricks] for the Yaśodās;
"Thou art the maker of abundance"—five for the Bhūyaskṛts;
"Thou art seated in the waters"—five forms of Agni.
"Upon the earth's wealth I set thee"—these are the five *draviṇodās* (12). "Protect my breath"—these are the six *āyuṣyās* (13).
"O Agni, that which is thy highest heart-name"—this is the *hṛdayam* of Agni (14).

"Yāvā ayāvā"—these are the seven seasonal bricks (15). "O divine brick, giver of life, thou who art near; lie down near me, as a wife lies near her husband. "O divine brick, giver of out-breath, giver of in-breath, giver of diffused breath, giver of sight, giver of hearing, giver of speech, giver of self, giver of earth, giver of mid-air, giver of heaven, giver of light, giver of maidens, giver of abundance, first to be approached, giver of young women, thou who art near; lie down near me, as a wife lies near her husband"—thus there are sixteen "near-lying" bricks (16).
Thus ends the fifth section.
Abhīṣāt, abhiṣavī, abhivayās, ūrdhvavayas, bṛhadvayas, savayas, sahvān, sahamānas, sahasvān, and sahīyān—these are the ten names of Indra.
(1) Agninā viśvāṣāḍ—these are the twenty-two bodies of Indra. (2) Prajāpatiḥ, manasāndhas, acchetas—these are the thirty-three bodies of the sacrifice. (3)
"Thou art luminous, I set thee down"—with these twelve [bricks] he places the luminous ones.
Having first laid down the Paurṇamāsī brick with "Full behind," he then lays down the Nakṣatra bricks to the east, facing westward, not touching one another, with "The Kṛttikās are the lunar mansion.
Having laid down the first, he lays down each subsequent one up to the two Viśākhās.

To the south, he establishes the row beginning with the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, using the formula "That which the gods assigned to thee" (*yatte devā adadhuḥ*). Having placed the *Amāvāsyā* brick behind it, he places the remaining bricks one after another, ending with the *Āpabharaṇī* bricks.
To the north, he establishes the row beginning with the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
Up to the full moon day (paurṇamāsī),
he appends [the formulas] "For radiance thee, for luster thee" to all the Nakṣatra bricks.
Thus ends the sixth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," one places eight *sarit* bricks;
with the verse, "Viśvakarman is the lord of the quarters," five *hiraṇyeṣṭakā* bricks—one in each direction and one in the center.
With the formulas, "For breath thee! For sight thee! and so on, one places four *svayamātṛṇā* bricks in the respective directions.

"O Agni, come for the feast! We choose Agni as our messenger. By Agni is Agni kindled. May Agni strike down the Vṛtras. O Agni, we meditate upon the effective hymn that touches the heavens today, desiring the wealth of the god. These are the forms of the five days. Then he lays down the Vrata-bricks:
"I settle thee with the eastern direction," and so on; he places five bricks in each of the directions and one in the middle.
With the verses, "saṃyac ca pracetāś ca" (VS 34.1–5), which are five addressed to the Viśvedevas, while meditating in his mind upon that which he hates;

and with the Vāmadevya hymn: "kayā naścitra ā bhuvat... (RV 4.31.1), "ūtī sadāvṛdhaḥ sakhā... (RV 4.31.2), "kayā śaciṣṭhayā vṛtā... (RV 4.31.3), "kastvā satyo madānāṃ maṃhiṣṭho matsadandhasaḥ... (RV 4.31.4), "dṛḍhā cidāruje vasu... (RV 4.31.5), "abhī ṣu ṇaḥ sakhīnāmavitā jaritṝṇām... (RV 4.31.6), and "śataṃ bhavāsyūtibhiḥ" (RV 4.31.7). Thus ends the seventh section.
To the south, upon oneself:

"Indra, with the bones of Dadhyañc, irresistible, has grown powerful, fierce, and unconquered"—thus the ten *atiṣakta* verses of the *Atharvaśiras* are found in the eastern half of the head. The extraction (*nirūhaṇa*) of the head is performed there.

"It is not found"—this is another [verse]. "To thee, O Hero, we cry out, like unmilked cows; to the Lord of this moving world, the beholder of heaven, the Lord, O Indra, of that which stands still—the Lord, O Indra, of that which stands still. No other like thee exists, whether celestial or terrestrial; none has been born, nor shall be born. Desiring horses, O Maghavan Indra, and desiring cattle, we invoke thee as those seeking booty. With these words, the *Rathantara* [Sāman] is on the right wing; its completion is within the self (*adhyātman*). Having laid down the first [brick], then the second, and then the *viśayā* [brick].

Half [of the hymn] is for oneself, half on the wing: "For we, the poets, invoke thee for the winning of booty; thee, O Indra, the lord of heroes, do men invoke in battles, thee in the races for the prize. "Thee in the races for the prize. "As such, O wonderful one, wielder of the thunderbolt, boldly grant us [wealth], O great one, being praised, O wielder of the stone! "O great one, being praised, O wielder of the stone! Bestow upon us cattle, horses, and chariots, O Indra; grant us booty as if one who has won in every way. This is the *Bṛhat* [Sāman] on the northern wing.
Its ritual procedure is like that of the *Rathantara*.

Thus ends the eighth section (kaṇḍikā). "Yajñāyajñā vo agnaye... girāgirā ca dakṣase... prapra vayamamṛtaṃ jātavedasaṃ priyam mitraṃ na śaṃsiṣam... priyam mitraṃ na śaṃsiṣam... ūrjo napātaṃ sa hināyamasmayuḥ... dāśema havyadātaye... dāśema havyadātaye... bhuvadvājeṣvavitā bhuvadvṛdhaḥ... uta trātā tanūnām"—this is the *yajñāyajñiya* [sāman] at the tail.
Its ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is like that of the *rathantara*.
Having laid down the Ṛṣabha brick with the verse, "O Agni, you the bull," he lays down the Prājāpatyā brick with the verse, "The image of the year.
Then, with the five Ājyānī verses beginning, "For him who has a hundred weapons, who has a hundred powers," he places one in each direction and one in the middle.
With the four Vajriṇī verses beginning, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt," he, holding a stone in his hand, lays them down in each direction.

"Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra, the protector of our bodies, the watcher against [enemies]. May he who seeks to harm us from above, who would attack us—may he strike this stone!"—thus some recite the fifth [verse] in the middle.
(6) "For the earth thee! For the atmosphere thee! For the sky thee!"—these are the three *lokeṣṭakā* bricks.
(7) "For Agni the Purifying thee! For Agni the Cleansing thee! For Agni the Bright thee!"—these are the three *pāvamānī* bricks. (8)

Thus ends the ninth section (kaṇḍikā). "I settle you with the *ṛc* metre; I settle you with the *vaṣaṭ*-call metre; I settle you with the *hiṅ*-call metre; I settle you with the *prastāva* metre; I settle you with the *pratihāra* metre; I settle you with the *udgītha* metre; I settle you with the *nidhana* metre"—these are the seven *chandasīyā* bricks.
Having first laid down four *rāṣṭrabhṛt* bricks with the formula "O glorious Agni," he lays down the bricks in the form of gold on all sides facing every direction.
"It is said that one lays down the *gāyatrī* in the east.

Now, according to some: "One lays down the *gāyatrī* in the east, the *triṣṭubh* on the south, the *jagatī* in the west, the *anuṣṭubh* on the north, and the *paṅkti* in the middle. With all these [verses], one lays down [the altar] facing in every direction. The *gāyatrī* and the others [beginning with the east] end with the *paṅkti*.
"Agni is the head; of the world; the guardian of the people; thee, O thou of most wonderful renown; O Agni, that horse today"—these [verses] are recited.
With these, including "O Agni, come hither for the feast," he lays down [the brick] facing in all directions.
Some say [he does so] with the *lokapṛṇā* verses.
Or here he should place the *vikarṇī* and the *svayamātṛṇā* bricks.

From the *lokaṃpṛṇā*s up to the end of the layering (the *citi*), he touches the piled fire-altar with two verses: "O Agni, yoke those [horses] which are yours... and "Yoke those who best invoke the gods..."; then, with the formulas beginning "May the Vasus protect you from the east with the Rudras," he sprinkles the piled fire-altar with clarified butter according to their respective marks; in the middle, he does so facing east with the final formula.
Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).

Standing upright, he sprinkles the fire toward each of the directions with a thousand pieces of gold, using the formula "Thou art the measure of a thousand," with two hundred pieces at a time; he uses the final two hundred while facing eastward in the center.
With the formula "O Agni, may these bricks of mine be milch-cows," the sacrificer makes the bricks into milch-cows.

Having touched the fire-altar with the *aiḍikī* verse, the Adhvaryu offers the Śatarudrīya oblation with either a gruel of wild sesame (*jartila*) or a gruel of *gavīdhuka* seeds, or with wild sesame flour mixed with *gavīdhuka* flour, using *kusaya*-grass butter or goat’s milk or doe’s milk; standing facing north on an *arka* leaf, he offers it at the northern corner of the northern wing, at the *vikarṇī* joint, upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, moving around the altar from left to right.

Having divided these Anuvākas beginning with *namaste rudra manyave* into three parts, or alternatively, starting from the first [Anuvāka], while holding [the ladle] at knee-height for the section ending with *namastakṣabhyaḥ*; then starting from *namo rathakārebhyaśca vaḥ* and holding it at navel-height for the section ending with *namaḥ svāyudhāya*; and having offered the remainder while holding it at mouth-height for the sections up to *pragavātānebhyaḥ*, he offers the ten *avatāna* oblations with *sahasrāṇi sahasraśaḥ* and then offers the *anvāroha* oblations. 4.

Holding [the ladle] at the height of the knees while reciting, "Homage to the Rudras who are on earth"; at the height of the navel while reciting, "Homage to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space"; and at the height of the mouth while reciting, "Homage to the Rudras who are in heaven. Having offered these oblations and caused the sacrificer to recite these same formulas, he offers these same oblations in reverse order. Having offered them, he throws a leaf of the *arka* tree into the path of the cattle. If he should hate someone, he should go away toward the north along that person's path and perform the recitation of the Rudra hymns; this is the ritual procedure when one intends to harm the offspring or cattle of another. This is the ritual not connected with a formal sacrifice. Thus ends the eleventh section.
With the verse, "Rudra who is in the fire," he prepares a *gāvīdhuka* pap for Rudra.
By means of this sacrificial formula (*yajus*), he establishes it upon whichever brick he offers the *śatarudrīya* oblation.

Having given a bow with three arrows to a Brāhmaṇa without asking, the sacrificer worships [Rudra] with the verses beginning, "O Rudra, that wealth which is before you," according to their respective characteristics.
Taking a water-pitcher, the Adhvaryu goes around the fire three times from left to right, sprinkling water while reciting, "In the stone is strength.
Having set down the pitcher, he goes back around three times without sprinkling, reciting, "May there be hunger for you in the stone; may pain reach so-and-so whom we hate.
If he should practice sorcery, he should empty the pitcher into either the southern or the northern corner, saying, "Here I cut off the life of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so."
Having tied an *avakā* plant, a reed branch, and a frog together on a long bamboo pole, he drags the fire with seven or eight [verses] beginning with "Thee, O ocean, with the *avakā*" (VS 13.25).
While dragging it, having followed after it and enticed away all the vital breaths of the frog, he throws it onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
With these same verses, he should touch him whom he hates.

He worships with the *pṛṣṭha* chants: with the *gāyatra* from the front; with the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* for the two wings; with the *ṛtusthā* and *yajñāyajñiya* for the tail; with the *vāravantīya* on the southern hip; and with the *vāmadevya* on the northern hip.
On the side-wing (*apipakṣa*), he sings the Sāmans of Prajāpati without their verses, beginning with "Father Mātariśvan. The Hotṛ recites the *ukthya* litany over the piled altar.
When the Hotṛ has ceased his desire [for the recitation], the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite the formula for the milking of the Stotra and Śastra:
"Thou art the praised praise" (*stutasya stutam asi*). At this point, he causes the Pravargya vessel to be removed.
Thus ends the twelfth section.
Having taken five portions into the *juhū* ladle, [he recites] the two verses beginning with "svayaṃ kṛṇvānaḥ":

"Bestowing the *atisarga* upon Mānava, while beholding the straight path, the Maruts took pleasure in this sacrifice—the rain of the gods, the immortal, the light-finder. Turning back in the midst of the world, transforming the progeny and generating diverse forms, may Saṃvatsara, the Supreme Lord who maintains his vows, protect our sacrifice from the eastern region of the mid-air. May Parivatsara grant us offspring, and may Dhātṛ, being well-disposed, grant it to us."

"May the many, diverse, and multiform [waters], united by a single vow, enter into me! Having offered five *anvāroha* oblations and having taken another fivefold portion of clarified butter, he puts on two sandals made of black antelope skin:
one with the formula "For the built one," the southern one; and the other with "For the unbuilt one," the northern one.
The sacrificer does likewise.

"This is the gathering-place of the waters; homage to thy heat and thy flame"—with these two verses he ascends the fire. With the [verses] beginning "I have stepped upon the earth," the sacrificer [ascends].

Having poured [clarified butter] over the fire—either on the high altar (*uttaravedi*) or on the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick—with the five [verses] beginning "To the man-seated one, vaṭ! and with the two [verses] beginning "O gods who belong to the gods," he sprinkles the fire from left to right with curds mixed with honey using a handful of *darbha*-grass. Having made it marked with the pattern of a tortoise, he descends with [the verses] "Giver of out-breath, giver of in-breath. Then, with the two [verses] beginning "Agni with the sharp [flame]," having offered one oblation to Agni Anīkavant, [the rite is completed]. Thus ends the thirteenth section.
Having filled the *sruk* ladle with sixteen portions [of clarified butter], he offers the Vaiśvakarman oblations.
With the two separate hymns, "He who, offering up all these worlds... and "The father of the eye, for he is wise in mind," he makes two offerings.
It is said that for one whom he desires, "May he be released from evil for a long time," he should offer one by one.

If he should find him in water, he should take a handful of water and offer it into the waters with the verse, "To the ocean, the wise one... This is a ritual procedure not connected with a formal sacrifice. 4.

With the verse, "Lead him upward," he places three fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood, soaked in clarified butter, into the fire—one at a time—with three verses; then he leads forward the fire as in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). 5.
Having lifted up the fire with the verse, "Thee, O Viśve Devās," he carries it from the *āgnīdhra* shed with five verses beginning, "The divine five directions. 6.

With the hymn beginning "Swift, sharpening," the Brahman—or the Maitrāvaruṇa or the Pratiprasthātṛ—follows from the south with ten verses. With this [hymn], he should follow one whom he desires to become a ruler when they are girded for battle. When a battle has joined, it should be offered.
The sacrificial wood is made of *taijana* or *māndhuka*; this is a ritual procedure not connected with the sacrifice.

Having placed a stone in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed with the two verses beginning "This celestial chariot stands in the midst of heaven," and having gone as far as the tail [of the altar] with the four verses beginning "The all-people have strengthened Indra," [this concludes] the fourteenth section.

Having ascended the fire-altar with the five verses beginning "Toward the eastern quarter," he offers a ladle made of Udumbara wood, filled with curds, upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the two consecutive verses beginning "Night and Dawn" and "O Agni, thousand-eyed."
With the verse *naktoṣāsā*, he offers an oblation of milk from a black cow that has a white calf;
some say he sprinkles [the altar] with milk.

Having recognized the signal from the Hotṛ with the verse *ūrṇāvantaṃ prathamaḥ sīda yonim*, and having placed the animal-related materials (*saṃbhārāḥ*) there, he establishes the fire upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the three verses beginning *suparṇo 'si garutmān*, and then places a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood upon it with the verse *preddho agne dīdihi puro naḥ*.

With the verse, "We have kindled thee at thy highest birth, O Agni," he offers a fuel-stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood; with the verse, "That wonderful [splendor] of Savitṛ, the most excellent," he offers one of *śamī* wood. Having offered two oblations with the verses, "I offer consciousness, O Agni" and "This horse today, O Agni," and having filled the *sruk* ladle with twelve portions of clarified butter, he offers the *pūrṇāhuti* (full-offering) with the seventy-verse hymn beginning, "Seven are thy fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues."
Meditating with his mind on Agni from the quarters, he thinks, "May he be here for me as I offer this.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.
