Having performed the sprinkling of the altar, he initiates the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of Vaiśvānara.

Having prepared the Veda and strewn grass around the fire, he undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the washing of the hands (pāṇiprakṣālana). (2) The arrangement of the vessels is according to the requirements. (3) At the time of the pouring out of the oblation-materials, having poured out the portion for Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds, he pours out seven portions for the Maruts on seven potsherds each. (4)
They proceed silently.
At the time of the summons, he issues the summons with the exception of the wife.
At the time of taking the clarified butter, he takes it from the *dhruvā* ladle alone.
He proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* waters (8).

At the time of spreading the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), having spread it to the west of the fire, he places the *dhruvā* ladle and the *sruva* spoon down (9). He modifies the mantra to "these two have sat down" (10).

Having set down the Veda, he proceeds with the *sāmidhenī* verses. (11) He does not issue a call (*saṃpraisha*), he does not perform the cleansing (*saṃmarśana*), and he does not offer the *prayāja* oblations.

(12) Having performed the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, having spread an underlayer of ghee in the *juhū* ladle, and having taken a portion of the entire *vaiśvānara* cake, he pours ghee over it twice and calls for the *śrauṣaṭ* response loudly for Vaiśvānara. (13)
He offers the Māruta oblations entirely with low-voiced recitation (upāṃśu). 14.
Sitting down, he offers the Māruta oblations with the seven verses beginning "īdṛṅ cānyādṛṅ ca," pronouncing each group [of verses] with his hand. 15.
According to some, he offers them in the middle of the forest, verse by verse, group by group. 16.
"By means of the Maruts, he encloses Vaiśvānara on all sides," so say some (17).
"Svatavān, Praghāsī, Sāṃtapana, Gṛhamedhī, Krīḍī, and Sākī—these six are traditionally handed down as the Ugiṣī" (18).
"And the Mitās and the Saṃmitās, O [Maruts]"—he appends this phrase everywhere (19).
Thus ends the sixteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

If he should desire, "May the ruling power (*kṣatra*) be more powerful than the common people (*viś*)," he should run through three or four words of the *grāme'nuvākya*, then run through the *araṇye'nuvākya*, and then offer the oblation with the remainder of the *grāme'nuvākya*.
(1) Having offered thus with the first three groups, he should offer with the *araṇye'nuvākya*. (2)
As with the first three groups, so it is with the three subsequent groups.

(3) If he should desire, "May the commoners (viś) be more powerful than the nobility (kṣatra)," then, having offered with the three groups from the beginning as they are recited in the text, he should offer with the *araṇye’nuvākya* after placing six groups within the six intervals between the words of the *araṇye’nuvākya*.
(4) As with the first three, so it is with the three subsequent groups. (5)

He does not give the summons, he does not wipe [the ladle], and he does not offer the after-offerings (anūyājas). If one should desire of someone, "May I strike his ruling power (kṣatra) with his own ruling power; may he be displaced from his own abode," then for him, one should break a part of the chariot-stand (rathavāhana) that stands nearest the fire with a verse recited in the forest. This is a ritual procedure (kalpa) unconnected with the sacrifice. Having offered four spoonfuls with the mantra, "O Agni and Viṣṇu, being of one accord," he takes a ladle made of Udumbara wood, one fathom in length, smeared with clay, provided with a spout at the back, and fills it with ghee. Then, with the formula, "Strength for me, impulsion for me," he offers a continuous stream of wealth (vasordhārā) until the conclusion of the mantra.

If one should desire, "May I cut off his vital breaths and his food," it is said that he should do so by taking separate mouthfuls for him. Whatever clarified butter remains, having cooked a *brahmaudana* (Brahman’s rice) in it, he should feed four Brāhmaṇas; or, having cooked four *śarāva*-measures of rice, he should feed them with that as their condiment. To those who have eaten, he should give four milch-cows.
"From the ocean comes the wave"—these are three verses. (12) Thus ends the seventeenth section.

The gods found the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) placed in three ways within the cow, hidden by the Paṇis. Indra produced one part, Sūrya produced one, and from Vena they fashioned one by their own inherent power (*svadhā*). These flow from the ocean of the heart, moving in a hundred channels, not to be perceived by the enemy. I gaze upon the streams of clarified butter; the golden reed stands in their midst. Like rivers, the milk-streams flow together, being purified within the heart by the mind.

These surges of clarified butter flow forth like deer fleeing from a swift bowman; like the rapid currents of a river on its course, the mighty streams, overtaking the wind, fly along. The streams of clarified butter, like a ruddy steed, break through the barriers, swelling with their waves. Like beautiful women smiling as they go to a gathering, they hasten toward Agni. The streams of clarified butter reach the fuel; finding them pleasing, Jātavedas desires them.

Like a maiden going to her wedding, I gaze upon you as you are being anointed with ointments. Where the Soma is pressed, where the sacrifice is performed—there the streams of clarified butter flow toward it. Flow toward our excellent praise in the contest for cattle; bestow auspicious riches upon us. Lead this sacrifice of ours to the gods; the streams of clarified butter flow sweetly. Upon your foundation the entire world is supported: within the ocean, within the heart, and within all life.

"In the encounter, in the battle, may we obtain that wave of yours which is rich in sweetness, when it has been offered or is being offered"—with these words, the sacrificer recites the consecratory formula over the oblation.
Thus ends the eighteenth section.
He offers the *vājaprasavīya* oblations.
There are seven cultivated plants and seven wild plants.

Having liquefied these separate foods, he offers the cultivated ones with a dipping-spoon (*sruva*) made of *udumbara* wood, reciting, "The impulse of strength has impelled this," and then he offers the wild ones.
After each offering, he pours the residue into a vessel.

Having established an Audumbara stool facing south, and having spread upon it a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair upward, he sprinkles the sacrificer seated thereon while he maintains contact with the fire by means of the remnants of the oblations.
(5) A tiger skin for a Kṣatriya; a goat skin for a Vaiśya; a black antelope skin for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
(6) Some say a goat skin for one desiring prosperity (*puṣṭi*). (7)

Having recited "Thee for the God," he says, "I consecrate thee with the sovereignty of Agni"—this is for a Brāhmaṇa. "With the sovereignty of Indra"—this is for a Rājanya. "With the sovereignty of Bṛhaspati"—this is for a Vaiśya.
Some prescribe a reversal of these mantras for the Rājanya and the Vaiśya.
Standing facing west, he sprinkles him who is seated facing east from the top of his head, and lets the water flow down over his face.
Regarding this they say: "One must certainly offer; for one who has performed the consecration does not descend [from his status] toward anyone.
Having offered with the milk of a black cow that has a white calf with the verse, "Night and Dawn," he offers the twelve *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations in six turns.
Thus ends the nineteenth section.
Having recited the section beginning with "ṛtāṣāḍ ṛtadhāmā," he offers the first oblation with the formula "svāhā to him. With the formula "svāhā to them," he offers the subsequent one.
In this same manner, he distributes the other sections.
The thirteenth [oblation] among the seven oblations of the sections is that of the section beginning with "bhuvanasya pate."
By this, the rite with the verse "O Lord of the world" (bhuvanasya pata) is explained: he offers five oblations at the front of the chariot, or ten;
according to some, he offers over the head of the chariot while it is being held above the Āhavanīya fire.
Having lifted up the *abhihuta* [oblation], they carry it to the residence of the *adhvaryu*.
They lead forward three horses, or four. He gives them, together with the chariot, to the *adhvaryu*.
"Vaḍabā," say some; "vaḍabe," say others.

(10) With the mantra, "Thou art the ocean, full of wind," he offers three oblations of the names of the wind with his joined palms. (11) For it is known that there is no cutting off of portions for this [wind]. (12)
Some say that one offers the wind-oblation with a fold of a black antelope skin.

Having offered five oblations of clarified butter with the verses, "O Agni, from the ocean... your arrow named Yuvan," he offers six serpent-oblations of curds mixed with honey, moving around the fire clockwise, with the verse, "Thou art the converging one, the eastern quarter.
He offers the six great oblations with the verse, "The weapons are thy name," in the same manner as the serpent-oblations.
"O golden cauldron, svāhā!"—with this, he offers five *arka* oblations (16).

"Those splendors of yours, O Agni, which are in the sun"—with these, he offers three *ruc* oblations (17). He then commences the ritual pertaining to the Soma sacrifice, beginning with the strewing of the sacrificial altar (18).
Having performed that which is prior to the pouring of the hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*), [he does so] according to the twentieth section (Kaṇḍikā 20).
With the anuvāka beginning "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations" (*mamāgne varco vihaveṣvastu*), he piles the hearths with bricks, using each mantra for each brick.
He places nine stones on the Āgnīdhrīya hearth;
twelve, sixteen, twenty-one, or twenty-four on the Hotṛ’s hearth; eleven on the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s hearth; six on the Mārjālīya hearth;
and it is known that he places eight stones each on the other Dhiṣṇiya hearths.
The hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*) are either square or circular;
for each of them, there are as many pebbles (*śarkarā*) surrounding it as there are bricks.

"For thy glory the mountain opened wide; when thou, O Aṅgiras, didst release the herd of cattle. With Indra as thy ally, O Bṛhaspati, thou didst unbind the ocean that was encompassed by darkness. O Bṛhaspati, [overcome] whatever the enemy deserves."

"Bṛhaspati has won all treasures; this god [has won] great stalls full of cattle. Desiring to win the waters, confident in the light of heaven, Bṛhaspati slays the enemy with his hymns"—these three [verses] are for the seat of the Brahman priest. 7.

Yama has supported the earth; Yama has supported this entire world. To Yama belongs all that stands here, and all that breathes, protected by Vāyu. As are the five, as are the six, as are the fifteen seers—whosoever knows Yama, he shall speak as the one seer understands. With the *trikadruka* verses he falls; the six wide ones, this one great [hymn], the *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, and all the meters—all these are placed in Yama. Thus [one recites] three times at the *mārjālīya* fire-altar. This is the twenty-first section.

"Be gracious to us, O Rudra; grant us happiness. May we obtain your benevolence through sacrifice to the gods, O bounteous Rudra, ruler of heroes. Approaching us with goodwill, come to our people; with our heroes unharmed, let us offer the oblation to you. We invoke for our protection the fierce Rudra, the accomplisher of sacrifice, the swift one, the seer. May he cast far away from us ill-will and anger; we choose his benevolence. Thus [he recites] three verses at the *catvāla*.

"Make the oblation pleasing; mix the oblation; cook the oblation; bake the oblation; you are the oblation; for the oblation you, for the oblations you, sit in the oblation"—these eight [verses] are at the *śāmitra* fire. "May your heat descend," "Up the highest," and "I entreat you for that"—these three are at the *avabhṛtha* bath.
They move about during those [rites].

The *khaṇḍāḥ*, *kṛṣṇāḥ*, and *lakṣmaṇāḥ* [trees] he throws aside. Having split those that remain, he performs whatever was previously done prior to the measuring out of the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*). Then he measures out either a single post or eleven posts.
Of these, on the day before [the sacrifice], he [measures] the one standing near the fire (*agniṣṭha*); here itself he [measures] the others; or else, on the following day.

He dedicates the animals of the *vaikādaśina* group at a single sacrificial post. He offers the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice; he subsequently offers the eight oblations of the Devasū.
However, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* portions are common [to all].
Thus ends the twenty-second section (kaṇḍikā).
Before the Prātaranuvāka, he yokes the fire while touching it with the three verses beginning "I yoke Agni. 1.

If a former rival should be threatening him, he should place eight Gāyatrī verses before the Bahiṣpavamāna; eleven Triṣṭubh verses before the Mādhyandina [Pavamāna]; and twelve Jagatī verses before the Ārbhava [Pavamāna]. 2.

Or else, there is another [procedure] which is the reverse of this. They are placed above the *pavamāna* chants. At the time for the animal sacrifice, he dedicates the *savanīya* animal to Agni, or the eleven [animals].

At the time for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he looks at a golden vessel filled with honey, weighing one hundred *mānas*, prepared and decorated with the verse "The bright [face] of the gods" (*citraṃ devānām*), causes a horse to smell it, and gives it to the Brahman priest.
He gives auspicious sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) to the *adhvaryu*.
If he piles the fire-altar for him, when the *yajñāyajñīya* hymn has been commenced with one verse, he touches the fire-altar with two verses, "Homage be to thee;
do not harm me," and then offers eleven *samiṣṭayajus* oblations.

Having offered the nine oblations pertaining to the sacrifice, he offers the tenth and eleventh with the formula, "The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus. (9) When the omentum of the *anūbandhya* cow has been offered, having filled a ladle made of *udumbara* wood with clarified butter, he offers the oblation for the release of Agni with the verse, "Suck this breast, full of strength, of the waters. (10) When the offering of parched barley flour has been performed, having offered the ten *ākūti* oblations with the formula beginning "From what intention," he descends [from the sacrificial ground] and worships [Agni] with the verse, "Mind has returned, life has returned; breath has returned, intention has returned. Vaiśvānara, increasing with his rays, stands within as the guardian of immortality. (11)
With the verses beginning "The fires that belong to the soil," the sacrificer, when about to depart, worships the fire with the *āpti* formulas.
Thus ends the twenty-third section.
Having seen the fires of others, having piled the fire-altar, and having performed the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, he should also offer a curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. 1.

For one year, he should not descend [to a lower level] toward anyone, nor should he approach women; he should not eat birds. For as long as he lives, he should not eat the brain, nor should he run while it is raining.
If he runs, he should turn back.

Having piled the second [fire-altar], he should not approach another woman. Having piled the third, he should not approach any woman at all, nor even his own wife. If, after piling the fire-altar, one should fail to achieve success within this year, he may, when undertaking a sacrificial session (*kratu*), pile it with a single layer (*ekacitīka*). With the eight mantras beginning "For the sake of the waters" (*salilāya tvā*), he should place them on the high altar (*uttaravedi*) using separate formulas. Then follow the *lokapṛṇā* bricks as required, and then the loose earth (*purīṣa*).
Now, he who might not find firm support should, while undertaking a sacrificial rite (*kratu*), pile up [the altar] in a single layer (*ekacitīka*).
He should place five bricks with distinct formulas on the *uttaravedi*, namely "saṃyac" and "pravetā. The *lokapṛṇā* bricks are placed according to their purpose, and then the loose earth (*purīṣa*).
Some authorities record the two desires (*kāma*) in reverse order.

Furthermore, the *cit* is heard of in three senses: for the purpose of hearing (*śravaṇa*), for the purpose of prosperity (*samṛddhi*), or for the purpose of continuity (*saṃtāna*). We shall explain [the *cit*] for the purpose of hearing.
"If one sacrifices with an *iṣṭi*, or with an animal sacrifice, or with Soma"—having caused that fire of his which was previously [there] to settle down, he should sacrifice.

Alternatively, one should place eight bricks with the mantras beginning "yenarṣayaḥ" on the *uttaravedi*; then the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks according to their respective places, and then the loose earth (*purīṣa*). This is the twenty-fourth section. Alternatively, while the fire is being held over the *uttaravedi*, one should touch the *uttaravedi* with the formula: "May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm."
Alternatively, there may be three *svayamātṛṇā* bricks;
the rule for their placement is as follows:
one *svayamātṛṇā* brick has a *sāman*-verse as its *purīṣa*; the second is prepared in the same manner; the third is without *purīṣa*.
Alternatively, there are three *svayamātṛṇā* bricks and three *viśvajyotis* bricks.
5. The procedure for their laying out is as follows: 6.

The *svayamātṛṇā* is the *sāmapurīṣa*, and then the *viśvajyotis*. Thus is the second [set] prescribed. In the third [set], however, the *viśvajyotis* is first, then the *svayamātṛṇā*, and then the *sāmapurīṣa*. 7.
Or else, there are eight *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks and a layer of loose earth (*purīṣa*). Or eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks and a layer of loose earth. Or twelve *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks and a layer of loose earth.
(8) Having piled the fire-altar, he who would sacrifice with Soma should pile these thirty-one *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks upon the high altar (*uttaravedi*) and then sacrifice.

(9) But one piling [the altar] for the sake of prosperity should, in the second layer, place eight bricks with the formulas beginning "By whom the seers... (*yenarṣayaḥ*), each with its own mantra, upon the high altar; then eight *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks, and then a layer of loose earth. (10)

On the next day, he should place these same various bricks and eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks, and then the *purīṣa* (filling soil). 11. On the next day, he should place these same various bricks and twelve *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks, and then the *purīṣa*. 12.

But when building the third layer for the sake of continuity, one who builds the third layer should place eight bricks with the various mantras beginning with “yenarṣayaḥ” on the *uttaravedi*, the *lokaṃpṛṇā*s according to their respective places, and then the *purīṣa*. 13.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth section. Now, moreover, they say: "It should not be piled. For it has been said, "This Agni is indeed Rudra. The "piled according to the meters" refers to the optional rites; these have been enumerated in the *Śulbasūtra*.

The consecrations (*dīkṣā*) last for a year while the fire is being heated; the *upasad* rites last for a year. Prior to the *upasad* rites, he offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni; thus, for four months at a time, he offers with each *upasad* mantra for four months.
Following the *upasad* rites, he piles the fire-altar (*agni*).
Two months for each layer; four [layers] at the end.

For three months each, the observances consist of the four-breasted, three-breasted, two-breasted, and one-breasted [forms]. He remains for a year performing the laying down of the bricks with the *ṛṣis* and the *āgneya* [verses].

It is understood that this altar of Yājñasenī belongs to the seers and is dedicated to Agni (9). Or rather, one should lay it down with those hymns addressed to Agni which occur in the ten Maṇḍalas (10).
The bricks are of various mantras, equal in number to the hymns; the Lokampṛṇā bricks are according to their purpose, and then the loose soil (11).
In the third year, he should sacrifice with either the Abhijit or the Viśvajit. He gives away his entire property (*sarvavedasa*).

Having moved out [of the sacrificial ground], he puts on a red cow-hide with the hair outside—along with its ears, tail, and hooves, or including the dewclaws—and having wrapped his head from left to right with a turban, he takes up a cup made of *udumbara* wood. He also takes up a wooden scraper (*abhri*) made of *udumbara* or bamboo, variegated and of the same dimensions as before.

For three nights, staying in a wild fig tree (*audumbara*) forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, they live by means of a digging-stick. Having dug up a root, they place it in this vessel and both take it from one another—the wife and the sacrificer. They do not drink from an earthenware vessel.
The sacrificer may desire to eat [the food] with a *samūhaka* or a *khanātaka* [spoon]; the wife, according to some, with an *upavīkṣāya* or an *upavikṛnta*.
He shall dwell for three nights among Niṣādas; for three nights among Vaiśyas; for three nights among Rājanyas; or for three nights each among Brāhmaṇas.
He shall not beg for a year; nor shall he refuse what is being given. If [he cannot obtain food] for a year, [he may do so] for twelve days at a time.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter.
In autumn, a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya desiring prosperity should sacrifice with the Vājapeya. 1.
Some recite [the ritual] as if it were permanent;
he attains Prajāpati;
its ritual procedure is like that of the sixteen-fold [Soma sacrifice].
Everything is seventeenfold:
there are seventeen initiations (dīkṣās), three Upasad days, and the Soma-pressing on the twenty-first day.
Or else, there are thirteen initiations, three Upasad days, and the Soma-pressing on the seventeenth day.
The sacrificial post is made of Bilva or Khadira wood, seventeen cubits long, hornless, and four-cornered; its top-ring (caṣāla) is made of wheat flour or a braid of wheat. 8.
When that which precedes the Upasad rites has been performed, the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the Surā according to the ritual procedure for Surā. 9. It becomes a *parisrut* [fermented liquor]. 10.
At the time for preparing the *khara* mounds, the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares a second *khara* below and behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart for the sake of the *surā* cups (11).
At the time for the girdles, he encircles the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with seventeen cloths (12).
At the time for arranging the vessels, having set out the vessel for the *atigrāhya* cup dedicated to Indra, he sets out five *atigrāhya* vessels for Indra in its vicinity (13).
The ritual procedure for these has been explained previously. 14.
Having employed the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, he employs seventeen *prājāpatya* Soma-cups near it. 15.
The ritual procedure for these is like that of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. 16.
At the next pressing, the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares seventeen earthen vessels for the cups of *surā*.
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
At the time of the drawing of the cups, having drawn the *atigrāhya* cup for Indra, he draws five *atigrāhya* cups for Indra with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; thee, the man-seated. 1.
The ritual procedure for these is as before.

Having drawn the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, he draws seventeen Soma cups for Prajāpati with the verse, "When he, bestowing his works, came into existence... (RV 10.54.3). The ritual procedure for these is like that of the *ṣoḍaśin*.
At the second pitch, beginning with the verse "kuvidaṅga," the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the cups of *surā* with seventeen *upayāma* formulas.
Some authorities prescribe that the two methods of drawing the cups are reversed.
He draws the *surā* cups in an interlocking manner with the *soma* cups.
The Adhvaryu draws first; the Pratiprasthātṛ follows later. He places the Soma cups in front of the axle and the Surā cups behind the axle.
At each pressing, beginning with the Savana, he offers oblations with the mantra "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]," or he offers them at the commencement of each ritual act.
On the day of the Sutyā, the priests wearing golden garlands perform the rites.
At the time for the animal sacrifices, having dedicated three *kratupaśu* animals, he dedicates a barren cow to the Maruts and a ewe to Sarasvatī that has no missing teeth.
Having dedicated the ram to Sarasvatī, he dedicates seventeen animals to Prajāpati—black, hornless, and uniform in appearance.
They immolate the animals that have been carried around the fire, ending with those dedicated to Sarasvatī, as prescribed previously;
they hold back those beginning with the ones dedicated to Sarasvatī for the subsequent rites.
It has been stated that there are two blades of sacrificial grass (barhis) for each animal.

Having performed the rites prior to the offering to Mahendra, and having set aside the midday *puroḍāśas*, he sets aside the *paśu-puroḍāśa* for Sarasvatī, and then offers the *naivāra* (millet) *caru* for Bṛhaspati in seventeen *śarāva* measures. He offers twelve portions with a mantra; the others are offered silently.
He cooks it in milk.
Having offered the two *dākṣiṇa* oblations...
Thus ends the second section (kaṇḍikā).

Having brought down the chariot with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt," they cause the horses to enter the water and bathe them in the water. With the formula, "O Son of the Waters," he wipes the forehead-ornaments.

With the formula, "Either Vāyu shall yoke thee, or Manu shall yoke thee," he yokes the chariot drawn by a team of four horses. He yokes the other sixteen chariots silently. At the time of the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā), he bestows seventeen chariots; seventeen garments, seventeen horses, seventeen elephants, seventeen gold neck-ornaments (niṣkas), seventeen female slaves, seventeen goats, seventeen ewes, seventeen garments, and seventeen hundred cows.

Now, according to some: he gives seventeen hundred cows; seventeen yoked chariots, seventeen horse-chariots, seventeen elephants, seventeen gold neck-ornaments (*niṣkas*), seventeen female slaves, and seventeen drums. This is the Vājapeya sacrifice as performed by the Āptas. Now follows the Kuru-Vājapeya.
He gives seventeen birds of each age;
the birds range from one year old up to five years old.
When the sacrificial gifts have been assigned, he gives to the Adhvaryu the one yoked with a Yajus formula.
The remainder is common [to all]. 11.
In front of the Āhavanīya fire, they station chariots facing either north or east. 12.
Among them, the one on the south is the "yoked by sacrificial formula" (yajuryukta). 13.
The prince, having stationed himself in front of the Āgnīdhra shed, shoots seventeen arrows.
Where the last one falls, there he fixes a post of Udumbara wood as a marker.
Thus ends the third Kaṇḍikā.
Having performed the rites prior to the offering to Mahendra, he brings clarified butter to the *naivāra* grain and places it in the *cātvāla* pit.
1. A prince guards it. 2. Having fixed a piece of wood shaped like a chariot axle into the *cātvāla*, he fastens a seventeen-spoked chariot wheel made of *udumbara* wood upon it. 3.
On the northern corner of the altar, they tie seventeen drums.
With the words, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," the sacrificer approaches the chariot.
With the words, "The two hooks, the two descending hooks," he touches the two wheels of the chariot, or its two side-pieces.
"Speak words for Indra!"—thus they cause the drums to resound.
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize, may I win the prize"—with these words, the Brahman ascends the chariot wheel made of Udumbara wood.
He says to him: "Sing the Sāman of the prize-winners."
He causes the wheel to revolve three times clockwise. While it is revolving, Brahmā sings:
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I ascend the highest firmament through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize. Thereupon, the sacrificer mounts [the chariot] which is yoked by the Yajus formula.

"O seekers of the prize, you who are swift, having won the prize and about to run for the prize, about to win the prize—smell the portion of Bṛhaspati! With these words, he causes the two horses yoked to the poles to smell the *naivāra* (wild rice) offering. Or, [he says], "Smear yourselves with the portion of Bṛhaspati," and he wipes away the remnants from all their nostrils.
Taking the horse-whip, the Adhvaryu mounts the chariot yoked with a sacrificial formula, saying, "Thou art a steed; thou art the seven-stepper," and with that whip he strokes the horses together.
(16) The other chariots follow behind without placing [the whip] down. (17) He consecrates the running horses with the four verses beginning, "O prize-winners, run for the prize. (18)
With the verse, "Agni with one syllable," he causes the sacrificer to recite the *ujjitī* formulas while they are running.
(19) Having reached the mark, they turn toward the north and then turn clockwise.
(20) With the four verses beginning, "O swift runner," he consecrates them as they run back. (21)
Thus ends the fourth section (kaṇḍikā).

Having offered the oblation with the verse, "May the impulse of strength come to me," when the drums have been struck, he causes [the sacrificer] to smell the *naivāra* rice again. With the words, "Having run together," he wipes away the remnants of the grease.
With the words, "This was that true compact of yours," he performs the oblation for the release of the drums.
He touches the water for purification three times;
he gives a *kṛṣṇala* weight [of gold] to each of the *vājasṛt* priests.
Having taken those back, he gives them to the *brahman*. And he gives a golden honey-spoon made from a *śatamāna* weight of gold.
Here he introduces the hymn for Mahendra.
While it has not yet been chanted, the sacrificer puts on a garment of silk (tārpya) with the formula, "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatra.
The wife puts on one made of darbha grass with the formula, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra."
Thinking, "My husband will come," the sacrificer addresses his wife: (9) "Let us two ascend! she replies.
He addresses her three times; she replies three times. (10–11)
"I shall not ascend to the heavenly world for both," [thinking thus] the sacrificer, at the end,

having offered the twelve *vājaprasavīya* oblations with "Vāja and Prasava," ascends the sacrificial post by means of a ladder with the ten formulas beginning with "May life be fashioned by the sacrifice.
Having reached the top, he mutters, "We have gone to the heavenly world, O gods."
"May I be united with my offspring; may my offspring be united with me," he says while looking toward the house.

(15) Then the Vaiśyas present him with baskets made of *aśvattha* wood—either filled with *āsa* grass, or filled with *ūṣa* grass, or both—toward each of the four directions. Or else, the *mahartvijas*, having tied them to long poles, present them.

(16) "For food, thee!"—thus the Adhvaryu from the east. "For the eating of food, thee!"—thus the Brahman from the south. "For strength, thee!"—thus the Hotṛ from the west. "For the winning of strength, thee!"—thus the Udgātṛ from the north. (17)
They strike him from the front (18).
He turns back against the one who strikes him (19).
"This [is] for you, O King, for friendship, for restraint, for support, for cultivation, for security, for wealth, for prosperity," with these words he descends (20).
Having spread a goat-skin with its neck pointing eastward and the hairy side upward in front of the sacrificial post—
thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā)—
the sacrificer, having placed a piece of gold weighing one hundred mānas upon it, sets his right foot upon the gold with the formula, "Thou art immortality. 1.
"Thou art nourishment, thou art procreation"—with these words, he places the left [foot] upon the goat-skin;
therefore, he ascends the throne-seat.
"Ascend the wide-based throne-seat; having ascended it, look out over the single-minded men"—with this he addresses him as he is ascending.
With seven [verses], he offers seven prior *annahoma* oblations. 5.
He is consecrated at the *māhendra* stotra, as in the *agnicityā*. 6.
In the middle *ukthya-paryāya* of the midday pressing, when the *brahmasāman* has been introduced, they immolate here the subsequent animals beginning with the one for Sarasvatī. 7.
He proceeds with their omenta without having first basted them.
(8) Having proceeded with the omentum of the Sarasvatī animal, he takes portions from the other animals and proceeds with their omenta.
(9) Having proceeded with the sacrificial cake of the Sarasvatī animal, he proceeds with the one made of *nīvāra* grain. (10)

The *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* portions are common [to all]. (11) The great officiating priests (*mahartvij*) become entitled to eat the remnants of the sacrificial oblation (*havirucchiṣṭa*). (12) They consume the remains of the oblation at the *āgnīdhra* shed. (13)

14. Here, he proceeds with the deities up to the Sārasvata [offering] according to the sequence of the *saṃvāda* (dialogue) up to the *iḍā*. Or, at the proper time, having performed the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice and having drawn the cups beginning with the *hotṛ-camasa*, he introduces the *bṛhat* stotra.
15. At the time of the performance, the Adhvaryu takes the *hotṛ-camasa*; the Camasādhvaryus take the other cups; and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) take the other Soma vessels. 16.
The Pratiprasthātṛ takes the principal *surā* cups; the Vājasṛt takes the other *surā* cups.

This is the sixth section (*kaṇḍikā*). "You are united; unite me with prosperity," saying this, the Adhvaryu hastens forward with the Soma cups. "You are separated; separate me from evil," saying this, the Pratiprasthātṛ hastens backward with the *surā* cups.
They stand by the Āhavanīya fire with the Soma-cups; they stand by the Mārjālīya fire with the Surā-cups.
He proceeds with the Soma-cups.
At the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls, they shake the Surā-cups after [the Soma-cups].
The consumption of the Soma has been explained.
[With the words] "of the Virāj metre," he modifies the consumption mantra.
They present the portions to be cut from the Māruta offering and the Soma cups to the officiating priests; and the portions not to be cut and the Surā cups to the Vājasṛt priests.
Having crushed them on the southern corner of the altar (vedi-śroṇī), they consume them. 8.
The prince, the protector of the *kakud*, or the protector of the *naivāra* grains, should eat [the *kakud*]; or else, the entire *kakud* is [eaten] after all the *soma* offerings.
9. At this point, he proceeds with the deities beginning with Sarasvatī. 10.
"It is known that they proceed with the sacrifice in the sacrificial forest (yajñāraṇya).

At the point where the after-offerings (anūyāja) have been performed and the offering-spoons (sruk) have not yet been separated, they should proceed with these [formulas]. However, one should not do it in that way. "For the sacrifice falters when they act in this manner.

Therefore, at whatever point they proceed with the omenta (vapā) of the former [animals], there they should proceed with the others; and at whatever point they proceed with the oblations (havis) of the former, there they should proceed with the oblations of the others.
The Vājapeya sacrifice is concluded. 14 Having sacrificed with it, one should perform the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, or with curdled milk (āmikṣā) for Mitra and Varuṇa.
15 For as long as he lives, he should not descend [from his high status] toward anyone. 16
Or he should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava or the Pratyavarohaṇīya;
it is known from tradition that [the sacrificer] becomes one who possesses a white umbrella.
Thus ends the seventh section.
A king desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Rājasūya;
the sacrificial fee is one hundred thousand [cows];
the first day is an Agniṣṭoma consisting of five concluding rites (apavarga).
He gives five thousand [cows] at the Pavitra; thirty at the Abhiṣecanīya; thirty at the Daśapeya; ten at the Keśavapanīya; twenty at the Vyuṣṭidvirātra; and five at the Kṣatrasya Dhṛti.
Or rather, there are four at the Abhiṣecanīya; the other days consist of thousands each.
"The Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa states: 'He gives thirty-six thousand [cows].
(7) Likewise, he should lead the sacrificial fees so that his days may have their proper times. (8) He assigns the remainder. (9)

On the following day, he sacrifices with the eight [deities] beginning with Anumati, one after another. 10. While grinding [the grain], he causes the portion for Anumati to fall behind and to the north. 11.
That which falls to the west of the yoke-pin is for Nirṛti, as a cake on a single potsherd. 12.

Those [stalks] which are turned upward, having gone toward the north, he should dig up an ant-hill with the formula, "Here I expiate the *kṣetriya* (hereditary disease) of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so. Having offered an oblation upon the ant-hill with a shell, he should cover the ant-hill with that very shell, saying, "Here I shut off the *kṣetriya* of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so.
Some say that one offers with an ant-hill and covers with an ant-hill.
Having set down the *ānumata* cake, he proceeds with the rite for Nirṛti.

Having offered an oblation of rice with the formula "Vīhi svāhā" in the Gārhapatya fire, he takes a single burning brand from the Dakṣiṇāgni that is still smoking. Having gone to the southern-western intermediate direction, having kindled a fire on a natural salt-flat or in a cleft, he offers the entire portion to Nirṛti as a *sarvahuta* oblation with his two thumbs or with two stalks that have fallen off, saying: "This is thy share, O Nirṛti. A black garment with a black fringe is the sacrificial fee.
Some say that the garment should be black with frayed edges;
they proceed without looking back, as it is known from scripture: "By means of concealment from Nirṛti.
Thus ends the eighth section.
"svāhā! Homage to him who has done this! Having returned and offered in the *gārhapatya* fire, he proceeds with the rite accompanied by the *anumata* (consent) formula.
1. A cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
2. Having sacrificed day after day with these [formulas], "The *caru* for Āditya," etc., he undertakes the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices. 3.
He sacrifices with them for one year;
he does not combine the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice.
Thereafter, he sacrifices with the four-oblation [rite] consisting of the Indraturīya.
"A cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (7); "a reddish-brown cow is the sacrificial fee" (8);
with that [offering], one should cause a man who has rivals or one who is dear [to him] to sacrifice (9).
On the night of this very same day, he performs the Pañcedhmīya sacrifice.

Having divided the Āhavanīya fire into four parts according to the directions and having placed the fifth in the middle, and having separately added fuel to each of the fires, he takes five portions of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle and offers oblations with the verses beginning "The gods who sit in front," according to their respective characteristics. With the fifth verse, "The gathered guard," he piles the fuel together in the middle, adds fuel all at once, takes another five portions of clarified butter, and offers the next five oblations with the formula: "To Agni, the slayer of Rakṣases, svāhā! and so forth.
A chariot drawn by four mares is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or one drawn by five;
with this one should sacrifice who fears Rākṣasas or Piśācas. When the dawn has broken, before the Agnihotra, they perform the oblation of Apāmārga plants.
Having fetched Apāmārga plants from a place where waters converge and having ground them into flour, he takes a single glowing ember from the Dakṣiṇāgni fire while it is still smoking.

Having gone to the north-western intermediate direction and having kindled a fire on a natural salt-flat or in a cleft, he recites the formula "By the impulse of the god... and offers the oblation with a spoon made of Parṇa wood, saying, "I offer the slaying of the Rakṣas.
Having cast the spoon into the fire with the words, "The Rakṣas is slain," he stands over it worshipping with the words, "We have struck down the Rakṣas."

Whatever you possess, that is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or else a chosen boon (*vara*). It is known from tradition: "They proceed without looking back, so as to remain hidden from the *rakṣases*.
This is the ninth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
Having performed the Agnihotra, he offers the oblations for the Devikās:
(1) a cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ—these are five; (2) a pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee.
Even an animal is to be sacrificed here for the sake of the Creator (Dhātṛ), or not.
There are three oblations: one on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, and so forth.
Of these, with the first, one desiring a village should sacrifice; with the second, one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); with the third, one desiring cattle.
Some say it is "the birth of a hero.
He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara;
gold is the sacrificial fee.
A *caru* of barley for Varuṇa, one *prādeśa* on all sides; 10.
a horse that has not yet been harnessed is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); 11.
a *caru* for Bṛhaspati—these are the twelve oblations of the Ratnins offered daily. 12.
In whose house he performs the offering, from that house come the distribution of the sacrificial food and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 13.
A pot of cooked rice (caru) for Bhaga is in the house of the favorite wife; 14. a four-year-old cow with a miscarried fetus is the sacrificial fee. 15.

Some say that the sacrificial cake for Nairṛta is made entirely from the size of a thumb-joint. (16) There is a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu as the thirteenth offering, at the house of a carpenter and a chariot-maker. (17) All-iron implements are the sacrificial gifts. (18)
According to some, [the offering is] for a carpenter or a chariot-maker (19).

In the house of an akṣāvāpa or a govikarta, there is a *raudra* oblation of *gāvīdhuka* grains in a pot (20). The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of a halter with tassels, or a sword bound with hair, or a brindled bull (21).

"It is known [from tradition] that he is three years old. (22) A *barāsī*—a cow-hide mat with its hair on the inside, its fringes bound with the hair of a she-goat, and its straps made of leather—is provided; or else a spotted yearling calf. (23) According to some, the horse has reddish-brown ears. (24)
With the formula "Svāhā to the road," he offers an oblation in the house of the Pālākala.
25 They call him Anṛtadūta.
26 Three arrows made of leather and provided with feathers are the sacrificial fee; or a bow encased in cane. 27
In the house of the sacrificer, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman; [he also offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Aṃhomuc.
28. A bull is the sacrificial fee. 29. According to some, a gold necklace and armor [are also given]. 30.
Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the Adhvaryu mutters: "May this king, the slayer of Vṛtra, having become king, slay Vṛtra.
He fashions a four-cornered vessel for Mitra from a branch of the *aśvattha* tree that has fallen of its own accord.
They milk a white cow with a white calf into a white vessel made of clay;
they carry that [milk], which has solidified by itself, away together;
they place that, which has been churned by itself, in the sun.
That ghee becomes melted by itself. 6.
On the following day, he commences the initiations for the *Ukthya* sacrifice that is part of the consecration (*abhiṣecanīya*). 7.
The initiation offering (*dīkṣaṇīyā*) is dedicated to Mitra and Bṛhaspati. 8.

The altar is self-made; the sacrificial grass is self-cut; the fuel is self-prepared. Now, according to some, they prepare half of the altar; half is self-made. They cut half of the sacrificial grass;
half they bind together as it is self-cut. They chop half of the fuel; half is self-chopped.
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is to be sprinkled with water; some say the same applies to the fuel-wood (*idhma*).
At the time of arranging the vessels, he places the *caru* for Bṛhaspati and the vessel for Mitra in the place where the potsherds would normally be.
He separates the rice grains that have been husked three times according to the verse for division, distinguishing between those with broken kernels and those without.
"Some say [the portions] are both the smallest and the largest. 14.
Those ears which are in the milk belong to Bṛhaspati. 15. When it has been cooked, he then covers it with a vessel belonging to Mitra. 16."
He causes the two [spoons] to be placed into that clarified butter which has itself melted; he pours the two ear-rings into it;
he makes them upper and lower.
Thus they become simultaneous. 20.
Having reached the month of Bārhaspatya, he reaches the month of Maitra. 21.
Thus he proceeds. 22.
A white-backed ox is the sacrificial fee for [the offering] to Bṛhaspati; a horse is that for Mitra. And that same white cow with a white calf [is the fee].
This is the eleventh section.
Likewise, he extends the initiations of the consecration-ceremony (abhiṣecanīya) Ukthya sacrifice so that the Daśapeya will take place when ten nights remain of the year.
He purchases the Soma for both the Abhiṣecanīya and the Daśapeya sacrifices together. He transports it together;
he deposits half of the King (Soma) in the house of the Purohita for the sake of the Daśapeya.
He offers the animal-cake of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, followed by the eight oblations of the Devasū offerings.
The *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* portions are the same [as in other sacrifices].
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the Brahman priest takes the hand of the sacrificer with the formula, "May Savitṛ impel you for all impulses.

Then he announces him to the recipients of precious gifts (*ratnin*), saying: "This is your king, O Bharatas! To one of the Kuru lineage he says, "This is your king, O Kurus! To one of the Pañcāla lineage he says, "This is your king, O Pañcālas! Or to the Kurus and Pañcālas together, "This is your king, O Kurus and Pañcālas! To other kings he says, "This is your king, O people! (or "O clansmen!").
"Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas," the Brahman priest mutters.
(8) "Thou hast been established in that name and sovereignty," with two verses addressed to Varuṇa, the sacrificer wipes his face.
(9) "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he takes three strides toward the east as the Viṣṇu-strides. (10)

Having performed the rites prior to the offering to Mahendra and having set aside the midday *puroḍāśa* cakes, he offers a cake on twenty-one potsherds to the Maruts and a curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) to the Viśvedevas.

He places the potsherds for that [Marut cake] with the groups of verses beginning with the third *araṇye’nuvākyā*, using the two [verses] beginning with "īdṛṅ cānyādṛṅ ca. Having covered [the altar] in the middle with the *araṇye’nuvākyā*, he draws the cups of water.
In the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, the Vāyavya cups are drawn;
sixteen or seventeen oblations are offered,
and an equal number of cups are drawn.
Thus ends the twelfth section (kaṇḍikā).
Having offered oblations into the waters of the Sarasvatī with the formula "Artha" and "Stha," he takes [the water] with this same mantra.
In the same way with the subsequent [formulas]. With that by which he offers, with that he takes.
"Lord of the waters"—this refers to those belonging to the ocean, or to the Sindhu river, or whatever other male-streamed watercourse there may be.
When a man or a beast has entered [the water], one wave fights against the current while another follows the current.
"You are the bull"—this refers to the one that goes against the current; "you are the bull-army"—this refers to the one that follows the current.
"O you who dwell in the cow-pen," for those that flow downwards;
"O strength of the Maruts," for those that flow upstream, or for those that are hail-like;
"O you who flow forth," for those that, having surged up, pour back down into that very place.
"Flowing around" is for rivers that flow in all directions;
"having the brilliance of the sun" is for those that rain;
"having the skin of the sun" is for those in which forms are clearly visible.
The *māndās* are [the chants] for stationary plants;
the *vāśās* are for dewdrops;
the *śakvarīs* are for the offspring of cattle.
"O supporter of all," [is the formula] for the milk;
"O source of people," for the curd;
"O brilliance of Agni," for the ghee.

"The essence of the waters, the essence of the plants"—this [formula] belongs to honey (18). "The divine waters, rich in sweetness, have taken hold"—this he appends everywhere to both the oblation and the taking (19).

"You are givers of the kingdom; grant the kingdom, svāhā!"—this is used when connected with an oblation. "You are givers of the kingdom; grant the kingdom to so-and-so"—this is used when connected with the taking (20).

Having poured the cups together into a vessel made of *vetasa* wood with the formula, "O divine waters," and having set them down between the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths of the Hotṛ and the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin with the formula, "Sit down, unassailable ones," he places a *śatamāna* gold coin upon it with the formula, "Thou art the destroyer. Having purified [the water] with that [gold] using the formula, "I purify your bright [waters] with the bright," he distributes it among four vessels—those made of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *nyagrodha*—with the formula, "These [waters], which are companions at the feast, full of splendor and strength.
Having gone northward to where the residue remains in the vessel, he offers it on the Āgnīdhrīya fire with the formula, "O Rudra, that highest name of yours which is secret."
Thus ends the thirteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

With the words, "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatriya," the sacrificer puts on a garment of fine linen (tārpya). With the words, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatriya," he puts on a second turban, white and pale-yellow;
they call white "pāṇḍara."
Some [use] three white garments and turbans;
he places a turban upon his head. Then he purifies him with one hundred and one tufts of *darbha* grass; he anoints him with one hundred and one [tufts].
With fifty [verses] he [anoints] the right eye; with fifty-one, the left.
Then he causes him to eat curd and shoots of the *udumbara* tree.
Some authorities record that these acts—rubbing [the eyes], anointing [the body], eating, and putting on the garment—are to be performed in this successive order.
These rites are performed by the Āgnīdhra:

having caused [the sacrificer] to touch water, while making the sacrificer recite the *āvida* formulas beginning with "Agni has found us," he leads him out to the exterior. Having said, "This is your king, O Bharatas," he hands the bow to the sacrificer with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt.
He gives three arrows equipped with feathers, saying, "Thou art the repeller of enemies."
He recites the mantra, "Protect me from the west," over the [soma] being offered. 12.
While offering it, the Adhvaryu mutters, "Protect me from the east, protect me from the west, protect me from the north.
13. The sacrificer raises his right arm with the words, "Thou art Mitra," and his left arm with the words, "Thou art Varuṇa. 14.
Or else, this is reversed:
he consecrates the two raised [stones] with the verse "Hiraṇyavarṇau" (VS 28.33).
Then he establishes him in the five directions.
Thus ends the fourteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
"Place the fuel-stick," he says; he follows along mentally.
Or, at this point, one may offer the oblation to the Maruts.

Having placed him upon the sacrificial grass, they embrace this tiger and urge on the lion for great good fortune. Like the ocean, he stands as one who is well-invoked; they groom the leopard within the waters. Striking the sacrificial cake with the wooden sword (sphyá) while performing a malevolent rite, whatever clings to the wooden sword and whatever crumbles away, that he offers to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.

In front of the *praśāstṛ*’s hearth, having set down a stool made of *khadira* or *udumbara* wood, he spreads upon it a tiger skin with the neck pointing eastward and the hair facing upward, saying, "Thou art the splendor of Soma. Upon that, saying, "Thou art immortality," he places a *śatamāna* weight of gold. Then, saying, "O lightning, protect me," he places the golden *śatamāna*—weighing one hundred *kṛṣṇalas* and consisting of one hundred syllables—upon the head of the sacrificer.

Mounting it, the sacrificer throws a piece of lead with his right foot toward a eunuch, saying, "May the biting serpents be driven away! He throws a piece of red iron with his left foot toward a hair-cutter, saying, "The head of Namuci is cast out!
They both throw these two outside the sacrificial altar. With the formula, "To Agni, svāhā," he offers six *pārtha* oblations prior to the consecration.
"To the earth, svāhā!"—with these [formulas] he offers six oblations to the elements. 9.
While he stands with his arms raised, he consecrates him during the *māhendra* hymn. 10.
Having consecrated him with the mantra "Soma is King," he says: "I consecrate thee with the splendor of Soma. 11.
Thus ends the fifteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
With a palāśa [wood] in front, the adhvaryu [acts];
likewise the others.

The Brahman priest stands to the south with a staff of Udumbara wood; or a Rājanya may do so. To the west, a Vaiśya uses one of Aśvattha wood. To the north, a friend or ally uses one of Nyagrodha wood.

He addresses the one being consecrated with the mantra: "Thou art the lord of the Kṣatriyas among the Kṣatriyas. (6) With the mantra "They have come together," he wipes away those drops which flow down as the remnants of the one being consecrated. (7–8)
With the formula, "Thou art the womb of Indra, the bearer of people," he unfastens the garments with the black antelope horn— either one, two, or all of them—
and throws them onto the rubbish-heap with the formula, "Protect beyond the sky. With the formula, "Svāhā to Indra," he offers six terrestrial oblations after the consecration.
With the formula "To the waters, svāhā! he performs the six *aveṣṭi* offerings for the elements.
Or, at this point, he may offer the *prareka*.

If he should desire of a wife, "May her offspring be a kingdom," then, having caused the fire to be established in her *aupāsana* hearth, he should offer two *nāmavyatiṣañjanīya* oblations from the remnants of the smearings that have been left in the vessels, with the verses beginning "O Prajāpati, not these... and "These, O Prajāpati."
"‘He is the son of such-and-such; she is the daughter of such-and-such’—thus he interchanges their names; some say ‘their names’ [in the plural]. This is the sixteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

Having brought down the chariot with the formula, "Thou art the thunderbolt of Indra," he yokes the chariot drawn by side-horses with the formula, "By the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the directors, I yoke thee.
With the formula, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," the sacrificer approaches the chariot.
The Kṣatriya who has been appointed as his deputy takes hold of him from behind.
With the verse, "O thou who art invoked by many, thou hast prevailed," the Brahman priest follows from the south. With the words, "May I conquer at the impulse of the Maruts," he sets forth.
The Rājanya, equipped with his bow, stands stationed to the north-east.
Therefore, he shoots these arrows, thinking, "The mind has been reached.
Having released each one in turn and conquered it, he turns clockwise, saying, "I am equal to this sense-faculty in vigor.
Wherever he departs, that [conquered sense] remains established.
With the formula, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt," he drives away the wife and the horses with the tip of the bow.

With the formula, "This is the thunderbolt, the winner of booty; by it may our son win booty," he hands the bow to the wife. Having fastened on two boar-skin sandals with the formula, "Thou art the wrath of cattle," and having consecrated the earth while about to descend with the formula, "Homage to the mother," he descends and puts on the amulets. With the formula, "Thou art this much," he puts on the silver one; with "Thou art vigor," the one made of Udumbara wood; with "Thou art yoked," the golden one.
Some prescribe a golden vessel in the middle.

Having offered the oblations for unyoking the chariot with the formula, "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā! he places the chariot upon the chariot-stand together with the charioteer, using the verse, "The swan dwelling in purity... (RV 4.40.5). Once it has been placed there, the charioteer descends.
Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā).
With the words "Thou art Mitra," the sacrificer draws down his right arm; with "Thou art Varuṇa," his left. Or rather, it may be the reverse.

With the words, "Together with all the gods," he lowers his hands over the *āmikṣā* dedicated to the Viśve Devās; or, according to some, they recite, "May it be seated in my seat, may it be abundant for me," over the *āmikṣā* dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
In front of the *Āgnīdhra* shed, they construct a measured hall with four sloping drains, elevated in the east and sloping downward toward the west.

Having established a stool made of *khadira* wood upon it with the words, "Thou art pleasant, a good seat," and having spread a woolen garment over it with the words, "Thou art the navel of the ruling power (*kṣatra*)," he fastens the girdle around her with the words, "Be firm for the sake of the people in the lower garment.
(6) Having seated her with the words, "Sit on the pleasant one; sit on the good seat," the sacrificer sits down beside her with the words, "May he not harm thee; may thou not harm me.
(7) He addresses her as she sits with the verse, "He has sat down, firm in his vows. (8)

The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the jewel-bearers (*ratnin*) sit down around him from all sides: the *adhvaryu* to the east, the *brahman* to the south, the *hotṛ* to the west, and the *udgātṛ* to the north.
Once they have sat down, the *brahman* addresses the *adhvaryu* and the King.
"O King, you were Brahmā," the other replied.
(11) In this manner, [the others addressed] the Brahmā, the Hotṛ, and the Udgātṛ. (12) With each successive mantra, the others replied. (13)

With the formula, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt," the Brahman priest hands the wooden sword (*sphya*) to the King; the King to his deputy; the deputy to the family priest (*purohita*); and the family priest to the jewel-bearers (*ratnin*). They hand it down from one to another until it finally reaches the keeper of the dice (*akṣāvāpa*). With that [sword], the keeper of the dice, having raised up the gaming-ground and sprinkled it with water, should pour down the dice.
Thus ends the eighteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

Four [men]—a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra—who are associated with those [dice], play with more than a hundred or more than a thousand golden dice; they call out for the cooked rice while gambling with a four-year-old cow.
The two former fire-carriers of this ritual are the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Those two are to be given to the Brahman priest.

"To the King [belongs] the Audbhidya"—having thus cast four hundred golden dice for them and having conquered the quarters, [the sacrificer says], "This king has come forth"; he then presents five dice to the King.
The king calls out to him whose name is auspicious: "Suśloka! He calls to the charioteer: "Sumaṅgala! He calls to the distributor of portions: "Satyarāja!"
Having summoned the steward Nīti, he gives those four-footed animals to the Brahman;
they become the witnesses.
Or, at this point, he should offer two oblations with the *nāmavyatiṣañjana* formulas.
He causes the *Śaunaḥśepa* narrative to be recited, consisting of verses interspersed with songs, numbering more than a hundred or even more than a thousand.
Seated upon a golden cushion, the Hotṛ recites it.
Standing between the two golden bunches of grass, the Adhvaryu responds.
12. "Om" is the response for a Ṛc verse; "So be it" is the response for a Gāthā. 13.
When the Śaunaḥśepa episode has concluded, he gives a golden cushion to the Hotṛ, two golden bunches of grass to the Adhvaryu, and two gold plates for the consecration. 14.
Here he proceeds with the offering to the Maruts and the Vaiśvadeva; however, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* are the same.
When the *iḍā* has been invoked, having untied the amulets, he gives them to the Brahman priest.
Thus ends the nineteenth section (kaṇḍikā). One commences the ritual procedure for the Mahendra offering beginning with the *pracaraṇa*. It is the same up to the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath).
Having performed the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) rite, he offers an oblation into the waters with the formula: "To the grandson of the waters, svāhā! (3).

Having offered into a clump of *darbha* grass, or into a stump, or into the mound of an anthill with the formula: "To the grandson of strength, svāhā!", and having returned and offered into the *gārhapatya* fire with the formula: "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā!", he immolates the *anūbandhyā* cow for Indra. (4).
For that [cow], he prepares a *paśupuroḍāśa* cake of wild rice from the four-footed slaughter-ground. (5)
It is known that there is a substitution for the cart-offering.

On the following day, to the west of the sacrificial ground used for the Soma sacrifice, one should sacrifice with either ten or seven *saṃsṛp* oblations, beginning with the cake on eight potsherds for Agni.
One settles at each successive sacrificial ground from the preceding one.

Where the Āhavanīya fire is in the eastern [hall], there the Gārhapatya fire is in the northern one; in the last [hall] the Āhavanīya is in the Prāgvaṃśa and the Gārhapatya is outside. Having sacrificed with these, he initiates the procedure for the Daśapeya in the afternoon.
They initiate him immediately;
12 they purchase the Soma immediately;
13 in place of the initiation water, he puts on a garland of twelve lotuses. 14
He purchases Soma with ten castrated young bulls;
he does not bargain, nor does he carry it away;
he merely effects the purchase.

There is one initiation and three *upasads*. Before the *upasads*, he offers a *caru* of rice for Soma; in between, a cake on eight potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ; and after them, a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu.
For these [offerings], the same procedure as that of the *upasads* applies regarding the *prastara* grass-bundle and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
The Bhārgava becomes the Hotṛ priest;
the Śrāyantīya is the Brahman’s Sāman; the Vāravantīya is the Agniṣṭoma Sāman;
he takes the Sarasvatī waters.
Thus ends the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā).
On the following day, at the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out ten additional goblets (camasas).
At the time of filling them, he fills those [ten].

At the time of consumption, ten Soma-drinking Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma from each individual cup, having drunk the Soma in an uninterrupted lineage for ten generations. 3. This must be recounted back to the tenth generation; he becomes the performer of that consumption. 4. One hundred Soma-drinking Brāhmaṇas enter the Sadas. 5.

At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives a golden vessel with a lid to the *adhvaryu*; a golden garland to the *udgātṛ*; and a gold plate to the *hotṛ*, according to the traditional recitation. Now, according to some, he gives a cow that seems to be leaping about to the *unnetṛ*; a bull to the *grāvastut*; a goat to the *subrahmaṇya*; an ox is to be given to the *neṣṭṛ*; another to the *agnīdh*; and a one-horse cart laden with barley to the *acchāvāka*. He concludes the sacrifice with the *diśām aveṣṭi* offerings.
"An offering on eight potsherds for Agni"—thus [there are] five [offerings].
(9) With this [rite], a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya who desires splendor (*tejas*) should sacrifice.

(10) If it is a Brāhmaṇa who sacrifices, having placed the offering to Bṛhaspati in the middle, he should sprinkle each oblation as it is offered over it. If it is a Rājanya, [he should place the offering] to Indra. If it is a Vaiśya, [he should place the offering] to the Viśvedevas. (11)
In the afternoon, he should sacrifice with the animal offering consisting of two animals.
He immolates a large, pregnant ewe for Āditya, and a spotted heifer for the Maruts.
He causes the announcement for the offering to Āditya to be made loudly; he proceeds with the offering to the Maruts in a low voice.
The *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta* formulas are whispered (15).
On the following day, he performs the three-oblation sacrifice for the messengers of Satya (*sātyadūtānām*). [He offers] a cake on twelve potsherds to the Aśvins and Pūṣan (16).
A bow with three arrows and a dry leather water-skin are the sacrificial fee (17).
Thus ends the twenty-first section (kaṇḍikā).
Some say [the staff] is made of boar-horn or of *upāmaha* wood;
others say it is a staff, or a dried one, or a leather water-skin, or worn-out sandals.
Having bathed those [vessels], he sends them to the rival kings;
he announces, "I have been consecrated, I have become king.
In the afternoon, he sacrifices with the six Prayuja oblations, beginning with the cake on eight potsherds for Agni.
The southern draft-ox of the chariot-pole is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 6.
On the following day, with the six northern [verses], 7. the northern draft-ox of the chariot-pole is the sacrificial fee. 8.

Having performed the Agnihotra for a year, he sacrifices with the Keśavapanīya Atirātra. 9 The mantras containing references to shaving, such as "Those long-haired ones who first sat for the sacrificial session," are used. 10 With those beginning with the first reference, he has his hair shaved at the beginning; with those ending with the last reference, he has it shaved at the end. 11
Immediately thereafter, he performs the Vyaṣṭidvirātra sacrifice.
The first day is an Agniṣṭoma; the second is an Atirātra. The first day falls on the full moon; the second on the Vyaṣṭakā.
Or on the day before the new moon; or on the following day when [the moon] has risen;
or on whichever two days of the waxing fortnight may be auspicious.
On the first day they immolate five animals of the set of eleven; on the second day, six.

For Kṣatriyas, there is the Dhṛti-Ṛtu, consisting of the Triṣṭoma and Agniṣṭoma with five concluding rites (pañcāpavarga). 18 One should perform this sacrifice at the end. 19 Thus the Rājasūya comes to a conclusion. 20
Having performed that [sacrifice], he should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī or with a curd-mixture (āmikṣā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
21. The days [of the sacrificial session] have different purificatory baths (avabhṛtha), except for the first day of a two-night rite.
22. Thus ends the twenty-second section.
Thus ends the eighteenth question:
Three days prior [to the sacrifice], having purchased young grass from a eunuch with lead and having tied it in a linen cloth, he sets forth the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the Sautrāmaṇī.
Its ritual rule (*kalpa*) is like that of the Nirūḍhapaśubandha.

Having added fuel to the fires, prepared the *veda* grass-bundle, and strewn around the fires, he proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the washing of his hands (3). He arranges the vessels according to their purpose; he places a cooking-pot (*sthālī*) in the place of the potsherds (4).
At the time of the pouring out [of the grain], he pours out an abundant quantity of rice for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman (5).

The ritual procedure for the sacrificial porridge (caru) has been explained. Having cooked it, one digs a pit in front of the Gārhapatya fire; in that pit, one prepares the surā according to the ritual procedure for surā.
A strainer (parisrut) is used.
With the formula, "Sweet thee with the sweet," he mixes the *surā* with young grass shoots.
It remains mixed for three nights.
He cuts down a single sacrificial post.
He does not construct this altar;
he accomplishes his purposes by means of what has already been done.
It is known from tradition that one sacrifices on the third part of the Soma-altar.

While the *uttaravedi* is being prepared, the *pratiprasthātṛ* fetches earth from the *cātvāla* pit and, having fashioned a mound (*khara*) to the south of the *uttaravedi*, prepares a second mound in front of the *anvāhāryapacana* fire for the purpose of the *surā-graha* cups.
(15) When the fire is being led forward, the *pratiprasthātṛ* takes fire from the *dakṣiṇāgni*, places it upon the mound to the south of the *uttaravedi*, and kindles it.
(16) At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out three vessels for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman: a vat with a hair-strainer, a hawk-wing-shaped vessel, and the cooking pots. (17)

Before the immolation of the animals, having performed the rite of breaking open [the vessel] and having placed the *surā* on the head of a Brāhmaṇa or upon a donkey, he purifies the *surā* with a filter made of hair, using the formula: "May the *parisrut* purify thee.
(18) For one who has vomited Soma, [he uses] "Soma has flowed forward"; for one who has passed through the Soma filter, "Soma has flowed backward.
(19) Having set down the purified [liquor] in its proper place, he immolates the animals at a single sacrificial post. (20)
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā). [The animal victims are]:
a smoky-colored goat for the Aśvins, a ram for Sarasvatī, and a bull or a young male for Indra;
and a fourth for Bṛhaspati, for one who has vomited Soma or for one who has passed Soma excessively.
When the omenta have been offered, he gives a gold ornament, a bull, and a swift mare;
they say she must be one that has been lost and recovered;
a mare with a foal is the sacrificial fee.
According to some, there are two *śatamāna* weights, one of gold and one of silver (6).
Having performed the purification at the *cātvāla* pit, they draw the cups of *surā* on the second mound (7).
For all [the cups], there is one introductory verse (*puroruca*), one invitatory verse (*puro’nuvākya*), one direction (*praiṣa*), and one offering verse (*yājyā*) (8).

"Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, the flawless one, with the flawless [ladle], acceptable to the Aśvins"—with these words the Adhvaryu takes the draught for the Aśvins. With "for Sarasvatī," the Pratiprasthātṛ or the Āgnīdhra takes the draught for Sarasvatī. With "for Indra," the Brahman or the Sacrificer takes the draught for Indra.

(9) He mixes the draught for the Aśvins with *kvala*-grains and lion’s hair; the draught for Sarasvatī with jujube-grains and tiger’s hair; and the draught for Indra with *karkandhu*-grains and wolf’s hair. (10)

In the absence of those, the Adhvaryu should mentally meditate on lions; the Pratiprasthātṛ on tigers; and the sacrificer on wolves. Having wiped all of them with the *śyenapattra* [leaf], he deposits them in their respective places according to the deity and the station, saying, "This is your womb.
Or, they may be milk-draughts (*payograha*).

Having taken the animal-related portions of clarified butter (*pāśukāni vājyāni*), they should draw the cups (*grahān*). Then he offers the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśān*): having offered the animal-cake for Bṛhaspati, he offers one for Indra on eleven potsherds.
Having set those three down, they proceed with the cups.
Those who take [the cups], the Adhvaryu gives the two calls:

"Recite for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman the Soma-pressings accompanied by *surā*! and "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman the Soma-pressings accompanied by *surā*! Or alternatively: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the Soma-pressings accompanied by *surā* that have been set forth. 17–18.

"O Aśvins, lords of beauty, drinking the *surā* together with the Asura Namuci, you two protected Indra in his deeds. O Aśvins, like parents protecting a son, protect us both through your deed and your wondrous powers (*daṃsanā*). When you drank the *surā* with your skills, O Maghavan, Sarasvatī was constantly by your side"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the offering to all the gods (19).
This is the second section.
He performs the after-offering (*anuyāja*) with the words: "O Agni, enjoy the Soma. (1)

"O Agni, the oblation has been poured into your mouth, like clarified butter into the ladle, like Soma into the cups. Bestow upon us wealth that wins booty, accompanied by brave sons, praiseworthy, glorious, and great—wealth in which horses, bulls, oxen, barren cows, and rams are released and offered as oblations. To the one who drinks the sweet draught, whose back is sprinkled with Soma, the Ordainer—I generate a beautiful hymn from my heart for Agni. With these words, the sacrificer consecrates the oblation either when it has already been offered or while it is being offered. (2) He should hire a Brāhmaṇa to drink the remnants of the offering. (3)

"For separate indeed is your divinely ordained seat; do not mingle in the highest heaven. You are the spirited Surā, and this is Soma; do not harm me as I enter my own womb. Whatever remains here of the pressed juice, which Indra drank by his powers—that portion of it, with a gracious mind, I consume here as King Soma," or he may drink it himself. 4

"I have heard of two paths of the fathers, and of the gods and mortals; by these two this entire world comes together, between the former and the latter sign"—with these words, he should pour [the mixture] into an anthill. 5.
On the southern fire, he holds a vessel containing a hundred blades of grass, tied up. 6.

Having spread the filter with its fringes pointing northward over the mouth of that vessel, and having placed a piece of gold weighing a hundred mānas upon it with the verse, "My mind which has gone away... he pours the remainder of the *surā* into it with the formula, "O Fathers, whose faces are like Soma, may you be satisfied," or alternatively, "O Fathers, whose faces are like Soma, may they rejoice; may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods. Drunk by Indra, far-seeing, may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods.
They worship the flowing stream with three verses addressed to Soma and containing the word "Fathers," each subsequent verse being recited after the preceding one.
These verses beginning with "Thou, O Soma, art observant" are those traditionally handed down.
The Adhvaryu stands to the east, the Brahman to the south, and the Hotṛ to the west.
With the verses beginning "O Agni, Kavyavāhana," he establishes the Śatātṛṇā bricks on the southern fire, if a Brāhmaṇa performs the sacrifice.
This is the third section (kaṇḍikā).

Now, if a Rājanya or a Vaiśya should not care to carry forward the southern fire, he himself should sit consuming the remainder of the *surā* as his sacrificial food (*vrata*). Having performed the offering of the animal-cake for Bṛhaspati, he proceeds with the animal sacrifices, and then with the [other] cakes.
The *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* offerings are the same [as in the animal sacrifice]. 4.
The ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice begins with the words, "O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings (*upayaja*)," and so forth. 5.
They perform the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the heart-spits, the *māsara* mixture, and the vessels. 6.
He offers [the mixture] according to the ritual procedure for *māsara* and *mṛjīṣa*. 7. They call the dregs *māsara*. 8.

"O divine Varuṇa, that bond of yours which has the *gāyatrī* metre—by this [offering] I release it for you; *svāhā*! With these words, he casts the cup of the Aśvins into the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). By the same formula, substituting "that which has the *triṣṭubh* metre," he casts the cup of Sarasvatī.
"Jagatī is its metre"—this is for the offering to Indra. "Anuṣṭubh is its metre"—this is for the *sata*, the *vālasrāva*, and the *śyenapattra*. "Paṅkti is its metre"—this is for the *śūla* spears.
(9) The returning [of the victim] is performed silently.

(10) With this [rite], one should cause the sacrifice to be performed for one who has vomited Soma, one who has passed over the Soma, one whose king is being driven away, one who has been driven away, one who is being consecrated, or one who has been consecrated. (11)

One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should perform this sacrifice; likewise one performing malevolent magic, or one desiring food, or desiring offspring, or desiring cattle. It is prescribed for all consecrations (abhiṣeka).
By means of that [sacrifice], a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya who desires splendor should sacrifice.
Thus ends the fourth section (kaṇḍikā). Now, therefore, we shall explain the Kaukilī sacrifice. Its ritual procedure is as before.
At the time of the offering, he immolates an animal for Indra; a bull is the sacrificial fee;
[he offers] a pap for Āditya.

6. Beforehand, having purchased rice, barley, and *śyāmāka* with black iron, black sulphate of iron (*kālānuśātana*), black [pigment], and a fine hair-sieve, they make the rice-grains into *tokmāni* (germinated grains) when tied in a linen cloth; the barley-grains are slightly parched. 7–8.
Having mixed those powders with curd or whey, he wraps them around with *darbha* grass and sets them down.
That *māsara* (9);
those same coarse powders, sprinkled with the *saṃsrāva* liquid, are the *nagnahu* (10).

Having made groats of *śyāmāka* grain, at the time of fermenting the *surā*, one mixes the *surā* with sprouts (*tokma*), *māsara*, and *nagnahu*; having scattered a third part of the groats around it and sprinkled it with the milk of one cow while reciting "Pour forth the pressed juice" (*parīto ṣiñcatā sutam*), and having scattered another third part around it, one sprinkles it with the milk of two cows using the same formula; and having scattered yet another third part around it, one sprinkles it with the milk of three cows using that same formula. Thus mixed, it remains for three nights. (11)
Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā).
Some authorities prescribe a basket with a wide mouth at the place of the pit.
It is made of split bamboo and bound with leather.
Into that [vessel], he places a bamboo tube with a snout-shaped opening;
its opening is covered with a piece of leather.
Whatever flows out into it becomes the *parisrut*.

At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out three vessels for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman. 6. He places three types of groats—of barley, wheat, and *upavāka*—either in a winnowing-basket with ears of grain or in a wooden trough (*droṇa*). 7.
The strainer for the Adhvaryu is made from the wool of goats and sheep; that of the Pratiprasthātṛ is from the hair of cows and horses. 8.
Having set aside the clarified butter, the Adhvaryu pours out an abundant quantity of milk into a wooden trough (droṇa).
Regarding this, Āśmarathya says it should be done with a mantra; Ālekhana says it should be done silently. Having purified the clarified butter, he purifies the milk with a tuft of wool.
"Eastward Soma has flowed too much," [he says] for one who has vomited Soma; "Westward Soma has flowed too much," [he says] for one who has passed Soma through the filter excessively.
