"The Brahman and the Kṣatra purify themselves," [with these words] the Pratiprasthātṛ [takes] the Surā.
Having taken the clarified butter portions pertaining to the animal sacrifice, the Adhvaryu takes the milk-draughts.
"Kuvid aṅga": for all [these verses], there is one *puroruc*, one *puro'nuvākya*, one *praiṣa*, and one *yājyā*.
This is the sixth section (*kaṇḍikā*).

Having taken [the draught] with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the Aśvins," and having mixed it with barley-meal, wiped it around with a strainer, and set it down with the formula, "This is thy womb; for splendor thee," he then takes [another draught] with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Sarasvatī," and having mixed it with wheat-meal, wiped it around with a strainer, and set it down with the formula, "This is thy womb; for vigor thee," he then takes [the third draught] with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra Sutraman," and having mixed it with *upavāka* meal.
Having wiped it with the strainer, he deposits it with the formula, "This is thy womb; for strength thee! and worships it with the following verses according to their respective characteristics.
When the *surā* is being poured, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the *surā*-cups from the stream.

For all of them, there is one introductory verse (*puroruca*), one invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākya*), one direction (*praiṣa*), and one offering verse (*yājyā*). These are indeed distinct, for a separate seat has been prepared for you by the gods.
"Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the Aśvins, as their splendor. Having thus taken it and wiped it with a strainer, he deposits it with:
"This is thy womb; for delight, thee! "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Sarasvatī, as her vigor. Having thus taken it and wiped it with a strainer, he deposits it with:

"This is thy womb; for bliss, thee! "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra Sutrāman, as his strength. Having thus taken it and wiped it with a strainer, he deposits it with: "This is thy womb; for greatness, thee!"
The *surā* vessels and the *vacchrayaṇa* filters [are prepared].
With the remainder of the *sanna* section, the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer perform the worship; and with the subsequent section.
Thus ends the seventh section (*kaṇḍikā*).

As before, he dedicates the animals, with the exception of the one for Bṛhaspati; the procedure is the same up to the carrying of fire around them. During the middle round of the fire-circumambulation, he places a portion of a firebrand upon the mound (khara) and adds fuel to it.

Having carried fire around the remainder with the rest [of the butter], he leads forward this very [fire] for the purpose of cooking the animal victim. When the omenta have been offered, he gives forty cows as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), along with a young colt and a mare.
Or, at this point, they may draw the cups (grahas).

The instruction for the ritual command has been stated. Āśmarathya maintains that all [libations] should be offered in the Āhavanīya fire; Ālekhana maintains that the *surā* cups are offered in the southern fire.
He offers the milk cups with the verse, "O you who possess the *surā*," and the *surā* cups with the verse, "That essence of yours which is gathered."
Having offered the oblation with a silent *anuvaṣaṭ* call, the Adhvaryu consumes the portion for the Aśvins with the formula: "O Aśvins, that which [belongs] to Namuci... (10).
The Pratiprasthātṛ and the Agnīdhra consume the portion for Sarasvatī with the formula: "Whatever here is smeared... (11).
The Brahman and the Sacrificer consume the portion for Indra with the formula: "This oblation... (12).
The procedure for the liquor has been explained.

13 To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he gives the remainder of the milk to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, saying: "To the fathers who partake of the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Adoration! 14 He worships [the ancestors] with the verse: "May the Soma-loving fathers purify me. 15
Thus ends the eighth section (kaṇḍikā).
Now they offer two oblations: the Adhvaryu with the verse "Those who are equal," and the Pratiprasthātṛ with "Those who are kinsmen.
At the time of the Manotā hymn, he places the broth of the animals separately in individual vessels.
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he performs the secondary oblations (*upahoma*) with the horns and hooves.
There are eight *kuṣṭhikā*-hooves for each [deity].

Having filled a *kuṣṭhikā* and a hoof with the broth of the [victim] dedicated to the Aśvins, he offers with each pair of *kuṣṭhikā*-hooves using two mantras at a time from the eight-verse hymn beginning with "sīsena tantram."
He attaches [the parts] to the highest horn;
having offered oblation after oblation, he pours the remnants into his own consecration vessels and thrusts the hoof-bones and hooves into the Āhavanīya fire.
In this same manner, he performs the rite for the Sarasvatī with the following eight-verse hymn.
With the entire Anuvāka dedicated to Indra (9),

he establishes the Audumbara throne-seat— having a head-rest one cubit high, with side-boards reaching to the navel, and legs reaching to the knees, its slats woven from Muñja grass (10)— at the sacrificer’s station with the formula, "Thou art Mitra; thou art Varuṇa" (11).
The acts of approaching, sitting down, and consecrating with mantras are as in the Rājasūya sacrifice. 12.

While he is seated facing east upon that [seat], [the officiant] stands facing west and sprinkles him with the residues of the Aśvin cups, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you with the healing power of the Aśvins for the sake of splendor and Vedic luster. 13. In the same way, he sprinkles him with the Sārasvata cup using the subsequent mantra. 14.
"By the highest [glory] of Indra"—this is the ninth section (kaṇḍikā).
Having touched his two hands together with the words "Who art thou? Which one art thou?", the Adhvaryu offers the vyāhṛtis.

In this case, as in the *Rājasūya*, having summoned one who has an auspicious name, he touches his limbs according to their respective characteristics, saying, "May prosperity be my head," and so forth; then, having descended with the words, "With my two shanks, with my two feet," and having murmured, "I am established in power, I am established in the kingdom," he offers oblations with the verse, "The three gods... and touches his limbs according to their respective characteristics, saying, "My hair is effort," and so forth. (2) From the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the procedure is the same up to the *Avabhṛtha*.

(3) Regarding the *Avabhṛtha*, Āśmarathya says that one should offer five oblations with the verse, "O gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed... whereas Ālekhana says they should be offered in the *Āhavanīya* fire. (4)

Having consecrated the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) with the mantra, "O *avabhṛtha*, O *nicaṅkaṇa*," the sacrificer, having immersed himself while reciting, "May the waters be friendly to us; like one released from a wooden post," and having worshipped the sun with, "We have risen above the darkness," throws [the grass-bundle] toward the edge of the water with, "The noose of Varuṇa is loosened.

(5) The placing of the fuel-sticks and the worship are as in the animal sacrifice. (6) Having worshipped with, "He has returned," and having offered an oblation with, "Bhūḥ svāhā," the *Pitṛyajña* (ancestral sacrifice) is performed as before. (7)
One sacrifices an animal to Indra, the bestower of vital strength; 8.
a bull is the sacrificial fee; 9. [one offers] a pap of cooked rice to Āditya; 10.
And it is known from scripture: "He gives the calf to the eastern [quarter] and the mother to the northern. Thus the Kaukilī sacrifice is concluded.
"Desiring heaven, one should sacrifice with that"—
this is the tenth section.
"Desiring heaven, one should pile the Sāvitra [fire]."
In the animal sacrifice (paśubandha), the altar is piled.

When he is about to pile it, he procures one hundred and eighty-five gold bricks, as many pebbles as there are joints on the topmost phalanx of his finger, anointed with clarified butter; four *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks, and an unlimited number of *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.
Beginning with the formula "The six-heater," he proceeds with the ritual actions pertaining to the animal sacrifice.
It is known from tradition that one should sacrifice on the third day of the moon.

Having performed the northern boundary-marking (parigraha), one should drive a wooden pin (śaṅku) into the center of the site for the high altar (uttaravedi). Having drawn a circular line around it with the circumference of a chariot wheel for the Sāvitra fire-altar, one should fetch a green clump of Darbha grass with its roots, plant it in the center of the fire-site, and take five portions of clarified butter in the Juhū ladle. Having offered five oblations upon the Darbha clump with the formula "In unison with the year, with the months... and having leveled and sprinkled the ground, one completes the high altar up to the final sprinkling (vyāghāraṇa). Within the line, there are nine circular [enclosures].

Having drawn the line, having strewn it with sand, and having covered it with *darbha* grass, he fills the outer line with curds mixed with honey and with sugar-grits, and then dwells there. (6) When the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, he touches the *uttaravedi* altar with the formulas: "May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! Having taken the fire into himself with the two verses, "I take Agni first" and "The fire which belongs to us, O Fathers," and having touched the self-piled altar with the verse, "Those logs of yours, O Agni," he pours down sand with the formula, "Thou art the ash of Agni. He pours down saline earth with the formula, "Consciousness. (7)
While scattering them, he offers [the black portion] into the moon, meditating in his mind: "Let that which is black in the moon be here.

Having mixed the saline earth (*ūṣāḥ*) and the sand (*sikatāḥ*) with the verse, "Those bodies of yours which are dear," and having mixed the saline earth and the sand with the verse, "You are piled up, you are piled around," he encloses [the altar] with an unlimited number of pebbles (*śarkarāḥ*). Then, with the verses, "Swell up; let [the waters] come together unto thee," he spreads out the sand.
He does not confuse the lines.
On the inner half of the rear part, he places a water-pot with the formula: "Speech, I place thee upon the ocean; bringing good offspring, winning increase of wealth, for me, O vigorous one!
This is the eleventh section (kaṇḍikā).
On the ninth outer line, he places fifteen bricks representing the days of the waxing fortnight with the formulas beginning, "Consciousness," "Discernment," and so forth.
In the intervals between these days, he lays down fifteen *muhūrta*s with the formula, "The bright banner...
(1). Then, in the interior [of the altar], he lays down fifteen nights of the waxing fortnight with the formula, "The visible, the seen...
(2). In the intervals between those nights, he lays down fifteen *muhūrta*s of these nights with the formula, "The giver, the bestower... (3).
Then, within [the space], he lays down fifteen [bricks] for the days of the second fortnight, beginning with "The Prastuta" and "The Viṣṭuta.

(5) In the intervals between these days, he lays down fifteen Muhūrtas, beginning with "Savitṛ, the Impeller. (6) Then, within [the space], he lays down fifteen nights of the second fortnight, beginning with "The Pressed" and "The Pressing. (7)

In the intervals between these nights, he lays down fifteen *muhūrta*s with the formula, "The accuser, the one who permits" (8). Then, in the next [interval], he lays down twelve *pūrvapakṣa*s (the first fortnights) with the formula, "Purifying, about to purify" (9).
Then, in the next [interval], he lays down twelve *aparapakṣa*s (the latter fortnights) with the formula, "The powerful, the more powerful" (10).
Then, within the inner [space], he lays down thirteen bricks named after the months, beginning with "Aruṇa, Aruṇarajas. Then he lays down sand, beginning with "ejatkā, jīvatkā.
Then, within the inner [space], he lays down fifteen bricks representing the muhūrtas, beginning with "idānīm, tadānīm."
Then, within the intermediate space, he lays down six sacrificial rites and three names of four syllables: "Agniṣṭoma," "Ukthya," and "Agni-ṛtu.
Then, at the navel, he lays down four names of the year: "Prajāpati," "Saṃvatsara," "Mahān," and "Ka.
He lays down four *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks in the quarters with the formulas: "Bhūḥ! Agni and the earth and me," and so forth.

He lays down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the formula, "Fill the world. Having brought earth from the *cātvāla* pit, he spreads it over the altar with the verse addressed to Vaiśvānara, "Thou art asked about heaven. That constitutes the layer.
He mutters the *ārohaṇa* (ascending formula); he mutters the *avarohaṇa* (descending formula). He worships with the *upasthāna* (homage): "Thou alone knowest thyself; who thou art, that thou art.
He performs [the rite] as if accompanied by a thousand.
Having made the cows [the offerings], the sacrificer worships them with the formulas for their gathering and dispersal: "Thou art the *saṃvatsara*, thou art the *parivatsara*," and so on.
(23) To the north of the highest brick, he offers goat’s milk with an *arka* leaf.
(24) With the formula, "O Agni, thou art Rudra," he throws the *arka* leaf upon a place where cattle do not pass, or he places it within a termite mound. (25)
Sitting behind the fire facing east, the Hotṛ recites the *saṃcita-ukthya* with the Anuvāka beginning "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.
Thus ends the twelfth Kaṇḍikā.

He commences the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-karma*) beginning with the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) and following the Cāturhotra ritual, which is the same up to the *atimukti* offerings.
Having offered the *atimukti* oblations, he offers four ladlings (*caturgṛhīta*).
(2) "Thou, O Agni, art Rudra"—this is the form of the *Śatarudrīya*. Another four ladlings (3) "O Agni and Viṣṇu"—this is for the *Vasordhārā*. Another four ladlings (4).
"O food-eater," with these words, he performs the oblation of food. Another portion taken four times [with the ladle]:
"Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues"—this is the Viśvaprī offering.

Another portion taken four times: "I offer you with the intent of the Vasus, with the wave of the Rudras, with the splendor of the Ādityas, with the will of all the gods, with the love of the Maruts—Svāhā!"
With the residue of those [libations], the sacrificer wipes his face with the section beginning, "The queen, the radiant one" (RV 10.75.8).
Then he offers twenty-one oblations, one by one with each mantra, according to the section beginning, "To Asu, svāhā! To Vasu, svāhā! (TS 4.4.11).

From the gathering of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) onwards, the ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) is undertaken; it is the same up to the offering of the omentum (*vapā*).
When the omentum has been offered, he gives four-year-old female mules as the sacrificial fee for each brick.

(11) If he is unable to provide so many fees, he should have the Brahmins drink as many bowls of stirred gruel, or have them eat as many portions of boiled rice. (12) By that very means, his desire is indeed fulfilled. (13)
One should give a pregnant heifer, or gold, and a garment.
Having performed that which precedes the *manotā* [verse], he takes a draught of broth for Mṛtyu with a vessel made of udumbara wood, using the formula:
"For the wise Pavamāna. The taking and the setting down [of the draught] are performed with these two verses.
"Furthermore, the Nāciketa fire itself should be the 'seizer of death' (mṛtyugraha). 17.
After its *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, there is a subsequent oblation (*anuhoma*). 18.
When about to offer it, he should touch water, [reciting]: 'Thou art lightning; strike away my evil. 19.
Then he offers [the oblation] with the mantra: "Away death, away hunger.
(20) Then, having offered, he should touch water with the mantra: "Thou art rain; cut off my evil. (21) His consumption [of the portion] follows the *iḍā*. (22)

He consumes [the portion]; he is a consumer of it, thus "one who consumes the nectar" (amṛtabhakṣa). Having consumed it, he establishes the vital breaths within himself with the remainder of the section beginning "Mandrayābhibhūtiḥ. From this point onward, the ritual procedure regarding the animal sacrifice is the same.
"The Sāvitra [fire] is completed.
Thus ends the thirteenth Kaṇḍikā. By this, the Nāciketa [fire] is explained. 1.
There are no lines here.

Twenty-one gold bricks, or pebbles smeared with clarified butter, are placed upon the navel itself at the time of laying down, using the formulas of the Anuvāka "Thou art the world; thou art heaven," one for each brick, whether the altar be square or circular.
Regarding this, some build it on the Uttaravedi during the Paśubandha sacrifice; such are the variations explained in the Brāhmaṇa.
We shall enumerate them:

at an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), a *soma* sacrifice, a sacrificial session (*sattra*), a thousand-fold sacrifice, or a sacrifice where all one's possessions are given away; or wherever the greatest number of oblations (*āhuti*) are offered—there the fire-altar is to be built.
At a sacrificial session, one who desires firm standing, fame, offspring, cattle, heaven, or prosperity should build it according to the available space and as prescribed in the traditional texts.

In all cases, the commencement is from the east, the movement is clockwise, and the conclusion is toward the north. (8) One desiring cattle should pile it in the *pāṅkta* manner: five bricks in each direction and one in the center.
(9) One who desires preeminence, glory, or progeny should pile it in the *trivṛt* manner: seven in the east, three in the south, seven in the west, three in the north, and one in the center. (10)
One who desires preeminence should begin from the middle and lay down the line toward the north. 11 One who desires heaven should begin from the west and lay down the line toward the east.

12 If he should desire, "May I be radiant, glorious, and possessed of spiritual luster," he should creep forward from the [Dhiṣṇya] hearths of the Agnīdhra and the Mārjālīya toward the Hotṛ’s Dhiṣṇya, saying: "That which has gone eastward, the glorious one—may it cover me with radiance, glory, and spiritual luster. 13

Now, if he should desire, "May they have great faith in me; may they bring abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās)," then while the sacrificial fees are being brought, he should offer an oblation with the sruva-spoon into the Āhavanīya fire, having drawn [the ghee] with the formula: "Come hither, O East!
Come hither, O East! May the East, enjoying it, partake of the clarified butter, svāhā!
The subsequent ritual from the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick onwards is the same.
The Nāciketa [fire-altar] is completed. 17. By this, the Cāturhotra [altar] is explained. 18.
As many bricks or pebbles as there are words [in the formulas], they are smeared with ghee. 19.

At the time of placing the supporting bricks, he places them facing north in front of a clump of *darbha* grass, reciting the *daśahotṛ* formula with each respective mantra: four bricks of the *saṃbhāras*, two of the wives, [and one] for the heart-cup (*hṛdayagraha*).
In the same manner, he places the *caturhotṛ* formula facing east to the south; the *pañcahotṛ* formula facing north behind.
To the north, facing east, [he places] the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ; 23 above, facing east, the Saptahotṛ;
24 there are five steps here for the *saṃbhāra* materials, and the remaining ones for the wives. 25
The subsequent [rites] beginning with the *svayamātṛṇā* are the same;
thus concludes the Cāturhotra [offering].
This is the fourteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
By this, the Vaiśvasṛja rite is explained.
1. As many as are required, gold bricks or pebbles are smeared with [clarified butter] according to the mantra. 2.

At the time of laying them down, starting from the front of the northern navel, he piles around the fire toward the right with these three anuvākas beginning with "That which is immortal and that which is mortal. 3.
There are three layers, corresponding to three sections (anuvākas). 4. From the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick onwards, the procedure is the same as before, except for the recitation (*anuśaṃsana*).
5. He performs the recitation with this section: "The eastern direction of the verses is called the great one. 6.

In the *rātrisattras* ending with the hundred-night sacrifice, in the three *sārasvata* sessions accompanied by the *mahāvrata*, in the *kāṭhaka-cāturmāsyas*, in the six-day periods of the *sādhyas* (excluding those), in the *viśvasṛjām ayana*, and in the two thousand-year sacrifices of Prajāpati, the *vaiśvasṛja* fire is prescribed.
(7) If they should perform sorcery while setting out, he should touch the site of the *uttaravedi* with these mantras.
(8) Or rather, on the third turn, he should offer the *vaiśvasṛja* [oblation] for one who is very dear to him and well-known. (9)
One who is performing the Sāvitra, Nāciketa, Cāturhotra, Vaiśvasṛja, and Āruṇaketuka [fires] together should pile them even at a Soma sacrifice.

The Sāvitra is the first layer; the Lokampṛṇā is the second; the Nāciketa is the third; the Lokampṛṇā is the fourth; the Cāturhotra is the fifth; the Vaiśvasṛja is the sixth; and the Āruṇaketuka is the seventh.
He draws a cup from the broth of the *savanīya* animal for Death. 12.
He who builds these fires either separately or by combining them gives both kinds of sacrificial fees: the fees for the ritual (*kratu*) as prescribed, and the fees for the fire-altar (*agni*). 13.
In this case, they are not combined because they are performed separately. 14.

Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī; [one should sacrifice] with the curdled milk (*vāmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. The Āruṇaketuka is explained in the Brāhmaṇa.
One desiring heaven should sacrifice day by day with the *divaḥ śyenī* [oblations] and with the *apādyā* [oblations].
These have been explained by the Brahmana. 18.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.
One should sacrifice with the animals intended for specific desires on either the new moon day or the full moon day. 1.
The ritual procedure for these is like that of the established animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*).
"To Vāyu, a white [animal]"—these have been explained by the Brāhmaṇa.

In the places belonging to the *āvāpika* (inserted) offerings, he deposits six verses according to the respective deity: two each for the omentum (*vapā*), the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and the oblation (*havis*).
"Pīvo'nnāṃ rayivṛdhaḥ sumedhāḥ"—these [verses] are recited in their respective order according to their characteristic marks (liṅga). 5.

In all rites involving malevolent magic (ābhicaraṇika), the officiating priests (ṛtvij) proceed wearing red turbans (uṣṇīṣa), red garments, and with the sacred cord (nivīta) suspended around the neck; they are "malhāḥ. 6.
This means they are "maṇilāḥ" (wearing neck-ornaments). 7.
"One should sacrifice an uneven [number]," so it is said; regarding the deity, there is an inquiry:
it may be for Āditya, or for Prajāpati, or for the deities of the Ekādaśinī, or for whichever deity the pregnant ones belong to. "Paryāriṇī" means one who has given birth after a long interval.
"The wooden sword is the sacrificial post"—this refers to a sacrificial post shaped like a wooden sword, or one belonging to the fire-hall attendant (agnyāgārika).
"The horse of Tvaṣṭṛ"—this refers to a male horse which he mounts. "At the junction of the waters and the plants"—this occurs either during the rainy season or at the onset of autumn.
Alternatively, at the junction of water and plants, there is the "bifurcated sacrificial post" (viśākha-yūpa);
that which is above the cord is the bifurcated part. Or rather, from the top, both branches—each having eight facets—should be provided with a head-piece (caṣāla). [The animals] are:
a bull with horns pointing forward, a bull with horns pointing downward, a cow, a heifer, a milch-cow, a calf, a young bull, an ox, one released again, and a gayal; these are the bovine animals.
One sacrifices a barren cow to Anila; a barren cow to Vāc; a barren cow to Śraddhā; a bull to Brahmán. 17.
"The cows have come," are the secondary offerings (upahoma). 18. A barren cow to Mṛtyu. 19.
Therein, one should offer the husband [as an oblation] (20). To Sūrya and Candramas, one offers a white and a black [bull] at a single sacrificial post (21).
To the Waters, a cow that miscarries (22).
Therein, one should offer water with the mantra,
"To Bhaga, the female [animal].
For those animals that follow the Āśvina [offering], the procedure is according to the sequence of the hymns (sūkta).
Thus ends the sixteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

When the bull has grown old among the cows, one should whisper into the ear of a young bull with the two verses beginning, "Of tawny form" (RV 6.28.1) and "That [Soma] of ours, the most potent" (RV 9.101.7).
Then he lets it loose among the cows with the verse, "This young one" (RV 10.190.1).
Then he seizes the Jīrṇa animal—either one dedicated to Prajāpati, Indra, or Tvaṣṭṛ.
He recites "Homage to the Greatness" during the introductory rite (upākaraṇa).
With the third verse he offers the omentum; with the fourth, the oblation; with the fifth, the portion for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Having offered an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, he immolates a barren goat.
"One desiring prosperity should immolate [an animal] for Vāyu"—thus the deities have been stated.
He performs the introductory rite with the verse addressed to Vāyu: "O Vāyu, come hither, thou who drinkest the pure."
While the fire is being carried around [the victim], he offers oblations with the words: "For intention thee! For desire thee! (9).
He recites over it as it is being led toward the north: "Thou art the fourth, the controller, the mistress" (10).
He recites over it as it is being struck down: "Thou art a goat, the abode of wealth" (11).
"Stretching the thread," with these words he offers the omentum (vapā). "Weave it without flaw for the two who urge on," with these words he offers the oblation (havis).
"Thou art the oblation of the mind," with these words they consume the remnants of the oblation.
It has been said that this [cow] belongs exclusively to three [persons].
Regarding this very cow, there is only one non-sacrificial ground (*adevayajana*): namely, when a cloud appears over her once she has been seized.
If a cloud should appear over her once she has been seized, he should either cause her to enter the waters, or the sacrificer himself should consume her entirely day after day.

The *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* have been explained by the Brāhmaṇa. (18) One appends [the formula] "In this Brahman... to the *abhyātāna* offerings. (19) It is known from scripture: "If one should desire success through a particular ritual act, one should offer [these oblations] therein; he indeed succeeds through that ritual act. (20)
Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā).
One should perform the optional sacrifices (kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ) on either the new moon day or the full moon day. These have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa.

Between the *samidhyamānavatī* and the *samiddhavatī* verses, he places two *dhāyyā* verses containing the word "pṛthu-pāja. Or rather, they follow the specific instruction; the two *ājyabhāga* offerings should contain the verbal root corresponding to the desire for which the sacrifice is performed, because they serve that purpose and possess its characteristic mark. Or they may have those same deities. Or they may be the archetypal ones.
In the absence of an instruction, the archetype is to be understood.
The two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter: "O you of most wondrous fame...

and "O Agni, mortals bearing oblations praise you, the god; I deem you Jātavedas; may you carry the offerings in succession. These two are thus handed down in the tradition. 7. Regarding the verses beginning with "I invoke both of you, Indra and Agni," the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* formulas are determined by their characteristic marks (*liṅga*) according to the order in which they were previously handed down. 8.

In the former case, the *puro'nuvākyā* is that which has the deity's name in the first half-verse (*ardharca*), while the *yājyā* is that which has it in the latter half-verse. Or rather, it may be the reverse of this. The remaining [options] are for the purpose of providing alternatives.
Alternatively, the subsidiary offerings (upahoma) there are uncertain;
we shall enumerate them [later].
One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rakṣoghna on the night of the new moon, because of the efficacy for the successful completion of that rite.

There should be a reduction of the time for the new moon (amāvāsyā) by fifteen [muhūrtas]. He recites the *sāmidhenī* verses beginning with "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ," which are directed against demons (*rakṣoghnī*) and recited in their regular order.
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are "vi jyotiṣā" and so forth.
Thus ends the eighteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
One who is about to set out for battle should offer a pap (caru) to Āditya.
Having reached the battlefield, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds (dvādaśakapāla) to Vaiśvānara.
With the same rope by which one would capture an excellent cow, he should address the rival's cow; or he should leave it in his stall. He should bind *balbaja* grass to the fuel-bundle.
He should sprinkle those [grass blades] together with the fuel.
With the verse beginning "Sarasvatyājyabhāge," clarified butter becomes the oblation (6).
Since it is said, "The sprinkling is with clarified butter; they purify themselves with clarified butter," all the sprinklings and purifications are performed with clarified butter (7).
One should employ two *dhāyyā* verses from the *Mānava-ṛc*, specifically two out of these [verses] beginning with "makṣū devavata" (8).
One should perform this very sacrifice after going to a place of habitation;
one should perform this sacrifice after going to the field of an enemy.
There, having dug up the southern half of the altar, one should spread the sacrificial grass over that with half [of the usual amount], and one should add half of the fuel-wood.
One who desires a village should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra and an oblation on seven potsherds to the Maruts.
12. He places the offering for Indra over the Āhavanīya fire; he places the offering for the Maruts over the Gārhapatya fire.
13. At the proper time, he sets down the offering for Indra; while the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, he sets down the offering for the Maruts. 14.

Now, where [the call is] "Recite for Indra," the *puro'nuvākyā* is dedicated to Indra; "Sacrifice to the Maruts," the *yājyā* is dedicated to the Maruts; "Recite for the Maruts," the *puro'nuvākyā* is dedicated to the Maruts; "Sacrifice to Indra," the *yājyā* is dedicated to Indra. One desiring a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and one on twelve potsherds to the Viśvedevas. In that case, having first made the cutting from the portion for Indra, he should make both cuttings from the portion for the Viśvedevas; then, the remainder of the portion for Indra is offered subsequently.
"Recite for Indra and for all the gods; sacrifice to Indra and to all the gods," he issues the command.
"In battles, [we invoke] Indra"—these are the invitatory and offering verses (yājyānuvākye).
This is the nineteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
The sacrificial fee is a garment previously worn by a teacher;
that is to say, one with variegated borders.
Having offered the *saṃjñānī* separately and having taken portions from all [the other offerings], he recites the invocation for all the deities and issues the command.
The invitatory and offering verses for the sacrifice to all the deities are "Agni is the first with the Vasus" and so forth.
One who has been expelled or is being expelled should offer a portion containing the word *dhārayat* (supporting) and remain [in that state] until they no longer expel him.
Now, one who is being expelled should take a footprint of the person expelling him while saying, "O Aditi, give your consent," and then depart.
From the house of one who speaks vulgarly about another, he should fetch rice grains;
he should separate the white ones from the black ones.
Those which are white, for them he should offer a *caru* oblation to Āditya.

Those [stalks] which are black, having bound them together on a black antelope skin and set them down, he releases his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*). Then, with the verse, "Come hither, O bounteous Maruts," he approaches the sacrificer.
With the words, "May the blessing be true," he scatters a portion of the footprints upon the upper garment of the sacrificer.
With the words, "Here is the mind," he pours the remainder over his chest.
The sacrifice is concluded successfully.

(13) If he should not obtain [the person], he should offer this portion to the Ādityas, pronouncing the name of the obstructer and that of the clan: "I set aside this portion for the Ādityas, so that such-and-one from such-and-one clan may be obtained.

(14) If he still does not obtain him, he should drive seven stakes of *aśvattha* wood into the middle of the sacrificial post, saying: "I bind the Ādityas here, so that such-and-one from such-and-one clan may be obtained. Three [stakes] toward the east and four toward the north. (15)
If he should not understand this, he should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) to this very Sun; 16.
he should also bind the rays onto the fuel-bundle (idhma); 17.
he should place them upon the fire together with the fuel-bundle. 18.
Having understood [the omen], he offers a *caru* oblation of black rice (*kṛṣṇavrīhi*) to Varuṇa. 19. The sacrifice is concluded in the established manner.
20. Thus ends the twentieth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
One desiring long life should offer an oblation to Prajāpati consisting of one hundred kṛṣṇalas.
(1) One hundred gold kṛṣṇalas are equal in weight to either a kākiṇī or a māṣa.
(2) He pours them into clarified butter accompanied by the purifier-mantra. (3)
The cooking consists of mere dharma-materials.
At the time of the ritual performance, he cuts portions for eight deities; four for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, two for the *prāśitra*, and eight for the *iḍā*.
At the time of dividing into four parts, having gathered all [portions] into the *prāśitra*, he presents them to the *brahman* priest as a single unit.
Brahmā consumes them;
for the others, there is the removal of the consumption. He places the *caru* for Sūrya, enclosed by two gold plates, upon the altar.
At each fore-offering (prayāja) of that sacrifice, he offers a kṛṣṇala weight of gold. Having set aside the two golden plates, he proceeds with the sacrificial porridge (caru).
These very two golden plates constitute the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
"To Agni the Giver, a cake on eight potsherds"—these are three [offerings].
Of these, the third is an offering of mixed substances dedicated to Prajāpati.
Some say it consists of curd, honey, ghee, water, parched grains, and rice; for them, it is a modification of the clarified butter (ājya) offering.

When honey and water are mixed, the primary rule regarding their respective natures applies. 16. "The clarified butter is not purified; both are well-shining"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. 17.
"One should cause the offerings to Agni and Soma to coalesce in [the offering] to Indra"—this means that one should place the sacrificial oblations together. 18.
He should apply this plaster to this [altar]. 19.
"O Brahman, may I destroy the people," [with these words] everything belongs to Bṛhaspati. 20.
He should employ two verses addressed to the Maruts as the invitatory and offering verses. 21.
Then he places this three-layered [cake] upon eleven potsherds arranged in rows. This is the twenty-second section (kaṇḍikā).

Having placed the first sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) on the fire and performed everything up to the heating around it, he places the second, larger one upon that; having performed everything up to that point for it as well, he places the third, largest one upon that.

At the time of the performance, one should sacrifice to the first deity from the southern half, to the second from the middle, and to the third from the northern half. It has been stated that one cuts portions while making them reach all [the deities]. One recites three verses beginning with "In the eastern direction, you, O Indra," alternating their order.

Having recited the first [verse] as the invitatory formula (*anuvākyā*), one should sacrifice with the middle [verse]. Having recited the middle [verse] as the invitatory formula, one should sacrifice with the last [verse]. Having recited the last [verse] as the invitatory formula, one should sacrifice with the first [verse].
In this way, all the sacrificial offerings (*yājyās*) and invitatory formulas (*puro’nuvākyās*) come to be. He offers the *sarvapṛṣṭhā* oblation.
With the formula, "For Indra, [the offering] belonging to the Rathantara," he places the twelve cakes upon the upper potsherds according to the traditional recitation.
At the time of the ritual performance, he sacrifices to the first deity from the eastern half. In this manner, he sacrifices to the others, moving clockwise, ending in the north.

It is said that he recites [the hymn] all around. (11) He recites the six verses beginning with "abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ" in alternating order. (12) He should not utter the *vaṣaṭ* call upon a *bṛhatī* verse. (13)
One should cause the four syllables of the *anuvākyā* to pass into the *yājyā*.
We consider that they thus complete both the *anuṣṭubh* and the *paṅkti* meters.

Having recited the verse, "We cry out to thee, O Hero, like unmilked cows; to the Lord of this world, the beholder of heaven," ending with "O Indra, the Lord," one should sacrifice with the verse, "For we invoke thee alone. (14–16)
Thus ends the twenty-second section (*kaṇḍikā*).

Having recited [the verses] beginning with "We poets indeed invoke thee for the winning of booty; thee, O Indra, the lord of the virtuous, men invoke in battles" and ending with "Thou art a fortress," he should sacrifice with the verse "O Hero, we praise thee, the possessor of light.
He places the fourth verse of these [verses], "Never indeed art thou neglectful," [in its proper position].
It has been stated: "To Agni Bhrājasvat, a cake on eight potsherds.

At the time of the fourfold division [of the cake], having set aside three balls for Sūrya, he gives those balls to the sacrificer with the verses: "Upward that Jātavedas," "The seven bay horses in the chariot," and "The bright face of the gods has risen. (Sūtra 4) The sacrificer eats them. (Sūtra 5)
One desiring a village should offer the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
He cooks it in fresh butter.
With the formulas beginning "Thou art firm," he lays the enclosing sticks around the fire, one by one with each mantra.
"Thou art the support," [with these words] the secondary offerings (upahoma) are made. 9.
For one who has been long ill, or for one who desires, "May I reach the full span of life," he should offer this sacrifice. 10. There are five [oblations] beginning with that to Agni.
At the time of setting out the vessels, he employs a four-cornered vessel made of *khadira* wood. And a golden ear-ring (*pravarta*) made from a *śatamāna* weight of gold. 11.
Furthermore, it should be of such a measure as he thinks will suffice for as many years as he intends to live.

Having looked at the clarified butter with the words, "That which was fresh became butter," and having silently taken four portions of butter into a vessel of *khadira* wood at the time of taking the butter, he places that *khadira* vessel to the north of the *dhruvā* at the time of setting it down, and puts the stirring-stick (*pravarta*) into it.
Thus ends the twenty-third section.
At the time of the subsidiary offerings (upahoma), he offers four oblations with the formulas "Thou art the breath of the Aśvins," etc., one by one.

Having offered each oblation, he pours clarified butter over the fire-wood (pravarta) with the formulas, "Thou art the ruler (rāj)," "Thou art the far-ruler (virāj)," "Thou art the sovereign ruler (samrāj)," and "Thou art the self-ruler (svarāj).
Having carried the clarified butter from the khadira-wood ladle around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it on the southern corner of the altar (vediśroṇi).
Then the sacrificer looks at it, saying, "The stream of clarified butter, the path of immortality.
Then the Brahman priest takes his right hand;
the other officiating priests, having taken hold of the hand of the Brahman, lead the sacrificer around him, saying, "With the purifying hymn (stoma), we [lead] thee."
Then the sacrificer drinks the clarified butter from the gold vessel with the verse:
"O Agni, bestow this [butter] upon me for life and splendor. He addresses the one who is consuming it with the same formula.
Having lifted up the gold and washed it, he hands it back to the sacrificer with the verse: "Bestowing long life upon you from every side."

Then the sacrificer, having sipped water and taken hold of it, ties it on his right ear from left to right, saying: "Thou art life; thou art all-encompassing life; thou art complete life; thou art total life; may total life be mine; may I attain total life. (10) With the remainder of the section beginning "Agni is long-lived," the Adhvaryu takes hold of his right hand. (11) The sacrifice is concluded in the established manner. (12)
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section (kaṇḍikā).
Having offered the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) for Indra and Varuṇa, he should offer the curd-mixture (payasyā) for Indra and Varuṇa.
Having removed it from the fire and decorated it, he places the sacrificial cake into the curd-mixture.
With this very [verse], he covers it and places it down.
Then, from this [spot], he spreads out the *payasyā* toward each direction with the verse, "O Indra and Varuṇa, that body of yours which is to be hidden.
With these same [verses], he gathers it back together again.
With the words "unreleased," he joins the ends of the mantras.
He cuts portions from the cake together with the curd-mixture.
"O Indra and Varuṇa, whoever is weary in your fire"—these are the secondary offerings (upahomas).
It has been stated: "To Agni Saṃvarga, a cake on eight potsherds.
(9) He recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses beginning with "Harness, O you who best invoke the gods! (10) He concludes with the regular verse. (11)
*kuvitsa* and *gaviṣṭaye* are the invitatory and offering verses (12);
*yasyājuṣat* and *vidmā hi te* are the two concluding offering verses (13).
On the full moon day of the Citrā constellation, one should perform the Citrā sacrifice; it consists of seven offerings beginning with that to Agni (14).
"O Agni, come to us with cattle"—these are the secondary offerings (upahoma).
Having settled in a place where the stars are abundant, one desiring rain should sacrifice with the Kārīrī offering.

Having added fuel to the fires, the sacrificer, having passed behind the Āhavanīya fire to the south and sat down, puts on a black garment with a black fringe, saying: "Thou art of the Maruts; thou art the vigor of the Maruts. 17.
With the mantra, "O Maruts, delight the illusory hawk," he drives back the wind from behind. With "Come, O Wind," he generates the east wind.
A black horse stands in front, facing westward.
He crushes him with this garment [while reciting], "Roar!
(21). If he should cry out, shake himself, or void excrement or urine, one should know: "It will rain" (22).
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section.

Having offered the eight oblations named after the winds, beginning with "The east wind rains," he spreads a black antelope skin within the altar-site with its neck to the east and the hair upwards. Upon it, having mixed dates or *karīra* fruits with honey and black sesame, he forms three balls. Wrapping them in lotus leaves and lifting them up, he secures the ends of the black antelope skin with a black cord, saying, "Thou art the tethering-rope of the stallion. (1) On the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) stands a three-pole cart with its pole pointing eastward. (2) This refers to the roof-coverings. (3)
With the words, "The gods who possess wealth," he should fasten a black antelope skin to the front post;
this remains attached for a day and night.
If it should rain, he should offer only the *piṇḍī* oblations.
If it should not rain, he should fasten [the offering] to the middle post with the verse, "O gods, grant us protection.
(7) It remains fastened for a day and night. (8) If it should rain, he should offer only the *piṇḍī* [cakes]. (9)
If it should not rain, he should tie [the offering] to the hind leg with the verse, "May the gods grant us prosperity" (RV 7.104.16).
It remains tied for a day and night.
If it should rain, he should offer only the *piṇḍī* cakes.
If it does not rain on the day of the *śoṣa*, he offers three oblations of black rice, beginning with the *dhāmacchat* [and others].
Having placed those [oblations] down, he spreads a black antelope skin upon the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
The officiating priests proceed wearing black turbans, black garments, and with their sacred cords suspended over the right shoulder.
"Trvaṃ tyā cidacyuta" are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses (16).
At the time of the secondary offerings (*upahoma*), he binds the balls (*piṇḍī*) with each of these mantras, beginning with "divā cit tamaḥ kṛṇvanti" (17).
Some say he offers them as oblations (18).
Then he consecrates their smoke with the mantra:
On the heap of rubbish, he fills a black, unbaked pot with water, saying, "Create rain.
If it should break, one should know that it will rain.
It is tied to either a support-post of the cart or to a peg with a black sheepskin.
He sprinkles it with the formula, "Thou art born from the water" (abjā asi). Upon it, he acquires knowledge concerning horses.
Having established a clump of *varṣāhū* grass on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he offers the *varṣāhū* with the verse, "Make the earth swell up" (unnambhaya pṛthivīm).
Some say that he offers a ladle full of water.
Then he throws it into the Āhavanīya fire.
Then he recites the mantra over its smoke: "Golden-haired, in the expansion of the atmosphere..."
With the verse, "The gods who have their portion in heaven," he shakes the black antelope skin over the Āhavanīya fire with its neck pointing upward; the dissection is performed from the outside.
A black garment, a black horse, and a black cow are the sacrificial fees.
Then follows the Sākamedha sacrifice: an oblation on eight potsherds for Agni, free from obstacles.

Its subsidiary offerings are the names of the winds (*vātanāmāni*), with which he binds the balls of dough and with which he offers oblations, and with which he consecrates the smoke. As before, he places it on the fire in three layers; however, the middle layer consists of barley.
There is an oblation for Indra and Viṣṇu.
He places the two *dhāyyā* verses, *pra so agne* and *itthā hi soma*, in the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters (17).
He concludes with the verse containing the word "three": *agne trī te vajrin trī ṣadhasthā* (18).
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* are the two verses beginning with *saṃ vāṃ karmaṇā ubhā jigyathuḥ* (19).
The two concluding *saṃyājyā* verses are used for the subsequent offerings. 20.
Gold, a linen garment, and a cow constitute the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). 21.
One should offer a pap (*caru*) dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati upon the birth of a Kṣatriya. 22.
"A golden chain is the sacrificial fee, the sacrificial fee.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section (kaṇḍikā).
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter (praśna).
A universal monarch should perform the horse sacrifice; even one who is not a universal monarch may do so when he settles at a sacred place of sacrifice named Citrā,
where the waters to the east are pleasant, easy to enter, and flow away.
On the full moon day of Caitra, he performs the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice. On the subsequent new moon day of that month, he performs the Saṃjñānī sacrifice.

On the subsequent new moon day of that month, they bring the great officiating priests who do not travel by foot.
Every day they bring the other [formulas] up until the Subrahmaṇyā. Having performed the New Moon sacrifice, he proceeds toward the sacrificial ground.

With the thirty-one salutations: "Homage to the Seer, homage to the Overseer, homage to the Observer; homage to the Proclaimer, homage to the Proclaimer-nearby, homage to the Proclaimer-along; homage to the Hearer, homage to the Listener-nearby, homage to the One who exists, homage to the One who does not exist, homage to the Born, homage to the To-be-born, homage to the Past, homage to the Future; homage to the Eye, homage to the Ear, homage to the Mind, homage to Speech, homage to Brahman, homage to Austerity, homage to Peace," he worships the rising sun with these thirty-one salutations.
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
With the verses beginning "Homage to Agni, who dwells on the earth," he offers oblations according to their respective characteristics.

Having entered the *prāgvaṃśa* hall through the eastern door with the verse "Those paths of yours, O Savitṛ," and having placed a fuel-stick of cane (*vaitasa*) upon the Āhavanīya fire, he offers eleven full-spoon oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*). He offers eight with the verse "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," and three with the verse "O gods, exert yourselves among the gods."
Water is brought together from the four quarters;
in it he cooks the *brahmaudana* (the sacrificial rice for the Brahman).

Having placed a silver plate in a vessel, having taken out the *brahmaudana* into it, having poured abundant clarified butter over it, and having put a golden plate on top, he offers it to the four great officiating priests who are descended from Ṛṣis, drawing it across without breaking the connection.
To those who have consumed [the food], he gives four thousand gold coins (*niṣkas*), four chariots drawn by mules, and these two golden ornaments.
The girdle is made of *darbha* grass or *muñja* grass, twelve or thirteen *aratnis* in length.
He anoints it with the remnants of the *brahmaudana*.
They prescribe the forms of the horse: black, white, tawny, dappled, or reddish-tawny;

or one should sacrifice a white horse that has a small amount of black. It should be well-bred on both maternal and paternal sides, capable of bearing a load on its back, well-trained, a drinker of soma, and the son of two such soma-drinkers.

It is known that he is indeed a soma-drinker whom they cause to drink soma when he is a newborn infant before he has eaten grass. These two are indeed soma-drinkers: those two infants whom they cause to drink soma when they are born before they have eaten grass.

With a hundred princes, the Adhvaryu priest, standing in front facing west, sprinkles [the horse], saying: "Having sacrificed with this pure horse, may this king slay Vṛtra.
With a hundred fierce non-princes, the Brahman priest, standing on the south side facing north, sprinkles [the horse], saying: "Having sacrificed with this pure horse, may this king be unassailable."

Accompanied by a hundred charioteers and village headmen, the Hotṛ priest, standing behind and facing east, sprinkles [the horse] with the formula: "Having sacrificed with this pure horse, may this king become the ruler of this people—possessing many cattle, many horses, many goats and sheep, much rice and barley, much beans and sesame, much gold, many elephants, many male and female slaves, wealthy, prosperous, and possessing abundant increase of riches.

Accompanied by a hundred attendants and collectors, the Udgātṛ priest, standing to the north and facing south, sprinkles [the horse] with the formula: "Having sacrificed with this pure horse, may this king attain a full span of life."

Having submerged the reed-mat (*aiṣīka*) and having made the horse step onto the waterless spot between the place where it stood and the place where it steps, he recites over the horse's footprint three verses addressed to Viṣṇu—*idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, *pra tad viṣṇuḥ*, and *divo vā viṣṇuḥ*—and then consecrates the drops of the horse with the formula: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā!

Now he sprinkles it toward each of the directions:

With "To Indra and Agni, thee," [he places it] to the south facing north;
with "To Vāyu, thee," to the west facing east; with "To the Viśve Devas, thee," to the north facing south.
With "For the gods, thee," [he sprinkles] below;
with "For all the gods, thee," above; and with "For the earth, thee! For the intermediate space, thee! For the sky, thee! he sprinkles the remainder.

Having caused the sacrificer to recite the names of horses into the right ear of the horse, saying, "Vibhū [is] the mother; Prabhū [is] the father," and having offered the preliminary oblations with the formulas, "To Agni, svāhā! Svāhā to Indra and Agni!", he releases the horse with the formula, "Thou art the earth; for the past thee, for the present thee, for the future thee. He entrusts it to the guardians of the quarters with the words, "O gods, guardians of the quarters!
(9). A hundred men wearing armor guard it (10). They follow the horse without turning back (11).

one hundred princes mounted on chariots, equipped with armor and accompanied by armored charioteers; one hundred fierce non-princes, equipped with armor and accompanied by armored charioteers; one hundred Vaiśyas without paths; and one hundred Śūdras with protective enclosures.

15. Whosoever does not know it, having defeated him, they should take from his house food and drink. 16. Whatever food is prepared for non-Brāhmaṇas, that is their food. 17.

He offers an eight-potherd cake to Savitṛ in the morning.
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of that sacrifice, he makes oblations with the ladle turned upwards, saying: "Svāhā to the going forth! Svāhā to the departure! (1–2).
He offers the horse's tracks, saying: "Svāhā to the sound 'īm'! Svāhā to that which has been made 'īm'! (3).

"To the reddish-brown one, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā! To the white one, svāhā!"—these are the forty-eight forms of the horse; there is one extra. Here, a Brāhmaṇa who is a lute-player sings three verses: "Thou hast given," "Thou hast sacrificed," and "Thou hast cooked. At midday, [he offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Savitṛ Prasavitṛ; in the afternoon, [he offers] a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ.
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, the Hotṛ sits upon a golden cushion, desiring to recite the *pāriplava* and the *bhauvanya* sections.
To the south of that golden cushion sit the Brahman and the sacrificer; to the east, the Adhvaryu sits on a golden mat.
To the south, the lute-players and musicians sit down.

this year consists of thirty months. 4.
When the sacrifices have concluded, he gives to the two lute-players a hundred [cows] and a chariot yoked with horses;

(11) If [the animal] does not come to the deer-trap, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.

At the time for the animal sacrifice, he dedicates the *savanīya* animal to Agni, or alternatively, the eleven animals of the *aikādaśina* set.

At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), whatever wealth is located in the various directions belonging to non-Brāhmaṇas, he distributes it equally among the four quarters over a period of three days, giving it day by day.

(14) Thus ends the ninth section (*kaṇḍikā*). [He gives] the eastern direction to the *adhvaryu*; the southern to the *brahmán*; the western to the *hotṛ*; and the northern to the *udgātṛ*. He gives the chief queen to the Brahman priest; the favorite wife to the Hotṛ; the discarded wife to the Udgātṛ; and the Pālākalī to the Adhvaryu—so it is known. The day concludes with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. When the day has ended, they construct thirty-six couches made of Aśvattha wood around the Āhavanīya fire.

When the sun has set, the thirty-six Adhvaryus ascend their platforms and offer oblations of food throughout the entire night with ladles made of *khadira* wood. [The materials are: clarified butter, honey, rice grains, flattened rice, parched grain, flour-cakes, roasted grains, groats, lentils, and *priyaṅgu* rice grains.
Some authorities prescribe four groups of these. He offers with clarified butter; he offers with parched grain; he offers with roasted grains; he offers with groats.

With the formulas beginning "Svāhā to One," from these Anuvākas, he offers the odd-numbered verses with clarified butter and the even-numbered verses with food; finally, he concludes with clarified butter.
In this regard, some authorities recite the application of the mantras already employed and those yet to be employed.
Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).
"Vibhūrmātrā, prabhūḥ pitrā"—these are the names of the horses.

Having offered the *Aśvastomīya* oblation with the verse, "When you first cried out at birth," he recites these sections beginning with "Svāhā to One! over and over again as repetitions until the end of the night.
