He offers with "Svāhā to the one brought near" when [the horse] has been brought near; with "Svāhā to the one seized" when it has been seized; with "Svāhā to the one sacrificed" when it has been sacrificed. 6.
The wives adorn the horse—the chief queen (*mahiṣī*), the favorite (*vāvātā*), and the discarded one (*parivṛktī*).
7. Each of these has a hundred attendants. 8. [There are also] princesses, the wives of the *ugras*, non-royal [warriors], charioteers (*sūta*), and village headmen (*grāmaṇī*).

A thousand times a thousand gems—gold, silver, and those from the ocean—are woven into the hair-locks. With the word "bhūḥ," the chief queen (*mahiṣī*) places the gold ones on the left side of the forehead; with "bhuvaḥ," the secondary wife (*vāvātā*) places the silver ones on the right side of the forehead up to the ear; with "suvaḥ," the discarded wife (*parivṛktī*) places the ocean-born gems on the right side of the ear.
Maidens tie shells and gems into the hair-locks so that they do not slip out; or they may not.

Then they anoint him with his own country's clarified butter: "May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre," [saying this] the Mahiṣī anoints him with *gaulgulava* resin; "May the Rudras... [saying this] the Vāvātā anoints him with *kāsāmbava* resin; "May the Ādityas... [saying this] the Parivṛktī anoints him with *maustakṛta* resin. 12.

"Perfumed with guggulu resin, the horse has been brought forward for sacrifice. About to go forth to the gods, O steed, be a giver of splendor and a conqueror of worlds. "Perfumed with kāsāmbu resin, the horse has been brought forward for sacrifice. About to go forth to the gods, O steed, be a giver of splendor and a conqueror of worlds. "Perfumed with mustakṛta resin, the horse has been brought forward for sacrifice. About to go forth to the gods, O steed, be a giver of splendor and a conqueror of worlds"—with these mantras, one by one.
(13) Thus ends the fifteenth section. With the verse, "They harness the ruddy one," he yokes the horse to the pole on the right side of the yoke. (1)
With the verse, "They harness his two beloved [steeds]," he fastens the two side-pieces; with the verse, "Making a banner for those who have no banner," he attaches the flag to the chariot;
with the verse, "Like a cloud," he puts on the armor.
With the words, "With the bow, the cattle," he takes up the bow.
With the words, "As if about to speak," he touches the bowstring. With the words, "They move toward each other," he touches the two ends of the bow.
"Father of many, he whose son is many"—with these words he fastens the quiver upon his back.
"Standing on the chariot, he drives the steeds"—with this he consecrates the charioteer.
"They make loud noises, they whose hands are like bulls"—with this [he consecrates] the horses.
With the three verses beginning, "The fathers who sit at the sweet draught, bestowers of vitality," he worships the ancestors.

Having touched himself with the verse, "O straight-flying one, avoid us," and having taken the horse-whip with the words, "Not striking," he consecrates the driver's seat with the mantra, "Like a serpent with its coils.
With the fifth verse, "O tree, may you be firm of limb," he addresses the chariot.
"O you who are not bewildered, turn these back!"—thus sounding the drums with banners.
"The steed has stepped across with his strides; the steed has transcended"—having thus proceeded toward the northern limit, the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite, "O Savitṛ, those paths of yours.
Having made the horse smell the water with the words, "Smell the waters yourself, O steed," he turns it clockwise with the verse, "When the wind went to the waters."
From whence it departs, there it remains.

Having unyoked this horse with the formula, "I unyoke thee," and having placed the chariot upon the chariot-stand with the formula, "The oblation is its name," he cleanses the back of the horse with the formula, "May heaven be thy back.
Lājī3!
"O horse, eat this; let there be food for me," with these words the wives scatter the remnants of the horse's food. 29
"Whatever he eats that has been scattered [as seed], by that his offspring and kingdom prosper.
This is the sixteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

Having consecrated the horse with the mantra, "The steed has stepped forth; the steed has stepped across; heaven is your back," and having harnessed it according to the prescribed ritual, he sprinkles it and makes it drink.

If the fire, while being offered the drink, does not drink, one should offer it with the mantra: "The animal was Agni. 2. With the verses beginning "Kindled, anointing the heart of prayers," they become the *āprī* verses for the horse. 3. While the fire is being carried around, he offers the *apāvya* oblations with the verse: "May the ram protect thee with cooked offerings. 4.
They release the forest animals after they have been circumambulated by fire; a mare and a man-woman are also released.
A goat is led in front of the horse.

Having spread a garment of *tārpya* fiber, a woolen covering, and a golden cushion upon a branch of the *vetasa* reed, and having placed a golden disk (*rukmam*) on top, they slaughter the horse, the hornless goat, and the *gomṛga* upon it; the other animals upon branches of the *plakṣa* tree.
They quiet the horse with a blade of *śyāmūla* grass or with linen; the other animals with cords.
While the animal is being quieted, he offers two oblations with the formulas, "To the out-breath, svāhā! To the diffused breath, svāhā! Or [he offers them] once it has been quieted.
The *prastotṛ* priest stands in attendance with the *yāma-sāman*. 11.
With the words, "O Mother, O Ambālī, O Ambikā," the *pratiprasthātṛ* priest leads the wives forward. 12.

Having tied up their right-side hair-braids and loosened their left-side ones, and striking their right thighs while fanning themselves with their garments (*sig*), they circumambulate the horse three times from left to right, saying, "May you protect us. 13.
Having tied up their left [hands] and let down their right [hands], they walk around three times, striking their left thighs but not fanning themselves;
finally, they proceed clockwise as before,
completing nine rounds.
"O Amba, O Ambālī, O Ambikā!"—having thus addressed the queen as she lies down beside the horse;
this is the seventeenth section.

Having consecrated [the horse] with the mantra, "We invoke thee, the lord of hosts," he says, "May I be thou; mayst thou be me; may we be born of the lineage of Surā. Then, having interlaced these four feet, they lie down, interlacing the feet. This is the first section.
"Let us two together extend our four feet," saying this, they both extend their feet. 2.
"O fortunate one, dweller of Kāmpīla!"—having thus covered the queen and the horse with a linen garment, the Adhvaryu consecrates them with the mantra, "A bull for you two. 3.

"Place the testicle between your thighs"—having joined the male organ with the female organ, [the Adhvaryu says]; then the queen reproaches the horse with the words, "O Mother, O Motherly One, O Child of the Mother. 4.
"May he raise her upward"—thus the wives meditate upon her;
the chief queen murmurs three times, and the other wives murmur three times each with the subsequent verses.

Having murmured at the end all the verses containing the word *surabhi*, beginning with "I have performed [the praise] of Dadhikrāvan," and having sprinkled [the horse] with the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses, the chief queen (*mahiṣī*) prepares the incisions for the knife on the horse's back with golden needles according to the two verses beginning with "The Gāyatrī and the Triṣṭubh," from the shoulder-joint forward. Likewise, the favorite wife (*vāvātā*) uses silver needles according to the next two verses, from the shoulder-joint backward to the navel. Likewise, the discarded wife (*parivṛktī*) uses iron or lead needles for the remainder.
7. They prepare the incisions for the knife on the backs of the hornless goat and the Gomṛga silently.
8. With the verse, "Who flays you? Who dissects you? he flays the skin of the horse. 9.
"Candram" refers to the fat. One extracts it; there is no omentum for the horse, but one extracts it from the others.
Having cut off the ear, he fastens it onto the three limbs.
(13) There is no anus in a horse.
(14) When the omenta have been cooked, he places the omenta of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal upon a branch of cane to the north, above the fire. (15)
Thus ends the eighteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
To the south, on the branches of a Plakṣa tree, are the other animals.
Having offered the two preceding omenta—the Mahiman and the Parivapya—he takes portions from the omenta of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal, and issues the command.

"Recite the invitatory prayer for the omenta and the fat of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal for Prajāpati! "Give the command for the offering of the omenta and the fat of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal for Prajāpati!"—these are the two calls. Or alternatively: "Recite the invitatory prayer for the omenta and the fat of the moon[-dedicated] animals," or "Give the command for the offering of the omenta and the fat of the moon[-dedicated] animals.
Having taken portions from all the other omenta together, he issues the call:

"Recite the invitatory prayer for the omenta and the fat of the oxen, the goats, and the rams for the Viśvedevas! "Give the command for the offering of the omenta and the fat of the oxen, the goats, and the rams for the Viśvedevas!"—these are the two calls.

Having scattered the two additional portions of soil and offered the oblations, and having performed the purification at the *cātvāla* pit, they sit down on both sides of the *āgniṣṭha* post for the *brahmodya* (theological debate). The *brahmán* sits to the south; the *hotṛ* sits to the north.
The questions belong to the *hotṛ* from this section beginning with "What was the first thought? (*kiṃ svid āsīt pūrvacittiḥ*), while the answers belong to the *brahmán*.
They signal the northern victory to the *brahmán*.

For Prajāpati, they perform the dismemberment of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal, using their bones and hair without piercing them crosswise, acting according to the injunction: "Dissect the pig's dissection! 9.
He sets aside the blood of the horse for the sake of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. 10. He sprinkles the hoof of the horse and the thorn of the gayal over [the sacrificer] at the Māhendra hymn. 11.

He offers six oblations dedicated to Prajāpati with the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," prior to the consecration; and six oblations dedicated to the Prāṇabhṛts with the verse, "This one was born as the foremost.
He is consecrated upon a tiger skin or a leopard skin.
This is the nineteenth section.
They hold a bull’s hide over him as he is being consecrated.

With the verse, "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads," he places a golden image of the Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa—weighing a hundred mānas, consisting of a hundred syllables, and weighing a hundred kṛṣṇalas—upon the head of the sacrificer. He consecrates him with the residue of the two *mahiman* cups, saying: "At the impulse of Prajāpati, on the navel of the earth, with the arms of the atmosphere and the hands of heaven, I consecrate you with the sovereign rule of Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin. Thus he sprinkles him.

"Some say he sprinkles him with [water] belonging to Vāyu. (4) He makes offerings over the one being consecrated with the names of the months: "Madhu and Mādhava... (5) [He offers] six times to the seasons: "Svāhā to Spring! Svāhā to Summer! and so forth. (6)

"O Indra, strike down our enemies; cast low those who attack us. Whoever seeks to harm us, send him down into the lowest darkness. Drive away the Rakṣas, drive away the adversaries; break apart the jaws of Vṛtra. O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, crush the wrath of the enemy who seeks to harm us. With these two verses addressed to the Dispeller of Enemies (*vaimṛdhī*), the sacrificer wipes his face.
"His fuel-sticks stand upright," with these *āprī* verses dedicated to Prajāpati, he takes the hand of the one being consecrated.

"Prajāpati moves within the womb. Worship first Prajāpati, the one to be worshipped at the head of the gods worthy of sacrifice. May he grant us wealth and heroic strength; may he release for us the abundance of riches at our navel. These worlds are yours—the intermediate quarters, the cardinal directions, the distant realms, the hollows, and the heights. O Prajāpati, creator of all, source of life, O God, graciously accept this our oblation. With these six verses addressed to Prajāpati, he offers oblations after the consecration. (9) "The eastern direction of the directions... with these six verses, he offers the Apānabhṛt oblations. (10)
"Here the sacrificer performs the Viṣṇu-strides belonging to the Jagatī meter.
This is the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā).
At the time for the animal sacrifice, to the north and above the fire, he arranges the horse limb by limb upon a mat of vetasa reeds, facing eastward.
In this manner, he places the hornless goat facing west in front; behind it, the Gomṛga facing east;
and to the south, he places the other animals on branches of the Plakṣa tree.
The performance regarding the omenta follows the standard procedure.
He bows down at the end with the words "of the oblation.

With the verses, "The steed has stepped across with his strides," and "The steed has stepped across; heaven is your back," he offers the horse as a complete oblation (*sarvahuta*) along with the donkey, the hornless goat, and the *gomṛga* upon a mat of reeds (*vaitasa*). He makes offerings over the horse with the formulas, "To the young bull, svāhā! To the draft ox, svāhā!
At this point, he throws the mat after [the horse].
"It is known from scripture: 'All those who smell the fragrance of the horse that has been offered as an oblation become possessors of the worlds of merit.

Having performed the ritual with the *havis* and having made a portion of clarified butter (*ājya*), he offers the body-oblations (*śarīra-homa*) with each of these fourteen sections (*anuvāka*), beginning with 'The porcupines with his tusks, the frogs with his jaws.
The fifteenth is the *Divākīrtya*. The sixteenth is the *Araṇye'nuvākya*. The seventeenth, beginning with 'Heaven is your back,' is offered with clarified butter alone."
With these three sections beginning with "When you first cried out at birth," he offers thirty-six oblations of the Aśvastomīya;
[he offers] this thirty-sixth [oblation] with the verse, "With his strides he has stepped across.
According to some, he offers eighteen [oblations].
"Which worlds shall we now establish?"—with these two-footed verses (RV 10.129.6–7).
14. At the end, he makes an offering to the *Sviṣṭakṛt* with the cooked blood of the horse.
15. Thus ends the twenty-first section (*kaṇḍikā*).
He offers the first oblation with the neck of a wild ox; the second with a horse-hoof; the third with an iron water-pot.
The day concludes with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.
On the following day, the Sarvastoma Atirātra sacrifice with the Bṛhat-sāman is commenced.

At the time for the animal sacrifice, they immolate eleven oxen dedicated either to Prajāpati or to the Viśvedevas. A twelve-year-old bull, hornless, of every color, is to be immolated for all desires as the twelfth. [The ritual] is the same up to the *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory bath). Having performed the *avabhṛtha*, one causes an Ātreya man—named Śipiviṣṭa, bald, leprous, white, with reddish-brown eyes, and covered in moles—to descend into the *avabhṛtha* water; then one offers oblations upon his head with three [mantras]: "To Death, svāhā! To the murder of an embryo, svāhā! To Jumbaka, svāhā! 6.
To him he gives a hundred [cows] yoked with a cart;
some say "a hundred and a cart-yoked [cow].
Together, both the doers of merit and the doers of evil, grasping each other's hands, go forth toward the village. It is known from scripture: "They all become inhabitants of the world of merit."
There are nine white barren cows for Sūrya as the Anūbandhyā victims.
Now, according to some, there are red ones for Indra, white ones for Sūrya, and white-backed ones for Bṛhaspati.
Or, in this case, he sacrifices them in pairs.
The spotted goat, the kikidīvi bird, and Vidīgaya—these three, belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, are offered;
the one for Pātnīvata, the one for Agni, the one for Indra-Agni, and the one for the Aśvins are sacrificed at the Viśāla sacrificial post.
Thus ends the twenty-second section (kaṇḍikā).

Now, according to some: among the Traita animals, he sacrifices the first-born to Kālakābhra and the Aśvins at the middle Viśālayūpa; their middle-born to Ūrj at the southern [Viśālayūpa]; and their last-born to Pṛthivī at the northern [Viśālayūpa]. Following these, he offers the animal-cake oblations for them—a ten-oblation Mṛgāreṣṭi beginning with "To Agni Amhomuc, a cake on eight potsherds.
However, the Sviṣṭakṛt and Iḍā portions are the same.
The invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) are according to their respective characteristics, beginning with "I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise one" (RV 10.2.7).
4. He performs the *traidhātavīya* sacrifice. 5. At that [sacrifice], he gives a thousand [cows]. 6.
Having moved out [of the sacrificial ground], some authorities prescribe a large sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

Regarding this, they say: "When the sacrifice is completed, one should offer twelve *brahmaudana* rice-messes; one should sacrifice with twelve offerings. However, one should not do it in that way. When the sacrifice is completed, one should offer exactly twelve *brahmaudana* rice-messes. At these, he gives twelve hundred [cows] on each successive day.
"Three tawny ones for the spring"—with these seasonal animals he sacrifices throughout the year.

Now, according to some: those for the spring belong to Agni; those for the summer belong to Indra; those for the rainy season belong to the Maruts or Parjanya; those for the autumn belong to Indra and Varuṇa; those for the winter belong to Indra and Bṛhaspati; and those for the cool season belong to Indra and Viṣṇu.
"For the year, with a broad chest"—with these sacrificial animals he performs the Paśubandha sacrifice every two months.
The Aśvamedha is concluded. (13) Thus ends the twenty-third section.
The Puruṣamedha consists of five days. (1)
Either a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya may sacrifice;
he obtains vigor and heroism, and he attains all individual successes. There are eleven Agniṣomīya victims at eleven sacrificial posts.
The days [of the sacrifice] are like those of the Pañcaśāradīya. The Agniṣṭoma is the penultimate [day].
Having offered the three Sāvitrī oblations—"O God Savitṛ," "That of Savitṛ," and "All things, O God Savitṛ"—on the middle day, he dedicates the animals.
Having dedicated two sets of eleven [animals], he dedicates the human victims.
"He offers a Brahmin for Brahman"—this is according to the traditional recitation. 8.
They hold these [animals] between the sacrificial posts. 9.
Having stood to the south of those animals that have been dedicated, the Brahman priest recites the Puruṣa hymn, beginning with "The thousand-headed Puruṣa," followed by the Nārāyaṇa hymn. 10.

Having led them toward the north while fire has been carried around them (*paryagnikṛta*) and having released them, he offers oblations to those deities with clarified butter and concludes the sacrifice with the two sets of eleven victims.
At the time of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives whatever wealth the non-Brāhmaṇas possess in their respective directions, together with the land, just as in the Aśvamedha.
If the sacrificer is a Brāhmaṇa, [he gives] his entire property (*sarvavedasa*).
On this very day, there is an ablution like that of the Aśvamedha. 14.

There are eleven Anūbandhya victims, dedicated either to Sūrya, to the Viśvedevas, or to Prajāpati. 15. Having performed the Udavasānīyā sacrifice with the Traidhātavīyā offering, having consigned the fires into separate fire-drills, and having worshipped the sun with the Uttara-Nārāyaṇa hymn, he should dwell in the forest. 16.
"Or, having entered a village, he should sacrifice with the Traidhātavīya.
This is the twenty-fourth section (kaṇḍikā).
[He should sacrifice] with the Sautrāmaṇī, with the Maitrāvaruṇī curd-mixture (āmikṣā), with the Sākamprasthāyīya, with the five-holed sacrificial pot (caru), and with the Pañcaśāradīya. 1.

The *pañcabila* (five-holed) oblation is known [as follows]: in the eastern hole is an offering of clarified butter for Agni; in the southern, curds for Indra; in the western, boiled milk—or milk mixed with curds—for the Viśvedevas; in the northern, water for Mitra and Varuṇa; and in the middle, milk for Bṛhaspati. 2.
The *sarvamedha* (all-sacrifice) consists of ten nights. 3.
A king who desires, "May I become this entire world," should perform it. 4.
The fire is of one hundred and one kinds. 5.
The Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma is the first day; everything belongs to Agni. 6.
The Indrastut Ukthya is the second; everything belongs to Indra. 7.
The third Ukthya is dedicated to Sūrya; it consists entirely of [hymns] for Sūrya. 8.

The fourth Ukthya is dedicated to the Viśvedevas; it consists entirely of [hymns] for the Viśvedevas. 9. The middle fifth day belongs to the Aśvamedha. On that day, one sacrifices the horse fit for sacrifice. 10.
The sixth [offering] is the middle *puruṣamedha*. In that [rite], there are eleven men.
The seventh is the *aptoryāma*. In that [sacrifice], he immolates all those fit for sacrifice. He offers the omenta of those possessing omenta; having flayed the skins, [he offers] the omenta.
Having cut down dry and moist medicinal herbs and forest trees, they scatter them into the Āhavanīya fire.
At the morning pressing, when the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been set down, he offers food after food;
it is known from scripture that this is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything.
In this same manner at the midday pressing and the third pressing:
the eighth [stoma] is the twenty-sevenfold (triṇava), and the ninth is the thirty-threefold (trayastriṃśa).
The Viśvajit, with all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras, is an Atirātra; it is the tenth day.

At the time of giving the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), whatever wealth non-Brāhmaṇas possess in the various directions, he gives that along with the land and the people, just as in the Aśvamedha, just as in the Aśvamedha.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section.
Thus ends the twentieth question:
By means of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), one is indeed born; he conquers the heavenly world and becomes firmly established in these worlds. 1.
It is accompanied by the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*). 2.
And [the rule applies] to both the *sattra* and the *ahīna*.
Those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*) may officiate for those who have not been initiated in an *ahīna* sacrifice.
In a *sattra*, these same persons are both the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificers (*yajamāna*).
Therefore, it is known: "One should not officiate at a twelve-day sacrifice for the sake of warding off evil.
(5) He prospers who sacrifices with the twelve-day rite. (6) Some say that he also prospers who receives [the sacrificial gifts]. (7)
Concerning the officiating priests and the sacrificer, it is said:
"Fat, he undergoes initiation; lean, he performs the sacrifice. Whatever of his limbs wastes away, that indeed he offers as an oblation"—so it is understood.
"He who would be without austerity, his sacrifice would be disjointed. He should be austere; thereby he joins the sacrifice together"—so it is understood.
One should sacrifice with the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). Three, six, twelve, or thirteen [priests] [should officiate]. 11.
Among them, they initiate the thirteenth during the *upasad* days. 12.
Therefore, some say that on the twelfth day there should not be a thirteenth Brahman priest. 13.

Fifteen should undergo initiation for those whose abode is the half-month; seventeen for those desiring offspring or cattle; twenty-one for those desiring stability or splendor; thirty for those whose abode is the month; thirty-three for those desiring vigor or strength; forty for those desiring sacrifice; forty-four for those desiring sensory power; and forty-eight for those desiring cattle. "An unlimited number may undergo initiation," he says finally.
Whatever other modes there are besides the seventeen, they belong to the Ahīna sacrifice.
Regarding these seventeen [priests], there is freedom of choice as one desires (17).
All are established in the duties of the sacrificer (18).
They should all perform the duties of the sacrificer, whatever it may be, provided it does not interfere with their priestly functions (19).
"The office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) is stronger when it causes conflict" (20).
This is the first section (*kaṇḍikā*).
All [the priests] have already performed their first sacrifice; or rather, only the householder (*gṛhapati*) has. 1.

The rites for the sake of others belong to the *gṛhapati* alone, such as the anointing of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-añjana*) and the seasonal offerings (*ṛtuyājya*). They should proceed according to the ritual procedure for the *sāmidhenī* verses and the ritual procedure for the portions (*avadāna*), as well as whatever other rites of this nature there may be.
For the Vasiṣṭhas and Rājanyas, the verse "Thou, O Varuṇa" (*tvaṃ varuṇa*) is the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*).
"Ājuhotā" is for the other *gotras*;
"Nārāśaṃsa" is the second *prayāja* for the Vasiṣṭhas and Śunakas;
"Tanūnapāt" is for the other *gotras*.
They undergo initiation in the cool season (śiśira) and rise from it in the spring;
for this [sacrifice], the departure is in the cool season and the rising is in the spring.
It is known: "He prospers who, knowing thus, undergoes initiation in the cool season and rises in the spring."

When six days of the waxing fortnight of Caitra have passed, they should undergo initiation (dīkṣā). Those intending to offer the Sāvitra oblations should churn the fire and then pour it back together; thereafter, they should pour it out again. Those intending to sacrifice with five animals should pour it back together; thereafter, they should pour it out again.
Those about to undergo initiation should pile up their fires together;
for them, the fires remain thus piled until the *audavasānīyā* offering.
The Adhvaryu, having initiated the householder (*gṛhapati*), initiates the Brahman; then the Udgātṛ; then the Hotṛ.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having initiated him, initiates those who receive half; 17.
Then the Neṣṭṛ, having initiated him, initiates those who receive a third; 18. Then the Unnetṛ, having initiated him, initiates those who receive a quarter. 19.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ initiates him;
thus ends the second Kaṇḍikā.
Or another Brāhmaṇa [may initiate him]. 1.
Once initiated, he omits [the rites] one by one until the conclusion of the *tantra*. 2.
Thus, whatever sacrificial duties (*yājamāna-dharma*) belong to these [sacrificers] that are not shared (*avibhavin*), they follow this same sequence.

3. Regarding those of the same lineage (*samāna-gotra*), some hold that the selection of ancestral seers (*ārṣeya-varaṇa*) must be repeated whenever there is an intervention by persons of different lineages (*nānā-gotra*). 4. Others hold that even when there is such an intervention, it remains a single *tantra*.
Some authorities prescribe initiation on the very same day; others prescribe daily initiation.
One may undergo initiation on the second day, or one may undergo initiation on the third day—in this manner, one proceeds by increments up to twelve days.
Regarding one who is about to undergo initiation, Āśmarathya maintains that everything pertaining to the initiation ceremony should be repeated.

Having established the fires, one should proceed with the consecration of oneself alone; Ālekhana says that the ritual procedures (*tantra*) shall consist of the oblations alone. 8. They consecrate the wives in the very place of the wives. 9.
The sequence of their duties has been explained by the rules pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). 10.
The initiated ones take hold of the *adhvaryu* from behind; the wives take hold of the initiated ones.

Then, while they are thus holding on together, he offers an oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "Let death depart; let immortality come to us. May Vaivasvata grant us fearlessness. Like the leaf of a tree, may wealth fall upon us. May the Lord of Power (*śacīpati*) attend to us, svāhā!
(12) For the other two fires, the offering is made excluding the wives. (13)

Thus ends the third section (kaṇḍikā). "Go away, O Death, along your own path, which is other than the path of the gods. To you who have eyes and hear, I speak: do not harm our offspring, nor our heroes. [With this verse] he offers into the *dakṣiṇāgni*. "We have now come to this better dwelling, which wins cattle, wins wealth, and wins horses. May riches fall upon us like the leaf of a tree; may the Lord of Power attend us, Svāhā! [With this verse] he offers into the *āhavanīya* fire.
They remain consecrated for twelve days. 3.
At the *sattra*, they do not send out those who carry away the sacrificial fees. 4.
Having performed the *prāyaṇīyā* offering, having purchased the King (Soma), and having bound him, he deposits him, acquired for the twelve-day rite. 5.
The *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice lasts sixteen years; the *somakrayaṇī* cow [is used]; during the *upasads* of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), he recites the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas;
according to some, he causes the sacrificer to recite them.
There are twelve *upasads*. (9) For four days at a time, he offers oblations with each individual *upasad* mantra. (10) Following the *upasads*, he piles the fire-altar. (11)
Each layer (citi) consists of one day each for two days;
the final [layer] consists of four days.
The observances (vrata) consist of three days each, corresponding to the four-uddered, three-uddered, two-uddered, and one-uddered [cows].
If one should wish to fulfill their vow, having drawn one spoonful of curd, he should not draw another.
(15) The *sadas* has twenty-one roofs. (16) The two pressing-boards are joined together. (17)
The Upavasatha day is straightforward.
This is the fourth section (kaṇḍikā).
On the following day, the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is extended.

The Vaiśvānara Atirātra is the introductory sacrifice (prāyaṇīya). It is the same [as the standard procedure] up to the bringing down of the King Soma. One should perform as much as one considers sufficient for a single day.
Having tied it up in one garment, he unfastens the other and brings it down. 5.
In this manner, day by day, there is the binding and the unbinding of the fire-altar.
6. On the first day he binds it; on the last day he unbinds it. 7.
Some authorities prescribe the two ritual releases (yogavimoka) every day.
At the time of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives twelve hundred [cows] every day during the *ahīna* sacrifice.

But at the *sattras*, having offered the two *dākṣiṇa* oblations with the formula, "This I, myself, lead as a sacrificial fee for auspiciousness, for fame, and for the heavenly world," the sacrificers, shaking their black antelope skins, proceed northward by the southern path.
In this manner, day after day,
on the final day alone they release their friendships and cast away the black antelope horns.
On the very same day, he takes up the *vasatīvarī* waters for the sake of the following day’s *yajñāyajñiya* stotra.
While the *atirātra* sacrifice is still in progress, he issues instructions regarding the milks for the following day.

When he recognizes the formula of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest—"Proclaim the Soma for Indra and Agni, for the All-gods, for the Brāhmaṇas who drink Soma, for those entitled to the Soma-drink; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā"—[he acts accordingly].
Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā).

Then the Āgnīdhra, having entered the Āgnīdhra shed, issues the command: "Tomorrow there is the Soma-pressing; I announce the Soma to Indra and Agni, to the Viśve Devas, to the Brāhmaṇas who partake of Soma, and to those who drink Soma; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā!
Regarding this, Āśmarathya says that he should indeed say, "Tomorrow there is the Soma-pressing," while Ālekhana says, "Today there is the Soma-pressing."
Thereafter, he should say, "The Soma-pressing is tomorrow.
3. The day concludes with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. 4. When the day has concluded, the Brahman releases his speech. 5.
They pour water for the wives; they go out carrying firewood;
having returned, they place [the wood] upon the Āhavanīya fire.
In this manner, day after day, they then perform the Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma sacrifice characterized by the Rathantara Sāman.
With the word "chariot" (ratha), he introduces the Māhendra hymn.
The sound [of the drum] takes the place of the mantra.
On the following day, they perform the fifteen-fold Ukthya sacrifice with the Bṛhat Sāman. He begins the chant for the Mahendra cup with the sound of a drum.
If there should be thunder, that very sound shall take the place of the mantra.

On the following day, they perform the seventeen-fold Ukthya sacrifice with the Vairūpa Sāman. At the place of the sacrificial grass (barhis), he introduces the chant for the Mahendra hymn with the Ādhāva verse.
When the animal has been brought forward, the Sāman becomes uncommenced (18). Then the Udgātṛ runs forward and shakes [the skin] (19).
Thus ends the sixth Kaṇḍikā.
On the following day, they perform the twenty-first [stotra], the Ṣoḍaśin, with the Vairāja as its Sāman. 1.
On this day, there is a Nyūṅkha. 2.
In place of the sacrificial grass (barhis), he introduces the chant for the Mahendra cup using the two kindling woods (araṇī). 3.
The Sāman that has been introduced becomes uncommenced.
Then, having covered the right thigh of the Udgātṛ with Avakā plants, he churns fire upon it.
When it has been produced, the Udgātṛ, having uttered the sound *hiṅ*, hands it to the Prastotṛ; the latter, in turn, hands it to the Adhvaryu.

The Adhvaryu, having carried it around the north of the Dhiṣṇiya hearths and having offered it into the Āhavanīya fire, makes an offering over it with the Virāj verse: "O Agni, being kindled, shine forth.

On the following day, they perform the Ukthya sacrifice characterized by the Triṇava Stoma and the Śākvara Sāman. At the place where the sacrificial grass (barhis) would normally be, he introduces the chant for Mahendra with those waters that have been soaked in avakā plants.

The Sāman that has been introduced becomes uncommenced. Then, three cows with bulls go northward along the path of the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇāpatha), passing in front of the Sadas and behind the Āgnīdhra fire-hall.
On the following day, they perform the Trayastriṃśa Ukthya sacrifice characterized by the Raivata Sāman.
On this day, there is chanting of the *nyūṅkha*.
The Adhvaryu himself performs the *ṛtuyāja* offering; the Gṛhapati himself [performs his].

Having recognized [the signal], "O two Adhvaryus, sacrifice! O Gṛhapati, sacrifice!", the Adhvaryu enters the *havirdhāna* shed and sacrifices with the verse following the *praisha*, or rather, with the *praisha* followed by the verse.

"O Aśvins, drink the pressed [Soma], you who shine with fire and possess pure vows, according to the season, O bearers of the sacrifice! According to the season, drink the Soma—*vauṣaṭ*!"—if [the day] is not intercalated (16).

But when it is intercalated, [he recites]: "Today, harness the hitherward-turning, swift chariot that carries heroes; here is your place of unyoking. Mix the oblations with honey, for indeed, come! Then drink the Soma, O lords of wealth! According to the season, drink the Soma—*vauṣaṭ*! The performance for this [day] takes place with the Marutvatīya cups (17). Thus ends the seventh section.
The Māhendra cup has not yet been drawn.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having stretched the cord toward the north along the north of the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, ties the calves to it. To the south of the Mārjālīya fire, they confine the mother-cows.

At the place of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he begins the *stotra* for Mahendra with water and dūrvā grass spread out. (4) Once the *sāman* has been introduced but before it has been chanted, they then unite these calves with their mothers and cause them to low together. (6)
They lead them out by the northern path from the front of the *sadas* and behind the *āgnīdhra*, toward the north.
Thus concludes the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.
When it has concluded, they consume clarified butter or honey.
"It is known from scripture: 'Just as Uṣas would drive toward him, so it is.

Then they enter upon the tenth day, which is the Avivākya. It is a Caturviṃśa Agniṣṭoma with the Rathantara Sāman.
Here, no one at all may speak out against anyone who has been struck down or obstructed.

"In the end, he says, 'That indeed is what is to be spoken of.

On whichever day [the sacrifice] might be impaired, he completes it with an *anuṣṭubh* verse. On this day, they bring two kinds of fuel: the regular ones and those made of *udumbara* wood.
They place the regular ones on the fire first.
To the north of the Āhavanīya fire, they place an Audumbara post.

Then, while [the priests] have taken hold of one another, he offers two oblations on the Gārhapatya fire with [the verses]: "Those [waters] which are near the sun, or those with which the sun is together—may they speed our sacrifice. Here is delight, here is pleasure, here is enjoyment; may you find enjoyment here; may your enjoyment be here, svāhā!
Having offered with these two [verses], beginning with "Releasing the support," he then goes to the Āhavanīya fire.

"Exceeding desire they stand near; this thousandfold vision of the seers is the thought, the light, the law. The sun has brought together the converging dawns. Spotless, dwelling in the same abode, like-minded, of the same seed, full of spirit even in their own place, they have come.
(Thus ends the ninth section.
Then they proceed toward the Prājāpatya Manograha cup.
When [the Soma] has flowed forth, he draws [the cup] with the Upāṃśu vessel, saying: "With this vessel, the earth; with the essence, I draw thee, acceptable to Prajāpati, for the ocean.

One view is that he should draw it from the open space. Another view is that he should let the Soma of the third pressing remain until as much as is sufficient for one group of goblets together with the draught-cup is reached.
The commencement of the Stotra is performed mentally; so too are the Prastāva, Udgītha, and Pratihāra.
He responds mentally six times to the three *sarparājñī* verses if he recites them by half-verses; nine times if he recites them by quarters. 5.
The *hotṛ* recites the *caturhotṛ* formulas.
6. "Om" is the response for the *daśahotṛ*; "Tathā" (So be it) for the *caturhotṛ*; "Om" for the *pañcahotṛ*; "Tathā" for the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*; and "We have succeeded, O *hotṛ*" for the *saptahotṛ*. 7.
In the mind, there are the *pratyāśruti* (response), the *yājyā* (offering verse), the *vaṣaṭkāra*, and the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*.
Having offered mentally, he takes away the portion for consumption.
When they look at one another, that is the mutual invitation (*samupahava*).
"They consume it mentally;
they discourse on the Brahman," so it is known.
One view is that there should be a discussion after they have sat down. Another view is that the officiating priests (ṛtvij) should sit around the householder (gṛhapati) himself and question him.
The Adhvaryu asks him:

"By Prajāpati as their householder, indeed, they prospered; by him they created offspring"—this is the reply. (2) The Brahman asks: "When the Caturhotṛs performed a sacrificial session, by which householder did they prosper? By whom did they create the plants? (3) "By Soma as their householder, indeed, they prospered; by him they created the plants"—this is the reply. (4)

The Hotṛ asks: "When the Pañcahotṛs performed a sacrificial session (sattra), by what householder did they prosper? By whom did they drive away the Asuras from these worlds? By whom did they win their cattle? 5. "By Agni as their householder they indeed prospered; by him they drove away the Asuras from these worlds; by him they won their cattle"—this is the reply. 6. The Hotrakas ask: "When the Ṣaḍḍhotṛs performed a sacrificial session, by what householder did they prosper? By whom did they arrange the seasons? 7.

"By whom as their householder did they succeed? By whom did they arrange the seasons?"—this is the question. "By Dhātṛ indeed as their householder did they succeed; by him they arranged the seasons"—this is the reply. (8) The Udgātṛ asks: "When the seven Hotṛs performed the sacrificial session (*sattra*), by which householder did they succeed? By which [householder] did they go to the heavenly world (*suvar*)? By which did they extend these worlds? (9) "By Aryaman indeed as their householder did they succeed; by him they went to the heavenly world; by him they extended these worlds"—this is the reply. (10)
Or rather, this is the explanation of that which is silent and mental; or it is when the Hotṛ recites the Caturhotṛ formulas, for it is known from scripture: "They praise Prajāpati. 11–13.
Thus ends the eleventh section (kaṇḍikā).
"This Prajāpati is indeed unskilled who created gadflies and mosquitoes, and [created] thieves"—this is a censure of Prajāpati.
Alternatively, they recite mantras that constitute a censure of Prajāpati.

These are to be understood: "Whatever Prajāpati created—the wildernesses, the fortresses, and the mountains—that was not auspicious for him; let that which is auspicious be bestowed upon me. That which is joined with frost and darkness, that which burns most fiercely in the day, and the waters and the heat that scorch during the summer of Prajāpati—whatever thieves, wolves, gadflies, mosquitoes, and malevolent beings there are—that indeed is your sin; this is your vow, and it is not my intention."
"Divide the tenth day among Prajāpati; [assign] the thought of the sages, the bull among men. He, bestowing fair praise and excellent wealth, purified and free from sin, shall depart to the world.

Thus [he says]. Then he chooses a boon, saying, "May that be ours," whatever he desires. For indeed, a Brāhmaṇa may have many desires. "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! May I be rich in offspring through my offspring, rich in heroes through my heroes, rich in splendor through my splendor, and rich in nourishment through my nourishments"—thus he ordains this.
Having explained the Caturhotṛ formulas and closed the two doors, he seats the wives according to their respective hearths (dhiṣṇiyas) and then offers them the introductory speech (vāc). 6.
Having embraced the Audumbarī post with the words, "Here is support, here is self-support, here is delight, here is enjoyment," they stand silent, touching it with their bellies. 7.
When the sun has risen above the trees, they move forward together, holding onto one another. 8.

"O Indra and Parvata, you who fight from the front, strike down each one who would attack us; strike him down with the thunderbolt, strike him down! May it be pleasing to him who stays far away, even if he reaches the thicket. O Hero, may the shatterer shatter our enemies on every side—on every side! With these words, moving eastward while holding mats or reed-brooms in their right hands, they go past the northern *havirdhāna* shed and utter five formulas: "Speech! Let Speech come! Let Speech approach! Let Speech meet me! Let Speech come to me! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! (9)
Having meditated on the night during the day, when the sun is over the trees, he releases his speech with the *subrahmaṇyā* formula and offers fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood. The tenth day concludes.
Thus ends the twelfth section.

They perform the Udayanīya [concluding rite] like the Prāyaṇīya [opening rite]. 1. Here, the continuities of the Ahīna [sacrifice] do not occur. 2. Those actions which are performed on the previous day for the sake of the following day constitute the continuities of the Ahīna. 3.
If it is a *sattra*, they shave their hair including the top-knots at the time of shaving.

Having performed the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice and chosen other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), they perform the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice, which is a *jyotiṣṭoma-agniṣṭoma* with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of one thousand.
Now follows the arrangement of the cups (*graha*).

On the tenth day, at the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* rites, he draws the *pṛśniprāṇagraha* cups. Having recited the original *yajus*-measure interspersed with the Soma-measures, he measures out ten measures of the *pṛśnigrahas* with the ten formulas for the *pṛśnigrahas*: "Thou art Vāyu, named Prāṇa," and so forth. Having recited the subsequent *yajus*-measure, he measures out ten measures of the *prāṇagrahas* with the ten formulas for the *prāṇagrahas*: "This one is Purobhuvas," and so forth.
In this way he interlinks the subsequent measures:
there are ten mantras for nine new stalks;
or rather, he measures with nine [stalks] at a time.

The remaining options concern the meaning of the alternatives: (13) Or rather, having followed the measurement, he should pour [the grain] with the *pṛśni* verses; (14) or he should pour it with the breath;
(15) or he should pour the breath and the measurement with the two *pṛśni* verses.
Then, with the *pṛśni* [verse], one should pour out the breath by measure. 16. The two subsequent sequences are prescribed in this same manner.
17. That which was the first becomes the fourth; that which was the second becomes the fifth. 18.

He takes nine new *navāṃśu* cups [on the first three days]. On the last three days of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, he takes three *atigrāhya* cups: one for Agni on the twenty-one-fold day, one for Indra on the twenty-seven-fold day, and one for Sūrya on the thirty-three-fold day.
The Vājasaneyins prescribe these for the first three-day period.
Where the Gaurīvīta Sāman is used, there one takes many *atigrāhya* cups.
Thus ends the thirteenth section. We shall now explain the *tryanīkā* [rite]. 1.

The Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya days have the Aindravāyava cup first, as does the tenth day. Now, among the other nine days, the first day has the Aindravāyava cup first; then the Śukra cup first; then the Āgrayaṇa cup first.
In this manner, the three-fold series (tristryanīkā) proceeds in rotation, provided it is not expanded (avyūḍha).

In the *vyūḍha* (expanded) arrangement, however, the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* days have the cups beginning with that for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyavāgra*). Now, among the other ten days: first, a day beginning with the cup for Indra and Vāyu; then one beginning with the *śukra* cup; then two beginning with the *āgrayaṇa* cup; then one beginning with the cup for Indra and Vāyu; then two beginning with the *śukra* cup; then one beginning with the *āgrayaṇa* cup; then two beginning with the cup for Indra and Vāyu. 5. Now follows the preparation of the sacrificial animals (*paśukḷpti*).
On the *prāyaṇīya* day, they immolate a victim for Agni. On the following day, a ewe for Sarasvatī. 7.
They immolate these eleven animals, thus prepared, day after day.
On the concluding day, they offer an animal to Agni, or one to Indra and Agni;
or one to Surya for one who desires spiritual luster.

If there is a set of eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī), one should erect the posts one by one on each successive day; or [alternatively], all of them on the Upavasatha day. Every day, a post for the animal victim (upaśaya) is brought forward.
On the Udayanīya day, he dedicates the animal at the post standing nearest the fire (agniṣṭha).
Twelve Agniṣṭomas with the Rathantara Sāman;
that is the Bharata-dvādaśāha.
Thus ends the fourteenth Kaṇḍikā.
By means of the Gavāmayana, they attain progeny, prosperity, and abundance; they conquer the heavenly world and become firmly established in these worlds.
1. Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the twelve-day sacrificial session (*dvādaśāha-sattra*). 2. They prescribe seventeen days of initiation (*dīkṣā*). 3.
It has been stated that those intending to undergo initiation for the year-long sacrifice (saṃvatsara) should be initiated on the Ekāṣṭakā day.
They should be initiated four days before the full moon;
Āśmarathya says [it should be] the full moon of Māgha, while Ālekhana says [it should be] the full moon of Caitra.
It is the same up to the Prāyaṇīya [day]. (7) Having performed the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra, they enter upon the Caturviṃśa Ukthya as the Ārambhaṇīya.
(8) These two become the Śaya days. (9)

Then they enter upon the *abhiplava* six-day period: the *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma* with the *rathantara* *sāman*; the *go* *ukthya* with the *bṛhat* *sāman*; the *āyus* *ukthya* with the *rathantara* *sāman*; the *go* *ukthya* with the *bṛhat* *sāman*; the *āyus* *ukthya* with the *rathantara* *sāman*; and the *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma* with the *bṛhat* *sāman*. They enter upon four such prescribed *abhiplavas*. At the conclusion, they perform the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period.
In this manner, they enter upon five months as prescribed.
Then follows the Saṃbhārya [Sāman],
three Abhiplava [six-day periods], the Pṛṣṭhya six-day period, the Abhijit Agniṣṭoma, three Paraḥsāman Ukthyas or Agniṣṭomas, and the final two Śaya days;
thus [constitute] the six months.
Then they enter upon the Viṣuvat day, an Agniṣṭoma with twenty-one stomas, having the Divākīrtya Sāman as its chant. (16) When the sun has risen, he begins the Prātaranuvāka.
(17) This day is characterized by the Divākīrtya. (18)

In the latter fortnight, the groups (gaṇas) are repeated, except for the twelve-day period and the ten-night period. Then they perform three Ukthya sacrifices with the *arvāk-sāman* chants, or rather, Agniṣṭomas;
[finally] the Viśvajit Agniṣṭoma.
Those four days of lying down;
having performed the reversed *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, they perform four *abhiplava* periods in reverse;
thus they proceed for five months as prescribed.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.
Then follows the *saṃbhārya* [period]:
two *abhiplava* periods, the *go* and *āyus* [days], the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the final four *śayāna* days, the *mahāvrata*, and the *atirātra*.
Thus are the twelve months; 3. Thus is the Śāṭyāyanaka; 4. Now, the Tāṇḍaka; 5.
After the Viśvajit, following the latter fortnight, having undertaken the reversed *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) and three reversed *abhiplava* periods,
those together with the preceding ones constitute twenty-eight *śaya* days. Having undertaken the reversed *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, four reversed *abhiplava* periods are completed in the assembly.
They spend these four months arranged in this manner;
thereafter come the two *saṃbhārya* days, three *abhiplava* periods, the *āyus*, the *go*, and the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*).
There are another twenty-eight *śayanī* days, the *mahāvrata*, and the *atirātra*;
thus [there are] twelve months;
thus ends the *Tāṇḍaka*.
Then there is the Bhāllavika [sacrifice]:
the Abhijit Agniṣṭoma before the last Pṛṣṭhya of the eastern wing;
the Viśvajit Agniṣṭoma after the first Pṛṣṭhya of the northern wing.
The rest is the same as in the Śāṭyāyanaka.
Alternatively, having completed the year-long sacrifice, in the final month, during the ten-night period belonging to the twelve-day rite, they should perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants only once;
in that case, the *abhiplava* days should be substituted for the positions of the *pṛṣṭhya* days.
After the twelve-day period, following the ten-night rite, comes the Mahāvrata;
thus ends the sixteenth section.
Then they proceed to the Mahāvrata, which is a Pañcaviṃśa Agniṣṭoma.
They praise verse by verse.
The Adhvaryu chants with nine unresponded verses addressed to Indra. Or rather, the wives do not join in the singing of the *bhadra* chant.
The performance for that [rite] proceeds with the Marutvatīya cups;
the Māhendra cup has not yet been drawn.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ executes the artistic crafts associated with the Mahāvrata.
Ten pieces of Audumbara wood are whetted for the neck of the lute;
on each whetted piece, he weaves ten threads of Muñja grass.
That is the *vāṇa* consisting of one hundred strings.

Now, according to some: "Thirty-three threads are for *bhūḥ*," with these words the Adhvaryu spreads out thirty-three; "Thirty-three threads are for *bhuvaḥ*," with these words the Hotṛ spreads out thirty-three; "Thirty-three threads are for *suvaḥ*," with these words the Udgātṛ spreads out thirty-three. The Gṛhapati places the highest Udumbara stool upon the Udgātṛ's seat, provided with a woven band of Muñja grass.
He fastens an Udumbara swing to the Hotṛ's seat with a cord of Muñja grass.
The Adhvaryus place [the vessels] upon a board made of Udumbara wood; or they place them on two mats.
The Hotraka priests, the singers, and the wives sit upon mats.
The wives take up their musical instruments: the apāghāṭalikā, the stambalavīṇā, and the piccholā.
The lute-players, the conch-blowers, the nālīs, and the tūṇava-players take their positions.
The religious student and the harlot, intending to sing the *ārti* hymns, take their places in front of the southern door of the sacrificial hall.
They enclose the harlot and the bard within the northern corner of the altar.
Thus ends the seventeenth section (kaṇḍikā).

They tie drums to the quarters, or to the corners of the great altar (mahāvedi). To the west of the Āgnīdhra fire-altar, they dig a pit for a ground-drum (bhūmidundubhi), half of which is within the altar and half outside the altar.
Having stretched it out with a moist hide, wool-side up, and having fixed it around with stakes, he places this tail-section here for the purpose of striking; 3.
To the east of the Āgnīdhra, a Śūdra and an Ārya take their positions, intending to compete in cutting the hide; 4.
To the north of the Āgnīdhra, they stretch out a moist hide upon a heap of straw or a heap of reeds and hold it upright for the purpose of piercing it. 5.
In front of the Āhavanīya fire, the armored men equip themselves upon their chariots.
At the edge of the Mārjālīya fire-altar, eight young slave-girls arrange water-jars.
"May speech be auspicious, may the mind be auspicious, may pride be auspicious; may that which is auspicious for us [be ours]"—with this, he should circumambulate three times.
Having sharpened the arrow with a blade of *kaṭa*-grass, a stalk of sugarcane, a stalk of bamboo, or a stalk of reed, the Udgātṛ begins the *māhendra* hymn with it;
it is known that he plays [the arrow] while doing so. The Udgātṛ hands it to the Prastotṛ; he [the Prastotṛ] gives it to the Adhvaryu; the Adhvaryu gives it to another.
He sits at the front of the Sadas, facing the southern door-post, making it resound.
This is the eighteenth section.
When the *māhendra* stotra has been commenced, they utter all kinds of speech.
The sacrificers perform the *utkroda* rite;
the wives play the *apāghāṭalikā*, the *stambalavīṇā*, and the *piccholā* lutes.
The lute-players, conch-blowers, flute-players, and tabor-players sound together.
The religious student and the harlot feel aversion when embracing the right arm of the door;
the harlot and the bard come together;
they run the race.
They beat the drums; with the tail-staff, they beat the earth-drum.
A Śūdra and an Ārya strive together over the hide-worker’s task—a fresh, white, circular skin—within the altar for the Brāhmaṇa and outside the altar for the Śūdra.
The Śūdra reviles; the Brāhmaṇa praises.
"These have succeeded; these have done well," says the Brāhmaṇa. "These have been driven out; these have done ill," says the Śūdra.
Having conquered him, the Brāhmaṇa spreads his skin upon the Āgnīdhra altar. Those wearing armor exchange positions with this skin.
He instructs each of them one by one, saying, "Do not miss; do not over-pierce. They pierce it, but they do not let it fall through.
According to some, princes pierce it.
Having gone northward for an immeasurable distance and having returned, they release [the horse]. 17.

At this point, these slave-girls, having placed water-jars upon [the ground], dance three times around the Mārjālīya fire in a clockwise direction, stamping their right feet while singing, "This is honey. 18. "This very [substance] is the honey of the bees; this is the Soma pressed here. Drink of it here until you are satiated; we are great!"—they should sing only, "This is honey! This is honey! says Āśmarathya. 19.
Now follows the section on *ālekhanas*.
[This concludes] the nineteenth *kaṇḍikā*.
Two *hillukās* should be sung; two *himbinīs*; two *hastāvārās*; and two *saṃvatsaragāthās*. 1.

"May Vāgveda Hillukā sing this Sāman for the sounding of Prāṇa; may she, being sung, protect the sacrificers here. May Vāgveda Himbinī sing this Sāman for the sounding of Prāṇa; may she, being sung, protect the sacrificers here. May Vāgveda Hastāvārā sing this Sāman for the sounding of Prāṇa; may she, being sung, protect the sacrificers here. (2)

Then follows the *Saṃvatsara-gāthā*: "Cows indeed are fragrant; cows have the scent of bdellium. Cows are the mothers of clarified butter; may they be most numerous here. Truly, the cows drank the water of the Gaṅgā at Maṅkīra; they drank from the river Sarasvatī and plunged into the eastern waters. We swim across these as if crossing with oars. Having scattered them for you in the midst, I draw them in like a hawk. When the two Aśvins speak of the breaking, O leaf of Truth, [tell] who it was that struck."

When both Rākhāḍya and Aṅkīradāśaka speak of the blemish of what has been revealed and what has not been done, and when they speak vulgarly, the village suffers for its misfortune, like a man carrying a load of reeds. "This the Kalmāṣyas drank; this Soma produced; here they fixed the stakes with gold—this was the breaking of the thighs.
"Haimahā! This honey! Hillu! Hillu!"—this is the rule at the end of all verses.
At this point, these Dāsa maidens, having poured out their water-jars, go as they please.
Following the praise of Mahendra, the sounds subside.

The Sun, the purifier, the measurer of the mid-world (*rajas*), purifies all the worlds of the gods. Heaven and Earth, in harmony, yielding milk, pour forth clarified butter and the immortal nectar. The Sun, the purifier, the measurer of the mid-world, purifies all the worlds of the gods. "May we attain the light of heaven, great glory, a firm footing, and a secure foundation"—having ascended the two boards or the two mats, the Adhvaryu responds to the recitation (*śastra*). The Mahāvrata rite concludes.
Thus ends the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā).
The Udayanīya and Pṛṣṭhaśamanīya sacrifices have been explained.
Now follows the arrangement of the cups (graha-kḷpti).

In the three *paraḥsāman* days, he draws three *atigrāhya* cups: on the first day, he draws it with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the waters and the plants"; on the second day, "To the plants thee, to the progeny thee"; on the third day, "To the progeny thee, to Prajāpati thee.
He performs these same rites in reverse order in the *arvāksāman* days.
Those [cups] are drawn upright and not turned back at the Viṣuvat day; in their midst, he draws the cup for Sūrya with the verse, "Upwards that Jātavedas...
On this very day, he draws the Vaiśvakarman Atigrāhya as the eighth, with the verse, "Vācaspati, Viśvakarman, for our protection..."
On the following day, he takes [the draught for] Āditya with the verse, "The great mother... (RV 8.69.2).
In this very manner, he takes them alternately until the Mahāvrata day.
On the Mahāvrata day, he takes both together, as well as the Prājāpatya draught in five vessels.
On this day, he takes thirty-three *atigrāhya* cups.

There are ten for Agni, ten for Indra, ten for Sūrya, one for Viśvakarman, and the Āditya cup as the thirty-fifth; thus there are thirty-three. Four *atigrāhya* vessels are placed in the four directions, with the fifth in the middle.
In the first half [of the verse], he takes [the draught] with the formula:

"Having recited 'Indra, him the singers...'," and having taken it with "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra accompanied by the *ṛk*," he deposits it with "This is thy womb; for Indra accompanied by the *ṛk*, thee.
In this same manner, everywhere, he adapts both the taking and the depositing of the draughts.
"Abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ"—this [verse] is in the southern half.
Thus ends the twenty-first section (kaṇḍikā).

"Imā nu kaṃ bhuvanā sīṣadhem indraś ca viśve ca devāḥ | yajñaṃ ca nas tanvaṃ ca prajāṃ cādityair indraḥ saha sīṣadhātu | ādityair indraḥ sagaṇo marudbhir asmabhyam bheṣajā karat"—this is in the western half. 1.

"Tvāmid dhi havāmahe"—with this [verse], he pours [the Soma] into the northern half [of the vessel]; "Tad id āsa bhuvaneṣu jyeṣṭham yato yajña ugras tveṣanṛmṇaḥ | sadyo jajñāno ni riṇāti śatrūn anu yaṃ viśve madanty ūmāḥ"—with this, he pours into the middle [vessel].
Having poured all of them into another vessel, he draws them all into the middle [vessel] with [the verse]: "Tve kratum api vṛñjanti viśve."

Now, according to some: if one were to offer separately, he would cut off his own limbs; if he were to collect the oblations and hold them back, the sacrificers would likewise be held back. Therefore, the drops alone, having been brought back to himself, should be offered. Thus it is known: "He bestows his limbs back upon himself; he does not withhold the oblations, nor does he interrupt the sacrifice. (5) He consumes it [the remnant] with the formula: "I consume your greatness; I consume your vigor; I consume your enjoyment; I consume your food. (6) We shall now explain the *tryanīkā* (the threefold array). (7)
The first day has the cup for Indra and Vāyu as the first; then the cup for Śukra is first; then the cup for Āgrayaṇa is first.
Thus arranged, the threefold series rotates from here upwards prior to the Viṣuvat day.
After the Viṣuvat, it rotates in reverse order on each successive day.
The Viṣuvat day has the Śukra as its first [stotra]. 11.
Now follows the preparation of the sacrificial animals: 12.
On the Prāyaṇīya day, they immolate a victim for Agni; on the following day, a ewe for Sarasvatī. 13.
Thus, they immolate the eleven animals prescribed for each day on successive days.
This is the twenty-second section.
On the Viṣuvat day, a victim for Sūrya is to be immolated. 1.
As they proceed in this manner, at the seventeenth Ukthya of the ten-night period within the twelve-day rite, thirty-two Ekādaśinīs are concluded;
nine days remain over.

Among these, they immolate animals that are not in excess of the number of cows: a dwarf animal dedicated to Viṣṇu at the twenty-first [stoma]; one for Indra and Agni at the twenty-seven-fold; one for the Viśvedevas at the thirty-three-fold; a milch-cow for Heaven and Earth at the first *chandoman* day; its calf, dedicated to Vāyu, at the middle [day]; a barren ewe for Āditya at the last; one for Mitra and Varuṇa on the *Avivākya* day; a hornless bull for Prajāpati at the *Mahāvrata*; and one for Agni at the *Udayanīya* sacrifice. Thus say the followers of the Pāliṅgāyana school. Now, the followers of the Kāṭhaka school: 1. *teṣu gavyānatiriktapaśūnālabhante* — Among these, they immolate animals that do not exceed the number of cows. 2. *vaiṣṇavaṃ vāmanamekaviṃśe* — A dwarf animal for Viṣṇu at the twenty-first [stoma]. 3. *aindrāgnaṃ triṇave* — One for Indra and Agni at the twenty-seven-fold. 4. *vaiśvadevaṃ trayastriṃśe* — One for the Viśvedevas at the thirty-three-fold. 5. *dyāvāpṛthivyāṃ dhenuṃ prathame chandome* — A milch-cow for Heaven and Earth at the first *chandoman* day. 6. *tasyā eva vāyavyaṃ vatsaṃ madhyame* — Its calf, dedicated to Vāyu, at the middle [day]. 7. *ādityāmaviṃ vaśāmuttame* — A barren ewe for Āditya at the last [day]. 8. *maitrāvaruṇīmavivākye* — One for Mitra and Varuṇa on the *Avivākya* day. 9. *prājāpatyamṛṣabhaṃ tūparaṃ mahāvrate* — A hornless bull for Prajāpati at the *Mahāvrata*. 10. *āgneyamudayanīye* — One for Agni at the *Udayanīya* sacrifice. 11. *iti pāliṅgāyanikāḥ* — Thus say the followers of the Pāliṅgāyana school. 12. *atha kāṭhakāḥ* — Now, the followers of the Kāṭhaka school.
They immolate the animals of the *aikādaśinī* group either by distributing them individually or without distribution, at the *Prāyaṇīya* and *Udayanīya* sacrifices.
(7) The animal for Agni is offered when the *Rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, and the one for Indra when the *Bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*.
(8) Alternatively, the animal for Agni-Indra is offered when the *Rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, and the one for Indra-Agni when the *Bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*. (9)
In those very [days], there are nine animals of good quality;

there is a modification in that regard. On the thirty-third day, a white-backed animal for Bṛhaspati; on the last day, a spotted one for Vāc; at the Mahāvrata, a hornless bull for Viśvakarman; and on both sides of that, a two-colored one.

If there should be sufficient sacrificial animals, they should offer them daily, increasing the number as in the case of the *kratupaśus*. Or, according to the Vājasaneyaka, they should offer the eleven animals distributed [over the days].
Or, indeed, the offering to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*) may be performed everywhere.
Thus ends the twenty-third section (*kaṇḍikā*).
The Utsarginām Ayana and the Gavām Ayana are modifications characterized by specific qualities.
Should one abandon them? Or should one not abandon them?
Thus it has been said:

"If they should omit days, having completed the first *pṛṣṭhya* [period], and having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters for the following day, having placed a lump of earth in the *vasatīvarī* waters, and having set out the *sāṃnāyya* offering for Indra, they observe the fast.
On the next day, having omitted the day, they immolate an animal sacrifice for Prajāpati."
At the appropriate time, having performed the offering with its omentum, he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Vasumat and curd for Indra.
For these two, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* portions are common.
When the *iḍā* has been invoked, they partake of the *sāṃnāyya* after having jointly invoked it.

At the time of the midday pressing, having performed the ritual with the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), he offers a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra accompanied by the Maruts (marutvat) and a pap (caru) for Indra. Having completed the oblation of the sacrificial food (havis) starting from the offering up to the *iḍā* portion, at the time of the third pressing, having performed the ritual with the animal, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśvedevas and a pap for the Viśvedevas. He should complete the two offerings as previously described.
Alternatively, these sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) themselves take the place of those oblations; or else, the ritual of the Adhvarakalpa begins with the words,
"O Agnīdh, bring the embers for the Upayaj offerings," and so forth, following the procedure for the animal sacrifice.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section.
From this point forward, having completed the months with six-day periods (*ṣaḍaha*), they omit the seventh and perform this: 1.
Five *jyotis* [days] are omitted prior to the *viṣuvat*. 2.
There are four [days] for the Trayastriṃśa [stomas], and one light-day (jyotis) above; these are to be combined.
According to some, one should not omit the first and seventh days.
Now, according to others: those days which are subject to omission should consist of Ekatrika-stotras only.
They should omit one *stotrīyā* verse from each of these [days]. Or rather, on the last day of the year, they should omit only a single *stotrīyā*. Thus it becomes both omitted and not omitted.
Now, according to some, on the very day they would omit [the verses], they should perform them again on the following day.
One should not do it in that way; for that would be a fragmentation of the year. (9) Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, they should return to those very same [fires].
(10) If they were to discontinue [the fires] on the new moon day, there would be twelve [months]; if on both [new and full moon days], there would be twenty-four. (11)
This very [rite] is conducive to grandchildren, cattle, long life, and heaven. It concludes with the Utsarginām Ayana, the Utsarginām Ayana.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section (kaṇḍikā).
This is the twenty-first question:
regarding the *ekāhas* and *ahīnas*, does one give the archetypal (*prākṛtī*) sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇās*), or according to what is specifically prescribed? 1.
The *agniṣṭoma* is the archetype for all sacrifices; however, among those belonging to a class (*nikāyin*), the first is the archetype everywhere. Or, [the fees are] as specifically directed. 2.
The Jyotis, Gaurīvīta, and Āyu are the Trikadruka days;
the first is an Agniṣṭoma, or all may be Ukthyas; on the Jyotis day, one gives a thousand [cows].

By the rule of the Śyaita [Sāman], the Bṛhat is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra for one who has rivals; the Gaurīvita is for one who has rivals. The Āyuṣya is for one desiring heaven. But the Agniṣṭoma is for one who has rivals. The Viśvajit Agniṣṭoma is for one desiring preeminence. The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is a thousand, or all one's possessions, or as many as there are stotriya verses in the sacrifice.
In a sacrifice where everything is given away as a fee (*sarvavedasa*), one should exclude the eldest son from the distribution and exchange it for knowledge.
(8) At the time of the sacrificial fees, he should give whatever constitutes his entire property, with the exception of his land and his male slaves.

(9) Having brought the highest sacrificial fee and having settled [the ritual], he should sit facing east to the south of the *audumbarī* post and say: "Whatever debt I have here, that I now give all of it. (10)
Having moved away [from the sacrificial ground], [he performs] the Rohiṇī sacrifice with a calf-skin; the rest is the same. 11.
Indra’s Abhijit Agniṣṭoma is for the victory of one who has not yet conquered. 12.
Both the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are used, or it may have the Pṛṣṭha-stotras performed out of sight (parokṣa). 13.
There are eleven animals for the Hotṛ priest at a single sacrificial post;
the sacrificial fee consists of either a thousand choice items or one hundred and twelve.
By means of the Sarvajit Agniṣṭoma, one obtains everything and conquers everything.
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
He becomes an eater of food.
For him, the Mahāvrata, the Pṛṣṭhya, and the Ārkya are recited.
The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a thousand, or twenty, or twenty-eight.

3. There are four [sets] of a thousand. 4. The first is the *Jyotis* Agniṣṭoma with the *Rathantara* Sāman; one becomes firmly established in the vital breaths and in the eating of food. The second is the *Gauḥ* Ukthya with the *Bṛhat* Sāman; one becomes firmly established among cattle. The third is the *Sarvajyotis* Agniṣṭoma with both Sāmans; one obtains everything and conquers everything. The fourth is the Agniṣṭoma equal to the three-night sacrifice (*trirātra*) with the *Bṛhat* Sāman; one obtains the fruit of the three-night sacrifice. 5.
There are four *sādyaskra* sacrifices.
Their distinction is as follows:
the first has the *rathaṃtara-sāman*, the *bṛhat-sāman*, or both *sāmans*.
In that [sacrifice], there are desires regarding rivalry, the desire to overcome an enemy, heaven, or cattle.
On the day before, there are animals dedicated to Agni, Soma, and Bṛhaspati. These are the forms of the set of eleven animals.
If these [materials] are not obtained, there is a cake on eight potsherds for these deities; the first is a caru, and the other two are likewise.
12 He maintains the Āhavanīya fire. 13 He sprinkles the Uttaravedi with clarified butter. 14
He eats food mixed with clarified butter (15).
Having placed gold in his mouth, he lies between the thighs of his beloved wife while observing celibacy, thinking: "Tomorrow I shall sacrifice with an *iṣṭi* or an animal sacrifice" (16).
The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are chosen by mutual consent (17).
Having placed those [carts] according to the light, the *somapravākas* run in all directions with horse-carts carrying milk-pails.
(18) One should pour into the clarified butter (*ājya*) whatever fresh butter (*navanīta*) may rise from them.

(19) With a four-yoked [cart], one should go two *krośas* in the eastern direction; with a three-yoked [cart], three *krośas* to the north; with a two-yoked [cart], two *krośas* to the west; and with a single-yoked [cart], one *krośa* to the south. (20)
Or there may be a single chariot drawn by mules (21).
The release [of the horse] takes place by circling it clockwise to the east (22),
or at a distance of one *yojana* or even two *krośas* (23).
The gift of a horse-chariot is the sacrificial fee (24). A three-year-old castrated bull is the means for purchasing the Soma (25).
Thus ends the second section.
When the sun has risen and he is consecrated, the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) takes place before sunset.
During the Upasad rites, he should close his eyes three times; or having closed them, he may proceed with the ritual. Or else, there are no afternoon Upasad rites.
The sacrificial altar (vedi) is a furrow of barley.
The threshing floor of barley is the high altar (uttaravedi); the two Havirdhāna sheds are the ascent; the measured hall is the Sadas.
The sacrificial post is a wooden splinter (sphyo), or it may be a threshing-fence post with a splinter at its top, or the pole of a plow; the top-ring (caṣālam) is a bundle of grass.
At the time of the offering to Agni and Soma, one should take the Vasatīvarī waters from the house of the sacrificer.
At the time of the *savanīya* offerings, one sacrifices the animals together: the *agnīṣomīya*, the *savanīya*, and the *anūbandhyā*. 10.

In place of the *agnīṣomīya* animal, there is a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Soma. In place of the *anūbandhyā*, there is clotted curd (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa. 11. At the time of its sacrificial fee, a white horse with a dark mane is the fee. 12.
One should give it to a rival belonging to the lineage of Aṅgiras;
or, having chosen a Brahmin who is an object of hatred, one should give him a horse adorned with a golden ornament. In the absence of that, a white cow.
For one year, he should avoid washing his feet, meat, women, untruthfulness, elevated beds, and the application of collyrium and ointments.
That is the initiation (dīkṣā).
If he is unable to do so for a year, he may observe it for twelve days.
Thus ends the third section (kaṇḍikā).
By this, the subsequent [sections] are explained.

Having made the Agniṣṭoma-sāman of the second [stotra] the Pañcadaśa, one should cause one who suffers from illness, or one who desires food, or one who desires offspring, or one who desires cattle, to sacrifice.
The inferior, the younger, and the lowly are the imitation;
its two subsequent Pavamāna lauds consist of eighteen verses.
The horse-sitter, the Soma-announcer, and the leather bag of curd announce [the arrival] at the end of three krośas.
A female cow is the price for purchasing the Soma;
the sacrificial post has its tip sharpened;
the best field of rice is the altar.
The threshing floor of rice serves as the high altar (uttaravedi).

Bhāradvāja is the Hotṛ priest. The fourth [day] is the Viśvajit, characterized by artistic skill, featuring all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras, all the Stomas, and having the gift of one's entire property as the sacrificial fee.
He attains the production of all kinds of food.
12 One practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena.
13 The two chariots are the two Havirdhāna sheds. 14
The sacrificial post (yūpa) is made of *tailva* or *bādhaka* wood and has a pointed top like a wooden sword (*sphya*). 15.
The two pressing-boards (*adhiṣavaṇaphalaka*) are made of *śyena* wood. 16.
For Agni accompanied by Rudra, there is a red animal victim. 17.
They set down the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups;
the sacrificial grass is made of Śara reeds;
the Prastara bunch is from Udumbara wood.
The fuel-sticks are made of Vibhītaka wood (21); the enclosing sticks are provided with arrows (22);
the officiating priests proceed wearing red turbans and red garments, with their sacred threads suspended around the neck (23).

There are twenty-four [sacrificial animals] with ninefold sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*): those with deformed horns, those with missing ears, those that are one-eyed, those that are maimed, and those that are crippled.
(24) At the time of giving the sacrificial fees, they should pierce these with thorns.

(25) If he desires, "May he be slain," he should perform the *Rathantara* at the *Pavamāna* [laud] and the *Bṛhat* as the *Pṛṣṭha* [laud]. If he desires, "May he perish," he should do the opposite of this. (26)
"May he go to the furthest distance and not find a firm footing"—as before, one should perform the *plava* and the *brahmasāman*.
(27) The *ekatrika* Agniṣṭoma of Prajāpati departs after having pointed out all evil.
(28) He gives twenty-four cows as the sacrificial fee. (29)
Thus ends the fourth section (kaṇḍikā).
There are three Vācastomas:
the first two are Agniṣṭomas with the Rathantara-sāman; the latter is an Atirātra consisting of all the Stomas.
In that [sacrifice], all the Ṛg-verses, all the Sāman-chants, and all the Yajus-formulas are employed. 3.
For the Vrātyas who have gone abroad, there are the Vrātyastoma Ukthya sacrifices characterized by the Rathantara Sāman; or alternatively, a second Agniṣṭoma. 4. [The equipment consists of:

a turban, a goad, a bowstring, a chariot with uneven wheels, a chariot covered with wooden planks, a horse and a mule as the two draft animals, a garment of black wool, two skins—one black and one white—and a silver neck-ornament (niṣka). 5.
In that case, the householder's [rope] has its ends frayed like a *balūka* bird, while those of the others have their ends frayed like a *dāma-tūṣa* bird;
there are two ropes each, and two pairs of sandals each.
There are two sets of sacrificial skins.
Thirty-three [priests] approach the householder [sacrificer] with thirty-three [cows] each;
these are the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās).
Or rather, they should win sixty-six cows;
moreover, they say that they should give whatever is their own property, for that is the wealth of a Vrātya.
The Ṣaṭṣoḍaśin is for those who are censured; the Dviṣoḍaśin is for the youngest; the Ūrdhvastoma is for the eldest; and the Catuḥṣoḍaśin is for all.
The *prayati* of the Ādityas is the *ukthya*, the first of those who sit upon the firmament (15);
they go forth free from evil and rivalry (16);

the others are *agniṣṭomas*. The second belongs to the Aṅgirases; the third to the Sādhyas; with the fourth, one attains vigor and heroism for the Maruts; the thirty-three-fold [stoma] is the fifth (17).
"One desiring heaven overcomes his rival through the Abhibhū; he repels his rival by means of the Vinutti.
Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā). "The Citistoma is for one desiring progeny."
A Brāhmaṇa desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) [should perform] the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice with the Gāyatrī metre and the Rathantara Sāman.
(2) The two Agniṣṭomas with the Gāyatrī [metre] are the first sacrifices.
(3) By the first, the Brāhmaṇa obtains splendor and spiritual luster; by the second, the Kṣatriya obtains a fierce and unshakable kingdom. However, they do not become possessed of many cattle. (4)
