One who has not been purified should sacrifice with the Trivṛt Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma.
The Puroruks are addressed to Agni; the Subrahmaṇyā formula is addressed to Agni. They chant the Stotra in verses addressed to Agni; a goat and gold are the sacrificial fees.

Having performed this very Catuṣṭoma sacrifice, a learned Śrotriya who has been struck by dice, struck by a woman, struck by lust, or struck by his own conduct should sacrifice. A dark-grey horse is the sacrificial fee; it is to be given to the Brahman priest.

Having made the Pañcadaśa-stoma the Agniṣṭoma-sāman for this same sacrifice with Vāyavyā verses, one should cause a person afflicted by disease, or one desiring food, offspring, or cattle, to sacrifice. Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman for this same sacrifice with Revatī verses, one should cause one desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) to sacrifice. Having performed this very Catuṣṭoma, one should cause one desiring a village to sacrifice. 10.
"Some say they are without the *pravargya* rite.
One desiring food should perform it with the *trivṛt* stoma;
one desiring vigor, with the *pañcadaśa*."
One who has failed in a sacrifice, or in whatever rite he may have stumbled, should perform the seventeen-fold Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma.
For one who speaks, the first [stotra] is the Trivṛt;
for one who strikes down [the enemy], it is the Pañcadaśa, which is explicitly defined.
The seventeenth [stoma] is for eating food that should not be eaten;
the twenty-first is for traveling to Gandhāra, Kaliṅga, Magadha, Pāraskara, or Sauvīra;
the twenty-third is for one desiring vigor.
The Trayastriṃśa [sacrifice] is for one who desires heaven; or rather, in the Agniṣṭoma form of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, one may desire all desires—
thus ends the sixth section (kaṇḍikā).
There are four Agniṣṭoma sacrifices characterized by the *trivṛt* stoma and having the *rathaṃtara-sāman* as their principal chant.
One desiring a village should sacrifice with the first of these, which is *anirukta* (undefined).
According to some, the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) is *nirukta* (defined).
A white horse is the sacrificial fee; it is to be given to the Brahman priest. 4.
The Bṛhaspatisava is the second [sacrifice]. 5.

A Brāhmaṇa who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) or the office of domestic chaplain (*purodhas*), or one whom they might consecrate for the position of a ruler (*sthapati*), should perform this sacrifice. 6.
The Hotṛ is one who wears a wreath, is ruddy, and has squinting eyes; he is the Triśukra.
With the verse, "O Bṛhaspati, be pleased with us," he draws the Atigrāhya cup for Bṛhaspati.
An animal dedicated to Bṛhaspati is to be immolated.
At the morning pressing, when the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down, he assigns eleven sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). 10.

At the midday pressing, with clarified butter, he sprinkles him while he is seated upon a black antelope skin, or with the residue of the *śukra* and *manthin* vessels, [reciting]: "O Bṛhaspati and Indra, you two are masters of celestial wealth and also of that which is earthly. Bestow riches upon the singer who praises you! Do you all protect us evermore with blessings! 11. There are twelve horses at the midday pressing; eleven at the third pressing. 12.
He disposes of both of them.
Alternatively, there are eight at the morning pressing, eleven at the midday pressing, and twelve at the third pressing; or all of them at the midday pressing.
They lead the horse to each pressing in three turns.
Or rather, one should meditate upon the other two pressings with the mind. Or even not with the mind at all.
Having performed the *iṣu* *viṣṭuti* for the third pressing, one who practices sorcery should sacrifice.
The rest is the same as in the Śyena sacrifice.
A dark-brown horse is the sacrificial fee; it is to be given to the Brahman priest. 19.
The fourth [sacrifice] is the *sarvasvāra*, the *śunaskarṇastoma*. 20.
One who desires death should perform this sacrifice, he who should desire: "May I go to the heavenly world while free from disease. 21.
A parrot-green animal dedicated to Yama is to be sacrificed. 22.
Cooked food is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 23.

While the Ārbhava Pavamāna is being chanted, having wrapped himself with a new garment with its fringes pointing downward, with his head toward the south, he lies down and says: "O Brāhmaṇas, complete my sacrifice. 24.
At that very time, it is completed. 25.
One desiring prosperity should sacrifice with the Bhū-ukthya, having the Rathantara as its Sāman. 26.
A cow is the sacrificial fee. 27.
Thus ends the seventh section.
Truly, the merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices becomes inexhaustible.
In the world of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, there is the Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma.
The animal sacrifice is for the Viśvedevas; the *anūbandhyā* cow is dedicated to Bṛhaspati. He subsequently offers the Vaiśvadeva oblations following the morning pressing cakes.
However, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* portion are the same.
They do not erect a sacrificial post; they do not prepare the high altar.
They bind the animal to the enclosing stick, or to a firebrand, or to the sacrificial grass. In the subsequent rites, they erect the sacrificial posts and they prepare the high altar.

Then, after four months, in the world of the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings, there is an Agniṣṭoma or an Ukthya; or both an Ukthya and an Agniṣṭoma. There is an animal sacrifice for the Maruts, and a second one for Varuṇa. The Anūbandhyā cow belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa.
The oblations of the Varuṇapraghāsa are like those of the Vaiśvadeva.
On the *mārjālīya* altar, they proceed with the *karambha* vessels.

Then, after four months, in the section of the *Sākamedha* sacrifices, there is an *agniṣṭoma*, an *ukthya*, and an *atirātra*. There is an animal sacrifice for Agni; a second one for Indra and Agni; on the third day, eleven animals or one for Prajāpati; and a *saurya* *nūbandhyā* as the concluding offering.

On the first day, they perform the *prātaḥsavanīya* offerings for Ānīkavat; the *mādhyaṃdinīya* offerings for Sāṃtapana. When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, they proceed with the *gṛhamedhīya* offering.
On the following day, when the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) has been commenced, they proceed with the *pūrṇadarvya* offering.
The Kraiḍinas [offer] the oblations of the morning pressing; the Svātavasas, those of the midday pressing; and the Mahāhavis, those of the third pressing.
(18) When the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been set down, they proceed with the Pitṛyajña on the Mārjālīya fire-altar enclosed by a screen.
(19) Having performed the Traiyambaka rites, they return and proceed with the Āditya offering. (20)
Thus ends the eighth section (kaṇḍikā).
Then, after four months, in the place of the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice, there is the Jyotiḥ Agniṣṭoma; the animal victim is dedicated to Vāyu; the Anūbandhyā cow is dedicated to the Aśvins.
The oblations for the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice are like those of the Vaiśvadeva;
the intermediate vows are like those of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices;
throughout, he emerges from the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) wearing unwashed (new) garments.

Every day he gives fifty cows as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); on the final day, one hundred and twelve. Or, in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, they are according to the season or according to their own specific rule. At the third pressing, the calves are given together with their mothers.
One who desires a village should sacrifice with the *Upahavya* *Agniṣṭoma*, which is undefined (*anirukta*).
Some say that the Nirukta is the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana). A white horse is the sacrificial fee; it is to be given to the Brahman priest.
One desiring heaven [should sacrifice] with the Ṛtapeya Agniṣṭoma, using the Bṛhat Sāman.

There are six *dīkṣā*s or nine; there are six *upasads*. (12) He observes the vow of clarified butter. (13) The vow lasts for as long as it takes to traverse the first joint of a finger once the *soma* has been purchased. (14)
With each successive section he undertakes the vow.

15 At night, having turned toward the Āhavanīya fire, he remains seated; by day, [he remains seated] toward the sun. 16 Having uttered "Ṛta," they proceed forward. 17 Reciting "Ṛta," they consume [the food].
A four-cornered cup made of udumbara wood, filled with soma, is to be given to a dear Brahmin of the same lineage.
(18) Through an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice accompanied by abundant gold, one attains the world of oxen and conquers the luminous worlds.
(19) One gives twelve mānas of gold at the Dīkṣaṇīyā offering; twice that amount at the Prāyaṇīyā offering. (20)

Thus, from this point upward, by doubling the practice, he gives an additional hundred oxen at the *atithyā*, during the performance of the *upasad*s, at the omentum of the *agnīṣomīya* animal, at the omentum of the *savanīya* animal offered to Agni and Soma, and at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) of the *savanīya* when the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down.
Thus ends the ninth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
A golden garland with six or twelve lotuses is for the Udgātṛ at the Avabhṛtha sacrifice, the Udayanīya, the Anūbandhyā, and the Udavasānīya offerings performed during the Yajñāyajñīya stotra. 1.
A Brāhmaṇa desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should perform the Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, characterized by the Trivṛt stoma and the Rathantara Sāman.
2. A Rājanya desiring heroic power (vīrya) should perform the Indrastut Indraṣṭoma Ukthya sacrifice, characterized by the Pañcadaśa stoma and the Bṛhat Sāman.
A Vaiśya desiring cattle should sacrifice with the seventeen-fold Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma, using the Kaṇvarathantara Sāman;
it has been stated that the morning pressing is performed with the Pratidhuṣa [stotra].

One should cause a person afflicted by disease, or one desiring food, offspring, or cattle, or one who has fallen away from prosperity, to sacrifice with the Tīvrasut Ukthya, using either the Rathantara Sāman, the Bṛhat Sāman, or both Sāmans.
They milk a hundred [cows] for the *āśira* mixture;
these constitute the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).
The methods of mixing the soma are like those of the *vaiśyasava*.
Or, at the third pressing, they draw up the Soma-mixtures with the *nītamiśra* formula;
the officiating priests smell them but do not consume them.
They consume [the soma] during the Acchāvāka’s chant (stotra). (13) The Hotrakas seek permission for the Brahman.
(14) Both Adhvaryus and all the Camasādhvaryus respond to the Acchāvāka. (15)
The eastern set of eleven [stakes] is brought together;
they dig up the altar as far as the sacrificial post;
a white mare, pregnant, is the sacrificial fee.
By the Marutstoma, the king and the domestic priest attain union (sāyujya).
Now, this is the Rāḍ: he who, desiring a kingdom, does not obtain it, should perform this;
one desiring food, by means of the Virāj; one desiring stability, by means of the Svarāj.
Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).

He who, having accepted much [as a gift], might feel as if he has swallowed poison, should perform the Punastoma sacrifice; or likewise after eating food that should not be eaten, or, according to some, after officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom it is forbidden to officiate.
He who is light, as it were, and unstable,
should perform this twenty-first [stoma] when desiring offspring;
in each stotra, one additional stotrīyā verse is produced.
"May the Gandharvas and Apsarases rejoice," [he says] at the morning pressing;
when the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been set down, he places the *pūta* stalk underneath.
"May the Gandharvas, the gods, rejoice," [he says] at the midday pressing. "May the Gandharvas, the fathers, rejoice," [he says] at the third pressing.
One who has rivals [should perform it] with a *chadana* [stoma].
In each stotra, one *stotrīyā* verse falls away.
It is known that as that [verse] falls away, the rival falls away after it.

For one who desires by means of the *sarvatomukha* sacrifice, "May I become all this," the *gārhapatya* fire is in the center; the sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*) for the Soma rites are in each direction: the *trivṛt* stoma in the eastern direction, the *pañcadaśa* to the south, the *saptadaśa* behind (to the west), and the *ekaviṃśa* to the north.
For one desiring food, there are the *rāśimarāyū* and the *catuṣṭoma*.
He gives a heap of grain in the east; a heap of grain in the north.
15 For one desiring cattle, there are the Gotama and Catuṣṭoma sacrifices.
16 The subsequent [sacrifice] is an Ukthya with the Ṣoḍaśin cup. 17
You two are like neuter sacrificial animals (18).
One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid* and *valabhid* [sacrifices] (19).
Having sacrificed with the *udbhid*, one should sacrifice with the *valabhid* after a year has passed (20).
He enters upon the intermediate space with a cake on eight potsherds for Agni.
On both occasions, he gives complete Gāyatrī verses as the sacrificial fee. Thus ends the eleventh section.
Eight and eight [verses]. 1.
One desiring honor [should recite] with two verses of honor.
2. Both [days] have the same *sāman*. 3.
For those two, a chariot with horses was the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of four yokes;
all the horses were capable of a hundredfold performance;
that [chariot] was golden, trembling, adorned with every ornament, and radiant.
His retinue consists of tiger-skins; his armor is made of leopard-skin and bear-skin. He mounts [the chariot] fully equipped, with his charioteer likewise equipped and surrounded by two attendants.
It is known that the charioteer wears a golden ornament and a garland.
With the two bird-sacrifices accompanied by the piling of the fire-altar, for one who should desire, "May I move through the luminous heavenly worlds like a bird," [one should perform them].
With the Bull-Agniṣṭoma and the Rathantara Sāman, one should cause a king to sacrifice when a battle is joined.
Whatever they may obtain therein, from that [total] a hundred and twelve is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One who desires heaven [should sacrifice] with the Vyoma [stotra].
13 Both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara [sāmans] are used.
14 Everything is seventeenfold. 15
The Agniṣṭoma-sāman consists of twenty-one verses.

With the Gosava sacrifice, characterized by thirty-six [verses], an Ukthya-stotra, using either the Rathantara-sāman, the Bṛhat-sāman, or both sāmans, one who desires self-sovereignty [should perform it]. The Kaṇvarathantara is used as the Pavamāna-stotra.
The sacrificial fee is ten thousand.

To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, on ground not yet dug up for the altar, he is consecrated during the Bṛhat-stotra with the verse: "Born with wealth, increased by power, the best sustainer of princely authority among princes, the bestower of vigor—great in greatness, do thou stand firm; be watchful over the princely authority and the kingdom! I consecrate thee with the self-sovereignty of Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin.
Thus ends the twelfth section.
Having sacrificed with that [offering], he remains for one year under a vow regarding cattle:

he should drink water only after bringing it near, and he should cut grass only after bringing it near; he may approach his mother, his sister, or a woman of the same lineage. Wherever he finds excrement, there he should urinate.
By means of the Stoma of the Maruts, one conquers infinite prosperity.
4 One should cause two or three [persons] to sacrifice with this [rite]. 5 It is for Agni Kulāya for one who desires food. 6
The two *kulāya* sacrifices for Indra and Agni are for one who desires heaven.
(7) With the *Indrastut*, the *Indrastoma*, the *ukthya* sacrifice, and the *Bṛhat-sāman*, a *rājanya* desiring heroic power [performs the sacrifice]. (8) A bull is the sacrificial fee. (9)
One should cause both a king and his domestic priest to sacrifice with the *stoma* of Indra and Agni for the attainment of prosperity.
Splendor and spiritual luster belong to the Brahmin; the king enters into the people. By means of the *vighana*, one strikes away evil and the rival; by it, all adversaries are struck down.
One practicing exorcism [uses] the *vajra* with sixteen [verses]; one practicing exorcism [uses] the *saṃdaṃśa*.
The ritual procedure for these two is explained by that of the *śyena*.
There are thirteen *atirātra* sacrifices.
One desiring prosperity through light [should sacrifice] with the Sarvastoma; one wishing to thrive [should sacrifice] with the Ekādaśina animal offerings.
Because the sacrificial animals would otherwise fall away, [one should perform] the Aptoryāma; by it, one obtains everything and conquers everything.
(19) One who desires offspring [should perform] the sacrifice with nine and seventeen [stomas].
(20) The son of the eldest wife [should perform] the Viṣuvat [day]; he obtains preeminence. (21)
One desiring prosperity should perform the Goṣṭoma; one desiring long life, the Svargakāma;
and one desiring cattle, the Abhijit.
One who has rivals should perform the Viśvajit sacrifice; one desiring food should perform the Trivṛt sacrifice;
one desiring vigor should perform the Pañcadaśa sacrifice.
With the seventeenfold [stoma] one desiring offspring;
with the twenty-onefold, one desiring firm standing—
thus ends the thirteenth section.
The Ahīna sacrifices beginning with the Dvirātra and extending beyond the Atirātra up to the Ekādaśarātra have their ritual procedure explained by that of the Ahīna-twelve-day sacrifice (Dvādaśāha).
For the Dvirātra, the first day has the Aindravāyava cup as the first, and the subsequent day has the Śukra cup as the first.

And this [first day] of the three-night sacrifice has the Āgrayaṇa cup first; 4. And this [first day] of the four-night sacrifice has the Aindravāyava cup first; 5. And this [first day] of the five-night sacrifice has the Śukra cup first; 6.
In a six-night sacrifice, it changes twice; 7.
In a seven-night sacrifice, this [sequence] and that which begins with the Aindravāyava; 8. In an eight-night sacrifice, this [sequence] and that which begins with the Śukra; 9.
In the nine-night rite, it revolves three times;
this same [rite] of ten nights has the draught for Indra and Vāyu as the first;
this same [rite] of eleven nights has the draught for Śukra as the first.
In the twelve-night sacrifice, it is performed four times (13).

The drawing of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup occurs on the second day of the two-night sacrifice (14), and it is to be drawn on the middle day of the three-night sacrifice; on every fourth day in the various *ahīna* sacrifices beginning with the four-night sacrifice (15).
There are four two-night sacrifices.
The first is the Vyuṣṭi-dvirātra; it has been explained by Āṅgīrasa: he who might be virtuous yet as if lacking [in prosperity] should perform this.
The Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma is first; the Sarvastoma Atirātra is second. By means of the Kāpivana [sacrifice], whatever desire one desires, that he attains; he becomes free from scorching heat.
The Jyotir-ukthya or Agniṣṭoma is first; the Atirātra is second.
By means of the Caitraratha [Sāman], one becomes firmly established in the vital breaths and in food.
22. The Agniṣṭoma is the first; the Atirātra is the latter. 23.
Thus ends the fourteenth Kaṇḍikā.

By means of the Garga-trirātra sacrifice, one attains progeny and abundance, conquers the heavenly world, becomes firmly established in these worlds, and ascends after the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas.
1. The *traidhātavīyā* is the initiation offering (*dīkṣaṇīyā*).
2. A red, brown, or tawny one-year-old, two-year-old, or three-year-old cow is the *somakrayaṇī* (the cow for purchasing the Soma). 3.
The Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, and the Atirātra; the Rathantara, Vāmadevya, and Bṛhat as the Pṛṣṭha-stotras;
a thousand as the sacrificial fee.

On the first day he gives three hundred and thirty-three; likewise on the second and the third. A thousand is exceeded by the *rohiṇī*, the *upadhvastā*, the *dvirūpā*, the *ubhayata-enī*, or the *anyatarata-enī*.
"Whichever cow is excellent" is what has been stated.

On the first day, the *udbhṛṣṭi* (the bull that has been rubbed) is the principal one. He consecrates it with the mantra: "O Agni, bring us a thousand; you have burst open the skin of the powerful one. Bring us a thousand along with offspring and cattle; may wealth enter into me again. On the second day, the *vehad* (the cow that miscarries) is the principal one.

He consecrates it with the mantra: "Thou hast become rich in sap through the sap of the waters and the plants; as such, bestow upon me a thousandfold, together with offspring and cattle; may wealth return to me again. (13) Regarding the dwarf [image] on the third day: (14) He consecrates it with the mantra: "Thou art the foundation of a thousand; thou art the dwarf belonging to Viṣṇu; as such, bestow upon us a thousandfold, together with offspring and cattle; may wealth return to me again. (15)
"It is said that he should lead her north of the Āgnīdhra fire.
This concludes the fifteenth section (kaṇḍikā).

Or, having led her south of the altar, he should make her smell the Droṇakalaśa vessel between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya fire, [reciting]: "Smell the vessel! [This may be done] at the Āgnīdhra fire-shed or at the Havirdhāna shed.
Having led it northward to the Āgnīdhra shed, he places a garment of fine silk upon its back;
in that [garment] there is a knotted representation of the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths.
Then, while she stands facing west in front [of the fire], he should offer the oblation with the verse: "Both of you have conquered."
He offers as oblations the forms that exist in her;
some recite [the formulas] pertaining to the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Having led [the horse] to the western corner of the *sadas* and standing near it, he should whisper into its right ear: "O *iḍā*, O delight! (1.5.7).

Having abandoned consciousness, he departs. If [the fire] has been carried eastward, one should know: "This sacrificer, being favored by the Person, has won the auspicious world. If it has been carried southward, he will quickly depart from this world. If it has been carried westward, he will possess abundant grain. If it has been carried northward, he will become superior in this world.
The sacrificer consecrates it with the mantra: "May she lead me to the heavenly world."
Of the thirty-three [cows], taking three from each group, he should bring them together and give them to the Āgnīdhra, the Brahman, the Hotṛ, the Udgātṛ, the Unnetṛ, or the Adhvaryu;
or, having chosen two Unnetṛs, he should give them to whichever of the two does not call for the *śrauṣaṭ*;
or he may give two shares to the Brahman and a third to the Āgnīdhra.
Or she may be assigned to all the members of the assembly (sadasyas).
Or, having been set apart with water, she may live according to her own will. It has been stated that he who accepts her without knowing [the ritual] incurs a fault.
Having ransomed her with gold weighing one hundred mānas, he releases her into the cow-pen of the sacrificer.
Thus ends the sixteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
On the first day, they milk ten cows for the *āśira* mixture; on the second, twenty; on the third, thirty.
Prepared food is to be given on the first day; gold, a cow, and clothing on the second; a wagon, a chariot, a horse, an elephant, and a man on the third.
One should not give anything in excess of a thousand;
some say one may give.
If one gives, when the omentum of the *anūbandhya* animal has been offered, while leading the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), one should lead no fewer than ten.
Because, when one intends to give a single cow, one should dedicate a set of ten to those [ten priests];
if two, to five; if five, to two.
In this manner, it continues up to a hundred or even a thousand.
Having taken the best sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and having settled down, [he performs] the Śabalī-homa:

"Thou art the ocean, all-encompassing; the first-born of the gods, the Brahman of the cosmic order (*ṛta*). Thou art food, thou art pure, thou art light, thou art immortality. We know thee, O Śabalī, as the shining one. Of thee, the earth is one foot, the atmosphere is one foot, the sky is one foot, the ocean is one foot. Such art thou, O Śabalī; we know thee. Do thou milk for us food and strength, the stream of wealth, O Śabalī, most powerful among creatures; may I follow thy enclosure, Svāhā! Thus he offers the Śabalī-homa. This is the seventeenth section.
The Aśvamedha consists of the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, and the Atirātra. The Pṛṣṭha-stotras are the Rathantara, the Mahānāmnī verses, and the Bṛhat.
A king who desires, "May I become all this," should perform this sacrifice.
One desiring self-sovereignty performs the Baidatrirātra sacrifice.
There are three Trivṛt Atirātras, each equipped with the Ṣoḍaśin cup; the Pṛṣṭha stotras are the Rathantara, Vāmadevya, and Bṛhat.
By means of the Garga-trirātra, the three days of the latter [period] with their *pṛṣṭha* stotras have been explained.
(7) One desiring cattle [should perform it] with the Chandoma-pavamāna; (8) by means of the Antarvasu, one obtains cattle. (9)
One desiring heaven [should perform] the Parāka [fast];
there are four four-night [sacrifices];
of Atri, the first is the Caturvīra.
"Four heroes are born in his lineage," so it was said regarding Suhotra (13).
The Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Atirātra, and the four Catuṣṭomas belong to Atri alone (14). "Atri, whose deity is faith," so it was said (15).
One desiring prosperity [should perform this sacrifice] by means of the son of Jamadagni (Jāmadagnya).

(16) The Upasad rites consist of sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa). (17) There are: a cake on one potsherd for Agni; a cake on two potsherds for the Aśvins; a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu; a cake on four potsherds for Soma; a cake on five potsherds for Savitṛ; a cake on six potsherds for Dhātṛ; a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts; a cake on eight potsherds for Bṛhaspati; a cake on nine potsherds for Mitra; a cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa; a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra; and a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśvedevas. (18)

The *darvihoma* offerings take place. (19) Thus ends the eighteenth section (*kaṇḍikā*). O Agni, perform the office of the Hotṛ; perform the sacrifice. Bring hither Vaiśvānara the Father for our protection. May it be pleasing to Indra and to the gods; may they enjoy the oblation, *svāhā*! O divine Aśvins, with the honeyed stalk, sprinkle the sacrificer at this sacrifice. O divine Viṣṇu, stride forth after this sacrifice for the sake of the sacrificer. O divine Savitṛ, well-inspire today at this sacrifice for the sake of the sacrificer. O divine Dhātṛ, being a good disposer, be present today at this sacrifice for the sake of the sacrificer.

"O divine pressing-stones, speak today at this sacrifice a honeyed word for the sacrificer! O divine Aditi, favor this sacrifice today; be present for the sacrificer! O divine Anumati, approve this sacrifice today; think favorably of the sacrificer! O divine waters, bow down today at this sacrifice for the sake of the sacrificer! From seat to seat, may the Ṛbhu, possessing offspring and rejoicing, [be present]. O divine Indra, be present today at this sacrifice as the bestower of power for the sacrificer! O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, the bestower of good seed, be present today at this sacrifice for the sake of the sacrificer! Having thus recited these responses, the oblations are offered.
"To Indra, to the gods, may the oblation be pleasing; Svāhā!"—with these words he appends [the formula] everywhere.
Thus ends the nineteenth section (kaṇḍikā).
This is the "Crawling" (saṃsarpa) of Vasiṣṭha. He who is virtuous but as if deficient should perform this [rite].
The *Saṃjaya* sacrifice belongs to Viśvāmitra; one who has rivals should perform it. There are five five-day periods.
It is said: "In the beginning, this [universe] was indeed one, the year. 4.
The second is the Abhyāsaṅgya; whatever desire one desires, that one attains. There are three Ukthya sacrifices, an Agniṣṭoma, and an Atirātra.

Two [pressings] have the *trivṛt* stoma, one has the *pañcadaśa*; two have the *pañcadaśa*, one has the *saptadaśa*; two have the *saptadaśa*, one has the *ekaviṃśa*; two have the *ekaviṃśa*, one has the *triṇava*; two have the *triṇava*, one has the *trayastriṃśa*.
By means of the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice, one becomes more prosperous. Year after year, he performs the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*).
They bring seventeen spotted bulls five years old; seventeen spotted heifers three years old that have not yet calved.
They release the bulls after they have been sprinkled with water and carried around the fire; they immolate the heifers.
We shall describe their colors in order.
Having sacrificed female oxen that are speckled like lotuses, soft as butter, reddish, tawny, dappled, and of the finest quality, they undergo the consecration (dīkṣā).
14. There is a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma*, a fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*) *ukthya*, a seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) *ukthya*, another fifteen-fold *ukthya*, and a seventeen-fold *atirātra*. 15.
These bulls are the sacrificial animals for the Soma-pressings (*savanīya*). 16.
Every day they sacrifice three [bulls] each; on the final day, fifteen bulls for Indra and the Maruts, and heifers for the Maruts. If Rudra should take ill-will toward the bulls...
Thus ends the twentieth section (kaṇḍikā).
One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by Rudra;
[one should offer] a pap to Aponaptr if [the victim] should fall into the water.
If [the sacrifice] should fail, [he should offer] a *caru* to Nairṛta;
if it has failed or become shattered, a *caru* or a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) to Bhauma;
if it is crippled or crooked, a *caru* to Bṛhaspati.
If it should be lost, [he should offer] a pap to Vāyu (6).
If he should encounter a threatening army, [he should offer] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Jayat (7).
If they should lead him away by force, [he should offer] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Prasahvan (8).
If he should become blind, [he should offer] a pap for Sūrya or a cake on one potsherd; 9.
If he should fall into a pit, a pap for Viṣṇu; 10.
If he should die from an unknown wasting disease, a pap for Prajāpati or a cake on twelve potsherds. 11.
The fourth [sacrifice] is the Antarmahāvrata.
One who has rivals should perform it:
a Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma, a Pañcadaśa Ukthya, a Mahāvrata, a Saptadaśa Ukthya, and an Ekaviṃśa Atirātra.
The Puruṣamedha is the fifth [sacrifice]. 15.
The days are like those of the Pañcaśāradīya. 16.

On the first day he gives ten thousand (ayuta); on the second, a hundred thousand (niyuta); on the third, a million (arbuda) and ten million (nyarbudam). As it is for the first two days, so it is for the two following. 17.
Thus ends the twenty-first section (kaṇḍikā).
There are four six-day periods (ṣaḍaha):
the first belongs to the Sādhyas.
"It has been said that the Sādhyas were indeed gods who desired heaven" (3); "one desiring offspring [should perform] the second [form] of the seasons" (4);
"the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha" (5).

By means of the third [set], the *trikadruka*, he attains whatever desire he may wish for from above. 6. The *agniṣṭoma* is the *trivṛt*; the *ukthya* is the *pañcadaśa*; the *ukthya* is the *saptadaśa*; and the *atirātra* is the *jyotis-gaur-āyus*. 7.
By means of the fourth [set], he is indeed procreated with offspring and cattle. 8.
The five-day sacrifice with repeated *abhyāsa* chants, ending with the *viśvajit* *atirātra*, [is one];
there are eight seven-night sacrifices; [and] the *kausurubinda* for one desiring cattle. 9–11.
That has been explained. 12.
With the second [sacrifice] for the Seven Seers, one who desires heaven [performs it]. 13.
It consists of a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, the *mahāvrata*, and an *atirātra*. 14.
One desiring offspring [should perform] the Prājāpatya;
the Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha, the Prājāpatya Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra [are included].
One desiring cattle [should perform] the Chandomapavamāna.
The Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha with Chandoma Pavamānas and the Mahāvrata at the Atirātra (18);
one desiring food should perform the Pṛṣṭhyāvalamba (19);
the Pṛṣṭhyastoma-ṣaḍaha with the Mahāvrata and Atirātra (20).
Thus ends the twenty-second section (kaṇḍikā).
One desiring food should perform [the sacrifice] measured by a sattra;
the days are like those of Kausurubinda.
One desiring vigor [should perform] the Aindra sacrifice.
Then there is Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus, Abhijit, Viśvajit, Sarvajit, and the Sarvastoma Atirātra.
By means of Janaka’s seven-night rite, one attains progeny and abundance, conquers the heavenly world, and becomes firmly established in these worlds.

There are four nine-night sacrifices (*navarātra*) beginning with the *agniṣṭoma*: the *viśvajit*, the *mahāvrata*, the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and the *vaiśvānara* *atirātra*. (6) One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should perform the eight-night sacrifice; it has been explained. (7) There are three nine-night sacrifices. (8)
By the first [sacrifice], one who desires long life [performs] the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, the *jyotis*, the *go*, the *āyus*, and the *atirātra*. By the second, one who desires spiritual luster.
The *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma*, the *pañcadaśa* *ukthya*, the *saptadaśa* *ukthya* as an *abhyāsaṅgya*, the five-day rite (*pañcāha*), and the *viśvajit* *atirātra*. 12.
One desiring food [should perform] with the *śalalīpiśaṅga* [sacrifice]. 13.
The *jyotis-gau-āyus-jyotis-gau-āyus-gau-jyotis* *atirātra*. 14.
There are four ten-night periods.
(15) One who is about to undergo initiation for a ten-night rite should, having mentally recited the *daśahotṛ* formula, offer it with the *graha* into the *āhavanīya* fire.
(16) The *trikakud* is the first; one becomes a *trikakud* among his offspring and equals. (17)

The Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma, the Pañcadaśa Ukthya, the Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma, the Saptadaśa Agniṣṭoma, the Ekaviṃśa Ukthya, the Saptadaśa Agniṣṭoma, the Triṇava Agniṣṭoma, the Trayastriṃśa Ukthya, the Triṇava Agniṣṭoma, and the Viśvajit Sarvapṛṣṭha Atirātra. Thus ends the twenty-third section (Kaṇḍikā).
One who is being harmed by the magic of the gods [should perform this].

The Jyotis Agniṣṭoma with the Triṣṭomasaṃstha; the Abhijit Agniṣṭoma with the Triṣṭomasaṃstha; the Gaur Ukthya; the Abhijit Agniṣṭoma; the Viśvajit Agniṣṭoma with the Ukthya; the Viśvajit Agniṣṭoma; and the Sarvastoma Atirātra.
(2) By means of this Chandomavat sacrifice, one obtains a person, cattle, vigor, and strength.
(3) The Abhyāsaṅgya six-day period, three Chandomas, and an Atirātra. (4)
Now, according to some: there is an Abhyāsaṅgya, five Ahaḥ-sacrifices, four Chandomas, and an Atirātra (5).
According to Kausurubinda: it becomes more abundant than the Bahu (6).
There are three Agniṣṭomas with the Trivṛt-stoma, three Ukthyas with the Pañcadaśa-stoma, three Ukthyas with the Saptadaśa-stoma, and an Ekaviṃśa Atirātra (7).
The Pauṇḍarīka is an eleven-night sacrifice with a sacrificial fee of ten thousand [cows].

Day by day he gives thousands; at the final day, he gives a thousand horses or a hundred horses. By means of this, he attains all prosperity, reaches the state of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), conquers the heavenly world, and becomes firmly established in these worlds.
The Abhyāsaṅgya consists of a six-day period with four *stomas*, an *agniṣṭoma*, three *chandomas*, and an *atirātra*. 11.
Now, according to some: the Abhyāsaṅgya consists of a five-day period, four *chandomas*, a *mahāvrata*, and a *viśvajit* *atirātra* with all *pṛṣṭhas*. 12.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section (*kaṇḍikā*).
Now, the Bṛhaspatisava among the Savas has been explained.
A Vaiśya desiring prosperity [performs it].
He offers seven oblations beginning with that for Agni.
A speckled heifer is offered to the Maruts.
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, having spread the skin of a bull on the sacrificer’s seat with its neck toward the east and the hair upward, he sprinkles the sacrificer, seated upon it, with curds.
This applies when the sacrificer is a Brahmin desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
He offers eight oblations beginning with that for Agni (the Āgneya).
Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, having purified the clarified butter with gold, he sprinkles him while he is seated upon a black antelope skin with that [butter].
Now follows the Somasava.
Whatever belongs to the Rājasūya, with the exception of the Soma sacrifice, all that takes place here.
Having completed the offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati, he immolates a barren cow for Soma.
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of that [cow], he sprinkles him with water while reciting the verse addressed to Soma: "He who has spread himself in battles and in armies... (RV 6.75.1). 10–12.

Having completed the remainder, he performs the sacrifice with the *saṃsṛp* oblations, the *diśām aveṣṭi*, the animal sacrifice with two animals, the *sātyadūta* oblations, and the *prayuja* offerings. (13) One desiring cattle performs the *pṛthisava*. (14) Whatever belongs to the *rājasūya* that does not require the high altar (*uttaravedi*), all that takes place here. (15)
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the *maitrābārhaspatya*, he sprinkles [the sacrificer] with water while reciting the *nārāśaṃsī* verse, "Those fifty of mine... (RV 10.87.16). 16.
The subsequent portion is the same as the preceding one, with the exception of the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). 17.
The *gosava* has been explained. 18.
One who desires food and drink should sacrifice with the Odanasava;
he should sacrifice under the Rohiṇī asterism and cook the oblation before sunrise;
it is a Darvihoma offering.

When the sun has risen, having offered four oblations of boiled rice with the formulas "A lion! and "A tiger!", he offers them with the respective mantras: "Thou art a sovereign (rāḍ)," and "Thou art a universal ruler (virāḍ).

22. This is the twenty-fifth section. They prepare churned drinks: a Brahmin prepares a churned drink of clarified butter, a Kṣatriya a churned drink of milk, a Vaiśya a churned drink of curds, and a Śūdra a churned drink of water. 1.

"O Indra, for you who are radiant, I mix you, the radiant one, with the flour-meal"—having thus mixed the clarified butter with the meal, the Brāhmaṇa consecrates it with "Thou art radiance," and gives it to the sacrificer with "I give this to thee.
2. Having received it with "May my mouth be radiant," he consumes it.
3. In the same manner, for the others, each subsequent mixing, consecration, giving, and consumption is performed according to their respective characteristics. 4.

Having consumed all [the portions], the sacrificer gives gold to a Brāhmaṇa; a bow with three arrows to a Rājanya; a goad to a Vaiśya; and a bowl of beans to a Śūdra. The sacrificer eats the remainder of the cooked rice.
He consecrates him as he eats with the mantra: "O Agni, make this [person] for long life and splendor. (ŚGS 4.15.5–7)
He ties gold to the sacrificer [with the mantra]:
"Thou art life; thou art all-encompassing life. While it is being tied, he mutters [the mantra].
They take up the water-drawings (apām graha) for those who prepare the stirred offerings (mantha), with each respective mantra beginning: "The essence which is in the flowing of the waters."
With these [verses] joined together, he sprinkles him with the formula: "From whence the wind, swift as thought...

(RV 10.168.4). Having consecrated him with the formula: "Like the ocean art thou in depth... (RV 10.168.5), he then purifies him with three bunches of *darbha* grass. It is known that this serves as a substitute for the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
The chariot stands positioned in front of the Āhavanīya fire. (14) "Go forward!"—with these words, the sacrificer approaches it.
(15) "Mount, O increaser of friends!"—with this, he addresses the sacrificer as he is mounting. (16)
He touches the two chariot wheels with the words, "The two hooks, the two hooks. Or [he touches] the two sides.
With the five verses beginning, "Mount, O slayer of Vṛtra," he mounts.
It is known from scripture: "He becomes worthy of being seen and beautiful to behold, who sacrifices with this."
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section. The Odanasava sacrifice is concluded. The Pañcaśāradīya has been explained.
Likewise, for the Agniṣṭut sacrifice: its *puroruc* verses are as follows:

"O Agni, these thy ages are ageless" (*asyājarāso agne āyūṃṣi*) is that of the Aindravāyava cup; the second is that of the Maitrāvaruṇa cup; the third is that of the Āśvina cup; the fourth and fifth are those of the Śukra and Manthin cups; and the sixth is that of the Āgrayaṇa cup.
He binds another [animal] dedicated to Agni for the Ukthya sacrifice;
those [animals] for the Dhruva are constant;
he binds [animals] for the Aindrāgna and Vaiśvadeva sacrifices.

"O you who possess the splendor of Agni"—these three [verses] are for the Marutvatīya cups; "Hear us, O you with hearing ears"—this next one is for the Māhendra cup; "Aditi, of all [gods]"—these three are for the Āditya cup; the last one is for the Sāvitra cup.
He binds [the animal] for the Vaiśvadeva cup;
the [verse] is constant for the Pātnīvata cup.
He joins [the cup] for the Hāriyojana.
One who desires power or one who desires vigor should sacrifice with the Indra-stuti, the Indra-stoma, and the Ukthya.
The Puroruc verses belong to Indra.

"Stay, O two bay horses; whose bull [is it]?"—this is for the cup for Indra and Vāyu. The third [verse] is for the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa; the fourth for the cup for the Aśvins; the fifth and sixth for the cups for Śukra and Manthin; the seventh for the Āgrayaṇa cup.
The [verses] prescribed as constant are for the Ukthya cup.
He yokes the Dhruva, Aindrāgna, and Vaiśvadeva cups.
The verses beginning with *nityā* are for the cups dedicated to Marutvat and Mahendra (18).

The three verses beginning with *ā no viśvābhirūtibhiḥ* are for the cup of the Ādityas; the last one is for the Sāvitra cup (19). He fastens [the cords] for the cups of the Viśve Devās and the Pātnīvata (20).
The [verses] for the Hāriyojana [cup] are fixed. 21.
The Aptoryāma has been explained. 22.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section (kaṇḍikā).

When the king is about to be consecrated, while the people of the countryside have assembled, he prepares a sacrificial mound on the first of two auspicious days, kindles the fire, and having strewn grass around it, he dwells there overnight.

When the sun has risen, having offered two oblations with the verses, "O long-haired ones... and "Without prayer...", he establishes an Udumbara throne at the place of the sacrificer with the formula, "Thou art a ruler, thou art a sovereign.
The king mounts it.

He addresses the one who is mounting [the cart] with the words, "Mount the seat. 4. At this point, he gives a gift. 5. Sitting upon that [cart], he has his hair shaved with the verse, "With the razor wherewith Savitṛ shaved [the beard of]... 6.
With the verse, "May no one [cut] your hair," he consecrates the hair as it is being scattered (7).
Having gathered them together, he places them upon a bunch of *darbha* grass with the formula, "This is the deposit for them" (8).

Then he anoints him with milk mixed with clarified butter: with the formula, "Strength in your two arms," he anoints the arms; with the formula, "When you [crossed] the parting," he anoints the head (9).

Having offered seven oblations with the formula, "This tiger [is] in the fire," he spreads a tiger skin on the sacrificer's seat with the formula, "Thou art heaven; thou art earth," with its neck to the east and the hair upwards. The King sits upon it.
He consecrates him as he sits with the mantra, "A tiger, a tiger-skin-clad one."
Then he sprinkles him with water containing young shoots of *tokma* or shoots of *dūrvā*, beginning with the verse, "The waters which are divine... (VS 11.50), up to the end of the *pāṅkta* hymn.

Having consecrated him with the mantra, "Thee, the ruddy wolf... (VS 11.52), and having extended his arms with the words, "Forward, O arms... (VS 11.53), he lowers him with the words, "Of Indra, thee, the strength-maker...
(VS 11.54). A chariot stands positioned in front of the fire.
"Go forward!"—with these words, the king approaches him. (16) "Mount, O best slayer of Vṛtra!"—with this he addresses him as he is mounting.
(17) "Aṅka and Nyaṅka"—with this he touches the two wheels of the chariot, or the two side-pieces. (18)
He consecrates the domestic priest with the mantra, "Homage to you, O seer" (19); [he addresses] the charioteer with "Stand up on the chariot" (20);
he takes hold of the reins with "The reins hither" (21).
With the six verses beginning "Mount [the chariot], O slayer of Vṛtra," he addresses the one who has mounted it (sūtra 22).

Having caused him to recite the two verses beginning "May the armies avoid me," he consecrates him with the three following verses and makes him look up at the sun with the verse beginning "May the waters flow" (sūtra 23).
With the verse beginning "Of those possessing food," he gazes upon the inhabited lands (sūtra 24).
The royal consecration is completed (25).
The Vighana [rite] has been explained (26).
All the Sava [offerings] are completed (27).
Thus ends the twenty-eighth section.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter:
"Twenty-four at most should sit for the sacrificial session (*sattra*). 1.

The ritual procedure for those [sacrifices] that precede the year-long cycle is explained by means of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) performed as a sacrificial session (*sattra*). For the others, it is by means of the *gavāmayana*.
There are *atirātra* rites at both ends.
Having omitted the third fifteen-night rite, there is also the sacrificial session of the Kuṇḍapāyins.
By means of the eleven-night rite of the seasons (*ṛtu*), they create progeny; they obtain progeny; they find progeny; they become possessed of progeny.
5. [The sequence is: the *Jyotis* Atirātra, the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, three Chandomas, and an Atirātra. 6. Two thirteen-night rites. 7.
Whatever desire they desire, that they attain.

[The sacrifice consists of] an Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, a Sarvastoma Atirātra, four Chandomas, and an Atirātra. Those desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should undertake this as a second [performance].
The Atirātra, twelve days of the Dvādaśāha, ten days, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra; (11) three Caturdaśarātras; (12) whatever desire they may desire, that they attain. (13)
An Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha performed in reverse, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, and an Atirātra (14).
This second [sacrifice] they may consider for use on a couch, in water, or at a wedding (15).
An Atirātra, the Jyotis, Go, and Āyu three-day periods, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, the Āyu, Go, and Jyotis [three-day periods], and an Atirātra (16).
Those desiring supernatural power (ṛddhi) should undertake the third [sacrifice]:
an Atirātra, the Go and Āyus [Sāmans], ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra.
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā).
There are four fifteen-night sessions:
(1) he goes to the state of divinity; (2) on the new moon day is the *prāyaṇīya*, on the eighth day the *mahāvrata*, and on the full moon day the *udayanīya*; or rather, this is the reverse order.
An Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, the Mahāvrata, and a reversed Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha followed by an Atirātra;
(this) second [sacrificial session] those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake.
An Atirātra, a Trivṛt Agniṣṭut, Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyuḥ—this is a three-day period; a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, Āyuḥ, Gauḥ, Jyotis, and an Atirātra.
By the third [set], they obtain both types of desires: that which is in the *sattra* and that which is in the *ahīna*.
The *trivṛt*, the *agniṣṭut*, the *jyotis*, the *gauḥ*, the *āyuḥ*, the three-day period, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and the *atirātra* [constitute it].
By the fourth, they are indeed procreated with offspring and cattle.
An Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyu—this is the three-day period; ten days of the twelve-day sacrifice, and an Atirātra [make up the forty-nine-night sacrifice].
(10) Those desiring vigor should undertake the sixteen-night sacrifice dedicated to Indra. (11) These same [days], including the Mahāvrata, [constitute the seventeen-night sacrifice]. (12)
Those desiring food and sustenance should undertake the seventeen-night sacrifice:
an Atirātra, a Jyotis, a Go, an Āyus, a Go, an Āyus, a Pañcāha, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra.
Those desiring cattle should undertake the eighteen-night sacrifice.
An Atirātra, an Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra—[this constitutes] the nineteen-night sacrifice.
By means of this nineteen-night sacrifice, they are propagated with offspring and cattle.
These same [days], together with the Mahāvrata, [constitute the twenty-night sacrifice].
By means of the twenty-night sacrifice, they become endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and eaters of food.

[The structure is: an *Atirātra*, an *Abhiplava* six-day period, the *Abhijit* and *Viśvajit*, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and an *Atirātra*. This is the second section (*kaṇḍikā*).
Two [sessions] of twenty-one nights:
they attain whatever desire they may desire.
An Atirātra, an Abhiplava ṣaḍaha, an Atirātra; two Abhiplavas, an Atirātra.
Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake the second [rite].
A victim for Soma and Pūṣan is to be immolated.
The *manorṛc* verses are the *sāmidhenī* verses.
The Nidāgha [sacrifice] consists of:
the Atirātra, the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, three Svarasāman days, the Divākīrtya day, three Svarasāman days, the reversed Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, and the Atirātra. 9.
By means of the twenty-two-night sacrifice, they obtain food from these worlds, from yonder sun, and from the year.
10. It consists of an Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyuḥ; a three-day Abhiplava; a six-day period; the ten days of the twelve-day rite; the Mahāvrata; and an Atirātra. 11.
Those desiring cattle should undertake the twenty-three-night sacrifice. 12.
An Atirātra, a Jyotis, a Gauḥ, an Āyus, a Gauḥ, an Āyus, a Pañcāha, an Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra.
(13) Two Caturviṃśatirātras. (14) Whatever desire they may desire, that they attain. (15)
An Atirātra, two Abhiplava [six-day periods], ten days of the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha), and an Atirātra—thus [is the twenty-four-night sacrifice].
This is the third section.

An Atirātra, a Caturviṃśa Ukthya as the introductory day, or a Trivṛt; then the Pṛṣṭhya-stoma Ṣaḍaha; the thirty-third day is undefined, followed by a defined thirty-third day, a Triṇava, two Ekaviṃśas, a Triṇava, and a defined thirty-third day; then an undefined thirty-third day, the Pṛṣṭhya-stoma Ṣaḍaha turned back (pratyaṅ), an undefined Trivṛt day, the Jyotiṣṭoma Vaiśvānara Atirātra. 2. Those desiring cattle should undertake the twenty-five-night sacrifice: an Atirātra, two Abhiplavas, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (Dvādaśāha), the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra. 4.
Those desiring heaven should perform the twenty-six-night rite:
an Atirātra, the Go and Āyus [Sāmans], two Abhiplava [ṣaḍahas], the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra. Those desiring food should perform the twenty-seven-night rite.
An Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyu—this is a three-day period; two Abhiplavas; ten days of the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha); and an Atirātra.
(8) Those desiring cattle should undertake the twenty-eight-night rite. (9) These same [days] are accompanied by the Mahāvrata [day]. (10)
In twenty-nine nights they conquer immeasurable prosperity:

the Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, the Āyus, the Gauḥ, the Āyus, the Pañcāha, two Abhiplavas, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and the Atirātra. Those desiring food should undertake this thirty-night rite.
An Atirātra, three Abhiplava [six-day periods], ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra— thus ends the fourth Kaṇḍikā.
Those desiring food should undertake the thirty-one-night sacrifice.
These same [sacrifices], including the Mahāvrata,
should be performed for thirty-two nights by those desiring a firm foundation:
an Atirātra, the Go and Āyus [Sāmans], three Abhiplava [six-day periods], the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra.
Three [sets of] thirty-three nights;
they attain whatever desire they may desire. An Atirātra, three Pañcāhas, a Viśvajit Atirātra, one Pañcāha, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra.
Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake the second [sacrifice]:

an *atirātra*, an *abhiplava* six-day period, an *atirātra*, an *abhiplava* six-day period, an *atirātra*, an *abhiplava* six-day period, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the *mahāvrata*, and an *atirātra*.
Those desiring prosperity (*ṛddhi*) should undertake the third [sacrifice].

An Atirātra, three Pañcāhas, an Atirātra, three Pañcāhas, an Atirātra—this is the thirty-four-night sacrifice; those desiring power should perform it. An Atirātra, the Jyotis, Gaus, and Āyus [Sāmans], three Abhiplava periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra.

Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā). Those desiring cattle should undertake the thirty-five-night sacrifice: an Atirātra; Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus; Gauḥ, Āyus; a Pañcāha; three Abhiplavas; the ten days of the Dvādaśāha; and an Atirātra.
Those desiring heaven should undertake the thirty-six-night sacrifice:
an Atirātra, four Abhiplava periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (Dvādaśāha), and an Atirātra.
Those desiring food should undertake the thirty-seven-night sacrifice.
These same [rites], including the Mahāvrata,
they should perform for thirty-eight nights if they desire cattle:
an Atirātra, the Go and Āyus [Sāmans], four Abhiplava [six-day periods], the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra.
By a forty-nine-night rite, they conquer infinite prosperity. [The structure is:
an Atirātra, the Jyotis-Gau-Ayu three-day period, four Abhiplava six-day periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (Dvādaśāha), and an Atirātra.
By a forty-night rite, they become firmly established in the supreme Virāj.
"These very [rites] are accompanied by the Mahāvrata"—
this is the sixth section (kaṇḍikā). There are forty-nine nights for the *vidhṛti* rites, one for each.
By means of the first [set], they turn away from evil and from the rival.

There is an *atirātra*, three *agniṣṭoma*s consisting of the *trivṛt* stoma, an *atirātra*, ten *ukthya*s with the *pañcadaśa* stoma, a tenth day consisting of the *ṣoḍaśin*, and an *atirātra*. Twelve *ukthya*s with the *saptadaśa* stoma, an *atirātra*, a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), and an *atirātra*. Twelve *ukthya*s with the *ekaviṃśa* stoma and an *atirātra*. This *atirātra* is the second *yama*.
Whichever among these becomes prosperous—Mitra, Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Indra, and Vivasvat—they attain the prosperity of these deities. 5.

An Atirātra, two Abhiplavas, the Go and Āyus, two more Abhiplavas, the Abhijit and Viśvajit, two more Atirātras, one Abhiplava, the Sarvastoma, nine Saptadaśas, two Atirātras, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra. 6.
The third [day] consists of the application of collyrium and ointment. 7.
When they do not know [the names], yet they anoint them and anoint them over, they recognize them; they place beauty within themselves.
(8) With *gulgulu* resin at the morning pressing, with fragrant substances at the midday pressing, and with *pautudrava* resin at the third pressing.
(9) An *atirātra*, four *abhiplava* periods, an *atirātra* consisting of all the *stomas*, two *abhiplava* periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and an *atirātra*. (10)
The fourth [sacrificial session] lasts for a year;
they attain the prosperity of the year.

It consists of an Atirātra, a Caturviṃśa Ukthya as the introductory rite, a Trivṛt, three Abhiplavas, the Abhijit, three Svarasāmans, a Divākīrtya, a Mahāvrata, three more Svarasāmans, a Viśvajit, one reversed Abhiplava, the Āyu, the Gau, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (Dvādaśāha), the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra.
Thus ends the seventh section (kaṇḍikā).
The fifth [section] is the "Summits of Savitṛ" (Savituḥ Kakubhaḥ).
They proceed toward the production of all kinds of food.

The Atirātra; nine Trivṛt days beginning with an Agniṣṭoma; then a Ṣaḍaha; then three days—an Agniṣṭoma on both sides and an Ukthya in the middle; likewise nine Pañcadaśa days; likewise nine Saptadaśa days; likewise nine Ekaviṃśa days; the ten days of the Dvādaśāha; the Mahāvrata; and the Atirātra.
(3) Those desiring a firm foundation should perform this sixth [form].
(4) The Atirātra; four Abhiplava periods; the Mahāvrata; two Abhiplavas; the ten days of the Dvādaśāha; and the Atirātra. (5)
By means of the seventh [day], other offspring come into being; they become most vigorous. 6.
[The sacrifice consists of] an Atirātra, six Abhiplava [six-day periods], the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra. 7.
Those desiring prosperity should perform the sixty-one-night sacrifice. 8.
"O God Varuṇa, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods. Having settled upon the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), he offers the oblation.

9 The sequence consists of: an *atirātra*, a twenty-four-fold (*caturviṃśa*) *ukthya* as the introductory day (*ārambhaṇīya*), a *trivṛt* *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), three *abhiplava* periods, the *abhijit*, three *svarasāman* periods, the *divākīrtya* day, three *svarasāman* periods, the *viśvajit* with its reversal, a reversed *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, one *abhiplava* with its reversal, the *āyuḥ* and *gauḥ* days, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the *mahāvrata*, and an *atirātra*. 10 By means of the hundred-night rite of the gods (*devānāṃ śatarātra*), they attain a full lifespan and become more prosperous. 11
An Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyu—this is the three-day period; fourteen Abhiplava periods; the ten days of the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha), the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra.
12 They press [the Soma] while marching forward, or they do so in one place.
13 Thus ends the eighth Kaṇḍikā.
By means of the Ādityānām ayana, they attain procreation and abundance, they conquer the heavenly world, and they find firm footing in these worlds. 1.
This has been explained by [the description of] the Gavāmayana. 2.
All [the days] are abhiplava [six-day periods]. 3.
The months consist of the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* [stomas], with the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] occurring in the middle.
4. In the place of the *abhijit*, there is the *trivṛt* Bṛhaspatisava; in the place of the *viśvajit*, there is the *pañcadaśa* Indrastoma Ukthya. 5.
Immediately following that, having passed over the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* [days], there are the expanded (*vyūḍha*) Agniṣṭomas of the twelve-day period, which are *trivṛt*. 6.
With the *udbhid* and *valabhid*, a month less two days is completed.

(7) Having performed the *āyuṣa* and the *gavya*, there follows the *chandoma* and the ten-night rite; then the *aṣṭācatvāriṃśa* facing westward, the *catuścatvāriṃśa*, the *catvāriṃśa*, the *ṣaṭtriṃśa*, the *dvātriṃśa*, the *triṃśa*, two *aṣṭāviṃśas*, the *pañcaviṃśa*, and the *caturviṃśa*.
(8) With the *mahāvrata* and the *udayanīya*, a month less two days is completed. (9)
By this, the Aṅgirasa-ayanam is explained. Those desiring heaven should undertake it.
There are *abhiplava* periods consisting of the *trivṛt* stoma.

The *pṛṣṭhya* periods consist of months prior to the *viṣuvat*. After the *viṣuvat*, the *pṛṣṭhya* periods consist of fifteen-versed chants. 13. The *chandoma* ten-night period consists of ascending stomas: the twenty-four-fold, the twenty-five-fold, two twenty-eight-fold, the thirty-fold, the thirty-two-fold, the thirty-six-fold, the forty-fold, the forty-four-fold, and the forty-eight-fold.
14. By means of the *mahāvrata* and the *udayanīya*, the month is completed minus two days. 15.

Now, according to some: they call those [sacrifices] which include the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] "the traversing" (*ākṣyantī*) of the Ādityānāmayana, and those which include the *abhiplava* [ṣaḍaha] "the traversing" (*ākṣyantī*) of the Aṅgirasāmayana; whatever is other than the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* [ṣaḍahas], they call that "the traversing. This is the ninth section.
By means of the Dṛtivātavatorayana, whatever desire they desire, that they attain.
There are Atirātra sacrifices on both sides.

For one month [the Soma-pressing is] with the Trivṛt-stoma; for one month with the Pañcadaśa; for one month with the Saptadaśa; for one month with the Ekaviṃśa; for one month with the Triṇava; for one month with the Trayastriṃśa.
Then follows either the Viṣuvat day or the Mahāvrata.
These same months that follow have thirty-three as their opening elements and the Trivṛt-stoma as their final element.
In the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, they remain consecrated for one month.
Having performed the Prāyaṇīya ceremony, having purchased and bound the King Soma, they set him down.

Having performed twelve *upasad* days, they sacrifice with the *haviryajñas*. For one month they offer the *agnihotra*; for one month they sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*; for one month with the *vaiśvadeva*; for one month with the *varuṇapraghāsas*; for one month with the *sākamedhas*; for one month with the *śunāsīrīya*. For one month [they sacrifice] with the *trivṛt*, for one month with the *pañcadaśa*, for one month with the *saptadaśa*, for one month with the *ekaviṃśa*, for one month with the *triṇava*. There are eighteen days of the *trayastrimśa* stoma, ten days of the *dvādaśāha*, the *mahāvrata*, and the *atirātra*—these constitute the twelve months.

All of them indeed become [the officiants], and they all accomplish every supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). (10) They consume [the Soma] from ladles that lack handles (*atsaruka*). (11) He who is the *hotṛ* is the *adhvaryu*, he is the *potṛ*. He who is the *udgātṛ* is the *neṣṭṛ*, he is the *acchāvāka*. He who is the *maitrāvaruṇa* is the *brahmán*, he is the *pratihartṛ*. He who is the *prastotṛ* is the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, he is the *grāvastut*. He who is the *pratiprasthātṛ* is the *agnīdh*, he is the *unnetṛ*. The *gṛhapati* is the *gṛhapati*. The *subrahmaṇya* is the *subrahmaṇya*. (12)
Thus ends the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).
Those desiring heaven should undertake the Tapaścitāmayana sacrifice.
There are initiation rites (dīkṣās) for one year; there are subordinate rites (upasadās) for one year.
For four months at a time, he offers oblations with each individual *upasad* mantra.
He piles the fire-altar following the *upasad* rites. Each layer (*citi*) consists of two months; the final one consists of four months.
They observe the vows for three months each, consuming [milk] from four teats, then three teats, then two teats, and finally one teat;
for one year they remain in a state of continuous flow.
Through this twelve-year rite dedicated to Prajāpati, they attain the prosperity of Prajāpati.
Three years of the *trivṛt* [stoma], three of the *pañcadaśa*, three of the *saptadaśa*, and three of the *ekaviṃśa*.
Those desiring heaven should undertake this very [rite] of the Naimiṣīyas.

Nine years of the *trivṛt*, nine of the *pañcadaśa*, nine of the *saptadaśa*, and nine of the *ekaviṃśa* constitute the thirty-six-year sacrifice of the Śāktyas, featuring the *tarasa-puroḍāśa* offering, with the Kāpyas as the Adhvaryus and the Āgastyas as the Gṛhapatis.
On each day that has passed, the householder goes out hunting.

The sacrificial cakes made from the flesh of the wild animals he kills serve as the *tarasa-puroḍāśas*. By means of this very *tarasa-puroḍāśa*, Gaurivīti Śāktya attained prosperity both in the world of the gods and in the world of men; indeed, they attain prosperity in both worlds.
There are twenty-five years consisting of threefold stomas, twenty-five of fifteenfold stomas, twenty-five of seventeenfold stomas, and twenty-five of twenty-onefold stomas.
This is the eleventh section (kaṇḍikā).
By means of a hundred-year sacrifice, the Sādhyas, together with their cattle and their men, go to the heavenly world.
Through the *sahasrasāvya* of Agni, they attain the impulsion of all food.
2. An *atirātra*, a thousand *trivṛt* days, and an *atirātra*.
3. There are three *sattras* dedicated to Sarasvatī: the first belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa, the second to Indra and Agni, and the third to Aryaman. 4.
They undergo initiation at the immersion in the Sarasvatī.
Having performed the introductory sacrifice (prāyaṇīya) and having purchased and bound the King Soma, they set it down.
Having performed twelve Upasad rites and having reached the introductory Atirātra, on that day they drive away the calves.
When the Prāyaṇīya [offering] has been completed, they sacrifice with the Sāṃnāyya.
When that has been completed, the Adhvaryu throws a wooden pin (śamyā) eastward;
where it falls, that is the Gārhapatya fire-place.
Therefore, he strides thirty-six steps toward the east;
that is the Āhavanīya fire-altar.
The Sadas, the Havirdhāna sheds, and the Āgnīdhra shed are provided with wheels.
The Havirdhāna shed and the Āgnīdhra shed are made of *aśvattha* wood.
The sacrificial post has its base in a mortar; having been dragged [into place], it is simply strewn with earth. They do not dig out the *uparava* holes.
They proceed during this waxing fortnight with the new-moon oblation;
on the full moon day, they perform the Goṣṭoma sacrifice characterized by the Bṛhat-sāman;
when that is completed, they sacrifice with the full-moon rite.
They proceed through this dark fortnight with the full-moon oblation;
on the new moon day, they undertake the Āyuṣṭoma sacrifice characterized by the Rathantara Sāman;
when that is completed, they sacrifice with the Sāṃnāyya offering.
In this very same manner, they proceed in reverse order along the southern bank of the Sarasvatī.
This is the twelfth section (kaṇḍikā).
Shouting, they go eastward. 1.
At the confluence of the Dṛṣadvatī, they offer a *caru* oblation to Apām Napāt and proceed [to the next stage]. 2. Among ten cows, they set free a bull for every hundred. 3.

When they have completed ten hundred, that is one completion; or when they have completed a hundred thousand; or when the householder dies; or when they lose all their property; or when they reach the Plākṣa spring. 4.
Having reached Plakṣaprasravaṇa, they perform a sacrifice to Agni Kāma;
in that sacrifice, having given a mare and a human female as two milch-cows, they proceed toward Kārapacava and enter the river for the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
On the second day, there is the Trivṛt-Bṛhaspatisava, the Go and Āyus offerings, and the Indra-kukṣis.
Other offspring become even more powerful; they become most vigorous. 8.
In the third [year], there is the Jyotis, Gaur, Āyus, Ayana, Viśvajit, and Abhijit, and the two Indrakukṣis. 9.
They ascend the path of Aryaman and go to the world of the gods. 10.
In the Dārṣadvata sacrifice, one should guard the cows of a Brāhmaṇa for a year without losing any; 11.
For a year, one should maintain the sacred fires at Naitandhava on the Vyarṇa river; 12.

Having encircled the fire and established it, one should proceed along the southern bank of the Dṛṣadvatī with an offering on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni, casting the sacrificial yoke-pin (śamyā) as far as it reaches. 13.
Three times he descends to the *avabhṛtha* bath at the Plakṣa tree on the Yamunā;
at that very moment, he becomes invisible to human beings.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.
By means of the *turāyaṇa* fast, one attains all prosperity.
(1) One who is not initiated puts on a black antelope skin; by that, he attains human prosperity.
(2) When he performs austerity, by that he attains divine prosperity. (3)

He observes the vow of eating the remnants of the sacrificial oblation for a year. During that time, he performs sacrifices according to the procedure of the *savana* (Soma-pressing) rites: an offering on eight potsherds for Agni, one on eleven potsherds for Indra, and one on twelve potsherds for the Viśvedevas. Some say there should be a cooked rice oblation (*caru*) instead.

Or rather, at the morning pressing, they all remove old age through the sacrificial session of the serpents; their radiance is like that of the Ādityas. Every year consists of ten-month periods, and the twelfth is the Viṣuvat day.

The Gavāmayana lasts for three years; it belongs to the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases. They attain procreation and abundance, they conquer the heavenly world, and they become firmly established in these worlds.
By means of Prajāpati’s thousand-year sacrifice, they attain the prosperity of Prajāpati.
An Atirātra, a thousand threefold (trivṛt) years, an Atirātra—this is the Viśvasṛj-sahasrasaṃvatsara sacrifice.

There are fifty-five threefold years, fifty-five fifteenfold (pañcadaśa) years, fifty-five seventeenfold (saptadaśa) years, and fifty-five twenty-onefold (ekaviṃśa) years. By means of this, the Viśvasṛjs indeed created this universe; because they created the universe, they are called the Viśvasṛjs. Everything is born after them.

Regarding this, there is a verse: "The creators of the universe performed their first sacrificial session for a thousand years, proceeding with the pressed soma. From that was born the golden bird, the guardian of the world, whose name is Brahman.
(16) "They attain union with Brahman and residence in the same world who practice this, who practice this.
(17) Thus ends the fourteenth section.
Thus ends the twenty-third question.
We shall now explain the sacrifice (yajña). It belongs to the three social classes (varṇas): the Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, and the Vaiśya.
It is prescribed by three Vedas:
the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda;
the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) are prescribed by the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda.
The Agnihotra is performed with the Yajurveda; the Agniṣṭoma with all [three Vedas];
the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda are recited aloud.
Inaudibly, according to the Yajurveda;
except for the *āśruta*, *pratyāśruta*, the announcement of the *pravara*, the dialogue, and the *saṃpraiṣa* formulas.
It is to be recited in the interval between the *sāmidhenī* verses.
With a low tone before the two *ājyabhāga* offerings and at the morning pressing;
with a medium tone before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and at the midday pressing;
with a loud tone for the remainder and at the third pressing.
And the rapidity of speech is likewise [to be understood]. 15.
With the Ṛgveda, the Hotṛ priest performs [his duties]. 16.
With the Sāmaveda, the Udgātṛ priest [performs his duties]. 17.
The Adhvaryu [should act] with the Yajurveda (18);
the Brahman with all [the Vedas] (19);
or another may perform [the duties] by virtue of a specific injunction or because of a prohibition [of others] (20).
The office of officiating priest belongs to the Brāhmaṇas (21).
For all sacrifices, the fires are established once and for all (22).
When it is enjoined that "one offers," one should understand clarified butter (sarpis) as the sacrificial ghee (ājya) (23).
The Adhvaryu is the performer; 24. the *juhū* is the vessel; 25.
when [the *juhū*] is occupied, [he acts] with the *sruva*. 26.

The offering is made in the Āhavanīya fire (27). From the time of their consecration until the end of one's life, the vessels are maintained (28). Their purification is performed for each ritual performance (29).
The Mantra and Brāhmaṇa constitute the authority for the sacrifice (30).
The designation "Veda" applies to both the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa (31).
The Brāhmaṇas consist of injunctions regarding ritual acts (32).

The remainder of the Brāhmaṇas consists of explanatory passages (arthavāda), censure (nindā), praise (praśaṃsā), the deeds of others (parakṛti), and ancient legends (purākalpa). 33. Other than these are the mantras. 34.
However, those not specifically recited as such are non-mantras, such as the choosing of the *pravara* and the utterance of names. 35.

The sound of a chariot and the sound of a drum [are occasions for interruption]. (36) There is no suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) regarding the recitation of mantras during these [sounds], because they are distinct from the ritual act itself. (37) Ritual acts are performed with a single mantra. (38)
Furthermore, [the rules apply] to actions involving numbers, conjunctions, separations, and the production [of results] (39);

At the time of sifting the flour, he sifts the rice grains; 26. At the time of placing [the vessel] on the fire, he pours in the rice grains with the mantra for placing on the fire; 27. Without removing [the vessel from the fire], he sets down the *caru* oblation; 28.

and the *vaiśvadeva*, *varuṇapraghāsa*, *sākamedha*, and *śunāsīrīya* [offerings] belong to the [four-month] seasonal sacrifices.
The cake on one potsherd for the Vaiśvadeva is [the model] for cakes on one potsherd; 38.
the curdled milk (āmikṣā) for the Vaiśvadeva is [the model] for curdled milk; 39.
in that case, the modification would be understood through general similarity. 40.

those with two deities are modifications of the Agnīṣomīya; 42. and likewise those with many deities. 43.

The substitute for the master, the fire, the deity, the word, and the action is excluded by three reasons:
by direct injunction, by prohibition, and by the disappearance of purpose.
The *agniṣṭoma* is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*).
The Dvādaśāha is the first among the multi-day sacrifices (ahargaṇa); the Gavāmayana is the first among the annual sacrifices; and the first [sacrifice] of the Nikāyins is likewise [the first].
The *uttaravedi* is used in the *agniṣṭoma*; the fire-altar (*agni*) is used in the subsequent sacrifices,
except for the *sādyaskra* sacrifices, the *vājapeya*, the *ṣoḍaśin*, and the *sārasvata sattra*.

At the beginning of a sacrifice, he should desire the fulfillment of the sacrifice; at the beginning of a sacrificial limb, the fulfillment of that limb. Where there are fewer mantras and more ritual acts, he should divide them equally and have the former acts performed with the former mantras and the latter acts with the latter mantras.

When there are fewer ritual acts and more mantras, one should perform [the rite] with each individual mantra. The remaining [mantras] are for the purpose of providing options, just as in the case of the materials for the sacrificial post (yūpa). (Sūtra 13) There may be either an omission at the end or an expansion. (Sūtra 14) Since the original form (prakṛti) has been previously stated, that which is new (apūrva) should occur at the end. The *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice should not take place in a modified (*vikṛti*) rite, because it falls within the time-period of the archetypal (*prakṛti*) rite; for it has already been performed for the sake of that [archetype].
Alternatively, it should indeed take place, because the time is not exhausted [by the archetype], and because there is a distinction between the commencement [of the archetype and the modified rite].
For each purpose, he brings forward the fire; when the ritual act has concluded, it becomes a common (laukika) fire, as in the case of one that has been mounted [on the kindling sticks].
This is the fourth section. We shall now explain the *pravara* lineages. 1.

He chooses the lineage of the seers (*ārṣeya*). "He goes to his kinsman, and also for the sake of continuity," so it is known. 2. He does not choose the lineage of seers among gods nor among men; "he chooses the lineage of seers only among the seers," so it is known. 3. He recites the lineage of the seers; "for by means of the seer the gods recognize the man," so it is known. 4.
It is known from scripture: "He who, being one [person], chooses another by means of the latter's ancestral seer (*ṛṣi*), that seer indeed takes away his sacrifice and his enjoyment.
5. He chooses three; he chooses the makers of the mantras. It is known from scripture: "One should choose the makers of the mantras according to their respective seers.
6. Now, according to some, it is known from scripture: "One chooses one; one chooses two; one chooses three; one does not choose four; one does not choose more than five. 7.
It is known from tradition: "From there upwards the Adhvaryu chooses [the ancestors], and from here downwards the Hotṛ.
It is known from tradition: "The king chooses by means of the Pravara of his domestic priest (purohita). It is known from tradition: "The king chooses by means of the Pravara of his domestic priest."
We shall explain those of the Bhṛgus first.

10. The Vatsas are descendants of Jamadagni. 11. Their *pravara* consists of five ṛṣis: Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jāmadagna. [The invocation is: "As Bhṛgu, as Cyavana, as Āpnavāna, as Aurva, as Jamadagni. 12.
Some [recite] the *ārṣeya* [formula] as: "Bhārgava, Aurva, Jāmadagna"—that is, "as Bhṛgu, as Urva, as Jamadagni.

This same [formula] remains unaltered for the Sāvarṇi, Jīvanti, Jābāli, Ai-tiśāyana, Vairohi, Āvaṭa, Maṇḍu, and Prācīnayogya lineages. Now, for the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, there is a fivefold *ārṣeya*: "Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Anūpa"—that is, "as Anūpa, as Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, as Āpnavāna, as Cyavana, as Bhṛgu."
Some, however, prescribe three *ṛṣis*: Bhārgava, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and Anūpa—that is, as Anūpa, Ṛṣiṣeṇa, and Bhṛgu.
This is the fifth section.
Now follow Vītahavya, Yāska, Vādhūla, Mauna, and Mauka.
For them, there is a tri-ārṣeya: Bhārgava, Vaitahavya, Sāvedasa—[the latter being] like Saveda, like Vitahavya, and like Bhagavat. 2. Now, the Gārtsamadas are the Śanakas.
3. For them, there is a single ārṣeya: Gārtsamada, [is the invocation for] the Hotṛ; Gṛtsamada-vat, [is the invocation for] the Adhvaryu. 4.
Now, the Vādhryaśvas, who desire friends:
they have a single *ṛṣi* lineage; the *hotṛ* priest says "Vādhryaśva," and the *adhvaryu* says "like Vadhryaśva.
Then there are the Pārthas of Vainya.
Their *ārṣeya* (ancestral invocation) consists of three names: Bhārgava, Vainya, and Pārtha; [the sequence being] "like Pṛthu, like Vadhu, like Bhṛgu. These Bhṛgus have been explained.
Now, therefore, follow the Āyāsyas and Gautamas among the Aṅgirases.
Their *ārṣeya* consists of three names: Āṅgirasa, Āyāsya, and Gautama. [The invocation is: "As Gautama, as Ayāsya, as Aṅgiras. 11. Now, there are the Ucathyas, who are Gautamas.
12. Their *ārṣeya* consists of three names: Āṅgirasa, Aucathya, and Gautama. [The invocation is: "As Gautama, as Ucathya, as Aṅgiras. 13.
Now, the Auśijas Gautamas:
their *ṛṣi*-lineage consists of three ancestors—Āṅgirasa, Auśija, and Kākṣīvata—and they invoke them as "like Kakṣīvān, like Auśija, and like Āṅgiras.

Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: Āṅgirasa, Vāmadeva, and Bārhadukthya; that is, "as Bṛhadukthya, as Vāmadeva, and as Aṅgiras. (17) Now, for the Bharadvājas, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja; that is, "as Bharadvāja, as Bṛhaspati, and as Aṅgiras.

[The rules apply] to the Kukkas, Agniveśyas, and Urjayanas, and to all those whose names contain the word "stamba" or "stamba.
